Ten young Danes will compete against more than 400 participants at the European Cybersecurity Championship in Bochum, Germany, from Monday to Friday.
Denmark won silver last year, but national coach Jens Myrup Pedersen, a cybersecurity professor at Aarhus University, believes the team can win gold this year.
“Technically speaking, the team this year is completely at the top. They are exceptionally good at collaborating, and they have the will to fight for and with each other,” he said.
The competition is open to hackers between ages 14 and 25. Denmark’s participants were selected after competing in the national cybersecurity championship in May.
During the first day of competition, teams must identify information in vulnerable applications, websites and network traffic. On the second day, they must protect their own server while attempting to exploit weaknesses in other teams’ servers.
Denmark’s team has finished among Europe’s five best for the past five years and won gold in 2022.
The Danish Defence Intelligence Service, known as FE, established the team in 2017 to develop talent capable of addressing Denmark’s growing cyberthreats.
The team is also supported by universities, European organizations and Industriens Fond, a foundation supporting the competitiveness of Danish industry.
Aarhus will host the European Cybersecurity Championship next year.
Denmark’s autumn holiday to bring sunshine, rain and overnight frost
Denmark’s autumn holiday will bring a mixture of sunny, dry periods and rainy weather, with temperatures falling to around freezing early in the week.
“It is an autumn holiday that looks really nice for most people,” Danish Meteorological Institute meteorologist Kasper Bonde Niebe said.
“There will be periods where it is a bit wetter, but there are also periods with some really nice days with sun and dry weather for much of the country.”
Light frost was recorded in central Jutland overnight into Monday. Monday morning temperatures will range from zero to five degrees in Jutland, while eastern Denmark will be slightly warmer because of cloud cover.
Showers and clouds will remain in eastern Denmark during the morning before giving way to sunshine and dry weather in the afternoon.
Temperatures could fall slightly below freezing in central Zealand overnight into Tuesday. No further overnight frost is expected during the rest of the week.
Tuesday will begin sunny before a rain front moves across Denmark from the west. Temperatures will reach between 11 and 15 degrees.
Wednesday is expected to be dry and stable, with temperatures up to 15 degrees. Thursday will remain dry but become cloudier, with temperatures reaching 17 degrees.
Another weather front will arrive overnight into Friday, bringing widespread rain during the day.
Danish foreign minister warns US-Russia diesel deal could help finance war
Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen of the Moderates has warned that a new diesel agreement between the United States and Russia could provide additional funding for Russia’s war in Ukraine.
“It is regrettable if this secures additional revenue for Russia,” Rasmussen told Danish public broadcaster DR on Saturday.
“In the EU, we have put a lot of work into tough sanctions and into reducing dependence on Russian energy, and that work must not be undermined,” he said.
“We must continue to pressure Russia’s economy and stand together in support of Ukraine.”
US President Donald Trump said Friday that he and Russian President Vladimir Putin had reached an agreement under which Russia would immediately supply 300,000 tons of diesel to US and global markets.
The US Treasury Department has issued a temporary authorization easing sanctions to allow Russia to sell diesel internationally. The authorization is valid until April 7, 2027, Reuters reported.
A British government spokesperson said the United Kingdom would maintain pressure on Russia through what it called the strictest sanctions regime the country has implemented.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also said the deal would provide Russia with more money to wage war.
The agreement comes after gasoline and diesel prices rose sharply across the United States, increasing costs for consumers and businesses and contributing to higher inflation.
Danish business emergency network grows to 223 members
The number of companies and organizations in Virksomhedsberedskabet, Denmark’s business emergency preparedness network, has risen from 63 to 223 in just over 10 months.
Together, its members represent about 350,000 private-sector employees.
The network coordinates resources from private companies so they can help maintain essential services during serious crises.
“It is about having this conversation about what one already has on the shelves, and how it can actually be repurposed for a crisis and support critical infrastructure,” director Maja Broløs said.
Fitness centers could provide shelter, baby stores could supply essential products and department stores could make their buildings available. Companies participating in the network include SATS Denmark, BabySam and IKEA.
Virksomhedsberedskabet is part of a broader effort to strengthen Denmark’s emergency preparedness. In February, the government launched a total defence preparedness initiative and allocated 1.2 billion DKK to the area.
Broløs said more members would be needed to respond effectively to a nationwide crisis.
“If it is a major regional crisis, we are in a pretty good position. But if it is nationwide, then those are completely different numbers we need to reach,” she said.
The network aims to exceed 1,000 members by 2029. By 2028, it plans to be capable of mobilizing members’ resources nationwide within six hours.
DTU Aqua to create 40 fish nurseries near Bornholm
DTU Aqua, the National Institute of Aquatic Resources at the Technical University of Denmark, will establish 40 fish nurseries and spawning grounds near Bornholm over the next five years.
The artificial nurseries, known as biohuts, will be placed in the ports of Rønne and Hasle, Danish broadcaster TV 2 Bornholm reported.
The project aims to increase the number of young fish around the biohuts by 30 percent and raise local perch and pike populations by 20 percent.
Researchers will examine whether local restoration initiatives can strengthen fish stocks and reverse biodiversity loss. DTU Aqua will also develop a monitoring system for coastal and marine areas.
Bornholm is one of nine European islands participating in the EU-funded Isla Bonita project. Each island will establish a “Living Lab” where local groups will collaborate on nature restoration.
The projects will reflect local needs. Santorini will focus on reducing plastic pollution, while Scotland’s Orkney Islands will restore oyster reefs.
The islands are located across the Atlantic, Arctic, Mediterranean, Baltic and North seas.
The EU is providing 16.2 million euros, equivalent to nearly 121.1 million DKK, for the project. It involves 51 organizations from 16 countries.
This year, oxygen depletion was recorded in 38 of Denmark’s 108 coastal waters, compared with 33 in 2025 and 34 in 2024.
`123456’ password used in massive Danish CPR data breach
At least three accounts at the company linked to a major breach of Denmark’s CPR register reportedly used the password “123456”, including an administrator account.
At least three user accounts at the Funen-based IT company Pays used the password “123456” when hackers gained access to Denmark’s CPR register, Politiken reports.
One of them was the company’s administrator account.
The breach exposed information linked to around 8.8 million CPR numbers. The CPR system is Denmark’s central civil registration database and contains personal information on people living or previously registered in Denmark.
The newspaper Politiken reviewed data from the breach that the hacker allegedly used to gain access to the system.
Jens Myrup Pedersen, professor at Aarhus University’s Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, described the company’s password security as “hopeless”.
“There is really no security, it is an open door. A password like ‘123456’ is one of the very first things you would guess if you took a list of common passwords,” he told Politiken.
“I find it hard to see that you could have worse security. It was a matter of time before things went wrong.”
Pays ApS, based in Odense, confirmed to TV 2 on Friday that it was the company whose access had been compromised.
“We can confirm that we are the company that has been subjected to an attack where our legal access to search for information in the CPR system has been abused,” managing director and owner Sophie Laursen said in an email to TV 2.
The hacker had access to the CPR register from 10 September for a total of 21 days and 17 hours.
An anonymous hacker told Politiken on Thursday that they were behind the attack and claimed gaining access had not been particularly difficult.
According to the hacker, access was initially obtained using a leaked password belonging to a former employee of a small Danish company. The hacker then allegedly created two computer programs to retrieve information from the CPR system and store it externally.
The hacker told Politiken that there were no plans to sell or publish the information.
Private companies and associations can be granted access to information in Denmark’s CPR register when they have a legitimate need, for example to obtain address information about customers or members.
According to Denmark’s Central Business Register, Pays ApS had two employees as of July 2026.
One in four Danish driving penalty points linked to mobile phone use
Danish motorists received almost 21,000 penalty points for using handheld mobile phones while driving last year – the highest number in four years.
Mobile phones are playing a growing role in traffic offences in Denmark.
In 2025, motorists received 20,910 penalty points on their driving licences for using a handheld mobile phone behind the wheel, according to figures from the police case management system POLSAS.
That means mobile phone use accounted for roughly one in every four of the 84,056 penalty points issued for traffic offences during the year.
The number of mobile-related penalty points increased by 7.5 percent compared with 2024 and reached its highest level in four years.
On average, police issued 57 penalty points every day for handheld mobile phone use.
Britta Bjerregaard, claims director at insurance company Alm. Brand, described the development as deeply concerning.
“Most people know full well that the phone should stay put while driving. Still, it can be tempting to just answer a call, reply to a message, or change the song,” she said.
“Traffic does not pause while you look at the screen.”
89 metres without watching the road
The Danish Road Safety Council considers inattention one of the major risks on Danish roads, with mobile phones posing a particular problem.
“The mobile phone takes an incredible amount of attention if you use it behind the wheel,” deputy director Karina Petersen said.
“If you look at the screen for four seconds at country road speed, you are driving 89 metres blind.”
However, Petersen cautioned that the increase in recorded offences does not necessarily mean that more drivers are using their phones.
The rise could also reflect more police checks or improved camera equipment used for traffic enforcement.
What are the rules in Denmark?
Using a handheld mobile phone while driving in Denmark results in a DKK 1,500 fine and a penalty point on your driving licence. An additional DKK 1,000 contribution to the Victims’ Fund is also charged.
The rule applies even when the car is stationary in traffic or waiting at a red light.
Drivers may briefly operate a phone if it is securely mounted, and using a vehicle’s built-in screen is also permitted.
The ban on handheld mobile phone use also applies to cyclists, electric scooter users and drivers of other motorised vehicles.

Minister of Defence Jeppe Bruus (S) calls a Russian TV report about the incident where a Russian frigate fired flares at a Danish military helicopter in September a “misinformation campaign”.
He says this to DR.
The minister says that, according to the Defence Command, part of the material does not originate from the day in question.
– This confirms to me that what is underway here is a Russian misinformation campaign, which is about trying to see whether they can sow distrust in the Danish authorities, the minister says to DR.
On Thursday, Russian state TV showed a report about the incident on 14 September, in which a Russian warship and a Danish helicopter were involved.
According to DR, the footage shows how close the Danish defence helicopter allegedly came to the Russian warship.
In the report, it is mentioned that the helicopter “intruded into the ship’s security zone”, DR writes.
The firing of the two flares itself does not appear in the report from the TV channel Rossiya 1.
On 14 September, two flares were fired from the Russian frigate Soobrazitelny, which was in international waters off Gedser.
According to the Defence Command, one of the flares passed 10-15 metres from a Danish Fennec helicopter.
According to the Defence, the firing occurred without warning in connection with a routine mission where the helicopter was taking pictures of the frigate in international waters.
Russia’s ambassador to Denmark, Vladimir Barbin, has stated that the Danish helicopter acted “provocatively” in the lead-up to the firing of the flare.
According to Denmark’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, Lars Løkke Rasmussen (M), the Russians will not be able to present evidence that supports this,
– It does not budge our perception of that situation an iota, he said to TV 2 News in September.

73-year-old charged with reckless wrong-way driving
A 73-year-old man has been charged with reckless driving after he made a U-turn on the Esbjerg Motorway on Friday afternoon and briefly drove against the direction of traffic.
This was stated by South and South Jutland Police in an update on the messaging service Politi Update on Friday evening.
While the wrong-way driver was driving against the direction of traffic, another motorist had to make an evasive maneuver, which led to a traffic accident.
No one was seriously injured, duty officer Rikke Rosenberg stated earlier in the evening.
Following the incident, which occurred at 16:35 at exit 73 Korskro in South West Jutland, police appealed for witnesses.
According to surveillance footage, the black car slowed down and pulled into the emergency lane on the right side of the road before turning around and driving back toward the exit.
From the surveillance footage, police were able to see the car’s registration number and thereby find the owner.
After the accident, the first lane was briefly closed.

Hacker retained access to Danish CPR register for nearly 22 days before breach was discovered
An unauthorized user had access to Denmark’s national Civil Registration System (CPR) for nearly 22 days before authorities discovered the security breach, according to documents obtained by TV 2.
The access began September 10 and was stopped October 2, lasting 21 days and 17 hours.
However, preliminary investigations suggest the unauthorized activity ended September 20, approximately 10 days after it began, according to a report submitted by the CPR office to the Danish Data Protection Agency.
The Ministry of Research, Education and Digitalization announced Monday that personal information belonging to approximately 8.8 million people had been exposed, including names, addresses and CPR identification numbers.
The breach occurred through a small Danish company with legitimate access to the register.
According to DR, the company is based on Funen and shares ownership and an address with a larger business. Its identity has not been publicly confirmed.
Authorities discovered the incident after receiving an unusually large invoice for searches conducted through the company’s account.
Approximately 14 million CPR searches had been made using its access credentials.
“The number far exceeds the company’s customer base, and the company has indicated that they did not perform the lookups themselves,” the CPR office stated in its report.
Private companies and organizations can pay to access certain CPR information.
Research, Education and Digitalization Minister Christina Egelund of the Moderates party acknowledged that security measures had been inadequate.
She has requested a security review of the register following the breach.
The company had not responded to DR’s requests for comment as of Friday morning.
Sardine sales surge in Copenhagen as social media skincare trend gains popularity
Canned sardines are selling rapidly across Denmark, particularly around Copenhagen, as supermarkets report rising demand and occasional shortages.
Four major grocery retailers, Coop, Salling Group, Nemlig.com and Dagrofa, confirmed significant sales increases to TV 2 Kosmopol.
Coop, which operates 365, SuperBrugsen, Brugsen and Kvickly, reported a 170 percent increase in sardine sales in Denmark’s Capital Region between June and September 2026 compared with the same period last year.
Nationwide, Coop’s sales rose 163.5 percent.
Jacob Herbst Lassen, Coop Denmark’s press manager, said the sudden popularity has left some shelves with fewer products while purchasing teams work to replenish supplies.
Salling Group also reported pressure on availability, although spokesperson Alma Lyhne Kristensen said the company remained adequately stocked overall.
Online supermarket Nemlig.com said Greater Copenhagen and North Zealand accounted for 75 percent of its sardine sales.
Dagrofa, which operates Meny and Spar stores, reported that sales in the capital area had more than doubled compared with last year.
The surge may be connected to the social media trend “eat your skincare,” which promotes foods believed to benefit skin health.
Sardines have attracted attention for their omega-3 fatty acids, collagen and protein.
However, dermatologist and researcher Cæcilie Johansen cautioned that evidence linking sardine consumption directly to healthier skin remains limited.
She said some studies suggest omega-3 fatty acids may help with eczema, but the research involved large quantities.
Johansen emphasized that avoiding smoking, limiting alcohol and using sunscreen are more important measures for protecting skin health.
Denmark resumes citizenship and immigration cases after criminal records error
Denmark’s Ministry of Immigration and Integration has resumed processing citizenship applications that were suspended because of errors in the country’s Central Criminal Register.
The ministry announced the decision in a press release after the National Police concluded that the errors had only a very limited impact on the register.
Immigration authorities have also been instructed to restart affected cases involving permanent residence permits and family reunification, according to an update from the Danish Immigration Service.
The applications had been placed on hold September 7 while authorities investigated the problem.
The errors became public in early September when National Police Commissioner Lasse Boje informed politicians at Christiansborg, the seat of Denmark’s parliament, that some criminal records had been deleted incorrectly.
Authorities had discovered the problem in June.
The National Police said further investigations would determine whether the errors had affected decisions made by other public authorities.
If problems are identified, police will work with the relevant authorities to determine how those cases should be handled.
The errors also disrupted the issuance of child protection certificates, which are background checks used to identify certain criminal convictions relevant to working with children.
Applications for these certificates were temporarily suspended while police reviewed the affected records.
The National Police reopened applications September 18.
During its review, police restored 43 decisions that had been removed from the Criminal Register earlier than they should have been.
Those decisions were relevant to child protection certificates.
The ministry has not specified how many citizenship, permanent residence or family reunification applications were affected by the suspension.
Danish court rejects detention request for two Kosovo prison officers accused of assault
Two prison officers from Kosovo accused of assaulting an inmate at Copenhagen’s Vestre Prison will remain free while police investigate the allegations.
Denmark’s Eastern High Court rejected prosecutors’ request to hold the two men in pretrial detention Friday afternoon.
The decision upheld a ruling by Copenhagen City Court on Wednesday, which found insufficient grounds to detain them.
Both courts concluded there was no significant reason to believe the men would flee Denmark before a possible criminal trial.
The officers, aged 29 and 24, are undergoing training in Denmark ahead of assignments at Gjilan prison in Kosovo, which Denmark is renting to house prisoners.
According to police allegations, the two officers assaulted an inmate inside a cell at Vestre Prison around 4 p.m. Monday.
The inmate was allegedly pushed onto a bed before being punched in the face and body.
Police arrested the officers Tuesday morning, and prosecutors requested their detention the following day.
Both men deny using violence against the inmate.
During Wednesday’s hearing, a Copenhagen City Court judge found reasonable grounds to suspect the officers had committed the alleged assault.
However, the judge ruled that detention was unnecessary because both men reside in Denmark and are employed by Danmarks Fængsler, the Danish Prison and Probation Service.
Prosecutors challenged that decision, but the Eastern High Court reached the same conclusion Friday.
The investigation remains ongoing, and no decision has been made on whether the officers will face trial.
Once police complete their investigation, prosecutors will determine whether there is sufficient evidence to bring criminal charges before a court.
Fire near Aarup disrupts train services across Denmark throughout Friday
A fire in a railway signaling cabin near Aarup on Funen is causing major train disruptions across Denmark on Friday, with repairs potentially taking several weeks.
Michael Dyrborg, an area manager at Banedanmark, the state-owned company responsible for Denmark’s railway infrastructure, told Ritzau that almost everything inside the cabin had burned.
“It is too early to talk about a timeframe. We are getting an overview of the extent of the damage, but virtually everything inside has burned away,” he said.
A relay cabin is a small technical building along the railway that houses electronics and equipment used by the signaling system.
The fire has caused signal faults on the railway line between Middelfart and Odense. Dyrborg expects train services on the affected routes to remain disrupted for the rest of Friday.
“We are looking into whether it is possible to create some technical solutions so we can increase the speed and make traffic flow more smoothly,” he said.
Banedanmark has not yet said when normal train services are expected to resume.
The disruption is affecting services across Funen and other parts of the country.
According to DSB, Denmark’s national passenger railway operator, all trains between Fredericia and Copenhagen are experiencing delays, while all regional trains between Odense and Fredericia have been canceled.
Intercity trains running between Copenhagen and Fredericia via Roskilde are only operating as far as Odense, DSB said on its website.
Rail replacement buses have been deployed to replace the canceled regional trains on Funen. According to P4 Trafik, six buses were operating between Fredericia and Odense.
Passengers traveling between Jutland, Funen and Zealand can continue their journeys using some of the other trains still running, DSB said.
DSB employees are available at Odense and Fredericia stations to assist and guide passengers.
Both Banedanmark and DSB are urging travelers to check Rejseplanen, Denmark’s national journey planner, for updates.
Government unveils security-focused budget proposal
The Danish government has presented a proposed budget for 2027 that prioritizes national security, with more money allocated to defence amid an increasingly tense international security situation.
The proposal, titled “A stronger defence of Denmark – a strengthened Denmark to defend”, was presented by Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard of the Social Democrats (S) at the Ministry of Finance on Friday morning.
The government wants to ensure that defence spending reaches 3.5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) by 2030.
Hummelgaard said the proposal reflected the need to make “hard priorities” in response to the current security situation. He also described the Danish economy as being “in top shape”.
“The government’s proposal for the finance bill shows that we take responsibility upon ourselves, and that we lead the way in working for a greener, freer, and more equal Denmark,” Hummelgaard said.
Pia Olsen Dyhr of the Socialist People’s Party (SF), the minister for economic and interior affairs, also highlighted the security situation.
“We do not solve all the challenges we have in Denmark with this finance bill. But we are well on our way,” she said at the press conference.
“I also think everyone must remember that we are in an escalated security policy situation,” Olsen Dyhr said.
Much of the proposed budget had already been announced, either in the government’s policy platform or through statements by ministers in recent weeks.
The proposal allocates 1.2 billion DKK to children’s services and education in 2027, including Denmark’s public primary and lower secondary schools, known as folkeskole.
It also sets aside a total of 10.1 billion DKK in 2030 for tax cuts. These include abolishing the intermediate income tax and the top-top tax, as well as reducing corporation tax.
“We are simplifying the tax system,” said Taxation and Growth Minister Jakob Engel-Schmidt of the Moderates (M).
The tax measures will be negotiated separately as part of a tax reform. While the budget proposal includes tax cuts, the government also plans to freeze several tax thresholds, which would increase the tax burden for some taxpayers as incomes rise.
The liberal think tank Cepos estimates that the government’s various plans will result in a net tax cut of 2.2 billion DKK in 2030.
Business and Competitiveness Minister Martin Lidegaard of the Danish Social Liberal Party (R) highlighted investment in young people and education.
“We are significantly strengthening knowledge, general education, and formal education in Denmark, from ABC to PhD. It is good for the individual young person, but it is also good for Denmark’s future,” Lidegaard said.
Unlike in recent years, when the government’s fiscal room for manoeuvre helped fund much of its budget plans, this proposal includes several measures to find additional savings.
These include cuts to the Danish student grant (SU), savings on senior pension payments, a proposed tax on cruise ships and further reductions in state administration costs.
The government must now negotiate with other parties in the Danish Parliament, the Folketing, to secure a majority for the 2027 budget.
The proposal includes a negotiating reserve of 500 million DKK annually from 2027 to 2030, which other parties can seek to use to fund their own priorities.
Business groups warn 200 DKK cruise passenger tax could drive tourists away
Two Danish business organizations are warning that a proposed tax of 200 DKK per cruise passenger could lead cruise ships to skip Danish ports, reducing tourism revenue for cities and smaller destinations.
Dansk Industri (DI), the Confederation of Danish Industry, and Dansk Erhverv, a business organization representing companies across several sectors, are responding to the government’s proposal to introduce the tax from 2028.
“A cruise tax at this level will hit both the major cities and rural districts,” said Lars Bertolt Winther, head of tourism, culture and experiences at DI, in a press release.
Jesper Kronborg, industry director for transport at Dansk Erhverv, also criticized the proposal.
“In Dansk Erhverv’s view, it is a bad proposal, or at least a proposal that requires a very thorough analysis,” he said in a press release.
The government expects the tax to generate an additional 300 million DKK in annual revenue from 2028.
The aim is to make cruise tourism contribute more toward the costs associated with ships, including pollution, noise and congestion.
Figures from Statistics Denmark show that 1.1 million cruise passengers visited Denmark in 2025. The number of cruise ships calling at Danish ports increased by 16% compared with the previous year.
Copenhagen, Aarhus, Skagen and Rønne on the island of Bornholm are the country’s main cruise destinations. Together, they account for more than 98% of cruise passengers.
DI and Dansk Erhverv argue that cruise visitors generate local revenue through port fees and spending at shops and other businesses.
Both organizations point to Iceland, where a similar tax was introduced before being reduced.
“Following the introduction of a high passenger tax, bookings dropped significantly, especially to the smaller ports, and the tax was subsequently lowered to limit the damaging effects,” Winther said.
“There is no reason to believe that Denmark does not risk the same,” he added.
According to the industry organization Danske Havne, which represents Danish ports, Iceland now charges 85 DKK per cruise passenger, while Greenland charges 50 DKK.
Tine Kirk, director of Danske Havne, described the proposed Danish tax of 200 DKK as “unreasonably high.”
“The cruise ships can very easily opt out of Denmark. We fear that the shipping companies will either bypass Denmark completely or concentrate their port calls in the largest cities,” she said in a written comment.
Drop in exports to the US drags down Danish exports
Danish exports fell by 3.3 percent in August, driven in part by a decline in goods exports to the United States, according to Statistics Denmark.
Total exports of goods and services amounted to 194 billion DKK in August, down 3.3 percent from July. Goods exports fell by 6.2 percent, while services exports rose by 0.7 percent.
Søren Kristensen, chief economist at AL Sydbank, described the overall decline as “worryingly large”.
“But it is part of the story that a large part of the decline is concentrated around the US, where we also see fluctuations from month to month,” he wrote in a comment.
Exports of goods and services to both the US and the United Kingdom fell in August. Total exports to the US amounted to 31.7 billion DKK, down 2.8 billion DKK from July.
Goods exports to the US fell by 3.3 billion DKK, while services exports rose slightly.
Kristensen said fluctuations in the prices of products such as medicines sold by Danish companies in the US could partly explain the decline. He therefore cautioned against drawing too negative a conclusion from the latest figures alone.
The August decline followed an increase in exports in July. Overall, Danish exports of goods and services rose by nearly 19 billion DKK, or more than 10 percent, between August 2025 and August 2026.
According to Kristensen, Danish exports have so far held up despite geopolitical unrest, higher energy prices and rising interest rates.
Still, the August figures are bad news for the Danish economy when viewed in isolation.
“However, it will take several months of this development before we become worried,” Kristensen wrote.
Hacker claims simple password allowed access to 8.8 million Danish CPR numbers
An anonymous hacker has claimed responsibility for accessing nearly 8.8 million Danish CPR numbers, telling newspaper Politiken that a weak password made the breach possible.
CPR numbers are personal identification numbers used in Denmark’s national Civil Registration System to identify residents and access public services.
The hacker told Politiken that the breach occurred on September 11 through a small Danish company with access to the CPR register.
According to the hacker, a leaked password belonging to a former employee allowed entry into the system. The password was reportedly “123456.”
After gaining access, the hacker said they created two computer programs to retrieve CPR information and store it outside the system.
The person’s identity has not been made public, and their account has not been independently confirmed.
The hacker told Politiken they had no plans to sell or publish the personal identification numbers and were “really shocked” by the security weaknesses they encountered.
To describe the situation, the hacker compared it to someone leaving dangerous material unattended.
“Someone leaves a suitcase with 10 kilos of plutonium unattended at a train station. Then a homeless person steals it,” the hacker said.
“Yes, of course you shouldn’t steal other people’s suitcases. But you also shouldn’t leave nuclear material at a train station.”
The hacker provided Politiken with a file containing the CPR numbers.
The newspaper forwarded the file to Emil Hørning, an IT security expert at Danish cybersecurity company Defend Denmark.
Hørning said the hacker’s account appeared credible and that the described method was plausible.
Politiken conducted its interview with the hacker in English through an encrypted communication service.
Danish government proposes tighter senior pension rules to save 800 million DKK annually
The Danish government wants to change how workers qualify for senior pensions, potentially saving 800 million DKK annually by 2030, according to Jyllands-Posten.
Currently, people whose health limits their ability to work to 15 hours a week or less can receive a senior pension up to six years before reaching the state retirement age.
Their work capacity is assessed against their most recent job. Under the proposal, applicants would instead be assessed against all types of employment.
The Finance Ministry estimates savings of 200 million DKK in 2028, rising to 800 million DKK in 2030.
The proposal has divided political parties and organizations.
Anders Vistisen of DF, Dansk Folkeparti, the Danish People’s Party, said his party would oppose the changes.
“We are not going to cut for the worn-out,” he told Jyllands-Posten, citing Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen’s promises of more dignified retirement.
Ældre Sagen, Denmark’s senior citizens’ advocacy organization, also criticized the proposal.
Deputy Director Michael Teit Nielsen warned that applicants could face longer assessments to determine whether they could work in another profession.
However, Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry, Denmark’s main employers’ association, welcomed the proposal.
Deputy CEO Søren Kryhlmand said assessing workers against the entire labor market would allow those capable of other jobs to remain employed.
The government also plans to increase the separate Arne early retirement pension by approximately 3,000 DKK monthly. Its current maximum is 15,650 DKK per month.
Changing the senior pension scheme, introduced in 2019, requires agreement among the parties behind it before a general election.
Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard is scheduled to present the budget proposal today.

“We are significantly strengthening knowledge, general education, and formal education in Denmark, from ABC to PhD. It is good for the individual young person, but it is also good for Denmark’s future,” Lidegaard said.
Unlike in recent years, when the government’s fiscal room for manoeuvre helped fund much of its budget plans, this proposal includes several measures to find additional savings.
These include cuts to the Danish student grant (SU), savings on senior pension payments, a proposed tax on cruise ships and further reductions in state administration costs.
The government must now negotiate with other parties in the Danish Parliament, the Folketing, to secure a majority for the 2027 budget.
The proposal includes a negotiating reserve of 500 million DKK annually from 2027 to 2030, which other parties can seek to use to fund their own priorities.

Climate Change Is Accelerating Faster Than We Can Respond, Scientists Warn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:00:03 UTC
23:00:03 KST

The climate is warming up faster than we can respond. According to a new report published Oct. 14 in the journal BioScience, “Earth’s climate system is moving deeper into uncharted territory.”
The State of the Climate, an annual report that tracks the Earth’s “vital signs,” monitors several climate related indicators—ranging from greenhouse gas concentrations and temperature changes to tree cover loss due to wildfire. The researchers found that, of the 16 planetary vital signs, seven are currently at record extremes. This includes sea levels and greenhouse gasses in the atmosphere. Meanwhile several others, such as areas burned during wildfires and ocean heat levels, show evidence of acceleration or abrupt shifts.
The researchers warn that the rate of global warming appears to have accelerated, from about 0.05°C per decade between 1880 and 1970 to roughly 0.36°C per decade between 2010 and 2024—and the 2°C threshold meant to limit planetary damage could be reached before 2050 they warn. These accelerating and intensifying changes could raise the risk of reinforcing feedback loops and crossing tipping points—critical thresholds that, when crossed, can lead to accelerating and often irreversible environmental changes. In 2025, the Earth passed its first climate tipping point, as rising ocean temperatures, acidification, overfishing, and pollution are combining to cause coral bleaching and mortality.
"Earth’s life-support systems are being pushed beyond stable limits," the report states, "with changes unfolding faster than our ability to respond."
This year, a number of extreme weather events made the impacts of an acceleratingly warming planet impossible to ignore. July 2026 was the hottest month on record for the contiguous United States, with ocean temperatures also reaching a record high that month. Back-to-back heat waves in Europe lead to an estimated 35,000 excess deaths, preliminary reports show. A number of regions—including Utah in the U.S., Ontario, Canada, along with France, Spain, Britain, and Belgium have either experienced their worst wildfire years in history or are on track to do so. While we don’t yet know enough to link these individual weather events to climate change, research shows that it is supercharging extreme weather events.
Concentrations of greenhouse gases—including carbon dioxide, methane, and nitrous oxide—all reached record levels in 2026, the researchers say. In May 2026, atmospheric carbon dioxide exceeded 428 parts per million, roughly 50% above pre-industrial levels and generally higher than any time in the last 2 million years.
The authors of today’s report also tracked indicators of the human activities driving these planetary changes, like energy use, food production, and economic growth. Fossil fuel consumption remains the dominant driver of these changes. Fossil fuel consumption rose by 0.9% in 2025, the report found, with oil, coal, and gas all reaching record highs, and annual energy-related carbon dioxide emissions surpassed 41 gigatons for the first time—the equivalent of emissions released by over 10,800 coal-fired power plants in one year.
There have, however, been some signs of progress, the report notes. Low-carbon sources provided roughly 43% of global electricity generation in 2025, and solar and wind energy consumption grew by approximately 18%. That was before the war in Iran laid bare the world’s reliance on fossil fuels, and triggered a global green energy boom.
But cutting carbon emissions will no longer be enough on its own, the report states. Adaptation measures—ranging from shifts towards plant-based diets, to restoring mangroves to better protect against storm surges—will be key to adjusting to a changing climate.
The report underscores an unavoidable truth. "We are witnessing the rapid destabilization of the Earth’s climate system,” it states. “This is no longer a warning for the future; it is a diagnosis of the present.”

“The initial versions of Hurjet will be manufactured and delivered by Turkish Aerospace Industries. But with contributions from subcontractors in Spain and additional certification there, we will deliver a version that could become a joint platform for the two countries,” he said.

Organized by the OSTIM Defense and Aviation Cluster with support from Türkiye's National Defense Ministry and Defense Industries Secretariat, the event opened at Congresium Ankara. Anadolu serves as its global communication partner.
Defense exports exceed $7.4B
Gorgun said Türkiye's defense industry exports had exceeded $7.4 billion this year, already matching the previous year's total.
He said the sector comprises more than 4,000 companies and nearly 130,000 employees, with an average age of 34.
Highlighting the seasonal pattern of defense exports, Gorgun said shipments in the final two months typically significantly exceed the monthly average, supporting expectations that annual exports would surpass last year's level.
He attributed the industry's progress to Türkiye's industrialization model, which has enabled a transition from direct procurement to indigenous designs and platform exports.
Felipe Javier Carrasco Torres, deputy industry minister of Spain's Valencia region, said cooperation with Türkiye could help expand the region's defense and security industries.
Valencia has industrial clusters spanning traditional manufacturing and emerging technologies, including semiconductors, photonics, aerospace and drones, he said, adding that its companies currently serve mainly civilian markets.
Torres invited Turkish industrialists to a defense and security industry event planned in Valencia next September, emphasizing that cooperation with other countries and institutions would help the region develop capabilities more quickly.

EU provides EUR 228 bln to Ukraine since 2022 - commissioner
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:58:06 EEST
22:58:06 KST

The European Union’s support for Ukraine since Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022 has reached EUR 228 billion, European Commissioner for Economy and Productivity Valdis Dombrovskis said at the 10th ministerial roundtable on support for Ukraine on Wednesday, on the sidelines of the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank in Bangkok.
“The EU is doing its part: EUR 228 billion in support of Ukraine since the start of the full-scale invasion, and that is not all, more to come,” he said on X after the roundtable, which was closed to the press.
Dombrovskis stressed that international partners must join these efforts.
He did not give Interfax-Ukraine other details, but a meeting of the Ukraine Financial Coordination Group with the commissioner is scheduled for Friday, October 16, on the sidelines of the annual meetings.
Several roundtable participants told Interfax-Ukraine that it did not address specific commitments that Kyiv’s partners are ready to make in the future, but that in general they confirmed their readiness to keep supporting Ukraine.
The Ukrainian side outlined its external financing needs for 2027 and said its sources must be confirmed before the IMF mission in November for the combined second and third reviews of the Extended Fund Facility (EFF) program.
IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva traditionally took part in the roundtable and left after a while, and the fund was then represented by First Deputy Managing Director Daniel Katz, an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent said. Before joining the IMF last year, Katz was U.S. deputy treasury secretary and worked on creating the American-Ukrainian investment fund.
World Bank Vice President Antonella Bassani, European Bank for Reconstruction and Development President Odile Renaud-Basso, International Finance Corporation (IFC) Managing Director Makhtar Diop and IFC Vice President Alfonso Garcia Mora, and European Investment Bank President Nadia Calvino were also present.
Prime Minister Serhiy Koretsky spoke for Ukraine online, as did Finance Minister Serhiy Marchenko, who stayed in Kyiv because of his report to the Verkhovna Rada on Monday and the adoption of laws important for external financing later in the week. National Bank of Ukraine Governor Andrei Pyshnyy, Economy and Environment Minister Oleksandr Kravchenko and Deputy Finance Minister Olha Zykova also attended.
During the IMF annual meetings, which run on October 12-18, the Ukrainian delegation will discuss with the fund the implementation of the new four-year EFF program of $8.1 billion, approved in late February this year. It is part of total external financing of $136.5 billion in 2026-2029 under the base scenario.
In July, the fund completed the first review of the program and released a second tranche of about $690 million, bringing total financing under the new program to $2.2 billion. Delays in meeting some of the program’s structural benchmarks were recorded. The program, updated after the first review, gained eight structural benchmarks, seven of them fiscal.
The plan now is to combine the second and third reviews and bring them to the executive board by December, together with approval of the combined third and fourth tranches totaling about $1.65 billion.
“Bringing this to the board depends on receiving sufficient and reliable financing assurances to cover the projected funding gap on terms consistent with ensuring Ukraine’s debt sustainability,” IMF spokeswoman Julie Kozack said in early October.
Marchenko said that before the IMF mission’s expected visit in November it would be desirable to get confirmation of all sources of the $52.6 billion of external financing of the state budget in 2027, while about $32.6 billion of that still needs additional confirmation.
He said Kyiv counts on the EU to keep its commitment to cover two-thirds of Ukraine’s external financing needs next year as well, which would add about $17.5 billion to confirmed financing. As for the remaining roughly $15 billion, there are a number of sources for covering it, he said, including bilateral financing and guarantees and programs with international financial institutions.
The first such roundtable took place at the IMF and World Bank spring meetings on April 21, 2022, and the second at the autumn meetings on October 12 that year. They have been held twice a year at these events since.
At the first meeting, the IMF head pointed to Ukraine’s monthly need in 2022 of $5 billion to finance the state budget deficit amid the war Russia unleashed. At the second, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy proposed that the global financial community take three urgent steps in support of Ukraine: create a ‘financial Ramstein,’ ensure economic recovery and help for Ukrainians, and create a mechanism to support investment and insure it against war risks.
At the third, Zelenskyy asked the IMF and World Bank to approve a Support Program to cover priority Rapid Recovery projects worth $14.1 billion, and urged them to work out specific mechanisms for using frozen Russian assets to compensate for the damage Russia caused.

Ukraine charges five Russian scientists with war crimes over excavations in annexed Crimea
Ukraine is investigating criminal cases against five Russian archaeologists over excavations in occupied Crimea, BBC Russia reported, citing prosecutorial and court documents obtained by the outlet.
The archaeologists have been designated as suspects in absentia in war crimes investigations. BBC names two of the suspects: the leaders of an excavation at the medieval site of Solkhat: Mark Kramarovsky, an 86-year-old Soviet and Russian scientist who founded the excavation in 1978 and has led it ever since, and Emil Seydaliev, a senior researcher at the Institute of Archaeology of Crimea.
The Ukrainian outlet Graty reported in August that Ukraine had formally designated Kramarovsky and Seydaliev as suspects. Ukrainian investigators said the scientists carried out illegal excavations at Solkhat, helped Russia appropriate the valuables found there in violation of international humanitarian law, and damaged the cultural layer beyond repair.
BBC does not name the other three scientists.
Since 2014, the excavation has received permits from Moscow, BBC said, and its finds have been handed over to the Crimean Tatar Museum of Cultural and Historical Heritage, established by Russian authorities. All the objects have been entered into Russia’s museum fund. Ukrainian prosecutors believe this has led to the “illegal appropriation of Ukrainian cultural heritage.”
Emil Seydaliev was born in Crimea, held Ukrainian citizenship and later obtained a Russian passport. He has worked in Crimea his entire life and called the criminal case against him and his colleagues a farce.
In December 2025, Polish security services detained Russian archaeologist Alexander Butyagin, who had conducted excavations in Crimea for many years. Since 1999, Butyagin had led the Myrmekion archaeological expedition, which studies the ancient site of Myrmekion in present-day Kerch. He said he kept working in Crimea after 2014 because he considered it necessary and right for the site. Ukrainian prosecutors believe he conducted illegal excavations in Crimea after 2014 and destroyed a cultural heritage site. Ukraine had sought Butyagin’s extradition, but in April 2026 Poland handed him over to Russia as part of an exchange.
Ukraine initially accused Butyagin of partially destroying a cultural heritage site and causing damage exceeding 201.6 million hryvnias ($4.8 million). After his release, Ukrainian authorities reclassified the case as a war crime: “looting of national treasures in occupied territory” by prior conspiracy. A court in Kyiv authorized an in-absentia investigation into a new case against him, allowing him to be tried in absentia. The previous charge did not allow for that, BBC said.

Two Veterans With Prosthetic Legs Conquer 6,476-Meter Himalayan Peak in Tribute to Ukraine’s Defenders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:57:00 UTC
22:57:00 KST

Two veterans who each lost a lower leg while defending Ukraine have summited Mera Peak in Nepal, reaching an altitude of 6,476 meters (21,247 feet) and dedicating their ascent to Ukrainian service members fighting Russia’s full-scale invasion and those who have died in the war.
Christopher John Park-Greenwood, a former British soldier who served in Ukraine’s military, and Roman Havryliak, a Ukrainian veteran, completed the climb using prosthetic legs as part of an expedition organized with Second Wind, a Ukrainian community supporting service members and veterans with limb loss through adaptive mountain sports.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The expedition began on Oct. 1, Ukraine’s Defenders Day. The climbers dedicated their ascent to those continuing to defend the country and to the memory of those who have given their lives.
According to Second Wind, the team faced demanding high-altitude conditions, including temperatures below freezing, up to three meters of fresh snow and avalanches in close proximity. The multi-day expedition required gradual altitude gain and acclimatization before the final push to the summit.
For Greenwood and Havryliak, Mera Peak marked another milestone in a mountaineering journey that began after their combat injuries. The climb followed their ascent of Mount Ararat in Turkey, which stands at 5,137 meters (16,854 feet), in the summer of 2026.
From combat injuries to high-altitude mountaineering
Both climbers spent more than a year preparing for the expedition through regular training, climbing-gym sessions and increasingly challenging routes in Ukraine’s Carpathian Mountains.
Kyiv Mayor Faces Questioning as Russian Attack Triggers Fresh Water Cuts
Greenwood, originally from Yorkshire, England, is a career soldier who previously served in the British Army and the French Foreign Legion.
Following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, he joined the Armed Forces of Ukraine’s (AFU) 73rd Naval Special Operations Centre. He sustained a severe combat injury in 2023 that resulted in the loss of his lower leg.
                                                                                                                                                                         Two veterans summited Mera Peak in Nepal with the support of the Second Wind Foundation team. (Photo courtesy of the Second Wind Foundation)                             
Havryliak, known by the call sign “Hava,” is from the Lviv region. He volunteered to join the AFU following the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion and served as a drone operator with the 80th Separate Air Assault Brigade. He also sustained a severe combat injury that led to the loss of his leg.
After more than a year of treatment and multiple surgeries, Havryliak set himself a new goal: returning to the mountains.
Both veterans subsequently became active members of Second Wind, a charitable foundation and community that brings together Ukrainian service members and veterans who use prostheses, taking part in its training sessions and mountain programs.
The expedition was accompanied by Gennady Gazin, Anna Vozna and Oleksii Aleksieienko, the founders of the organization.
Second Wind grew out of the documentary project Second Wind, which followed five Ukrainian service members who climbed Mount Kilimanjaro, Africa’s highest mountain. The foundation currently runs regular adaptive mountain sports programs in Ukraine and organizes mountain expeditions for its community members.
Ukrainian veterans turn to mountain climbing for rehabilitation
Ukrainian veterans are increasingly taking on mountain-climbing challenges at home and abroad as part of their rehabilitation after severe combat injuries.
Many of these expeditions involve service members who have undergone amputations and climb using prosthetic limbs, demonstrating how adaptive mountaineering can help veterans return to physically demanding activities.
In early 2025, five Ukrainian veterans completed a group ascent of Mount Kilimanjaro, Africa’s highest peak, at 5,895 meters (19,341 feet). The expedition was described as a world first for a group of veterans with combat-related injuries.
The participants included Roman Kolesnyk, known by the call sign “Dobriak,” a veteran of the 3rd Assault Brigade who underwent an amputation after a severe injury; border guard Vladyslav Shatilo, known as “Shatia,” who lost a limb; and Mykhailo Matviiv, or “Grizzly,” a member of the Omega Special Forces Detachment of the National Guard of Ukraine who was injured by a landmine near Vuhledar.
The group also included Oleksandr Mikhov, known as “Ragnar,” an Omega special forces fighter who uses a prosthesis, and a servicewoman known by the call sign “Vysota” (“Height”), who sustained severe injuries twice while serving at the front.
In May 2025, Ukrainian military intelligence veterans Ivan Taran and Oleksandr Dashko, both of whom had undergone major amputations, reached the Everest Base Camp in Nepal at an altitude of approximately 5,400 meters (17,717 feet), using prosthetic limbs. The expedition was organized by Ukrainian mountaineerc Tetiana Yalovchak.
Veterans have also taken on mountain challenges within Ukraine. Volodymyr Voropai, a veteran of the 73rd Naval Special Operations Centre who lost a leg during the war, helped pioneer climbs of Mount Hoverla (2,061 meters, or 6,762 feet) for veterans with amputations.
In October 2026, service member Maksym Bashynskyi, who was wounded near Huliaipole, climbed Mount Vysokyi Verkh in the Carpathians, which stands at 1,176 meters (3,858 feet), as part of the Travel Therapy project. Volunteers assisted him using a specialized all-terrain mobility cart known as “Julietta.”
Group ascents of Mount Hoverla have also brought together dozens of veterans. Among the initiatives reported in late 2025 and 2026 were a climb involving 50 veterans from the Kyiv region and an ascent by Special Operations Forces (SSO) personnel who carried a fellow veteran with an amputation to the summit of Ukraine’s highest mountain.

Restriction of access

- Sternenko speculated that SpaceX had acted at the request of US President Donald Trump’s administration.
- Zelensky’s external adviser Beskrestnov later confirmed the reports on Telegram.

- In his view, "this action cannot be a coincidence and has to do with the current political situation."
- Ukraine once again received no intelligence warning from its Western partners last night, Vladimir Zelensky said.
- The US warned Ukraine that it could suspend intelligence sharing, Zelensky said in an interview with NPR. According to him, Ukrainian generals reported that they had been notified of this possibility at the military level.
- Ukraine received no intelligence warnings regarding the first wave of Russian ballistic missile launches overnight into October 14, but warnings about subsequent attacks did come in, RBC Ukraine quoted Ukrainian Air Force Spokesman Yury Ignat as saying.
Consequences
- A slowdown in Starlink service is making it virtually impossible to launch medium-range drones, and some missions involving them have already been cancelled since the start of the day, the 7th Corps of the Ukrainian airborne assault troops reported on Telegram.
- The Ukrainian armed forces rely entirely on Starlink satellite internet, so the Kiev authorities must travel to the US to negotiate the lifting of access restrictions, Verkhovna Rada lawmaker Alexey Goncharenko (listed in Russia as a terrorist and extremist) said.
- The Ukrainian army will no longer be able to counter Russian jet-powered drones due to the reduced speed of the US Starlink satellite Internet service, Zelensky’s external adviser on communications and unmanned systems, Beskrestnov, said.
- As the adviser pointed out, Kiev uses Starlink to counter jet-powered drones, but restrictions on its operation will now prevent the Ukrainian military from doing so.
- Beskrestnov said that through their actions Ukraine’s partners "actually deprive" Kiev of one of the few chances to intercept such drones.
- The slowdown of Starlink terminals caught the Ukrainian military by surprise, occurring entirely without warning, the British newspaper Financial Times (FT) wrote citing sources.
- The report says that Ukrainian drones relying on Starlink terminals are experiencing signal disruptions at speeds above 160 kmph.
- The reduction in intelligence-sharing from the United States, combined with Starlink's operational restrictions, is seriously hampering the Ukrainian military, unmanned aviation expert and CEO of the Center for Integrated Unmanned Solutions Dmitry Kuzyakin told TASS.
- According to him, the Kiev regime’s unchecked actions are irritating both the US president himself and a segment of the American establishment that has heavily invested in Ukraine.
- A number of cyber operations by the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) against Russia may be disrupted or delayed due to SpaceX restricting the speed of Starlink satellite Internet terminals used by Ukrainian security agencies, Sergey Trukhachev, a technical and digital security expert, told TASS.
- He also noted that the SpaceX restrictions would directly impact the Ukrainian armed forces as well.

HAMBURG, October 14. /TASS/. The first hearing in the case of the Nord Stream gas pipeline explosions took place at the Higher Regional Court in Hamburg, Germany, amid tightened security measures.

TASS has compiled the key details about the hearing.
Defendant
- Ukrainian national Sergey Kuznetsov is the defendant in the case.
- He was detained in Italy in August 2025 and transferred to Germany.
- During the first hearing, Kuznetsov confirmed his identity and said that he had been born in Omsk on January 2, 1976.
- Another Ukrainian citizen was detained in Croatia recently.
Charges
- The Office of Germany’s Federal Prosecutor believes that Kuznetsov’s actions should be considered a war crime, a TASS correspondent reported from the courtroom.
- The suspect and his accomplices, also service members, acted on orders from Ukrainian government agencies, a prosecutor from the German Federal Prosecutor's Office said during the Hamburg hearing.
- Investigators believe that the saboteurs used forged documents to rent a sailing yacht from a German company and transported explosives to the Nord Stream pipelines.
- Earlier, the court admitted the indictment against the Ukrainian national for trial on the merits and opened the main proceedings.
- Judges came to the conclusion that there was enough evidence to suspect Kuznetsov of committing a war crime using banned methods of warfare by attacking civilian facilities, carrying out a blast, damaging property, and disrupting public services.
- Kuznetsov declined to speak to the court, exercising his right to remain silent.
Defense team’s stance
- Kuznetsov’s defense team said that, as a service member, he was unable to discuss the circumstances of the incidents, the people who gave him orders and the details of those orders.
- According to his lawyer, this makes a fair trial is impossible.

- The defense team plans to seek a dismissal of the charges.
Trial
- The first hearing of the case took place at the Hamburg Higher Regional Court.
- The hearing lasted a little over two hours.
- The next hearing is set for October 27.
- The court has scheduled 24 hearings through the end of the year.
- Further hearings are planned for February, but they have yet to be finalized.

Nord Stream blast case

Who met Egypt's intelligence chief? Israeli security officials all deny receiving pre-Oct. 7 warning
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:55:32 UTC
22:55:32 KST

One by one, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the former head of the National Security Council and senior Israeli security officials all denied Wednesday any involvement in a meeting with whoever arrived at Ben Gurion Airport aboard an Egyptian aircraft on September 26, 2023, just 11 days before the October 7 massacre. According to reports, Egypt's then-intelligence chief Abbas Kamel was the man on the plane and he came to warn those he met of "a major attack being planned by Hamas."
In an interview with Channel 14 on Tuesday night, Netanyahu acknowledged, contrary to his previous statements, that Kamel had indeed arrived in Israel. However, he insisted that the Egyptian intelligence chief "did not meet with me because I was at a memorial ceremony for fallen IDF soldiers."
Former Mossad chief David Barnea and former Shin Bet director Ronen Bar also said they had not met with Kamel. Both said they believed reports of the visit were fake news, arguing that it would have been unlikely for Kamel to visit Israel without meeting them.
The Mossad said no representative of the agency had met with Kamel.
Ghassan Alian, who was then coordinator of government activities in the territories and was heavily involved in efforts to maintain calm in Gaza, also denied meeting Kamel that day. Former National Security Council head Tzachi Hanegbi similarly said he had not met with the Egyptian official.
Israel's embassy in Egypt, another body that maintains contact with the Egyptian intelligence chief, was excluded from the meeting.
Two days after the October 7 massacre, Ynet journalist Smadar Perry reported, following an Associated Press report about an Egyptian warning, that Kamel had contacted the Prime Minister's Office and conveyed a message warning of "something unusual, a massive operation" expected to originate from Gaza.
The Prime Minister's Office denied the report at the time. Yet, at least as things appear now, it made no urgent effort over the following three years to establish whether any messages had indeed been conveyed by the Egyptian side, even if not directly to Netanyahu.
As for Netanyahu's claim that he could not have met whoever arrived on the aircraft because he was attending a ceremony marking the 50th anniversary of the Yom Kippur War at Mount Herzl, The Atlantic reported that the ceremony took place about two hours after Kamel's arrival.
Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana suggested Wednesday morning that "it was one of the heads of the security establishment." However, the IDF chief of staff, Mossad director, Shin Bet chief and police commissioner were all seated alongside Netanyahu and President Isaac Herzog at the ceremony.
'Reinforcing the deep state narrative'
A former senior Israeli official commenting on the reports Wednesday said: "It is unlikely that Abbas Kamel would come to Israel to meet with anyone below the level of prime minister. Netanyahu has met him before, contrary to what he said on Channel 14. He also met his successor, Hassan Rashad, last year.
"In any case, it is clear that when the Egyptian intelligence chief arrives, a minister and President el-Sissi's No. 2, he meets at the very least with the prime minister and also with the president. It is unlikely that Abbas Kamel did not meet the prime minister. You cannot hide something like that."
The former official continued: "When a senior foreign official arrives, his aircraft enters a special route managed by the Israel Airports Authority. There are cameras and digital location records. Bibi is manipulating things here and laying the groundwork for his continued portrayal of himself as a victim: 'Why wasn't I informed?'
"Netanyahu is reinforcing the deep state narrative. But it is not difficult to check these things. The prime minister is claiming there was a breach of trust. He says a plane arrived. For years, I didn't care. Now I'm saying it happened.
"So the attorney general can order all the digital evidence to be seized, examine the computer records and see who was in a restricted area that day. A plane lands, and its crew is supposed to be registered. Did anyone get off the plane? Did anyone come to meet them?"
Netanyahu's son, Yair Netanyahu, responded with a post on X.
"To all the 'left-wing journalists,' stop your propaganda already! My father was referring to the fact that a prime minister does not meet the intelligence chief of another country 'alone,' as the blood libel against him claimed.
"The meeting they showed from 2021 with the Egyptian intelligence chief also included his Israeli counterparts, such as the head of the National Security Council, Israel's intelligence minister and others.
"During the Egyptian intelligence chief's one-hour visit to Ben Gurion Airport in 2023, 11 days before the massacre, my father was at a ceremony commemorating the Yom Kippur War."
Yair Netanyahu concluded: "Now the question is: Who did meet with the Egyptian intelligence chief at the time? And why has this been concealed from the prime minister and the public for three years? Why are they still refusing the prime minister's request to reveal who met the Egyptian intelligence chief in Israel?"
'We do not dismiss any threat'
Last month, The Atlantic reported that Kamel had arrived in Israel for an exceptionally brief visit on September 26, 2023, during which he "warned that Hamas was preparing a major attack and urged Israel to introduce economic relief measures to prevent escalation."
According to the magazine's investigation, a chartered aircraft linked to Egyptian intelligence services landed at Ben Gurion Airport and remained in Israel for just 67 minutes before departing for Cairo.
A former Israeli official who spoke to the magazine said the Egyptian intelligence chief's decision to make such a short and unusual visit should itself have conveyed the urgency of the warning.
"The messenger was the message," the official said.
Approximately two hours after the Egyptian aircraft landed, Netanyahu attended a ceremony in Jerusalem marking the 50th anniversary of the Yom Kippur War. "As a central lesson from that war, we do not dismiss any threat," Netanyahu said at the time.
The Wall Street Journal separately reported that Kamel called Netanyahu in early October 2023 to warn him of an impending attack from the Gaza Strip, after two earlier Egyptian warnings had gone unheeded.
"Kamel began to grow concerned," the newspaper reported, lending further support to Smadar Perry's reporting in Ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth in the days following the massacre about an Egyptian warning.
Netanyahu, however, continues to deny that he spoke with Kamel.

A North Korean Missile Already Supplied to Russia Just Got a Much Longer Reach
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:55:18 UTC
22:55:18 KST

- Category
- World
A North Korean Missile Already Supplied to Russia Just Got a Much Longer Reach
North Korea launched a KN-30 ballistic missile more than 910 kilometers during an October 12 test, demonstrating substantially greater range than in the weapon’s earliest known trials.
The same missile type has previously been transferred to Russia and could potentially be used in strikes against Ukraine, according to Militarnyi on October 14.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
North Korea’s state-run KCNA released images from the launch but did not publicly identify the missile or disclose its range.
Based on photographs of the five-axle mobile launcher, the secretary general of the Korea Defense and Security Forum identified the weapon as the Hwasong-11Da-2.5, also known in Western reporting as the KN-30.
The KN-30 is a solid-fueled short-range ballistic missile and an enlarged member of North Korea’s Hwasong-11 family. Pyongyang has claimed that the weapon can carry a 2.5-ton warhead, although that figure has not been independently confirmed.
At least two ballistic missiles were launched toward the Sea of Japan on October 12. Japan’s Defense Ministry said one traveled roughly 220 kilometers, while the second flew more than 910 kilometers and reached an altitude of about 70 kilometers.
KCNA said the test was intended to verify improvements made to key components of the missile system. North Korea did not specify which components had been upgraded, leaving open the question of whether the longer flight reflected changes to propulsion, guidance, payload configuration, or another part of the weapon.
The reported 910-kilometer flight is particularly notable compared with earlier KN-30 tests. When North Korea first tested the missile in March 2021, Pyongyang claimed a range of 600 kilometers, while Japanese and South Korean military assessments placed the actual distance at roughly 420 to 450 kilometers.
The KN-30 was first publicly displayed during a military parade in Pyongyang on January 14, 2021. It is launched from a mobile transporter on a five-axle wheeled chassis and uses a solid-fuel motor, allowing it to be prepared and fired more quickly than liquid-fueled ballistic missiles.
Russia has already received KN-30 missiles from North Korea. Their presence in Russian stocks has raised concern that Moscow could add the weapon to the growing inventory of North Korean ballistic missiles used or available for strikes against Ukraine.
Earlier, reports emerged that more than 50% of the identified electronic components in North Korean Hwasong-11 (KN-23) ballistic missiles recovered in Ukraine were found to be fake.

A New Report Sheds Light on the Secretive Race to Build Self-Improving AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:55:01 UTC
22:55:01 KST

For months, Anthropic and OpenAI have warned that AI may be on the verge of improving itself.
This tipping point, known as “recursive self-improvement,” or RSI, could mean that new AI capabilities arrive faster than ever. But the advent of RSI might also be highly perilous for humanity, potentially marking the stage at which developers lose control of AI systems entirely.
Even as AI companies warn about the potential dangers of RSI, they have shared remarkably little about how they’re pursuing it. A new report, published Wednesday by the firm Gladstone AI, attempts to change that. It gives one of the most detailed pictures yet of how RSI could work and how AI companies are progressing toward it. The report is based on what the authors say are conversations with half a dozen researchers inside the top AI companies.
The report, exclusively shared with TIME ahead of its publication, emphasizes that AI companies are “actively working on” automating all parts of the AI development pipeline, including generating new ideas, running experiments to test those ideas, and interpreting the results. Most of the insiders Gladstone spoke to “believe RSI will start within the next 3 to 12 months, and possibly sooner, assuming there’s no U.S. government intervention or slowdown,” the report states.
Read More: Inside the Race to Make AI Build Itself
“There's a fair amount of [disaster] prepping and bio-bunker purchasing going on” among these researchers, says Edouard Harris, Gladstone’s chief technology officer.
The aim of the report, Gladstone’s executives tell TIME, is to give lawmakers a better understanding of how RSI works, and, in turn, a greater ability to regulate it.
“Our goal here was to define recursive self-improvement well enough that people can have a sane conversation about it, especially in Washington,” says Jeremie Harris, Gladstone’s CEO. (The pair are brothers.) “There are all these bills proposed to ban superintelligence, which are really interesting attempts to grapple with this problem. But what we're more interested in is: what is the process that needs to be regulated?”
How RSI could work
The report gives a simplified outline of how the AI research pipeline currently operates inside AI companies—and how those companies are beginning to automate the process.
For the first phase of training an AI model, known as pretraining, much of the emphasis is on finding ways to squeeze more intelligence out of a model with less and less computing power, known in the industry as “compute.”
The AI companies take a portfolio approach to testing these ideas. Researchers allocate a small amount of compute to each idea, using it to train a series of models. The models that reliably perform better as they scale up are selected for another round of training, using larger amounts of compute.
Companies don’t have infinite compute, which limits the number of promising ideas they can test at larger scales. This means that even if AI companies can train an AI that is able to generate ideas that seem promising, it matters greatly how many bad ideas it generates simultaneously. If companies need to spend huge amounts of time or compute filtering good AI-generated ideas from bad ones, it might make sense to continue to rely on human researchers with sound intuition.
Conversely, AI companies with access to more compute are able to test more ideas—potentially allowing them to reach RSI first. With more compute to throw at experiments, companies may also be likelier to catch ideas that the Gladstone report describes as the rarest and most desired by AI companies: those that perform better as more compute is thrown at them, even if they appear to be duds at smaller scales.
Being able to tell when those ideas are found—and particularly whether AI is helping find them—“is just such a critical part of this process that right now legislators have essentially zero visibility into,” says Jeremie Harris.
One of the traits that makes regulating RSI tricky is that it is a gradual process. “This is actually one of the reasons why we went to pains to describe it in so much detail,” says Edouard Harris. “So that it is possible to point to a part of this process and say: a human needs to be there.”

Russian forces attacked Epicentr’s hub in Khmelnytskyi, a city in western Ukraine, 10 times on 13 October, starting five large fires that destroyed about 85% of the goods stored inside, the company said.
Epicentr is a Ukrainian chain of home-improvement and household-goods stores. The attack adds pressure to Ukraine’s logistics network, already damaged by Russian strikes. On 10 September, Ukrainian entrepreneur Ruslan Shostak, co-owner of the popular retail chains Eva and Varus, said that 2.1 million square meters of Ukraine’s modern warehouse space had been destroyed since Russia’s full-scale invasion began. He put the country’s total modern warehouse space at approximately 5 million square meters. The strike on the hub came the same day Russia opened a barrage of 39 ballistic missiles on Ukraine’s power grid.
About 30 drones in the sky kept the fire from being put out, and the hub burned down completely overnight, Epicentr said. None of its people were hurt, the company said.
“The most important thing is that all our people are alive,” Epicentr wrote.
Russia had earlier completely destroyed Epicentr’s two largest logistics complexes, in Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast, the company said. The Khmelnytskyi hub had remained effectively its only surviving large warehouse complex. Goods were sent from there to the company’s shopping centers, and people worked there every day “so that millions of Ukrainians could buy what they need,” it wrote. Epicentr described every such attack as a blow to Ukrainian businesses’ ability to operate, pay wages, preserve jobs, and support the country’s economy.
Epicentr’s earlier losses
Epicentr said in August that 10 of its shopping centers had been completely destroyed since February 2022. Another 13 retail sites had been damaged, and one in Melitopol remained under Russian occupation, it said. At the time, the company operated 70 shopping centers, down from 80 at the end of 2021.
Earlier, during a Russian missile attack overnight on 5 August, Epicentr’s logistics center in Kyiv burned down completely, Epicentr’s Yulia Chudnovets said. The company’s ceramic tile plant in Kalynivka, one of the largest in Ukraine, was effectively lost, she said. One employee was killed and three were injured, she added.
A fourth Ukrainian pharmaceutical warehouse has burned in a Russian strike since the start of the month
On 25 May 2024, Russian airstrikes on an Epicentr hypermarket in Kharkiv killed 19 people, Interior Minister Ihor Klymenko said.
Attacks across Khmelnytskyi Oblast
Fires broke out at enterprises in Khmelnytskyi and Shepetivka districts on 13 October, Serhii Tiurin, head of the Khmelnytskyi Oblast Military Administration, reported. He did not name the enterprises. On 14 October, Tiurin said one of the fires had been put out, and crews were still fighting the other. Khmelnytskyi Mayor Oleksandr Symchyshyn said six people were injured in Khmelnytskyi district that day, where Russian strikes damaged private enterprises, a gas station, and a medical facility.
