Ikrame Imane Kouachi
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Jordan said Wednesday that Colombia’s opening of an embassy in West Jerusalem constitutes “a violation of international law and international legitimacy resolutions.”
In a statement issued following the embassy’s opening, the Jordanian Foreign Ministry said the kingdom condemns and rejects the move.
The ministry stressed that any measures or decisions aimed at changing the status or legal standing of Jerusalem are “null and void, illegitimate and without legal effect.”
It said the only way to achieve a just and comprehensive peace is to establish an independent, sovereign Palestinian state along the June 4, 1967, lines, with East Jerusalem as its capital.
Earlier Wednesday, the Palestinian Foreign Ministry said Colombia’s opening of the embassy violated international law and relevant UN resolutions, calling on the country to reverse the move.
On Aug. 28, 1980, Colombia informed the United Nations of its decision to move its diplomatic mission from Jerusalem to Tel Aviv in compliance with UN Security Council Resolution 478, before returning it to the occupied city 46 years later.
Adopted on Aug. 20, 1980, Resolution 478 calls on states not to recognize Israeli measures aimed at changing the character and legal status of Jerusalem and urges countries that had established diplomatic missions in the city to withdraw them.
In addition to Colombia, the US, Guatemala, Honduras, Kosovo, Papua New Guinea, Paraguay, Fiji, Nauru and Somaliland have moved their embassies to Jerusalem or opened embassies in the city.
Jerusalem remains at the heart of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and is widely regarded as one of its most sensitive issues.
While Israel claims the entire city as its capital, Palestinians view East Jerusalem – occupied by Israel since 1967 – as the capital of a future Palestinian state, in line with longstanding international consensus and UN resolutions.

No more Dolphins in NL: government moves to ban breeding
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:33:37 UTC
22:33:37 KST

No more Dolphins in NL: government moves to ban breeding
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Dolphin breeding is to be banned in the Netherlands within two years, and imports of the animals will be restricted.
Junior agriculture minister Silvio Erkens told parliament in a letter on Wednesday that keeping dolphins in captivity prevents them from expressing their natural behaviour and can cause health problems.
“Dolphins are intelligent animals that need to be constantly challenged and have a natural need to be able to dive deep and swim long distances,” said Erkens. “That cannot be provided in captivity. Life in chlorinated pools can also cause health problems.”
An immediate ban on dolphin captivity is not wanted because it would mean killing 22 bottlenose dolphins at the country’s Dolfinarium in Harderwijk, Gelderland.
But eventually, by preventing breeding and limiting importation, captivity for entertainment or education will be phased out entirely. The Dolfinarium criticised the cabinet, saying breeding is an essential aspect of welfare and will damage the dolphins’ health.

EU allocates $188.2M to boost defence production
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:33:04 UTC
22:33:04 KST

The European Commission has allocated $188.2 million (€168.2 million) to eight projects aimed at boosting Europe's defence production capacity under the European Defence Industry Programme.
The projects are expected to mobilise $1.41 billion (€1.26 billion) in industrial investments to accelerate and expand the production of energetic components used in missiles, drones, and ammunition, according to a statement on Wednesday.
The projects, which will become operational from 2027, are expected to reduce manufacturing times by up to 90% and enable annual production of more than 20,000 tonnes of energetic materials, 3,500 drone and missile propulsion systems, 200,000 loitering munition warheads, and 60 million rounds of ammunition.
The investments will cover 17 production sites across 14 member states and Norway, while also strengthening their protection against growing physical and cyber threats.
The initiative builds on the EU's Act in Support of Ammunition Production, an emergency instrument introduced to address production bottlenecks and increase ammunition manufacturing capacity following the start of the war in Ukraine.

Meanwhile, the euro dropped 0.7% to $1.112 as the dollar strengthened.

Core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, accelerated to 2.6% annually from 2.4% in August. Monthly core inflation remained at 0.3%.
The acceleration in both headline and core inflation highlighted persistent price pressures as investors assessed the outlook for Federal Reserve monetary policy.
Higher US interest rates can support the dollar by making dollar-denominated assets more attractive to investors.

Closer EU trade ties greater prize for UK than making separate deals, minister says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:31:55 UTC
22:31:55 KST

Britain will benefit from much closer trading relations with the EU even if that means giving up its ability to negotiate free trade agreements, the Scotland secretary has said.
Douglas Alexander helped negotiate deals with India and the US when he was a trade minister under Keir Starmer.
But he has told the Guardian he thinks joint trading arrangements with the EU – whether under a customs union or full membership – would be a bigger economic prize, not least because the EU has now negotiated its own similar deal with India.
When Starmer was prime minister, ministers would argue against rejoining the EU because it would mean having to abandon trade agreements with other countries.
Alexander’s comments show how much Starmer’s successor, Andy Burnham, who called this week for a “serious dialogue” on the UK’s relations with the EU, including possible re-entry, has shifted the government’s position.
Speaking to the Guardian from a trade delegation to India, Alexander welcomed the progress made since the Indian agreement came into force earlier this year, since when the price of scotch whisky in India has fallen by 10-15%.
But he said the economic benefits of trading agreements with the EU would be greater.
“In trade policy, geography still matters,” he said. “The Channel is just 21 miles wide. Our largest trading partner is and will remain the European Union in the years to come. We trade almost twice the amount with the European Union that we do with the United States, the largest single-country trading partner.”
He said: “It’s no secret that I was not a supporter of leaving the European Union, and I called out early as trade minister what I described as the ‘post-imperial delusions’ of the Brexiteers. Back in 2016, they promised a world of Britain as a buccaneering free trade nation in a world where barriers were coming down. Sadly, what we’ve witnessed in the year since is a more protectionist, more regionalised world in which barriers have been going up.
“At the time we joined the Pacific trade grouping, the CPTPP [Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership] – which undoubtedly makes a lot of sense geopolitically for the UK – our own analysis made clear that the long-term boost to UK GDP from membership is less than a tenth of 1%. If you compare that with estimates of the structural damage to the UK economy from Brexit, you get a sense of just how important Europe remains to our future trade and prosperity.
“We’re already paying a real economic price for putting up new barriers to our European neighbours who, with almost half of total UK trade, remain easily our largest trading partners.”
Alexander was speaking in Mumbai, where he was joined by the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, and the environment secretary, Angela Eagle, as well as a group of mayors from northern England. He made it clear he did not support any particular method of achieving closer relations with the EU.
The ministers spent much of their time in meetings with Indian officials as they attempt to iron out what they say have been “teething problems” with the early implementation, especially for smaller businesses.
“There are always teething problems,” Alexander said. “We’re also having a conversation at the level of regulation to see how do we overcome non-tariff barriers that can prove to be an inhibitor to the kind of progress we want to see unless they’re addressed.”
Many in the government say a bigger prize will be to reach an agreement at next month’s EU summit, where Burnham hopes to sign new trading deals for emissions, electricity and agricultural products.
One hurdle to delivering that is the UK’s desire to discuss the protectionist “Made in Europe” policy, which British manufacturers fear will shut them out of a key market. EU leaders say they are willing to discuss British entry into that scheme, though they are also pushing for the UK to impose tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles, without which they fear the UK will become a back door into the European market.
Reynolds told the Guardian this week he would not impose tariffs simply because of pressure from Brussels.

Sanchez posted a playful response to the appeal made by Luciana Littizzetto on the TV show *Che tempo che fa* (broadcast on channel Nove), where she read a letter inviting him to come to Italy to lead the centre left. 
"Thanks for the kind words, Luciana," Sánchez wrote on social media, "but I have to stay in Spain and cook paella for at least four years. 
"And anyway, I really can't imagine anyone better for Italy than Elly Schlein." He signed off by quoting a song by late entertainment icon Raffaella Carrà—which Littizzetto had referenced in her appeal—writing: "Yours always, Pedro Pedro Pedro."
Amid the centre left's chronic inability to pick a leader, many on the left have said it should first forge a common platform for the general election. One of the main areas of contention is further defence spending and aid to Ukraine, which the M5S is against. Schlein's watchword for years has been that she is "stubbornly in favour of unity". However, she recently pointedly observed that the PD has twice the votes of the M5S.

Behind the scenes: Kyiv Independent's September digest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:31:04 UTC
22:31:04 KST

Welcome to the Kyiv Independent's monthly digest, where we share company updates, milestones, and the stories behind our work.
In September, we gave our travel series a home of its own, launched a new way to reach readers, saw our community's support translate into practical help for journalists on the front line, and met our community at events in Brazil and the Netherlands.
What's new at the Kyiv Independent
On Sep. 11, the Kyiv Independent War Crimes Investigation Unit presented its latest investigative documentary, Last Seen in Crimea, which investigates a system of secret prisons in Russian-occupied Crimea where Ukrainian civilians have been held without contact with the outside world, often without formal charges, and subjected to torture and other forms of abuse.
Olesia Bida, the film author, shared that the main goal of the investigation was to identify those, who are directly responsible for these unlawful detentions. “Systems like this do not operate on their own — they depend on those who run them and those who carry out their orders,” she says.
The documentary is available to watch on the Kyiv Independent Youtube channel.
Our travel series, Dare to Ukraine, now has its own YouTube channel. The series explores Ukraine beyond the headlines, from its culture and history to its landscapes and, above all, its people. All 11 episodes from both seasons are now available in one place. As our deputy chief editor, Toma Istomina, put it, the series "captures the heart and soul of Ukraine." We hope the new channel will help even more people discover it.
We've also launched a WhatsApp channel, giving readers another way to follow our work. It brings our field reports, investigations, analysis, and long-form stories straight to your phone, alongside a weekly recap of the most important developments in Ukraine.
We also have an update on a project made possible by our community. In May, ahead of World Press Freedom Day, we launched our No News is Bad News collection to help protect journalists reporting near the front line. Through sales of the collection, plus additional donations, our community raised more than $24,000.
The funds enabled the Institute of Mass Information to purchase 26 Vydun 7.5 FPV drone detectors for independent regional journalists working near the front line, exceeding our original goal of funding 20 detectors. The Institute had been seeking funding for the equipment for months, as many potential donors were unable to support purchases of equipment suitable for military use. The detectors provide early warnings of approaching drones, giving journalists crucial time to seek cover.
Thank you to everyone who contributed.
Events
Our editor-in-chief, Olga Rudenko, spent part of September meeting audiences and fellow journalists abroad.
First, she traveled to São Paulo for the Festival piauí de Jornalismo, held under the theme "In the eye of the hurricane: editors-in-chief in times of turmoil." Joining newsroom leaders from eight countries, Olga spoke about what it takes to lead an independent newsroom in a country under attack.
Later in the month, she traveled to Deventer to speak at the Nederlands Journalistiek Festival. In a session titled "The Kyiv Independent: building independent journalism in wartime," she joined Wendelmoet Boersema, the editor-in-chief of Dutch newspaper Trouw and a former correspondent in the post-Soviet countries.
Their conversation explored the challenges of journalism under fire, the importance of holding those in power to account, and why independent reporting is particularly vital when a country is fighting for its future.
In the meantime, Francis Farrell and Olena Zashko travelled to Bucharest, Romania for a screening of Can You Hear Me? The Invisible Battles of Ukrainian Military Medics, the Kyiv Independent documentary co-authored by them. The film follows a group of Ukrainian military medics as they travel from the front-line in Ukraine to the quiet forests of Sweden, for a short mental health retreat.
In other media
September also brought opportunities to share our journalists' experiences and perspectives with international audiences.
Our deputy chief editor, Toma Istomina, spoke to Canadian Affairs about daily life in Kyiv under the threat of Russian aerial attacks. The city is now under round-the-clock air-raid alerts, forcing residents to weigh the risks of carrying on with their lives against the need to seek shelter. Toma also shared her mother's experience of receiving a cancer diagnosis and undergoing treatment during the war, explaining how interrupted sleep and the constant stress of attacks make recovery even harder.
Olga's visit to Brazil also drew interest from local media. In an interview with Marie Claire Brasil, she discussed leading an independent newsroom in wartime. She also spoke to Poder360 about the debate over holding elections in Ukraine during wartime.
For a deeper look at the issue, you can also watch Olga Rudenko and our deputy chief editor, Oleksiy Sorokin, discuss wartime elections on the Kyiv Independent's YouTube channel.
Meanwhile, Helsingin Sanomat, Finland's largest daily newspaper, featured Kyiv in a story exploring how younger Ukrainians view President Volodymyr Zelensky. Its reporters traveled to the Ukrainian capital to hear their perspectives firsthand.
Special recognition
September also brought us two awards that recognized not only our journalism, but also the work that makes it possible to keep that journalism free to read.
Our chief operating officer, Zakhar Protsiuk, was named among INMA's 2026 30 Under 30 honorees. The International News Media Association's awards recognize young professionals making an impact on the news industry. INMA highlighted Zakhar's role in growing the Kyiv Independent's membership from 6,000 to more than 35,000 members, with reader revenue now covering more than 70% of our budget.
We also received the 2026 Online Journalism Award for Innovation in Revenue Strategy from the Online News Association, in the Medium Newsroom category. This marks our second consecutive win in the category. The judges praised our "authentic and transparent membership model" and its central principle: keeping independent journalism freely accessible during wartime.
Neither milestone would have been possible without the people who choose to support us. Consider joining our community of members today.

French president acknowledges young people’s concerns amid high school protests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:30:35 UTC
22:30:35 KST

Seyma Erkul Dayanc
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
French President Emmanuel Macron has acknowledged the “legitimate anxieties” of young people amid nationwide high school protests, while condemning violence during demonstrations, government spokesperson Maud Bregeon said Wednesday.
Bregeon said Macron believed young people’s concerns had been “politically exploited and transformed into urban violence.”
The president denounced what he called “unacceptable scenes” of violence during the demonstrations, particularly on Tuesday, she said.
Macron has asked the government to provide “clear and concrete answers” in the coming weeks, including measures to protect teachers and an assessment of school buildings.
The government has assigned 2,000 of the 3,000 substitute teachers it had pledged to deploy, Bregeon said.
Education Minister Edouard Geffray said earlier Wednesday that more than one-third of the 3,000 substitute teachers had already been deployed to work with students.
The movement’s demands include greater education spending and opposition to the Parcoursup university admissions platform.
Macron urged demonstrators to remain calm and respect people and property.
More than 6,800 people, overwhelmingly minors, have been detained since the movement began, according to Le Parisien. The national police watchdog, IGPN, has opened 24 investigations into suspected police violence.

‘Dune: Part Three’ Cowriter Brian K. Vaughan Has a New Comic on the Way
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:30:00 UTC
22:30:00 KST

Brian K. Vaughan would like to apologize. He knows everyone is dying for details about Dune: Part Three, which he cowrote with director Denis Villeneuve, but his lips are pretty sealed until December 18 when the film finally hits theaters.
“Sorry to be coy,” he says as we’re about to leave the New York coffee shop where we’ve been chatting. “I hope the day will come where I’m able to say much, much more. It was truly so awesome. I can’t believe it happened.”
Vaughan is in the city for New York Comic Con, but not to talk about Dune. Ostensibly, he came to the convention to talk about Paper Girls, the comic he created with Cliff Chiang that was turned into a 2022 Amazon Prime Video series. During the Paper Girls panel, however, the pair announced that they’re working on a new comic, Roam, a superhero sci-fi series set to come out in February of next year.
Roam, Vaughan tells me, came from a deep desire to work with Chiang again. They’d considered doing a short eight-page story or maybe a one-shot, but eventually they said “Fuck it. Let’s do an ongoing series.”
Vaughan has the kind of career writers of a certain ilk would kill for. He started working on comics in the 1990s and has been the pen behind favorites like Saga, Y: The Last Man, and Marvel’s Runaways. (Those last two got turned into TV series; the outlier, Saga, is a story people have wanted to see adapted for years.) He also served as a writer on Lost and created CBS’s adaptation of Stephen King’s Under the Dome.
Still, his heart remains in comics. “I think sometimes people are like, ‘Oh, are you just going to sell out, Vaughan? Are you just going to go to Hollywood full-time?’” he says. “But I’m only able to do work in Hollywood because I have comics.”
Here, he speaks about Roam, his worries about AI, and maybe a little bit about Dune: Part Three as well.
On Roam, his forthcoming comic with Cliff Chiang:
It's completely unlike Paper Girls, completely unlike anything I've ever done. It’s set in the distant, distant future. The logline, as it were, is that in the future, everyone will get to be a superhero, but only while they're young. We're trying not to reveal too much more than that.
I remember seeing The Matrix, and having no idea what the fuck it was gonna be about. That was such a delight. So we're trying to do that here. I've been doing this for 31 years. I started when I was a teenager. I have a Spider-Man story here and there. I did a little Batman, and Ex Machina was my sci-fi political comic that sort of deconstructed the superhero. But this is certainly my first true superhero book.
On his fears about AI impacting comics, film, and TV:
It's terrifying. My friends who work in previsualization and as storyboard artists, these jobs are going away. I've heard about editors going away as well. Show business is a business, first and foremost. I’m lucky to sort of have been grandfathered in. I think there will always be people who are interested in bespoke human-made stories. But the future is terrifying and unknowable, and coming at us very, very quickly.
I’m heartened by the fact I've got two teenagers who are so disgusted by AI and grossed out if they ever hear I used it—and I’ve certainly never used it for anything creative. But I do think we're getting pretty close to the day that someone could be like, “I'm tired of waiting for the next issue. Give me the next issue of Saga.” That's when you get to the point of, do you just want content, something that's a distraction?
In Roam there's an element of this as well; AI is a component in the story. So, it's something I guess I need to write about with my human meat machine to process, but I'm in the middle of thinking about it, as you are, every day.
OK, a little bit about Dune: Part Three, which he has seen:
I can't say very much other than it’s a tremendous, insane, ridiculous honor to be involved with it, and my contributions are modest. Denis’ true cowriter on this is Frank Herbert. The novel is the star. And it's obviously the greatest cast and crew ever assembled. It's a fucking beautiful movie. It's my favorite of the three. which I can say with genuine humility. I can't say anything other than it's just as wonderful as you can imagine.
I got special thanks in the first movie. I was doing a tiny amount of consulting. I was working at Legendary [the media company that owns the rights to Dune] at the time, and they just invited me in to see an early cut, which was as fantastic as the finished product. But I just ended up talking to Denis, honestly. Never before has a director been that talented, also that decent and warm as a human being. I wasn't anticipating getting this call at the beginning of three, but it's obviously a call I could not refuse.
I should probably just be discreet at this point. The movie doesn't need me to promote it. I'm reluctant to do anything that makes me sound more important to this process.
On the future of Hollywood:
I am a small worker in the world of Hollywood. It is changing so rapidly that who knows what it's gonna be like tomorrow, six months from now.
But again, I've got teenagers and I see how delighted they were by Backrooms, by Obsession. It feels like Gen X has been force-feeding them a lot of my childhood stories that we have gussied up, and they are clearly hungry for something new.
On why he doesn’t write adaptations of his own comics:
I've taken stabs at it in the past. Richard Price, the novelist, I once heard him say in response to “Why don't you adapt your own stuff more?” that adapting your own work is like being a dentist and giving yourself a root canal. Just because you can do it, doesn't mean you should. Let some other motherfucker handle that. I believe those were Mr. Price's words.
It's been constructive and a thrill to adapt other people, and I like getting to watch other people adapt me, but I've also been doing a lot of it for the last decade, where it feels like I've either been adapting or being adapted. I think that was part of the siren song of Roam. It’s time to break some new ground.
Denis says that to adapt something you love is to do violence to it. When I've been adapted, that has always been what I've told people. It is much more important for this to be good than to be faithful. He's a master of cinema, and cinema is rarely about people sitting in a room having dialog. How do you transliterate this to cinema? That's an alchemy that I don't understand. He's just unparalleled at that.
On Lost and why writing for commercial breaks was a challenge:
I love my prestige drama without commercials, but there was a degree of difficulty working on Lost and having a cliff-hanger five times an episode. To have that was such a challenge and so rewarding when you were able to pull it off. Can you write something where people are like, “OK, I'll just wet my pants. I cannot risk not coming back [before the break is over].”

Deputy Prime Minister Radosław Sikorski takes part in Warsaw Security Forum 2026

Unknown Publisher

Deputy Prime Minister Radosław Sikorski takes part in Warsaw Security Forum 2026
13.10.2026
On 13 October, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs Radosław Sikorski attended a ministerial panel during the Warsaw Security Forum. Together with his counterparts from Norway, Germany, and the UK, he discussed the future of Europe in the context of ongoing changes in the global security architecture.
Minister Radosław Sikorski’s interlocutors during the panel were: Norway’s Minister of Foreign Affairs Espen Barth Eide, UK’s Secretary of State for Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Affairs Ed Miliband, and Germany’s Federal Minister for Foreign Affairs Johann Wadephul.
Minister Sikorski emphasised that Europe is capable of playing the role of a global player even in a situation where, instead of the order based on international law which we prefer, we are heading for lower predictability. In his remarks, Sikorski also highlighted Europe’s enormous economic potential, which Poland is currently seeking to translate into specific defence capabilities to ensure security by deterring potential aggressors. The head of Polish diplomacy also recalled that the EU remains attractive in terms of culture and investment.
We don't just need to have culture and to be in the right in facing evil. The side that is right has to have the power to defend it. And, you know, we had all the right in the world in 1939. We didn't have the power. We had to create it
said Minister Radosław Sikorski.
He also noted the region’s constant determination in its responsibility for the security of Europe. As its example, Minister Sikorski pointed to, among other things, the growing Baltic–Nordic cooperation, which illustrates these countries’ commitment to building a strong regional wing of NATO. This was a particularly important issue, as Norway is the Partner Nation of this year’s Warsaw Security Forum.
Livestream: WSF2026 (DAY2) 13.10: The Return of Power Politics: Europe Between War and Rivalry
The ministerial panel provided an opportunity to exchange views between representatives of countries of key importance to European security. Such meetings also serve to improve the coordination of efforts aimed at strengthening European defence and Europe’s position in the world.

Australian premier, Jordan's king discuss strengthening defense, trade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:29:14 UTC
22:29:14 KST

Saadet Gökce
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Jordanian King Abdullah II discussed strengthening defense, trade, and climate cooperation during a meeting in the capital Canberra on Wednesday, according to a joint statement.
The leaders welcomed closer defense ties, including training, technology, defense industry cooperation, joint operations and counterterrorism efforts, and condemned terrorism and violent extremism.
They also discussed the situation in the Middle East, expressing concern over tensions and calling for de-escalation through diplomacy.
Australia condemned Iranian attacks on Jordan and expressed solidarity with the country.
The two leaders reaffirmed their commitment to a two-state solution in the Middle East, rejected attempts to annex the West Bank and the displacement of Palestinians, and called for full implementation of the Gaza Peace Plan and unhindered humanitarian aid delivery.
They also reaffirmed support for Syria's unity and sovereignty and Lebanon's efforts to strengthen state authority, as well as condemned Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia.
In opening remarks at Parliament House, Albanese said "it's never been more important for countries to work together in the interests of international security," highlighting cooperation on defense and security, humanitarian efforts, resources, and energy.
Abdullah also pointed to military and intelligence affairs as areas for enhanced bilateral cooperation.
Bilateral goods and services trade totaled Australian $348.7 million ($242 million) in 2024-25, including A$217.2 million in Australian exports and A$131.5 million in imports, according to the Australian Embassy in Amman. Major traded products include meat and fertilizers.

Deputy Minister Marcin Bosacki at FAC meeting in Luxembourg
Poland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:29:05 CEST
22:29:05 KST

Deputy Minister Marcin Bosacki at FAC meeting in Luxembourg
12.10.2026
On 12 October, MFA Secretary of State Marcin Bosacki took part in a Foreign Affairs Council (FAC) meeting in Luxembourg. The deputy head of Polish diplomacy spoke about the need to exert pressure and tighten Russia sanctions, European security, and an offensive approach in combating Russian disinformation. The largest round of individual sanctions since the onset of Russia's aggression against Ukraine was adopted on Poland's initiative.
Europe’s pressure on Russia
In a discussion among foreign ministers on Russia’s aggression against Ukraine, Deputy Minister Bosacki stressed that the pressure on Russia should continue. The deputy head of Polish diplomacy thanked the gathering for adopting—on Poland’s initiative—the largest round of sanctions listings since Russia’ aggression began. The sanctions encompass nearly 1600 companies and individuals from the Russian military and industrial complex, people involved in the illegal election to the Russian Duma on occupied Ukrainian territories, and entities that facilitate circumventing the sanctions. The deputy foreign minister stressed that the Council’s adoption of the package on 12 October 2026 proves our resolve in supporting Ukraine.
Deputy Minister Bosacki called on the EU to reexamine the matter of using immobilised Russian assets to Ukraine’s benefit. He also urged the member states to tighten the visa policy towards Russia. The deputy minister noted that Poland does not issue tourist visas to Russian citizens. He found it incomprehensible that Russian tourists travel freely around the Schengen area while Russia bombs Ukraine’s civilians and infrastructure.
EU enlargement—security dimension
In a discussion on European security, Deputy Minister Bosacki emphasised the crucial role of EU enlargement in that regard. He offered an example of candidate countries that contribute their relevant experience, referring to Ukraine with its new defence and industrial capacities, topped with experience in operations during conventional, hybrid, and cyber conflict.
Deputy Minister Bosacki spoke about the possibility to draw on Ukraine’s military experience in ensuring broader European security, including in the EU’s missions on the territory of European neighbourhood. He also extended a reassurance that Poland is ready to assist Western Balkan EU candidate countries in combatting Russian disinformation.
Need for countering FIMI
During an unofficial debate in the Council on countering foreign information manipulation and interference (FIMI) and strategic communications, Deputy Minister Bosacki welcomed a more offensive approach to the matter proposed by High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas.
He conveyed Poland’s readiness to share its experience and expertise in order to enhance the EU’s strategic communications. Also, the deputy foreign minister emphasised that sanctions are essential in combatting Russia’s FIMI ecosystem and called for strengthening the Union’s sectors responsible for proceeding on proposed sanctions. He observed that the EU’s messages must be communicated also to Russian-language audiences.

Publishers: Libraries' survival as important as national defense
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:29:00 UTC
22:29:00 KST

Publishers: Libraries' survival as important as national defense
The Estonian Publishers' Association has issued an open letter urging the state and local governments to pay greater attention to libraries and literature as pillars of education, culture and mental well-being.
"The Ministry of Culture recently announced that state funding allocated to public libraries for purchasing books and other materials will be cut by €100,000. As the average price of books has also risen due to small print runs and increased costs, this will significantly reduce libraries' ability to purchase new books and make them available to readers," the Estonian Publishers' Association stressed in its open letter.
The association is calling on both the state and local governments to pay greater attention to libraries and literature as essential pillars of education, culture and mental well-being.
"The decline in deep reading among children and young people is not merely a cultural issue. It affects vocabulary, concentration, imagination, academic performance and the ability to understand oneself and others. These skills are essential for learning, working and participating in society as informed citizens."
"The 2025 reading survey 'Estonians Read 2025,' co-authored by Marju Lauristin, highlights a generational concern: 22 percent of people aged 50 to 60 and older are active readers with diverse literary interests, compared with just 11 percent of those aged 15 to 24. A strong interest in books among young people generally develops in homes with plenty of books. Public libraries must therefore help bridge disparities between households by providing every child with free, age-appropriate reading materials, good recommendations and opportunities to discover books, even when their family's book collection or financial circumstances do not allow it," the association explained.
According to the association, libraries are essential for readers of all ages who want to keep up with literature but find new books too expensive or live far from bookstores.
"Libraries are also important community centers. Without libraries and literature in our native language, it is impossible to ensure the survival of the Estonian language. This requires sufficient funding for libraries to maintain up-to-date and diverse collections of newly published works, support readers, authors and publishers through book purchases, and ensure that libraries do not become yet another disappearing community service."
The association said supporting the survival of libraries and access to literature in Estonian is just as important as what is traditionally understood as national defense.
"If we have no culture in our native language, what exactly are we defending?"
--
Editor: Kaspar Viilup, Marcus Turovski

2 Iraqi military personnel killed in blast from terror group remnants in Kirkuk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:28:49 UTC
22:28:49 KST

Fekry Abdeen and Ikram Kouachi

Petition to cut mobilization age to 55 gets 25,000 votes
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:28:21 EEST
22:28:21 KST

A petition on the Cabinet of Ministers website calling for the upper age limit for mobilization to be lowered to 55 has gathered the number of votes needed for consideration, according to the government's petition platform.
The petition was submitted on July 27 and had collected the required 25,000 votes by October 14.
"Practical experience of carrying out combat and special tasks shows the need to review the rule and lower the age limit to 55," the petition says.
Its author believes that men aged 55-60 in most cases have persistent age-related health changes and chronic diseases, which significantly reduce their physical endurance in extremely difficult field and combat conditions.
She also believes that staffing units with personnel according to their physical capabilities would improve the overall combat readiness and mobility of military units.
In addition, she said, citizens in this age group are highly qualified specialists whose work in the civilian sector and at critical infrastructure enterprises provides significant support to the economy.
The author proposes drafting and submitting to the Verkhovna Rada a bill amending the laws 'On Military Duty and Military Service' and 'On Mobilization Preparation and Mobilization' to lower the upper age limit for military service under martial law from 60 to 55 for privates, sergeants, petty officers and officers. It would also establish the right of servicemen who reach 55 under martial law to leave military service at their own request.
General mobilization is in effect in Ukraine, covering men liable for military service aged 25-60.
Earlier petitions on the Cabinet website calling to allow demobilization of servicemen over 55 who have served more than three years, to lower the upper draft age from 60 to 58 and to demobilize men over 55 who have earned the right to a civilian pension for work in hazardous conditions did not gather the votes needed for consideration.

Russian drone debris damages artwork of famous contemporary artist at museum in northwestern Ukraine
Debris from a Russian drone damaged artwork by one of Ukraine's most prolific contemporary artists at the Korsak Art Museum in Lutsk, a northwestern Ukrainian city, the museum staff reported on Oct. 14.
Petro Antyp's polyptych "Cosmogony," a Ukrainian interpretation of the world's origin, spans thousands of square meters. The museum's founder, Viktor Korsak, described the damage inflicted upon the panel "The Future" as a "symbolic and at the same time terrifying coincidence."
The museum was damaged in a fire caused by a Russian drone attack against Lutsk on Oct. 13, the staff said.
"Now the war itself has intervened in a work about the future. And I wonder: perhaps we should not fully restore the damaged section? Perhaps these traces of war should remain as a historical artifact and a warning to future generations? But the most important thing is that we continue to create!" Korsak wrote.
Established in 2018, the Korsak Museum is the country's largest museum of contemporary Ukrainian art. The museum has received international recognition for its curatorial work, including a Special Commendation at the 2025 European Museum of the Year Awards.
Although the Oct. 13 attack damaged part of the collection, Roman Korsak, Viktor's son and the museum's owner, told the Kyiv Independent that the museum continues to operate. 
"We know the collection remains at risk. But we believe the greater loss would be to hide art away from people and close our doors at such a difficult time," Korsak said. 
Ukraine's cultural heritage has long been a target of Russian aggression. The Culture Ministry reported that, as of September 2026, Russia has damaged or destroyed at least 2,161 cultural heritage sites and 2,665 cultural institutions since the start of the full-scale war. 
Tens of thousands of artworks are also estimated to have been looted by Russia from Ukraine's museums in the occupied territories and active combat zones.
Russia attacked Ukraine's northwest again on Oct. 14, exacting a deadly toll: at least six people were killed and 20 injured in Volyn Oblast, including Lutsk, and in neighboring Rivne Oblast.

Holidays remain a ‘spending priority’, but ‘cost-conscious’ travel is on the rise, report reveals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:26:24 UTC
22:26:24 KST

Travellers are planning on booking cheaper accommodation and eating out less while away, rather than giving up holidays completely.
It has been quite the year for the travel industry, with the Middle East conflict and heatwaves causing major disruption for holidaymakers while the cost of living crisis has seen people tightening their belts.
But that hasn’t stopped people from prioritising their vacations, with 70% of adults planning to travel abroad in the next 12 months, according to ABTA’s Holiday Habits report 2026/27.
Based on polling of more than 2,000 adults based in the UK, the new research shows that holidays are still a “priority”, but that “cost-conscious” travel is on the rise.
Just 7% of people said that the cost of living crisis would mean they would not go on holiday at all next year, but 21% said they would book cheaper accommodation, and 19% would eat out less while away.
Package holidays are proving popular as a result of the cost of living crisis, with 48% of those booking one saying they were doing so as it was the best value option for the price, up from 43% last year.
While the percentage of people who took a cruise in 2026 is stable (13%), the percentage of people planning to do so next year is rising (17%), and the reasons for doing so are reflecting the need for cost-conscious trips.
Some of the main reasons cited for booking a cruise are value for money (52%, up from 49%) and being able to pay for everything up front (40%, up from 38%).
“We continue to love our holidays and the desire to travel remains strong; this looks set to continue despite the ease of getting away, for some, being affected by geopolitical and economic challenges,” Mark Tanzer, chief executive of ABTA – The Travel Association, said.
“When times are uncertain, booking with an expert ABTA member gives holidaymakers added confidence. And, in a ‘value for money’ market, they are excellently placed to find people a fantastic holiday at a budget that works for them.”
City breaks overtake beach escapes
City breaks were the most popular holiday type in the last 12 months for UK travellers, with 53% of those polled going on one, up from 48% last year, while 49% of people went on a beach break.
Of those surveyed, the third most popular type was a countryside break (23%), followed by a multi-destination trip (16%), adventure holiday (14%), cruise (13%), lake and mountains (10%), and wellness (9%).
Europe remained the most popular choice for holidays, with certain destinations seeing an uptick in visitors as people avoided the Middle East or avoided travelling via the region.
For Brits, the top country over the past 12 months was Spain, with 36% of those surveyed having visited.
Portugal overtook Germany as the sixth most visited destination, behind France (24%), Italy (15%), the US (14%) and Greece (12%), with 11% having visited.
The top 10 was rounded out by Türkiye, Australia and Cyprus.

How AI apps are offering free substitutes for Big Tech software
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:25:35 UTC
22:25:35 KST

How AI apps are offering free substitutes for Big Tech software
AI-developed ArtCraft is challenging Adobe after disrupting legacy software’s economic model.
As AI development rapidly expands, people are replicating paid-for desktop and mobile apps with free apps, potentially changing the future of legacy software.
Last week, a Reddit user named Brandon Thomas shared a project called “ArtCraft” – essentially a free rebuild of the Adobe Creative Suite, which includes programmes such as Photoshop and Adobe PDF. The recreated services have been named PhotoCraft and PdfCraft.
This software package usually costs individuals $779.99 per year if paid upfront or $69.99 per month on an annual contract.
Earlier this week, ArtCraft also released copies of the Microsoft Office suite.
As with the Adobe package, ArtCraft has announced WordCraft, DeckCraft, and GridCraft, taking on Microsoft Word, PowerPoint, and Excel. While the software engineer behind the new packages is based in the United States, the programmes are available worldwide.
Here’s what we know:
Who is Brandon Thomas and what did he do?
Reddit user “u/ai_art_is_art”, the person behind ArtCraft, has been revealed as Atlanta, US-based software engineer Brandon Thomas.
Using AI platform Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 and Rust software, Thomas said he was able to reverse engineer Adobe’s creative suite.
Announcing his project on Reddit, Thomas said that this is not a “one-off flash in the pan that will die”.
“I’m not just some casual vibe coder. I’m a 15-year industry veteran who has written everything from six-nines payment rails that move billions of dollars of transaction volume a day to advanced robotics and optics automation. I’ve used Rust extensively for about a decade, and I know how to build and maintain large-scale Rust projects,” he said.
“Six-nines payment rails” refers to online payment infrastructure which provides 99.9999 percent operational availability, while Rust is a programming language.
Thomas said he had become fed up with being hit with cancellation fees on software products and wanted others to be able to access them for free.
He wrote on the social media and news site, Hacker News: “We’ll replace Google Search, we’ll build our own smartphones, we’ll build better infra. We’ll remove all the ads and de-enshi**ify the entire tech world.”
What is ‘vibe coding’ and how common is it for app development?
While Thomas denies he is “just some vibe coder”, vibe coding is at least partly what he has done.
Vibe coding is a new term in software development which refers to prompting AI tools to generate code rather than writing it manually. This means that people who do not have technical knowledge of programming can describe an idea to an AI tool and have it create it for them.
According to the IBM technology company, vibe coding is a “shift toward intent-driven software development, where AI systems assist developers by generating code from natural language instructions”.
The phrase was introduced by computer scientist and OpenAI cofounder Andrej Karpathy in February 2025, who wrote on X that AI users could “fully give in to the vibes, embrace exponentials, and forget that the code even exists”.
Vibe coding has become more common as AI has taken off and new apps have flooded Apple’s App Store.
The New York Times reported that Sensor Tower, a global market intelligence and digital analytics platform, estimates that new apps doubled in the first half of this year to about 560,000.
Are there copyright concerns?
There is a legal grey area around replicating software which has already been established without infringing on intellectual property.
On Reddit, Thomas described his Adobe-similar apps as “clean-room” replacements, meaning that they were built from scratch from publicly available file-format specifications, rather than from Adobe’s proprietary source code.
However, there is still little information about how much of the code Claude wrote and how much Thomas wrote, according to Technollama, a blog written by Professor Andres Guadamuz, a reader in intellectual property law at the University of Sussex.
“We also do not know whether the claimed ‘clean-room process’ stands up to scrutiny,” he said.
Could AI coding kill legacy software?
Possibly.
The downfall of legacy software is unlikely to make apps like Adobe Creative Cloud or Microsoft completely obsolete, but it could make them far less profitable if there are free-to-use substitutes available.

Scandinavian government leaders criticise Trump–Putin diesel deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14

Government representatives in Sweden, Denmark and Norway have criticised US President Donald Trump’s announced agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Russian diesel supplies. Their central concern is that additional revenue for Moscow could help finance its war against Ukraine, weakening allied efforts to increase economic pressure on Russia.
On 9 October, Trump announced that, following talks with Putin, Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tonnes of diesel to US and global markets. The US president presented the agreement as a way to reduce fuel prices. The announcement came ahead of the US congressional midterm elections on 3 November.
Sweden: Energy Revenues Sustain Russia’s War Chest
Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson expressed regret over the US agreement with Russia on 10 October. According to Swedish media outlet EFN, the prime minister emphasised in a post on X that energy revenues play a central role in financing Russia’s war.
Kristersson said Sweden’s position had remained unchanged since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine: support for Ukraine must continue for as long as necessary. He argued that pressure on Russia should increase, alongside stronger assistance for Ukraine. The prime minister pointed to further EU sanctions targeting Russia’s military industry as one means of achieving this.
Denmark: Sanctions Must Not Be Undermined
Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen warned that additional Russian revenue generated by the agreement could ultimately finance the war in Ukraine.
Speaking to Danish public broadcaster DR, Rasmussen stressed that the EU had invested considerable effort in imposing tough sanctions and reducing dependence on Russian energy. Those efforts must not be undermined, news agency Ritzau reported.
Rasmussen reaffirmed Denmark’s commitment to maintaining economic pressure on Russia and supporting Ukraine together with its partners.
Norway: US Decision Moves in the Opposite Direction
Norwegian Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide described the agreement as a step in the opposite direction to the policy pursued by Norway and its allies.
Aftenposten reported on 10 October that Eide had emphasised the need to increase economic pressure on Moscow to weaken Russia’s ability to continue the war. In his assessment, the US decision to permit Russian diesel supplies does not advance that objective.
A common position runs through the three governments’ responses: efforts to lower fuel prices should not weaken pressure on Russia or undermine support for Ukraine. Sweden and Denmark explicitly reaffirmed their existing policies, while Norway highlighted the contradiction between the US decision and allied efforts to restrict financing for Russia’s war.

Gold prices fell below $4,100 an ounce on Wednesday after stronger-than-expected US inflation data fueled expectations of more Federal Reserve interest rate hikes.
Gold traded at $4,094.57 an ounce, down 1.61% as of 1310GMT, its lowest level since early August. Silver also declined sharply, falling 3.9% to $59.80 an ounce.
US annual consumer inflation accelerated to 3.7% in September, exceeding market expectations of 3.6%, with higher energy prices driving the increase.
Consumer prices rose 0.6% month-on-month, their biggest increase in five months. Core inflation, which excludes food and energy, also exceeded expectations, reaching 2.6% annually and 0.3% monthly.
The figures prompted investors to reassess the Fed's interest rate outlook, weighing on precious metals, which offer no interest income and tend to become less attractive when borrowing costs rise.
Markets priced in around a 50% probability that the Fed would leave rates unchanged at its October meeting, down from more than 78% before the inflation report.
The probability of a December rate hike rose to nearly 99%, compared with 88% previously.
Although recent Fed communications had offered little indication of consecutive rate increases in October, the stronger-than-expected core inflation reading brought that possibility back into focus.

Bushehr: Where Iran’s history meets the Persian Gulf
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:23:25 UTC
22:23:25 KST

Bushehr: Where Iran’s history meets the Persian Gulf
TEHRAN - On Iran’s southern coast, where the Zagros Mountains descend toward the Persian Gulf, Bushehr offers a distinctive blend of history, architecture, nature and living traditions. The sea has shaped almost every aspect of life here, from trade and fishing to cuisine, music and the design of traditional houses.
The provincial capital, Bandar-e Bushehr, occupies a peninsula extending into the Persian Gulf. Its historic neighborhoods, shaded alleys, merchant mansions and waterfront reflect a time when the port connected Iran with trading networks across the Persian Gulf and the Indian Ocean. Beyond the city, the province unfolds into a varied landscape of archaeological sites, date-palm plantations, mountain villages, sandy beaches and unusual geological formations.
For travelers interested in Iran beyond its better-known destinations, Bushehr offers an opportunity to discover a region whose identity has been shaped by maritime exchange, ancient civilizations and the resourcefulness of coastal communities.
A port shaped by history
Bushehr’s strategic position has made it an important center of settlement and commerce for centuries. Archaeological evidence points to human activity in the region during different historical periods, including the Elamite, Achaemenid, Parthian and Sassanian eras.
The port regained prominence during the Afsharid period and developed further under the Zand and Qajar dynasties. Its maritime connections attracted merchants, travelers and foreign commercial interests, bringing wealth and cultural influences to the southern Iranian coast.
The wider province also contains archaeological remains associated with ancient Iranian kingdoms. Ruins of palaces and settlements in Dashtestan, along with historic sites scattered across the region, demonstrate that Bushehr’s significance extends well beyond its more recent commercial history.
Bushehr province was formally established in 1973. Today, it combines a busy industrial and commercial economy with a heritage that remains visible in its historic towns, coastal villages and archaeological landscapes.
The old city, architecture adapted to the heat
One of the best ways to understand Bushehr is to walk through its historic urban quarter, a district of traditional houses, merchant mansions, courtyards and narrow lanes.
The old city includes four principal neighborhoods: Behbahani, Kuti, Dehdashti and Shanbadi. The area flourished particularly during the Zand and Qajar periods, when the port played an important role in maritime commerce.
Its architecture reflects generations of adaptation to the hot, humid coastal climate. Traditional builders used materials such as stone, timber, lime and stucco, arranging buildings to provide shade and encourage air circulation. Narrow streets, internal courtyards, wooden shutters and shaded balconies helped make everyday life more comfortable under the southern sun.
Walking through the old quarter reveals how these features work together. Weathered balconies overlook narrow alleys, traditional doors open onto courtyards, and old residences stand alongside shops and cafés. The neighborhood is not simply an architectural attraction but a record of the relationship between the port’s inhabitants and their environment.
Historic mansions and maritime heritage
Several buildings offer a closer look at the prosperity and international connections that once characterized Bushehr.
For instance, the Malek Mansion, one of the city’s best-known landmarks, is associated with Mohammad Malek ol-Tojjar, a wealthy merchant. Built during the Qajar period, the large complex features balconies, columns, spacious interiors and elaborate wooden doors. Its design reflects local architectural traditions alongside influences that circulated through Bushehr’s international commercial connections. The mansion later served different purposes, including military accommodation, and has undergone restoration.
The Dehdashti Mansion, also known as the Oil Edifice, is another prominent historic property. The Taheri Mansion, formerly called Amiriyeh Mansion, now houses an ethnographic museum that introduces visitors to local occupations, domestic life, handicrafts and maritime traditions.
Other attractions include Golshan House, Tabib Mansion, the Qavam Water Reservoir, St. George’s Church, the English cemetery and the Maritime Museum of the Sea and the Persian Gulf. Together, they reveal different aspects of life in a port shaped by trade, religious diversity, water scarcity and contact with other cultures.
The historic market provides another glimpse into everyday life. Visitors can browse local food products, handicrafts and household goods while observing the commercial traditions that remain part of the city’s character.
Tangestan: A legacy of resistance
Bushehr’s history is also associated with resistance to foreign intervention. In Tangestan, the name of Rais Ali Delvari remains closely linked to the struggle against British forces during World War I.
Delvari, a local leader who mobilized fighters in southern Iran, became a symbol of resistance and the defense of national independence. His former home in Delvar, a coastal settlement near Bushehr, has been converted into a museum, preserving objects and accounts associated with the resistance movement and local life.
Tangestan offers other attractions, including historic castles, traditional qanats and the Tal-e Kushk site in Shahrabad. The Qucherak hot springs near Ahram provide a different reason to explore the area.
Combining these sites with coastal excursions offers travelers a broader understanding of a region whose history encompasses commerce, agriculture and political struggle.
Dashtestan: Palaces, caves and palm groves
East of Bushehr, Dashtestan offers a landscape where archaeological remains and date-palm plantations stretch across the plains.
Borazjan, the county’s main urban center, is known for its date production and its position along routes linking the coast with inland Iran. The surrounding area contains the ruins of the Black Bardak Palace near Dorudgah village and remains traditionally associated with the Great Cyrus Palace southeast of Borazjan.
The Chehel-Khaneh Caves near Sadabad are another notable attraction. Rock-cut chambers and openings in the cliffs create a striking landscape whose original functions and historical associations invite further exploration.
Date palms are central to the region’s economy and food culture. Their cultivation supports local livelihoods, while fresh and dried dates, date syrup and sweets made from date paste feature prominently in the province’s markets and kitchens.
Siraf, a window onto the maritime world
Further southeast along the coast, the historic port of Siraf offers one of Bushehr Province’s most compelling links to the wider history of the Persian Gulf.
Siraf flourished as a maritime trading center during the Sassanian and early Islamic periods. Its merchants participated in commercial networks connecting Iran with the Arabian Peninsula, India, East Africa and China. Goods, people and ideas passed through the port, helping establish its reputation as a center of maritime exchange.
Today, archaeological remains include ancient wells, rock-cut tombs, traces of historic buildings and remnants of settlements extending toward the surrounding hills. The combination of ruins, rugged terrain and sea gives Siraf a distinctive atmosphere.
Its history also reflects the vulnerabilities of coastal settlements. Earthquakes and other changes contributed to the decline of the historic port, leaving parts of its former urban landscape scattered across the area.
Unlike a single monumental complex, Siraf reveals its history gradually, through the relationship between the archaeological remains, the hills and the shoreline.
Jashak Salt Dome and coastal nature
Bushehr’s attractions extend beyond historic settlements. Inland, the Jashak Salt Dome, between Dashti and Deyr, offers a dramatic contrast to the blue waters of the Persian Gulf.
Part of the southern Zagros geological landscape, the formation features white salt surfaces, colored mineral bands, caves and unusual erosion patterns. Some formations resemble glaciers or waterfalls, although they are shaped by salt and water rather than ice. Shades of white, orange, yellow and gray create a striking natural spectacle.
The terrain can be difficult to navigate, particularly in hot weather. Visitors should arrange suitable transport and guidance, carry sufficient drinking water and avoid exposed areas during the hottest hours.
Another important natural destination is Nayband National Sea Park, near Asaluyeh. Its coastal habitats, beaches, marine environments and mangrove ecosystems support wildlife, including migratory birds and marine species. The protected area offers opportunities for nature-based tourism, provided visitors respect its sensitive habitats.
Ganaveh combines a lively commercial atmosphere with coastal scenery. Its large market attracts shoppers from across Iran, while its beaches offer space for seaside walks and relaxation. In Jam, gardens, mountain landscapes and historic water infrastructure provide further opportunities for travelers exploring the province beyond the main port.
Music, handicrafts and local traditions
Music is an essential part of Bushehr’s cultural identity. Local traditions accompany celebrations, social gatherings, work and religious ceremonies, reflecting the region’s varied cultural influences and maritime connections.
The neyanban, a bagpipe-like instrument, is closely associated with regional music. Percussion instruments such as the damam and senj play prominent roles in mourning ceremonies, where rhythmic performances accompany traditional forms of lamentation.
Bushehr’s handicrafts also reflect its natural environment. Palm leaves are woven into mats, baskets, brooms and other household items, while shells are used to create jewelry and decorative objects. Carpet and kilim weaving, gabbeh production, pottery and boatbuilding contribute to the province’s craft heritage.
The flavors of the Persian Gulf
Seafood is at the heart of Bushehr’s cuisine. Fish and shrimp are prepared with aromatic herbs, garlic, tamarind and spices, often producing the bold, tangy flavors associated with southern Iranian cooking.
Among the best-known dishes are ghalieh mahi, a spicy fish stew, and ghalieh meygoo, prepared with shrimp. Both are commonly served with rice. Other local specialties include steamed fish, lakh-lakh, a rice dish cooked with fish and seasonings, and fish tah-andaz, in which fish forms a flavorful layer beneath the rice.
For a meat-free option, yatimak combines eggplant, beans, onion and seasonings. Bushehri variations of traditional Iranian stews and lentil dishes offer further tastes of local home cooking.
Dates are equally important. Fresh dates, dried dates, date syrup and sweets made from date paste are widely available. Ranginak, a dessert made with dates and other ingredients, and date halva are among the treats visitors should look for. Local pickles, herbs, date bread and palm-derived products also make distinctive souvenirs.
Traditional restaurants and local eateries are good places to sample these dishes, while markets offer opportunities to discover regional ingredients and handicrafts.
When to visit
Bushehr has hot summers, with high humidity along much of the coast. Temperatures can exceed 50 degrees Celsius on exceptionally hot summer days, making autumn, winter and early spring the most comfortable seasons for sightseeing.
The cooler months are well suited to walking through the historic quarter, exploring archaeological sites and visiting coastal communities. Excursions to Jashak Salt Dome and other remote areas require advance planning, appropriate transport and attention to weather conditions.
Accommodation ranges from hotels and guesthouses to locally run houses and ecotourism lodgings. Staying in traditional or locally operated accommodation can provide opportunities to experience regional food, hospitality and everyday customs. Travelers should confirm current availability and access arrangements before visiting individual attractions.

4,700-year-old amphorae discovered near Türkiye's Kekova Island
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:23:05 UTC
22:23:05 KST

Ozcan Yildirim and Halis Sunnetci
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Culture and Tourism Minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy announced on Wednesday that underwater excavations near Kekova Island in Türkiye's southern Antalya province uncovered amphorae dating back 4,700 years.
Ersoy shared details of the discovery on social media, describing the site as the world's oldest shipwreck.
"In the Blue Homeland, we are bringing to light the traces of the world's oldest shipwreck," he said.
The ancient vessels, believed to have transported olive oil or wine, provide evidence of maritime trade and cultural exchange across the Eastern Mediterranean, according to Ersoy.
Clay analyses suggest the amphorae may have been produced in workshops in the Jordan Valley, while similar examples discovered in Egypt, Troy and Crete point to extensive ancient maritime trade networks, he said.
Ersoy highlighted one amphora featuring nine distinct markings and two holes in its body.
The vessel, believed to have been used as a churn for making cheese or butter, could offer clues about whether ancient seafarers produced food during long voyages, he added.
The minister said Türkiye would continue uncovering Anatolia's maritime history while preserving underwater cultural heritage for future generations.

Iran says container ship sank after striking naval mine in Strait of Hormuz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:21:28 UTC
22:21:28 KST

Mohammad Sio and Ikram Kouachi
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said Wednesday that a ship carrying more than 2,500 containers sank after striking a naval mine while attempting to cross the Strait of Hormuz through “an unauthorized” route.
In a statement carried by Iranian state broadcaster IRIB, the IRGC Navy said the vessel struck a mine and caught fire while attempting to navigate “a dangerous and unauthorized” passage through the strategic waterway.
The ship sank in waters south of the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday morning after the fire intensified, the statement said.
The IRGC Navy urged local vessels and fishermen to exercise extreme caution when navigating the area, warning that containers from the sunken ship were floating on the water's surface.
The statement did not identify the vessel, its flag or operator, or provide details on the fate of its crew.
String of maritime incidents
The reported sinking came amid a series of maritime incidents in the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has imposed restrictions on commercial shipping, including designated transit routes and requirements for prior authorization from the IRGC Navy.
The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported on Wednesday two incidents from the previous day in which container ships were struck by unidentified projectiles in the Strait of Hormuz.
It said in a statement that a 50,000-ton vessel conducting an inbound transit, was struck at 1640UTC, while the other, a 19,000-ton vessel conducting an outbound transit, was hit at 1700UTC.
Both vessels reported minor damage and no casualties and were able to continue their passages, according to the agency.
Earlier this week, the IRGC Navy reported that several oil tankers had struck naval mines or come under attack while attempting to navigate unauthorized routes through the waterway.
Since April, Iran has imposed restrictions on maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, including designated transit routes and a requirement for prior coordination with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy.
On May 30, Tehran announced that vessels passing through the strait would be required to obtain prior authorization from the IRGC Navy, warning that transit without permission would constitute a “security threat.”
The developments come amid continued tensions between Iran and the US over navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most important strategic routes for energy and commodity supplies and a key issue in negotiations between the two sides.
The war began with US and Israeli attacks on Iran on Feb. 28, before a ceasefire was reached in April. Clashes between Washington and Tehran later resumed as negotiations stalled despite the two sides signing a framework agreement in June.

Planned capacity of 12,000 interceptors a year, under 100 seconds to target: US firm pitches a low-cost drone killer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:21:17 UTC
22:21:17 KST

US defense-tech company CHAOS Industries introduced its Vespid interceptor family in Washington on 12 October, as the Association of the US Army (AUSA) annual meeting opened there, the company announced. CHAOS pitches the drones as low-cost defense against small and mid-size drones and one-way attack munitions. The company expects initial production capacity of 12,000 interceptors a year, expandable to 50,000 as demand grows.
The pitch lands as Russia moves its strike drones to jet power. Russia has stopped building the Geran-3, an earlier jet model, and makes about 3,000 faster Geran-4s and Geran-5s a month, Ukraine’s military intelligence (HUR) told Militarnyi in August. In mid-September, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said two Ukrainian companies had passed combat tests with interceptors against such drones, while 67 were still working on them. Ukrainian defense outlet Defense Express measured the new US drones against exactly that threat.
One to carry, one to launch in batches
The Mk 1 made its first public appearance on 12 October aboard a Forterra MESA autonomous ground vehicle, Army Recognition reported. It fires from tubes on launchers such as the 10-round ISS Aerospace HAL10. It takes midcourse guidance from CHAOS radars or external command systems, then an AI-assisted infrared seeker handles the final approach, the company says. An electric ducted fan rather than a jet engine drives it, which CHAOS says cuts cost and logistics compared with turbojet interceptors.
The smaller Mk 0 is man-portable and needs no operator input once fired, its product page says. Both are rated to reach a target in under 100 seconds, with a listed range of 10+ km. Defense Express called that range a serious weakness that more launchers around a city could offset.
Most drone interceptors ram or explode. This Ukrainian one just throws a net—six shots to a module
CHAOS lists cruise speeds of 100 m/s (360 km/h) for the Mk 0 and 150 m/s (540 km/h) for the Mk 1. Defense Express said those speeds may be enough to intercept the Geran-4 and Geran-5, which it puts at 340 km/h and 450–600 km/h.
Ukrainian makers say their interceptors already down jet Gerans
Wild Hornets’ Sting interceptors downed several of the slower jet-powered Geran-3s in November 2025. An unnamed Wild Hornets representative told NV, in an interview published on 22 September, that the company’s new interceptor had destroyed about ten Geran-4s and several Geran-5s in limited use. The company plans mass production within a month of finishing combat tests.
On 12 October, former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov said he and Pavlo Yelizarov, commander of Lasar’s Group, had created a new interceptor with troops and engineers. He said it downed two Geran-5s headed for Kyiv.
Crews from Lasar’s Group, which Fedorov has called a National Guard special unit, flew those combat tests, he said. Separately, Fedorov reported in August that a Ukrainian jet interceptor with a top speed above 600 km/h had entered combat testing.

NATO may eventually have to shoot down missiles over western Ukraine – former Polish security chief
Former Head of Poland’s National Security Bureau Stanisław Koziej said this in an interview with Ukrinform, answering a question about whether NATO countries would eventually be able to agree on shooting down missiles over western Ukraine.
According to Koziej, he has been proposing for the past two or three years that NATO establish what is known as an advanced missile defense zone, which would provide for the interception of at least dual-purpose missiles, including those capable of carrying nuclear warheads.
Koziej acknowledged that reaching consensus within the Alliance on such an initiative would be difficult. At the same time, he believes that further escalation of Russian aggression and an increase in the number of aerial incidents could force NATO to take this step.
Koziej separately emphasized the need to deepen security cooperation between Poland and Ukraine.
“We need to be as close to each other as possible. We should put political and emotional disputes aside as soon as possible and move toward pragmatic cooperation in the security sphere, especially along the border,” he said.
According to the former head of Poland’s National Security Bureau, the two countries need to exchange information about drones and missiles in order to respond to threats in advance. He also stressed the importance of ensuring an uninterrupted supply of aid to Ukraine and urged that historical disputes not be allowed to obstruct efforts to address urgent security issues.
Koziej described Russian disinformation as one of the problems that Poland currently finds most difficult to counter. At the same time, he said Poland is beginning to pool efforts in this area, including by establishing a special center to counter disinformation.
He expressed hope that the center’s work would help develop a strategy to protect society from Russian manipulation aimed at exacerbating divisions between Poles and Ukrainians.
As Ukrinform reported, unidentified debris was found on a beach in Karwia, Pomeranian Voivodeship, Poland. Preliminary findings indicate that it may be drone debris, but the type of object has not yet been established.

Finnish cities pushing for mandatory school attendance law
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:18:17 EEST
22:18:17 KST

Helsinki and five other Finnish cities are calling for stricter laws on homeschooling.
According to Helsinki Mayor Daniel Sazonov (NCP), homeschooling should only be allowed in exceptional cases, for example for health reasons.
In practice, the cities are proposing that in-school attendance should be compulsory.
"Going to school is much more than just learning defined academic content, it is also a social process," Sazonov said.
Attending school is also a tool for integration, according to the mayor.
"In Helsinki, many pupils speak a language other than Finnish or Swedish as their mother tongue; it is also essential from an integration perspective that they are at school and part of the school community," he said.
Homeschooling is not a widespread phenomenon in the capital. Just over 200 children in Helsinki were being home-schooled this year, accounting for about 0.4 percent of all pupils. The number has increased in recent years, however.
A total of around 1,000 children in Finland are home-schooled, with many choosing the option for health or wellbeing reasons.
Last week, the Helsinki City Council decided to tighten supervision of homeschooled pupils.
Supervision abilities limited
But according to Sazonov, the jurisdiction of municipalities regarding homeschooling is limited.
Not all home-school instructors have accepted more active supervision, Sazonov said.
He noted that there have been no major problems with homeschooling in Helsinki. However, he did point to concerns raised by the Finnish Security and Intelligence Service (Supo) that homeschooling can carry the risk of promoting radicalisation.
Supo's national security review suggested that homeschooling could, over time, heighten security risks linked to social fragmentation. Its report warns that isolated educational settings may enable the spread of extremist ideologies, including radical Islamist or far-right teachings.
Helsinki University terrorism researcher Leena Malkki noted that Finland should not close its eyes to these concerns.
"Finland is a society built on trust. Supervision, and even support, is not always the strictest when it comes to home schooling," she said.
Tampere is among the cities calling for educational law change. But according to Tampere Deputy Mayor for cultural services, Anne-Mari Jussila, radicalisation risks are not the reason.
"I would prefer to see children among their peers at school, learning together with other children," she said.
Tampere currently has about 50 home-school pupils.
Jussila emphasised that radicalisation is not a problem in Tampere, even though it may be a problem elsewhere.
Newspaper Helsingin Sanomat on Tuesday queried parliamentary groups regarding homeschooling.
Left Alliance leader Minja Koskela told HS that Finland needs to introduce mandatory school attendance, arguing every child has the right to education.
Some Swedes have moved to the Åland Islands, attracted by the option of homeschooling.
