Iraq’s PM tells Saudi crown prince Iraqi territory will not be used for attacks
Saudi Arabia’s East-West oil pipeline was struck by drones last month in an attack that originated in Iraq.
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Faleh al-Zaidi has assured Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) that he will not allow Iraqi territory to be used to launch attacks against Saudi Arabia, the Iraqi News Agency (INA) has reported.
Al-Zaidi arrived in Riyadh on Wednesday for his first visit to the kingdom since taking office in May.
He also said he would not allow attacks against other regional countries to be launched from Iraq.
“Iraq’s firm position is not to allow its territory to be used as a launching pad for any attacks or actions that affect the security of the kingdom and the countries of the region, and to be keen on adhering to the principles of good neighbourliness and respecting the sovereignty of Iraq and brotherly and friendly countries,” Al-Zaidi’s office said in a statement, cited by INA.
Saudi Arabia’s East-West oil pipeline was struck by drones last month during the Houthis’ lightning offensive in Yemen.
The attack forced Riyadh to temporarily shut down the export route, which Saudi Arabia has used as an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz.
The pipeline, which has a maximum capacity of seven million barrels per day, has since resumed operations.
Saudi Arabia said the drone attack originated in Iraq. Baghdad conducted its own investigation and concluded that the strikes were launched from Iraqi territory.
There was no claim of responsibility for the attack, but Iraq is home to numerous Iran-backed armed groups.

Netherlands denies visas to 3 Russian athletes, barring them from world championships
Dutch authorities refused to grant visas to three Russian gymnasts, preventing them from taking part in world gymnastics championships held in Rotterdam later this month, the Russian Gymnastics Federation said on Oct. 13.
Angelina Melnikova, Viktoria Listunova, and Anna Kalmykova were denied entry as "one or more Schengen area member states consider the athletes a threat to their international relations," the federation said on its Telegram channel.
Participation of Russian athletes in international competitions remains controversial and, in some sports, restricted due to Russia's ongoing full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
At the same time, Dutch authorities approved visas for five other gymnasts, the Russian Gymnastics Federation said later on Oct. 13, noting that 47 of the 61 members of the Russian delegation had been granted entry so far.
Listunova publicly expressed support for Russian aggression in Ukraine and was previously denied visas for a gymnastics competition in Croatia in August.
Melnikova has also voiced backing for Russian President Vladimir Putin and even ran as a candidate for the ruling United Russia party in local election primaries last year.
Both Melnikova and Listunova are Olympic gold medalists.
Kalmykova, in turn, holds a sports contract with the Russian National Guard, according to Kyiv.
The Russian Gymnastics Federation denounced the decision and said it would appeal to the International Olympic Committee and World Gymnastics.
Rotterdam will host the World Artistic Gymnastics Championships from Oct. 17 to 25, serving as the first stage of team qualification for the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles.
World Gymnastics imposed sanctions on Russian and Belarusian gymnasts at the outbreak of the full-scale war in 2022, but allowed them to compete as "neutral athletes" two years later.
The international association finally lifted its ban in May 2026, allowing Russian and Belarusian gymnasts to compete under their national flags, as part of a broader loosening of restrictions on Russian athletes.
Kyiv continues to urge global sports organizations to maintain sanctions against Russian and Belarusian athletes.
Russia's all-out war has taken a heavy toll on Ukraine, with hundreds of Ukrainian athletes and coaches killed and hundreds of sports facilities destroyed by Russian missile and drone attacks.

US annual inflation rises to 3.7% in September as gasoline prices surge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:47:09 UTC
21:47:09 KST

Mücahithan Avcıoğlu
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
US annual consumer inflation accelerated to 3.7% in September, exceeding market expectations of 3.6%, as surging gasoline prices drove a sharper monthly increase, official data showed Wednesday.
The annual inflation rate rose from 3.4% in August, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
On a monthly basis, the Consumer Price Index (CPI) increased 0.6% in September, up from 0.4% in August.
Gasoline prices jumped 9.1% over the month, accounting for more than half of the overall monthly increase. Energy prices rose 5.2%, accelerating from a 2.1% gain in August.
Shelter costs also contributed to price pressures, increasing 0.4% after rising 0.3% the previous month.
Food prices were unchanged overall, as a 0.1% decline in grocery prices offset a 0.2% increase in the cost of eating out. 
Core inflation also accelerates
Core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, rose to 2.6% annually in September from 2.4% in August.
Monthly core inflation remained at 0.3%.
Prices increased across several categories, including recreation, used cars and trucks, education, airline fares, and apparel.
Used vehicle prices rose 0.7% over the month, while airline fares increased 1.2% and recreation costs climbed 0.5%. Communication prices fell 0.2%.
On an annual basis, energy prices surged 20.4%, with gasoline up 34.2% and fuel oil rising 74.2%.
Electricity prices increased 4.4% from a year earlier, while natural gas prices rose 5%.
Food prices climbed 2.5% annually, and shelter costs increased 3.2%.

Clash between security personnel and protesters during Delhi protests
NEW DELHI: The Delhi Police is investigating social media handles allegedly spreading rumours and inflammatory content during protests demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation in the national capital. The probe has traced the IP address of at least one suspicious handle to Pakistan, police said on Wednesday.Sanjay Bhatia, Additional Commissioner of Police in the Delhi Police’s Intelligence Fusion and Strategic Operations (IFSO) unit said that false claims about police action against demonstrators were circulated online to create panic and provoke unrest.The Intelligence Fusion and Strategic Operations (IFSO) unit has a dedicated cyber patrolling team to monitor such content and verify its authenticity, Bhatia told ANI, outlining the police's response to misleading posts."Delhi Police’s IFSO unit has a dedicated cyber patrolling team that monitors such posts to verify their authenticity and compliance with legal provisions. If we find a post to be factually incorrect, false, a rumor, a threat to public order, defamatory, or likely to incite anarchy, we take action in accordance with the law," he said.Bhatia said the investigation into the Pakistan-linked account was ongoing, along with other cases registered over social media content.
"When we sought registration details for one such specific handle, the IP address traced back to Pakistan; we are currently investigating that case. The process is ongoing, and we have registered other cases as well; investigations are underway, and we will share further details and evidence with you as they emerge," he said.Giving details of a post that allegedly claimed police were firing at demonstrators, Bhatia said the claim was false and could have heightened tensions."We found a post intended to incite chaos; the handle registered in Pakistan."He further claimed that the handle alleged that the police were opening fire on the demonstrators. "It was a deliberate attempt to whip up a volatile atmosphere based on falsehoods. Since the claim was untrue, we immediately requested the post's removal and registered a case; further action is underway," he said.
The Delhi Police had also recently debunked a viral social media video claiming that Rahul Gandhi's residence had come under attack and that gunfire had been reported.According to the police, the footage was from December 2019 and was unrelated to current events. The police said legal action was being initiated against accounts sharing the misleading content and urged users not to circulate unverified videos.
The investigation comes amid police action against three Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) activists over alleged attempts to disturb public peace and instigate others through social media. Sourav Das and Ashutosh Ranka were remanded to five days of judicial custody, while Ajinkya Shinde was bound down for six months to maintain peace and good behaviour.According to a Delhi Police statement, the action followed an incident on October 13 in which the three activists and 11 other CJP members allegedly entered the denotified Jantar Mantar protest site through private premises and obstructed police personnel. CJP has maintained that it will continue to demand the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and challenge the denotification of Jantar Mantar.

Israel has occupied most of Syria’s Golan Heights since 1967. Following the fall of Bashar al-Assad’s regime in December 2024, Israeli forces expanded their presence into the demilitarized buffer zone and other positions in southern Syria.
Damascus has repeatedly demanded Israel’s withdrawal from Syrian territory and reaffirmed its commitment to the 1974 Disengagement Agreement, which established a UN-monitored buffer zone between the two sides.

Rising oil prices are not saving russia’s budget from falling revenues - intelligence
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:42:41 EEST
21:42:41 KST

Rising oil prices are not saving russia’s budget from falling revenues - intelligence
Kyiv • UNN
In September, russia’s budget received only $5.28 billion in oil and gas revenues, down 22.3% year-on-year. Compensation payments to oil companies reached $25.7 billion.
The sharp rise in oil prices in September did not bring a corresponding increase in revenues for the Russian budget. The Kremlin is forced to return a significant portion of the taxes collected to oil companies, compensating them for the costs of supporting the domestic fuel market. This was reported by the Foreign Intelligence Service, UNN writes.
In September, gross receipts from oil and gas taxes amounted to about $10.16 billion. After compensation payments and tax deductions, only $5.28 billion reached the budget—22.3% less than in the same month of 2025. The state effectively returned nearly half of the funds collected to the sector
The largest increase was in fuel damper payments, from $2.30 billion in August to $3.56 billion in September. This was 55% more than the previous month and the largest amount since April 2022.
As the intelligence service notes, high oil prices only increase the amount of such compensation payments. The more profitable it is to sell oil on foreign markets, the greater the difference from domestic prices, which the state compensates fuel producers for.
The situation is worsened by declining refined-products production. Due to the fuel shortage, the Kremlin is restricting fuel exports and increasing imports. In August–September, seaborne deliveries of oil products to the Russian Federation amounted to about 350,000–370,000 tonnes per month. Compensation was also extended to imported fuel, shifting additional costs onto the federal budget.
From January through September, the Russian Federation’s oil and gas revenues fell by 17.2% year-on-year, to $63.82 billion. At the same time, oil companies received about $25.7 billion in compensation.
Against this backdrop, Russia’s Finance Ministry lowered its forecast for oil and gas revenues in 2026 to $88.4 billion—14.5% below its previous estimate. In the first nine months, the budget received about 72% of the new annual plan.
For the Russian budget, the problem is no longer only the price of oil. Declining refining and fuel shortages are forcing the Kremlin to spend increasingly more money on maintaining the domestic market. If disruptions at oil refineries continue, high oil prices will not offset these costs, and the oil and gas sector will remain a source of increasingly weaker budget revenues

Kremlin comments on restrictions on Ukraine’s access to Starlink, settlement process

Unknown Publisher

21:41:49 KST

MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. Reports about restrictions on Ukraine’s access to Starlink, the settlement process and the potential weaponization of artificial intelligence were among the main topics of the October 14 briefing by Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov.
TASS has compiled the Kremlin spokesman’s key statements.
On Ukrainian settlement
- Moscow has taken note of the risk that Europe could sabotage agreements on resolving the Ukraine conflict: "The risk of sabotage by European countries does exist."
- Unlike European countries, the US is working to steer the Ukrainian crisis toward a peaceful settlement: "The US, specifically its negotiators and President [Donald] Trump, is making efforts to help steer the settlement of the Ukrainian crisis toward peace."
- European countries, unlike the United States, which is seeking a peaceful solution, are doing everything they can to prolong the hostilities in Ukraine: "Europeans are taking a different approach: they are doing everything they can to ensure that this war continues."
- There is currently a lot of "media hype" around proposals for a settlement in Ukraine, and much of this hype does not correspond to reality: "There’s a lot of media hype around all of this right now, and much of it doesn’t correspond to reality; it’s pure fiction."
- Work on the possibility of an "energy ceasefire" is continuing.
- No international meetings on the Ukraine issue have been agreed upon at present: "There are no agreed-upon meetings on the agenda."
- Efforts to resolve the Ukraine conflict continue discreetly and will remain so: "This work is ongoing discreetly and it will continue discreetly."
On restrictions on Ukrainian army’s access to Starlink
- The Kremlin has seen media reports about restrictions on the Ukrainian army’s access to the Starlink satellite internet service but has no further information: "No, we know nothing beyond the media reports that we have read about it."
- Brilliant technologies such as Starlink would be better off not being used for military purposes at all: "In general, of course, it would be better if brilliant technologies such as Starlink were not used for military purposes at all."
- It is too early to conclude that Washington has changed its approach to military support for Kiev: "It is too early to draw any systemic conclusions. We proceed from the information available from the statements that are being made."
- "We have seen numerous media reports on the matter. On the one hand, there are statements that assistance continues to be provided, while on the other, there are reports of various technical restrictions and disruptions in information supplies to Ukraine. We have been carefully recording it all."
On Russian assets
- Russia sees difficulties in recovering assets frozen by the European Union but will fight to get them back: "In any case, the Russian side will make every possible effort on all fronts, including legal work, court proceedings and litigation, to fight for the return of its stolen assets."
On detention of Japanese journalist in Russia
- The detention of a Japanese journalist on Sakhalin is evidence that Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) is carrying out its duties to identify and detain spies: "The FSB has made relevant statements [on this matter]. The Federal Security Service is carrying out its duties: if there are spies, they are caught."
On AI
- Some countries are weaponizing artificial intelligence: "Attempts by a number of countries to turn these new technologies into weapons, the so-called weaponization of artificial intelligence, pose threats to entire sectors of any country’s economy, and, of course, we are no exception."
- The technology itself remains necessary, as it brings many benefits: "Artificial intelligence technologies bring many benefits, improve efficiency and do a lot of good."
- Russia must be prepared for its use as a weapon: "We must be prepared for these challenges."

Shape of Pope Leo's papacy more uncertain after cancer diagnosis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:41:02 UTC
21:41:02 KST

Shape of Pope Leo's papacy more uncertain after cancer diagnosis
VATICAN CITY, Oct 14 - When US Cardinal Robert Prevost emerged on the balcony of St. Peter's Basilica in May 2025 as Pope Leo XIV, the new leader of the Catholic Church, he struck a stark contrast from his predecessor Francis.
Leo, young for a pope at 69, appeared energetic, spoke in a strong voice and had no known history of health issues. Francis, who died at 88, had become increasingly frail during his 12-year papacy.
With the Vatican's announcement on Tuesday that Leo, now 71, was diagnosed with lung cancer after surgeons removed part of his right lung that afternoon, the world's 1.4 billion Catholics are again unexpectedly facing the reality of a sick pope.
Leo, the first US-born pontiff, has emerged as an increasingly influential voice beyond the Church, raising alarm about the risks posed by artificial intelligence and drawing the ire of US President Donald Trump by criticising the Iran war.
The future shape of Leo's papacy — once expected to be dynamic with many foreign trips and the pope stepping into a leading moral role on the global stage — is now more uncertain. Medical experts say the pope's prognosis will depend on several factors, including whether the cancer had spread to his lymph nodes, currently unknown.
"It's too early to say how this will affect Pope Leo's agenda and his ability to carry on the duties of the papacy," John Thavis, a Vatican expert and author, told Reuters.
"If his recovery is complete and no aggressive therapy is needed, the pope may be able to carry on as usual," he said.
PLANNED SOUTH AMERICA TRIP IN QUESTION
One immediate question Leo faces is whether to proceed with an 11-day tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from November 6 to 17. The trip is known to be a high priority for the pope, who spent decades as a missionary and bishop in Peru.
The original schedule, announced last month, would have made it one of the most intense foreign trips ever undertaken by a pope, with Leo leading some 50 events and giving 36 speeches across a 10-city tour.
Dr. Stephen Liu, a lung cancer expert at Georgetown University in Washington and division chief of hematology-oncology at MedStar Georgetown University Hospital, said the trip may need to be postponed, depending on Leo's recovery.
"A trip to South America that quickly is possible, if this is an early-stage lung cancer and no further therapy is needed, but it is a tight timeline, and recovery is highly variable," said Liu.
Leo had been keeping a rapid pace of foreign travel, already making four tours in 2026 and attracting large crowds. More than 800,000 people turned out to see him in Paris last month.
'ONE DAY AT A TIME'
Catholics have often witnessed a pope deal with illness. Francis, who had part of one lung removed as a young adult, was prone to respiratory infections. He was also hospitalised as pope for colon and hernia surgeries.
John Paul II began to suffer symptoms of Parkinson's disease in the 1990s, although the Vatican only confirmed his diagnosis in 2003.
John XXIII died in 1963 from stomach cancer that was not disclosed by the Vatican until after his death.
Benedict XVI however, who succeeded John Paul, was the first pope to resign in 600 years, stepping down in 2013 after he said he no longer had the strength for the job.
The Vatican, long reticent to discuss papal health issues, has been unusually transparent in Leo's case.
The pope himself announced to pilgrims in St. Peter's Square on Sunday that a "localized nodule" had been found in his lung and he needed surgery. He also said it was detected early and was well contained.
The Vatican later provided a detailed medical bulletin hours after Leo had undergone surgery.
Another statement may be released on Wednesday afternoon, but details on the pope's prognosis are expected to take a few days as doctors perform the necessary tests.
According to the American Cancer Society, the five-year relative survival rate for non-small cell lung cancer is 67% when the disease remains confined to the lung.
Dr. Giuseppe Cardillo, chief of thoracic surgery at Rome's San Camillo Forlanini hospital, said removal of lung cancer discovered at an early stage usually results in an "excellent" prognosis.
Elise Allen, author of a biography of Leo for Penguin Peru, said people should not "jump the gun" in making conclusions about how the pope will recover.
"Let's take it one day at a time," she said. REUTERS

Switzerland plans tougher social media rules to protect youth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:40:46 UTC
21:40:46 KST

Switzerland plans tougher social media rules to protect youth
The Swiss government plans to present a bill youth protection on social media platforms and search engines in June 2027.
On Wednesday, the government took note of the results of the consultation on the Act on Communication Platforms and Search Engines. Additional measures designed to protect young people are to be added to the preliminary draft. In addition, the reporting procedure is to be extended to cover all content suspected of being unlawful.
Specifically, this concerns the regulation of internet services provided by companies such as Google, Facebook and YouTube. According to the Federal Council, the public is increasingly turning to such platforms for information. As a result, these platforms are exerting a growing influence on public debate.
The new law is intended to strengthen users’ rights and oblige providers of platforms and search engines to ensure greater transparency.
Calls for better protection of minors
With the announced expansion of youth protection, the federal government is responding to demands from the Greens, who tabled motions on this issue in parliament. The aim is to enable minors to use the internet more safely by taking account of their right to participate in public discourse.
+ Too young to scroll? Rethinking consent in the digital age
The platforms and search engines concerned will be required to analyse the extent to which their services create or exacerbate risks for minors. Furthermore, they must take measures to reduce these risks, according to a statement released on Wednesday. In addition, large platforms are to be prohibited from displaying personalised advertising to minors.
Opposition to the bill
During the consultation period, which ran from October 2025 to February 2026, 214 responses were received, according to a report on the matter. A majority supported the Federal Council’s proposal.
Several political parties including the Centre Party, the Social Democratic party and the Greens support the proposal. Twenty-two cantons are also in favour.
The cantons of Schwyz and Thurgau, as well as some political parties including the right-wing Swiss People’s Party expressed their opposition. Reasons for the rejection include concerns regarding a potential threat to freedom of expression and freedom of information.
The Federal Council has now tasked the Federal Department of the Environment, Transport, Energy and Communications (UVEK) with drafting a dispatch by the end of June 2027. Parliament will then have to decide on the proposed legislation.

French minister accuses Elon Musk of ‘online harassment campaigns’ against European leaders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:39:22 UTC
21:39:22 KST

France’s foreign minister has accused Elon Musk of using his social media platform to orchestrate “massive online harassment campaigns” against European leaders as he took aim at foreign efforts to destabilise the country before next year’s presidential election.
Speaking at an Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development conference on Tuesday, Jean-Noël Barrot pointed to the role that social media had come to play in the global battle over democracy. “The forces seeking to undermine democracy now dominate the information landscape, where they employ tactics designed to polarise public debate,” he said.
The result was that “political movements with authoritarian aims”, which “play right into the hands of democracy’s declared enemies”, had been gaining ground in Europe and North America, he said.
“They exacerbate the polarisation of our societies,” he added. “Their ultimate goal is clear: to seize power and then create the conditions to never relinquish it.”
Barrot cited the 2027 presidential election in France, where the far-right leader Marine Le Pen is the frontrunner in the polls. “The enemies of democracy are doing everything they can to destabilise us,” he said. “They exploit our divisions and use immigration, secularism and the Israeli-Palestinian conflict to stoke hatred and tensions.”
He listed several other examples, from an unnamed Israeli company accused of creating fake French social media accounts to influence perceptions of the Israel-Gaza war, to accusations that Azerbaijan stirred up tensions amid deadly riots in the French Pacific territory New Caledonia.
Barrot also singled out Musk, the world’s richest man and owner of the social media platform X. “There are massive online harassment campaigns launched by Elon Musk against European leaders in order to influence debates by exploiting the virality of his social media platform.”
Musk did not reply to a request for comment.
Barrot also cited the protests that have rocked France in recent weeks, as schoolchildren, students and trade unionists blockaded schools and marched through cities. The events, said Barrot, had been exploited by “hostile narratives” from Russia, China and Iran, as well as those associated with the Maga movement in the US.
Last week Musk and the US president, Donald Trump, weighed in on the protests in France, seeking to recast them through a lens of mass migration and brushing aside protesters’ demands for better school conditions.
Barrot said his government was working to respond to a reality in which paid or commissioned influencers sought to explore the viral reach of digital platforms. “The Kremlin’s goal is explicitly stated: to put an end to our liberal democracies in favour of a new authoritarianism. Other actors are converging on this goal, seeking to dictate to Europe which democracies are ‘good’ and which are ‘bad’ based on whether they align with their own interests,” he said.
The French minister’s remarks come days after the British prime minister, Andy Burnham, said it was “clear” that Russia had interfered in the Brexit referendum.
Barrot said his government would work to counter these efforts by foreign entities. “We are uncompromising, because it is clear to us that they undermine the nation’s fundamental interests,” he said. “We do not tolerate any foreign interference, from wherever it may come. It is a matter of sovereignty.”

Constitutional values must underpin public ethics and youth upbringing — Tokayev
Chairman of the Kazakhstan Khalyk Kenesi (People's Council), Yerlan Koshanov, made a working visit to the West Kazakhstan region, where he attended the national forum "New Public Ethics: Culture, Moral Norms, and Values," Qazinform News Agency reports.
It is the first regional event organized by the constitutional consultative body to implement presidential directives.
The dialogue platform brought together over 1,000 community leaders, proactive women, and experts.
Opening the meeting, Yerlan Koshanov read a welcome letter from President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev to the forum participants. In the letter, the Head of State congratulated forum attendees and highlighted the event's importance for continuity in national upbringing and public culture.
“The Constitution is a sacred document opening the path to our country’s prosperity and a compass defining our people's identity in a new era. Therefore, our paramount goal is to thoroughly explain the Constitution's core values and meaning to our citizens, especially the youth, and to promote its provisions broadly. In today's volatile, unstable, and challenging times, it is particularly important to instill in the public consciousness the values of a progressive and advanced nation, while honoring our thousand-year history and statehood traditions,” the welcome letter reads.
The President stressed that building a civilized and prosperous state begins with the dedicated work of society as a whole in the Motherland's interest.
“Together, we launched the nationwide Taza Qazaqstan initiative. Clean-up campaigns are underway across the country, and the profound meaning of this concept is gradually taking root in the minds of our citizens, particularly the youth. Thus, cleanliness is becoming an integral element of our national identity and an inviolable value of our people. We are building a Fair, Safe, Strong, and Clean Kazakhstan where law and order prevail, with special emphasis on education, science, and innovation. Implementing this vital mission requires active involvement not only from state institutions, but from all of society—each family, each citizen, community activists, educators, and volunteers. I am confident that the constructive proposals and new ideas voiced today will contribute to achieving these goals,” the Head of State's letter reads.
In his address, Yerlan Koshanov emphasized that the Kazakhstan Khalyk Kenesi will actively support the implementation of the President's large-scale objectives. The constitutional consultative body primarily aims to unite society around the Head of State's reforms and initiatives.
“Today’s discussion is about our Motherland, families, and future. It is a dialogue on shaping a new quality of the nation through moral standards, behavioral culture, and public ethics. Along with the Constitution, profound and meaningful changes are occurring in people's consciousness and worldview. The President wants to see every Kazakhstani as an individual who respects their native language, honors traditions, respects elders, strives for knowledge, and remains open to the world. These qualities are nurtured within the family and must be reinforced through the principles of 'Law and Order,' 'Taza Qazaqstan,' and 'Adal Azamat',” Koshanov emphasized.
The Chairman of the Kazakhstan Khalyk Kenesi also highlighted that President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s reforms over the past seven years have driven significant transformations across all spheres of the country's life. The new economic course has helped diversify the economy and strengthen social justice. Over this period, Kazakhstan’s gross domestic product grew from $181.7 billion to $306 billion, while per capita GDP increased from $9,800 to $15,000. Additionally, 25,000 km of highways have been constructed, along with 1,300 new schools, including 217 built under the Keleshek Mektepteri (Schools of the Future) project.
In recent years, at the Head of State's initiative, the country has implemented reforms unprecedented since Independence. Today, Kazakhstan is entering a new stage of development not only in economic and social life, but also in the cultural and spiritual sphere.
“These modernization processes culminated in the new People's Constitution. Alongside it, deep and crucial transformations are occurring in people’s hearts and minds. Reforms are changing our country today, while values will determine what it looks like fifty years from now. That's why the President is consistently establishing civic guidelines that must become an integral part of daily life,” Yerlan Koshanov emphasized.
During the forum, participants discussed a wide range of issues, including youth upbringing, the role of moral values in society, the development of education, and the promotion of a reading culture.
Natalya Dementyeva, a member of the Kazakhstan Khalyk Kenesi, raised the issue of improving day-to-day conditions in military units. In this regard, the constitutional consultative body plans to assess the situation across military units and establish measures for continuous improvements.
Another key topic was youth employment. Arman Tulkubayev, head of the Zhana Mumkindik Civic Association, presented experience from the JOLTAP project, which helps people learn in-demand professions and find work. The forum also discussed prospects for expanding the project to regions, including in empowering rural youth.
Discussions on upbringing and public values continued with speeches by Nazipa Shanai, Chairwoman of the National Union of Mothers and member of the Kazakhstan Khalyk Kenesi, and Snezhanna Imasheva, a Qurultay deputy.
Other forum participants addressed public ethics, women's rights protection, and fostering responsible civic awareness. Tatyana Muradyan, Chairwoman of the Council of Mothers at the Nairi Association of Armenian Cultural Centers of Kazakhstan, spoke on the role of ethics in shaping behavioral culture.
Public figure Anna Mohammad, a member of the Afghan Ethnocultural Association, shared insights on raising honest and responsible citizens. Concluding this section, Gulsim Iskaliyeva, head of the Amangeldy Rural Library, highlighted the importance of reading culture and the need to build a reading nation.
The forum served as a platform for open dialogue between the state and society, pairing discussion of the country's strategic development goals with concrete initiatives to strengthen public values, civic responsibility, and standards of behavior.
As previously reported, Vice President Erlan Karin chaired a national meeting on strengthening interethnic harmony and implementing President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev's initiatives voiced at the first session of the Kazakhstan Khalyk Kenesi.

North Kazakhstan region claimed gold in the women's team sprint with a time of 1:34.14, followed by Astana (1:35.09) and Pavlodar region (1:35.91).
In the men's team sprint, Kostanay region took first place in 1:24.10, ahead of Astana (1:24.59) and Almaty (1:27.03).

Chinese company 'helping Houthis' improve missile capabilities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:37:04 UTC
21:37:04 KST

Breadcrumb
Chinese company 'helping Houthis' improve missile capabilities as fears grow for civilians in Taiz
The Houthis are trying to manufacture their own ballistic missiles, reportedly using components delivered by a Chinese company, according to information by Conflict Armament Research seen by the Wall Street Journal.
The Iran-backed group has bought a range of parts from a Chinese supplier and is attempting to locally produce Tehran's Kheibar Shekan missile, a cheap, precision-guided projectile that can evade air defences.
The Conflict Armament Research report says the missile would have a range of around 1,200 miles, enabling the group to launch strikes across the Gulf, Israel, Jordan and most of Egypt.
This is one of the first indications that the group is pursuing an advanced indigenous weapons programme independently of Iran.
The report was based on information given by Yemeni authorities in July after officials intercepted two shipments last year.
China has also emerged as one of Iran's biggest suppliers of dual-use components during its war with the US and Israel.
Customs data has shown hundreds of shipments have been delivered to Iran's defence ministry in recent months, providing it a vital lifeline to maintain military production during the war.
Advance on Taiz
The Houthis continued to advance towards Taiz on Tuesday, capturing the western entrance to the city.
The country's third-largest city is a major stronghold of the Saudi-backed Yemeni government's and has been a battleground since the long-running conflict was reignited in September amid the US-Iran war.
A Houthi offensive last week saw the group encircle the city, severing its last remaining supply lines.
Military sources told Reuters that clashes were ongoing in al-Dabab, 10 km from Taiz, and on Sabr Mountain, which overlooks the southern edge of the city.
Yemeni warplanes targeted Houthi forces in Dabab and Misrakh south of the city, government forces said in a statement on Tuesday.
Civilian casualties in the city are also mounting as the Houthis advance closer to the city. Yemen's internationally recognised government said Houthi shelling and drone attacks on Monday were responsible for the deaths of at least six people, including a child, and the wounding of another 17 in the city.
It accused the group of shelling residential areas of the city, damaging seven buildings.
Meanwhile, Houthi-affiliated media said one woman was killed and four others injured in an airstrike by the Saudi-led coalition outside the city.
Fears for civilians amid siege
Yemeni civilians in Taiz are facing a "devastating" humanitarian crisis as Houthi forces step up their attacks on the blockaded city, the UN has warned.
"We're alarmed by the intense hostilities across multiple front lines, particularly in Taiz, which is having devastating humanitarian consequences for civilians," UN spokesperson Stephane Dujarric said at a press briefing on Tuesday.
He warned that the blockade was beginning to cause shortages and drive up the prices of goods. Wheat and flour supplies could run out in less than three weeks, he said.
Dwindling fuel supplies are beginning to affect the water supply, risking water shortages for the estimated one million people who live in the city.
The World Health Organisation on Tuesday warned that the war is causing a resurgence in cholera. One quarter of the 8000 cases declared this year have occurred in the past four weeks alone, it said.
The resumption of the conflict last month has triggered a renewed humanitarian crisis across much of the country, displacing hundreds of thousands of people and putting millions at risk of famine.

19 teams, 30 days, one winner — the League of Legends World Championship begins in the US on Thursday

19 teams, 30 days, one winner — the League of Legends World Championship begins in the US on Thursday
Kyiv • UNN
The League of Legends World Championship will take place in the US from October 15 to November 14. Los Angeles, Allen and Brooklyn will host the tournament.
From October 15 to November 14, the United States will host the 16th League of Legends World Championship (Worlds 2026). The strongest esports teams on the planet will compete for the coveted trophy in three stages, hosted by Los Angeles, Allen and Brooklyn, reports UNN.
Details
The 2026 League of Legends World Championship is an esports tournament for the multiplayer online battle arena (MOBA) game, which will take place in the United States—in Los Angeles (California), Allen (Texas, part of the Dallas–Fort Worth metropolitan area), and New York City (New York)—from October 15 to November 14.
This will be the sixteenth League of Legends World Championship, as well as the fifth tournament hosted by the United States.
World Championship schedule
The tournament will take place in three stages: the preliminary stage will be held on October 15–18, the Swiss stage on October 23–31, and the playoff stage on November 3–14.
The preliminary stage (best-of-three) in Los Angeles will run from Thursday, October 15, to Sunday, October 18. All matches will begin at 21:00 Kyiv time
The Swiss stage (best-of-one, best-of-three), which will take place in Allen, Texas, will run from Friday, October 23, to Saturday, October 31. Matches will be held from 20:00 to 23:00.
The playoff stage (best-of-three) will also take place in Allen and Brooklyn. The quarterfinals and semifinals will begin at 1:00 from Wednesday, November 4, through Monday, November 9.
The tournament final will take place on Sunday, November 14, in Brooklyn. It will begin at 22:00.
List of participants
This year, the following teams will compete for the championship title:
-  China - Anyone’s
Legend (AL), Bilibili Gaming (BLG), TOP Esports (TES), Shanghai Invictus Gaming
Meituan (IG); 
-  South Korea - Gen.G
(GEN), Hanwha Life Esports (HLE), T1 (T1), Dplus KIA (DK); 
-  Europe - G2
Esports (G2), Movistar KOI (MKOI), Karmine Corp (KC); 
-  North America - Cloud 9
Kia (C9), Team Liquid Alienware (TLAW), LYON (LYON); 
-  Asia - Team
Secret Whales (TSW), CTBC Flying Oyster (CFO), MVK Esports (MVK); 
-  Brazil - LOS
(LOS), Team (TRICODE). 
It should be noted that participants in the League of Legends Champions Korea (LCK) are three-time defending champions.
World Championship format
In the preliminary stage, four teams will compete in a best-of-three format, with elimination after two losses. Opponents will be selected through a completely blind draw. Any team may face any other team.
The Swiss stage is a competition consisting of five rounds, during which teams will attempt to win at least three matches to advance to the playoff stage. Teams that lose three matches will be eliminated from the competition.
After the Swiss stage is completed, the remaining teams will take part in the quarterfinal draw. During this draw, the two teams with a 3:0 record from the Swiss stage will be randomly assigned opponents from among the two teams with a 3:2 record. The remaining four teams will then be divided into two more pairs through a blind draw.
Broadcasts will be available on Riot’s official Twitch and YouTube channels.

Ukraine

2026-10-14

The restriction on the operation of Starshield terminals (the "military package"), which SpaceX imposed unilaterally overnight into October 14 without warning the Defense Forces, complicates the work of UAV missions, including interceptors.
According to Interfax-Ukraine sources in Ukraine's Ministry of Defense, the ministry is now in contact with the United States, SpaceX and partners in NATO, and is collecting data from all units, while backup communication channels are being checked and used.

At least three seriously injured in Kiryat Gat Intel factory explosion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:34:50 UTC
21:34:50 KST

Three people were seriously injured in a blast at an Intel factory in Kiryat Gat on Wednesday, caused by what Israel Police suspect to be a gas cylinder explosion.
Israel's Fire and Rescue Authority initially warned that hazardous chemicals may have leaked following the explosion. Firefighters worked to identify the source of the chemicals and extinguish the ensuing fire, which has since been put out.
The Fire and Rescue Authority said the incident involved nitrogen trifluoride (NF3), a non-flammable gas with oxidizing properties.
Following the explosion, Mayor Kfir Suissa said, "After an on-site assessment of the situation in cooperation with all relevant parties, the fire at the factory was completely extinguished. As of this time, there are no special instructions for residents, and there is no danger to the public. We ask that you not come to the area of the incident, in order to allow the security and rescue forces to complete their work at the scene without interruption."
Intel’s Kiryat Gat factory, also known as FAB 28, manufactures semiconductor chips used in the company’s processors. The facility is one of Intel’s key manufacturing sites in Israel and plays a role in the company’s global semiconductor production operations.
Three in serious condition after Intel blast in Kiryat Gat
United Hatzalah medical teams treated three people who suffered burns across their bodies following the incident in Kiryat Gat, the emergency medical service said.
Yanaki Weinberg, deputy head of United Hatzalah’s Kiryat Gat branch, and paramedic Moshe Winfeld said they treated a man around 45 who was critically injured and suffered burns across his body. He was transported by a United Hatzalah ambulance to meet an intensive care ambulance while resuscitation efforts were underway. The team delivered two electric shocks using a defibrillator during the journey, and the man's heart miraculously began beating again. He was then transferred to Soroka Medical Center by intensive care ambulance.
Hila Rinkoff and Zvi Levin, paramedics with a second United Hatzalah ambulance team at the scene, said they evacuated another man, around 30, who was also critically injured, to meet an intensive care ambulance while resuscitation efforts were underway.
A third man, around 25, was treated at the scene and evacuated in moderate-to-serious condition, they added.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu spoke with MDA director-general Eli Bin to inquire about the condition of those injured in the explosion, the Prime Minister’s Office said later on Wednesday.
The prime minister wished the injured a speedy recovery and thanked the emergency responders for acting quickly and decisively, the statement added.

Annual inflation reached 73.6% in September, according to the Statistical Center of Iran.
Iran’s central bank launched a program in late September to sell up to $2 billion through state banks to support the rial.

Germany news: Merz attacks extremes for fueling division
Published October 14, 2026last updated October 14, 2026
What you need to know
- Chancellor Friedrich Merz accuses the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and socialist Left Party of fueling division and exploiting discontent for political gain
- The AfD leads national polls, while the Left Party has emerged as Berlin's largest party
- A man has gone on trial accused of playing a role in the 2022 explosion at the Nord Stream gas pipelines
Here is a roundup of all the headlines across Germany on Wednesday, October 14:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click hereto add DW as a Preferred Source on Google
Lufthansa wins bid for stake in Portugal's TAP
Germany's Lufthansa has won the contest to buy a 44.9% stake in TAP Air Portugal with an offer of €1.2 billion ($1.3 billion), Portuguese Prime Minister Luis Montenegro said.
Lufthansa beat rival Air France-KLM after months of efforts to privatize the state-rescued airline, Montenegro told journalists following a cabinet meeting.
Social justice and Christian references: DW's Berlin bureau chief weighs in on Merz's speech
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's overriding message was one of justice, especially between generations.
That was for the home crowd, trying to explain the governing coalition's reform plans of the social systems. Interestingly he also sprinkled in some Christian references, something he seems to be doing more recently.
Most likely the German chancellor is trying to show more empathy and a more positive vision of the future.
His own conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party colleagues have increasingly been demanding this after losses in three state elections this fall.
Merz warns of growing injustice between generations
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has warned that Germany faces a growing gap in fairness between generations unless it undertakes major reforms of its social security systems.
"A justice gap has opened up between the generations in our country, and this gap will grow unless we act," Merz told the Bundestag.
He said children and young people risked being forced to shoulder a greater burden than could reasonably be justified under principles of fairness.
Merz acknowledged that successive governments had paid insufficient attention to the long-term consequences of their decisions, explicitly including governments led by his own center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU).
The chancellor said his government had developed a broad reform program covering pensions, care, the labor market, economic competitiveness and the modernization of the state.
He argued that justice should mean equal opportunities, fair rewards for achievement and fairness between generations, rather than redistribution at the expense of those contributing to the economy.
Merz said the reforms were necessary to preserve Germany's prosperity and ensure that younger generations were not left carrying an unfair share of the costs.
Merz accuses political extremes of seeking chaos
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has accused political forces on the far left and far right of deliberately dividing society, spreading disinformation and downplaying the threat posed by Russia.
Speaking in the Bundestag, Merz said he could not understand why politicians at both ends of the political spectrum continued to minimize Russian aggression.
"One gets the impression that you want chaos because you hope to gain political advantage from it," he told lawmakers.
Merz warned that extremism was increasingly making its presence felt in Germany's national and regional parliaments, as well as everyday life.
However, he acknowledged that extremist movements could draw support from legitimate dissatisfaction and feelings of injustice, arguing that constructive political action was the only effective response.
"Justice for us does not come through the exclusion of minorities," Merz said, calling for policies that promote equal opportunities and fairness between generations.
He contrasted what he described as the destructive politics of division and exclusion with the responsibility of democratic parties to address genuine grievances and govern for everyone in Germany.
WATCH: Merz addresses Bundestag before crucial EU summit
Merz says Ukraine aid does not come at welfare's expense
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has rejected accusations from the far right and far left that support for Ukraine comes at the expense of social spending.
"Not a single euro is missing from social spending," he told parliament, speaking ahead of an EU summit in Brussels.
Merz said an exemption from Germany's constitutional borrowing limits allows spending on defense and assistance for Ukraine to be financed through additional credit.
He accused the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the socialist Left Party of seeking to divide Germany
AfD and BSW join forces against Ukraine support
In the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the far-right Alternative for Germany Party (AfD) won recent elections in a landslide, a new alliance has flexed its muscle.
The AfD put forward a motion to halt arms deliveries to Ukraine and lift sanctions against Russia. Instead, they argue, peace talks with Russia should be initiated.
The Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason (BSW), which holds five seats in the state parliament, again teamed up with the AfD to ensure a majority for the motion. The BSW combines left-leaning economics with right-wing populist positions on immigration and relations with Russia.
AfD and BSW also called for an immediate halt to financial support for Ukraine, to the extent that it goes beyond humanitarian aid.
The motion by the AfD and BSW has no more than symbolic value, as decisions regarding sanctions against Russia and aid to Ukraine are made not by the federal states, but by the federal government and the European Union.
But the new alliance of AfD and BSW has a wider significance. It is seen by observers as a sign of longer-term and closer cooperation between the two parties, which originate from very different ideological camps.
Although the AfD emerged as the clear winner of the state elections in September 2026, it lacks a majority to form a government. It has been searching for partners in the state legislature. So far, the BSW is the only party officially negotiating with the AfD on forming a government.
Merz to set out EU priorities after urging reforms
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is expected to outline Germany's priorities on Ukraine, European defense and economic competitiveness in a parliamentary address ahead of an EU summit in Brussels.
His government statement is scheduled for 14:05 local time (12:05 UTC), followed by a 90-minute debate. EU leaders meet on Thursday and Friday, with the Middle East, the bloc's next long-term budget and EU enlargement also on the agenda.
After the speech, the opposition Greens are set to put forward two motions calling for faster bloc enlargement and stronger measures to counter economic coercion and protect the bloc's market.
Merz's address follows a more domestic-focused speech on planned reforms at an employers' conference in Berlin on Tuesday. There, he said he would press ahead with changes to Germany's welfare system even at the expense of his own popularity, arguing that younger generations stood to benefit.
Energy prices push German inflation to 3.3%
Germany's annual inflation rate rose to 3.3% in September, its highest level since December 2023, as fuel and heating oil prices surged.
The Federal Statistical Office confirmed its preliminary estimate, up from 2.9% in August and 2.8% in July.
The increase was again driven by energy prices, said the office's president, Ruth Brand, highlighting higher costs at gas stations and for heating oil.
Energy prices rose 14.9% compared with September last year, their steepest annual increase since February 2023. That followed increases of 10.5% in August and 8.3% in July.
Motor fuel prices jumped 37.1%, while heating oil rose 74.9%. Firewood, wood pellets and other solid fuels became 15.6% more expensive.
However, electricity prices fell 5.5%, natural gas prices dropped 2.8% and district heating cost 1% less.
The office attributed those declines partly to government measures implemented since the start of the year.
Nord Stream sabotage trial draws protesters
The trial of a Ukrainian man accused of leading the operation that blew up the Nord Stream gas pipelines in 2022 has begun in Hamburg.
The 50-year-old, identified under German privacy rules as Serhii K., faces charges including a war crime, causing explosions, destroying structures and disrupting public services.
DW correspondent Matthew Moore was there as court doors opened at 07:30 local time in Hamburg.
A small pro-Ukraine protest held up a banner saying, "Russia is a terrorist". One participant from Germany told DW that they wanted to remind the world of "the war crimes taking place against the Ukrainian people."
Inside, a Ukrainian student also told DW that he and others had made the journey from Kyiv to show support for the defendant, Serhii K.
"Serhii K is a hero." In the eyes of the German prosecutors, it is another matter. They accuse him of carrying out a war crime. If found guilty of his part in the gas pipeline bombing, K faces a lengthy prison sentence.
Prosecutors allege that he planned the attack with other Ukrainian military personnel on behalf of unidentified Ukrainian state bodies. They say the aim was to prevent Russia from using gas export revenues to finance its war against Ukraine.
Serhii K., who was arrested in Italy last year, denies involvement. Ukraine's government has also denied any role in the attack.
Anti-nuclear activists block waste convoy
Police in the town of Dorsten, just north of the city of Essen, said that they had detained three people who were blocking the A31 motorway.
The group was attempting to stop trucks carrying radioactive waste.
After repelling down from a bridge above the highway, they unfurled a banner reading "stop this crap."
The incident was the latest in Germany's decades-long protest movement against nuclear weapons and atomic energy.
Although the last of the country's nuclear power stations went offline in 2023, transporting and storing the waste remains a divisive topic.
This particular convoy was headed for a facility in Ahaus, near the Dutch border. Authorities believe it could take until 2028 to safely store all the remaining waste from Germany's decommissioned atomic reactors.
Suicide rate increased significantly in 2025
The suicide rate in Germany has continued to climb, according to official statistics just released by the Federal Ministry of Health.
In 2025, at least 11,334 people killed themselves in Germany. That is a 9.3% increase on the previous year, and 15.6% higher than the average over the past decade.
This is higher than the number of deaths due to traffic accidents, AIDS, murder and manslaughter put together.
The data shows that this is partly due to more women (a 17.9% increase since 2021) taking their own lives, though most suicides are still carried out by men. The increase is also due to an increase in assisted suicides for the elderly and infirm, amounting to over 1,000 people.
In a 2020 decision, Germany's top court struck down a 2015 ban on organized assisted dying providers like Switzerland's Dignitas, and called on the Bundestag to create regulations for the practice. However, lawmakers have declined thus far to do so, putting assisted suicide in a legal gray area in Germany. Direct euthanasia by a single doctor remains illegal.
In August, the Health Ministry proposed reforms such as a national suicide prevention hotline, more support for local and state networks, as well as the creation of a federal office for suicide prevention.
However, medical groups and charities have both said that the proposed €1.4 million ($1.6 million) budget would come nowhere never covering such a scheme long-term.
Editor's note: If you are suffering from serious emotional strain or suicidal thoughts, do not hesitate to seek professional help. You can find information on where to find such help, no matter where you live in the world, at this website: https://www.befrienders.org/
Proposed sugar tax faces criticism
According to German media reports, the ruling coalition of Chancellor Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU) and the Social Democrats (SPD) has found a compromise for a planned tax increase on sugar.
The law would impact sugar drinks in particular, and is set to come into effect on July 1 of next year. There is reportedly going to be an exception for small-scale producers.
CDU state premier of Hesse, Boris Rhein, slammed the plan on Wednesday. Rhein told the Kölner Stadt-Anzeiger newspaper that this "expensive tax" (a phrase that rhymes in German) would simply result in companies passing on the extra expense to consumers.
Rhein accused the coalition of pretending the measure was about health when really it was so "the populace can continue to plug up holes in the federal budget at the cash register."
Nord Stream sabotage suspect goes on trial in Hamburg
The much anticipated trial of Serhii K., whose last name is withheld due to Germany's privacy laws, will begin in Hamburg today.
K. is accused by investigators of leading a group comprising professional divers, an explosives expert, and a boat skipper who plotted to travel to the remote section of the Nord Stream gas pipelines off the Danish coast and blow them up.
The series of explosions ruptured Nord Stream 1, which Moscow had switched off a month earlier, and destroyed Nord Stream 2, which had yet to come into operation at the time.
A former Ukrainian military officer, K's case has led some investigators to point at Kyiv as orchestrating the entire plan, as the pipelines controversially delivered Russian natural gas to Europe.
The attack came seven months after Russia's fullscale invasion of Ukraine, when European countries were taking steps to drastically decrease their reliance on Russian fuel.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has vehemently denied any official connection to the attack.
K. was apprehended in Italy in 2025 and extradited to Germany. His specific charges are: being an accomplice to a war crime by attacking civil energy infrastructure, disruption of public services, causing an explosion and destroying structures.
Welcome to our coverage
A hearty guten Morgen from the DW newsroom in Bonn.
It's a day for political and legal battles today, as a man suspected of being part of a conspiracy to blow up a major gas pipeline between Russia and Europe goes on trial.
Later, Chancellor Friedrich Merz will give a sweeping address on his future policies as government approval ratings sink to a record low.
All this and more is coming up in our Germany blog.

Starlink restrictions undermining Ukrainian army effectiveness — expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:33:05 UTC
21:33:05 KST

MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. The reduced scope of intelligence data received from the United States, as well as restrictions on Starlink operations, are undermining the Ukrainian armed forces’ capabilities, Dmitry Kuzyakin, an unmanned aviation expert and chief designer at the Center for Integrated Unmanned Solutions, told TASS.
"The United States is testing the Ukrainian regime’s strength and flexibility. They are twisting the Ukrainian armed forces’ arm by reducing the amount of intelligence data transmitted, cutting back on arms supplies, stopping direct payments ‘to keep them going,’ and artificially degrading Starlink satellite communications. The main reason for the current tightening of the screws on Ukraine is that the US State Department is beginning to lose control over the Ukrainian regime," he said. According to Kuzyakin, the Kiev regime's uncontrolled actions are irritating both US President Donald Trump personally and that part of the American establishment that has invested heavily in Ukraine.
On Wednesday morning, Sergey Beskrestnov, an adviser to Vladimir Zelensky on communications and unmanned systems, reported that SpaceX had limited the speed of Starlink satellite Internet terminals used by the Ukrainian army to 160 km/h overnight. According to him, this disrupted "a number of operations."

South Korea, US, Japan seek nuclear alliance against regional countries — Russia’s MFA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:29:04 UTC
21:29:04 KST

MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. South Korea, the United States and Japan are essentially working to create a nuclear alliance directed against other countries in the region, Konstantin Vorontsov, deputy head of the Russian Foreign Ministry’s Department for Nonproliferation and Arms Control, said.
"South Korea has decided to bring ‘peace and stability’ to the Korean Peninsula by brandishing the US nuclear bludgeon at North Korea," he pointed out at a meeting of the First Committee of the United Nations General Assembly.
"First, it deployed nuclear weapons to its territory in 1958-1991. In 1976, it started to engage in joint drills with the US that practice nuclear strikes and carpet bombings of North Korea, an activity that continues to this day. Now, building on this years-long aggressive policy, Seoul has teamed up with Washington and Tokyo, effectively seeking to form a nuclear alliance directed against the countries of the region," Vorontsov added.
The Russian diplomat highlighted "Seoul’s regular attempts to blame Russia for its own years-long deliberate escalatory moves, which are the root cause of the current crisis facing the Korean Peninsula."
"In Resolution 3390B, adopted at the 30th session of the UN General Assembly, the First Committee already outlined specific steps required to provide strong guarantees of peace on the Korean Peninsula, which include withdrawing all foreign troops stationed in South Korea and replacing the Armistice Agreement with a peace treaty," Vorontsov emphasized. "Since none of the above features in the long-term plans of Washington and Seoul, no comprehensive solution to the nuclear issue on the Korean Peninsula should be expected in the near future," he concluded.

European Union leaders plan to call for a ban on the export through EU territory of grain that Russia steals from the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine.
Source: European Pravda, citing the draft conclusions of the European Council summit on 15-16 October
Quote from the draft document: "The European Council emphasises the need to prevent the export through the EU of grain stolen by Russia from temporarily occupied Ukrainian territories."

Background:
- The European Council would also "express regret over the agreement reached between US President Donald Trump and Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin to supply Russian diesel".
- Furthermore, during the European Council meeting on 15-16 October, no additional decisions regarding financial aid for Ukraine are planned, nor is the question of using frozen Russian assets on the leaders' formal agenda, although the topic may be raised during discussions.
- The summit of EU leaders on 15-16 October will also call for assisting Ukraine in its winter preparations, particularly regarding the resilience of critical infrastructure and will address the consequences of Russia's blockade of Black Sea export routes.
- Consideration of the "Ukrainian matter" during the European Council meeting in Brussels is scheduled for 16 October. The attendance of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is expected.

Delivering the integrated force at DSEI UK in London
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:28:51 BST
21:28:51 KST

DSEI UK will run under the theme of delivering the integrated force in 2027, with four sub-themes covering innovation, industrial capacity, international collaboration and digital technology, the show’s senior defence adviser has told the UK Defence Journal.
Organisers are forecasting around 2,000 exhibitors and up to 60,000 visitors at ExCeL in September next year.
Air Vice-Marshal (Retired) Gary Waterfall CBE is senior defence adviser to Clarion Defence and Security, the company that runs the show. He left the Royal Air Force at the end of 2019, retiring from the Permanent Joint Headquarters as a two-star, and joined Clarion the following year. His job, he said, is to stand with his back to Clarion and look at the Ministry of Defence.
Themes have to be set at least a year ahead of the doors opening, “If you can tell me what’s going to happen in September 27, right here, right now, on the world stage, then please fire away,” he said.
The 2025 theme had to survive a defence review landing part-way through the cycle, and Waterfall said it did.
Sub-themes are built from research among the people who come to the show, Clarion’s own view of the market and talks with the department. “We don’t set the theme in isolation,” he said. “We confer with the Ministry of Defence.”
Defence and security exports used to sit in the Department for Business and Trade, and have now moved into the Ministry of Defence under the National Armaments Director. Waterfall said that gives the show one door to knock on in Whitehall, and he expects it to change what the department puts on its stand. “When it’s the MOD capability showcase, that’s going to be a much broader aspect,” he said.
Waterfall said the theme follows from the same reform drive, and that it is broad enough to mean something to everyone on the floor. “Everyone talks about integration and being that integrated force,” he said. “Therefore the theme for next year is delivering the integrated force. There’s a lot in those four words, but you can hang your hat on that.”
He said it applies to an SME with reservists on the books as much as to a prime, to CSOC or to a frontline command, and that it does not stop at the UK border. The four sub-themes are innovation and emerging technologies, supply chain and industrial capacity, deepening global defence collaboration and partnerships, and digital transformation, AI and cyber. Waterfall said the digital strand runs through all of them.
Choosing the wording for the collaboration sub-theme took some arguing inside the company. “We agonised, would you believe, over the global defence collaboration. Is that NATO?” he said. “It’s not just NATO.”
He cited Royal Navy, Royal Air Force and British Army units working with regional partners around Iran, and British activity in the High North through the Joint Expeditionary Force, both outside the alliance. Waterfall also made a case for the show itself as a form of deterrence. “Those that would wish harm to us will be sat there watching the power of DSEI, seeing it as that convening authority across the global allied defence sector,” he said.
Asked what rising British and European budgets will mean for the conversations on the floor, he spoke about procurement speed. Three years of war in Ukraine have made a 10, 15 or 20 year acquisition cycle impossible to defend, he said, and smaller firms have gained most from that.
“The winners are the small and medium enterprises that can work at a pace that outstrips the routine of a big prime,” he said. The primes have noticed, he added, and are buying into them while trying to leave them alone to work.
Waterfall said buyers now arrive wanting the part of a system that lets it keep changing. “I want it yesterday, please.”
James Samuel took over this year as managing director for live events at Clarion Defence and Security. The job covers DSEI UK, the company’s Japanese business and a conference portfolio that includes UDT in Europe and a UDT Australia launching in December. He has been at Clarion for seven years and has worked in exhibitions for 26.
Around 1,750 companies exhibited at the 2025 show, and Samuel is forecasting 2,000 to 2,100 next year, with the floor growing in square metres as well. The last edition drew 45,000 attendees and he expects 55,000 to 60,000 next time, “if there’s no tube strikes or DLR strikes during our week”.
Samuel said he judges the show on connections made instead off floor space sold. “We can’t just rely on the industry to meet itself,” he said.
Registration answers and what visitors then do on the show platform are used to push suggested sessions, events and contacts at them before they arrive. Samuel said the size of the venue makes that necessary. “It’s a kilometre from one end to the other. You could walk there three or four times and you’ve done that before you’ve even met anyone.”
The 2025 show hosted 114 official delegations from 66 nations, and Samuel said the list is drawn up with government. “This isn’t just us picking out who would like to come to the show,” he said, describing a test of whether there is real business for a delegation to do with British government and British industry.
Clarion is launching DSEI Germany in Hannover in March 2027, six months before London, and DSEI Japan follows in April. Samuel said its offices in Berlin and Tokyo let exhibitors and national pavilions carry one pitch across all three. “Their narrative continues, whether it be from Germany to London to Tokyo,” he said. Between shows the company runs smaller events of 150 to 200 people under the name DSEI Gateway, on the basis that four days every two years leaves a long gap.
Asked what he looks forward to most, Waterfall picked the first morning, telling me that he envisions, “There’s a Nigerian delegation talking to a Polish delegation. The interaction is just unbelievable,” he said. “We are facilitating this show for His Majesty’s government to stand on a stage and project soft power around the world, and that’s a real humbling factor.”
DSEI UK 2027 runs from 7 to 10 September at ExCeL London.

Lithuania’s government on Wednesday approved national asset freezes targeting Russian businessmen Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman, after the European Union lifted sanctions against the two.
The restrictions, proposed by the Foreign Ministry, will remain in force until the end of 2027. Both men were added to Lithuania’s list of undesirable persons in late September.

EU sanctions against Usmanov and Fridman were lifted following requests from several member states.
French officials cited national security grounds for seeking the removal of Usmanov from the sanctions list but did not publicly provide further details. Luxembourg sought the removal of Fridman, who had filed a €15 billion lawsuit against the country over the freezing of his assets.
In late September, EU member states agreed to extend sanctions for three years against nearly 3,000 individuals and entities linked to Russia’s aggression.

EU-China trade progress welcomed, yet trust issues linger

BRUSSELS — The EU and China are in a good place to talk after last week’s trade deal on hybrid cars, but challenges remain, panelists at POLITICO’s European Resilience Summit on Wednesday agreed.
“From the Chinese business perspective this is very welcome,” said Linlin Liang of the China Chamber of Commerce to the EU, calling the understanding reached in Beijing “quite balanced from our perspective.”
An agreement to halve China's exports hybrid vehicles to Europe was the main deliverable brought home by Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič.
Advertisement
The two sides said in a joint statement that they would keep talking about issues such as market access for medical devices and the Foreign Subsidies Regulation, an EU measure that scrutinizes foreign subsidies that distort competition in public procurement and corporate acquisitions.
Šefčovič will hold further talks with Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao in January, and they will meet again in March, as he pushes to rein in a €1 billion-a-day bilateral trade deficit.
Liang said Beijing stands ready to act if further talks go off track.
“I would like to remind all what MOFCOM mentioned: that they reserve the right to retaliate in case that things ... don’t go around as agreed,” she told the panel on Europe in global trade, referring to the Chinese Ministry of Commerce.
Kathleen Van Brempt, a Belgian MEP for the Socialists & Democrats, said the most important outcome of last week’s Beijing talks was that there was “some sort of trade deal or result.”
Yet Beijing’s aggressive subsidy policies remain a hurdle, the senior trade lawmaker said, referring to a widely cited OECD study which found that Beijing’s subsidies to industry are up to eight times higher than in other countries: “It’s not normal,” she said.
Advertisement
Liang said that China’s export success should not be attributed solely to subsidies, and was the result of “decades of investment in innovation.”
She also said there was “a super appetite” among Chinese businesses to invest in Europe, but that they needed to assess the profitability of the EU market just like European companies.
The discussion also revealed differences between policymakers and businesses over the EU’s proposed Industrial Accelerator Act, a flagship measure aimed at steering public procurement spending toward European companies in sectors ranging from renewable energy to steel and the automotive industry.
Van Brempt, the S&D group’s lead lawmaker on the file in the trade committee, said the parliament’s three co-leads are aligned on the bill. While the center-right European People’s Party was “very divided” over the measure, she said lawmakers should be able to come to a common position.
The bill’s “Made in Europe” provision is a cause for concern for industry, meanwhile, as it risks isolating the EU from global supply chains.
“I would be careful always saying, okay, localize, put fences up,” said Holger Weintritt of German pharmaceutical company Bayer. “Let’s make sure that we still remain globally connected and look for reliable partnerships instead of isolating ourselves .”
