Brig. Gen. Andriy Biletsky, commander of the Armed Forces of Ukraine’s (AFU) 3rd Corps, in a statement released to news agencies and social media said that his troops had successfully wrapped up the fourth and final phase of Operation Vivaldi, in the process liberating 101 km² (40 square miles) and hitting Russian troops in the north-eastern Lyman sector with 3,000+ new casualties.

Independent analysts have widely confirmed the Vivaldi Operation launched in July has gained substantial ground and seriously damaged Russian units, with the US-based Institute for the Study of War (ISW) in an Oct. 1 campaign review crediting Biletsky’s troops for re-capturing close to 300 square km (120 square miles) of Kremlin-controlled territory in operations east of Lyman.

During the fourth phase, Biletsky said on Wednesday, three more villages – Zelena Dolyna, Lypove, and Kolodiazi – had been liberated by Ukrainian troops. He did not mention his forces having taken Russian prisoners.
Ukraine’s Business Leaders to Tackle War Risks and Economic Resilience at 12th Kyiv International Economic Forum on Oct. 26
Third Corps forces carried out the attacks using combined arms tactics with dismounted and mounted infantry working in tandem with drone swarms, first to infiltrate to Russian positions and then to cut them off from supply and isolate them, before systematically mopping them up, Biletsky said.
“[T]he key to the operation was speed. We did not give the enemy time to replace his losses or to construct a viable defense. The disoriented commanders of the enemy made mistake after mistake,” Biletsky stated.
Overall, throughout Vivaldi operation, 3rd Corps forces returned Ukrainian control to “more than” 16 towns and villages and 277 km² (120 square miles) of Ukrainian territory, and inflicted total enemy losses of at least 8,000 troops, Biletsky said. Kyiv Post review of battle reports and OSINT trackers found battle lines in the Lyman sector generally consistent with Biletsky’s statements.
Accounts in 3rd Corps internal unit feeds reviewed by Kyiv Post found multiple reports of accumulating Russian casualties mostly to drone strike. Neither Russia nor Ukraine publish their own actual casualty counts.
“Vivaldi has demonstrated that an offensive is possible with outnumbered forces using asymmetric tactics. It is possible to, simultaneously, maintain an effective defense in other sectors,” Biletsky said.
In an evaluation generally shared by Ukrainian military analysts, Biletsky said that his 3rd Corps troops, by gaining ground and defeating defending Russian troops in positions east of Lyman, had scored an operational success by pushing Kremlin forces away from the logistically critical Slovyansk-Kramatorsk highway, thereby ensuring defenses in both those cities – named by Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin as top objectives for Russian conquest – would stay well-supplied.
A parallel offensive led primarily by Ukrainian air assault infantry and paratrooper units has since mid-summer used similar drone + infiltrating-infantry tactics to turn back Russian assaults further south in the Donetsk region, to the east of the cities of Slovyansk and Kramatorsk.
Together those successes made Ukrainian aggregate terrain gains in September 2026 slightly greater than Russia’s for the first time since June 2025.
Ukraine’s Slovyansk-Kramatorsk counter-offensive is still ongoing
Biletsky, in closing comments, suggested a possible follow-up to the Vivaldi Operation was being planned, saying, “At the very least there is still Wagner and Bach.”
Russia’s Defense Ministry during the Lyman/Vivaldi operation has steadfastly insisted Kremlin forces are holding their ground, and, in some places, advancing.
Russian milbloggers – even vehemently pro-Moscow content-creators, in contrast – have warned for weeks of a worsening situation and Russian forces under heavy pressure from Ukrainian drone swarms and infantry assaults.
Popular milblogger Mikhail Zvinchuk (450,000+ followers), in an Oct. 6 post on the Lyman battles, said Russian defenses were unable to stop infiltrating iUkrainian infantry, and that Ukrainian drone strikes were preventing Russian troops from digging in.
“The enemy has numerical superiority and a significant advantage in drones,” Zvinchuk wrote.
https://rybar.ru/limanskij-front/
In the Wednesday announcement, 3rd Corps named combat units participating in the Vivlaldi operation, many of which were among the most combat-experienced in the entire AFU.
Among 3rd Corps units involved in the offensive, Biletsky said, were the 3rd Assault Brigade, the 60th Separate Mechanized Brigade, the 125th Separate Territorial Defense Brigade, the 3rd Separate Reconnaissance Battalion, the 25th Separate Anti-Tank Battalion, and the 21st Separate Special Operations Battalion “Kraken,” a unit raised in Kharkiv at the start of Russia’s second invasion of Ukraine, in February 2022, from retired commando civilians at the time, who volunteered to return to service to fight Russia.
The 3rd Assault Brigade, a regular army unit raised in Kyiv originally as untrained militia on the first day of Russia’s second invasion, is widely considered one of the AFU’s most effective fighting outfits and an early proponent of closely coordinated infantry-drone tactics.
Reinforcements attached to the 3rd Corps included the 66th Separate Mechanized Brigade, the 3rd Border Detachment, the 10th “Dozor” Mobile Border Detachment, and commando groups from the 8th Special Operations Forces Regiment, Biletsky said.
Along with Kyiv’s 3rd Assault, four units participating in the Vivaldi offensive – the 3rd Reconnaissance, the 21st Kraken, the 10th Dozor, and the 8th Special Operations – are long-established, veteran infantry outfits with excellent fighting records, specializing in infiltration, raiding, and behind-the-lines operations supported by drones, Kyiv Post research found.
Biletsky named the National Guard’s “Lasar’s Group,” the special operations battalion from the regular army’s K-2 Regiment, and unmanned air vehicle (UAV) units from the Special Operations Center A as the drone units giving the Vivaldi operation air support. All three are long-established, crack flying outfits with average pilots having flown hundreds of combat sorties and experienced operators thousands.
The K-2 Regiment, formally known in the AFU as the 20th Separate Brigade Unmanned Systems K-2 (Ukrainian: 20-та окрема бригада безпілотних систем «К-2») was raised in 2017 as a squad of drone enthusiasts. According to AFU lore, it probably was one of the first military units in history to employ civilian MAVIC drones in a war and then modify them for combat purposes.
K-2 was, reportedly, the first AFU unit to convert a commercial drone into a bomber jury-rigged to drop grenades, and to employ 24/7 small drone presence with a “cab rank” of strike drones ready to attack over a battlefield target. In 2025, according to a unit statement, K-2 became the world’s first military unit to field a dedicated Unmanned Ground Vehicle (UGV) sub-unit.

DOE unveils global real-time dust source monitoring system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:09:37 UTC
21:09:37 KST

DOE unveils global real-time dust source monitoring system
TEHRAN – The Department of Environment (DOE) has unveiled a global real-time monitoring system designed to identify and track dust hotspots around the world.
The system also enables the analysis of dust patterns, the identification of populations at risk, more effective resource allocation, and the implementation of preventive measures to mitigate the impacts of dust storms.
The system comprises 13 stages organized into three main parts, including setting and initial analyses, identification and refinement of hotspots, and management analysis, IRNA quoted the head of Iran’s National Headquarters for Dust Storm Policy and Coordination, Behzad Raygani, as saying.
The official made the remarks on Tuesday while addressing the 24th meeting of the National Headquarters for Dust Storm Policy and Coordination. During the meeting, a decision-support system for managing dust storms was also unveiled in Khuzestan province.
“The system is described as global because it can generate reports on different regions around the world. Users can select their area of interest in the first section and specify a monitoring period, ranging from seasonal intervals to custom time frames. This feature enables more precise tracking of changes over time,” Raygani said.
Given that remote sensing analyses are subject to errors, a specific step has been incorporated for masking and eliminating errors and areas that do not generate dust, he added.
The second section focuses on identifying and refining dust hotspots. It includes extracting barren land areas, refining the identified hotspots, and generating the required outputs.
The third section makes it possible to examine wind conditions and analyze whether a dust event has originated from a specific source or not, he added.
The system also generates reports on populations exposed to dust and determines the timing, intensity, and location of the phenomenon within a specific region. It can provide reports on exposed populations at both provincial and urban scales.
In places where there are wetlands, the system also enables the estimation of the water volume needed to maintain moisture and prevent dust generation.
For her part, the head of the DOE, Shina Ansari, underlined the importance of boosting environmental diplomacy with neighboring countries, developing regional cooperation to curb sand and dust-storm sources, as well as monitoring the effectiveness of measures taken to address dust phenomena.
Referring to the global dust hotspot monitoring system and the decision-support system for managing dust storms launched in Khuzestan province, Ansari said the global system operates based on ground-based monitoring stations providing data on the location and severity of dust hotspots, affected people, and tracking the changes in the dust centers. The system enables real-time monitoring of dust at the national level, while utilizing global systems as well.
The second system, launched in Khuzestan province, helps make sound and timely decisions in response to dust events. Through enhancing collaboration and coordination among different organizations, the system helps accelerate interaction among the relevant agencies, she noted.
The system represents a strategic step towards strengthening governance capacity for dust storm management; an approach that has to be proactive, coordinated, and highly effective, she stressed.
To make the best use of these two systems, the training of the users must be put on the agenda, she further noted.
UNDP-backed assessment prioritizes 30 SDS hotspots in Iran
A national assessment supported by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) has identified and prioritized 30 critical domestic source areas for sand and dust storms (SDS) in Iran, providing an evidence base for targeted measures to reduce risks to communities, infrastructure and vulnerable ecosystems.
Sand and dust storms are an increasingly serious environmental and development challenge in Iran, affecting public health and livelihoods, damaging infrastructure and putting additional pressure on fragile ecosystems. More than 25 provinces are affected to varying degrees, highlighting the need to shift from responding to individual storms toward prevention, preparedness and long-term resilience.
Since 2023, UNDP has been working with Iran’s DOE and the National Secretariat for Policy Making and Coordination of Management for the Sand and Dust Storms Phenomenon to support this transition.
The national assessment combines data on SDS hazard intensity, ecological vulnerability and the exposure of populations and critical infrastructure. By bringing together environmental information with data on settlements, roads, railways and agricultural areas, the assessment identifies locations where vulnerable landscapes and exposed communities overlap.
The findings provide an evidence base for directing resources to areas where interventions can have the greatest impact, ranging from vegetation restoration and soil stabilization to wetland protection and measures to safeguard infrastructure and communities.
The assessment found that 20 percent of Iran’s territory falls within high- or very-high-risk SDS categories, underscoring the importance of targeted and preventive action.
“Sand and dust storms do not respect borders. Over the past three years, our partnership with UNDP has demonstrated what collective action can achieve, advancing mitigation and adaptation
Measures across four provinces and strengthening resilience to their impacts,” Raygani said.
At the same time, Iran is strengthening its capacity to anticipate and manage SDS events. With support from UNDP, forecasting and early-warning capabilities have been enhanced through fixed and portable monitoring systems. Technical work has also laid the foundation for a national and regional real-time SDS monitoring application.
The initiative extends from national systems to landscapes and local communities. Technical assessments in Khuzestan, Ilam, Yazd and Semnan have incorporated SDS considerations into biodiversity and landscape planning across approximately 47,000 hectares, linking SDS mitigation with ecosystem conservation and future investment decisions.
In Semnan’s Touran landscape, the integrated approach combines vegetation restoration, more efficient water use and improved grazing management with efforts to protect one of Iran’s most important biodiversity areas. SDS mitigation measures have also been implemented across 270 hectares of the Touran Protected Area, an important habitat for the endangered Asiatic cheetah.
Provincial capacity assessments in Ilam and Khuzestan have resulted in new action plans, clearer institutional responsibilities and stronger SDS working groups, helping translate national priorities into coordinated action at the local level. These efforts form part of a broader national shift toward proactive SDS management.

IEA warns global gasoil market tightness to extend into 2027
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
20:09:27 CST
21:09:27 KST

PARIS, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- Tightness in the global gasoil market is expected to extend into 2027 amid prolonged supply disruptions and escalating attacks on energy infrastructure in the Middle East, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said Wednesday.
In its October Oil Market Report, the IEA said global diesel exports fell by 700,000 barrels per day (700 kb/d) year on year in September, as prolonged supply disruptions led to counter-seasonal stock draws ahead of autumn refinery maintenance and peak winter demand.
Although global gasoil prices have eased from record highs of more than 200 U.S. dollars per barrel in September, benchmark prices remain nearly twice the level of crude oil prices and almost double their own pre-crisis levels.
The IEA warned that record gasoil prices were already having widespread economic consequences, raising the cost of goods and affecting real incomes, economic activity and inflation.
The IEA said the gasoil market balance is expected to remain tight well into 2027, depending on a recovery in product supplies from the Middle East. It added that without such a recovery, further demand reductions may be needed to balance the market, potentially at a high economic cost.
Global oil demand is forecast to fall by 2.5 million barrels per day (mb/d) year on year in the fourth quarter of 2026 and by an average of 2.6 mb/d over the full year. A partial recovery of 2 mb/d in 2027 is expected to leave global oil consumption 620 kb/d, or 0.6 percent below 2025 levels, it said.
Global oil supply is projected to decline by an average of 5.8 mb/d to 100.7 mb/d in 2026, before rebounding by 7.7 mb/d in 2027. However, renewed attacks in the Gulf are threatening to undermine the recovery, the IEA said.
A recovery in Middle Eastern oil supply was well underway in September, with Gulf crude oil exports approaching pre-war levels. However, escalating attacks on regional energy infrastructure and tanker traffic are threatening further gains, the IEA said, adding that Brent crude futures have risen by 13 percent since the beginning of September to around 107 dollars per barrel.
In the absence of a resolution to conflicts in the Middle East, oil markets may experience more turmoil in the months ahead before any eventual surplus emerges in 2027, the IEA said. ■

Chinese mainland insurer issues inaugural "sidecar" ILS in Hong Kong
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
20:09:22 CST
21:09:22 KST

HONG KONG, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- The Financial Services and the Treasury Bureau of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (HKSAR) government on Wednesday welcomed an inaugural issuance of insurance-linked securities (ILS) in the form of "sidecar" by the PICC Property and Casualty Company Limited in Hong Kong.
With a size of 12 million U.S. dollars, the issuance provides quota share reinsurance protection for offshore wind farm property insurance businesses on the Chinese mainland.
Christopher Hui, secretary for financial services and the treasury of the HKSAR government, said this move will enable Hong Kong to unleash the synergy effect of multilayered risk transfer and pooling mechanisms through ILS and other tools, thus consolidating the city's strategic role as a regional and global catastrophe and specialty risk management hub.
Since the establishment of the bespoke regulatory regime for ILS and the launch of the pilot grant scheme in 2021, seven catastrophe bonds and one "sidecar" have been issued in Hong Kong to date, with a total issuance amount of about 6.3 billion Hong Kong dollars (about 802 million U.S. dollars), securing protection against catastrophe and other specialty risks on the Chinese mainland and overseas.
A "sidecar" is an ILS structure through which investors provide capital to support a specific insurance or reinsurance portfolio. A "sidecar" is typically capitalized through equity or a debt instrument (such as preference shares or participating notes), and enables investors to share, on a quota-share basis with the sponsor, the premiums, claims and underwriting results of a designated insurance or reinsurance portfolio. ■

THE HAGUE, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- Dutch semiconductor equipment maker ASML said Wednesday it is exploring ways to expand production capacity beyond the previously announced 30 percent increase planned for 2028, as growing investment in artificial intelligence (AI) drives stronger demand for its equipment.
ASML President and Chief Executive Officer Christophe Fouquet said in a statement that customers continue to raise their short- and medium-term equipment demand forecasts, driven primarily by their expectations for the scale and duration of AI-related investment. Given the improved visibility into future demand, some customers are expressing interest in placing orders for 2029 and even 2030.

Feature: Impaired but unbroken, China's disabled build a living
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
20:08:37 CST
21:08:37 KST

Liang Kaiyu improves his artificial leg at his studio in Liangshan County, Jining City of east China's Shandong Province, July 7, 2026. (Xinhua/Zhang Liyuan)
JINAN, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- After losing most of his left leg in an accident, Liang Kaiyu spent so much time perfecting his prosthetic that it eventually became his livelihood.
The prosthetic he first ordered frequently buckled mid-stride and needed constant charging. So Liang set to work, modifying it until it fit him like a glove.
Since then, he has made or refitted more than a dozen artificial legs. One has a mountain bike shock absorber at the ankle. Another has a thruster for swimming. Some of them have electronic knees and ankles he programmed himself.
Going by "Steel Leg" online, Liang posts videos of his work, repairs prosthetics for other amputees and makes a living from it. "Every day there's something I want to do," he said. "I tinker with a part, solve a problem, and when it works I'm happy."
Liang is among more than 2 million registered residents with disabilities in east China's Shandong Province. Late last year, the province announced a three-year plan running through 2027, with targets for job training, self-employment and supported work. At least 45,000 disabled people will receive vocational training.
The plan encourages local governments to reserve space for disabled entrepreneurs in government-funded business incubators and startup parks. Eligible entrepreneurs can apply for guaranteed startup loans of up to 300,000 yuan (44,828 U.S. dollars).
The province is also promoting a "community micro-business" model that requires government-run convenience service outlets to set aside at least 10 percent of their stalls for disabled workers.
WHERE THERE IS A NEED, THERE IS A WAY
Like Liang, people with reduced mobility sometimes become entrepreneurs, driven by needs that aren't otherwise met.
Gong Yuben runs an online shoe store in the port city of Yantai that sells shoes one at a time, not in pairs. He lost his right leg in a traffic accident in 2012, when he was a teenager. Because shoes are sold only in pairs, he accumulated too many new but useless right shoes over the years.
This year, he began working with suppliers to split pairs and sell them individually. His store soon drew a small group of clients who also recommended it to friends with similar needs. Sales are modest, but they answer a real need. "To someone who actually needs it, one shoe is a complete pair," Gong said.
Zou Jiahao's entrepreneurship was driven by a different need: a good cup of coffee from his wheelchair. His wheelchair-accessible cafe in his home city of Qingdao has a ramp at the entrance, a wide doorway for wheelchairs, and a lower counter set at the ideal height for customers on wheels and for him on the other side.
Zou said the initial investment for the 60-sqm shop was about 100,000 yuan, spent mostly on coffee machines and furniture. The local federation for people with disabilities helped negotiate favorable rental fees.
"Equal employment means having the chance to learn a skill, use it, and earn the life you want," Zou said, adding that he is betting on customers, with disabilities or not, to keep coming back for his coffee and service.
China has an estimated 86 million people with disabilities as of 2023, according to the National Bureau of Statistics. In 2025, more than 8.9 million were employed, the China Disabled Persons' Federation (CDPF) reported earlier this year.
China's plan for the protection and development of people with disabilities during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030) outlines a wide range of priorities and initiatives to enhance social protection, life-cycle care and rights protection for disabled citizens.
A major target is to create a million new jobs for people with disabilities in urban and rural areas, said Cheng Kai, chairman of the CDPF.
BUILDING ON WHAT THEY CAN DO
Guangming Experience Hall, a darkness exhibition in Jinan, Shandong's provincial capital, hires visually impaired people exclusively as guides, turning their navigation skills into a new profession. Though "Guangming" means "light," the museum invites visitors to make their way around in the dark, simulating experiences like a bus ride or a shopping trip -- relying only on touch, sound, and smell.
When it opened in early 2024, only six of the about 60 visually impaired applicants were hired. They became familiar with every corner of the hall and learned to "read" visitors' moods from their voices.
Chang Wanxiu, 29, said the job has boosted her confidence and made her feel like everyone else. "With this job, I need to leave home, take the bus, and talk to different people," she said. "At first I was nervous. But after walking through it again and again, I found my footing."
A government-backed program also trains visually impaired therapists for community health centers and helps them open private clinics. "People with disabilities have their own strengths and potential," said Tang Jianquan, head of the Shandong provincial association for the visually impaired. "Once put in the right place, they can prove to be valuable workers for their enterprises as well as for their personal fulfillment."
Despite being hearing impaired, Xiao Wei (not his real name) is as well-prepared as any seasoned food deliveryman. When a customer calls, his smartwatch buzzes, an AI assistant answers and converts the conversation to text, and he quickly replies with one of dozens of pre-edited messages stored on his phone.
The delivery service center trained him and paired him with veteran riders. "I don't feel like a disabled person on the job," he typed in response to Xinhua. "I can feel my own sense of value."
A Starbucks outlet in Qingdao's Shibei district began recruiting and training hearing-impaired workers in 2021 with the municipal disabled persons' federation. Training usually takes a month, but at least twice as long for a hearing-impaired employee, said store manager Lyu Yan. "It's important to slow down the training but keep the same standard, so that all our employees are treated as equals."
To help them, the store installed screens that convert speech to text in real time and lower counters that make it easier to read customers' lips.
Lu Lin, chairman of the China Association of Persons with Physical Disability, said helping people with disabilities find work is a complicated project and one needs to get every step right, from their leaving home to settling into a job.
These often involve infrastructure such as accessible roads and transport, as well as fair wages, social insurance, adequate labor protections and personal development opportunities. "We want more job opportunities for them and every support they need, so that they can live with independence and dignity." ■
Zou Jiahao brews coffee for customers at his wheelchair-accessible cafe in Qingdao, east China's Shandong Province, July 21, 2026. (Xinhua/Zhang Liyuan)

Russia will introduce visa requirements for citizens of Montenegro in retaliation to Podgorica’s decision to end its bilateral visa-free travel agreement with Moscow as it seeks to join the EU in 2028.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova confirmed that Montenegro’s foreign ministry notified Moscow of its intent to cancel the 2008 mutual travel agreement on Sept. 28.
“In practice, this means that starting Nov. 1, our citizens will only be able to enter and remain in Montenegro with visas. Accordingly, citizens of Montenegro will also have to obtain visas for trips to Russia,” Zakharova said.
Montenegro announced in July that it would end visa-free access for citizens of Russia, Belarus, China, Saudi Arabia and Turkey to align with EU standards.
Zakharova argued the decision would curb Russian tourism, harm local businesses and degrade Montenegro’s investment climate.
Montenegro has for years remained one of the few European countries to offer visa-free entry to Russians for up to 30 days and absorbed a large wave of anti-war Russian emigres after the invasion of Ukraine.
Local media reported earlier this year that two-thirds of registered Russian residents had left Montenegro in anticipation of the new visa rules.
“It’s pointless for Montenegro to expect Brussels to compensate them for their inevitable losses,” Zakharova said.
She warned that EU accession would require prospective members among the Balkan nations to adopt a “confrontational anti-Russian course” that would go against their national interests.
The subject of tightening border controls recently drew the attention of the founder of the popular pro-war Telegram channel Rybar, who was detained and deported from Montenegro on claims that he was seeking to film a documentary portraying EU integration as an externally imposed process.
Russian-Montenegrin relations have been strained since 2016, when Podgorica accused Russia of plotting a failed coup with Serbian ultranationalists. The Kremlin denied that claim.
Ties worsened further after Montenegro joined NATO in 2017 and aligned with EU sanctions over Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Montenegro has also banned Russian state media and expelled Russian diplomats for espionage, prompting Moscow to add the country to its list of “unfriendly” states.

Ukraine-NATO AI built to forecast Russia’s front-line drone attacks from past data and weather is ready to plug into the army
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:07:38 UTC
21:07:38 KST

Ukraine and NATO have unveiled two artificial intelligence (AI) tools in Vilnius, Lithuania, Ukraine’s Defense Ministry reported on 13 October. One forecasts Russian drone attacks near the front and is ready to join the Armed Forces’ situational awareness systems. The other helps plan artillery fire and is still in testing.
A forecast of where, when, and which drones will fly targets the main source of losses near the front. In March, Ukraine’s military put the share of front-line casualties caused by FPV drones at up to 80%. In May, Ukraine’s drone forces commander Robert Brovdi said Russia was copying Ukraine’s model to grow its drone forces. A month earlier, Presidential Office head Kyrylo Budanov wrote that adding more drones no longer fundamentally changes the battlefield. The next stage, he said, is full integration of AI.
Forecasting Russian drone attacks
The NATO-Ukraine Joint Analysis, Training and Education Center (JATEC) presented both at a three-day seminar in the Lithuanian capital. NATO’s Allied Command Transformation and Ukraine’s Armed Forces built the tools with JATEC’s support.
“The solution has already been validated using real-world datasets. It has been refined and is ready for integration into the Armed Forces of Ukraine's situational awareness systems,” the ministry said.
Model No. 13 works from past data, weather, and the current battlefield situation. The ministry said it can identify the intensity of attacks, the areas, the time windows, and the types of drones with a high probability.
Ranking artillery options
Model No. 32 is a decision-support module. It tests whether artillery plans can be generated automatically. It weighs the mission’s requirements and current operational data, including available weapons, ammunition, firing positions, and constraints.
Ukraine’s new military AI does more than watch the battlefield—it helps commanders plan what comes next
First, it applies logistics, ballistics, and impact-zone parameters to throw out unworkable options. Then it scores and ranks the rest. That means less hand-based comparison, faster decisions, and a more efficient fire loop, the ministry said. The prototype is now with the Ukrainian military for trials. If the trials succeed and it is validated, it could be expanded to other units that strike Russian forces.

Remains of Ukrainians killed in 1944 attack by Polish Home Army found in Poland – photos

Unknown Publisher

Remains of Ukrainians killed in 1944 attack by Polish Home Army found in Poland – photos
A Ukrainian expedition has discovered around 30 sets of human remains belonging to Ukrainians killed in the village of Łasków in Poland. The remains were found in individual and mass graves at an Orthodox cemetery. Residents of Łasków were killed in an attack by units of the Polish Home Army (Armia Krajowa) and Peasants' Battalions in March 1944.
Source: Ukrainian Institute of National Remembrance on Facebook
Details: The expedition is being conducted in the Lublin Voivodeship with the permission of the Polish authorities as part of the implementation of agreements reached by the Ukrainian-Polish Working Group on Matters of Dignified Burial.
Search operations are underway in Łasków based on historical records of the mass killing of Ukrainians on 10 March 1944. Historians estimate that more than 300 people were killed at the time.
Experts from Ukraine and Poland have so far established information about 327 residents of Łasków who were killed. However, some historians believe the death toll was higher, at around 350. Further research is expected to establish the number of victims.
"The preliminary findings confirm accounts given by former residents of Łasków who managed to survive the horrific events of March 1944. We plan to continue searching for burial sites, with the next stage involving exhumations, the reburial of the victims and a dignified commemoration of their memory," said the head of the Dolia municipal company, which is conducting the work in Łasków.
This is the second expedition by Ukrainian experts to Poland since a lengthy break that began in 2016. The last similar work, during which human remains were discovered, took place that year. The expeditions resumed in autumn 2025 in the village of Jureczkowa.
Background: Earlier, a search for the remains of Polish Army soldiers who died in September 1939 during a battle with the German Wehrmacht was completed at the old Holoskiv Cemetery in Lviv. The search uncovered 113 complete sets of remains of Polish Army soldiers, as well as the remains of 17 Wehrmacht servicemen.

Leonardo DRS wins $500M slot to supply counter-drone radar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:06:53 UTC
21:06:53 KST

- Leonardo DRS won a three-year counter-drone contract with a $500 million ceiling from Joint Interagency Task Force 401.
- The company can now compete for orders for its tactical radars, but it disclosed no initial task order or funding.
Leonardo DRS has won a spot on a Pentagon counter-drone contract worth up to $500 million, giving the company a path to sell its tactical radars to Joint Interagency Task Force 401, the U.S. Department of War organization set up last year to speed anti-drone gear to troops.
The company announced the three-year indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity award on Oct. 14 in a press release, saying it will be eligible to compete for task orders covering integrated counter-drone sensing for force protection and low-altitude air defense. The $500 million figure is a ceiling for orders rather than money committed, and Leonardo DRS did not report any initial task order or say how much has been obligated.
“Our counter UAS and air defense radars have demonstrated proven detection, tracking, and force protection performance in operational environments,” said Max Cohen, senior vice president and general manager of the Leonardo DRS RADA Technologies business unit.
That business traces back to Israeli radar maker RADA, which merged with DRS in 2022 and builds compact tactical radars designed to spot small drones, rockets and mortar rounds. Its Multi-mission Hemispheric Radar flies on the U.S. Army’s Stryker-based Maneuver Short-Range Air Defense vehicle, for which Leonardo DRS also integrates the mission equipment package. According to the company, the same family of sensors supports counter-rocket, artillery and mortar missions as well as short-range air defense for deployed forces.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth ordered JIATF-401 created in August 2025 to replace the Joint Counter-small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Office. The task force reports to the deputy secretary of war, is run under the U.S. Army, and has a director who can approve up to $50 million per counter-drone effort without going through the usual acquisition chain.
Leonardo DRS is one of several companies to receive a JIATF-401 contract with an identical $500 million ceiling this year. The first went to Perennial Autonomy in May, covering Merops interceptors and Bumblebee quadcopters among other drone-killing systems. Since then, CACI, AeroVironment, Digital Force Technologies, DroneShield and SRC have announced similar vehicles, most of them tied to Domestic Shield, the task force’s push to protect military bases and other sites inside the United States.
Radar maker SRC is the closest comparison, having received a $10.24 million first order for its Gryphon radars alongside its own $500 million vehicle earlier this month. Leonardo DRS framed its award around expeditionary and deployed forces, and its release does not mention Domestic Shield.
“This JIATF IDIQ positions DRS to accelerate the delivery of integrated C-UAS sensing technologies through rapid fielding of operationally relevant capabilities that help protect forces and strengthen low-altitude air defense as new threats emerge,” said John Baylouny, president and chief executive officer of Leonardo DRS.

12:06:05 UTC
21:06:05 KST

Portugal has chosen Lufthansa to buy a 44.9% stake in TAP, completing the first phase of the airline’s privatisation. The deal still needs regulatory approval.
The Portuguese government announced after Wednesday's cabinet meeting that German carrier Lufthansa had been chosen to buy a 44.9% stake in TAP as part of the Portuguese airline’s privatisation.
"The government is successfully bringing to a close the first phase of the privatisation of our national airline. A process conducted with strict respect for competition, a stringent approach to negotiations and complete transparency vis-à-vis the Portuguese public," Portuguese prime minister Luís Montenegro said.
The prime minister then announced that, after assessing the bids, the government had opted for the Lufthansa Group, "whose financial offer is 16% higher than the rival proposal and carries a lower degree of uncertainty."
The transaction will bring in "€1.201 billion in this first phase" and the state will retain a majority stake of 50.1% in the company. "Lufthansa will be responsible for executive and operational management," he said.
"This is an offer that gives the airline a total valuation of €2.552 billion. A figure far above the independent valuations put forward a few years ago or even just a few months ago," he added.
Montenegro also stressed the "ambitious strategy" in the aviation sector, particularly when it comes to airport infrastructure.
As a result, "we are ensuring the growth of TAP, the growth of the fleet, the growth in passenger numbers, the growth in destinations and routes, and also the growth in investment, not only in TAP but across the entire aeronautics sector in Portugal," he said.
The proposal will support further investments, including €500 million to set up a new pilot training school in Tancos, an innovation centre in Aveiro and a corporate services centre, in addition to the already announced investment by Lufthansa Technik in Santa Maria da Feira.
Montenegro also pointed to plans to create jobs. "We are envisaging 3,000 associated jobs linked to TAP's projected growth and a total of 5,500 direct and indirect jobs across all these investment initiatives in our country."
Miguel Pinto Luz, minister for infrastructure and housing, set out the offer in detail, highlighting plans to expand the fleet to 117 aircraft by 2035 and 130 after 2035. Up to eight Airbus A350-900s are also due to be transferred to TAP from 2030 onwards.
The proposal also includes investment in Francisco Sá Carneiro Airport, the strategic base for the entire operation, as well as in Faro Airport and the airports in Portugal’s autonomous regions.
At the end of September, Air France-KLM and Lufthansa submitted their respective final bids to acquire 44.9% of the Portuguese airline's share capital, according to Parpública, the company that manages state holdings.
A further 5% of the company’s shares are reserved for employees. However, under the decree-law on TAP's privatisation, published in August and cited by Lusa, the chosen private investor — in this case Lufthansa — may also buy any shares not bought by employees. The state will retain the remaining 50.1%.
According to Portugal's business press, TAP posted a loss of €99.2 million in the first half of 2026, 40% higher than a year earlier.
The finance minister, Joaquim Miranda Sarmento, said last week that the privatisation process would only be concluded in 18 to 24 months, in 2028, after approval from the European Commission.

MI5 Director: Russia, Iran, and AI pose greatest threats to Britain
Unknown

2026-10-14
12:06:01 UTC
21:06:01 KST

Sir Ken McCallum, the Director of the British intelligence agency MI5, has stated that more resources are currently being spent on countering threats to national security than during the Cold War, the BBC reports.
McCallum noted that threats from hostile foreign states have quadrupled over the past decade; while Russia remains the primary aggressor, there is also rising aggression from Iran targeting sites linked to Jewish communities and Israel, as well as military bases. He pointed out that Russia is waging hybrid warfare at a time when artificial intelligence is intensifying the cybersecurity race between attackers and defenders. McCallum also warned of threats from far-right terrorists seeking to utilize artificial intelligence—including by integrating the latest technologies into drones—though the most significant danger stems from extremist groups attempting to create new biological weapons or exploit existing ones with the help of AI. At the same time, the MI5 Director highlighted the extensive scale of efforts to counter terrorism and prevent threats to the country, noting that significant changes are underway.
McCallum stated that Russia has stopped just short of conventional conflict with NATO, seeking instead to sow insecurity across Europe, while its full-scale war in Ukraine has stalled and is exacting a horrific toll in lives.
Hybrid attacks are largely carried out by hiring proxies, and Russia—despite the evidence—consistently denies involvement. McCallum explained that MI5’s success in identifying and expelling Russian spies has forced the Kremlin to rely on paid proxies to commit crimes. He noted that nearly 1,000 Russian spies have been expelled since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine; 
with its own capabilities depleted, Moscow is resorting to paying criminals to do its dirty work.
 He added that a major power possessing strategic superiority would not act in such a manner. Following his speech, McCallum was asked about recent remarks by British politician Andy Burnham regarding Russian interference in the Brexit process; the MI5 Director replied that information about Moscow's attempts to influence events was nothing new, though he emphasized the distinction between attempts to interfere and actually achieving a result. He noted that there had been coverage of the referendum in Russian media and activity by so-called bot farms and internet trolls, but maintained that the outcome of the 2016 referendum was not in question. McCallum added that he was somewhat concerned about current discussions regarding Russian interference, noting the importance of not playing into the enemy's hands or exaggerating the scale of the troll activity.
McCallum reported that Iran is expanding its hybrid influence campaigns. Over the past year, more than 50 arrests linked to Iran have been made. Much of this aggression is directed at Jewish communities, though other targets—such as military facilities—are also at risk. 
McCallum did not explicitly mention arrests linked to the alleged plot to attack the Royal Air Force base at Fairford, but he later told reporters that the incident was not unique
 and that Iran had shown interest in other military sites as well.
The MI5 director also addressed the threats posed by artificial intelligence. He noted that AI could be used to create propaganda and radicalization materials tailored to specific individuals. The agency has reportedly intercepted terrorists seeking ways to leverage AI to enhance their reconnaissance capabilities and attack methods, with AI-enabled drones representing a new development. While AI-generated biological weapons have not yet become a reality, the technology holds the potential to raise the stakes.
McCallum also highlighted the unknown threats that AI could pose, observing that humanity has no historical precedent for contending with something more intelligent than itself.

Scientists reveal why some workout recovery tricks can backfire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:04:20 UTC
21:04:20 KST

Scientists reveal why some workout recovery tricks can backfire
- Date:
- October 14, 2026
- Source:
- The Conversation
- Summary:
- Ice baths, massages, compression garments, and recovery supplements promise faster muscle recovery, but research suggests their benefits are often overstated, and some techniques may even undermine long-term gains. Scientists say the most effective recovery methods are far simpler and cheaper: getting enough sleep, eating well, and giving muscles time to rebuild.
- Share:
Finishing a tough workout always feels good. That is, until a few hours later when those uncomfortable muscle aches start setting in. This discomfort can linger for days – making easy, everyday tasks a challenge.
In search of relief, some recreational gym-goers are adopting the kind of recovery techniques once reserved for elite athletes. Social media and professional sport have helped popularize everything from ice baths and compression garments to massage and recovery supplements.
While many of these products promise faster recovery, reduced soreness and improved performance, the science is often more nuanced.
Ice baths
Few recovery strategies have received as much attention as ice baths. This involves immersing oneself in water that is below 15°C to boost recovery. But the evidence for this benefit is mixed.
Ice baths help ease inflammation, which research suggests can reduce muscle soreness and help athletes recover muscle function more effectively in a 24-hour period.
But there’s a catch. While inflammation causes soreness, it also triggers adaptations that build muscle. Dampening this response with ice baths may limit some of the long-term benefits of training – particularly if they’re used regularly.
When it comes to ice baths, side-stepping short-term pain may sacrifice long-term gains. It’s best to only use them when rapid recovery is vital.
Compression garments
Compression garments are commonly worn after exercise to speed recovery. The idea is that the external pressure they apply supports circulation, enhances blood flow to the muscles, and reduces swelling.
But while compression garments might make you think they’re helping as they reduce soreness, evidence showing they actually improve muscle recovery is generally less convincing.
A study from 2022 put them to the test. One group was given compression garments; the other group was given a placebo tablet that they were told was equally as effective as compression.
The compression garments were shown to improve circulation and muscle blood flow, while the placebo had no effect on these measures. This suggests the effects of compression garments on recovery are physiological and aren’t simply due to expectation or perception.
However, whether these changes meaningfully improve performance is less clear. Although emerging evidence suggests compression garments genuinely affect some markers of recovery, this is unlikely to directly restore muscle function.
So, compression garments may mainly help because they make you feel better recovered.
Massage
Massage is one of the few recovery interventions with relatively consistent scientific support. It can reduce soreness and improve perceived recovery after exercise.
It’s not currently clear what mechanisms actually trigger the recovery benefits of massage. But it could be due to the fact that massage reduces muscle stiffness, improves circulation and boosts relaxation.
But although athletes feel less sore and perceptions of recovery are improved after a massage, objective measures of performance and muscle function are modest and inconsistent.
Massage might ease the discomfort of training, but don’t expect miraculous performance restoration.
Recovery supplements
The nutrition supplement market is a big business, with hundreds of brightly coloured recovery drinks and capsules promising reduced soreness and faster recovery. But not all supplements are created equal. Some appear to confer small benefits, while some come with hype that science doesn’t back up.
Whey protein, for instance, is a well-researched supplement. Rich in amino acids (the building blocks of protein), it stimulates muscle protein synthesis – the process which helps your muscles grow. Whey protein is shown to have small-to-moderate benefits for muscle recovery – but evidence that it can alleviate soreness is inconsistent.
Branch chain amino acids (BCAAs) are widely-used supplements that typically contain a mixture of the amino acids leucine, isoleucine and valine. BCAAs are popular because it’s believed the leucine they contain switches on protein synthesis.
Yet despite their popularity, BCAAs appear less effective than complete protein sources for muscle recovery. This is because muscle repair requires all essential amino acids – not just the ones found in BCAAs. Food sources such as chicken, beef, salmon and tofu contain all the essential amino acids.
Tart cherry juice is a relatively new supplement in the fitness world. It’s rich in polyphenols – plant compounds that are said to have anti-inflammatory and antioxidant (reducing or preventing cell damage) effects. It’s for these reasons that tart cherry juice is thought to help reduce muscle damage and soreness.
Although this is still an emerging area of research, evidence suggests these compounds have small-to-moderate effects on reducing soreness after workouts, and may also help restore muscular strength and power.
Omega-3 (fish oil) supplements are often championed as a way to reduce inflammation and accelerate recovery after exercise. While some research suggests they can modestly reduce muscle soreness and help preserve muscle function after strenuous exercise, results are far from consistent. As such, omega-3 supplements are unlikely to vastly improve recovery.
Importantly, all of these nutrients can be obtained from a healthy, balanced diet. Science also shows that it’s better to get these nutrients from whole foods over expensive supplements, as whole foods provide other important nutrients that may interact synergistically to support health.
What actually works?
Popular recovery techniques might have small benefits for reducing feelings of soreness, but they don’t actually tend to restore muscle function all that much. Instead, the strongest evidence for good recovery comes from the basics:
- Prioritize sleep: Get 7-9 hours of sleep per night so the body can conduct vital recovery and adaptive processes.
- Fuel properly: Consume 20-40g of protein after exercise for muscle repair and adequate carbohydrate intake to replenish energy stores.
- Train smart: Pair good sleep and nutrition with a sensible, well-structured training plan. This includes allowing rest days between sessions, challenging yourself a bit more each time, and scheduling easier sessions when needed to allow recovery.
So, perhaps the biggest lesson here is that recovery cannot be bottled and sold.
Story Source:
Materials provided by The Conversation. Original written by Max Davis, Postgraduate Research Student, Centre for Nutrition, Exercise and Metabolism, University of Bath. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

More than 2.2 million dengue cases and nearly 1,200 deaths were reported across 97 countries and territories in the first eight months of 2026, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).
In October, Bangladesh's reported total surpassed 103,000 cases and 300 deaths, while Cuba has recorded 11,235 cases so far in 2026. Florida is also experiencing the largest dengue outbreak in any US state in decades, with nearly 300 locally acquired cases reported this year.
One of the world's fastest-growing mosquito-borne viral diseases, dengue has expanded its geographic reach in recent decades. Climate crisis-linked rising temperatures and rapid urbanisation are among the factors contributing to its spread.
About half the world's population is now at risk, with an estimated 100–400 million infections occurring annually, according to WHO.

Known criminal serving as police agent aids in mass arrest of 28 drug traffickers across Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:01:59 UTC
21:01:59 KST

Police arrested 28 suspected drug traffickers in raids across Israel early Wednesday following a 10-month undercover operation in which a known criminal recruited as an agent helped gather evidence against dozens of suspects involved in supplying drugs to Jerusalem.
The agent, a known criminal who had spent years building connections in the underworld, was recruited by the Jerusalem District Police's Central Unit (YAMAR) and helped establish an evidentiary basis against dozens of suspects involved in drug trafficking.
The operation was designed to reach dealers behind the drug supply chains operating in Jerusalem. According to police, the reputation the agent had built in the criminal underworld allowed him to gain the trust of dealers and carry out dozens of controlled drug transactions under the direction of YAMAR's undercover agents division.
During the operation, the agent purchased commercial quantities of cocaine, ecstasy, and other drugs, with a total value of hundreds of thousands of shekels. The transactions were conducted under the supervision of the Jerusalem District Attorney's Office, and the evidence gathered was used to build cases against the suspects.
When the investigation entered its overt phase, officers from the Jerusalem District and other police districts, along with Border Police officers, National Guard personnel, and the canine unit, launched the arrest operation.
During searches, police seized more than NIS 100,000 in cash, drugs, and 12 vehicles suspected of having been used to transport drugs and carry out transactions. Police intend to seek the forfeiture of the vehicles as part of the subsequent legal proceedings.
Operation aimed to undermine trust among criminals, police say
At a ceremony on Wednesday marking the agent's public unveiling, Jerusalem District Police Commander Maj.-Gen. Avshalom Peled said the operation was intended not only to target drug suppliers but also to undermine trust among criminals.
"We can certainly say this morning that we achieved the two main objectives we set for this operation. The first was to strike at the criminals operating the supply chains and bringing drugs into the capital, targeting those in their closest circles. The second was to undermine the trust between criminals and their ability to rely on one another, thereby making it harder for them to operate," Peled said.
He added, "No criminal involved in this field knows this morning whether the next deal will be the one that ends his criminal career and puts him behind bars."
The suspects are expected to be brought before a court later Wednesday for hearings on extending their detention. The investigation remains ongoing.

First ever Israeli fashion museum anticipated to open in Tel Aviv in early 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:01:41 UTC
21:01:41 KST

Israel's first museum dedicated entirely to fashion as a cultural field is expected to open in Tel Aviv in early 2027, marking a new chapter for fashion exhibitions in the country.
The Tel Aviv Fashion Museum, a joint initiative by Azrieli Group and fashion historian and curator Dr. Ya'ara Keydar, will be housed at Azrieli Sarona.
In Paris, London, and New York, fashion museums have long been part of the cultural landscape, while fashion exhibitions at the Metropolitan Museum of Art attract blockbuster crowds. In Israel, by contrast, fashion has entered exhibition spaces only through a handful of shows. The opening of the new museum is expected to change that.
The museum is a joint venture between Azrieli Group, led by CEO Dana Azrieli, and Keydar, and the project has been underway for about three years. Located at Azrieli Sarona, it will cover approximately 1,150 square meters across three floors and include exhibition spaces for rotating shows, an auditorium for lectures and events, and a museum shop.
Alongside the exhibitions, the museum plans to offer educational activities, guided tours, and themed evenings. Its founders aim to attract more than 250,000 visitors annually.
Azrieli malls intertwined with fashion industry
The choice of location is no coincidence. Azrieli operates some of Israel's largest shopping malls, and the museum continues the group's ties to the fashion industry.
"The group's malls are spaces where the public encounters brands, designers, and trends from Israel and around the world, and the museum expands on that encounter," Dana Azrieli said.
She also described a personal connection to the world of fashion: Her grandfather, Rafael Hirsch Azrilovich, was a tailor and workshop owner in Poland.
Keydar is perhaps the figure most closely associated with bringing fashion into Israeli museums. Over the past decade, she has curated 12 exhibitions in Israel and abroad, including four presented at the Design Museum Holon: an exhibition dedicated to Ronit Elkabetz, The Ball, an exhibition on Alber Elbaz, and Heroines. Together, the four exhibitions attracted more than half a million visitors.
A graduate of the fashion design department at Shenkar College of Engineering, Design and Art, Keydar holds a master's degree from New York University and a doctorate from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem. She also trained at the Metropolitan Museum of Art's Costume Institute.
Museum will promote Israeli designers, build relationships with institutions abroad
According to Keydar, the museum will present original exhibitions, promote Israeli designers, and develop relationships with institutions abroad.
"Especially in a complex reality, we need spaces of beauty," she said.
Ilan Jarbi, the group's director of strategic content initiatives and a partner in establishing the museum, added that the opportunity to build a museum from scratch makes it possible to rethink both exhibitions and the visitor experience.
The theme of the museum's inaugural exhibition will be revealed at a later date.

====================================================================================================

Elections delayed: A generation of Palestinians is being denied its right to choose - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:01:40 UTC
21:01:40 KST

What pains me most about the postponement of the Palestinian elections is that I know the faces of those who were waiting for them. I spoke with them, heard their dreams, and saw how the prospect of voting restored some of their confidence in themselves and their country. They were not expecting a miracle. They wanted a simple right: to choose their representatives and have a say in their future. Then the door was closed.
Based on my close observation of the political process leading up to the decision, I hold Vice President Hussein al-Sheikh and Jamil Mezher primarily politically responsible for pushing for this postponement. This does not absolve others of responsibility. But it prevents those who drove the decision from hiding behind vague phrases about “national consensus” and “creating the right conditions.” Palestinians have the right to know who closed the door, and why. Those responsible have a duty to answer.
In my assessment, Sheikh worked persistently to prevent the election decree from being issued last July. Once it was issued, he continued his efforts to cancel the date it had set. He succeeded in securing the postponement. The painful irony is that his success in closing the path to elections followed a series of failures in areas that should have opened a way out of the crisis.
Postponement of the elections
Internal dialogue within Fatah and national dialogue were used to justify the postponement. Yet these are two processes the vice president helped lead over many years. Numerous capitals hosted lengthy meetings without achieving reconciliation or ending the division.
How does the failure of dialogue become a reason to deny people elections? Why should citizens pay the price for their leadership’s failures and then be denied the democratic means to hold it accountable?
As for Palestinian-American relations, where is the breakthrough ordinary citizens can see? And as for civilian coordination with Israel, ask the worker cut off from his job, the student arriving late to university, or the employee who leaves home before dawn without knowing when he will arrive.
The occupation bears direct responsibility for the checkpoints, restrictions, and humiliation. But the Palestinian official entrusted with coordination must also be held accountable for the results he has achieved in protecting people’s interests. It is not enough for the office to remain in place while citizens’ lives become harder every day.
Holding leadership accountable
I have known Sheikh since his release from prison in the early 1990s, after many years of detention. At the time, I headed Fatah’s youth movement in Jerusalem and served in its leadership across the West Bank and Gaza Strip. He was a member of Fatah’s Higher Movement Committee: well liked, cheerful, and close to ordinary people and the youth movement’s activists. We had a strong relationship, as he did with many leaders of our generation.
I do not know what these long years have done to the leader we once knew. But I know that the young man who once defended his generation’s right to participate has now become, in my assessment, one of the leading figures denying that same right to a new generation.
These young people are present within Fatah, too. In recent weeks, I saw its members and activists eager to stand as candidates and participate. According to the information I followed, more than 430 people in Hebron alone applied for a place on the movement’s electoral list, including many young grassroots leaders. This was a clear expression of a desire to take part in political life, and of talent waiting for an opportunity, even within the organization to which the vice president belongs.
As for Mezher, deputy secretary-general of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine, who holds a leading role while Secretary-General Ahmad Sa’adat remains imprisoned, his responsibility raises a question no less painful: How can an organization with such a substantial political history and popular following accept a role in closing the path to political renewal?
For me, that question has a face and a name: Nidal al-Rabadi.
He was my friend and schoolmate, and a supporter of the Popular Front. During a demonstration in Jerusalem in 1988, a bullet struck him and he fell beside me. We were 15. Lying on the ground, he looked at me and spoke his last words: “Don’t leave me.”
I have never left him behind in my memory. To this day, I keep his photograph in my home beside those of my children, and I cannot hold back my tears whenever his name is mentioned.
When I think about Mezher’s position on the elections, I remember Rabadi and ask: How do we honor that generation by denying its children the right to choose? What future do we preserve for their sacrifices if young people remain outside our institutions, waiting for permission to participate from those who have held their positions for decades? I invoke Rabadi because politics, to me, means responsibility toward people’s lives and toward those who died believing their sacrifices would open a better path for future generations.
The Popular Front was once the second-largest force in the Palestine Liberation Organization, with a clear grassroots presence during the First Intifada. In my assessment, that presence has diminished considerably over the years. Recently, I have witnessed young people and activists moving from its ranks to other political groups and electoral lists, including Masar Jadid.
This phenomenon extends beyond any single organization. Many of my colleagues in Masar Jadid and I came from other political movements. We brought our history and convictions with us, but we sought a space where we could work, make a difference, and participate. When organizations fail to make room for their members’ abilities, people look for other doors. Postponing elections will not resolve this alienation. It will deepen it.
The cost of delay
The cost of waiting is visible in almost every Palestinian household. Employees receive delayed portions of their salaries, workers have lost their incomes since October 2023, and families borrow money to pay rent and buy food. I have met people overwhelmed by loans, checks, and obligations they can no longer meet. Fear of creditors and the courts has become part of their daily lives.
In education, the financial crisis affects both regular schooling and teachers’ lives. When a teacher must seek additional work or sell goods on the street to support a family and afford the journey to school, the future of all our children is at risk.
In Gaza, families – many displaced into tents – are approaching a third winter since the war began. Mothers and fathers spend their days searching for the bare minimum of food, water, and medicine for their children.
Amid these conditions, I spoke for hours every day with young men and women from Gaza by phone, Zoom, and social media. Their education, knowledge, and capacity to think and act impressed me. I was moved by the hope in their voices simply because a political organization existed that allowed them to express their views and participate.
For them, elections offered a chance to become decision-makers in a society accustomed to treating them as recipients of aid. How painful it is to see these abilities buried once again beneath a closed bureaucracy and leaders who refuse to make room for them.
There are Palestinians approaching 40 who have never once voted in a national election. There are leaders who have held their positions for most of these young people’s lives. This imbalance cannot be corrected through more waiting or through dialogue that continues for years without restoring people’s rights – especially when the cost of postponement extends beyond our internal affairs.
French President Emmanuel Macron invested significant political effort in supporting recognition of Palestinian statehood and advancing an international path toward a two-state solution. Those efforts were linked to Palestinian commitments to reform, renew democratic legitimacy, and hold elections.
When we postpone this vote again, we confront our partners with a difficult question: How can they defend support for Palestinian institutions that deny their own people the opportunity to choose their representatives?
I cannot say with certainty that donor countries will freeze their assistance. But I fear this decision will weaken their willingness to honor their commitments and make it harder to defend support for us before their parliaments and taxpayers.
When our institutions and public services depend on that support, international trust becomes a direct Palestinian interest. Squandering it places an additional burden on citizens who are already suffering. Even so, I still see an opportunity to correct course, and I place cautious hope in it.
President Mahmoud Abbas has the authority on the Palestinian side to bring the date forward. Macron can use his diplomatic influence to support that correction and link the reform process to a clear electoral timetable in the near future.
We may have missed the opportunity to hold elections on November 28, 2026, but that does not justify waiting until September 11, 2027. I call for presidential and legislative elections to be brought forward to no later than March 2027, with preparations beginning immediately and conditions created that allow all Palestinian lists and political forces wishing to stand to carry out their preparatory work and activities on the ground.
Elections alone will not solve all our crises. But they give people a peaceful means of demanding accountability, open institutions to new talent, and rebuild trust between citizens and their leadership. Every day we postpone this opportunity makes it harder to recover.
At Masar Jadid, we will continue reaching out to everyone who can help. We will use the political, administrative, and legal means available to advocate for an earlier date. We will participate in every serious national dialogue that leads to a clear outcome: returning the decision to the people.
I hold Sheikh and Mezher politically responsible for pushing for the postponement. I call on Abbas to correct the decision he signed, and I urge Macron to help protect the opportunity that remains.
Thirty-eight years ago, Rabadi told me: “Don’t leave me.”
Today, in those words, I hear the voice of an entire Palestinian generation waiting for someone to open the door.
We have a duty not to leave them behind.
Samer Sinijlawi is a Palestinian political figure from Jerusalem and the founder and president of Masar Jadid (New Path), a Palestinian political movement advocating democracy, nonviolence, reform, and regional peace.

Iran's stock market climbs despite US blockade, energy shortages, collapsing currency

Iran’s stock market has recently rallied despite its plummeting economy.
Iran International reported on Tuesday that the Iranian stock market has seen an influx of Investments, despite increasing power outages, a shortage of foreign currency, and the rate of the rial tanking.
The report noted that this could mean one of two things: either investors believe Tehran and Washington will reach a peace deal soon, or they have no other way to stop their savings from losing value.
Iran International points to a few competing analyses of the situation to better explain investors’ choices.
One analysis from Farau indicates that a lack of foreign exchange currency in the country, energy shortages, and uncertainty over the war are the primary stressors for Tehran’s economy.
Why is Iran's stock market rallying?
Iranian oil exports have effectively stopped under the US blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, leaving Iran with a dwindling supply of foreign currency.
The report noted that Khabar Online cited a 35,000-toman rise ($.003495) in the free-dollar market in the last month alone.
Additionally, energy shortages in Iran are exacerbating the problems. Iran's energy sector was already underfunded before the war began, and strikes on Iranian energy infrastructure have further strained production.
On top of that, Iranian investors are unsure what comes next. The economic effects of a third round of war would be disastrous, but diplomatic efforts continue.
Businesses that rely on imported goods are feeling these effects, as they face higher operating costs with less access to foreign currency, Iran International added.
These factors significantly complicate long-term investment and leave Iranians seeking assets that will preserve their value.
Some analyses indicated that investors are optimistic about a deal.
Rouydad24 argued that investors expect a deal and believe more access to international markets is on the horizon.
However, Iran International noted that other analyses show a different picture.
Just because the market is rising does not mean that investors in Iran are optimistic about the country’s economic prospects. Instead, it might indicate that Iranian’s lack alternatives for preserving their wealth.
The rial’s value has tanked, property is losing value, and bank deposits are losing purchasing power, making domestic equities more attractive to investors, the report noted.
This could offer a more stable assessment than the first: investors may be buying domestic stocks out of fear that cash will lose value in the country.
This comes as the International Monetary Fund forecasted that Iran’s economy would contract by 7.6% in 2026, as compared to the rate of 5.4% projected in July.
Notably, Iran International noted that the Middle East and Central Asia were expected to contract by 0.3%.

Kraków’s new mayor withdraws patronage of LGBT+ equality march
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14

21:01:37 KST

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
In one of his first policy announcements since being elected on Sunday, the new mayor of Kraków, Poland’s second-largest city, has declared that he will withdraw official patronage of its annual LGBT+ equality march.
Łukasz Gibała, who has been supportive of LGBT+ rights in the past and has previously attended the march, argues that the event has become too “partisan”. He stood for election as an independent and has pledged to depoliticise city hall.
His decision does not prevent the march from taking place. But it means that it no longer has the official support of the city.
Łukasz Gibała: Nie obejmę patronatem Marszu Równości. Polityka progresywna nie zawsze się sprawdza https://t.co/vIw8ZsSPQK
— Radio Kraków (@RadioKrakow) October 12, 2026
Kraków’s equality march, which was first held in 2004, draws thousands of participants when it takes place each year in May. The event is used to demand greater LGBT+ rights in Poland, which is ranked as one of the worst countries in Europe for LGBT+ people.
In 2021, the city’s former mayor, Jacek Majchrowski, became an honorary patron of the march. In 2024, his successor, Aleksander Miszalski, became the first mayor to attend the event, declaring that Kraków should be “a home for everyone”.
However, Miszalski was removed from office earlier this year in a recall referendum, necessitating a new election, which was won by Gibała. He beat Monika Piątkowska, who, like Miszaski, is a member of the centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party of Prime Minister Donald Tusk.
Kraków's new mayor has announced that he will attend the city’s LGBT parade next week, something his long-serving predecessor never did.
"I want to build a tolerant Kraków, a home for everyone," says @OlekMiszalski, who took office this week https://t.co/ZQ9SzZiHp4
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 9, 2024
The day after his victory, Gibała was asked by local broadcaster Radio Kraków if he would continue city hall’s patronage of the equality march. The new mayor, who takes office next week, declared that he would not, saying he “will avoid sponsoring events that have a partisan character”.
“I have the impression that, over the past three years or so, the community that organises equality marches has simply become partisan,” said Gibała. “These are people who ran for parliament and local government on the lists of specific political parties.”
Gibała did not indicate who he was referring to. However, one of the organisers of the equality march in Kraków is Magdalena Dropek, who has three times stood as a candidate for The Left (Lewica), one of the groups in Tusk’s ruling coalition, in elections to the Polish and European parliaments.
Gibała emphasised that he has himself attended equality marches in the past “and does not regret it”. He was previously an MP for both KO (when it was known as Civic Platform, PO) as well as for the liberal Palikot’s Movement (Ruch Palikota), later known as Your Movement (Twój Ruch).
During the recent mayoral election campaign, Gibała told broadcaster TVN that, as an MP, he had supported the introduction of same-sex civil partnerships in Poland, and said that his views had not changed.
When asked if that meant that, as mayor, he would continue the city’s practice of transcribing foreign same-sex marriages into the civil registry – as Poland was ordered to do last year by the Court of Justice of the European Union – Gibała said that he would.
However, he added that he was doing this as a “legalist” who respects the current legal situation. “If a different political party wins [parliamentary elections] next year and changes the law in Poland, it [recognition of foreign same-sex marriages] won’t happen,” he told Radio Kraków.
In fact, although the current government supports recognition of foreign-same sex marraiges, it has not changed the law in that regard. Polish law still does not recognise any form of same-sex union.
The government, aware that opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki would veto any change to the law, instead issued a regulation (which does not require presidential approval) empowering local authorities to transcribe foreign same-sex marriages into their registries.
Many municipalities, especially more liberal larger cities, have begun to do so (some even did before the regulation was issued). But others, especially in more conservative places, have refused to, often arguing that there are legal doubts around the issue.
Data provided to the Polish Press Agency (PAP) by the digital affairs ministry last week showed that 516 foreign same-sex marriages have so far been registered in Poland. The largest numbers were in Warsaw (209), Wrocław (73) and Kraków (46).
The Polish government has granted same-sex couples who married abroad the same tax rights as other married couples
It follows an EU court ruling ordering Poland to recognise such marriages even though domestic law does not allow any form of same-sex union https://t.co/3gE1PQU9AQ
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 25, 2026
In the same interview this week with Radio Kraków, Gibała was asked if he would “return to your political roots” and be a “progressive mayor”. He responded by saying that, while “there are some issues where progressive policies actually work, there are others where they don’t”.
Asked for an example of the latter, Gibała said that, “if we look, for example, at what’s happening in western European cities, there are entire neighbourhoods in which there is a fear of entering for people of our skin colour”.
