Police hold 11 in raid on Turkey pro-opposition Halk TV
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
08:30:00 UTC
17:30:00 KST

Breadcrumb
Police hold 11 in raid on Turkey pro-opposition Halk TV
Turkish police raided the headquarters of the pro-opposition Halk TV, halting its live broadcasts and arresting 11 people, the channel and prosecutors said early Wednesday.
"Police raid at Halk TV headquarters! A trustee (manager) has been appointed, broadcasts have been halted," the channel wrote on X shortly before 7:00 am (0400 GMT).
Halk's news channel and the live broadcasts on its YouTube site were both offline.
It was the latest crackdown on the pro-opposition media and came just two weeks after the authorities shut down the website and social media accounts of T24, a leading digital news website, citing its "LGBT propaganda".
In a statement to Turkish media, prosecutors said they had issued a warrant for 17 people, 11 of whom had been detained as part of an investigation into Halk's chairman Cafer Mahiroglu on suspicion of "bribery", "rigging tenders," and "money laundering."
It said companies co-owned or managed by Mahiroglu had been seized and that the authorities put a government-appointed trustee in charge of them.
Of the remaining six people named in the warrant, four were abroad, one was in a correctional facility, and the last was still being sought for, it said.
Mahiroglu was not among those detained as he lives abroad.
'We're under a blockade'
In several posts as dawn was breaking, Halk journalists said they were unable to get into the building.
"The police have sealed off the entrance to our building. That's the situation... There's nothing left to say," wrote Onur Dalar on X, his words echoed by a colleague.
"At Halk TV, the management is now under a trustee. Broadcasting systems have been seized. Our channel is literally under blockade. I still can't get into the institution where I've worked for 5 years—none of us can. The police haven't left the building," wrote Gamze Altunay.
The move came just hours before the start of the defence's arguments in the sprawling corruption trial of jailed Istanbul mayor Ekrem Imamoglu and some 400 other defendants.
The move drew a furious reaction from the main opposition Yeni Parti and the Turkish Journalists' Union (TGS)
"In recent years, the lawlessness used by the political authorities to overcome every problem has once again struck freedom of the press today... We do not accept this tyranny!" wrote TGS on X.
And opposition leader Ozgur Ozel also lashed out against a TV channel "watched by millions" describing the government's action as "weak and cowardly".
"Storming a TV channel with a police raid at dawn and appointing a trustee is something only dictators do. Unfortunately, they have brought our country to this state," he wrote.
He said it was no coincidence the raids came just hours before the start of the defence arguments in Imamoglu's trial.
"They did this on the very day the defence was to begin in Turkey's biggest political trial. Those who appoint trustees to municipalities and usurp the will of the people have now appointed a trustee to Halk TV, watched by millions. Because they are WEAK and COWARDLY!"
Last year, Halk TV—which has faced repeated sanctions from Turkey's broadcasting regulator—was threatened with possible closure over its critical tone towards the government of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

Bank and fintech: How partnership is transforming the auto lending market
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
08:29:41 UTC
17:29:41 KST

Bank and fintech: How partnership is transforming the auto lending market
Today, creating a financial product that meets market demand requires more than simply issuing a loan. It is important to make the entire customer journey fast, convenient and digital. That is why banks are increasingly combining their financial expertise with the technologies of fintech companies. Bank RBK and Sapa Digital Finance demonstrate how this approach works in practice, Qazinform News Agency reports.
Stronger together
The global financial market is gradually changing its traditional development model: instead of building all the infrastructure themselves, banks are engaging technology partners. This allows them to launch products faster, automate processes and scale their businesses without unnecessary operating costs.
For Kazakhstan, this approach is particularly relevant in auto lending. According to the First Credit Bureau, the market grew by almost 44% over two years, from 2023 to 2025, reaching 2.39 trillion tenge. Amid growing demand, competitive advantage is determined not only by loan terms but also by how quickly and easily customers can obtain financing.
From application to car purchase — a digital process
Bank RBK and Sapa Digital Finance (SDF) have been cooperating since 2023. The partners have combined their competencies: the bank provides the financial component and sets lending parameters, while SDF is responsible for technological support, process automation and interaction with customers and partners.
“Today, a bank’s competitiveness is determined, among other things, by its ability to quickly turn technology into tangible benefits for customers. Our partnership with Sapa Digital Finance allows us to leverage an established technological infrastructure, scale our auto lending business and make the financing process more convenient. This is an example of how combining expertise helps create products that meet market demand and develop business,” says Natalya Akentyeva, Chairwoman of the Management Board of Bank RBK.
Since the partnership began, 65,000 Kazakhstanis have received auto loans. SDF’s technological platform brings together all participants in the process within a single digital environment, providing access to financing through a partner network across different regions of the country.
Loan applications are assessed in real time using artificial intelligence, while the loan application process, including collateral registration, can be completed on the same day. This is particularly important for those who need a vehicle not only for personal use but also for work: more than 10,000 auto loans have been issued to individual entrepreneurs over the course of the partnership.
At the same time, lending speed should not come at the expense of loan portfolio quality. Amid increased market attention to the quality of auto loans, modern credit scoring models play a particularly important role, allowing lenders to comprehensively assess borrowers’ creditworthiness and determine credit risk levels more accurately. Their application helps make well-informed lending decisions, combining access to financing with a responsible approach to loan portfolio management. Technology therefore not only speeds up processes but also enhances the quality of lending decisions.
Another area of cooperation is subsidizing the purchase of domestically manufactured vehicles, which helps make them more affordable for buyers and supports demand for cars assembled in Kazakhstan.
Technology at the service of customers
“For us, the importance of technology lies primarily in how it helps people. Today, customers want not only to obtain an auto loan on favorable terms but also to complete the process quickly, conveniently and without unnecessary complications. Together with Bank RBK, we have combined the bank’s reliability, our AI-based technologies and an extensive network of car dealerships to make the car-buying process simpler and more accessible. The use of AI helps us accelerate processes, reduce waiting times and offer customers more convenient services. Behind the 65,000 auto loans issued are real people, their needs and their plans. For us, this is the main result of the partnership and confirmation that modern technology should, above all, serve the interests of people,” says Yeldar Tenizbayev, Chairman of the Supervisory Board of Sapa Digital Finance.
The partnership between Bank RBK and SDF reflects a key trend in the financial market: technology delivers the greatest impact when combined with banking expertise. The bank gains opportunities to scale its lending operations, the fintech partner provides the technological foundation, and customers benefit from simpler and faster access to financing.
This is precisely the new logic of the financial business: rather than building everything independently, partners combine their strengths to offer customers higher-quality and more accessible solutions.
Bank RBK is one of Kazakhstan’s largest commercial banks, ranking 5th in terms of corporate loan portfolio size, 7th in total assets and 10th in equity.
Sapa Group is a Kazakhstan-based technology group of companies developing solutions in fintech, artificial intelligence and business process automation.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that Bank RBK led Kazakhstan’s banks in term deposit growth, recording a 47.8% year-on-year increase.
License No. 1.1.821.135, issued by the Agency for Regulation and Development of the Financial Market of the Republic of Kazakhstan on July 15, 2026.

Kazakhstan’s vice minister calls for labeling AI-generated content
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
08:29:27 UTC

Kazakhstan’s vice minister calls for labeling AI-generated content
Kazakhstan’s First Vice Minister of Culture and Information Kanat Iskakov has called for labeling content created using artificial intelligence. He made the remarks during a panel session at Astana Media Week 2026, Qazinform News Agency correspondent reports.
According to Iskakov, viewers, readers and online users should be aware when AI technologies have been used to produce news and other media content. He described this as one of the key principles for building a transparent media environment and strengthening public trust.
Iskakov also stressed the need to develop professional and ethical standards for the use of artificial intelligence. At the same time, journalists and editorial teams must remain responsible for the content they publish.
“We greatly overestimate the capabilities of AI. It is a tool, a way to speed up the preparation and delivery of documents and materials. But the most important thing is responsibility, and that responsibility lies with the journalist,” the vice minister said.
Speaking about the future of the media industry, he also suggested that digital technologies would gradually erase the traditional boundaries between different types of media.
“In the near future, there will be no distinction between websites, television and news agencies. Information will be delivered through multiple channels and in multiple formats. We will have an entire information ecosystem,” Iskakov said.
Astana Media Week, which is celebrating its 10th anniversary this year, is taking place in the Kazakh capital from October 14 to 16. The forum focuses on the transformation of the media industry, the impact of artificial intelligence on journalism and new approaches to building trust in information.
Earlier,Qazinform News Agency reported that new AI transparency requirements came into effect in the European Union on August 2. The rules require the labelling of deepfakes and certain other categories of AI-generated content, including text on matters of public interest published without human editorial oversight or review.

Moscow, Washington vs. Kyiv: Can Trump Force Ukraine to Capitulate?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
08:29:26 UTC
17:29:26 KST

US President Donald Trump’s recent statements have by now fully aligned with those coming from the Kremlin.
Meanwhile, on the front line, the Russian army has had no advantage for almost a year. Indeed, the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) is counterattacking and liberating settlements in the Donbas itself – the region Putin has identified as a key objective for the Russian military.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Against this backdrop, Trump has partially lifted energy sanctions on Russia and announced an agreement to import several hundred thousand tons of diesel fuel from Russia to the US.
Then, under the guise of a peace plan, Trump began issuing ultimatums to Ukraine, demanding that it stop striking Russian oil refineries, and calling for “no strikes on oil refining facilities.” The plan is supposedly bilateral but is, in practice, one-sided in Ukraine’s case, since Ukraine has only one oil refinery, which Russia has already destroyed.
After the ultimatum, Trump went further, declaring that Ukraine “should get” a new president because he was dissatisfied with Zelensky’s refusal to sign a “peace agreement.”
Predictably, this was followed by threats to stop supplying Ukraine with intelligence about Russian ballistic missile strikes against Ukrainian civilian targets.
By Oct. 13, after the initial emotions and passions had subsided, new US proposals for a peace agreement were revealed by Washington Post columnist David Ignatius. There has been some progress: the Russian demands for territorial concessions are no longer repeated.
US-Russia Diesel Deal: What’s The Big Idea?
Ukrainian reaction
The reaction of most Ukrainians to the latest developments is extremely sharp.
“Trump’s energy truce means that Ukraine does not strike Russian oil refineries that are operating, while Russia does not strike the Ukrainian refinery that is not operating. The next step in Trump’s incredible plan will be to announce a ceasefire. Ukraine will have to promise not to strike the Russian army, and Russia will give its word not to strike the Russian army. And peace will immediately follow,” investment banker Serhiy Fursa wrote.
“The overall strategy has long been clear: blame Ukraine for your own miscalculations and use Russian oil refineries as an example, while shielding a target that is genuinely painful for the Russians. The figures for Russian diesel supplies to the US are not what matters here. What matters is the violation of laws passed by Congress, as well as the creation of new precedents for cooperation and business with the Russian war machine,” said Olha Aivazovska, head of the OPORA civil society analytical group.
“By refusing to provide us with intelligence on the trajectories of missile attacks against Ukraine, America is, in effect, becoming complicit in Russia’s murder of Ukrainian civilians,” said Oleksandr Shvets, editor-in-chief of the Fakty newspaper.
A member of the Cabinet of Ministers told Kyiv Post that Trump’s move had come as a complete surprise to Ukrainians.
“This is simply unthinkable. It is a betrayal of every allied position. It is worse than the Russians,” he said.
Why do Trump and Putin need the diesel deal?
The US president’s motives are clearly an attempt to forestall an Election Day disaster for Republicans on Nov. 3. He hopes, at the very least, to convince Americans that he is doing something about sky-high fuel prices.
Putin’s motives, however, are more perhaps more complex. Despite the negligible export volumes, Russian experts believe he can present the deal to a war-weary Russian population as a victory –signaling renewed warming of relations and rapprochement with the US.
“What does Putin need this for? To damage Trump’s relations with Zelensky and Europe, which, like Zelensky, has condemned the deal. And to try to use it as leverage, so that Trump pressures Zelensky to restrict Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries,” wrote Russian economist Kirill Rogov.
Zelensky is presented as the problem… again
Among other things, Trump said that Ukraine should “have a new president” because, supposedly, Zelensky did not want to sign a peace agreement – a capitulation in a war that Ukraine is not losing.
Numerous analyses have been published in Ukraine and elsewhere showing that the various peace-plan proposals put forward by Russia through US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were effectively one-sided. They took into account only the aggressor’s demands, in a form that was absolutely unacceptable to Ukraine. In particular, Russia wanted to obtain, without a fight, territories where its army had made no progress over the preceding four years despite suffering heavy losses.
Trump’s statements about the need to replace Ukraine’s president are fundamentally at odds with the principles of a democratic country – the kind of country Trump represents.
First, elections cannot be held in Ukraine during wartime because most people living near the front line, in occupied territories, or as refugees, as well as those currently fighting on the front line, would be unable to vote.
Second, holding elections during the war without the participation of Zelensky’s main competitors – who are senior officers or generals and therefore cannot leave their posts while martial law remains in force – could produce a result Trump would not expect: Zelensky would have a strong chance of winning.
Third, the issue goes far beyond the president. According to opinion polls, the overwhelming majority of Ukrainians do not want to make concessions to Moscow. Nor is there any evidence of declining morale in the army or of soldiers wanting to hand over anything to Russia.
The main reason is that everyone understands that as soon as Putin gets one territory, he will use it as a base to attack others and demand those as well – endlessly.
“The issue is not Zelensky. It is the Ukrainian army and Ukrainian civil society that do not want to capitulate to Moscow. To think that changing the president will change Ukrainians’ approach to the war is nonsense. But Donald Trump has demonstrated a complete lack of understanding of the nature of Russian aggression against Ukraine since the very beginning of his presidency. He likewise fails to understand the essence of Ukrainian resistance,” said writer and journalist Radomyr Mokryk.
Not even the ‘peace party’ can accept capitulation
Ukraine’s political discourse includes not only the determination to continue resisting Russia but also a willingness to hold peace talks with Russia and make some concessions to the aggressor as a compromise for peace.
This tendency is represented by various politicians. Some are trying to establish themselves among the military “heavyweights,” while others are seeking to appeal to Trump. Still others are simply trying to capitalize on the war fatigue felt by part of society, along with constant power outages and the fear of being killed by shelling far from the front line.
These politicans from different parties are not taking part in one initiative, but informally known among journalists as the “peace party” (with ironic sense of this term).
Among them - many politicians associated with this tendency are figures of varying stature.
They include popular lawmakers Oleksiy Honcharenko and Danylo Hetmantsev, Kharkiv Mayor Ihor Terekhov, etc.
It is important to note, however, that none of them supports capitulation exclusively on Russia’s terms, let alone handing over territories that the Ukrainian army firmly controls.
For example, Honcharenko, who has faced a wave of public condemnation and accusations of “capitulationism” (in commentsaries on his pages in social media), explained his position as follows:
“Peace cannot be achieved with a single decision. Yes, we will have to discuss compromises, but compromise is not capitulation. It means finding terms under which Ukraine can end the war, obtain real security guarantees, and preserve its national interests. We must not give Russia anything. Every agreement must take Ukrainian interests into account,” Honcharenko said.
Even with such wording, however, he faced criticism on social media.
The issues of existential survival and capitulation lie largely outside the political sphere and do not depend on the identity of the president or members of parliament.
Attempts to change or dismiss this reality are naturally perceived as a form of coercion into capitulation, and anyone engaged in such efforts is seen as Putin’s accomplice and complicit in Russian aggression.
This is the dividing line between “peace” and “capitulation.”

Türkiye plans QR code age checks for cigarette sales to address privacy concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
08:27:00 UTC
17:27:00 KST

Türkiye is preparing to introduce a QR code-based age verification system for cigarette purchases, allowing retailers to confirm that customers are at least 18 without accessing their personal information, as authorities seek to restrict minors’ access to tobacco products.
The Health Ministry and the ruling Justice and Development Party’s parliamentary group are working on draft legislation that would introduce electronic identity verification at tobacco sales points, modeled on similar practices in Japan and South Korea, according to reports in local media.
Under the proposed system, customers would present a QR code generated by the relevant public authority and scanned using their phones. The system would cross-check the code against the buyer’s Turkish identification number to determine whether they have reached the legal age for purchasing tobacco.
The planned approach aims to address privacy concerns by allowing sellers to verify a customer’s eligibility without accessing their name, exact age or other personal details. Authorities are considering applying the system to physical outlets, including supermarkets, grocery stores and kiosks, as well as online tobacco sales.
The draft legislation cites findings from Türkiye’s 2017 Global Youth Tobacco Survey, which found that 73.3 percent of students aged 13 to 15 who smoked said they could easily purchase cigarettes from retail outlets, despite being under 18.
The proposed electronic verification system is intended to strengthen enforcement of the legal age limit and make it more difficult for minors to obtain tobacco products.
The draft also envisages using the electronic infrastructure to monitor not only buyers’ ages but also the quantities of tobacco products they can purchase daily, introducing an additional layer of oversight over retail sales.
Authorities aim to develop the system and put it into operation within one year, according to the report.
The Health Ministry is expected to establish the rules and procedures governing the electronic infrastructure after consulting the Agriculture and Forestry Ministry.
The measures remain at the draft stage, and further details on how the system would operate in practice have yet to be finalized.

MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. Air defenses shot down 902 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions overnight, the Defense Ministry said in a statement.
The attempted Ukrainian drone attack on the Moscow Region was one of the largest in two years, according to TASS calculations based on data published by Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin.
The drone attack paralyzed operations at Moscow’s four airports: Vnukovo, Domodedovo, Zhukovsky and Sheremetyevo suspended arrivals and departures for varying periods. All four airports resumed operations at 6:44 a.m. Moscow time [3:44 a.m. GMT].
One person was killed in the drone attack in Balakovo, Saratov Region. Several residential buildings were also damaged.
Later, Sber confirmed that a drone attack targeted a data center in Balakovo, Saratov Region, noting that all the company’s systems and services are operating normally.
TASS has compiled the key details of the aftermath.
Scale
- Air defenses on duty destroyed 902 Ukrainian unmanned aerial vehicles over the Belgorod, Bryansk, Volgograd, Voronezh, Vladimir, Kaluga, Kursk, Lipetsk, Novgorod, Oryol, Rostov, Ryazan, Saratov, Smolensk, Tver, Tula, Moscow, Krasnodar and Stavropol regions, as well as Crimea and the Sea of Azov, last night, between 8:00 p.m. Moscow time on October 13 and 8:00 a.m. Moscow time [5:00 p.m. to 5:00 a.m. GMT - TASS].
- The attempted Ukrainian drone attack on the Moscow Region was one of the largest in two years, according to TASS calculations based on data published by Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin.
- He said that 493 drones were heading toward the Moscow Region between 8:30 p.m. Moscow time on October 13 and 7:00 a.m. Moscow time on October 14 [5:30 p.m. to 4:00 a.m. GMT - TASS].
- Most were intercepted by air defenses before they approached Moscow, with 180 destroyed as they were closing in on the capital.
- More than 160 drones were destroyed overnight in Kamensk-Shakhtinsky and the Kamensky, Kasharsky, Millerovsky, Morozovsky, Tarasovsky, Tatsinsky, Chertkovsky and Sholokhovsky districts of the Rostov Region, Governor Yury Slyusar said on Max.
- Air defenses destroyed 20 Ukrainian drones over the Kaluga Region overnight, Governor Vladislav Shapsha wrote on Max.
- Air defenses destroyed 11 Ukrainian drones over the Tula Region, Governor Dmitry Milyaev said on Max.
- A drone attack was repelled in the Stavropol Region, Governor Vladimir Vladimirov wrote on Max.
Moscow Region airport operations
- On the evening of October 13, three Moscow airports, Vnukovo, Domodedovo and Zhukovsky, introduced temporary restrictions on arrivals and departures, the Federal Air Transport Agency reported.
- Sheremetevo later also suspended flight operations.
- All four airports resumed operations at 6:44 a.m. Moscow time [3:44 a.m. GMT] on October 14.
- Vnukovo did not handle flights for more than eight hours. During the restrictions, all passengers were returned from aircraft to the terminals.
- Sheremetyevo said that flight schedules could change and that departures would take place as aircraft became ready.
- Domodedovo also warned of possible schedule changes. Airport services are operating in an enhanced mode to dispatch delayed flights and receive arriving aircraft as quickly as possible.
- Aeroflot continues to adjust its flight schedule for October 14 to stabilize operations as quickly as possible following temporary restrictions at Sheremetyevo, the airline said in a statement on Max.
- The airline is also continuing to notify passengers of schedule changes using the contact details provided at the time of booking.
- Passengers waiting to have their tickets reissued at Sheremetyevo are being offered bottled water.
- Depending on the length of the wait, some are also being provided with drinks, meals and hotel accommodation.
- Aeroflot representatives continue to assist passengers at alternate airports.
- Flights to Moscow are being organized in accordance with crew working-hour regulations.
- Rossiya Airlines said on Max that it was adjusting the schedules of some flights, including those operated under its shuttle service between Moscow and St. Petersburg, due to the earlier restrictions on departures and arrivals at Sheremetyevo and Vnukovo.

- A woman was reportedly killed in a drone attack in Balakovo, Saratov Region, Governor Roman Busargin said on Max, citing preliminary information.
- Several residential buildings were also damaged.
- Emergency response services are working at the scene.

- All infrastructure facilities in Balakovo are operating normally, Busargin said later.

- Temporary accommodation will be arranged if necessary.

A bipartisan group of U.S. senators on Oct. 13 called on U.S. President Donald Trump to rescind his deal to buy Russian diesel, joining other colleagues in Congress who lambasted the controversial agreement.

"Granting Moscow the ability to sell Russian diesel freely in global markets damages American security interests and is a betrayal of the people of Ukraine, who continue to defend themselves from Putin's murderous, illegal war," the letter read.
The agreement was announced as Trump ramps up pressure on Kyiv to halt attacks against Russian refineries as part of his unilaterally announced energy truce, with his administration threatening to cut off intelligence and arms shipments to Ukraine.

Earlier, on Oct. 11, seven bipartisan members of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee released a statement condemning the decision, urging the White House to "immediately reverse course."

Russia strikes military-linked energy facilities across Ukraine (VIDEOS)
Russian forces launched an overnight barrage against energy and communications infrastructure across Ukraine, targeting facilities that support the Ukrainian military, the Defense Ministry in Moscow has said.
In a statement on Wednesday, the ministry said high-precision ground-based weapons and long-range attack drones were used to attack facilities in Kiev, its suburbs, and Kharkov Region.
In Kiev, the ministry said the strikes hit the Darnytskaya combined heat and power plant (CHP-4) and Kiev CHP-5, which it said were supplying power to Ukrainian military installations and defense manufacturers. It also reported that it hit the ATM Ukrsibbank data center, which was used for collecting intelligence about Russian forces.
In the region of Kiev, the targets included Kiev CHP-6, the Trypilska thermal power plant, and the Kievskaya electricity substation. According to the ministry, the facilities supplied power to military logistics hubs, weapons storage sites, and defense enterprises.
In Kharkov and the surrounding region, Russian forces struck Kharkov CHP-5 and the Zmievskaya thermal power plant, which supplied electricity to military-industrial enterprises and Ukrainian defense installations.
Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky confirmed the attacks, saying Russia launched 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 attack drones and loitering munitions overnight. “At least 600,000 people are currently, unfortunately, without electricity,” he said, warning that further outages are possible. He added that significant damage was done to 26 elements of Ukraine’s power system and four oil and gas facilities.
The Ukrainian Air Force reported that it shot down four missiles out of 39, amid reports of critically low stocks of US-made Patriot interceptors.
Kiev Mayor Vitaly Klitschko claimed that three people were killed and at least 22 were injured in the barrage, adding that the attacks caused extensive electricity outages.
The head of Ukrzaliznytsia, Ukraine’s state railway operator, Aleksandr Pertsovsky, also reported strikes on infrastructure in five regions – Kharkov, Kiev, Vinnitsa, Khmelnitsky, and Ternopol – with locomotive and carriage depots, maintenance facilities, railway stations, and rolling stock coming under attack. He described the material damage as substantial, adding that railway personnel did not suffer any casualties.
The attacks come amid growing tensions between Kiev and Washington over intelligence sharing. US President Donald Trump recently said “it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president,” as Zelensky’s term expired more than two years ago. He also urged the Ukrainian leader to stop striking Russian oil refineries. Zelensky replied that he is ready to do so if Russia stops attacking Ukrainian energy facilities.
Following the strikes, Zelensky said Ukraine’s Western backers failed to provide advance warnings about Russian ballistic missile launches for the second time that week. He also claimed that the US threatened to suspend intelligence sharing unless Ukraine stops attacking Russian refineries.
However, he stressed that cooperation has not been halted, echoing Trump’s earlier remarks in which he said the US is “helping [Ukraine], and we are sharing intel.”
The latest barrage came after the Russian Defense Ministry vowed earlier this month to intensify strikes on military-related facilities in Ukraine in response to Zelensky’s threat to step up attacks on Russian oil refineries.

Norstat: Isamaa extends lead in front of Center again
Support for Isamaa has risen slightly over the past four weeks, widening its lead over the Center Party, according to the weekly Norstat AS poll.
According to the latest results, Isamaa is supported by 24.3 percent of eligible voters, followed by the Center Party at 21.7 percent and the Social Democratic Party (SDE) at 15.4 percent.

The coalition parties have a combined support rating of 14.3 percent, while the opposition parties in the Riigikogu are supported by 75.6 percent of respondents.
The latest aggregated results cover the polling period from September 14 to October 12, during which a total of 4,000 voting-age Estonian citizens were surveyed. Norstat conducted the surveys September 14-19, September 21-27, September 28-October 3 and October 5-12.
To ensure the sample was as representative as possible, the surveys used a combination of telephone and online interviews, with telephone respondents making up the vast majority. The sample data was weighted according to key sociodemographic characteristics to reflect the proportional distribution of eligible voters and ensure the results were representative.
Voters who did not express a party preference were excluded from the calculation of the parties' relative support ratings.
The maximum margin of error depends on the proportion of respondents belonging to the largest group. In this survey, Isamaa supporters made up the largest group, giving a margin of error of plus or minus 1.6 percentage points. The margin of error is smaller for the other parties, standing at plus or minus 0.41 percentage points for Eesti 200, for example.

Deloitte Cyprus falsified documents to help Roman Abramovich hide $10 billion in assets, investigation says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
08:24:29 UTC
17:24:29 KST

Deloitte, one of the world’s largest accounting firms, falsified corporate documents in order to help billionaire Roman Abramovich conceal assets and avoid taxes, according to a joint investigation by The Bureau of Investigative Journalism, BBC Panorama, The Guardian and OCCRP. The assets involved were worth more than $10 billion, the investigation said.
The investigation found that Deloitte Cyprus and Meritservus, a firm spun off from it, falsified at least 1,000 corporate documents for Abramovich. Employees backdated records by as much as five years, and Deloitte later approved the accounts in its capacity as an “independent auditor.” The scheme allowed Abramovich to avoid paying millions of dollars in taxes.
The investigation said the schemes involving Abramovich’s assets also included Eugene Tenenbaum, Abramovich’s longtime right-hand man in London, and Demetris Ioannides, who headed Deloitte’s Cyprus operation before later founding Meritservus.
Sibneft shares
One of the central episodes involved Kravin Investments, a Cyprus-registered company that was among the offshore structures through which Abramovich held his stake in the Russian oil company Sibneft. In 2003, Kravin received $3 billion as the first installment in the sale of Abramovich’s Sibneft shares. About $2 billion of that sum remained in Kravin's bank accounts, where it generated interest income and thereby created substantial tax liabilities.
According to the investigation, in 2005 Abramovich’s aides began working with representatives of Deloitte and Meritservus to create large numbers of backdated documents in order to avoid having to pay taxes on the interest the money was earning. The paperwork claimed Kravin had transferred the $3 billion to another Abramovich-owned company and had merely been holding and investing the money on that company’s behalf, meaning it was not taxable.
A châteaux, yachts and private jets
In 2005, Deloitte prepared draft financial statements for Abramovich’s Cyprus company Amiscan Investments Ltd. Under new disclosure rules, the company was required to report its assets, which were valued at more than $600 million. They included a $38 million estate in Sussex, England, an $8 million London apartment, the Château de la Croë on the French Riviera, several private jets, various superyachts and helicopters, and a supercar.
However, when Amiscan’s audited financial statements were officially published, all of those assets had disappeared. As it turned out, Deloitte, Meritservus, and Abramovich’s business associates had prepared backdated agreements transferring the assets from Amiscan to its shareholder, Kelvedon Worldwide — a company registered in the British Virgin Islands, where disclosure requirements were less severe. According to the investigation, no one appeared to notice that Kelvedon did not actually own Amiscan at the stated time of the “agreement” and therefore could not have received the assets.
Deloitte knew the agreements were fictitious, the investigation said, as it already had a draft of Amiscan’s financial statements containing detailed descriptions of the assets. Deloitte nevertheless canceled that version and approved a new one, stating that it gave a “true and fair view” of the company’s financial position.
A “twin” company
At the top of Abramovich’s offshore network was Cyprus-registered Electus Investments Ltd., which controlled other holding companies and, through them, Abramovich’s stake in Sibneft. In 2003, Electus became subject to new Cyprus disclosure rules. Unlike Amiscan, however, it had no parent company to which the assets could be transferred, making the earlier workaround unavailable.
The documents reviewed as part of the investigation indicate that Deloitte had reserved the name of a duplicate company in the British Virgin Islands as early as late 2002. In November 2003, Deloitte formally incorporated the company and placed ownership in the name of a nominee shareholder. The leaked documents contained no information about the Electus “twin” until it began playing a key role in the alleged backdating scheme. Instead of disclosing or transferring the assets, Deloitte simply replaced Electus Investments Ltd with the previously registered duplicate. Assets worth more than $10 billion effectively “disappeared” from one company and “appeared” in another. And yet, the substitution went unnoticed for more than two decades.
The story has an even earlier dimension. In 2000, Abramovich wanted to take just under $100 million out of companies that owned Sibneft, which by then were held through Cyprus-based entities. According to the leaked records, it was important to Abramovich that the transaction not reveal the Cyprus layer of the structure and that the payment appear to be earned income. Deloitte proposed creating a package of backdated consulting agreements involving Abramovich directly.
Abramovich’s Sibneft-holding companies were to pay an intermediary, PB Mediapower Enterprises Ltd, $98 million for “consultancy services.” That company would then pay Abramovich 99.9% of the sum as a “commission” for acting as an “agent.” The supposed consulting services involved advice on buying and selling Sibneft shares among other companies owned by Abramovich. Because the share transactions had taken place approximately one year earlier, Deloitte identified a suitable dormant Cyprus shell company that had already existed at the time.
Deloitte signed the allegedly falsified documents and included them in the annual accounts. Abramovich’s commission was then structured as promissory notes — essentially IOUs — which he cashed in over the following three years. The leaked records include 50 of these notes bearing his signature.
Lawyers for Abramovich and Tenenbaum said their clients were unaware of any falsification of documents and did not take part in or authorize such actions. Deloitte Cyprus said it could not comment on the details because it no longer had access to correspondence “from more than 20 years ago,” adding that Deloitte Cyprus "acts in compliance with applicable laws.”

====================================================================================================

How do Iranians move money abroad to avoid US sanctions?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
08:24:02 UTC
17:24:02 KST

How do Iranians move money abroad to avoid US sanctions?
From currency brokers to crypto, Iranians find ways to circumvent sanctions, but each comes with its own problems.
Tehran, Iran – Decades of international sanctions have severely restricted Iran’s access to the global financial system, making cross-border payments difficult for individuals and businesses alike. The sanctions have only increased with the current US-Israeli war on Iran.
Unable to rely on conventional banking for international transactions, many Iranians have turned to alternative channels to pay for goods and services abroad.
And while each workaround channel offers a way to navigate some of the restrictions, it comes with its own costs and risks, often falling short of the security, reliability and efficiency of a functioning international banking system.
One alternative financial channel is relying on networks of currency exchangers that operate across borders, an informal system that matches those who need local currency in Iran with those who need foreign currency abroad. By balancing these opposing needs, transactions can be settled without money necessarily moving directly between Iranian and foreign bank accounts.
There are other similar methods.
Intermediary firms offer services comparable to currency exchange traders. Typically, a customer pays the intermediary in local currency in Iran, while the firm or an overseas partner arranges payment to the foreign supplier in a convertible currency, using funds held abroad.
Using currency traders or intermediary firms can help bridge gaps in international banking access, but both often involve additional fees, exchange-rate costs, delays and greater complexity.
Other Iranians don’t deal with companies, but resort to private arrangements with individuals, including people they do not know personally, to transfer money across borders. Those deals may offer a practical solution when formal channels are unavailable, but they rely heavily on trust rather than enforceable guarantees.
“The transaction involves strangers having to trust one another to conduct a deal without any legal documentation or proof,” said Reza, an Iranian IT manager in Germany, who did not wish to give his full name. “It relies entirely on trust, and either party can back out at any time, leaving the others out of pocket.”
The methods used – whether through companies or individuals – are informal and not the most secure. “We have to use informal exchange and remittance systems for international trade, which carries risks such as lost funds, fraud and high transfer costs,” explained Ashkan Bahrami, an Iranian trade expert.
These networks are also vulnerable to geopolitical shocks. Some operating through Gulf countries have been disrupted by the war, adding another layer of uncertainty for businesses and individuals dependent on them.
The crypto route
Cryptocurrency has offered another route, enabling users to transfer wealth without relying on conventional banks. But even these digital assets have not provided a fully reliable escape from sanctions. Earlier this year, the US Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) sanctioned several major Iranian cryptocurrency exchanges, including Nobitex, Wallex, Bitpin and Ramzinex.
Alireza Yaghoubi, chairman of Iran’s FinTech Association board, warned that crypto transactions are traceable, “and very bad things can happen, such as the sanctions imposed on multiple Iranian wallets, whether they belonged to individuals, the Central Bank, or other entities”.
The possibility of sanctions, combined with periodic internet disruptions, makes cryptocurrency an uncertain option.
Import delays
For businesses importing physical goods, the challenges extend beyond payment itself. War-related disruptions and restrictions, particularly after the US naval blockade on Iran, have complicated transportation, lengthened delivery times, and increased uncertainty over when shipments will arrive.
Arghavan Ghazanfari, CEO of Aron Trading Group, described the scale of the disruption facing importers using the port of Shanghai in China, a major gateway for goods shipped to Iran.
“Transit time used to be 26 days. But when it stretches nowadays to 102 or even 120 days, customers are bound to reconsider importing,” Ghazanfari said. “Unfortunately, the main problem now is that our supply routes are gradually being cut off.”
And even when Iranians find a way to make payments abroad – and are willing to accept the delays in receiving their goods – another problem remains: whether they can afford what they are trying to buy.
The Iranian rial’s sustained depreciation has sharply eroded purchasing power. Against the US dollar, Iran’s currency has lost more than 10 percent of its value over the past month, more than 55 percent over the past year and almost 90 percent over the past five years.
And there is little certainty that the pressure will ease anytime soon.
With the prospect of another escalation in the conflict looming over Iran and uncertainty clouding the country’s economic outlook, the question for many Iranians is not simply how to move money across borders. It is how long they can keep navigating an increasingly restrictive financial system, and what it will cost them to do so.

Africa records world's fastest gains in disaster resilience, new study shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
08:23:15 UTC
17:23:15 KST

The World Risk Poll, which surveyed 143,000 people across 140 countries, found North Africa up five points and Southern Africa up four, driven by expanding internet access and household preparedness. Yet 220 million people affected by disasters in the past five years received no warning.
Africa has recorded the world's fastest improvements in disaster resilience, a new major global study has revealed.
Research from Lloyd's Register Foundation shows that African regions have made the biggest gains in people's ability to withstand and recover from disasters and other major disruptions since 2023.
North Africa, for instance, recorded a five-point increase in resilience, followed by Southern Africa with four points. Eastern Africa and Central and Western Africa each improved by three points.
Expanding internet access, better household preparedness, and improved financial resilience in countries including Kenya, Egypt, Uganda, Algeria, and Nigeria propelled the gains.
The findings, however, expose a significant trial. In Central and West Africa, few disaster-affected adults received any warning, raising questions about whether resilience improvements are translating into better protection for vulnerable communities.
What is driving Africa's progress?
This is the outcome of the fourth edition of the World Risk Poll, which surveyed more than 143,000 people across 140 countries and territories in the year 2025. Conducted by Gallup, the study examines experiences of safety risks, including in countries where official data is limited.
Its Resilience Index measures people's ability to absorb and recover from major shocks on a scale of 0 to 100. The assessment covers four areas: individual resilience, household preparedness, community support and wider societal conditions.
Increased internet access can help people obtain information about potential dangers, while household preparedness can improve their ability to respond when emergencies occur.
The researchers identified Algeria, Nigeria, Kenya, Egypt, and Uganda as countries contributing to regional improvements, although the factors behind the gains varied. The findings, however, do not mean Africa has become the world's most resilient continent. Rather, its regions have recorded the fastest improvements over the period examined.
But why are millions still missing disaster warnings?
Despite the progress, the study discloses massive inequalities in access to potentially life-saving information. In Central and Western Africa, for instance, 47% of adults affected by disasters said they had received a warning.
Globally, people in low-income countries were almost twice as likely to have experienced a disaster over the previous five years as those in high-income countries.
Nearly one in three adults in poorer countries reported being affected, compared with 16% in wealthier nations.
Yet only 64% of disaster-affected adults in low-income countries received warnings, compared with 84% in high-income countries. Even when warnings were issued, many people could not respond.
Fewer than half of warned adults in low- and lower-middle-income countries took action before disaster struck, compared with 71% in high-income countries.
Nancy Hey, director of evidence and insight at Lloyd's Register Foundation's Global Safety Evidence Centre, said the results highlighted the importance of preparedness.
"A warning is only as good as what people can do with it," she said.
Can mobile phones help save more lives?
The research identifies mobile technology as a major opportunity to close gaps in disaster warning systems.
Worldwide, an estimated 1.1 billion adults experienced a disaster in the previous five years, but almost 220 million received no warning beforehand.
Of those not warned, 77% owned a mobile phone, or more than 170 million people.
The study also found that people were more likely to act when warnings reached them through several channels.
Only 37% of those receiving alerts through one channel took action, compared with 51% reached through two and 64% through three. These channels include text messages, television and social media.
Local preparedness is already evident in parts of Africa.
In Malawi, volunteers mobilised communities to clear storm drains ahead of extreme rainfall in January, according to the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies.
This initiative illustrates how communities can take practical steps before severe weather arrives.
Caroline Zastiral, acting global lead for disaster risk reduction and resilience, said effective warnings depended on people's ability to respond.
"Warnings lead to action when people have the trust, knowledge, time and resources to protect themselves, their loved ones and their assets," she said.
Challenge for rich and poor countries alike
While the study highlights poorer countries' greater exposure to disasters, especially amid climate change, it also challenges the assumption that national wealth necessarily makes people more resilient.
The research also states that societal resilience, including trust in national institutions, rose globally from 63 points in 2021 to a record 66 in 2025. However, individual resilience fell from 46 to 42, its lowest recorded level.
Lloyd's Register Foundation is urging governments and disaster management agencies to widen warning coverage and invest more in household preparedness.
Dr Andrew Tupper, chief of the Early Warning Services Section at the World Meteorological Organisation, said warnings must be part of a broader system that helps communities to respond.
"An early warning system is useless if it doesn't empower people to act," he said.

Ukraine held off strikes on Russian energy for two days after the announcement, Zelenskyy wrote on 13 October. Russia’s barrage opened that evening with a ballistic strike on Kyiv. For the second time in two days, it came without a launch warning from partners.
How the night unfolded
The Air Force described one massive combined strike that began at 18:00 on 13 October. By 09:00 the next day, it had counted 39 missiles on ballistic trajectories and 128 drones, aimed mainly at Kyiv, Kyiv Oblast, and Kharkiv Oblast. Air defenses downed or suppressed four missiles and 115 drones, but missiles and drones hit 22 locations, the Air Force said.
Russian ballistic missiles hit Kyiv before sirens, gap that lands hard amid fears that Washington could cut data that warns of launches

On 13 October, Trump said the US was still sharing intelligence with Ukraine.

Russia attacked all three of Kyiv’s combined heat and power plants and key facilities in Kyiv Oblast that power the capital, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said. He asked Trump for strong sanctions under the Lindsey Graham sanctions law, which he said was recently passed and signed. He also asked for additional Patriot interceptors.

This represents a 100,000 bpd downward revision from September, when the IEA projected a 2.5 million bpd drop. The agency notes that global oil demand will fall by 2.5 million bpd in the fourth quarter.
According to the agency, in the third quarter of 2026, supply volumes contracted by 3.7 million bpd year-on-year, indicating a slight improvement compared to the 5 million bpd slump seen in the second quarter. For most of the first six months of the conflict [in the Middle East], global demand remained close to 2019 levels. However, it is now expected to grow, driven by a gradual rise in supplies from Persian Gulf nations, the IEA stated.
The agency estimates that oil consumption growth will not return to positive territory until March 2027 at the earliest, which will drive a 2 million bpd demand increase for the full year 2027. According to the IEA, global oil demand in 2026 will average 102.377 million bpd, down from 104.994 million bpd in 2025. For 2027, the agency projects demand at 104.377 million bpd.

Swiss health group Galderma acquires US skincare brand for $1.5bn

Swiss health group Galderma acquires US skincare brand for $1.5bn
Swiss health group Galderma is acquiring the United States skincare brand ZO Skin Health for US$1.5 billion.
According to a press release issued on Wednesday, Galderma aims to strengthen its medical skincare business and drive growth in the segment of skincare products distributed through doctors with this acquisition.
An agreement has been signed with ZO Skin Health to acquire 100% of the company. The sellers include funds managed by Blackstone Tactical Opportunities and the family of the brand’s founder, Zein Obagi. The purchase price of $1.5 billion will be paid entirely in cash and covered by existing cash reserves and bank financing.
The all-cash transaction is expected to be completed in the fourth quarter of 2026 or early 2027, subject to regulatory approvals and other customary closing conditions. In the first full financial year following completion, the acquisition is expected to have a neutral impact on adjusted earnings per share (core EPS).
For 2027, Galderma anticipates a slight dilution of the adjusted EBITDA margin. From 2028 onwards, the margin is expected to return to approximately the Group average.
Complement to the existing portfolio
With ZO Skin Health, Galderma is expanding its skincare business, which already includes the Cetaphil and Alastin brands. According to the company, the two brands, ZO Skin Health and Alastin, complement each other particularly through their different areas of focus.
ZO Skin Health offers a wide range of medically-oriented skincare products for daily use. The treatments are based, amongst other things, on retinol and acids and follow structured skincare routines. Alastin, on the other hand, focuses primarily on regenerative skincare using peptides to support the skin before and after dermatological and aesthetic procedures.
By combining the two brands, Galderma will be able to provide more comprehensive coverage of both daily skincare and care relating to medical and aesthetic treatments in future, it is said.
The group expects this to bring additional growth opportunities and a stronger position amongst dermatologists, plastic surgeons and other specialists.
ZO Skin Health was founded by dermatologist Zein Obagi and is headquartered in Irvine, California.

Iran have been drawn in Group B alongside Iraq, South Korea and the Philippines. The Iranian team will face Iraq in its opening match on Friday at Aichi International Arena in Nagoya, Japan. Iran will then take on South Korea on Saturday before meeting the Philippines on Monday.
Dastyar highlighted the challenges the team faced during their journey to Japan, explaining that the lengthy trip had affected the players’ physical condition.
“We held our first training session in Nagoya on Wednesday. However, we had a 60-hour journey to Japan, which had a considerable negative impact on the players’ physical readiness,” he said.
The team travelled from Tehran to Istanbul, then continued to Manila before finally arriving in Nagoya. The demanding itinerary kept the players on the road for approximately three days, leaving some of them experiencing muscle stiffness and fatigue.
Despite these difficulties, Dastyar stressed that the team were focused on preparing for their opening match against Iraq.
“Fortunately, despite the problems we experienced during the journey, we held an energetic training session. We reviewed our tactical plans and worked on preparing the players for the first game. Our aim is to make a strong start to the competition,” he told Tehran Times correspondent’s Masoud Hossein.
The coach also referred to Iran’s absence from the recent Wheelchair Basketball World Championships in Ottawa, Canada. The Iranian team missed the tournament after visas were not issued to some members of its coaching staff.
According to Dastyar, missing the World Championships had a negative psychological impact on the players. However, a period of rest helped them recover mentally and move forward.
“That experience affected the players’ morale, but fortunately, they were able to recover mentally during their break and put the disappointment behind them. We now have a new challenge ahead, and our entire focus is on achieving the best possible results in Nagoya,” he said.
Iran will need to perform consistently throughout the group stage before facing a playoff match, with the ultimate objective of reaching the semifinals.
Dastyar expressed hope that his team would successfully navigate the demanding schedule and defend Iran’s reputation in wheelchair basketball.
Iran have an impressive record at previous editions of the Asian Para Games, having won one silver medal and secured two third-place finishes across the last four editions. The team now hopes to build on that record in Nagoya, overcome the challenges of their long journey and launch their campaign with a victory over Iraq.

2026-10-14
08:11:22 UTC

The move came just hours before the start of the defence's arguments in the sprawling corruption trial of jailed Istanbul mayor Ekrem İmamoğlu and some 400 other defendants.
Turkish police raided the headquarters of the pro-opposition Halk TV news channel, halting its live broadcasts and arresting 11 people, the channel and prosecutors said early on Wednesday.
"Police raid at Halk TV headquarters! A trustee (manager) has been appointed, broadcasts have been halted," the channel wrote in a post on X shortly before 7:00 am (0600 CET).
Halk's news channel and the live broadcasts on its YouTube site were both offline.
It was the latest crackdown on the pro-opposition media and came just two weeks after authorities shut down the website and social media accounts of T24, a leading digital news website, citing its "LGBT propaganda."
In a statement to Turkish media, prosecutors said they had issued a warrant for 17 people, 11 of whom had been detained as part of an investigation into Halk's chairman Cafer Mahiroğlu on suspicion of "bribery", "rigging tenders," and "money laundering."
It said companies co-owned or managed by Mahiroğlu had been seized and that the authorities put a government-appointed trustee in charge of them.
Of the remaining six people named in the warrant, four were abroad, one was in a correctional facility and the last was still being sought, it said.
Mahiroğlu was not among those detained as he lives abroad.
'We're under a blockade'
In several posts as dawn was breaking, Halk journalists said they were unable to get into the building.
"The police have sealed off the entrance to our building. That’s the situation...There’s nothing left to say," wrote Onur Dalar on X, his words echoed by a colleague.
"At Halk TV, the management is now under a trustee. Broadcasting systems have been seized. Our channel is literally under blockade. I still can’t get into the institution where I’ve worked for 5 years, none of us can. The police haven’t left the building," wrote Gamze Altunay.
The move came just hours before the start of the defence's arguments in the sprawling corruption trial of jailed Istanbul mayor Ekrem İmamoğlu and some 400 other defendants.
The move drew a furious reaction from the main opposition Yeni Parti and the Turkish Journalists' Union (TGS)
"In recent years, the lawlessness used by the political authorities to overcome every problem has once again struck freedom of the press today...We do not accept this tyranny!" wrote TGS on X.
And opposition leader Özgür Özel also lashed out against a TV channel "watched by millions" describing the government's action as "weak and cowardly."
"Storming a TV channel with a police raid at dawn and appointing a trustee is something only dictators do. Unfortunately, they have brought our country to this state," he wrote.
He said it was no coincidence the raids came just hours before the start of the defence arguments in İmamoğlu's trial.
"They did this on the very day the defence was to begin in Turkey’s biggest political trial. Those who appoint trustees to municipalities and usurp the will of the people have now appointed a trustee to Halk TV, watched by millions. Because they are WEAK and COWARDLY!"
Last year, Halk TV, which has faced repeated sanctions from Turkey's broadcasting regulator, was threatened with possible closure over its critical tone towards the government of President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan.

Poll suggests Swiss voters reject three of four referendum proposals
Swiss voters are set to reject a proposed VAT hike to fund 13th pension payments and tax changes for married couples, according to a Leewas poll commissioned by 20 Minuten and Tamedia.
The outcome of an upcoming vote on amending the War Material Act remains uncertain.
The proposal to fund the 13th monthly pension payment through a higher value-added tax met with the strongest opposition. Some 60% of respondents were against it, with just 36% in favour.
A plan to amend taxation of married couples also failed to secure a majority, with 51% saying they intended to vote ‘no’ and 38% tending ‘yes’.
The survey showed that the only initiative to receive broad support was the one to restrict fireworks, with 68% in favour.
A proposal to revise the War Material Act is more finely balanced, with 47% against and 44% in favour. A striking feature was the gender divide. Men tended to support the proposal, while women tended to oppose it.
According to Leewa, the survey shows that public opinion is still in its early stages.

U.S.-Russia deal on diesel is 'very risky choice,' Italy PM Meloni says

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy criticised the accord, calling it "an investment in a war that must be ended."

Meloni told parliament the 27 EU countries should appoint "an authoritative figure" to negotiate for Europe over the Russia-Ukraine war, without ruling out a formal mandate for the E3 Group comprising Germany, France and Great Britain.
"If France, Germany, and Great Britain believe they can do better on their own than we could all do together, and so far that is the choice they have made, then at least let them do so on behalf of everyone and with an official mandate," Meloni said.
In other remarks, she said the EU summit would discuss what she said had been an escalation in Russian hybrid attacks, referring to drone incursions, cyber attacks, sabotage and other covert operations aimed at weakening backing for Kyiv.
"We need to protect our critical infrastructure: energy grids, undersea cables, ports, airports, and the underwater domain, where Italy possesses outstanding expertise," she said. REUTERS
