Denmark’s biggest retailer is training robots for supermarket night shifts. When will they be ready?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
08:10:33 UTC
17:10:33 KST

For now, they are slower than supermarket workers, though the start-up says advances in AI will help improve their speed and precision.
In the Danish town of Lyngby, just north of Copenhagen, the supermarket night shift is getting some unusual trainees.
Humanoid robots are learning to restock shelves after closing time, part of a multi-year trial to take on routine tasks and free employees to help customers.
With their arms, legs and fingers, the robots can operate in spaces built for people without stores having to change their layouts, according to the Danish start-up, Hive Robots.
For now, they are slower than supermarket workers, though the start-up says advances in AI will help improve their speed and precision.
How do robots learn?
Getting robots to work in real-world settings takes training and data collected on the job.
In a corner of the store, a human operator uses virtual reality glasses and handheld controllers to guide a robot as it picks up pasta bags and places them on shelves.
His demonstrations provide data to teach the machines to perform the tasks independently.
“There are a lot of small things that we as humans don’t think about that basically we need to teach the robot,” said Roger Sala, a robot pilot at Hive Robots.
Training began in June at grocery chain Føtex, owned by Denmark’s largest retailer, Salling Group, which operates more than 2,100 stores across Denmark, Germany, Poland, Latvia, Estonia and Lithuania.
Hive Robots develops the software and trains the machines, which are manufactured by Chinese robotics company Unitree.
The Danish start-up hopes they can independently restock some products at night by early 2027, with stores paying by the hour for the service.
What could it mean for workers?
The deployment of humanoid robots in workplaces adds to the debate over whether AI will ease labour shortages or reduce demand for workers.
AI could change how around 60% of jobs across the EU are done, according to a 2024 report from the International Monetary Fund, helping workers perform some tasks while potentially taking over others.
The technology offers opportunities to improve productivity as well as risks of job displacement, the report said.
Salling Group says the purpose of its trial is to support employees rather than replace them.
The grocery store Føtex estimates that restocking accounts for 40% to 50% of staff time.
Hive Robots says the chain also struggles to recruit young workers for the task.
Føtex operations director Simon Kudsk says it could take up to five years to have robots in every store. Further tasks could include identifying missing or misplaced products, removing empty cardboard boxes and checking best-before dates.
“Our vision or the dream right now is that we eventually could have one or two humanoids in every Føtex store that could support our colleagues to make it more efficient and create more time for value-adding activities focused on customers,” Kudsk said.

====================================================================================================

The boldness Australia needs has no political home right now
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
08:10:08 UTC
17:10:08 KST

analysis
Boyer Lecture: The boldness Australia needs has no political home right now
This year's Boyer Lecture series explores the opportunities and challenges of Australia's engagement with Asia in the 21st century. Keynote speaker Sam Roggeveen, director of the Lowy Institute's International Security Program, gave his lecture Four Forces: Australia in the New Asia this evening. This is an edited extract.
The biggest change to Australia's region since World War II is underway. Three forces are reshaping Asia and Australia's place in it: the decline of one empire, the rise of another, and the emergence of a powerful neighbour on Australia's doorstep.
Amid this regional shift, a fourth potent force is at play: an unmistakeable change in the character of Western liberal democracy, including in Australia.
These four forces present a challenge not just to our place in the world, but to our politics and identity; we are a Western nation perched alongside Asia as it enters a post-Western era.
We can't stop these international forces, but we have a choice to make about how we meet the challenge, a choice about whether we leave our fate in the hands of others or take the harder road towards self-reliance.
The 'material dethroning of the West'
It doesn't take much persuading these days to convince Australians that China is an important part of their future, because it is already so conspicuous in our daily lives. It is a major source of immigrants, students and consumer products, our largest trading partner, and it is credited with keeping Australia out of recession during the global financial crisis.
But what China means to Australia is a fraction of what it means to the world. China is the largest trading partner to around 120 other countries, too. Roughly a third of all the physical objects produced in the world today are made in China. Its economy is now at least four-fifths the size of America's and may even be the largest in the world, depending on how you measure.
For the economic historian Adam Tooze, China's rise represents nothing less than "the material dethroning of the West as the central driver of world history".
Until not so long ago, China's economic rise was only good news. It was lifting hundreds of millions of its own people out of poverty, producing cheap goods for the world, and creating wealthy consumers for our goods and services. But China's rise was always going to create problems, including for our ally, the United States.
When the Cold War ended, the US became Asia's uncontested leader. The hope, at the time, was that China would simply go along with that arrangement. The plan in Washington was that even as China became richer, it would remain subordinate to the US. China would become something like Japan or Germany — economic powerhouses with no big independent foreign policy ambitions.
Clearly, that's not how things are turning out. China is building the world's biggest navy and quadrupling the size of its nuclear arsenal. It punishes American allies, including Australia, by imposing trade restrictions. Its behaviour in the South China Sea, where it has built artificial islands based on dubious legal claims, can be fairly described as territorial expansion. China is clearly not going to become a super-sized version of Germany or Japan.
We should assume China wants to lead in the region, and that means subordinating the US and its allies, and even pushing Washington out of Asia altogether. That's not because China is communist or because it's a dictatorship. It is those things, and that makes China harder to deal with. But this is a simple question of scale. China is big and big countries demand leadership.
Now, nothing up to this point would perturb any mainstream foreign policy commentator. But here's where I swerve off the beaten path. Because the consensus in Australia is that, whatever challenge China presents to us, the Americans will help us face it. In fact, our entire national defence is built upon this premise.
The US is weaker in Asia
China's rise has made America's position in Asia unsustainably weak. It used to be easy for America to make lavish promises to defend its partners and allies in Asia because no other country was strong enough to challenge it. That's not true anymore. It would now be incredibly costly for the US to meet the commitments it has made.
It is still assumed, on the Korean Peninsula and in Taiwan, and even in Japan and Australia, that the US will be willing to risk the lives of thousands of its troops, and perhaps even nuclear attacks on its own cities, to defend us. But the US simply has no vital reason to accept such risks. The sacrifice would not be worth it.
Now, it's important to stress: saying that America's position in Asia is weak is not the same as saying that America itself is weak. In fact, the United States has a reasonable claim to being the strongest and most secure nation in the history of the world. But that's part of our problem.
America has the world's biggest military, a huge economy, thousands of nuclear weapons, and is separated from China by a vast ocean. It is so secure that it simply doesn't need to be Asia's leader. It's nice to have, but not essential. So, when a challenger as big as China comes along, we should not assume that the US will bear the burden of resisting it.
If this is jarring, it's because it has happened relatively quickly. One of my predecessors as Boyer Lecturer, the distinguished Australian foreign policy thinker Owen Harries, titled his first address And Then There Was One, because in 2003 the US was the only superpower in the world. It's worth adding that Owen did not assume this would be a permanent condition.
You will note I haven't mentioned President Trump so far, who is so often the focus of our alliance concerns. And why not? He has threatened to annex Greenland, make Canada the 51st state, and throw Ukraine under the bus. Still, it's a mistake to focus on Trump because it invites us to believe that he was the cause of the power shift I am describing, and that things will return to something like "normal" after he leaves the world stage. They won't.
No previous US president could have prevented China's ascent, and no future US president is going to risk their nation's safety and prosperity by entering a competition with China that could lead to war.
So no, this is not a Trump phenomenon. It is a permanent shift.
AUKUS hits a jarring note
This is why AUKUS is such a jarring note in our national life. The agreement to supply Australia with eight nuclear-powered submarines, announced by the Morrison government in 2021 and now supported by the Albanese government, represents the biggest change to our alliance in its history. Yet it comes at exactly the moment when American reliability goes into permanent decline.
AUKUS is an illustration of one of the least attractive aspects of our national character: an insatiable desire to win the approval of Americans. Of course, the Americans sense this and they exploited it when we proposed AUKUS, which involves not just our biggest ever military purchase but billions of Australian dollars invested in US shipyards.
In the 1930s, America built the gambling mecca of Las Vegas, an entire city in the desert dedicated to fleecing gamblers. If AUKUS demonstrates anything, it is that the Americans still have a talent for separating fools from their money.
Australia should be sceptical of both China and America as one rises and the other declines. And from this dual scepticism flows an obvious conclusion: we must do more to look after ourselves.
Once we accept that our relationship with the US will become more transactional, the natural instinct will be to find a partner to replace it. But there is no replacement.
The sheer scale of the Asia Pacific counts against an alliance-like security partnership with Tokyo. Japan is pre-occupied with security threats far closer to home, and lacks the military capacity and ambition to be a significant power in our part of Asia.
What about India? It is in a slightly different category because of its size and still untapped potential — one day, it will likely surpass the US in GDP terms. But India is also too far away from Australia to be a close security partner. It is difficult to imagine that any security threat to Australia would ever be so vital to India that New Delhi would offer us help, and the same is true for Australia in its dealings with India.
There is one nation which, although it will never replace the US, does have vital interests that align with ours. It is close to Australia and has vast economic potential, enough to resist being pulled into China's orbit.
A great power on our doorstep
Indonesia matters to Australia because it is big and it is near.
Two hundred and ninety million people dispersed across an archipelago that covers Australia's northern approaches, and boasting consistent growth that will see it enter the top five economies in the world by the middle of the century.
Australia is about to have a great power on its doorstep.
For Australia's security, Indonesia ranks above every other nation. If we get this relationship wrong, the dangers are immense. Soon, Indonesia will be wealthy and strong, and we will not want it as an enemy.
We've had an antagonistic relationship with Jakarta before and even faced off against Indonesian troops in the so-called Konfrontasi of the early 1960s. But Indonesia was a poor country then, with little military power or influence on the regional stage. Today, Indonesia is South-East Asia's leader and soon its economy will surpass ours. From there, the gap will only widen.
For Australia, then, the stakes in the relationship continue to grow. The more powerful Indonesia becomes, the less we can afford a breach with Jakarta.
But if we get this relationship right, Indonesia offers a natural barrier against threats from third countries. And the good news is Canberra and Jakarta share one crucial interest: neither Australia nor Indonesia wants China to dominate our region. Right there is the kernel of a deeper partnership with Jakarta. It can be something like an alliance dedicated to ensuring that no outside power ever dominates the region we share.
Of course, that ambition remains distant and Jakarta may never be the partner we would like it to be. But with that vital interest in common, many barriers can be overcome, including the fact that Australia and Indonesia do not share what our politicians call "shared values".
If that sounds coldly transactional, then so be it. We Australians cherish our political traditions, but we've never insisted that our regional partners adopt our ways.
Lessons from the UK
The United Kingdom is, like us, a liberal democracy and an island lying just off a powerful continent. Ten years ago, the UK comprehensively sabotaged its own economy and its relationship with its neighbours.
I don't need to dwell on the damage Brexit has done over the past decade: according to The Economist magazine, it has taken at least 2.5 per cent, or maybe as much as 8 per cent, off Britain's GDP. Only a tenth of Brits now say Brexit has made their life better.
Why did it happen? We're told it was about xenophobia and anti-European sentiment. Yet despite some truly ugly outbreaks of racial violence, Britain remains a fundamentally liberal and tolerant society. And don't forget, the defining message of the Brexit campaign was not about keeping foreigners out, it was about taking back control.
That slogan — take back control — is a clue to what's really going on, not just in the UK but in every Western democracy touched by the rise of right-wing populism, including ours. I think the lesson of Brexit is not that British voters were xenophobic, but that they distrusted their own elites.
In every Western democracy, the gap between voters and their political leaders has widened to a chasm because the connective tissue between voter and government has withered and decayed. That connective tissue is the political party.
The decline of the big centre-right and centre-left parties that dominated Western democratic politics in the second half of the 20th century is the signature political phenomenon of our time. Those parties represented well-defined constituencies. The centre-left clustered around unions and the working class. The centre-right around business, small and large, and the middle class. But every force that once tied big political parties to a defined constituency — unionism, manufacturing, religion, class and even race — has withered.
The effect on the big parties has been catastrophic. It was the weakening of the Conservative Party at the hands of its own Eurosceptics and Nigel Farrage's UKIP that triggered the Brexit referendum. Major parties have declined all over Europe too, creating openings for new political forces.
In Australia, the collective membership of the Labor and Liberal parties couldn't fill the MCG. At the 2007 federal election, 43 per cent of us put Labor first. By 2025, even though Labor won the election convincingly, that figure was 33 per cent. The trends are roughly the same for the Coalition. Our primary votes are now split an even three ways, with independents and small parties also getting roughly one third.
The result is that modern Australian governments achieve power whilst never really feeling that they are in charge.
If a government doesn't feel it has a mandate, it sets about trying to manufacture one. Perhaps you've noticed that the term "social licence" has crept into our political vocabulary — that's an implicit acknowledgement of the democratic deficit I'm describing.
Our governments launch endless enquiries and establish expert bodies to make decisions that were once considered to be within their own remit. These are all signs of governments desperately searching for new indicators of public approval and devising mechanisms to work around its absence. No truly confident government would feel the need.
The Howard government was the last under the old two-party settlement. Not coincidentally, that was also when Australia had its last major economic reform. If we have indeed become a timid nation, as Paul Keating argues, then I think this is why.
The missing piece is a sense of authority arising from democratic legitimacy. That's what instils courage and policy boldness in governments.
Our future without a powerful regional ally
For the first time in our history, we face a future without a powerful ally committed to regional supremacy.
We face a future in which Asia will be led by an Asian superpower, one that has interests and ambitions that clash with ours. And we face a future in which our close neighbour, Indonesia, will have greater national power than us. All of this in a political environment undergoing its biggest realignment since the creation of the Liberal Party in 1944.
The changes to our region demand not just a new defence strategy or a new foreign policy, but an ambitious national reform agenda dedicated to creating a truly self-reliant Australia.
Yet our domestic political malaise is frustrating our ability to meet the regional challenges. The major parties are exhausted and fragile; they lack the energy and authority to embark on such a journey. The last big wave of Australian reform, in the 1980s and 90s, was built on consensus between our major parties. If there is to be another wave of reform it will need to be built on the ashes of the two-party system.
Right now, the boldness Australia needs has no political home. The far right offers nostalgia for a wholly imagined monoculture. The left is pre-occupied with conservation and flirts with de-growth. The major parties offer technocratic tinkering. There is not a single political force in Australia today focused squarely on building Australia's wealth and strength.
The most telling evidence is that Labor, the Coalition and One Nation are now all, to one degree or another, retreating from immigration.
Loading
Immigration retreat also one from Asia
Given the temper of our immigration debate, perhaps the least popular argument one can make right now is for Australia to get bigger. But immigration is our national superpower, and we do multiculturalism better than any country on earth.
Although many factors go into producing a strong nation, sheer size is vital. When Singapore got rich in the 1970s, the world applauded. When China got rich in the 2000s, the world shook. The difference is scale.
Australia should recommit to immigration not because "diversity is strength", to use the prime minister's anodyne phrase, but because scale is strength. Retreating from immigration will make us materially weaker. It will also raise the drawbridge to talented and industrious Asians who want to make Australia home. It will cut us off from our region. A retreat from immigration is a retreat from Asia.
Yet our politicians now propose to take us to the precipice. If the political mood against immigration holds until the next election, voters will be invited to consign Australia to a shrunken, inward looking, future — our own version of the Brexit referendum.
But Australia can't afford to turn its back on Asia the way the UK turned its back on Europe. Creating the conditions for an Australia that stands strong and independent in Asia begins with a simple act of recognition: we must look after ourselves.
If that sounds confronting, then I would close by reminding you that Asia is a source of immense opportunity, as well as risk. Although we in the West are passing through a moment of profound cultural pessimism, in Asia the future is still a source of optimism. And no wonder — the people living in its gleaming new cities are, in some cases, only one generation removed from rural poverty.
Young Australians are travelling freely around the region and imbibing its culture. They see Tokyo's urbanism, China's cityscapes, Singapore's garden-city infrastructure. These cities evoke a sense of promise.
Australia should want to capture the spirit of progress that animates those places, to be a country where the future feels exciting and abundant, maybe even a little glamorous.
Let that sense of optimism guide Australia as we navigate the difficult choices ahead.
Sam Roggeveen's keynote lecture will be on ABC TV and iview at 3:25pm October 17 and iview. This lecture and others from Louisa Lim, Mari Pangestu and Senior Minister Lee Hsien Loong will air on consecutive Sundays from October 18 on ABC Radio National's Sunday Extra program, at 8:05am.

Iran tensions, Syria talks put Iraqi Kurdistan at the center of Middle Eastern diplomacy - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
08:09:07 UTC
17:09:07 KST

The Kurdistan Region of northern Iraq has played an increasingly important role, often behind the scenes, in reducing tensions in the region. At a conference of the 2026 Middle East Research Institute (MERI) Forum in Erbil, a number of Kurdish leaders described recent initiatives the region has undertaken.
The new comments at the MERI conference illustrate how the Kurdish leadership sought to navigate the recent conflict between the US, Israel, and Iran. Although the Kurdistan Region came under more than 1,000 Iranian missile and drone attacks, the Kurdish leaders sought to reach out to Iran and the US. They also worked to broker talks between Damascus and Kurds in eastern Syria.
Who were the key leaders involved? Kurdistan Region President Nechirvan Barzani and Prime Minister Masrour Barzani played a major role. The two men are related and lead the Kurdistan Democratic Party. In addition, the members of the Talibani family, primarily Bafel and Qubad Talibani, from the rival Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) party were instrumental.
'We are part of the solution'
“We are very pleased today to see that Kurds are part of the solution - whether in Syria, as marked by the presence of Comrade Mazloum [Abdi] here, or in Iraq, where we are part of the solution,” Qubad Talabani stated at the 2026 Middle East Research Institute (MERI) Forum in Erbil.
Qubad Talibani is Deputy Prime Minister of the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG). Rudaw reported that Talibani told MERI, “Erbil expressed readiness to facilitate discussions between Kurds and the countries where they live in the Middle East, including in Iran.”
He also said, “We are very pleased today to see that Kurds are part of the solution - whether in Syria, as marked by the presence of Comrade Mazloum [Abdi] here, or in Iraq, where we are part of the solution.”
The report at Rudaw noted that Nechirvan Barzani played a key role in talks in Syria and Turkey. Nechirvan is a unique figure in Kurdish politics today because of his long experience and his ability to navigate the complex politics of Iran, Turkey, Syria, and Iraq.
The Kurdistan Region is involved in a variety of discussions in part because of its geographic position. Northern Iraq borders Iran, Turkey, and Syria. It sits at the crossroads of major regional policies.
For instance, US forces were concentrated in the KRG before the left on September 30. Iran, as noted, has targeted the region 1,000 times. This is mostly because Iran is targeting Kurdish Iranian opposition groups that are based in northern Iraq. Turkey is dealing with peace talks with the PKK, and the PKK has forces also in the KRG.
Most importantly, the KRG helped smooth discussions in Syria. The US was leaving Syria in 2025, and the US-backed SDF, which is Kurdish-led, was expected to integrate with the new government in Damascus. The Kurdistan Regional Government sought to make sure Kurds would not be harmed in Syria.
“As political forces in the Kurdistan Region, we stand ready for any coordination and role assigned to us,” Qubad Talibani added. “Furthermore, the Kurdistan Region has significantly contributed to the advancement of the integration process of the now-dissolved Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) into the Syrian state system,” Rudaw noted.
SDF commander Mazloum Abdi praised the Kurdistan Region for its support. This is important because there are still many tensions in Syria and the role of the KRG is likely not over. The Syrian Kurdish political authorities, called the AANES, never built a prosperous region like the KRG. They were also linked to the YPG and the PKK, and as such were generally rivals of the KDP. This is internal Kurdish politics, but it matters. When the chips were down, the Kurdish leadership in Erbil went to help Kurds in Syria, despite past disagreements among the politicians.
Not everything has been smooth sailing. Nechirvan Barzani was critical of the Kurdish Iranian opposition groups. These groups have bases and camps in the KRG. Some of the Kurdish Iranian groups are closer to the KDP or PUK.
However, Iran has made it clear it will continue its attacks until the KRG is able to assure Tehran that these groups are not a threat. Earlier in the year, in March, media reports suggested the US was willing to arm the Kurdish Iranian groups. The idea of US arms moving through northern Iraq to Iran was certainly seen by Iran as a threat.
“Rojhelat’s [western Iran’s Kurdish region] opposition forces, unfortunately, behaved very irresponsibly,” Nechirvan Barzani said speaking at MERI. This was tough criticism for these groups.
Barzani’s comments shed light on the issues facing the Kurdish Iranian groups
The Amargi, a local grassroots media network, noted that Barzani’s comments shed light on the complexities the Kurdish Iranian groups have faced. At least six of these groups exist. These include the centrist KDPI and PAK, as well as the more left-leaning Komala and PJAK.
PJAK is often believed to be closely linked to the PKK. Another group, Khabat, is part of the Kurdish Iranian opposition alliance. The groups formed an alliance in January and February, right before the US and Israeli strikes began. Iran may have seen this development as alarming.
“Meanwhile, the parties had begun preparing. According to accounts circulating within their ranks, former peshmerga fighters returned from abroad, while light weapons and vehicles were acquired. These preparations do not substantiate Trump’s allegations that Kurds diverted or kept weapons intended for Iranian protesters. The parties concerned rejected those accusations, which have not been publicly substantiated,” the Amargi noted.
“For some Iranian Kurds, including activists, party supporters and observers, the 39-day war appeared to offer a long-awaited opportunity after what they considered a missed chance during the Jin, Jiyan, Azadi (Women, Life Freedom) movement. They hoped that a weakened regime would pave the way for a ground operation, but events did not unfold as they had expected.”
The Amargi added that “Iranian Kurdish parties explained their decision not to intervene by pointing to the absence of international guarantees and protection. Without air cover, external coordination and a broader uprising in Iran, they feared that an operation would fail and leave civilians exposed to retaliation.”
Barzani’s critique of the groups may not be everything it seems on the surface. He may be trying to reduce tensions with Iran by showing that the KRG is listening to Iran’s concerns. So long as Iran believes that the KRG will rein in these groups, or at least prod them not to send forces over the border, then Iran may reduce its attacks. A recent statement from KDPI, one of the Kurdish Iranian groups, also indicated that KDPI will not send its forces over the border. KDPI tends to be politically close to the KDP, and it will not want to cause the KRG any trouble. KDPI members have resided in the KRG for decades and their facilities near Koya have been frequently targeted by Iran.
Iran knows it can’t eliminate all the Kurdish opposition. It likely prefers the groups weakened and abroad, rather than fighting in Iran. For this reason, Iran is willing to wait and see if the KRG can make sure the groups’ activity is curtailed. Barzani’s comments were aimed at reducing tensions with Tehran in this respect.

====================================================================================================

The Iran war has driven Trump crazy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
08:08:58 UTC
17:08:58 KST

More than seven months ago, Donald Trump started a war against Iran that was supposed to showcase America's military power and force Tehran to accept Washington's demands, but now this war has become a factor in eroding the American president's political credibility and restricting his room for maneuver. The Atlantic magazine's report on Trump's anger and confusion in the face of his inability to end the war against Iran presents a picture of the White House's deadlock and the consequences of Washington's miscalculations.
 
 
The Atlantic magazine, citing sources close to Donald Trump, the American president, has reported that his inability to end the war with Iran has made him extremely angry and at the same time has unusually restricted his decision-making and maneuvering power. According to this report, Trump, who is accustomed to attracting the attention of world leaders and the media, now faces a situation in which neither his threats have been able to force Iran to retreat nor have political and economic pressures produced the result Washington wanted.
 
In describing Trump's psychological and political condition, The Atlantic writes that he is losing control because Iran is not yielding to his demands. This report also refers to the resumption of tanker threats in the Strait of Hormuz and the rise in diesel prices in America; factors that have increased the economic costs of the crisis for American citizens and intensified Republicans' concern about its electoral consequences.
 
The Gap Between Washington's Objectives and the Realities on the Ground
 
The main problem for Trump is not only the prolongation of the conflict with Iran, but the gap that has formed between America's declared objectives and the results of this confrontation. The American government entered the war with the assumption that the weapons superiority and operational capability of American forces could change Tehran's calculations in a short period and provide the ground for imposing Washington's demands. However, military superiority alone does not guarantee the achievement of political objectives, and developments in this crisis have shown that converting military power into a strategic result depends on a set of factors beyond weapons capability.
 
Under such circumstances, the greater the gap between the initial objectives and the final result, the more the political costs of the decision to continue the conflict also increase. The American president must, on the one hand, be accountable for the expectations he created by promising a display of power and achieving a quick result, and on the other hand, face the economic and political consequences of the crisis's continuation. This situation can restrict the White House's decision-making power; because retreating without achieving the declared objectives carries the risk of weakening political credibility, and continuing the conflict also brings increasing costs.
 
The Strait of Hormuz and the Expansion of the Crisis's Costs
 
One of the most important dimensions of this crisis is the linking of the region's security developments with the global economy and the daily lives of American citizens. The Strait of Hormuz, due to its role in the transfer of oil and energy products, has a strategic position in global markets, and any disruption in maritime transit through this route can change market expectations and lead to an increase in transportation and energy costs.
 
The Atlantic report, referring to the average price of diesel in America exceeding six dollars per gallon, emphasizes one of the most important domestic consequences of this crisis. The rise in fuel prices is not limited to the direct costs of households; a large part of consumer goods in America are transported by truck, and the rise in fuel costs can increase transportation costs and ultimately the final price of goods. In this way, the consequences of a foreign crisis gradually become a tangible issue in the economic life of citizens.
 
For the Trump administration, this issue is important because public opinion usually links economic costs with the performance of the incumbent government. Promises related to reducing living costs, controlling inflation, and strengthening the economy face doubt when fuel prices rise and more pressure is placed on households and businesses. In such an atmosphere, claimed military achievements also cannot necessarily compensate for the dissatisfaction caused by the rise in living costs.
Republicans' Concern About Electoral Consequences
According to The Atlantic's report, Republicans are worried that the rise in energy prices will strengthen the Democrats' position in the midterm elections and lead to the loss of control of the House of Representatives and the Senate. This concern shows that the consequences of the war for the White House are not limited to the realm of foreign policy or military relations and can also affect the balance of power inside America.
The midterm elections are of particular importance for the American president; because a change in the composition of Congress can make advancing the government's programs more difficult and provide the ground for increased political and oversight pressures on the White House. From this perspective, the rise in fuel prices and concern about the economic situation is, for Republicans, not merely a livelihood issue, but a factor influencing the evaluation of the government's performance and determining the fate of electoral competitions.
Under such circumstances, Trump faces a serious contradiction. To maintain the image of a powerful president, he seeks to show success and the imposition of America's will; but the continuation of a crisis whose economic costs are transferred to American citizens can weaken this very image. The longer the crisis lasts, the more difficult it will be for the government to explain the reasons for its continuation and prove the necessity of bearing its costs.
Ukraine; An Attempt to Escape Responsibility?
In another part of its report, The Atlantic writes that Trump has been searching for someone to blame for the current situation and appears to consider Ukraine responsible for part of the problems. This is while attributing the rise in global oil prices to a country that is struggling to confront its own existential threats faces serious difficulties. From this perspective, blaming Ukraine can be seen as an attempt to divert public attention from the American government's decision to start the war against Iran.
Of course, determining the factors affecting global oil prices requires examining a set of variables including supply, demand, market expectations, and geopolitical developments, and all fluctuations in the energy market cannot be attributed to a single factor. However, what is important in The Atlantic's report is the way Trump confronts the consequences of his own decision and his attempt to transfer responsibility to others.
Overall, The Atlantic's report shows that the war against Iran has become a difficult test for Trump; a test in which America's military power alone has not been able to provide an easy way out of the crisis. The narrowing of political options, the increase in economic costs, and concern about electoral consequences can all reduce the American president's room for maneuver. For Washington, the issue now is not only how to continue the confrontation, but finding a way to end it without accepting heavy political and strategic costs; a dilemma that, the longer it continues, the more the contradiction between Trump's initial promises and the realities facing him will become apparent.
MNA

“The amount of easily available Oil is far greater than that of almost … anywhere in the World,” he wrote, quoting experts.
He did not give details of potential US involvement.
Last month, Trump reached a security deal with the leaders of Denmark and Greenland that expands the role of the US military on the island.
The agreement paves the way for two new military bases and Trump’s planned “Golden Dome” missile defence system, while reaffirming Danish sovereignty and Greenlanders’ right to self-determination.
The deal was aimed at ending an almost two-year-long crisis over Trump’s refusal to rule out the US seizing Greenland by force.
In his social media post on Wednesday, Trump also praised the security advantages that both the US and Europe have gained from last month’s pact as “second to none”.
He said that any aerial attack against the US could not be conducted without passing Greenland, arguing that Washington would be able to neutralise any threat as a result.
“Any future attack on the United States will have to come across Greenland, where our defence will routinely knock down drones, missiles, or any other form of weapon not yet even conceived,” Trump said.
“It gives us time, location, and sightline, like nowhere else in the world!”
There was no immediate comment on the US president’s post from the leaders of Greenland or Denmark.

CyberChess 2026 brings the international cybersecurity community together in Riga
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
08:08:26 UTC
17:08:26 KST

Riga once again will become a meeting point for the Latvian, Baltic and wider international cybersecurity community. On 14-15 October, the international cybersecurity conference “CyberChess 2026” will take place, an event that over more than a decade has grown into one of the key cybersecurity gatherings in the Baltics, neighbouring countries and among Latvia’s allies.
“CyberChess 2026” comes at a time when several high-profile incidents have brought cybersecurity issues into particularly sharp focus in Latvia. The cyberattack against the IT infrastructure of JSC “Latvijas valsts meži” (Latvia’s State Forests), the large-scale data security incident at the Road Traffic Safety Directorate (CSDD), and other events in recent months have demonstrated the importance of organisational preparedness and the ability to respond rapidly to cyber incidents.
“At CyberChess, we discuss cybersecurity not in theory, but in practical terms, looking at the most recent incidents and how they have been addressed. CyberChess brings together IT professionals who will be on the front line of the response when a major cyber incident occurs. In-person participants will also have access to closed sessions where CERT.LV and cybersecurity experts from other countries will share restricted information – technical indicators from incidents that have not been publicly disclosed, observed threat actor tactics and methods, as well as practical technical demonstrations. This is one of the greatest strengths of CyberChess: the opportunity to learn what is simply not discussed elsewhere,” says Dana Ludviga, cybersecurity expert at CERT.LV and member of the CyberChess Programme Committee.
The conference will bring together technical cybersecurity experts, policy and military experts, internet and telecommunications service providers, domain registry representatives and other industry professionals from Latvia and abroad. This year, more than 800 participants from 30 countries will attend CyberChess in person. Registration for in-person attendance has already closed, but everyone is welcome to follow the conference online.
From artificial intelligence to cyber crises and critical infrastructure protection
This year’s conference will focus not only on the cyber threats organisations currently face, but also on how to prepare for them in practice and build resilience in an environment where threats increasingly cross organisational and national borders. The programme will cover the use of artificial intelligence in cyberattacks and AI-powered defence solutions, cyber threat intelligence, vulnerability research and practical cyber defence techniques, cyber-physical systems security, as well as Domain Name System (DNS) security and governance.
The main plenary session will address strategic and policy aspects of cybersecurity at national and European level, while three thematic stages will run in parallel: #CyberStory – featuring real-world experiences and industry developments, #CyberShock – offering in-depth technical presentations and practical demonstrations and #BalticDomainDays – dedicated to DNS security, internet governance and the development of the domain name ecosystem.
Lessons from real-world incidents and a look at what lies ahead
One of the key strengths of CyberChess is bringing together those who shape cybersecurity policy and those on the front lines – experts who analyse attacks, hunt for threats and respond to incidents every day.
At the opening of the conference, Varis Teivāns, Deputy Head and Technical Director of CERT.LV, will examine both prevented and successful cyber incidents, current threats, as well as threat actors’ tactics and interests. He will also highlight the importance of timely incident reporting and active cooperation – both between institutions nationally and with international partners – in preventing and mitigating cyber incidents.
Real-world cyber incidents and the lessons learned from them will take centre stage in the practical experience sessions. Māris Kuzmins from JSC “Latvijas valsts meži” (Latvia’s State Forests), together with a CERT.LV expert, will share their experience of this year’s cyberattack and the subsequent recovery process, while Swiss cybersecurity expert Nadia Meichtry will examine recurring mistakes and patterns observed across cyber incidents affecting different organisations.
A series of technical presentations will focus on the practical application of artificial intelligence in cyber defence. Patrik Hammersborg from the Norwegian National Security Authority (NSM) will explore the use of machine learning to analyse attacker behaviour, while Ernesto Fernández Provecho from the Trellix Advanced Research Center will demonstrate how AI can accelerate threat hunting. Meanwhile, Ampyx News cybersecurity journalist Kerry Tomlinson will draw on a real investigation to reveal how scammers impersonating celebrities use deepfake audio, video and images alongside social engineering techniques.
The programme will also feature several unconventional technical and practical sessions. In his presentation “How to Rob a Bank”, Thomas Tom Freer from OPSWAT will explore the human factor and physical security, while Simon-Pierre Deschênes from Tessellate will examine vulnerabilities in autonomous systems in the context of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). Sébastien Garnault, founder and president of the Paris Cyber Summit, will discuss European cybersecurity in the new geopolitical reality. An international panel featuring experts from NATO, Canada and Europe will also examine cyber crises in which the compromise of a single organisation or critical infrastructure component can trigger cascading effects across national borders.
CyberChess 2026 is organized by CERT.LV, the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Latvia, the National Cybersecurity Centre of Latvia and Top level domain .lv registry NIC.LV in cooperation with ISACA Latvia Chapter, the Latvian Internet Association, the Institute of Mathematics and Computer Sciene University of Latvia and the operators of the .ee (Estonian Internet Foundation) and .lt (DOMREG) top-level domain registries.
The conference is co-financed by the European Union within the framework of the project of the Latvian National Coordination Centre of the European Cybersecurity Competence Centre (C-STRONG-NCC-LV).
Conference partners are SIA “Latvijas Mobilais telefons”, SIA “Tet”, VAS “Latvijas Valsts radio un televīzijas centrs”, ICANN (Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers), SIA “CYBER CIRLCE”, ESET Cybersecurity, Bitdefender, Versa Intel, Altacom, VMRay, Mattermost, Hermitage Solutions, Sentyron, Cognyte, Syteca, Squalio, IstroSec, Recorded Future, CLICO Baltic, Palo Alto Networks, Fortinet, Bite, ALSO, CISCO Distributor, Datakom, Woman4Cyber Latvia, the Embassy of Canada in Latvia, Trellix, Hack The Box and Blackwall.

"People were calm, no one was speaking. We were scared and all looking up at the sky," he added, requesting anonymity.

A strike on Riyadh's international airport on Saturday left 13 people dead and operations suspended in the worst attack since 2015.

He wrote on his Truth Social platform on Tuesday that "the Houthis are behaving very badly", accusing them of acting "probably at the behest of Iran".

The Houthis warned the US against intervention, with political bureau member Mohammed Al Bukhaiti stating they would target American interests in the region.
Bukhaiti said the purpose of the campaign against Saudi targets was to send a message to the crown prince "that he can no longer wage aggression against Yemen from a safe position".
The Saudi cabinet led by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman vowed earlier Tuesday that it "will not allow its security or freedom of navigation in the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb Strait to be threatened".
The Saudi-led coalition has supported Yemen's internationally recognised government militarily against the Houthis since 2015 in a long-running civil war that has created a dire humanitarian crisis.

Gazans harvest dregs of olive groves bulldozed and cut off by Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
08:05:38 UTC
17:05:38 KST

Gazans harvest dregs of olive groves bulldozed and cut off by Israel
GAZA/CAIRO, Oct 14 - Haidar Abu Middain, 60, lifts a desiccated bough of a fallen olive tree and tosses it aside in the barren dirt of what was once one of the most prosperous groves in central Gaza.
The family olive orchard he owned with his brothers and his uncles used to span 900 dunums — 220 acres — of trees that this time of year would be heavy with ripe fruit.
The whole clan would come out to gather the harvest — 1,100 to 1,500 tons of olives piled in bushels — some to be sold as fruit, the rest pressed into enough fragrant oil to fill as many as 900 of the 16-litre drums in which it is typically sold.
Today, nearly half of the orchard lies beyond the "yellow line" guarded by Israeli troops who bar Palestinians from even entering two-thirds of the Gaza Strip. The other half of the grove, though still accessible, has mostly been bulldozed.
Only around 20 or 30 trees are somehow still standing. Abu Middain reckons they will produce just two drums of oil, not even enough for his own family.
"The produce before the war was blessed, it was enough to earn a livelihood for our families," he told Reuters. "The harvest from here used to be enough to supply the entire central area, with both oil and olives."
PRIZE CROP AND SANCTUARY
Before the war, olives were the jewels of Gaza agriculture, pressed into enough rich oil to serve as a staple for the local diet, and a small surplus for export to Israel. The shady groves abutting Gaza's concrete cities were a sanctuary for families in one of the world's most densely populated territories.
But a year after a ceasefire ended major fighting, almost all of the once-proud orchards are bulldozed under.
Gaza's agriculture authorities estimate that of 2 million olive trees, barely 150,000 are still standing. They anticipate a harvest of about 5,000 tons of olives instead of the usual 40,000, producing only 700 tons of oil instead of 5,000.
THERE'S ZERO
Bushels of olives and drums of freshly pressed oil would normally be stacked high in Gaza's markets this time of year.
Nowadays there is barely any at all, and what does make it to market sells at around triple the pre-war price, nearly $500 a drum, well beyond what Gazan families can afford, said Imad al-Ajrami, 33, a shopper in Deir al-Balah market.
Authorities say only seven olive oil presses are still operating, down from about 40 before the war. They are barely functioning, said Fawaz Zidan, who has kept his press open in Deir al-Balah.
"Compared to years before the war, there's zero. Because there are no olives, all of it has been bulldozed, the olives are gone," he said as a handful of residents queued with plastic jerrycans to collect fresh oil from the spigot of the press.
In Deir al-Balah, a tiny part of central Gaza that Israeli forces declared a safe zone and held off from storming during the war, one of Gaza's few remaining olive groves still serves as a sanctuary at harvest time for Khalil Mansi and his family.
They were out gathering the green olives, the fruit pitter-pattering as it fell from the branches onto a white cloth laid out below. Barefoot boys climbed ladders to reach the higher branches. Girls sat below sorting the olives from leaves and twigs. Later the family sat for a picnic in the shade.
Ahmed Khader, 38, had come out for a rare day of work on the harvest. In the old days, the season would keep a labourer like him employed for two or three months, he said. Now he was grateful for a day's pay.
"But we still have to provide for our children with a bite to eat, and we want to try to get our daily bread." REUTERS

Ukrainian military’s access to Starlink satellite internet suddenly restricted
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
08:05:09 UTC
17:05:09 KST

Ukraine’s military has suddenly had its access to Starlink satellite internet terminals restricted as the Trump administration has increased pressure on Ukraine to halt long-range strikes on Russia’s oil industry immediately.
The terminals, which are distributed and managed by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, are a key component of Ukraine’s military operations and the sudden restrictions on the terminals travelling at high speeds on Tuesday evening led to the failure of several combat missions, said an adviser on military technology to Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
The sudden outage came as Russia launched ballistic missiles at Ukraine without any advance warning from the US for a second night. For years, the US has provided Ukraine with intelligence when strikes were about to take place.
Donald Trump has denied that his administration has cut intelligence sharing with Ukraine. Zelenskyy also indicated that the US was continuing to share intelligence with Ukraine in an interview with NPR aired on Wednesday, but confirmed that military advisers had received threats from the US that intelligence sharing could be limited.
Ukraine did not receive any warning before Russia launched its first barrage of ballistic missiles on Tuesday evening, according to Col Yurii Ihnat, a spokesperson for the air force. But it did receive warnings from “foreign partners” about three subsequent barrages, leaving further confusion about whether or not the US is intentionally withholding intelligence from Ukraine.
SpaceX did not confirm any changes to Starlink’s functionality and it was not immediately clear why the restrictions had been put in place. Terminals travelling at more than 100mph and using a version of Starlink for the military and other national security agencies suddenly lost connectivity, said Serhiy Beskrestnov, in what appeared to be a targeted outage meant to disrupt military operations.
“Our armed forces did not receive a warning about these restrictions and this led to the failure of a number of missions,” said Beskrestnov, who is also a popular military blogger. “It’s clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is connected to the current political situation.”
Limiting Starlink’s access speeds would have a significant effect on Ukraine’s air defences because it is being used, according to Beskrestnov, in “the most current effective solution”: interceptors that target the jet-powered Shahed drones now deployed in large numbers to bomb Ukraine.
“With their actions our partners are depriving us of one of the few chances we have to defend ourselves,” he added in a follow-up post. Shahed interception rates had already dropped from more than 90% to about 60% when Russia upgraded its engines to jet power in the early summer.
But there have been no reports that access for static Starlink terminals has been cut, meaning critical battlefield communications for soldiers should remain unaffected. The detection of incoming Russian missiles and drones relies on other technologies.
Musk, an ally of Trump, had previously cut off Starlink service to Ukrainian soldiers during an offensive that took a small amount of Russian territory. Musk has supported Trump’s calls for Zelenskyy to be replaced as Ukraine’s leader – an extraordinary act of political interference against a wartime ally – as a personal feud between the two presidents has burst into the open.
The reports that Starlink was being throttled on the frontlines were interpreted by some as further pressure on Ukraine to end the fighting and make a deal with Russia at any cost.
Serhii Sternenko, a political activist with close ties to the military, first reported the outage and later said that the speeds at which the loss of connectivity occurred had fallen even lower. “It is likely that the company ‘SpaceX’ resorted to such measures at the request of the Trump administration,” he said. “Ordinary satellite communication terminals are currently operational.”
Trump has demanded that Ukraine stop striking Russian oil refineries, which he has blamed for the high cost of diesel, although most analysts say that the closure of the strait of Hormuz has had a far larger impact on global energy prices.
Zelenskyy had suggested, though not said, that the US was intentionally withholding intelligence from Ukraine about impending Russian missile strikes.
Russia carried out a massive strike against Ukrainian energy infrastructure late on Tuesday evening, Zelenskyy said, launching 39 ballistic missiles and 120 attack drones against Kyiv and Kharkiv. The strikes hit five big power plants, key substations and other infrastructure that sustains major cities including Kyiv.
“The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale – Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States,” Zelenskyy said. “Russia does not consider the American president’s statements strong.”
At least 600,000 people were now without power, he said, adding that outages could become even more widespread.
Trump last week announced an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine that has not been confirmed by either side. Zelenskyy said he had not heard of the deal until Trump announced it on his Truth Social site, and the Kremlin on Wednesday claimed it was abiding by the ceasefire because Trump had not specified which energy infrastructure it included.
Dmitry Peskov, the Kremlin’s spokesperson, told reporters: “The energy truce proposed by Trump was not specified in detail, so it cannot be claimed that Russia is failing to observe it.”
Ukraine is observing a short-term moratorium on striking Russian refineries while Kyiv seeks to show that it is ready for talks with Russia. Zelenskyy arrived in London on Wednesday to meet Andy Burnham, Britain’s prime minister. He will also be received by King Charles.
Zelenskyy is seeking new negotiations with the US. He has sent proposals to the Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, the president’s son-in-law, saying Ukraine was ready to work towards a ceasefire and “Russia must also be part of this agreement”.

The Ukrainian government has expanded the state assistance program for installing autonomous power sources in apartment buildings, which was previously available in Kyiv, Kyiv region and Kharkiv region, to Dnipropetrovsk, Zaporizhia, Poltava and Sumy regions, Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhiy Koretsky said.
"Applications on behalf of co-owners may be submitted by homeowner associations, managers of apartment buildings, as well as housing construction and maintenance cooperatives. The program provides for the installation of equipment that will ensure the operation of lighting, water supply, heating, communications and elevators during power outages," Koretsky wrote on Telegram.
In addition to expanding the program's geographical coverage, the Cabinet of Ministers has also improved the mechanism for implementing the program itself, the prime minister said.
As reported, the government program SvitloDIM, a support initiative for apartment buildings that helps install autonomous power sources, was launched on January 28, 2026. It provides financial assistance of UAH 100,000 to UAH 300,000 to co-owners for purchasing autonomous power sources. This makes it possible to ensure the availability of electricity, water, heating and communications, as well as elevator operation, during power outages. Initially, the program covered the city of Kyiv and Kyiv region, and in early April the government extended it to Kharkiv region.
In June, the Cabinet of Ministers extended the SvitloDIM program through the end of the year.
The press service of the Ministry for Restoration, Infrastructure and Transport reported that, as of July 22, funding had been provided to 2,442 apartment buildings for a total of more than UAH 610 million, while 4,205 applications had been received by that date. By applicant type, 68% of the applications had been submitted by homeowner associations, 22% by apartment building managers and 10% by maintenance cooperatives. More than UAH 560 million had already been transferred by that time for the purchase of equipment. The funds are being used to purchase equipment that will ensure the stable operation of essential infrastructure in apartment buildings.

Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning made the announcement during a regular press briefing in Beijing.
“As agreed between China and the DPRK, the new Yellow River Bridge connecting the two countries will officially open to traffic on October 15th,” Mao said, adding that a joint inauguration ceremony would be held Thursday.
DPRK stands for the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea, North Korea’s official name.
Mao described China and North Korea as friendly neighbors connected by mountains and rivers.
She said the bridge would facilitate bilateral trade and people-to-people exchanges, bringing greater benefits to citizens of both countries.
The 3-kilometer (1.9-mile), bridge connects Dandong in China’s northeastern Liaoning province with Sinuiju in North Korea.
Its construction began in October 2011.
China remains North Korea’s largest trading partner, despite international sanctions imposed over Pyongyang’s nuclear weapons program.

Tories blame 'source error' for Badenoch's Right Way policy document overstating cost of net zero by almost £500bn
Peter Walker
Peter Walker is a senior Guardian correspondent.
Kemi Badenoch’s flagship Conservative party conference policy document overstated the estimated cost of net zero by nearly £500bn because of a “source error”, her spokesperson has said, seemingly meaning it was copied from elsewhere and not checked.
A chapter on net zero in The Right Way, a policy document produced for the Tory conference in Birmingham, said the Climate Change Committee (CCC) estimated in 2020 that reaching net zero by 2050 would cost £957bn.
This baffled experts, and the CCC said it did not recognise the figure. The claimed total was double the £478bn cited in the 2020 document, seemingly because someone tallied a row showing totals for each individual column, along with the figures which made up the totals, thus doubling them.
Badenoch’s spokesperson said:
That was a source error, and it has been corrected online.
The incorrect total was previously published in a report by the rightwing thinktank the Institute of Economic Affairs and also included in an article in the Spectator, from which it was seemingly copied.
Badenoch’s spokesperson defended the error, saying:
Quite frankly, the people who want to get upset about this should be upset more about the fact that net zero is costing us £500bn.
This is also incorrect. The 2020 estimate from the CCC was £478bn, but its most recent estimate puts the total at £110bn.
At least we learned one thing from PMQs – the Conservative party still has not settled on a reliable line of attack against Andy Burnham (and the one deployed by Kemi Badenoch today was possibly its worst yet.)
Various themes have been deployed: that Burnham is continuity Starmer; that he’s leftwing; that he’s just “eyelashes and a black T-shirt”; that he’s an unprincipled opportunist; and that he is a people pleaser who can’t say no or take tough decisions. There is a bit of truth in most of these assertions (and quite a lot in the final one, which in time may turn out to be the line most useful to the Tories), but none of them has stuck yet, and so today Badenoch tried another.
Badenoch sought to depict Burnham as a serial gaffe-merchant and she set this up with her opening question:
The prime minister has had a busy few weeks tying himself in knots, explaining why national security shouldn’t come at the expense of social security, bumbling into a row still ongoing about Manchester City.
He spent the last 48 hours trying to unsay that Russia influenced the 2016 referendum, when we all heard him say it. Does he ever get tired of putting his foot in his mouth?
What’s true about this is that, unlike his predecessor, whose instinctive response to a question was to recall the No 10 line-to-take and stick to it rigidly, Burnham is someone more inclined to answer questions and to say what he thinks. This has sometimes led to him having to take back something he said (as he did over Manchester City), or reframe an argument in different language (as he did after the PMQs national security/social security answer). But these are not grotesque errors, and any downside is probably more than compensated for by the appeal of a PM who can actually talk a human being.
Badenoch then proceeded to develop this argument by claiming that Burnham received a slap-down from the head of MI5 yesterday. (See 12.16pm.) Given that Ken McCallum told reporters yesterday “I strongly agree with what the prime minister said”, to get from there to Badenoch saying it “the first time I have ever heard the head of MI5 slap down a prime minister for doing Russia’s dirty work for them” required some extraordinarily ingenious spin. It was arguably clever – but also nonsense.
The detail is tedious, but it has to be explained. Essentially, it rests on two acts of misrepresentation. Burnham told the Rest is Politics that there was Russian interference in the 2016 Brexit referendum (which is true), but the Tories have suggested or said outright that Burnham was saying the Russians altered the outcome and that the result was illegitimate. Burnham has never said either of these things.
The second dodgy assertion came yesterday when CCHQ issued a press release saying McCallum had delivered “an extraordinary slap down to the prime minister”. This was in a response to McCallum saying Burnham was right about Russian interference in 2016. McCallum did also say that the impact of Russian interference was limited, and that it would be a mistake to go on about it too much because that would “play into our adversaries’ hands”. But, if that is the problem, you have to ask, who has been banging on it for the past three days? And who raised it at PMQs yesterday?
Burnham saw off the Badenoch attack quite easily. (Badenoch will probably get written up as having scored a great victory in the papers that have swallowed this hogwash, but if the Tories end up believing their own spin, they are in more trouble than they realise.)
One of Burnham’s strengths is that he does not seem to get rattled by this sort of rubbish. His decision to use his final response to Badenoch to praise what she said about race and Englishness at PMQs was a good one, and he even managed to adopt a cordial tone towards Nigel Farage. Being nice and personable does not guarantee success in politics, but it is a start and it helps to explain why Burnham is currently the most admired of the party leaders.

India remains a ‘natural partner’ for Russia – Jaishankar
India remains a natural partner for Russia as Moscow turns increasingly toward Asia amid its deteriorating relations with European nations, Indian Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar has said. Maintaining strong ties with Moscow serves the interests of both countries and the wider world, he added. 
Russia’s relationship with Europe has become “pretty much a broken, embittered relationship,” pushing Moscow to strengthen its ties with Asia, particularly China, Jaishankar told the Bloomberg New Economy Forum in New Delhi on Tuesday. 
He noted that Russia had historically considered itself a European country and valued its relationships with both Europe and the US, but that sanctions following the escalation of the conflict in Ukraine had pushed it toward Asia. 
The European Union on Monday adopted new sanctions targeting 826 Russian companies and 743 executives, saying the restrictions were intended to increase pressure on Moscow over the Ukraine conflict.
🇷🇺🤝🇮🇳 'India Is A Natural Option': Jaishankar On Russia’s Pivot To Asia The EAM asserted that it is in both 🇮🇳’s and the world’s interest that 🇷🇺 has other major options in Asia - framing New Delhi's 75-year partnership as an essential geopolitical stabilizer. https://t.co/vuzrW4JnXk
— RT_India (@RT_India_news) October 14, 2026
The Indian foreign minister said it is in New Delhi’s interest, and that of the wider world, for Russia to have multiple choices and maintain substantial partnerships with other Asian powers. “We are a natural option in that regard,” Jaishankar said, pointing to nearly eight decades of steady relations between New Delhi and Moscow. 
India has continued to assure Russia that despite changes in the international order and Moscow’s strategic calculations, the longstanding bilateral partnership remains intact, he said. 
The relationship has served both countries and contributed to the balance of power in Asia, Jaishankar added.
India and Russia have maintained close ties for decades, particularly in defense, energy, and space cooperation. The two countries formalized a strategic partnership in 2000 and elevated it to a Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership in 2010.
They are also targeting $100 billion in bilateral trade by 2030, compared with $68.7 billion in the 2024-25 financial year. Russian oil remains a major component of India’s imports, despite pressure from Washington to scale back purchases.
New Delhi has also stepped up its involvement in efforts to end the Ukraine conflict, which it has maintained should be resolved through dialogue and diplomacy.

China's foreign trade maintains sound momentum in first three quarters
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:00:06 CST
17:00:06 KST

The State Council Information Office (SCIO) holds a press conference on China's import and export of the first three quarters of 2026 in Beijing, capital of China, Oct. 14, 2026. (Xinhua/Jin Liangkuai)
BEIJING, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- China's foreign trade maintained sound momentum in the first three quarters of 2026, with both exports and imports growing rapidly and the overall growth rate reaching its highest level for the same period in five years, official data showed Wednesday.
The country's total imports and exports rose 18.8 percent year on year to 39.94 trillion yuan (about 5.94 trillion U.S. dollars) in the January-September period, according to the General Administration of Customs (GAC).
Growth accelerated through the year, with the expansion rate rising from 15.3 percent in the first quarter to 18.3 percent in the second quarter and 22.3 percent in the third quarter.
Foreign trade growth in the first three quarters was the fastest for the same period in the past five years, with both quarterly and monthly growth rates generally accelerating, said Wang Jun, GAC's deputy head.
"Latest international data show that such a growth rate ranks among the top among major economies, and China remains the world's largest trader of goods," the official told a press conference on Wednesday.
Exports increased 16.4 percent year on year to 23.2 trillion yuan, while imports expanded by 22.3 percent to 16.74 trillion yuan, GAC data showed.
In September alone, China's total imports and exports reached 5.16 trillion yuan, up 27.5 percent from a year earlier and crossing the 5-trillion-yuan mark for the first time. This figure also marked the sixth consecutive month of double-digit monthly growth.
Exports rose 29.6 percent year on year to 3.03 trillion yuan, while imports grew 24.6 percent to 2.13 trillion yuan for the month.
The country's trade with more than 180 countries and regions expanded during the first three quarters. Trade with free trade partners reached 19.55 trillion yuan, up 30 percent and contributing over 70 percent of the total trade increment. Meanwhile, trade with other APEC economies rose 23.9 percent to 24.07 trillion yuan.
Trade with ASEAN grew 22.7 percent to 6.84 trillion yuan, that with the European Union rose 8.4 percent to 4.78 trillion yuan, and trade with the United States increased 4.1 percent to 3.18 trillion yuan.
Exports continued to shift toward new and higher-quality growth drivers. The equipment manufacturing sector contributed nearly 90 percent of the export increment, while intermediate goods accounted for more than half of total exports, underpinning global industrial and supply chains, according to the GAC. ■

S. Korea's new jobless claims fall for 3rd month in September
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:59:58 CST
16:59:58 KST

SEOUL, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's new jobless claims fell for a third straight month due to a sharp contraction in the construction sector, government data showed Wednesday.
The number of new applicants for job-seeking benefits dipped 2.5 percent from a year earlier to 87,000 in September, keeping a downward trajectory since July, according to the Ministry of Employment and Labor.
The statistical breakdown highlighted a significant reduction in claims from the construction industry that was offset by moderate increases in healthcare and retail sectors.
The construction sector recorded the steepest decline of 22.4 percent last month, and the manufacturing industry followed with a decrease of 6.8 percent.
New jobless claims in the healthcare and social welfare and wholesale and retail sectors grew 7 percent and 2.5 percent, respectively, in the cited month.
The government offers the job-seeking benefits to help the unemployed find work, accounting for the majority of unemployment benefits. It is financed by the state employment insurance fund.
The number of benefit recipients totaled 601,000 in September, down 3.7 percent from a year earlier.
It was driven by a substantial contraction of beneficiaries in the construction industry, the number of which dropped 26.8 percent last month.
The total payout for job-seeking benefits declined 3.4 percent to 1.03 trillion won (about 771 million U.S. dollars) in the cited month. ■

China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:59:56 CST
16:59:56 KST

COLOMBO, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- Sri Lanka plans to introduce a new injectable HIV-prevention drug from the beginning of 2027 as the country seeks to curb a rise in new HIV infections and meet its 2030 elimination target, Dr. Nimali Jayasuriya, Consultant Venereologist at the National STD/AIDS Control Program (NSACP), said on Wednesday.
Jayasuriya said Sri Lanka expects to import injectable pre-exposure prophylaxis, or PrEP, which would be administered twice a year.
She said the country was working to overcome existing barriers and strengthen prevention efforts as it moves towards the goal of eliminating HIV as a public health threat by 2030.
According to figures presented by the NSACP, Sri Lanka recorded 874 new HIV infections in 2025, while another 487 infections were reported during the first six months of 2026.
The program said the increase in Sri Lanka comes against a broader global decline in new HIV infections, which it said have fallen by about 65 percent since 1994.
Jayasuriya said the introduction of injectable PrEP would form part of efforts to strengthen HIV prevention and reduce new infections in the country. ■

S. Korea's ICT exports hit record high in September amid AI boom
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:59:29 CST
16:59:29 KST

SEOUL, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's exports of information and communications technology (ICT) products hit a record high, driven by an unprecedented global boom in artificial intelligence (AI), government data showed Wednesday.
The ICT product shipments skyrocketed 195.8 percent from a year earlier to 75.15 billion U.S. dollars in September, topping 70 billion dollars for the first time in history, according to the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources.
The milestone surpassed the previous record of 59.98 billion dollars set just a month earlier in August, keeping an upward trajectory for 20 consecutive months since February 2025.
The ICT sector served as the primary driver of the country's export growth, accounting for 62.1 percent of South Korea's total exports last month.
Semiconductor exports spiked 262.8 percent to reach an all-time high of 60.33 billion dollars, marking a triple-digit increase for nine straight months.
The historic performance was propelled by expanding global AI infrastructure investments that led to higher demand and soaring prices for memory chips used in AI chipsets.
Display panel shipments shrank 11.5 percent to 1.70 billion dollars amid adjustments in release schedules for some smartphone models, but mobile phone exports jumped 28.2 percent to 1.90 billion dollars thanks to strong demand for premium models alongside rising exports of parts such as camera modules.
Shipments for computers and peripherals surged 393.0 percent to 7.16 billion dollars, fueled by robust demand for solid-state drives, while communications equipment exports fell 2.3 percent to 220 million dollars.
The country's imports of ICT products soared 55.3 percent over the year to 21.43 billion dollars in September, sending the trade surplus in the ICT industry to 53.71 billion dollars.
The ICT trade surplus exceeded 50 billion dollars for the first time in history. ■

At the Losvido training range in the Republic of Belarus, peacekeeping units practiced tactical procedures at a stationary checkpoint as part of the process of coordinating units and practicing joint actions during the command-and-staff exercise with the CSTO Peacekeeping Forces “Indestructible Brotherhood-2026”.
	 Today, at the Starodorozhsky training range in the Republic of Belarus, servicemen of the CSTO joint NBC protection and medical support formation began practical operations as part of the “Barrier-2026” special exercise.
	 Today, at the Losvido training range in Belarus, the CSTO Collective Peacekeeping Forces Commander was presented with a mandate to conduct a peacekeeping operation at the command post as part of the “Indestructible Brotherhood-2026” command-and-staff exercise.
	 Servicemen of the Combined Arms Army of the Central Military District (CMD) have arrived in the Republic of Belarus to take part in the command-and-staff exercise with the CSTO Peacekeeping Forces “Indestructible Brotherhood-2026” and the special exercise with the CSTO joint NBC protection and medical support formation “Barrier-2026”.
CSTO Peacekeeping Forces practice checkpoint procedures as part of the “Indestructible Brotherhood-2026” exercise
14.10.2026
At the Losvido training range in the Republic of Belarus, peacekeeping units practiced tactical procedures at a stationary checkpoint as part of the process of coordinating units and practicing joint actions during the command-and-staff exercise with the CSTO Peacekeeping Forces “Indestructible Brotherhood-2026”.
Checkpoints are designed to enforce access control, ensure security and maintain public order, prevent unlawful activities, and detain offenders.
The main tasks of peacekeepers at checkpoints are to demonstrate the presence of peacekeeping forces to all parties to the conflict and to the local population in the area of the operation, monitor the situation in their area of responsibility, inspect and control the movement of people and vehicles, and prevent the smuggling of weapons, ammunition, explosives and other prohibited items.
A standard checkpoint has been set up at the Losvido training range, demonstrating modern approaches to organizing security. The facility includes several fortified firing positions providing reliable protection for peacekeepers. Areas have been designated for personnel and armored vehicles, enabling a rapid response to changes in the situation. Special zones have been equipped for vehicle inspections, while gates on both sides of the checkpoint and warning signs around its perimeter enhance security and ensure orderly operations.
The actions of peacekeepers during the “Indestructible Brotherhood-2026” exercise demonstrate the high level of readiness of the CSTO Peacekeeping Forces to carry out peacekeeping and security tasks. The skills practiced at the Losvido training range will enable them to operate effectively in real-world peacekeeping operations.
The Republic of Belarus is hosting the command-and-staff exercise with the CSTO Peacekeeping Forces “Indestructible Brotherhood-2026” and the special exercise with the CSTO joint NBC protection and medical support formation “Barrier-2026”.
The exercises involve contingents of the CSTO Troops (Collective Forces) from the Republic of Belarus, the Republic of Kazakhstan, the Kyrgyz Republic, the Russian Federation and the Republic of Tajikistan. These include military contingents, units of internal affairs bodies (police) and the National Guard, as well as operational groups from the CSTO Joint Staff and Secretariat. The Russian military contingent is primarily composed of units of the Combined Arms Army of the Central Military District.
In total, more than 1,500 servicemen and over 300 items of weapons, military and special equipment are involved, including approximately 80 different types of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs).
