Personalised cancer vaccines take a leap forward – can Swiss pharma catch up?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

Personalised cancer vaccines take a leap forward – can Swiss pharma catch up?
Vaccines tailored to each patient’s tumour look increasingly promising after positive melanoma trial results. But a Roche-backed vaccine stumbled days later, raising questions about where the approach can succeed – and what it means for Swiss pharma.
For decades, the idea of a vaccine to treat cancer promised more than it delivered. That may be changing. This summer, the first successful Phase III trial of an mRNA vaccine designed around each patient’s own tumour was announcedExternal link by US-based Moderna and MSD (known as Merck in the US). It was given to people whose melanoma had been surgically removed, and it made the cancer less likely to return.
“It clearly has the potential to be a breakthrough,” said Olivier Michielin, head of oncology at Geneva University Hospitals. He was already working on experimental therapeutic cancer vaccines over 20 years ago. Back then, scientists could see that the vaccines were activating the immune system, but that wasn’t translating into notable health benefits for patients.
Cancer vaccines fall into two broad categories:
Preventive vaccines, such as those against HPV and hepatitis B, protect against infections that can later cause cancer; researchers are also testing vaccines to prevent cancer in people at high risk.
Therapeutic cancer vaccines are given to people who already have cancer or have been treated for it. They work as a form of immunotherapy, training the immune system to recognise and attack cancer cells.
This article focuses on therapeutic vaccines, and in particular on personalised ones designed around the mutations found in each patient’s tumour, and built with the mRNA technology that’s behind the Covid jabs.
But just nine days after Moderna and MSD’s announcement, Germany-based immunotherapy pioneer BioNTech and Genentech, a subsidiary of Swiss drug giant Roche, External linkstoppedExternal link a failing Phase II trial of their own personalised mRNA vaccine for colorectal cancer. The two companies are still testing the same vaccine in pancreatic cancer.
What do these contrasting results reveal about where personalised vaccines might work best? The answer has different implications for Switzerland’s two pharma giants: Roche has a stake through its long-term partnership with BioNTech, while rival Novartis hasn’t entered the field.
Encouraging results
Moderna and MSD’s vaccine, intismeran autogene, is personalised: each dose is made specifically for one patient, targeting their tumour’s mutations. Given alongside MSD’s immunotherapy pembrolizumab (marketed as Keytruda), the trial showed the vaccine significantly delayed the return or spread of melanoma compared with Keytruda alone, the companies said. They have yet to say whether it helps patients live longer.
Full results of the Phase III trial – the final stage of testing before the vaccine is submitted to regulators for approval – will be presented at the end of October. In an earlier, smaller study, the combination nearly halved the risk of the cancer coming back.
If the full Phase III results confirm the smaller study, it would be “clinically very significant”, said Michielin, especially because Keytruda on its own is already an effective treatment. He pointed out that this trial could validate several ideas at once: mRNA as a cancer treatment, mutations unique to each tumour as targets, and treatments made from scratch for individual patients.
Financial markets took noteExternal link: Moderna shares surged by as much as 60% in pre-market trading after the Phase III announcement. MSD shares also rose, although by a much more modest 6%. The gap is mainly a matter of size, said Stefan Schneider, senior equity analyst for pharma at Swiss investment firm Vontobel and a virologist by training. For Moderna, a successful cancer vaccine could be a major new source of income, while for MSD, one of the world’s biggest drugmakers, it would be a small addition to its business.
Why did one trial succeed and the other fail?
Michielin and Schneider point to several differences between the MSD-Moderna and Roche-BioNTech trials. The first is the cancer itself. Melanoma carries an unusually large number of mutations, giving a personalised vaccine plenty of targets, and it is one of the cancers in which immunotherapy already works best. By contrast, most colorectal cancers are “cold” tumours, which contain few cancer-fighting immune cells and often respond poorly to existing immunotherapies.
The second is how the vaccine was used. Moderna’s was combined with Keytruda, which stops tumours from switching off the immune cells that approach them. The vaccine by Roche and BioNTech, autogene cevumeran, was tested on its own in colorectal cancer.
But in an earlier trial Roche and BioNTech had also tested the same vaccine in melanoma, alongside Keytruda, and it failed to meet its main efficacy goal. Those patients had advanced disease that had spread, or the tumour could not be removed surgically, whereas Moderna’s trial treated patients after surgery.
Roche, however, is cautious about drawing conclusions . In a written response to Swissinfo, the company said its melanoma trial “was not designed to test whether the adjuvant setting is preferable to the metastatic setting” – that is, treating patients after surgery rather than at an advanced stage.
At this stage of research, no single factor can explain the different results – the colorectal patients were also treated after surgery. But together they suggest personalised vaccines may work best early, in cancers the immune system can recognise, said Michielin.
The main open question for Schneider is whether vaccines can also help in cold tumours, where immunotherapy currently does little. That is also where a vaccine could make the biggest difference, which – he suggested – may be why Roche is focusing on them.
Roche and BioNTech are testingExternal link their vaccine in pancreatic cancer, another cold tumour, in a trial that combines it with Roche’s own immunotherapy and chemotherapy after surgery. The outcome could help answer that question, but according to the trial registry, the results are not expected before 2031.
Personalised mRNA vaccines are being developed mainly by two partnerships.
Moderna and MSD are testing an mRNA vaccine (intismeran autogene) in nine mid- and late-stage trials, focusing on melanoma, lung, bladder, and kidney cancer. One large lung cancer trial tests the vaccine on its own.
Roche and BioNTech have tested an mRNA vaccine (autogene cevumeran) in four mid-stage trials. One continues, in pancreatic cancer, where it is combined with Roche’s immunotherapy and chemotherapy after surgery; results are not expected for several years. A colorectal cancer trial was stopped in August 2026 for lack of benefit, and an earlier trial in advanced melanoma failed in 2025. A trial in bladder cancer, combined with a rival company’s immunotherapy, was paused in 2025 after a safety issue and dropped in 2026.
Other personalised approaches, using technologies different from mRNA, are also being tested. French biotech Transgene, for example, is testing a personalised vaccine built on a modified virus, given on its own after surgery for head and neck cancer, now in a mid-stage trial.
Off-the-shelf vaccines, which target features shared by many patients’ cancers rather than being tailored to each individual, are also in late-stage testing. Among these, BioNTech is testing a vaccine in advanced head and neck cancer, and French biotech OSE expects Phase III results for a lung cancer vaccine in 2028. But it’s a highly risky business: Danish firm IO Biotech went bust this year after its melanoma vaccine narrowly missed its goal in a final-stage trial.
Overall, more than 2,000 trials of therapeutic cancer vaccines have been launched since 2000, according to a 2025 studyExternal link.
Two Swiss pharma giants, two different strategies
Big pharma has bet on RNA-based medicines before. Major drugmakers piled in some 25 years ago, then largely retreated around 2010 when progress proved slower than hoped, said Schneider. When they returned in the second half of the 2010s, they mostly did so through partnerships with specialists rather than by buying companies outright. Roche was among them: its US subsidiary Genentech teamed up with BioNTech in 2016 to develop personalised cancer vaccines, sharing the costs and profits.
For Schneider, Roche “has what it takes to be there”. Its diagnostics business can support the tumour testing needed to design personalised treatments; it has long experience matching therapies to the molecular features of a patient’s cancer; and its checkpoint inhibitor, Tecentriq, can be combined with a vaccine. The stakes are modest, though. Schneider does not include the vaccine in his valuation of Roche, and even a success would be a small addition to a company of its size.
Novartis, Switzerland’s other pharma giant, is not working on personalised mRNA cancer-vaccines, at least not publiclyExternal link, despite being active in both RNA technologies and oncology. In a written response to Swissinfo, it stated it “will pursue opportunities where we believe Novartis can make a differentiated contribution for patients”.
Schneider sees this approach as a business calculation: the company is focused on renewing products approaching patent expiry, and personalised vaccines would mean entering a new field, for a product whose profitability is still unclear.
The manufacturing bottleneck
Even if cancer vaccines obtain regulatory approval, there are still significant practical hurdles to overcome.
Each vaccine has to be made for one patient. “You have to take the tumour, sequence it, design the RNA, synthesise it, package it, send it back to the hospital and inject it,” Michielin noted. Today that takes around six weeks – for patients with a fast-moving disease, that wait alone can determine whether a personalised vaccine is a realistic treatment option.
Schneider said there are expectations the timeframe could drop to about four weeks, and Michielin hopes the process will become leaner, for instance by making vaccines on site at university hospitals rather than shipping everything to large factories.
The other issue is price. Most medicines get cheaper as production ramps up, but economies of scale are difficult to achieve for a product made for a single person. Michielin said cost must stay “very, very high among our priorities”. The treatment is likely to be expensive, Schneider noted, but he does not expect costs to sink the business case: cancer drugs already command high prices, and other personalised treatments, such as CAR-T cell therapies, have made it to market.
From trial success to the clinic
No personalised mRNA cancer vaccine has been approved yet, and Moderna and MSD have not yet applied for approval. Michielin advises interested patients to ask their oncologist whether a suitable clinical trial or access programme exists. Even with compelling final data, he cautioned, broader access would still take “many, many months”.
Cancer vaccines are not expected to replace existing treatments. Schneider sees them as “one additional option” for some patients. If they really deliver, Michielin expects vaccines to become an important tool for doctors, but not a cure-all. “In oncology, I think we have come to realise that it’s rarely just one strategy that wins,” he said.

Tel Aviv building under renovation collapses, police, MDA scan for trapped individuals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

A building in southern Tel Aviv that was unoccupied due to renovations partially collapsed on Wednesday morning.
The Tel Aviv-Jaffa Municipality said the building was slated for demolition prior to its unexpected collapse, and instructed residents to stay away from the scene.
No injuries were reported in the incident on Nahalat Binyamin Street.
Israel’s Fire and Rescue Authority said it was conducting searches at the site alongside Israel Police and Magen David Adom paramedics to rule out the possibility of additional people being trapped in the rubble.
The authority added that the five construction workers inside the building were able to escape the building moments before its collapse.
Footage from the scene shows people running from the site as the building came down, sending smoke billowing across the busy Tel Aviv street.
Police announced that, due to the collapse, several roads in the area had been closed.
Some 80,000 buildings in Israel in danger of collapse
In 2021, a residential building in Holon collapsed after authorities evacuated 16 families out of safety concerns.
The evacuation was carried out after reports there had been an explosion in the building on Serlin Street. When firefighters and rescue workers arrived at the scene, they observed cracks in the building. Some residents who tried to leave their homes said they could not open doors because the building’s infrastructure had shifted, police said.
Following the 2021 incident, the Israel Builders Association warned that as many as 80,000 buildings in Israel, with about 300,000 apartments, are in danger of collapsing and must be reconstructed in the coming years to avoid calamity.
“We published this in a report that we submitted to the government in 2017, but this is something we have been saying for years,” said the association’s then-deputy director-general Shay Pauzner.
“The message is that Israel needs to start thinking strategically about this, because we are in the danger zone.”

In August, media reports of a US oil company's preparatory operations in a remote region of eastern Greenland left locals and authorities on the island uneasy.
Trump signed a security deal with the leaders of Greenland and Denmark on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York in September.
Under the terms of the deal, shared online by the Danish Foreign Ministry, the US will be permitted to expand its military presence on Greenland through the modernisation and enlargement of its current Pituffik Space Base and the establishment of new defence areas at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig.
It will also allow the US "free access to and movement between" defence areas across Greenland, "including the Territorial Waters, by land, air and sea."
American aircraft may also fly over and land in any territory on the island, it states.
Both Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenland’s Premier Jens-Frederik Nielsen welcomed the agreement, which stopped short of Trump's wish to seize the territory for the US, a move he had argued was essential for the US' "national security."
In a statement, Frederiksen said the deal "strengthens our common security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic Area," while Nielsen said it was "to the benefit of us all."
The US is reported to have had 17 military facilities and over 10,000 troops on Greenland at the height of the Cold War.
It currently operates just one base on the island, the Pituffik Space Base, which is used for missile warning, missile defence and space surveillance missions, per the US Space Force.

Weekly regional transport strikes begin, to run until Christmas

Unknown Publisher

Weekly regional transport strikes begin, to run until Christmas
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Regional bus and train services across most of the country are disrupted by strikes as of Wednesday morning, which trade unions CNV and FNV organised over pay and working conditions.
Staff at regional operators Arriva, EBS, Qbuzz, Transdev and Keolis are taking part. National rail operator NS is running a normal service.
City transport in Amsterdam and The Hague, run by GVB and HTM, is not affected because it falls outside the regional pay deal. In Rotterdam, RET trams and metro trains are running but its buses are not. Few or no buses and trams are expected to run in Utrecht.
The strikes could continue every week until Christmas unless the unions’ demands are met. They want higher wages, quicker access to permanent contracts for staff, and better working schemes for older employees.
They will announce each week’s strike day only shortly beforehand, assuming their demands aren’t met. They also plan to pick a different day each week, so operators can’t prepare emergency timetables and the same passengers are not hit every week.

President's adviser: Estonia should not stay silent on Trump's diesel deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
06:59:00 UTC
15:59:00 KST

President's adviser: Estonia should not stay silent on Trump's diesel deal
Estonia should publicly express dissatisfaction with US President Donald Trump's remarks and actions if it disagrees with them, the new Estonian president's security adviser said.
Rainer Saks, whom Madise hired soon after being elected president in September, said Trump's frustration over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries stems from a domestic desire to keep fuel prices down ahead of the US midterms next month.
Trump said late last week Russia would immediately release over 300,000 metric tons of diesel onto US and global markets, with more shipments coming. This followed the US lifting of sanctions on Russian diesel exports.
Speaking at a press conference in Riga Tuesday while on her first official visit as president, Ülle Madise declined to comment directly on the deal.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy condemned the deal, prompting Trump to say it was time for Ukraine to choose a new president.
According to Saks, Trump's remarks carried personal frustration with Zelenskyy's actions. He added that it is important to distinguish what was based on fact from what was political assessment.
Speaking to "Ringvaade," Saks said he had advised Madise to first speak with the prime minister and foreign minister to take on board Estonia's position on the issue.
"The second thing I will certainly be telling the president is that if we are not satisfied with what President Trump has just done, then we have to express that somehow. We cannot simply ignore it when we are asked how we feel about all this," Saks said.
Trump has also once again threatened to suspend intelligence sharing with Ukraine. Saks said there was no need to make a big deal of that aspect. He also noted that even with manipulating world oil prices ahead of elections, Trump is not alone in the US, though the geopolitical situation has changed since his predecessor was in office.
"I would draw a parallel here: President Biden, towards the end of his term, when there was still a year to go until the presidential election, tried to curb Ukraine's actions towards Russia, precisely in order to control the oil price. Sanctions have been played with there, and in that sense President Trump is half right — some of the diesel fuel consumed will be coming onto the world market from Russia. But the bigger problem is that supply chains in the Middle East have collapsed," Saks explained.
In Saks's assessment, Trump is demonstrating his displeasure given the midterm elections are approaching and the Republicans are not in a strong position — something Russia knows and is capitalizing on.
"Trump's frustration is not so much caused by strikes on oil refineries. He wants to get the price of diesel and other motor fuels down in the US before the election. That creates weakness in him, and Russia exploits it quite skillfully," Saks said.
At Tuesday's press conference, Madise said she "can honestly say that the information about this so-called diesel deal is relatively new to me," adding that in her experience it is necessary to "get your facts straight" before taking a strong position on a significant issue — facts which Madise said she lacked at that point in time.
She added that "in abstract terms, it is undoubtedly clear that anything that helps the aggressor to wage war is bad," as is anything which harms Ukraine, which is fighting that aggressor.
Trump said Friday Russia was to release more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel to US and global markets, with another 500,000 tons in November and a further 1 million tons after that.

'BJP’s new Pakistanified Bharat': Opposition leaders slam Centre for the arrest of CJP leaders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
06:58:29 UTC
15:58:29 KST

Saurav Das, Ashutosh Ranka detained over attempt to enter Jantar Mantar
NEW DELHI: Opposition leaders on Wednesday slammed the Centre over the arrest of Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, who were sent to five days of judicial custody after protesting at Jantar Mantar against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. Trinamool Congress MP Abhishek Banerjee called the situation “BJP’s new Pakistanified Bharat”, while leader of opposition Rahul Gandhi said jailing young protesters for waving the Tricolour was “an act of cowardice”.Abhijeet Dipke, founder and leader of CJP, has also personally extended his gratitude to the leaders for speaking out against what he termed as the 'illegal arrest' of his fellow CJP leaders.
Rahul Gandhi: ‘Jantar Mantar belongs to people of India’
Leader of opposition Rahul Gandhi said waving the Tricolour at Jantar Mantar during a peaceful protest was not a crime and called jailing the two men “an act of cowardice”.
“Students. Youth. Journalists. The INDIA bloc. Different banners, one cause,” he said, adding that the groups were united in demanding their constitutional rights. “Jantar Mantar belongs to the people of India. We will reclaim it.”
MK Stalin offers legal support
Former chief minister of Tamil Nadu and DMK president MK Stalin questioned how many protesters the government could detain and how many young voices the BJP could silence. He said jailing more young people would prompt more ordinary citizens, including those without political affiliations, to take to the streets.
Stalin expressed solidarity with Das and Ranka and said the DMK was ready to provide them with all necessary legal representation and support.
Arvind Kejriwal questions arrests
AAP national convenor Arvind Kejriwal questioned whether waving the national flag in India could be considered a crime.
“Is waving our own flag in our own country a crime? This is absolutely ridiculous,” he said.
Aaditya Thackeray says protest will continue
Shiv Sena (UBT) leader Aaditya Thackeray said the two CJP leaders had been jailed for holding the Tricolour at Jantar Mantar. Asking when holding the national flag had become a crime for young Indians, he said the fight would continue until democracy was reclaimed.
Abhishek Banerjee targets BJP
Trinamool Congress MP Abhishek Banerjee accused the BJP of arresting Indians for unfurling and waving the national flag in their own country. He called the situation “BJP’s new Pakistanified Bharat”.
Mamata Banerjee condemns arrests
Former West Bengal chief minister Mamata Banerjee strongly condemned the arrest of CJP leaders Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, calling it an attempt to intimidate and silence an entire generation.
“We must never surrender our constitutional rights,” she said, urging people to unite to protect democracy. Banerjee also alleged that 14,000 people in West Bengal were facing police and political atrocities, and said young people could count on her support. “Your Didi is with you — today and forever!” she said.
Mahua Moitra expresses solidarity
Trinamool Congress MP Mahua Moitra expressed solidarity with the two arrested leaders, writing: “With you boys. We will reclaim this country from these thugs & looteras.”
D Raja calls arrests undemocratic, demands immediate release
Communist Party of India (CPI) general secretary D Raja called the detention and judicial custody of CJP leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka “undemocratic”, alleging that the case over trespassing amounted to harassment.
Raja pointed out that Jantar Mantar had been a designated protest site until two days earlier and accused the government of trying to curtail protests and silence dissent out of fear of public anger. He questioned when protesting against an “undemocratic order” had become a crime and demanded the immediate release of the two leaders.Raja said the denotification of Jantar Mantar would be challenged politically and legally. He added that the All India Students’ Federation (AISF) and All India Youth Federation (AIYF) had marched to reclaim the protest site and would intensify their struggle to restore the right to protest.
Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka were detained early Tuesday after allegedly breaching barricades and entering Jantar Mantar, recently denotified as a designated protest site, while raising slogans demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. They were sent to five days of judicial custody on Wednesday.Police have booked them on charges including trespassing, violating prohibitory orders, breaching a peace bond and obstructing a public servant. The arrests came amid protests by CJP and other organisations over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.

SpaceX restricts Starlink for Ukrainian military, disrupting combat missions
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:58:00 EEST
15:58:00 KST

SpaceX restricts Starlink for Ukrainian military, disrupting combat missions
SpaceX imposed restrictions on Starlink connectivity for terminals being used in moving vehicles overnight on 13-14 October, disrupting Ukrainian military operations.
Source: Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov, an adviser to the president and radio technology expert
Quote: "I can confirm that tonight SpaceX introduced a speed limit for Starlink terminals operating in motion. The restriction currently applies to the Starshield military service package and is set at 100 mph [approx. 161 km/h – ed.]."
Details: Beskrestnov noted that Ukraine's defence forces had not been warned in advance about the restriction. As a result, he said, a number of combat missions have been disrupted.
"It is obvious that this action cannot be a coincidence and is linked to the current political situation," he added.
The expert confirmed information previously reported by Ukrainian volunteer Serhii Sternenko about restrictions on Starlink operations.
Sternenko previously reported that Starlink connectivity began dropping out overnight on 13-14 October when terminals exceeded speeds of 160 km/h. He also said that standard Starlink terminals continue to function.
Sternenko suggested that SpaceX may have introduced the restriction at the request of US President Donald Trump's administration.
The Exilenova+ Telegram channel also reported overnight that its readers had flagged up restrictions on Starlink along the line of contact.
Update: Sternenko later reports that Ukrainian military personnel are saying restrictions on the use of Starlink terminals have been tightened further. Connectivity now begins to drop out at speeds of 60-70 km/h.
Update at 11:25: Ukraine's 7th Air Assault Corps also reported that problems with Starlink linked to data transfer speed restrictions began emerging overnight.
"Based on our observations, during UAV flights, the connection could be lost for 10-20 seconds at speeds of just 110-120 km/h. The drones continued moving, but these interruptions made them more difficult to control," the military said.
The corps said reduced data transfer speeds leave drones more vulnerable to being hit, while unstable connections could make it impossible to launch high-speed drones, including mid-range ones. Since the beginning of the day, one unmanned systems unit operating on the Huliaipole front has had to cancel some missions due to connectivity issues.
Update at 12:05: Beskrestnov later also noted that Starlink is used in interceptor drones designed to counter jet-powered Shaheds. He added that "in effect, by taking these steps, our partners are depriving us of one of the few options we have for defending the country against jet-powered Shaheds".
Background: Ukrainian company Stetman is working on its own UASAT-NANO satellite communications system. The project is intended to reduce the defence forces' dependence on Starlink.

'Ostentatious disrespect' — Zelensky says Russia defied Trump's energy ceasefire with latest missile strike

Moscow's forces deployed 39 ballistic missiles and over 120 drones against energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv, Kyiv Oblast, and Kharkiv, Zelensky said, calling it "ostentatious disrespect toward the United States."
At least three people were killed, and another 22 were injured as a result of the Russian strike that hit a residential building in the Desnianskyi district and power plants elsewhere in the city, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
Russia has ramped up aerial strikes against Ukrainian energy sites as winter nears, despite Trump's unexpected and unilateral announcement on Oct. 11 that both Kyiv and Moscow agreed to halt attacks against each other's energy infrastructure.
Even as Kyiv said it had halted attacks against Russian oil refineries since Trump's ceasefire announcement, Trump declined to blame the Kremlin for breaking the truce when asked by a reporter on Oct. 13.
"The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale," Zelensky noted, adding that at least 600,000 people are without power and reporting damage to 26 power facilities, as well as four oil and gas sites.
"Russia does not consider the American President's statements strong," the Ukrainian leader added.
The comments come as Washington piles on pressure on Kyiv to halt its aerial campaign against Russian refineries, which he linked to rising global fuel prices — a claim disputed by experts.
The Kyiv Independent has previously learned that the Trump administration threatened senior Ukrainian military and government officials with cutting intelligence sharing and arms sales unless it stopped attacking Russian refineries.
While Ukrainian and U.S. sources told the Kyiv Independent earlier this week that Washington has not yet stopped intelligence support, questions about the early warning provided by partners are mounting as strikes now hit Kyiv even before the alarm sounds.
Presidential Advisor Serhii "Flash" Beskretnov and Serhii Sternenko, an activist and former advisor to ex-Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, claimed on Oct. 14 that Elon Musk's SpaceX has limited the speed of Starlink terminals in Ukraine, causing disruption to "a number of critical missions."
"The American President has all the effective and necessary tools to bring peace closer through strength, justice, and pressure on the aggressor," Zelensky noted, urging Washington to impose sanctions on Russia under late Senator Lindsey Graham's sanctions bill and calling for additional supplies of Patriot interceptors.

-  Germany — more than $4.9 billion. 
The largest destinations for exports from Ukraine were:
-  Poland — almost $3.7 billion; 
-  Türkiye — more than $2.2 billion; 
-  Germany — almost $2.1 billion.

IMF warns rising borrowing costs intensify global debt pressures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
06:56:46 UTC
15:56:46 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Rising government borrowing costs are intensifying fiscal pressures worldwide, the International Monetary Fund warned on Wednesday, urging credible measures to contain deficits as global public debt heads above 100% of economic output by 2030.
In a blog post, the IMF said average 10-year government bond yields across the Group of Seven economies rose by more than 1 percentage point between February and September, reaching their highest level in nearly two decades.
The fund cited the oil price shock, persistent inflation, stronger investment demand and expectations of growth linked to artificial intelligence among the drivers.
High debt, spending pressures and expectations of large government bond issuance are also pushing yields higher, with borrowing costs in major economies potentially worsening debt dynamics elsewhere.
The effective average interest cost of government financing is projected to rise from 2.3% in 2021 to 3.7% by 2031.
US interest payments are forecast to increase from about 2.8% of GDP before the pandemic to 5.7% in 2031, roughly matching projected Social Security spending.
In low-income countries, interest payments already consume more than 15% of tax revenues.
Rising debt-servicing costs leave less room for investment and social spending while limiting governments' ability to respond to downturns.
The global primary deficit, which excludes interest payments, is expected to reach about 3.3% of GDP in 2026. Stabilizing the debt ratio would require reducing it to around 2.6%.
Shorter debt maturities are accelerating the transmission of higher policy rates to government financing costs.
The IMF urged advanced economies to adopt credible fiscal plans and emerging markets to strengthen debt management, warning that delayed action would require larger adjustments.

Mucahithan Avcioglu
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Dutch semiconductor equipment maker ASML raised the lower end of its full-year sales forecast Wednesday, saying strong artificial intelligence demand was prompting some customers to express interest in orders for 2029 and 2030.
The company reported third-quarter net profit of €4.96 billion ($5.55 billion), exceeding analysts expectations. Net sales totaled €11.66 billion, slightly below expectations.
ASML now expects annual net sales of €44 billion to €45 billion, compared with its previous forecast of €43 billion to €45 billion.
For the fourth quarter, the company projected net sales of €14.2 billion to €15.2 billion.
CEO Christophe Fouquet said customers continued to raise their short- and medium-term equipment demand forecasts, primarily reflecting their expectations for the scale and duration of AI-related investment.
Some customers were expressing interest in placing orders for 2029 and even 2030, he said, indicating demand visibility extending beyond the next few years.
Fouquet said ASML’s planned supply for 2027 and 2028 would not fully meet customer demand. The company was examining ways to expand capacity for 2028 beyond the 30% increase previously envisaged.
ASML is the world’s sole producer of extreme ultraviolet lithography machines, which chipmakers including Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company use to manufacture advanced semiconductors.
Its results are closely watched for indications of investment trends in the semiconductor industry, particularly spending linked to AI infrastructure.
During the quarter, TSMC and Samsung committed to using ASML’s next-generation High NA EUV machines, which support the production of increasingly advanced chips.
The company also maintained its forecast that China would account for 20% of total sales.
ASML faces restrictions on exports of EUV machines and certain less advanced deep ultraviolet lithography systems to China, where efforts to develop domestic chipmaking equipment have intensified.

Kazakhstan forecasts inflation at 7.5-9.5% in 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
06:54:35 UTC

Kazakhstan forecasts inflation at 7.5-9.5% in 2027
Kazakh Deputy Prime Minister - National Economy Minister Serik Zhumangarin presented the country’s socio-economic development forecast for 2027-2029 during a plenary session of the Qurultay, Qazinform News Agency reports.
According to Zhumangarin, the forecast was prepared taking into account current economic conditions, projections by international financial institutions for global economic growth, and external market trends.
He said that the IMF projects the global economy to grow by 3% this year and 3.4% in 2027.
Despite the improved global outlook, economic growth is expected to slow in Kazakhstan’s key trading partner countries.
He added international organizations and major investment banks have also revised down their oil price forecasts for 2027, with the consensus forecast lowered to 70.3 US dollars per barrel. The analysis considered three development scenarios based on external conditions.
The optimistic scenario expects oil prices to reach 85 US dollars per barrel, with average annual economic growth projected at 5.9%.
The pessimistic scenario assumes oil prices of 50 US dollars per barrel, with GDP growth averaging 3.2%.
The baseline scenario assumes an oil price of 70 US dollars per barrel. Under this scenario, Kazakhstan’s average annual real GDP growth is projected to exceed 5% between 2027 and 2029. Nominal GDP is forecast to increase from 199.3 trillion tenge in 2027 to 245 trillion tenge in 2029.
The Government forecasts inflation at 7.5-9.5% in 2027 and 6-8% in 2028-2029.
Primarily, non-oil sectors are expected to fuel economic growth. Manufacturing is projected to outpace mining, with metallurgy, machinery manufacturing, building materials, chemicals, and food production making the largest contributions.
Agriculture is also expected to remain a key growth driver, with annual growth averaging at least 5%.
In construction, growth is forecast to increase from 16% in 2027 to 17.3% in 2029, supported by infrastructure projects in transport, logistics, energy, water systems, housing, utilities, and social services.
The services sector is expected to maintain strong momentum, with trade growing by an average of 5.7% annually, transportation and warehousing by 10.4%, and information and communications by 9.2%.
Goods exports are projected to rise from 82.8 billion US dollars in 2027 to 88.5 billion US dpollars in 2029, while imports are expected to increase from 80.5 billion US dollars to 88.4 billion US dollars over the same period.
Earlier, he said Kazakhstan’s economy grew by 4.2% in the first nine months of 2026, driven largely by the non-resource sector.

Swiss rollercoaster maker investigates fatal US Six Flags accident
Swiss rollercoaster manufacturer Bolliger & Mabillard is investigating a fatal accident on one of its rides at Six Flags Park near Atlanta in the United States.
“We are deeply saddened by this tragic accident,” Olivier Bolliger told the US broadcaster ABC News.
“Our thoughts are with the family and those affected,” Bolliger added. Bolliger & Mabillard is actively investigating the incident and will not comment further until the circumstances have been clarified, the company also stated in a statement to the AP news agency.
On Monday, a 42-year-old man was thrown from the Goliath rollercoaster at the Six Flags Over Georgia theme park near Atlanta and died. According to the police, several other visitors were also injured in the incident. The cause of the accident remains unclear. The police and the relevant regulatory authority have launched investigations.
The rollercoaster, built by the Swiss company, opened in 2006. It is around 61 metres high and reaches speeds of up to 113 kilometres per hour. Passengers are secured with safety bars across their thighs and hips.
Further roller coasters closed
Following the accident, the theme park operator Six Flags shut down nine similar roller coasters in six parks across the US and Canada as a precautionary measure. Eight of these rides were also manufactured by Bolliger & Mabillard. It is not yet clear when they will resume operations.
Six Flags came under pressure on the stock market. On Tuesday, its share price fell by 14.4% to $10.20, closing at its lowest level since December 2009.
Furthermore, it was only at the end of September that Six Flags announced the permanent closure of the “X2” rollercoaster at Magic Mountain in California. This followed lawsuits filed by several visitors who claimed to have suffered serious brain injuries. A 22-year-old man also died in 2022 following a ride. The operator reached a settlement with his relatives. The ride was manufactured by the US firm Arrow Dynamics.
Bolliger & Mabillard was founded in 1988 and is one of the world’s best-known manufacturers of steel roller coasters. According to the specialist database RCDB, the company – which is based in Monthey in the canton of Valais and has its headquarters in Aigle – has built more than 130 roller coasters worldwide.

The hidden treasure in discarded wearable and fast tech
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
06:52:00 UTC
15:52:00 KST

Unused mini fans, vapes and smartwatches: A critical mineral gold mine
October 14, 2026
From mini fans and the cheap chargers to smartwatches bought as part of a New Year's health kick, some 44% of Europeans own at least six "fast-tech" gadgets. And more than half say they keep unused and broken e-waste items languishing at home or throw them in the regular trash instead of recycling.
That's according to a new report by Brussels-based e-waste association WEEE Forum. It describes fast tech, which is booming, as charging and lighting devices under €10 (circa $11), high-tech items like power banks and fitness trackers, and gadgets and lifestyle appliances like cheap mini blenders and fans, as well as single-use electronic vapes.
"So, these electronics are a bit like fast fashion," Magdalena Charytanowicz, WEEE Forum's Communication Manager, told DW.
Nearly 40% of buyers recalled discarding a fast-tech item without using it at all or within a month of buying it, and nearly 60% said they had used a product for no longer than six months. Yet the vast majority of respondents were generally satisfied with their gadgets despite short-lived functionality.
This suggests consumers accept the "fast-tech bargain" of poor quality that "does the job for a while" and is easily replaced — similar to fast fashion — according to the report.
The Great Wall of e-waste and what to do about it
About 62 million tons of electronics are discarded worldwide annually. "That's the Great Wall of China of e-waste that is produced every year," noted Charytanowicz, adding that the figure is set to grow to 82 million by 2030.
In Europe, roughly 40% of electronic waste is recycled, yet the rate worldwide is just 17%. This means valuable materials are lost, while electronic waste ends up polluting the environment.
In 2022, a million tons of critical raw materials were embedded in the 10.7 million tons of e-waste generated across Europe, including manganese, gold, copper and aluminum.
These materials are at "the center of geopolitical tensions," Charytanowicz said, referring to escalating global tensions over access to rare earths and other critical minerals.
"Even the smallest" devices are worth recycling if they contain a circuit board or battery, she said.
Groups like WEEE Forum say more awareness raising is needed on how to dispose of cheap electronic devices, and that recycling should be made as easy as possible.
But the best way to reduce a product's environmental impact is to extend its lifespan through better design and repair, as recycling raw materials is energy intensive.
Charytonawicz said clearer, harmonized EU rules now under consideration could help improve e-waste collection. The bloc's 20-year-old directive is "not really adapted to the changing reality," she said.
Healthcare's increasing digital waste problem
Another growing area of e-waste is digital healthcare. While devices such as diabetes sensors and blood pressure monitors are "transforming healthcare," many are designed to be disposable.
A study published in Nature in December 2025 found sales of wearable healthcare electronics, for example, could reach 2 billion devices annually by 2050, and generate a million tons of e-waste.
Jeremy Faludi, associate professor of sustainable design engineering at TU Delft in the Netherlands, says making health tech — particularly digital devices used in, or issued by hospitals — recyclable or reusable comes with some "much bigger challenges" than normal electronics.
That's in part due to the potential for patient contamination, particularly with digital surgical devices that come into contact with blood or other bodily fluids.
"The way that a lot of things are designed now, you can't recover the stuff because it can't be easily sterilized without the electronics," said Faludi.
He worked on the Digital Health in Circular Economy (DiCE) project, an EU-funded initiative, to help redesign digital healthcare devices to "recover critical materials and reduce environmental impacts without compromising patient safety."
A modular design, for example, allows electronic components to be separated from the parts that need to be replaced between patients, making devices easier to reuse.
The four-year DiCE project, which included citizens, hospitals and manufacturers across nine EU countries, found reusable ECG cables — which connect patients to heart-monitoring equipment — cut environmental impacts by up to 81-94%, for example. The sets are usually designed for single use.
Rules around medical waste can also make reuse and recycling more difficult, particularly when requirements differ between countries and often come down to perceived rather than actual risk, Faludi added. He says some 85% of hospital trash is not infectious but everything ends up in the same bins. Better sorting as well as EU-wide regulations around treating non-infectious hospital waste would help here.
'Green nudges' help citizens to recycle
Like with other tech, consumer health devices such as blood pressure and glucose monitors often risk being forgotten in drawers or ending up in the wrong waste, simply because people do not know how to dispose of them, said Charytanowicz of WEEE Forum, which is also involved in DiCE.
Pilot schemes in Belgium, Spain and Slovenia that offered free postal returns and collection machines in public places found that more than 60% of people were willing to return unwanted devices if it was a straightforward process.
"What's really important is the convenience so that it can be integrated in your daily routines," said Charytanowicz, adding that "nudges" such as messages that recycling a device could help the health of another person motivate people to "do the right thing."

Germany news: Merz attacks extremes for fueling division

Here is a roundup of all the headlines across Germany on Wednesday, October 14:

Fat-fingered cockpit error likely triggered Nuremberg hijack alert
A pilot's apparent mistake when entering a transponder code triggered the hijack alert that led to a major police operation at Nuremberg airport, German police said.
Investigators believe the pilot intended to report a radio failure but accidentally entered 7500, the code signaling a hijacking.
The Boeing 737-800's radio was defective, leaving the crew unreachable after takeoff from the Greek island of Corfu, police said.
Police spokesperson Michael Petzold said the pilot apparently did not realize the mistake. The pilot is not under investigation because police believe he acted unintentionally.
Military aircraft accompanied the plane in Croatian airspace, and Austrian interceptors were alerted. Two German Eurofighters then escorted it to Nuremberg.
A police team trained to negotiate with hijackers and a Bavarian support unit were deployed at the airport during the alert.
Officers had less than an hour between the emergency signal and landing to prepare, Petzold said. Police later gave the all-clear.
Lufthansa wins bid for stake in Portugal's TAP
Germany's Lufthansa has won the contest to buy a 44.9% stake in TAP Air Portugal with an offer of €1.2 billion ($1.3 billion), Portuguese Prime Minister Luis Montenegro said.
Lufthansa beat rival Air France-KLM after months of efforts to privatize the state-rescued airline, Montenegro told journalists following a cabinet meeting.
Social justice and Christian references: DW's Berlin bureau chief weighs in on Merz's speech
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's overriding message was one of justice, especially between generations.
That was for the home crowd, trying to explain the governing coalition's reform plans of the social systems. Interestingly he also sprinkled in some Christian references, something he seems to be doing more recently.
Most likely the German chancellor is trying to show more empathy and a more positive vision of the future.
His own conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party colleagues have increasingly been demanding this after losses in three state elections this fall.
Merz warns of growing injustice between generations
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has warned that Germany faces a growing gap in fairness between generations unless it undertakes major reforms of its social security systems.
"A justice gap has opened up between the generations in our country, and this gap will grow unless we act," Merz told the Bundestag.
He said children and young people risked being forced to shoulder a greater burden than could reasonably be justified under principles of fairness.
Merz acknowledged that successive governments had paid insufficient attention to the long-term consequences of their decisions, explicitly including governments led by his own center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU).
The chancellor said his government had developed a broad reform program covering pensions, care, the labor market, economic competitiveness and the modernization of the state.
He argued that justice should mean equal opportunities, fair rewards for achievement and fairness between generations, rather than redistribution at the expense of those contributing to the economy.
Merz said the reforms were necessary to preserve Germany's prosperity and ensure that younger generations were not left carrying an unfair share of the costs.
Merz accuses political extremes of seeking chaos
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has accused political forces on the far left and far right of deliberately dividing society, spreading disinformation and downplaying the threat posed by Russia.
Speaking in the Bundestag, Merz said he could not understand why politicians at both ends of the political spectrum continued to minimize Russian aggression.
"One gets the impression that you want chaos because you hope to gain political advantage from it," he told lawmakers.
Merz warned that extremism was increasingly making its presence felt in Germany's national and regional parliaments, as well as everyday life.
However, he acknowledged that extremist movements could draw support from legitimate dissatisfaction and feelings of injustice, arguing that constructive political action was the only effective response.
"Justice for us does not come through the exclusion of minorities," Merz said, calling for policies that promote equal opportunities and fairness between generations.
He contrasted what he described as the destructive politics of division and exclusion with the responsibility of democratic parties to address genuine grievances and govern for everyone in Germany.
WATCH: Merz addresses Bundestag before crucial EU summit
Merz says Ukraine aid does not come at welfare's expense
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has rejected accusations from the far right and far left that support for Ukraine comes at the expense of social spending.
"Not a single euro is missing from social spending," he told parliament, speaking ahead of an EU summit in Brussels.
Merz said an exemption from Germany's constitutional borrowing limits allows spending on defense and assistance for Ukraine to be financed through additional credit.
He accused the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the socialist Left Party of seeking to divide Germany
AfD and BSW join forces against Ukraine support
In the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the far-right Alternative for Germany Party (AfD) won recent elections in a landslide, a new alliance has flexed its muscle.
The AfD put forward a motion to halt arms deliveries to Ukraine and lift sanctions against Russia. Instead, they argue, peace talks with Russia should be initiated.
The Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason (BSW), which holds five seats in the state parliament, again teamed up with the AfD to ensure a majority for the motion. The BSW combines left-leaning economics with right-wing populist positions on immigration and relations with Russia.
AfD and BSW also called for an immediate halt to financial support for Ukraine, to the extent that it goes beyond humanitarian aid.
The motion by the AfD and BSW has no more than symbolic value, as decisions regarding sanctions against Russia and aid to Ukraine are made not by the federal states, but by the federal government and the European Union.
But the new alliance of AfD and BSW has a wider significance. It is seen by observers as a sign of longer-term and closer cooperation between the two parties, which originate from very different ideological camps.
Although the AfD emerged as the clear winner of the state elections in September 2026, it lacks a majority to form a government. It has been searching for partners in the state legislature. So far, the BSW is the only party officially negotiating with the AfD on forming a government.
Merz to set out EU priorities after urging reforms
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is expected to outline Germany's priorities on Ukraine, European defense and economic competitiveness in a parliamentary address ahead of an EU summit in Brussels.
His government statement is scheduled for 14:05 local time (12:05 UTC), followed by a 90-minute debate. EU leaders meet on Thursday and Friday, with the Middle East, the bloc's next long-term budget and EU enlargement also on the agenda.
After the speech, the opposition Greens are set to put forward two motions calling for faster bloc enlargement and stronger measures to counter economic coercion and protect the bloc's market.
Merz's address follows a more domestic-focused speech on planned reforms at an employers' conference in Berlin on Tuesday. There, he said he would press ahead with changes to Germany's welfare system even at the expense of his own popularity, arguing that younger generations stood to benefit.
Energy prices push German inflation to 3.3%
Germany's annual inflation rate rose to 3.3% in September, its highest level since December 2023, as fuel and heating oil prices surged.
The Federal Statistical Office confirmed its preliminary estimate, up from 2.9% in August and 2.8% in July.
The increase was again driven by energy prices, said the office's president, Ruth Brand, highlighting higher costs at gas stations and for heating oil.
Energy prices rose 14.9% compared with September last year, their steepest annual increase since February 2023. That followed increases of 10.5% in August and 8.3% in July.
Motor fuel prices jumped 37.1%, while heating oil rose 74.9%. Firewood, wood pellets and other solid fuels became 15.6% more expensive.
However, electricity prices fell 5.5%, natural gas prices dropped 2.8% and district heating cost 1% less.
The office attributed those declines partly to government measures implemented since the start of the year.
Nord Stream sabotage trial draws protesters
The trial of a Ukrainian man accused of leading the operation that blew up the Nord Stream gas pipelines in 2022 has begun in Hamburg.
The 50-year-old, identified under German privacy rules as Serhii K., faces charges including a war crime, causing explosions, destroying structures and disrupting public services.
DW correspondent Matthew Moore was there as court doors opened at 07:30 local time in Hamburg.
A small pro-Ukraine protest held up a banner saying, "Russia is a terrorist". One participant from Germany told DW that they wanted to remind the world of "the war crimes taking place against the Ukrainian people."
Inside, a Ukrainian student also told DW that he and others had made the journey from Kyiv to show support for the defendant, Serhii K.
"Serhii K is a hero." In the eyes of the German prosecutors, it is another matter. They accuse him of carrying out a war crime. If found guilty of his part in the gas pipeline bombing, K faces a lengthy prison sentence.
Prosecutors allege that he planned the attack with other Ukrainian military personnel on behalf of unidentified Ukrainian state bodies. They say the aim was to prevent Russia from using gas export revenues to finance its war against Ukraine.
Serhii K., who was arrested in Italy last year, denies involvement. Ukraine's government has also denied any role in the attack.
Anti-nuclear activists block waste convoy
Police in the town of Dorsten, just north of the city of Essen, said that they had detained three people who were blocking the A31 motorway.
The group was attempting to stop trucks carrying radioactive waste.
After repelling down from a bridge above the highway, they unfurled a banner reading "stop this crap."
The incident was the latest in Germany's decades-long protest movement against nuclear weapons and atomic energy.
Although the last of the country's nuclear power stations went offline in 2023, transporting and storing the waste remains a divisive topic.
This particular convoy was headed for a facility in Ahaus, near the Dutch border. Authorities believe it could take until 2028 to safely store all the remaining waste from Germany's decommissioned atomic reactors.
Suicide rate increased significantly in 2025
The suicide rate in Germany has continued to climb, according to official statistics just released by the Federal Ministry of Health.
In 2025, at least 11,334 people killed themselves in Germany. That is a 9.3% increase on the previous year, and 15.6% higher than the average over the past decade.
This is higher than the number of deaths due to traffic accidents, AIDS, murder and manslaughter put together.
The data shows that this is partly due to more women (a 17.9% increase since 2021) taking their own lives, though most suicides are still carried out by men. The increase is also due to an increase in assisted suicides for the elderly and infirm, amounting to over 1,000 people.
In a 2020 decision, Germany's top court struck down a 2015 ban on organized assisted dying providers like Switzerland's Dignitas, and called on the Bundestag to create regulations for the practice. However, lawmakers have declined thus far to do so, putting assisted suicide in a legal gray area in Germany. Direct euthanasia by a single doctor remains illegal.
In August, the Health Ministry proposed reforms such as a national suicide prevention hotline, more support for local and state networks, as well as the creation of a federal office for suicide prevention.
However, medical groups and charities have both said that the proposed €1.4 million ($1.6 million) budget would come nowhere never covering such a scheme long-term.
Editor's note: If you are suffering from serious emotional strain or suicidal thoughts, do not hesitate to seek professional help. You can find information on where to find such help, no matter where you live in the world, at this website: https://www.befrienders.org/
Proposed sugar tax faces criticism
According to German media reports, the ruling coalition of Chancellor Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU) and the Social Democrats (SPD) has found a compromise for a planned tax increase on sugar.
The law would impact sugar drinks in particular, and is set to come into effect on July 1 of next year. There is reportedly going to be an exception for small-scale producers.
CDU state premier of Hesse, Boris Rhein, slammed the plan on Wednesday. Rhein told the Kölner Stadt-Anzeiger newspaper that this "expensive tax" (a phrase that rhymes in German) would simply result in companies passing on the extra expense to consumers.
Rhein accused the coalition of pretending the measure was about health when really it was so "the populace can continue to plug up holes in the federal budget at the cash register."
Nord Stream sabotage suspect goes on trial in Hamburg
The much anticipated trial of Serhii K., whose last name is withheld due to Germany's privacy laws, will begin in Hamburg today.
K. is accused by investigators of leading a group comprising professional divers, an explosives expert, and a boat skipper who plotted to travel to the remote section of the Nord Stream gas pipelines off the Danish coast and blow them up.
The series of explosions ruptured Nord Stream 1, which Moscow had switched off a month earlier, and destroyed Nord Stream 2, which had yet to come into operation at the time.
A former Ukrainian military officer, K's case has led some investigators to point at Kyiv as orchestrating the entire plan, as the pipelines controversially delivered Russian natural gas to Europe.
The attack came seven months after Russia's fullscale invasion of Ukraine, when European countries were taking steps to drastically decrease their reliance on Russian fuel.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has vehemently denied any official connection to the attack.
K. was apprehended in Italy in 2025 and extradited to Germany. His specific charges are: being an accomplice to a war crime by attacking civil energy infrastructure, disruption of public services, causing an explosion and destroying structures.

Germany news: Merz attacks extremes for fueling division
Published October 14, 2026last updated October 14, 2026
What you need to know
- Chancellor Friedrich Merz accuses the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and socialist Left Party of fueling division and exploiting discontent for political gain
- The AfD leads national polls, while the Left Party has emerged as Berlin's largest party
- A man has gone on trial accused of playing a role in the 2022 explosion at the Nord Stream gas pipelines
Here is a roundup of all the headlines across Germany on Wednesday, October 14:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click hereto add DW as a Preferred Source on Google
Fat-fingered cockpit error likely triggered Nuremberg hijack alert
A pilot's apparent mistake when entering a transponder code triggered the hijack alert that led to a major police operation at Nuremberg airport, German police said.
Investigators believe the pilot intended to report a radio failure but accidentally entered 7500, the code signaling a hijacking.
The Boeing 737-800's radio was defective, leaving the crew unreachable after takeoff from the Greek island of Corfu, police said.
Police spokesperson Michael Petzold said the pilot apparently did not realize the mistake. The pilot is not under investigation because police believe he acted unintentionally.
Military aircraft accompanied the plane in Croatian airspace, and Austrian interceptors were alerted. Two German Eurofighters then escorted it to Nuremberg.
A police team trained to negotiate with hijackers and a Bavarian support unit were deployed at the airport during the alert.
Officers had less than an hour between the emergency signal and landing to prepare, Petzold said. Police later gave the all-clear.
Lufthansa wins bid for stake in Portugal's TAP
Germany's Lufthansa has won the contest to buy a 44.9% stake in TAP Air Portugal with an offer of €1.2 billion ($1.3 billion), Portuguese Prime Minister Luis Montenegro said.
Lufthansa beat rival Air France-KLM after months of efforts to privatize the state-rescued airline, Montenegro told journalists following a cabinet meeting.
Social justice and Christian references: DW's Berlin bureau chief weighs in on Merz's speech
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's overriding message was one of justice, especially between generations.
That was for the home crowd, trying to explain the governing coalition's reform plans of the social systems. Interestingly he also sprinkled in some Christian references, something he seems to be doing more recently.
Most likely the German chancellor is trying to show more empathy and a more positive vision of the future.
His own conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party colleagues have increasingly been demanding this after losses in three state elections this fall.
Merz warns of growing injustice between generations
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has warned that Germany faces a growing gap in fairness between generations unless it undertakes major reforms of its social security systems.
"A justice gap has opened up between the generations in our country, and this gap will grow unless we act," Merz told the Bundestag.
He said children and young people risked being forced to shoulder a greater burden than could reasonably be justified under principles of fairness.
Merz acknowledged that successive governments had paid insufficient attention to the long-term consequences of their decisions, explicitly including governments led by his own center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU).
The chancellor said his government had developed a broad reform program covering pensions, care, the labor market, economic competitiveness and the modernization of the state.
He argued that justice should mean equal opportunities, fair rewards for achievement and fairness between generations, rather than redistribution at the expense of those contributing to the economy.
Merz said the reforms were necessary to preserve Germany's prosperity and ensure that younger generations were not left carrying an unfair share of the costs.
Merz accuses political extremes of seeking chaos
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has accused political forces on the far left and far right of deliberately dividing society, spreading disinformation and downplaying the threat posed by Russia.
Speaking in the Bundestag, Merz said he could not understand why politicians at both ends of the political spectrum continued to minimize Russian aggression.
"One gets the impression that you want chaos because you hope to gain political advantage from it," he told lawmakers.
Merz warned that extremism was increasingly making its presence felt in Germany's national and regional parliaments, as well as everyday life.
However, he acknowledged that extremist movements could draw support from legitimate dissatisfaction and feelings of injustice, arguing that constructive political action was the only effective response.
"Justice for us does not come through the exclusion of minorities," Merz said, calling for policies that promote equal opportunities and fairness between generations.
He contrasted what he described as the destructive politics of division and exclusion with the responsibility of democratic parties to address genuine grievances and govern for everyone in Germany.
WATCH: Merz addresses Bundestag before crucial EU summit
Merz says Ukraine aid does not come at welfare's expense
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has rejected accusations from the far right and far left that support for Ukraine comes at the expense of social spending.
"Not a single euro is missing from social spending," he told parliament, speaking ahead of an EU summit in Brussels.
Merz said an exemption from Germany's constitutional borrowing limits allows spending on defense and assistance for Ukraine to be financed through additional credit.
He accused the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the socialist Left Party of seeking to divide Germany
AfD and BSW join forces against Ukraine support
In the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the far-right Alternative for Germany Party (AfD) won recent elections in a landslide, a new alliance has flexed its muscle.
The AfD put forward a motion to halt arms deliveries to Ukraine and lift sanctions against Russia. Instead, they argue, peace talks with Russia should be initiated.
The Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason (BSW), which holds five seats in the state parliament, again teamed up with the AfD to ensure a majority for the motion. The BSW combines left-leaning economics with right-wing populist positions on immigration and relations with Russia.
AfD and BSW also called for an immediate halt to financial support for Ukraine, to the extent that it goes beyond humanitarian aid.
The motion by the AfD and BSW has no more than symbolic value, as decisions regarding sanctions against Russia and aid to Ukraine are made not by the federal states, but by the federal government and the European Union.
But the new alliance of AfD and BSW has a wider significance. It is seen by observers as a sign of longer-term and closer cooperation between the two parties, which originate from very different ideological camps.
Although the AfD emerged as the clear winner of the state elections in September 2026, it lacks a majority to form a government. It has been searching for partners in the state legislature. So far, the BSW is the only party officially negotiating with the AfD on forming a government.
Merz to set out EU priorities after urging reforms
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is expected to outline Germany's priorities on Ukraine, European defense and economic competitiveness in a parliamentary address ahead of an EU summit in Brussels.
His government statement is scheduled for 14:05 local time (12:05 UTC), followed by a 90-minute debate. EU leaders meet on Thursday and Friday, with the Middle East, the bloc's next long-term budget and EU enlargement also on the agenda.
After the speech, the opposition Greens are set to put forward two motions calling for faster bloc enlargement and stronger measures to counter economic coercion and protect the bloc's market.
Merz's address follows a more domestic-focused speech on planned reforms at an employers' conference in Berlin on Tuesday. There, he said he would press ahead with changes to Germany's welfare system even at the expense of his own popularity, arguing that younger generations stood to benefit.
Energy prices push German inflation to 3.3%
Germany's annual inflation rate rose to 3.3% in September, its highest level since December 2023, as fuel and heating oil prices surged.
The Federal Statistical Office confirmed its preliminary estimate, up from 2.9% in August and 2.8% in July.
The increase was again driven by energy prices, said the office's president, Ruth Brand, highlighting higher costs at gas stations and for heating oil.
Energy prices rose 14.9% compared with September last year, their steepest annual increase since February 2023. That followed increases of 10.5% in August and 8.3% in July.
Motor fuel prices jumped 37.1%, while heating oil rose 74.9%. Firewood, wood pellets and other solid fuels became 15.6% more expensive.
However, electricity prices fell 5.5%, natural gas prices dropped 2.8% and district heating cost 1% less.
The office attributed those declines partly to government measures implemented since the start of the year.

Michelin-starred A Cut turns up heat with new live-fire restaurant in Taipei
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
06:51:00 UTC
15:51:00 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Michelin-starred steakhouse A Cut marked its 20th anniversary with the launch of a new live-fire restaurant brand in Taipei, taking its cooking beyond the hotel setting in which it has operated for two decades.
Located in Taipei’s Garden City shopping mall, The Grill by A Cut shifts the brand’s focus from the precision of traditional steakhouse cooking to the flavors and textures created by open flames. Longan wood burns beneath meat and seafood, adding a smoky aroma that changes how the ingredients taste and feel.
For beef, the focus moves beyond the creamy, cheese-like notes associated with dry-aged meat to the aromas that develop when fat meets intense heat. Seafood takes a similar approach, with high-heat grilling bringing out its natural sweetness and giving it a firmer texture than low-temperature cooking.
The Japan Kyushu ex-breed Wagyu striploin reflects this approach, using beef from mature cattle known for their firmer texture and deeper flavor. Grilled directly over the fire, the steak develops a deeply browned crust while remaining tender and rosy inside. As the fat renders, smoke from the longan wood adds subtle woody notes, giving the beef a more pronounced savory character than the soft, heavily marbled texture commonly associated with Wagyu.
The Australia Copper Tree Farms grass-fed bone-in ribeye offers a different take. The beef is wet-aged at a controlled low temperature before grilling, helping develop a tender texture and balanced flavor.
The fire forms a caramelized crust while the inside remains juicy. The bone adds savory depth, while fresh lemon cuts through the richness and brings the beef’s flavor into sharper focus.
The Taiwan black pork tomahawk chop pairs its grilled texture with a spiced sherry vinaigrette made with sherry vinegar and spices, adding gentle acidity and warmth. Honey apple sauce contributes sweet-tart fruitiness, while tomato and fresh rosemary bring brightness and a light herbal aroma.
The seasonal fish follows the same fire-driven approach, served with a sauce of tomato, capers and herbs that balances sweet, tart and savory notes. Crisp asparagus and fried basil leaves add texture and a fresh herbal touch.
The charcoal-grilled Maine lobster, meanwhile, develops a lightly charred aroma, complemented by rich spiced butter and a squeeze of lemon. Grilled asparagus provides a crisp counterpoint with a subtle smoky flavor.
Beyond grilled dishes, the menu includes a beef tartare made with chopped Australian Wagyu and layers of fried potato. One portion is topped with Japanese sea urchin, while another features Ossetra caviar, giving the familiar steakhouse appetizer a more elaborate presentation.
The raw scallop dish takes a lighter approach, pairing sashimi-grade scallops with cherry radish, kumquat vinaigrette, scallion oil, and chili oil. Miso and koji add savory depth, while shiso provides a fresh herbal finish.
Another seafood starter, yellowtail sashimi, is served with a cilantro and jalapeno sauce, lemon juice and olive oil. Citrus, herbs and a mild kick of heat balance the richness of the fish.
The live-fire concept extends to dessert with Baked Alaska, made with passion fruit sorbet and Meyer lemon ice cream beneath a layer of meringue. The meringue is torched until lightly browned, forming a crisp exterior around the cold, fruity center.
At the table, orange Cognac is poured over the dessert and ignited, sending a brief blue flame across the meringue. The combination of heat, citrus aroma and cold sorbet brings the fire theme through to the final course.
Another key difference between The Grill and A Cut is the menu format. Rather than requiring diners to commit to a traditional steakhouse set menu, The Grill allows guests to order individual dishes. The restaurant also draws on A Cut’s wine experience, offering a selection designed to complement its wider range of dishes and fire-driven flavors.
A Cut Executive Chef William Ling (凌維廉) said live-fire cooking requires an understanding of how heat and smoke can complement an ingredient without masking its natural character. At The Grill, fire serves not only as a source of heat but also as an element that shapes each dish’s aroma and texture, bringing an element of unpredictability to the dining experience.

The incident was the latest in Germany's decades-long protest movement against nuclear weapons and atomic energy.
Although the last of the country's nuclear power stations went offline in 2023, transporting and storing the waste remains a divisive topic.
This particular convoy was headed for a facility in Ahaus, near the Dutch border. Authorities believe it could take until 2028 to safely store all the remaining waste from Germany's decommissioned atomic reactors.
Suicide rate increased significantly in 2025
The suicide rate in Germany has continued to climb, according to official statistics just released by the Federal Ministry of Health.
In 2025, at least 11,334 people killed themselves in Germany. That is a 9.3% increase on the previous year, and 15.6% higher than the average over the past decade.
This is higher than the number of deaths due to traffic accidents, AIDS, murder and manslaughter put together.
The data shows that this is partly due to more women (a 17.9% increase since 2021) taking their own lives, though most suicides are still carried out by men. The increase is also due to an increase in assisted suicides for the elderly and infirm, amounting to over 1,000 people.
In a 2020 decision, Germany's top court struck down a 2015 ban on organized assisted dying providers like Switzerland's Dignitas, and called on the Bundestag to create regulations for the practice. However, lawmakers have declined thus far to do so, putting assisted suicide in a legal gray area in Germany. Direct euthanasia by a single doctor remains illegal.
In August, the Health Ministry proposed reforms such as a national suicide prevention hotline, more support for local and state networks, as well as the creation of a federal office for suicide prevention.
However, medical groups and charities have both said that the proposed €1.4 million ($1.6 million) budget would come nowhere never covering such a scheme long-term.
Editor's note: If you are suffering from serious emotional strain or suicidal thoughts, do not hesitate to seek professional help. You can find information on where to find such help, no matter where you live in the world, at this website: https://www.befrienders.org/
Proposed sugar tax faces criticism
According to German media reports, the ruling coalition of Chancellor Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU) and the Social Democrats (SPD) has found a compromise for a planned tax increase on sugar.
The law would impact sugar drinks in particular, and is set to come into effect on July 1 of next year. There is reportedly going to be an exception for small-scale producers.
CDU state premier of Hesse, Boris Rhein, slammed the plan on Wednesday. Rhein told the Kölner Stadt-Anzeiger newspaper that this "expensive tax" (a phrase that rhymes in German) would simply result in companies passing on the extra expense to consumers.
Rhein accused the coalition of pretending the measure was about health when really it was so "the populace can continue to plug up holes in the federal budget at the cash register."
Nord Stream sabotage suspect goes on trial in Hamburg
The much anticipated trial of Serhii K., whose last name is withheld due to Germany's privacy laws, will begin in Hamburg today.
K. is accused by investigators of leading a group comprising professional divers, an explosives expert, and a boat skipper who plotted to travel to the remote section of the Nord Stream gas pipelines off the Danish coast and blow them up.
The series of explosions ruptured Nord Stream 1, which Moscow had switched off a month earlier, and destroyed Nord Stream 2, which had yet to come into operation at the time.
A former Ukrainian military officer, K's case has led some investigators to point at Kyiv as orchestrating the entire plan, as the pipelines controversially delivered Russian natural gas to Europe.
The attack came seven months after Russia's fullscale invasion of Ukraine, when European countries were taking steps to drastically decrease their reliance on Russian fuel.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has vehemently denied any official connection to the attack.
K. was apprehended in Italy in 2025 and extradited to Germany. His specific charges are: being an accomplice to a war crime by attacking civil energy infrastructure, disruption of public services, causing an explosion and destroying structures.

This involves stopping and fining Chinese fishing boats that are illegally trawling or Chinese oil tankers polluting within the exclusive economic zone.
