He suggested that Taiwan learn from the Philippines’ successful appeal in the Permanent Court of Arbitration in 2016, concerning China’s illegal claims in the South China Sea.
“To win and retain world attention, Taiwanese public diplomacy needs to be inventive and fresh,” Blair said. It must not let China shape international opinion and allow its actions to be normalized, he added.
Blair called on Taiwan “to strengthen and publicize its own military and civil capabilities” in countering Chinese aggression. The nation can “further capitalize on its strong geographic position and can develop the military technologies that China cannot easily counter, such as anti-ship missiles, unmanned systems, (and) advanced electronic warfare capabilities,” he said.
Taiwan has purchased 100 sets of the land-based Harpoon Coastal Defense System, of which the first batch is expected to arrive by the end of the year. These actions can make the risks of an invasion so high that Beijing may decide it is not worth attempting, Blair said.

Tehran Auto Plaza aims to simplify the journey from car shopping to ownership
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
06:50:45 UTC
15:50:45 KST

Tehran Auto Plaza aims to simplify the journey from car shopping to ownership
TEHRAN – Buying a car can involve more than choosing a model and agreeing on a price. Prospective buyers may need to visit several dealerships, compare technical specifications, arrange financing, verify a used vehicle’s condition and navigate paperwork before completing a transaction. Tehran Auto Plaza is being developed around the idea that much of this journey could happen in one place.
Introduced to the media on Monday, October 12, the automotive complex on Tehran’s western outskirts aims to bring vehicle showrooms, specialist services and digital tools together in a single destination. Its plans include approximately 90 showrooms, facilities for vehicle maintenance and repair, a spare-parts hypermarket and services intended to support customers before and after a purchase.
The ambition is to make the process of buying and owning a vehicle more convenient, while giving customers a broader range of options to explore. Rather than concentrating solely on displaying cars, Tehran Auto Plaza seeks to connect several stages of the ownership experience, from comparing models and arranging a purchase to maintaining a vehicle and eventually selling or exchanging it.
For a market in which buyers must often weigh affordability, availability and the reliability of a transaction, the concept offers an alternative to searching for individual dealerships and service providers across the capital.
An idea shaped by the market
Amir-Parviz Farzan, manager of Tehran Auto Plaza, told the Tehran Times that the concept emerged from the experience of organizing Tehran Auto Expo and examining the difficulties encountered by consumers and automotive businesses.
The organizers subsequently began developing a model intended to address practical problems in the industry and make services easier to access.
“We wanted to design a model that could address the problems and concerns in the automotive industry and give consumers confidence that they could use services easily and transparently,” Farzan said.
That objective underpins the complex’s emphasis on bringing different sellers and service providers together. A customer considering several vehicles could, in principle, examine alternatives in one location rather than travel between separate showrooms. Access to technical specialists and related services would also give visitors the opportunity to investigate aspects of ownership beyond a vehicle’s appearance and advertised price.
The project is designed to accommodate customers with different budgets and preferences. Farzan said the planned selection would range from more economical vehicles to luxury models, while Iranian automakers would also have opportunities to present their products.
Negotiations with various automotive brands were continuing, he said, including discussions concerning dealership arrangements for vehicles that could be imported in accordance with government requirements.
The range of vehicles ultimately available will depend on those arrangements, market conditions and the pace at which individual showrooms become operational. Nevertheless, the proposed mix is intended to make the complex relevant to a broad customer base rather than limiting its appeal to buyers of premium cars.
A different approach to vehicle sales
A distinctive feature of the business model is the intention to manage sales through dealership arrangements rather than simply rent out display spaces.
Amirhossein Afrasiabipour, Tehran Auto Plaza’s deputy for strategy and business, said the complex itself would obtain dealership arrangements, assign specialists to its showrooms and take responsibility for vehicle sales.
This model is intended to create a more coordinated experience for visitors. Instead of entering a showroom and relying exclusively on the information available from an individual seller, customers would have access to specialists who could explain vehicle features and help them compare alternatives.
The value of such an arrangement will ultimately depend on the breadth of the available stock, the quality of advice and the clarity of the commercial terms offered. If implemented effectively, however, it could make the process more manageable for buyers who are unfamiliar with technical specifications or uncertain about which vehicle best suits their needs.
The planned services extend to the practical requirements of completing a purchase. Assistance with documentation, registration and license plates is envisaged, alongside financing and leasing arrangements through partner banks.
For some buyers, access to financing could be as important as the choice of vehicle itself. Bringing these services closer to the point of sale could help customers understand the overall cost of a purchase and assess whether a particular model fits their budget.
Tehran Auto Plaza also plans to accommodate customers who want to replace an existing vehicle. Under the proposed arrangement, owners could bring a used car to the complex for valuation and sale, then use the proceeds toward another purchase. Leasing services are intended to offer an additional option for people seeking to upgrade their vehicles.
These services could help connect the buying and selling processes, reducing the need for customers to arrange each stage independently. Their practical usefulness will depend on how valuations are conducted, how quickly transactions can be completed and what conditions apply to financing and leasing.
Bringing used-car transactions into the same setting
The used-car market presents a particular challenge for buyers, who may have to assess a vehicle’s mechanical condition, accident history, paintwork and maintenance record before committing to a purchase.
Tehran Auto Plaza’s planned technical inspection and vehicle-assessment services are intended to address some of these concerns. The complex also envisages facilities for checking a vehicle’s bodywork and paint, alongside repair and maintenance services.
Such assessments can provide useful information about a vehicle’s condition, although an inspection cannot eliminate every uncertainty or guarantee future reliability. Clear explanations of inspection methods and findings will therefore be important to building customer confidence.
A digital record of a vehicle’s condition and service history is another element of the proposed system. If supported by consistent inspections and reliable records, it could help buyers make more informed decisions and give sellers a clearer way to document the condition of their cars.
The complex also plans to facilitate used-car listings and exchanges, allowing customers to assess the approximate market value of their current vehicles and consider the additional amount needed to move to another model.
Together, these services are intended to make changing cars a more connected process. A customer could begin by assessing an existing vehicle, explore alternatives, obtain advice and consider a replacement without having to coordinate every stage with an unrelated business.
A digital companion for car ownership
The physical complex is only one part of the plan. A dedicated automotive application is being developed to connect customers with services at Tehran Auto Plaza and provide information useful throughout the ownership cycle.
Mehdi Moazzami, deputy for digital affairs, said the platform would allow users to book appointments for automotive services and arrange visits at designated times. Customers unable to take their vehicles to the complex themselves would also be able to request a vehicle-transfer service.
Under the proposed arrangement, a service vehicle would collect the customer’s car and transport it to the complex. Users would then be able to follow the progress of the requested work through the application.
The platform is also expected to support the purchase of spare parts and accessories. Customers would be able to order components suited to their vehicles, with free delivery planned, or visit the complex to have selected parts installed. Technical-inspection appointments are also envisaged.
Other proposed features include access to vehicle-fine and road-toll information, payment services and a digital wallet through which users could manage related transactions.
For motorists interested in upgrading their vehicles, the application is intended to provide recommendations for audio systems and other equipment based on vehicle specifications. Artificial intelligence would help identify suitable options and estimate their costs before the customer approves the work. Testing equipment before installation is also planned.
The aim is to make it easier for customers to understand what is compatible with their vehicles and what a proposed modification might cost before making a decision.
Helping customers choose
A planned intelligent car-buying assistant is intended to extend the application’s role beyond booking services and processing transactions.
According to Moazzami, users would be able to enter information about their budget, lifestyle and practical requirements. The system could then suggest vehicles that correspond to those needs, estimate the additional payment required for an upgrade and facilitate test-drive bookings.
Such a tool could be useful to customers who are overwhelmed by the number of models and specifications available. Someone looking for a family vehicle, for example, might prioritize space and everyday practicality, while another customer could focus on fuel economy, equipment or driving preferences.
The application is also intended to provide vehicle valuations based on market information and transactions involving comparable models. Following technical and bodywork inspections, a vehicle’s assessment could be recorded in its digital history.
The planned customer club would add another element to the platform, with users earning points through their activities and potentially receiving benefits such as car-wash services and discounts on selected offerings. The application is intended to be free to install, although the availability and terms of individual services will determine how customers can use them.
As with any digital service, the usefulness of these features will depend on the quality of the underlying information, the reliability of the system and the ease with which customers can access assistance when needed.
From a collection of services to a connected experience
Tehran Auto Plaza’s central proposition is straightforward: bring together services that motorists commonly need at different stages of buying, using and replacing a car.
The planned combination of showrooms, technical facilities, spare-parts sales, financing, inspections and digital services could save customers time and give them a clearer picture of their options. It could also create opportunities for businesses operating in different parts of the automotive sector to reach customers in one place.
The project is expected to generate more than 2,000 direct jobs, with Farzan estimating that the number could reach 2,300 to 2,400. He also projected the creation of another 7,000 to 8,000 indirect jobs. These figures are estimates rather than confirmed employment totals and will depend on the scale of operations as the complex develops.
For customers, the most important measure of success will be practical rather than architectural: whether the promised services are available when needed, whether prices and terms are clear, and whether the range of vehicles and expertise makes comparisons easier.
Tehran Auto Plaza is designed to offer an alternative to a fragmented search for cars and automotive services. If its planned facilities and digital tools work together as intended, the complex could turn what is often a series of separate errands into a more coordinated journey, from the first comparison of models to the ongoing care of a vehicle and the decision to replace it.

CPC will continue coordinating with its US counterparts, conducting project assessments, and seeking budget approval. The ministry said it would continue monitoring global natural gas markets and reviewing domestic demand forecasts to help ensure a stable energy supply.

‘To Be Ordinary’ brings Taipei family drama to Busan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
06:50:15 UTC
15:50:15 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Weber Yang (楊一展) admits he visited some dark personal places when building the character he plays in “To Be Ordinary,” the new film from acclaimed director Lee Yun-chan (李芸嬋).
But Yang did not really have much choice, given certain unmistakable similarities between himself and his character and the stages they are going through in life.
“Like this character I feel like I am now going through a midlife crisis,” Yang said. “I told the director this on the first day of shooting. It's actually very confusing.”
“There is a continuous loss of direction. You don't know if it's because of work, or because of your hormones, or the things around you.
“Simply from this perspective, I think if there is any inspiration at all from this movie, then I hope it is the message that you can still find a direction in life.”
“To Be Ordinary” — which made its world premiere in the main Competition section this past week at the 31st Busan International Film Festival — marks Lee’s return to feature filmmaking after a break of some 20 years.
It also reveals the filmmaker has not lost her ability to frame deep, sometimes unnerving family drama. The time away, including time spent making the series “Women in Taipei” (2022) for Disney+, seems to have simply sharpened it.
“To Be Ordinary” features Yang and Winnie Chang Shih-Ying (張詩盈) as a struggling couple whose son is hit by an elderly driver while riding his motorcycle — an accident that leads the guilt-ridden driver to offer various forms of compensation.
During the movie, the family’s fortunes and their individual relationships fall and rise as they move slowly toward some sort of acceptance of their lives and of each other.
“The whole story really wants to present the relationships between people in contemporary urban families in Taipei,” Lee said. “There are many unexpected events in a big city, and even the right decisions can have many incomprehensible results.”
The film is an almost immersive experience, bringing viewers up close and personal with the family in their trouble and grief as they slowly try to work their way through both. That the situations and dialogue feel so real comes down to the script Lee wrote and the strength of the central performances.
Both Yang and Chang said there were times when they struggled with the work and the characters they play, given the serious nature of the story. But there is no doubt their struggles were worth it.
“I think when you really encounter a major change, you have the opportunity to look back and see what it is that you have been moving towards in this lifetime,” Chang said. “Are you living for others or for yourself?”
For Lee, the film marks a welcome return to feature filmmaking, following the acclaim she received early in her career with “The Shoe Fairy” (2005), which starred Vivian Hsu (徐若瑄), screened at Busan and picked up two nominations at the Golden Horse Awards.
“When writing this script, I collected many stories from people around me because for the past 20 years, I have returned to family life,” the director said. “I have raised two children so I have insights into the different families living in Taipei.”
“You may face many sudden accidents and impacts and so having lived in Taipei my whole life, I wanted with this film to share my feelings about people's lives in general but especially in this city.”

Sigurd expands testing capacity with NT$2.2 billion Hsinchu acquisition
Unknown

2026-10-14
06:50:12 UTC
15:50:12 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Sigurd Microelectronics Corp. is expanding its testing capacity with a NT$2.2 billion (US$68 million) acquisition in Hsinchu.
The company said Tuesday that its subsidiary, Sigurd UTC Corp., won the bid to acquire a factory in Hsinchu Science Park. The acquisition comes as major US customers seek more advanced testing services for increasingly complex AI and high-performance computing chips, according to CTEE.
The site covers about 26,000 square meters of land and is expected to boost Sigurd's testing capacity by about 25% once fully operational. It will focus on developing testing equipment and services for high-speed optical communication chips used in AI data connections and silicon photonics.
The site will also offer wafer testing for application-specific AI chips, as well as testing services for chips packaged using chip-on-wafer-on-substrate, or CoWoS, technology. Other services will include testing and backend processing for general-purpose chips.
Sigurd is also increasing its production capacity at other sites. Its second plant in Hukou began production in the second half of this year, while its third plant in the Zhongxing area is scheduled to begin operations early next year.
The company reported cumulative revenue of NT$17.3 billion in the first three quarters. The figure was up 21.15% from the same period a year earlier, reflecting continued contributions from AI-related and high-end chip testing.
Packaging and testing is a key stage of semiconductor manufacturing that follows wafer fabrication. Packaging protects individual chips and provides the electrical connections needed to power them and link them to other components, while testing verifies that they function correctly and meet performance requirements, according to Gugu Fund.
As AI chips become more powerful and incorporate more components to handle growing volumes of data, testing must meet stricter performance requirements. This has increased the need for verification at multiple stages of production, from wafer testing to post-packaging checks and high-speed signal testing.
Meanwhile, advances in silicon photonics and co-packaged optics which bring optical communication closer to computing chips, are adding to the technical challenges of testing high-speed semiconductors. Analysts say companies that develop their own testing equipment and offer integrated services may be better positioned to secure higher-value contracts as these technologies advance.

The head of the International Monetary Fund on Wednesday called for countries to make "urgent repairs" to address fiscal balances as bond yields spike and pressure grows on governments to manage ballooning debt.

"Now is the time to enhance revenues, to rationalise spending and improve public financial management," she said.
The global economy "remains resilient in the face of very frequent repetitive shocks and in the face of uncertainty", Georgieva said. "But this resilience is reaching its limits."
The IMF is "ringing the alarm bell on excessive global economic imbalances growing", she added.
"To put it very simply, China needs to spend more, the US has to save more and Europe has to invest more," Georgieva said.
Her comments come as officials and experts gather in the Thai capital to discuss challenges facing the global economy as higher energy prices arising from US attacks on Iran drive up costs.
In its closely watched World Economic Outlook released on Tuesday, the IMF raised its 2026 global growth forecast by 0.1 percentage points to 3.1 percent.
However, it warned that while there is new economic activity sparked by rising investment in artificial intelligence, poorer countries are not benefiting as they deal with soaring energy costs.
On the United States, Georgieva said it cannot grow its way out of mounting public debt and needs to make other fiscal adjustments to put its debt on a more sustainable path.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, she points out, recognises that  US deficits and overall debt, now above US$40 trillion, are too high.
"The authorities very much rely on strong growth in the United States" to help reduce debt, Georgieva said. "At the fund,  we believe that  growth, of course, helps, but it cannot deliver  fast enough the necessary adjustments. So, some [fiscal] measures would be necessary. (Agencies)

China’s annual inflation edges up to 0.9% in September
Unknown

Mucahithan Avcioglu
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
China’s annual consumer inflation accelerated to 0.9% in September from 0.8% in August, slightly below market expectations of 1%, according to National Bureau of Statistics data released on Wednesday.
The reading marked the highest inflation rate since June, as increases in non-food prices were partly offset by a continued decline in food costs.
Non-food prices rose 1.5% from a year earlier, compared with a 1.2% increase in August. Prices for transport and communication climbed 4.3%, accelerating from 2.5% the previous month.
Healthcare prices increased 2.7% year-on-year, while education, culture and recreation costs rose 1.4%, both unchanged from August.
Clothing prices increased 1.2%, easing from 1.3% a month earlier. Housing costs fell 0.3%, matching the decline recorded in August.
Food prices declined for the sixth consecutive month, falling 1.7% from a year earlier after a 1.4% decrease in August. Pork prices dropped 10%.
Core inflation, which excludes food and energy prices, stood at 1% year-on-year.
On a monthly basis, consumer prices increased 0.2% in September, below expectations of 0.3% and slowing from August’s 0.4% rise.

New enforcement threshold and warning signs cut speed trap fines by €1 million a month
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
06:46:00 UTC
15:46:00 KST

New enforcement threshold and warning signs cut speed trap fines by €1 million a month
Since warning signs became mandatory for mobile speed cameras, the number of fines issued has fallen by nearly 90 percent, while revenue from fines dropped by almost €1 million in September.
In September last year, police issued €1,256,318 in fines using mobile speed cameras. This September, following the installation of warning signs ahead of the cameras and an increase in the enforcement threshold, fines totaled just €199,052, a decrease of nearly €1 million.
The drop in fine revenue was driven by a 90 percent decline in the number of fines issued. Raising the enforcement threshold nearly halved the number of violations, while the introduction of warning signs reduced it by roughly half again. As ERR has previously reported, citing police statistics, mobile speed cameras issued 26,228 fines in September last year, compared with just 2,939 across Estonia in September this year.
However, police spokesperson Taavi Kirss said revenue from fines has never been a priority for the police and will not be in the future.
"Our only priority has always been to make Estonia's roads safer and ensure that drivers obey speed limits. Higher speeds make it harder to spot hazards and lead to more severe consequences and more serious injuries in the event of an accident," Kirss said.
MP: The goal is to slow down traffic, not fill the treasury
Madis Timpson (Reform), chair of the Riigikogu's Legal Affairs Committee, who pushed for mandatory warning signs ahead of mobile speed cameras, told ERR that short-term police statistics may not provide a complete picture and that a longer period and more thorough analysis are needed to assess the actual impact.
"I think it's a little too early to draw conclusions based on just one month. We really need to look at a longer period than one or two months," Timpson explained. However, he said the decline in fines was a positive sign. "If the police say the number of fines has fallen by 90 percent, that's a good thing."
Commenting on the fact that the sharp drop in fines has left the state budget nearly €1 million short in a single month, with the trend likely to continue in the coming months, Timpson said issuing fines should never be an end in itself for either local governments or the state, even if it means forgoing millions of euros in potential annual revenue.
"The police have always said that the goal is not to issue fines but to calm traffic. If traffic has become calmer, that's a success," he said. "I certainly wouldn't want to live in a country where we try to fill the state coffers by issuing as many fines as possible," he added.
Timpson: I have not seen senseless speeding
Timpson disagrees with observations by some road users that drivers only obey the speed limit in the immediate vicinity of warning signs. The politician said his assessment is based on extensive personal experience driving between Tallinn and Viljandi every week.
"I drive between Viljandi and Tallinn several times a week. I don't think the situation is that bad. In my opinion, the overall traffic situation has improved considerably over the years," Timpson said, adding that it is wrong to regulate the behavior of all road users because of a few offenders.
"There have always been speeders, although there seem to be fewer of them lately. I haven't even noticed anyone driving recklessly fast," Timpson said.
Timpson also described his own negative experience with a mobile speed camera.
"I was once caught by a speed camera myself, doing 56 kilometers per hour. It was midday on a straight stretch of road with speed limit signs showing 90, 70 and then 50. I know because I drive that road several times a week. I switched off cruise control and coasted into the 50-kilometer-per-hour zone at 56. There were no cars coming from either direction, no other road users and the road was straight for three kilometers. Of course, I paid the fine, but it still left a bit of a bad taste in my mouth," Timpson recalled.
According to Timpson, however, his own fine was not the main motivation behind the legislative amendment. Rather, his decision to initiate the bill was a matter of principle: to restore fairness after police initially promised to install warning signs themselves but subsequently failed to do so.
"The bill actually originated from the fact that the police came to the Riigikogu in late 2018 and said they wanted to install mobile speed cameras and that warning signs would be placed ahead of them. In 2019, when the law was passed, this was reiterated on the floor of the Riigikogu. The law was passed, but the signs were never installed. In other words, the Riigikogu was deceived. If you went to your employer and promised to do something but then failed to deliver, what do you think would happen to you? I'd fire you," Timpson said.
On July 1, the Police and Border Guard Board (PPA) raised the enforcement threshold for mobile speed cameras on its own initiative. Mobile cameras now issue fines only when drivers exceed the speed limit by at least 6 kilometers per hour, up from the previous threshold of 3 kilometers per hour, to avoid penalizing momentary lapses in attention. The change applied only to the eight mobile speed cameras operated by the PPA across Estonia. Fixed speed cameras continue to enforce speed limits starting at 3 kilometers per hour over the limit.
In May, three Riigikogu members — Valdo Randpere, Madis Timpson and Marek Reinaas — introduced a legislative amendment requiring police to place warning signs ahead of mobile speed cameras. The amendment was passed despite police opposition and took effect on August 1.
A study published by the Estonian Transport Administration in September found that 77 percent of drivers exceed the speed limit on at least some types of roads, an increase from last year. Of those who speed, 22 percent have encountered a dangerous traffic situation as a result, a figure that has also risen.

Geometry that Generates Energy: The Solar Facade of Breidablikk Gården, Norway
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
06:45:00 UTC
15:45:00 KST

Solar panels are often treated as equipment added to a building. What happens when they become part of the architecture itself? Once integrated into the envelope, photovoltaics can generate energy while also influencing the building's form, construction, and environmental performance.
Roofs are often the most obvious location for photovoltaic panels, yet other parts of the building can generate power while performing additional architectural functions. Facades can provide shading, louvers can control sunlight, and ventilated rainscreens can combine weather protection with energy generation. Their orientation, position, and integration into the building envelope therefore become part of the architectural design rather than a separate technical decision.
For architects, this raises an important question: where should solar generation take place when the building is designed as a whole and is also expected to contribute to urban renewal? Breidablikk Gården in Haugesund, Norway, provides a case where the facade addresses several of these considerations. Designed by Asplan Viak, the office building combines roof-mounted photovoltaics with an integrated solar facade developed with SolarLab.
Its east and west facades use angled panels that turn toward the south, increasing energy production while also creating shading for the offices behind them. The result is a facade in which the photovoltaic system is coordinated with the building's energy strategy, climate, and urban setting. As Asplan Viak explains:
 The design stands out, attracting attention to itself, while simultaneously blending in with the city's overall aesthetic.
Where Can Photovoltaics Be Integrated?
A facade can provide another surface for energy generation while also contributing to the building envelope, with different panel sizes, colors, finishes, and mounting geometries offering ways to integrate photovoltaics into the architectural design. The approach used at Breidablikk Gården is one of several ways of incorporating photovoltaics into a building. In a ventilated facade, solar panels can replace conventional rainscreen cladding while maintaining a ventilated cavity behind the outer layer. This approach can be used for both new construction and refurbishment projects. Curtain wall systems offer another possibility, with photovoltaic elements integrated as replacements for selected spandrel or vision panels.
Louvers, or brise-soleil, can combine solar generation with solar control by mounting photovoltaic fins horizontally or vertically in front of windows. Roofs are another important location, especially when a large, unobstructed surface is available. These approaches mean the appropriate location for photovoltaics can be considered alongside the building's orientation, facade construction, shading requirements, and architectural expression, rather than decided separately.
Why Put Solar Panels on the Facade?
Haugesund's climate makes orientation particularly relevant. The city is located in southwestern Norway, where the sun remains low during winter months. Facades do not receive sunlight in the same way as roofs, but their orientation and inclination can still be used to influence solar production.
At Breidablikk Gården, the east and west facades could have been treated as conventional vertical elevations with photovoltaic panels simply mounted onto them. Instead, the panels are angled toward the south. The facade consequently forms a repeated zigzag up to 30 cm in and out at each window, turning the photovoltaic surfaces toward the sun while also creating shade at the openings. Together with screen curtains, this reduces solar exposure and the need for cooling.
The geometry therefore has a practical consequence beyond appearance. Changing the angle alters the relationship between the photovoltaic surface and incoming sunlight, while the same articulation creates depth around the windows. Solar collection and solar protection are addressed through the same facade element.
The project has a peak photovoltaic capacity of 39.9 kWp, while the facade can produce around 100,000 kWh of electricity per year. Breidablikk Gården also combines the facade system with roof PV and efficient building services and has achieved BREEAM-NOR Excellent.
A facade with customized photovoltaic geometry also changes the design process. SolarLab's method begins with scoping, using an architect's three-dimensional sketches or models together with local climate data to simulate potential electricity production. The results can be presented through three-dimensional visualizations and data graphs, allowing the design team to evaluate geometry and expected production during the design process. This type of process is particularly relevant for a facade such as Breidablikk Gården.
Turning an Energy System into an Urban Facade
At Breidablikk Gården, the solar panels form a ventilated rainscreen designed for the rainy and snowy Norwegian climate. The articulated panels are mounted on horizontal rails over the underlying structure, while the electrical system was designed to optimize production and remain resilient against partial shading.
The building uses low-carbon wood construction with prefabricated wall modules, placing the solar rainscreen outside the primary construction. The photovoltaic layer can therefore be understood as one part of a larger envelope assembly, working alongside the structural wall, ventilation cavity, weather protection, shading, and electrical system.
The facade also uses an iridescent coating that changes in appearance with the light and viewing angle, giving the articulated surface a changing presence within the city. The technology is integrated into the cladding rather than expressed as a separate layer of conventional solar panels.
Breidablikk Gården is located in a central part of Haugesund and was presented as an example of urban renewal. Its facade was designed to stand out while remaining connected to the character of the surrounding city. Here, the solar facade therefore combines several functions within a single envelope: its orientation supports energy production, its depth provides shading, its rainscreen construction protects the underlying building structure, and its surface treatment contributes to the building's appearance.

====================================================================================================

Young people grow out of peer pressure shenanigans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
06:43:00 UTC
15:43:00 KST

Young people grow out of peer pressure shenanigans
Most young people who break the law during adolescence eventually grow out of such behavior, with support, family relationships and teaching responsibility more effective than harsh punishment, experts say.
In criminology, there is a principle known as the age-crime curve, according to which young people's propensity for risk-taking is temporary. "People are most active in terms of criminal activity or breaking the law in their 20s. [...] Activity rises along this curve and then declines," criminologist Anna Markina explained on Vikerraadio's "Teise mätta otsast" program.
Nearly 80 percent of young people test boundaries during adolescence but move away from criminal behavior as they reach adulthood. Only a small proportion continue to lead troubled lives. According to clinical child psychologist Iiris Velling, this means that not every violation of the law warrants harsh punishment.
Teenagers often break the law to gain approval, recognition and a sense of belonging among their peers. "When young people make the decision to break the law in a particular moment, they don't even think about the long-term consequences," Velling noted. Social media amplifies this desire, as young people gain new followers and social capital by posting videos of their misdeeds.
Alongside their friends, the urban environment and leisure activities also influence young people's behavior. "At some point, our society decided that shopping malls would serve as public spaces. [...] These are now the public spaces where our young people gather," Markina pointed out. In such settings, boredom and peer pressure often lead to conflicts, with what begins as innocent recreation ending in young people damaging other people's property or shoplifting.
Don't punish, react!
Rather than focusing on punishment, Estonia has opted for an approach centered on responding to young people who come into conflict with the law. Since a reform introducing special treatment for minors took effect in 2018, Estonia's child protection and justice systems have dealt with each young person in a way tailored to their individual needs. "Punishment is generally understood to mean detention facilities. [...] However, we only use these when other measures cannot influence a child's behavior," Markina explained.
According to the criminologist, traditional prison sentences do not rehabilitate young people but instead make a criminal identity part of their personality. Behind bars, young people form new connections with peers from similar backgrounds. "When they are released, the consequences can be even more devastating for both the young person and society as a whole because they begin reinforcing each other's behavior," Markina explained.
According to Iiris Velling, rather than talking about punishment, it would be better to focus on consequences and teaching children to take responsibility. "Very often, we expect children to be punished for their actions. At the same time, we very often forget that many of these acts are not repeated by young people," she noted.
Home ultimately the biggest influence
Both guests agreed that the example set by adults has a significant influence on young people's behavior. Velling noted that children constantly imitate their parents' everyday choices. "When you're crossing the street with a small child, you see adults crossing against a red light or crossing in the wrong place. We know how important road safety is. Yet everyone is in a hurry without necessarily realizing it and people don't notice who is watching them, how they're crossing or where they're running across the street," she said.
Anna Markina also emphasized that whether young people behave with care or disregard for others begins at home. If parents tell their children not to use violence but resort to it themselves, that behavior carries directly over into interactions among young people. "Children see very clearly when violence is used to resolve conflicts or problems," the criminologist said.
According to the guests, young people who get into trouble often need support and help themselves. "Young people who end up in prison [...] are all very different, but one thing they have in common is that they all need love," Markina pointed out.
Velling agreed that many young people lack warmth at home and seek a substitute for the family they are missing in groups of peers. "The environment surrounding the family is also important. I know several families who have moved away because the neighborhood they lived in was not conducive to their child's development," the psychologist said.
To reduce crime, society needs genuine interest and empathy rather than condemnation. In the long run, family values can outweigh the negative influence of peers if parents maintain a trusting relationship with their children. "Research shows that [...] although friends' approval and belonging to a peer group are very important at a certain age, family values ultimately tend to prevail," Velling said.
--

China’s exports surge 36.3% in September as AI demand boosts trade

Mucahithan Avcioglu
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
China’s exports jumped 36.3% year-on-year in September, supported by strong global demand for artificial intelligence-related products, according to customs data released Wednesday.
Exports reached $447.18 billion, while imports increased 31% to $313.65 billion, leaving a monthly trade surplus of $133.53 billion.
Export growth accelerated from 25% in August to its fastest pace since February, while imports recorded their strongest increase since June, picking up from 28.2% the previous month.
Demand for components used in AI computing systems and data centers helped support overseas shipments, with rising product prices also contributing to trade growth.
The value of integrated circuit exports surged 136% from a year earlier, although the number of units shipped increased only around 1%, highlighting the gap between growth in export values and volumes.
Vehicle exports also expanded sharply. China shipped 1.18 million vehicles overseas in September, up 56.3% year-on-year, while their export value climbed 62%.
Exports to the US rose nearly 39.6%, outpacing overall export growth.
The strong trade performance comes as the world’s second-largest economy continues to face weak domestic demand, increasing the importance of overseas sales for economic growth.
Meanwhile, higher import values contrasted with falling volumes of some major energy purchases.
Crude oil import volumes declined at a double-digit annual rate for a sixth consecutive month, even as their value increased for the first time since May. Both crude oil and natural gas import volumes were lower over the first nine months of the year.
China’s exports totaled about $3.37 trillion in January-September, rising 21.3% from a year earlier, while imports increased 27.5% to approximately $2.43 trillion.
The figures put the country’s trade surplus at around $938.1 billion for the first nine months.

The Yemen conflict has resumed as a spillover from the wider US-Iran war that began with the US-Israeli attack on the Islamic Republic on February 28. Iran, Saudi Arabia's longtime regional rival, has offered to mediate between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, its foreign minister Abbas Araghchi said on Sunday in statements reiterated by the ministry on Monday.
The Conflict Armament Research report was based on information from Yemeni authorities in July after officials interdicted two shipments in 2025, which included the missile equipment hidden among a range of other goods, according to the WSJ.
“When you have imports like that, there is a possibility that they are already manufacturing or that they are trying and it doesn’t really work out,” Fabian Hinz, a senior analyst at Conflict Armament, told the Wall Street Journal, adding that because the Houthis weapons facilities are well camouflaged, it is unclear how far along missile production has proceeded.
China says it is respecting arms sales ban
China claims to be adhering to the UN arms embargo on the Houthis, per the WSJ. However, the report noted that while some of the Houthi-imported materials could have civilian uses, some were parts specifically designed for missile production.
The imported parts include custom-made metal missile components, including parts of the motor and of the airframe, the missile’s basic structure, the Wall Street Journal noted, adding that Yemeni authorities also found fins which stabilize the missile in flight and parts of a solid-propellant rocket motor of a Kheibar Shekan-series missile.
Yemeni authorities also seized tools, testing equipment, and raw materials, including the ablative material which protects sections of the missile from the intense heat produced by a ballistic missile, the WSJ added.
Why are Iranian Kheibar Shekan missiles particularly advantageous?
Iran has been using Kheibar Shekan missiles, cheap, mobile, and accurate missiles, which have a range of at least 1,400 kilometers in their strikes against US assets across the Middle East, the Wall Street Journal cited US officials as saying in July.
The solid-fuel, medium-range Kheibar Shekan missiles differ from older Iranian missiles that require prelaunch fueling, a lengthy process which the Kheibar Shekan can bypass by being kept fueled and are capable of being loaded quickly into trucks or other vehicles for launching, making it easier to evade US and Israeli warplanes seeking to knock out Iranian missile launch sites, military experts told WSJ at the time.
Danya Saperstein and Reuters contributed to this report.

IDF establishing new corps for countering low-altitude drones amid growing UAV threat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
06:40:26 UTC
15:40:26 KST

IDF Ground Forces Commander Maj.-Gen. Nadav Lotan is working to establish a new corps dedicated to countering low-altitude drone threats, as part of an effort to strengthen Israel's defenses against the growing threat posed by unmanned aerial vehicles, Walla learned on Tuesday.
For more than a decade, the IDF has been trying to address the threat posed by drones operating in the airspace close to the ground, using a variety of methods. However, these efforts have accelerated since the October 7 massacre, alongside a worldwide push to develop solutions.
The threat became evident during Hamas's attacks along the Gaza border at the beginning of the war and during the initial stages of the IDF's ground maneuver deep into the Gaza Strip. Hezbollah subsequently employed drones against IDF troops in southern Lebanon and civilians in Israel's home front.
The drone threat has also manifested itself in the smuggling of weapons and drugs across the Egyptian and Jordanian borders. Smugglers have used particularly heavy drones capable of carrying payloads weighing dozens of kilograms. There are also growing concerns that drones could become a significant threat in the IDF's Judea and Samaria Division and along the Syrian border.
The Defense Ministry and the IDF have accelerated projects to improve drone protection within the defense establishment. Some of these projects involve Israeli companies, while others entail purchasing technology from abroad.
Accordingly, the IDF has begun deploying various defense systems in the field to improve and refine protection against different types of drones, including fiber-optic drones. These pose a considerable challenge for conventional militaries because they are difficult to detect. As a result, armies generally counter them using nets, interceptor drones, and ground-based gunfire.
Five border defense battalions to form the foundation of new corps
The IDF recently decided to establish the new low-altitude airspace defense corps using the existing border infantry battalions as its foundation.
The corps will initially be based on five battalions that routinely protect the borders with Jordan and Egypt, as well as the security barrier area in the West Bank.
Under the plan, these battalions will assume an additional mission alongside their existing responsibility for defending Israel's land borders: protecting against mobile threats operating in the airspace close to the ground.
According to assessments, the corps' sixth battalion will be the tactical air defense battalion established during the war in response to threats from Gaza and Lebanon that emerged on an unprecedented scale.
IDF transferring Ground Forces resources to support new anti-drone corps
To support the new corps' establishment, the IDF will transfer significant resources from the Ground Forces to supplement the capabilities already available within the Border Defense Corps.
These resources will include additional training personnel to develop a drone school focused on defensive missions.
The IDF's Ground Forces already operate significant defensive drone capabilities, including intelligence-gathering operations conducted using drones by Unit 9900 of the Military Intelligence Directorate.
It can therefore be assessed that Military Intelligence will play a role in developing the emerging combat doctrine, operational methods, and the type and scale of procurement involving drones and associated technologies, as well as training.

Attacks on Saudi could have negative spillover 'everywhere', IMF chief says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
06:38:12 UTC
15:38:12 KST

International Monetary Fund head Kristalina Georgieva said on Wednesday that recent attacks on Saudi Arabia could impact people "everywhere", as conflict in the energy-rich region adds to wide-ranging economic concerns.
A violent battle between a Saudi-led coalition and Houthi militia has erupted in recent days, with missile strikes on airports and energy facilities across the kingdom.
The latest round of fighting was triggered by Houthi militia strikes on Riyadh's international airport at the weekend that left 13 people dead and operations suspended in the worst attack since 2015.
The escalation compounds fears about the impact of the Middle East crisis on global growth, with crude prices sent soaring since Iran effectively shut the crucial Strait of Hormuz after it was attacked by the US and Israel in February.
"The Saudi economy is important for the region and the world," IMF managing director Georgieva said at a news conference during the Annual Meetings of the Fund and World Bank in Bangkok.
"In that sense, these developments have potentially negative spillovers for everybody, everywhere," she said.
The warning comes as officials and experts gather in the Thai capital to discuss challenges facing the global economy, including higher energy costs and concerns about the sustainability of an artificial intelligence boom.
Other hurdles include ballooning debt in advanced economies, with bond yields at multi-decade highs as pressure grows on central banks to hike interest rates to cool inflation.
"What is our loudest call to policymakers right now? Make urgent repairs to the fiscal house before the cracks widen," Georgieva said.
"Now is the time to enhance revenues, to rationalise spending and improve public financial management."
'Reaching limits'
In its closely watched World Economic Outlook released on Tuesday, the IMF raised its 2026 global growth forecast by 0.1 percentage points to 3.1 percent.
However, it warned that while new economic activity has been sparked by rising investment in AI, poorer countries are not benefiting as they deal with soaring energy costs.
The global economy "remains resilient in the face of very frequent repetitive shocks and in the face of uncertainty", Georgieva said. "But this resilience is reaching its limits."
The IMF chief called for greater support for low-income countries to "strengthen their fundamentals so they can withstand shocks".
She noted that a global rise in interest rates had also caused debt servicing costs to increase from around six percent of government revenues a decade ago to 14 percent today.
And in its Global Policy Agenda released on Wednesday, the Fund warned that debt servicing challenges had become particularly acute for "low-income and vulnerable economies".
Georgieva said the IMF had been "ringing the alarm bell on excessive global economic imbalances growing".
"To put it very simply, China needs to spend more, the US has to save more and Europe has to invest more," she added.
Advanced economies have seen their debt-to-GDP ratios skyrocket since the COVID-19 pandemic and wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, with governments forced to increase spending to cushion the impact of those shocks.
Addressing the issue of how to tackle spiking bond yields, Georgieva admitted "there is no magic".
"You have to go in a direction of tightening debt (and) bringing it down," she said.
"(The) message that we are sending to our members: fundamentals matter. Get your house in order; otherwise, your people, your businesses will pay a price."

In short:
Controversial private health insurance changes have been effectively thrown out of parliament by the Coalition and crossbench.
The changes would wind back the rebate Australians aged 65 and over receive on their private health cover from April next year.
What's next?
Health Minister Mark Butler is vowing to press ahead and introduce the exact same bill to Parliament tomorrow.
Controversial private health insurance changes affecting older Australians are now on life support, after the legislation was effectively thrown out of parliament by the Coalition and crossbench.
The proposal would wind back the rebate Australians aged 65 and over receive on their private health cover from April next year, banking $3 billion over four years to be spent elsewhere in the aged care sector.
However, the legislation cannot continue through the Senate in its current form, after the Greens teamed up with the Coalition and Independent senator Jacqui Lambie on a motion to strike the bill from the parliamentary agenda.
Health Minister Mark Butler held a snap press conference on Wednesday afternoon, vowing to push ahead with the policy, flagging the government would reintroduce the exact same legislation on Thursday.
"This is an absolute travesty … [it] flies in the face of what I thought was a clear understanding across the parliament of the need to fund better aged care services,"
he said.
"What appears to be a rush of blood to the head by the new leadership of the Greens party, that's all become a bit of a pile on in the Senate and a discharge of a bill instead of a reasoned debate."
Shadow Health Minister Anne Ruston said Mr Butler should "take the hint".
"Don't try to sneak this cut back onto the agenda. Drop it for good," she said.
"Today the Senate stood with older Australians. Labor was left standing alone with its cuts."
With the Coalition vowing to block the legislation in the Senate the federal government had been counting on the Greens to try to get the bill through.
Last month, the ABC revealed about $1.6 billion of the forecast savings would be clawed back from pensioners which drew broad condemnation from the Opposition and crossbenchers like Monique Ryan.
Greens leader David Shoebridge said while the party supported reducing private health rebates, they did not want to "punch down" on pensioners, and would support the legislation if pensioners were exempt.
"It is plain offensive to see Labor looking for over a billion dollars in savings from cutting rebates to pensioners when they refuse to even consider taxing record gas export profits," he said.
"Labor has been told time and time again what we need for our support, and they refused to seriously engage."
Senator Lambie accused the government of trying to "balance the budgets on pensioners".
"Older Australians are already paying through the nose for private health insurance and many would have been forced to choose between putting food on the table and looking after their health. It's unbelievable that anyone should have to make that choice in modern day Australia."
Policy has been attacked on multiple fronts
The government has been counting on the legislation to secure some of the billions of dollars needed to fund crucial aged care commitments.
But the beleaguered policy has been attacked on multiple fronts, with the states and territories, aged care sector, private health industry, the Coalition and crossbench all arguing it could pile pressure on the public system.
In defending the legislation, Health Minister Mark Butler had said only 44,000 people would dump their private health cover as a result.
However, this week health department analysis was released under Freedom of Information laws, revealing that number was forecast to rise to a cumulative total of 78,000 by the end of the decade.
Mr Butler said the health department had indicated the smaller number was "the most reliable figure" and that the number of people with private health would continue to grow.
Outside parliament, many health economists have backed the policy, saying the impact on the system would be trivial and the money would be better spent elsewhere.
With the government's plans thwarted for now, an undeterred Mr Butler issued a plea to senators to recognise "hard choices" to fund aged care services needed to be made.
"It is important that the parliament have a proper debate, that these really important questions for older Australians are not held hostage to political stunts," he said.
However, Council on the Ageing (COTA) CEO Patricia Sparrow said the Senate had already sent a "clear message that the impact on older Australians, particularly those on low and fixed incomes, cannot be ignored".
"With the minister signalling his intention to reintroduce the Bill, we urge the government to seriously consider the concerns raised by older Australians and ensure any future changes don't leave them worse off," she said.

- EU leaders will debate the 2028-2034 budget, with Germany pushing deeper cuts and Ireland proposing a 17% cut to international aid.
- Beuze said cutting humanitarian and development aid could worsen hunger, schooling and refugee flows, while crises in Ukraine, Gaza, Sudan, Afghanistan and the Sahel still need funding.
AI generated
BRUSSELS – The UN’s refugee agency has warned the European Union against “short-sighted” cuts to international aid, as Germany spearheads a push to slash the size of the bloc’s next joint budget.
“It’s an easy target. It’s much more easy to explain to the taxpayers that we are going to spend less money abroad,” Jean-Nicolas Beuze, the UN High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) representative to the EU, told AFP in an interview on Oct 13.
“There is a short-sighted view of saying we are going to make savings by spending less abroad, but of course this will have negative consequences on our prosperity and our stability and security.”
EU leaders will wrangle over the 2028 to 2034 budget at a summit in Brussels from Oct 15 as they push to reach a deal by Christmas.
Ireland, which holds the EU’s rotating presidency, last week suggested shaving about €140 billion (S$200 billion) from an earlier €2 trillion proposal for the overall budget.
But that failed to satisfy a group of so-called “frugal” countries led by Germany, which are arguing for deeper cuts at a time when national budgets are under strain.
Foreign aid already looks like it could be on the chopping block.
Ireland has put forward cutting the part that covers international aid by 17% – while largely leaving sensitive areas such as funding for EU farmers untouched.
At the same time, Dublin pushed to ring-fence €25 billion for humanitarian assistance.
EU officials point out that the amounts on the table would represent an increase over the bloc’s last budget agreed in 2020.
“But it’s an increase, which is compensated with the number of crises that have erupted over the last 10 years,” Beuze said.
‘Missing an opportunity’
The UNHCR representative warned against cutting both humanitarian aid and broader development funding.
“Cutting the humanitarian aid would have an immediate and visible impact. It means that parents won’t be able to put food on the table, and children won’t go to school,” he said, pointing to a potential increase in refugees heading to Europe as a consequence.
“But we need the same efforts and focus on development if we want to get out of this vicious circle of creating dependency.”
The fate of the EU’s central funding has become even more pressing as numerous member states have cut back their own budgets and the US has slashed its role.
The EU and its 27 member countries are the world’s biggest providers of international aid.
“Being the largest provider of humanitarian development aid comes with responsibilities, but it’s also an opportunity to expand your sphere of influence in a very positive manner,” Beuze said.
“Not using this leadership role will mean missing an opportunity to shape the future of humanity, the future of the world.”
Unlike in its previous budget, the EU has put on the table a separate fund to support war-torn Ukraine, worth about €90 billion.
“Ukraine is critically important,” Beuze said.
But he pointed to other crises, including in Gaza, Sudan, Afghanistan and the Sahel, as also requiring the EU’s attention – and funding.
“All those crises are geographically, if you look at a map, really encircling the European Union.” AFP

China’s producer prices rose 5% year-on-year in September, their fastest increase since June 2022, as higher fuel costs increased pressure on businesses, the National Bureau of Statistics said on Wednesday.
The increase in the producer price index accelerated from 3.8% in August.
The bureau said coal prices also rose amid stronger demand for winter heating, temporary supply tightness in major coal-producing regions and expectations of higher international coal prices.
Consumer inflation, meanwhile, edged up to 0.9% year-on-year in September from 0.8% in August.

Food prices fell 1.7%, subtracting approximately 0.29 percentage points from headline inflation and partially offsetting the impact of higher fuel costs.
Core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, stood at 1%.
The figures showed a widening gap between producer and consumer inflation, with higher industrial costs accompanied by relatively modest consumer price increases.
China’s economy expanded 4.3% year-on-year in the second quarter, its slowest pace in more than three years. August figures also showed weaker-than-expected retail sales growth, while industrial output exceeded expectations.
The State Council signaled the possibility of additional economic support at a Sept. 28 meeting, calling for stronger countercyclical macroeconomic policy adjustments to address emerging challenges.
Lynn Song, chief economist for Greater China at ING, said in a research note that the meeting marked a shift in tone, suggesting further policy support was likely to help meet both short- and long-term growth objectives.
Those objectives include China’s 4.5%-5% economic growth target for 2026 and its longer-term goal of doubling GDP between 2020 and 2035, Song added.

Turkish police raid opposition TV station, halting live broadcasts
- Published
Turkish police have raided the headquarters of one of the country's most-watched news channels, halting its live broadcasts.
Reports in Turkish media said financial crimes police were searching the building of Halk TV, a pro-opposition channel, and that 11 people had been taken into custody in a raid linked to the channel's owner. The government also appointed a new administrator to run the channel.
It is the latest in a series of crackdowns on news sources deemed to be critical of Turkish President Tayyip Erdoğan and his government.
Halk journalists were initially unable to get into the building, although they later were allowed in, several reporters said on X.
There was a heavy police presence in the building, they said.
Halk's news channel and live broadcasts on its YouTube page were both offline early on Wednesday.
The channel has been seen by many in the country as being close to the opposition Republican People's Party (CHP). It often voices criticism of Erdoğan's ruling AK party.
Prosecutors said arrest warrants had been issued for 17 people as part of the investigation into Halk chairman Cafer Mahiroğlu on allegations of bribery, rigging tenders and money laundering, Turkish media reported.
Mahiroğlu, who was reportedly not in the country during the raid, wrote on social media that seven members of his family were among those detained.
"Today is a dark day for Turkey," he said in a video message. "The public's right to information is being seized for political reasons."
The Istanbul Bar Association denounced the move, which it noted came hours before Ekrem Imamoğlu, widely seen as Erdoğan's biggest political rival, was due to begin his defence against corruption charges in court, for which he has been in prison for over a year.
Özgür Özel, leader of the opposition New Party, called the raid "weak and cowardly".
"Storming a TV channel with a police raid at dawn and appointing a trustee is something only dictators do," he wrote on social media.
Özel set up the party after being removed as the CHP's leader by a court in May and replaced by a party veteran who had previously been voted out, in a move which further cemented Erdoğan's grip on power.
Turkey ranked 163rd out of 180 countries in the Reporters Without Borders (RSF) 2026 World Press Freedom Index, external.
The organisation stated that 90% of national media outlets were under government control and criticised the "abusive prosecution" of critical publications in the country, which Erdoğan has led since 2003.
The vast majority of Turkish media is seen as pro-government after years of state legal and financial pressure, corporate acquisitions and self-censorship.
In September, a court ordered the blocking of access to the website and social media accounts of T24, on the grounds that it had published "LGBT propaganda".
In October 2025, the authorities seized control of Tele1, another pro-opposition TV channel, appointing a trustee to oversee broadcasts, which were stripped of all hard-news content.
The channel still exists but its pro-opposition stance has been completely neutralised.
