Taxes, housing and tuition fees: 2027 budget measures impact family budgets in Portugal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
06:12:27 UTC
15:12:27 KST

From taxes and wages to pensions, housing and tuition fees, the 2027 State Budget contains several measures that will directly affect household incomes.
The draft State Budget for 2027 (OE2027) sets out changes that will affect the disposable income of Portuguese households, from taxes on wages to social benefits and spending on housing and education.
Key measures include a new update of the IRS brackets, an increase in the national minimum wage and a strengthening of some social benefits. On the other hand, tuition fees in higher education are expected to start rising again from the next academic year.
In addition, the evolution of prices for essential goods may swallow up part of the tax savings.
The draft must still go through the parliamentary approval process before being promulgated by the President of the Republic.
IRS: new update may boost disposable income
One of the main measures is the update of the IRS bracket thresholds. The rates planned for 2027 remain, according to the budget proposal, at the levels presented by the Government in September, but the income limits from which each bracket applies will be higher.
The IRS table presented sets out nine brackets, with rates between 12.2% and 48%. The first covers annual taxable income of up to 8,666 euros, followed by a rate of 15.2% for the slice between that amount and 13,075 euros. In the next two brackets, which go up to 18,530 euros and 23,985 euros, the rates are 20.7% and 23.6% respectively.
From there, the rates rise to 30.6% in the bracket up to 30,538 euros and to 34.6% in the next, up to 44,762 euros. Income between 44,762 and 48,373 euros is taxed at 43.1%, while the slice between 48,373 and 89,995 euros is taxed at 44.6%. The top rate of 48% applies only to the portion of annual taxable income above 89,995 euros.
The upper and lower limits for each bracket have been updated by 3.88%, a percentage lower than the reference value set for wage increases in collective bargaining, which in the Tripartite Agreement on Wage Enhancement and Economic Growth, agreed in Social Concertation, aims for an average wage rise of 4.5% next year.
Because the brackets are updated by around 3.9%, all taxpayers stand to gain, taking into account the progressive nature of this tax.
The Government also plans to update the specific IRS deduction, which excludes a portion of workers’ and pensioners’ income from taxation, but the exact amount is still unknown, as it depends on the update of the Social Support Index (IAS).
The IAS is set by a ministerial order that fixes the value in force each year from 1 January, but it is usually calculated a few weeks earlier based on inflation and economic growth.
There is also a change targeting higher incomes: the additional solidarity rate of 2.5% will apply only to taxable income above 89,995 euros a year. For income over 250,000 euros, the 5% rate remains in place.
The proposal to exempt from IRS productivity bonuses, performance bonuses, profit-sharing and balance-sheet gratuities up to a limit of 6% of a worker’s annual basic pay also remains, provided the company meets the wage enhancement criteria laid down.
Minimum wage rises to 970 euros
Workers earning the national minimum wage are set to move from the current gross 920 euros a month to 970 euros in 2027, an increase of 50 euros per month.
This figure is in line with the wage enhancement agreement reached in Social Concertation and represents a boost to the gross income of those on the minimum wage. The net amount will depend, among other factors, on each worker’s tax situation.
In the public administration, the proposal provides for a minimum salary update of 2.3% or 60.52 euros, raising the basic pay to 995.51 euros a month.
At present, the basic pay in the public administration stands at 934.99 euros.
Pensions to rise in 2027, with increases of around 3%
Pensioners will in 2027 benefit from the regular indexation of pensions, calculated on the basis of inflation and growth in Gross Domestic Product (GDP). Although the final figure is not yet known, available data point to an increase close to 3% for pensions of just over 1,000 euros a month or less, covering most pensioners.
This update is expected to add 824 million euros to public spending next year.
Before that, in December, pensioners with pensions of up to 1,611.39 euros a month will receive an extraordinary supplement, paid automatically together with their pension: 200 euros for those receiving up to 537.13 euros, 150 euros for pensions above that amount and up to 1,074.26 euros, and 100 euros for pensions above that level and up to the defined ceiling.
The aim is to strengthen pensioners’ incomes, especially those on the lowest pensions, although the regular 2027 increase can only be confirmed once the final inflation and economic growth data are known.
Older people to get an extra 50 euros in the Solidarity Supplement
Pensioners on the lowest incomes are among the beneficiaries of one of the social top-ups planned in the budget. The Solidarity Supplement for Older People (CSI) is expected to increase from 670 to 720 euros, a rise of 50 euros in the monthly reference amount.
The measure is designed to bolster the incomes of older people in situations of greater economic vulnerability. The Government is also maintaining its goal of raising this reference value to 870 euros by 2029.
Extra 60 million euros in spending on child benefit
Child benefit is also expected to see higher public spending, linked to indexation of amounts to inflation and the forecast increase in the number of beneficiaries.
The 2027 budget proposal states that spending on child benefit will rise next year by 59.5 million euros, "by comparison with the forecast outturn for 2026".
The Government explains the increase in the budget report by pointing to higher spending due, on the one hand, to "an increase in beneficiaries of around 1.1%" and, on the other, to "higher average amounts in line with the projected change in inflation".
Housing: benefit for landlords, IMT exemption for young people and public guarantees
On the rental market, there are changes with different impacts for landlords and tenants.
Landlords covered by the moderate rent tax regime will continue to benefit from an IRS rate of 10%, instead of the 25% previously applied.
The measure covers income earned up to 31 December 2029, in both new and existing contracts, but applies only to rents of up to 2,300 euros a month, the amount the Government set in September 2025 as a "moderate rent".
For tenants, the maximum IRS deduction on rents will increase from 900 to 1,000 euros in 2027. For taxpayers with lower taxable incomes, the ceiling may reach 1,100 euros. This change allows a larger share of spending on permanent housing to be offset against tax, within the applicable legal conditions.
Young people up to the age of 35 will continue to benefit from exemption from IMT property transfer tax and stamp duty when buying their first home, with updated exemption thresholds. The maximum value covered by the IMT exemption is expected to rise to 338,141 euros.
The Government also plans to reinforce the Porta 65 scheme, which supports young people renting a home, but gives no figures.
The continuation of the public guarantee scheme for the purchase of a first home is also described as likely, although, when presenting the budget, the finance minister clarified that a "formal decision" was still pending.
Tuition fees to be unfrozen
One of the measures that may mean an additional burden for families is the unfreezing of tuition fees in public higher education from the 2027/2028 academic year.
The current maximum fee for bachelor’s degrees and higher professional technical courses, set at 697 euros, is to start being updated in line with inflation.
The same rule will apply to certain master’s degrees that are required to work in a given profession or demanded by the relevant professional associations. For other master’s and doctoral programmes, the proposal states that updates should reflect the actual cost of providing the training.
This measure could raise annual expenses for households with children in higher education, especially when there are other associated costs, such as accommodation, transport and food.
The update of tuition fees had already been proposed by Luís Montenegro’s Government in last year’s State Budget, which envisaged raising the maximum fee for bachelor’s degrees to 710 euros, but the measure was eventually rejected during the detailed vote.
Support for parenthood
The budget provides for higher spending on parental benefits, reflecting expectations that eligibility conditions will be improved. The debate on extending the initial parental leave paid at 100% to 180 days could affect how these measures are implemented and how much they cost.
Spending on parental benefits is expected to increase by 349.1 million euros in 2027, reflecting "growth of 31.7% compared with the forecast outturn for 2026". The total budgeted amount comes to 1,452 million euros.
Parliament is in the final stage of detailed consideration of a citizens’ initiative that proposes extending initial parental leave paid at 100% to 180 days, or six months.
The 2026 State Budget already factored in the financial impact of extending payment of the initial parental benefit by two months.
According to the labour minister, Maria do Rosário Palma Ramalho, around 230 million euros had been set aside for this measure. However, that estimate was based on the Government’s proposal, under which payment of parental leave at 100% for six months would depend on a fair sharing of leave between both parents.
The group of citizens behind the proposal argue that full payment for the six months should be guaranteed regardless of how the parents split the leave. This solution would mean higher costs for the State, as all parents would be eligible to receive 100% pay while on parental leave.
Fuels and cars: no tax cuts announced
For those who use a car every day, the proposal does not provide for direct changes to taxes on fuel, either increases or decreases. The Government does, however, expect tax revenues from these products to rise by 5.2%, purely through higher consumption. That represents an extra 186 million euros.
The budget proposal does not spell out the Government’s plans for the future of the current 23-cent-per-litre tax discount on fuel. Part of this discount results from a mechanism used by the executive to refund, in petroleum tax, the extra VAT revenue generated by rising fuel prices.
Finance minister Joaquim Miranda Sarmento has said the Government will maintain its policy of responding to price shocks, with support for specific sectors and a refund of the tax windfall collected by the State.
The surcharge on diesel vehicles in the Single Circulation Tax (IUC) also remains. The rates for this tax are not changed in the budget, but the payment schedule will be different in 2027, a transition year to the new model.
Under the new schedule, IUC bills of up to 500 euros will fall due in October, with larger amounts paid in two instalments, the first in July. From 2028, IUC will be payable from April.
The executive is considering "new incentives for the purchase of zero-emission vehicles", but both the timetable and the budget envelope and conditions remain undefined, making it impossible to calculate how much support each household might receive.
The grant scheme for buying electric cars, opened in June, exhausted its budget of ten million euros in just a few hours. At the time, environment and energy minister Maria da Graça Carvalho said that "no further [funding rounds] are likely to open this year".
"Regressar" programme extended for another year
The Government plans to extend for a further year the benefits under the Regressar (Return) Programme, aimed at emigrants who come back to Portugal. The scheme is currently in force until the end of 2026, but the Government has decided to prolong it.
Created in 2019, the programme is aimed at former tax residents in Portugal who have spent at least five years abroad and then return to the country.
The benefit excludes from taxation 50% of employment income and business and professional income for a period of five years.

Estonia's minority goverment faces no-confidence motion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
06:10:00 UTC
15:10:00 KST

Estonia's minority goverment faces no-confidence motion
Center Party, Isamaa and EKRE have submitted a motion of no confidence in Prime Minister Kristen Michal's government, accusing it of undermining public trust and failing to address Estonia's challenges.
Those submitting the motion of no confidence, who also include nine independent MPs, believe that the Reform Party and Eesti 200 coalition government's actions have been marked by constant scandals that undermine public trust in the state and reinforce the belief that Prime Minister Kristen Michal has failed in his role.
Center Party parliamentary group chair Lauri Laats cited a recent Government Office public opinion survey in a press release, according to which 51 percent of people feel financially insecure and 85 percent of Estonian residents are concerned about rising everyday expenses.
"These are real concerns that people face and that need to be addressed — for example, by following the lead of neighboring countries and making decisions to reduce fuel or food prices and lower taxes that are stifling the economy. However, the government led by Kristen Michal is not listening to people's concerns. A series of tax increases has already been planned for the period following the 2027 Riigikogu elections, which will only exacerbate these problems," Laats said.
Isamaa parliamentary group chair Helir-Valdor Seeder said in a press release that the Reform Party-led government has undermined trust in the Estonian state both at home and internationally. Seeder considers the situation in national defense particularly critical.
"Public trust has been undermined not only by the current artillery shell procurement scandal. The government has repeatedly disregarded significant military advice from the commander of the Estonian Defense Forces, including on the development of drone defense capabilities. The current government is also damaging our international reputation: Estonia's decision to grant a sanctions exemption to the Rosatom-owned Solikamsk Magnesium Plant is yet another example in a long series of hypocritical decisions," Seeder said.
Martin Helme, chair of the Conservative People's Party of Estonia (EKRE) parliamentary group, added that every minister has significant shortcomings in their performance, making a motion of no confidence in the entire government fully justified.
"The finance minister lacks a substantive strategy and long-term vision for putting public finances in order, resulting in an uncontrolled rise in government debt. The climate and economy minister's inability to provide clarity on Estonia's energy future, security of supply and energy prices has jeopardized both industrial competitiveness and ordinary consumers' ability to make ends meet. Despite extensive analyses, the social affairs minister has failed to develop a substantive, evidence-based family policy amid the current demographic crisis. Through a series of hastily implemented reforms, the education minister has plunged Estonia's education system into a deep management crisis, with teachers burdened by ever-increasing bureaucracy," Helme said, listing the ministers' shortcomings.
As of Wednesday morning, the motion of no confidence in the minority government had been signed by 33 members of the Riigikogu. Its initiators have also invited the Social Democrats to join the motion, Andres Kalvik, media adviser to the Center Party's parliamentary group, said.
--
Editor: Mait Ots, Marcus Turovski

Hospitality bosses warn of empty cafes and kitchens under migration cuts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
06:08:37 UTC
15:08:37 KST

Hospitality industry warns of critical workers shortages as migration cuts loom
In short:
The hospitality industry has launched a campaign warning Australians of critical worker shortages if skilled migration is cut.
One Nation, the Coalition and the government have all pledged to slash migration numbers, but none have provided modelling of the economic impact.
What's next?
New research shows more than 70 per cent of businesses owners think workers born overseas are needed to fill roles.
The hospitality industry is the latest sector to push against sweeping cuts to migration, in a social media campaign depicting an Australia in which crucial jobs are left vacant due to a lack of migrant workers.
The AI-generated clip by the Australian Hotel Association (AHA) sets the scene for an Australia with a depleted workforce, depicting empty coffee counters, hotels where guests clean their own rooms, and elderly people saying goodbye to their carers.
AHA chief executive Stephen Ferguson said while businesses overwhelmingly wanted to hire "Australians first", there was already not enough people to fill vacancies.
"We have 7,000 chef and cook vacancies today. How many will that be in a year's time?" he said.
"All the major political parties have now issued migration policies, but none of them have included the economic impact on the cuts they are proposing".
More than 70 per cent of business owners agreed workers born overseas were important to filling critical roles, according to new research from the Federation of Ethnic Communities' Councils of Australia (FECCA).
Chief executive Prerana Mehta said the AHA ad highlighted the critical role migrant workers played in the economy.
"It is assisting individuals and members of the public to understand the impact that slashing migration would have, not just on the economy, but more broadly on their everyday lives," she said.
Growing chorus of voices against migration cuts
In August, big business and mining groups raised the alarm on weaknesses in the domestic workforce and warned Australia needed a steady flow of migrants to deliver on a number of projects already in the pipeline.
Earlier in the year, South Australian premier Peter Malinauskas admonished the major parties for engaging in a "political race to the bottom" with One Nation on migration policy.
One Nation is proposing net negative migration for three years before capping it below 130,000, while the Coalition would cut net migration to 100,000 for two years before gradually increasing it to 160,000.
Labor, meanwhile, is targeting 225,000 a year by 2028.
Migration policies explained
Read more
Labor:
The government is aiming for 245,000 net overseas migration (NOM) by June next year, and 225,000 by the middle of 2028. Those figures were forecast in the budget and are now a target.
In March, the NOM was 292,100, according to figures released last month by the Australian Bureau of Statistics.
Coalition:
The Coalition has announced an annual NOM target of 100,000 for the first two years if it wins the election.
It will aim for 130,000 in the third year and 160,000 in the fourth year.
One Nation:
The minor party unveiled a policy to slash immigration by 750,000 over three years, pushing the NOM into negative territory.
After that, it would aim for a "ceiling" of 130,000, to be reviewed every year.
Deputy Liberal leader Jane Hume said she had spoken with the AHA and was confident it understood the Coalition's position, saying Australia risked becoming a "guest worker economy" with an "imported underclass".
"That's not who we are, that is not Australian values," she said.
Immigration minister Tony Burke said the government was taking a "sensible approach to slowing immigration", with migrants critical to the workforce.
"Australia doesn't just benefit from migrant workers. We depend on them," he said.
"We need them to keep our hospitals and aged care homes open. We need them to build homes. We need them to work in hospitality and agriculture."
Independent Senator David Pocock said the migration debate was too focused on overall numbers rather than addressing workforce shortages, saying any reduction in migration should be accompanied by a focused approach to plugging skills gaps.
Critics online have said the ad reduces migrant workers to roles such as cleaners and baristas, overlooking those working in professions like engineering and healthcare, while depicting the people affected by service shortages as overwhelmingly white.
According to the Department of Home Affairs, more than half of GPs and nurses in Australia were born overseas.
Majority of business leaders see economic benefit of migrants
In September, FECCA virtually surveyed 500 business leaders across several sectors nationwide to gauge sentiment towards migration levels, multiculturalism and the economy.
The data, obtained by the ABC, found 87 per cent of those surveyed saw multiculturalism as an "economic strength", critical to growing trade, connecting with overseas networks and accessing skilled trades.
Two-thirds said multiculturalism made the economy "stronger".
Those surveyed reported concern about Australia becoming less welcoming to migrants, with 37 per cent fearing that would result in lost access to skilled workers.
Ms Mehta said business sentiments made it clear governments could not simply "stop migration" due to its impact on multiple sectors.
"I think our economy will be crippled … and small businesses, particularly, are going to be bearing the brunt of some of the policy inferences that are being made," she said.

Russian grain transit ban could cost hundreds of millions – Kulbergs explains why Latvia cannot impose it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
06:08:14 UTC
15:08:14 KST

Latvia is currently unable to increase railway infrastructure charges for Russian grain transit by 300% or impose a complete ban, Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs (United List) acknowledged following a government meeting on Tuesday. Until recently, Kulbergs had criticised LatRailNet, the company responsible for setting railway infrastructure charges, for acting too slowly to introduce substantially higher tariffs.
The prime minister noted that he would travel to Brussels this week to discuss the issue.
Last week, Kulbergs, Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal and Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda sent a joint letter to European Council President António Costa and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, calling for a ban on Russian grain transit through the European Union (EU).
“The biggest problem is that the EU has exclusive powers over both tariff and transit matters. We can take action under certain conditions, but that involves specific risks,” Kulbergs said.
He stressed that Russian grain has not been included in any sanctions so far.
Furthermore, according to the prime minister, the grain no longer belongs to Russia but to companies from Latvia’s strategic partner countries, including the United States, Switzerland and Japan.
“These are the companies buying the grain, some of the largest corporations in the world,” Kulbergs claimed.
He added that companies from these countries also purchase grain from farmers in the Baltic states.
According to Kulbergs, government ministers were informed on Tuesday that banning Russian grain transit could expose Latvia to immediate legal claims worth between 200 million and 800 million euros.
The prime minister claimed that Lithuania is currently involved in litigation over a similar case, with claims amounting to 12 billion euros.
He also asserted that Lithuania would most likely have to pay 450 million euros in connection with the proceedings later this year.
Kulbergs said he intends to present these examples in Brussels to support discussions on introducing a common EU-wide ban.
At the beginning of October, Estonia decided to introduce national sanctions prohibiting the transit of Russian and Belarusian grain through its territory.
However, Kulbergs pointed out that Estonia’s situation differs from Latvia’s.
According to the prime minister, Estonia had no existing grain transit contracts when it introduced the ban.
Latvia, by contrast, already has contracts covering the transit of 300,000 tonnes of grain.
Kulbergs acknowledged that he had previously been unaware of the potential costs associated with legal proceedings resulting from such restrictions.
The prime minister stressed that he must assess the risks these lawsuits could pose to the state budget.
If Latvia were required to pay substantial compensation, the question would be which other areas of government spending would have to be reduced.
Kulbergs also admitted that when the government decided to pursue a 300% increase in railway infrastructure charges, it had not been known that such a substantial increase could not be implemented.
Tuesday’s government agenda also included a proposal to change the institutional framework for setting railway infrastructure charges.
Under the proposal, responsibility for determining these charges would be transferred from LatRailNet, a subsidiary of the state-owned railway company Latvijas dzelzceļš, to the Public Utilities Commission (SPRK).
However, Kulbergs claimed that the issue had not been discussed during the meeting.
As previously reported, a decision adopted by LatRailNet takes effect on Tuesday, increasing railway infrastructure charges for Russian grain transit by an average of 25%.
LatRailNet board chair Justīna Hudenko told LETA that charges for different components of infrastructure use would rise by between 21.4% and 27.4%, resulting in an average increase of 25%.
According to Hudenko, the calculations take into account infrastructure costs associated with all grain shipments in the relevant transport category.
She explained that this approach makes it possible to increase infrastructure charges while justifying their level on the basis of the costs associated with the relevant freight services.
As previously reported, 
Kulbergs had suggested considering the dissolution of LatRailNet and transferring its responsibilities for setting railway infrastructure charges to the Public Utilities Commission.
The prime minister was dissatisfied with the pace at which LatRailNet was implementing politicians’ plans to impose substantially higher tariffs on grain transported from aggressor states.
On the 17th of September, the Saeima adopted urgent amendments to the Railway Law aimed at accelerating the revision of infrastructure charges for Russian grain transit shipments by the end of the year.
The amendments are intended to make it possible to increase infrastructure charges more quickly for grain transit shipments whose transport documents identify a departure station located in Russia.
The regulation will remain in force until the 31st of December, 2026.
The government has also previously approved changes allowing the Food and Veterinary Service to collect samples from grain shipments transported in transit and conduct laboratory tests to verify whether the declared country of origin is accurate.
Kulbergs has previously emphasised that Latvia wants to restrict Russian grain transit while maintaining opportunities to support exports by Ukrainian and Latvian farmers through Latvian ports.

Estonian students' interest in study loans skyrockets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
06:06:00 UTC
15:06:00 KST

Estonian students' interest in study loans skyrockets
Student interest in taking out student loans rose sharply this fall at two banks offering such loans, LHV and Swedbank.
"Interest in student loans has increased significantly this year. Compared with the same period last year, both the number of student loan applications and the total amount requested have essentially doubled," Eneli Nairis, head of small financing at Swedbank, told ERR on Tuesday.
"Compared with the same period last year, the total volume of student loans issued has tripled, while the number of applications has increased by 90 percent," said Catlin Vatsel, LHV's head of retail financing.
According to Nairis, the increase in interest is likely due to more favorable student loan terms introduced this fall. Students no longer need a guarantor or real estate collateral to take out a loan, interest rates have fallen and the repayment period has been extended.
"These changes make taking out student loans easier and more flexible for students than before," she said.
"We can clearly see that the changes to student loan terms have had an impact. We have not seen such a large jump in demand for student loans in previous years," Vatsel of LHV said.
Although the maximum student loan amount was raised to €6,000 last fall, not all applicants borrow the full amount. This year, the average student loan issued was €5,155 at Swedbank and approximately €5,400 at LHV.
More students studying abroad among applicants
Representatives of both banks said the number of Estonian students studying abroad among this fall's applicants has increased noticeably.
Vatsel also pointed out that approximately one-fifth of student loan applicants are over the age of 35.
"Studying has long since ceased to be something reserved for people in their 20s. The fact that one-fifth of our student loan borrowers are over 35 is a good indication of just how common it has become to pursue education later in life," LHV's head of retail financing said.
According to the Swedbank representative, the age distribution of student loan applicants has not changed significantly over the past few years. Approximately half of applicants are 25 or younger, while the other half are older.
According to figures provided by Vatsel, 12 percent of student loan applicants at LHV were rejected. The main reasons for rejection are failure to meet student loan eligibility requirements or issues with the applicant's credit history.
For example, student loans cannot be issued to students on academic leave or those who have already borrowed the maximum amount available at the same level of education. Not all levels of study qualify for student loans, while previous payment defaults or outstanding debts can also prevent applicants from obtaining a loan.
SEB, Coop Pank, Luminor and Bigbank do not offer student loans.

Hospitality is the key: Porto tops ranking as Europe's friendliest city, with Lisbon close behind
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
06:04:04 UTC
15:04:04 KST

Portuguese hospitality has once again won over international travellers. Porto was voted Europe's friendliest city, with Lisbon second in Condé Nast Traveller readers' ranking.
Portugal is often considered one of the most welcoming and hospitable countries in the world, with international studies and surveys repeatedly placing the Portuguese people at the top of tourists’ favourites. It is therefore no surprise that Porto has been awarded the title of "Europe's friendliest city".
The distinction comes from readers of Condé Nast Traveller in the Readers’ Choice Awards 2026, which also place the city of Lisbon in second position in this category.
The vote aims to identify cities where "hospitality is at its warmest" and "you find locals eager to help, whether you’re trying to make sense of a neighbourhood restaurant’s menu or looking confused on the metro".
The recognition now given to the Invicta, as Porto is known, "reflects the significant rise in Porto’s popularity as the ideal city-break refuge, both for lovers of good food and for culture enthusiasts", the magazine explains, also highlighting the city’s authenticity and relaxed atmosphere.
"Unwind in a stunning square lined with azulejo tiles or share petiscos – small portions of local delicacies – with residents in a neighbourhood restaurant," Condé Nast encourages, "and you will quickly realise how generous hospitality has made Porto a destination many of us end up returning to time and time again".
Lisbon appears in the next spot. "Few European cities are as picturesque as the sun-drenched Portuguese capital, famous for being built on the seven hills that punctuate the banks of the River Tagus", the magazine notes, describing it as "a wonderful city of winding alleys, soulful fado and creamy pastéis de nata".
"But what really ties it all together is the people. A youthful, inclusive atmosphere pulses through its steep neighbourhoods, and there are plenty of opportunities for travellers to get involved too. Experiencing the vibrant café culture is unmissable, where groups gather to savour their ritual morning espressos, or visiting during the Festival of Saint Anthony to see the cobbled streets fill with open-air parties", the publication recommends.
In the European ranking, the top five is completed by mentions of Amsterdam in the Netherlands, Stockholm in Sweden and Valletta in Malta.
The 15 friendliest cities in Europe
According to Condé Nast Traveller’s 2026 Readers’ Choice Awards:
- 1. Porto, Portugal
- 2. Lisbon, Portugal
- 3. Amsterdam, Netherlands

Businesses could be barred from non-essential water use amid supply threat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
06:00:48 UTC
15:00:48 KST

Three water companies are seeking to impose severe restrictions on businesses as the drought continues across most of England, putting rivers and wildlife under huge pressure.
Golf clubs and private schools could be barred from using mains water to irrigate playing fields and courses, and commercial car washes stopped from operating, under “non-essential use bans” being sought by the companies.
Eleven areas of England are still in drought, rivers are suffering from low flows, groundwater levels are declining and reservoir levels are at 54% – 21% below what is expected in the autumn.
Yorkshire was the latest area to move into drought status on 9 October. Parts of Wales are experiencing the first signs of drought recovery after the whole country was declared in drought in July.
Nineteen reservoirs or reservoir groups in England and Wales are less than 50% full, and eight are exceptionally low, up from five in August.
The Met Office says above-average rainfall is needed over a sustained seven-month period to bring all areas out of drought. But last month England received about 65% of its typical September rainfall, with eastern and southern areas experiencing the greatest deficit.
Businesses in drought-hit areas have been excluded from the hosepipe restrictions imposed on the public for the past three months. But South East, Southern and South West Water have applied to extend restrictions on water use to businesses via non-essential use bans in parts of their regions. If granted, water restrictions can be placed on golf clubs, private schools and commercial car washes to cut water use. Power hoses in car washes can use up to 25 litres of water per minute.
Permission from the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) is required, but the government has yet to respond to the water companies’ requests.
Pressure on wildlife and the environment from the drought is continuing. River flows in seven areas in England are exceptionally low, according to the latest Defra figures, affecting habitats, fish and wildlife. They include the River Derwent in the north-east, the rivers Yare and Ely Ouse in east England, and the River Tone and the Hampshire Avon catchments in south-west England.
When river flows fall to low flow levels they can take years to recover, with potentially severe effects on fish spawning and river health.
Mark Owen, the head of fisheries at the Angling Trust, said: “When rivers and fish are suffering from the ongoing effects of a severe drought, the Angling Trust supports further restrictions on non-essential water use, alongside urgent action to reduce huge leakage from water companies and unsustainable abstraction from rivers.
“We must continue to reduce unnecessary demand for water. It makes little sense to ban people from washing cars at home while commercial car washes can continue operating.”
In Hampshire, where the chalk aquifer is exceptionally low, Southern Water is seeking a drought order that would allow it to draw water from an internationally prized chalk stream and rare salmon habitat, even at levels below what is deemed ecologically safe. Southern said it was applying for the permit for the River Test owing to “a clear threat to supplies” in Hampshire and the Isle of Wight.
The company is seeking a non-essential use ban on commercial premises and businesses to reduce demand as it seeks to draw more water from the Test at levels that were previously deemed unacceptable.
As they seek permission to put restrictions on businesses’ water use, South East Water and South West Water have been allowed to alter the amount of water they draw from rivers to try to conserve water in their reservoirs.
The Ardingly reservoir, near Haywards Heath in West Sussex, which serves 280,000 people, is exceptionally low, holding 1.05bn litres of water. Its total capacity is 5.2bn litres.
In the south-west, Colliford reservoir on Bodmin Moor, which serves 255,000 households in Cornwall, is 37% full, holding 10.68bn litres against a total capacity of 28.5bn litres. Wimbleball in Somerset, which provides water for 390,000 people, is 18% full, with 3.8bn litres against a total capacity of 21.3bn litres.
Sam Bottomley, South West Water’s director for drinking water services, said the region was entering a critical phase of an exceptionally prolonged drought.
“Every day we continue to draw on our reservoirs to keep water flowing to homes, businesses and communities while river flows remain below the levels needed to support public water supply,” he said.
“Many people understandably think a drought is over once it starts raining. In reality, recovery takes much longer.
“Some rivers still remain at their lowest levels and with no significant rain forecast for the coming weeks, the immediate challenge is reducing demand and preserving enough stored water to maintain supplies until river flows and reservoir levels recover.”

Ukrainian soldier goes on trial over sabotage of Nord Stream gas pipelines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
06:00:47 UTC
15:00:47 KST

A former Ukrainian soldier has gone on trial in Hamburg accused of taking part in one of the most brazen acts of sabotage in postwar European history – the 2022 attack on the Nord Stream gas pipelines between Russia and Germany.
Serhii Kuznetsov, who was a special forces officer with the Ukrainian military, is accused by prosecutors of being an accomplice to war crimes by attacking civilian infrastructure, causing an explosion, damaging property and disrupting public services.
He appeared in court on Wednesday dressed in a grey suit, white shirt and black tie, and flanked by his lawyers. Kuznetsov saluted as he entered the court room. He and his legal team listened in silence for 10 minutes as the federal prosecutor general read out the indictment, which was simultaneously translated into Ukrainian.
Kuznetsov, 50, is alleged to have prepared and carried out the detonation of at least four incendiary devices of up to 27kg in weight at a depth of about 80 metres under the Baltic Sea, close to the Danish island of Bornholm.
He is believed to have had six accomplices, including four deep-sea divers, an explosives expert and a ship’s captain, who are alleged to have used a rented yacht and timer-controlled explosives. Both he and his country deny any involvement in the attacks.
Kuznetsov’s lawyers argued on Wednesday that the trial should not be taking place at all, telling the court that the defendant, who they said has been held almost entirely in solitary confinement for 11 months, was being treated “like a pawn on a chessboard”.
They stressed his inability to defend himself in the conventional manner due to his role as an army officer, which they said forbade him from speaking. It meant he was having to defend himself “with his hands tied”.
The explosions took place on 26 September 2022, badly damaging the pipelines which had been constructed to carry Russian natural gas between Vyborg in western Russia and Lubmin, near Greifswald in northern Germany.
The blasts caused the Nord Stream 1 pipelines – Russia’s main gas supply route to Germany before Moscow cut the supplies in August 2022 – to burst. They also damaged Nord Stream 2, which was ready to carry gas but was never put into operation after Germany suspended its authorisation process just before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The attacks happened as European countries were seeking to transition away from Russian energy supplies in reaction to the Kremlin’s aggression.
They exposed the dependence of Europe – and, in particular, Germany – on Russian gas as well as highlighting the murkiness of underground operations during wartime.
Security observers initially blamed Moscow for the attack. Russia has denied involvement, in turn blaming the US, which has denied it just as forcefully.
However, in July German state prosecutors accused Ukrainian “state authorities” of ordering the attack, arguing: “The aim was to permanently halt gas supplies via the pipelines and prevent Russia from using the revenue from natural gas trade to finance its war effort.”
The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has denied his country was involved.
Kuznetsov was arrested in August 2025 on a family holiday in Italy, with Italian police reporting that he surrendered without resistance. He had been travelling on a false passport. He was extradited to Germany last November, after legal efforts to prevent this failed.
A further suspect, Volodymyr Zhuravlyov, an air conditioner installer and hobby diver, was arrested on a European warrant in northern Croatia in August. He is fighting his extradition to Germany having applied for asylum in Croatia. He denies any role in the sabotage.
Aware of how potentially incendiary the trial could be, with Ukraine in effect in the dock for a crime committed against its ally – and one of its staunchest wartime supporters – the German government has declined to comment on the proceedings.
On Wednesday, a group of protesters gathered outside the court holding Ukrainian flags and placards. One of them, a Ukrainian man in exile in Germany, said: “It’s a scandal that a Ukrainian is being accused of a war crime here today, when Russia is constantly committing war crimes in Ukraine.”
The far-right populist, pro-Kremlin Alternative für Deutschland party, which is soaring in the polls, has seized on the Nord Stream plot to boost its argument that German aid for Ukraine must cease and the pipeline be reinstated so that cheap supplies of gas can help counter the cost of living crisis.
The pro-Ukrainian protesters who turned out on Wednesday were just a few feet away from a group of supporters of the far-left BSW party, which echoes the AfD’s stance on Russia and would also like to see the pipelines reinstated. They were holding placards demanding a parliamentary inquiry to investigate the political motives behind the Nord Stream attack.
Nord Stream was already a controversial subject before the attack, involving Russia’s leader, Vladimir Putin, who, with the then German chancellor, Gerhard Schröder, managed to bypass Ukraine as a transit country with Nord Stream 1. After Schröder left the chancellery, Putin appointed him as chair of the supervisory board of the company Nord Stream AG. Schröder was seen last week attending Putin’s birthday celebration.
A request by the Russians to participate as co-plaintiffs in the Hamburg trial was rejected by the court. The company Gazprom, which owns the Nord Stream 2 pipeline, had argued its right to do so due to what it has referred to as the severe economic consequences resulting from the attack. The court argued that while repair costs of the pipelines would be high, it would not be economically impossible to restore them.
According to reports, Kuznetsov, whose military ID indicates he was in active service at the time the pipelines were blown up, is expected to maintain his right to remain silent during the trial.
His legal team is expected to produce affidavits from two of his military superiors to support the argument that he is prohibited from revealing details of his actions as a soldier.
He is reported to have allegedly taken his orders from a man who is considered to be the mastermind behind the attack and is one of those who has sworn in his favour.
The trial will resume on 27 October.
Sixteen trial dates have been scheduled at Hamburg’s Hanseatic higher regional court up to and including 17 December, with further hearings likely in January and February.

Energy bills through the roof? Five signs your house is leaking heat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
06:00:47 UTC
15:00:47 KST

1. Cold draughts around windows, doors and loft hatches
Pick a day when there is a good breeze, and heat the house to its usual temperature. Then wander around with a candle or smoke pen (about £20). Alternatively, buy a thermal leak detector. This flashes blue for cold, green for normal and red for warm.
2. Water trapped between window panes
“Misting or water trapped between the panes of double glazing can point to a failed sealed unit,” says Antony Heath, the marketing and development director at Glevum Windows. “Once the seal has broken, the window may no longer insulate as effectively.”
3. Condensation on windows
Condensation on the inside of windows, particularly first thing in the morning, can indicate cold surfaces where heat is escaping, says Oliver Novakovic, technical and innovation director at Barratt Redrow. It can have several causes, including poor ventilation. Older single-glazed windows allow more heat loss, which exacerbates the problem.
4. The heating is always on, but your house still feels cold
If your home struggles to maintain a comfortable temperature, it may be losing heat through walls, floors or the roof. Uneven room temperatures can also be a sign that radiators are not working or heat is escaping faster in some areas. “The better a home is at retaining warmth through good insulation and airtightness, the less energy is needed to keep it comfortable,” Novakovic says.
5. Snow melts faster on your roof
If snow melts quickly on your roof while nearby properties remain blanketed – or it is a hotspot for birds – this can be a sign that heat is escaping. An older or uninsulated home can lose 25% of its heat through the roof.

How Europe’s most wanted cocaine trafficker turned Sierra Leone into the world’s first true narco state
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
06:00:46 UTC
15:00:46 KST

As abductions go, few have been more brazen. Alan Jalloh was with two friends outside Goodies supermarket, frantic as usual with late afternoon shoppers. Rush hour in downtown Freetown, Sierra Leone’s capital, was under way with familiar gusto.
A black Toyota Rav4 forced its way through the Peninsula highway traffic. Witnesses describe burly white men leaping out, yanking on balaclavas. Jalloh, 40, seemed to freeze. As did his two friends, one a famous Freetown footballer. All three were dragged into the waiting SUV. None of them have been seen since.
Two days later, on 25 October 2025, another three men disappeared. Within a week, nine people had been seized from the city’s streets, most in broad daylight. They were dismembered, police sources were told. At least one was beheaded. An officer investigating Jalloh’s abduction, says: “They were exterminated to hide the truth.”
No bodies have been found.
Five months after Jalloh disappeared, an ageing cargo ship, the Arconian, left Freetown. By May, it was navigating savage seas 100 miles off the coast of Morocco when Spanish civil guards boarded. Lucas Fernández*, clutching his assault rifle on the ship’s lower deck, stumbled across figures in the Arconian’s darkened cargo hold.
Fernández raised his gun, finger on the trigger. A man pointed an assault rifle back at him. Time stood still. Fernández says the man became agitated, yelling in English, incomprehensible above the storm outside. “It was crazy,” Fernández says.
Within minutes, he and his fellow officers had disarmed six gunmen found hiding in the bowels of the ship. Nearby, were 1,279 bales of cocaine wrapped in plastic; weighing between 30 and 45 tonnes, it is the largest amount of the drug ever seized.
Seventeen days later, the audience at Oxford University rose to applaud the guest speaker. Julius Maada Bio had nailed it once again. His address – eulogising robust leadership – was the latest in a whirlwind year for the president of Sierra Leone.
The chair of Ecowas – the Economic Union of West African States, a region home to more than 400 million people, Bio is among the most influential African voices in the UN. The EU sees Bio as one of its most reliable allies in Africa and has a long history of showering the impoverished country with aid stretching back more than 45 years.
But the most important figure in Sierra Leone is not this ambitious politician, but the man who ordered the abduction of Jalloh; the man responsible for the Arconian’s monumental cocaine stash. A man called Jos Leijdekkers. He also happens to be Bio’s son-in-law.
At 35, Leijdekkers is Europe’s pre-eminent cocaine baron. Intelligence assessments credit the Dutchman with importing volumes vast enough to repeatedly crash Europe’s cocaine market. Last year, he halved the drug’s wholesale price. Multiple intelligence sources confirm he has also transformed Sierra Leone into the world’s first true narco state.
“It is state capture by a criminal network on a scale never seen,” says a western official.
At least 14 people have been killed inside Sierra Leone on Leidjekkers’ orders. High-ranking police are believed to have been murdered on his say-so. Officers have fled the country fearing they will be next.
“If you get in his way, he wipes you out,” says an intelligence source.
Like most, they spoke on condition of anonymity, aware of Leidjekkers’ capacity to reach those who cross him.
Sierra Leone’s fate is a tale of western duplicity. Despite detailed intelligence of the extraordinary volumes of cocaine being exported to Europe, the EU continued to woo Bio and his government. The UN did the same: overlooking its own evidence.
And intelligence sources warn that Leijdekkers’ network is rapidly expanding. “The entire west Africa region is at risk,” says a Dutch official.
Leijdekkers’ prodigious transcontinental network brings deadly violence.
Dozens of his gunmen descended on a sleepy Dutch village last month intent on retribution. A European police source said: “We’ve had cocaine disputes before, but nothing like this. We’ve entered a new era.”
The first recorded sighting of Leijdekkers in west Africa came in October 2022. A six-vehicle convoy thundered down Aberdeen Road, towards Lumley beach, leaving Freetown traffic police baffled. No one had briefed they were expecting VIPs. “‘The convoy was bigger than our president’s,” says one officer.
Unaware of Europe’s most wanted cocaine trafficker, Freetown police were sufficiently concerned to begin surveillance on the mysterious convoy, which had stopped outside the Sky Bar, a nightlife institution in the city.
At 4am, the group were trailed to a waterfront house near Hamilton beach. There, the covert surveillance team were stunned: revellers included their own bosses.
At the time, western intelligence agencies had no idea of Leijdekkers’ whereabouts. One of Europe’s most wanted men had simply vanished. For years, authorities had tracked his rise in the Dutch underworld, watching how the local hitman from the well-heeled town of Prinsenbeek accrued key contacts for transatlantic cocaine shipments.
When Dutch intelligence traced Leijdekkers to Sierra Leone in 2024, he had created something remarkable: a sprawling cocaine empire from scratch.
“He’s very adept at adaptation, cultivating ties,” says an official. “A new country, but he won over its most influential people.”
That included marrying the president’s daughter, Agnes Bio, and starting a family. Sierra Leone’s top officials partied with the moneyed new guy. Immigration chiefs secured him a diplomatic passport. The person whose job it was to investigate cocaine traffickers became a drinking buddy.
Leijdekkers’ wealth corrupted. According to intelligence, he was generating a $150m (£113m) monthly profit – greater than the running cost of Sierra Leone’s entire state.
Hundreds of people were on his payroll, say sources, including senior military and police figures. But what Leidekkers coveted most was Freetown’s seaport: the Queen Elizabeth II Quay, perfectly sited between cocaine-producing South America and Europe’s booming markets.
In August 2023, his wife’s uncle, Yankuba Bio, became head of the port. Yankuba Bio denies a close relationship with “any individual called or identified as Jos Leijdekkers”. Sources, though, say port officials on Leijdekkers’s payroll make $2,000 a month – more than 30 times the national average.
In January 2025, the Dutch sent an extradition request to Sierra Leone for the fugitive, who had been sentenced in absentia to more than 100 years in prison for crimes including attempted murder.
Sierra Leone denied knowing the man. For Leijdekkers, it was a defining moment: he had state protection. His confidence culminated in the arrival into Freetown’s port on 18 April of the Arconian, a green cargo vessel the length of a football pitch. Over the next four days, about 30 tonnes of cocaine were hauled onboard, according to western intelligence.
“From experience, the maximum you can hide is eight tonnes. Thirty tonnes says you’re operating in plain sight,” says a UN agent. Yankuba Bio says such claims are “false, completely untrue and without foundation” adding that the port “does not engage in or facilitate the export” of cocaine.
On 26 April, a cryptic tip-off electrified European investigators. An unidentified vessel had left west Africa carrying 18 tonnes of cocaine, the second-largest such cargo identified in Europe.
Within 70 hours, the Arconian had been identified. At 8pm on 1 May, with the vessel pitching in brutal, black seas, Fernández, of Spain’s civil guard central operational unit, was first onboard.
Having arrested the 23-strong Filipino crew, the officer spotted a gun lying on the deck. “We started to search more deeply,” says Fernández.
After his team stumbled across the six-strong paramilitary detail guarding the cocaine, it became chillingly evident the gunmen had orders to kill anyone who threatened Leijdekkers’ drugs. They had no idea Fernández was a police officer.
“They thought we were an organisation come to rob the drugs,” he says. “It was very tense. Anyone – them, us – might have fired.”
It took interminable seconds for Leijdekkers’ men to appreciate the truth. “They knew then it would be worse to open fire.”
The Arconian seizure shattered previous understanding of cocaine trafficking. Firstly, Leijdekkers appeared certain that his €812m (£687m) cargo would reach Europe. No attempt was made to conceal the drugs. “There was a 60-metre-long corridor full of it,” says Fernández.
Such nonchalance corroborated intelligence assessments that Leijdekkers had repeatedly flooded Europe with shipments, utilising a vast narco fleet and driving the wholesale cocaine price to a record low.
In the weeks before the raid, the Arconian completely changed its identity. Analysis for the Guardian by the maritime AI company Windward tracked at least three “suspicious” vessels from Freetown in the months before the Arconian. All rebranded themselves before leaving Sierra Leone.
In January this year, a cargo boat changed its registration details just before arriving in Freetown. After a month, it left for an unspecified destination. On 15 March, the vessel loitered off the Canary Islands for four hours. Investigators say the Arconian intended to linger off the Spanish archipelago, offloading the cocaine to a flotilla of speedboats.
Last Christmas Eve, another suspicious ship altered its name, flag and identifying traits when anchored off Freetown. With no destination declared, it left on Christmas Day. Approaching the Canary Islands on 9 January, it slowed and remained there for 13 hours before heading to Libya, which was also the Arconian’s stated destination.
Exactly the same pattern was observed with a ship leaving Freetown on 15 December, too.
Another eight vessels with near-identical traits to the Arconian have departed Freetown for Libya via the Canary Islands since 2024.
These include the White Labeille, which left Freetown in November 2024, was tracked off the Canary Islands and later “went dark”, switching off locator devices. Four months earlier, the White Eagle departed Sierra Leone before going dark off Morocco and being mysteriously abandoned. On the same day, another vessel – the White Arrow – was discarded in Libya with its Filipino crew, weeks after leaving Freetown.
Other ships were found abandoned close to Freetown. One trawler, Sky 777, ran aground on Lumley Beach last year. No one has claimed it.
Months later, the Agios Basseterre drifted on to nearby Hamilton beach. Witnesses described white men hurriedly retrieving packages from the boat. It, too, was never claimed.
As investigators pored over the Arconian, Sierra Leonean authorities claimed its cargo originated from a mystery maritime transfer. However, analysis for the Guardian of its final voyage by Lloyd’s List Intelligence confirmed that the ship’s speed was consistent. There were no stops for a ship-to-ship transfer.
Something else did not seem right. Usually, the loss of even a modest cocaine cargo unleashes a wave of underworld violence. Intelligence agencies waited for the bloodshed.
Two days after the Arconian’s seizure, Leijdekkers chaired a Freetown summit to pinpoint what had gone wrong. Who gave the tip-off? Did he have a mole?
But no violence followed. “Mind-boggling amounts of cocaine had gone,” says a police source, “but Leijdekkers behaved like nothing had happened. Extraordinary.”
Perhaps Alan Jalloh underestimated Leijdekkers? Or maybe he was blinded by greed? Either way, intelligence indicates he was seen to have “betrayed” the Dutch fugitive over a cocaine deal. Police investigating the kidnapping made a swift breakthrough. Officers tracked down the black Toyota SUV. “We recognised it from our surveillance work on Leidjekkers,” says one.
Three kidnappers were arrested, but before they could be questioned, senior officers intervened. “They were released the same day,” says a source.
The investigating team’s caseload snowballed. Two days later, inquiries prompted a police raid on a Freetown warehouse. Inside were two teenagers and the property owner, guarding blocks of cocaine.
Halfway through the arrest, 40 armed troops turned up. At gunpoint, police were ordered to release the suspects. “Officers were told to leave everything with the military. Nobody saw those boys again,” says a police source.
Over the following days, other people went missing, including the owner of a Lumley beach bar. A name linking the disappeared kept cropping up: Leijdekkers. Detectives, though, felt their inquiry was increasingly thwarted. The lead investigator was abruptly transferred: Jalloh’s family could no longer contact them.
Nine people had disappeared, yet not a single police statement was issued. Such silence is even more striking because Jalloh, a shopkeeper, was related to Sierra Leone’s vice-president, and kidnapped alongside Alusine “Bokay” Koroma, a lauded Sierra Leonean international footballer.
Asked for details of its investigation, Sierra Leone police did not respond. The military also declined to comment. Western intelligence reports, though, are unequivocal: Leijdekkers’ enforcers murdered Jalloh. “His mercenaries were supported by the police and military,” says one report.
Witness statements reveal that hours before he was abducted, troops visited Jalloh’s Freetown Liquor Mart and looted its contents. Some of those kidnapped, police learned, were buried at Freetown’s police cemetery.
“Reliable sources say they were sliced with a power saw while alive. A pit was dug, the bodies dissolved with chemicals and concreted over,” said a Sierra Leonean police officer. Another source with knowledge of the burials informed investigators that a “head was missing”.
Other deaths occurred, such as John Conteh, who worked at Freetown’s port, checking container seals at the quayside. Intelligence sources reveal Conteh began “monitoring and inspecting containers” linked to Leijdekkers.
At about 1am on 2 June 2024, Conteh was crushed in work machinery. In the commercially sensitive heart of one of west Africa’s most critical ports, his death was apparently not caught on CCTV.
Conteh, who worked for Mediterranean Shipping Company (MSC), the world’s largest shipping group, is the only MSC employee to have died in Freetown since it started operations there 14 years ago.
Eight days after Conteh’s death, Sierra Leonean authorities concluded the incident was a “work-related accident”.
MSC declined to comment, referring to port authority statements. Sierra Leone police similarly chose not to respond. Western intelligence believe Conteh died in “suspicious circumstances”.
Even high-ranking police officers are at risk. On 8 April 2023, Supt Matthew “Boyka” Banya was in a marked police car near Makeni’s famous clock tower. Banya was adjusting to the northern city, having been ousted from Freetown after allegedly falling foul of Leijdekkers’ network.
An assassin shot Banya in his vehicle at point-blank range.
“Boyka wanted to expose Leijdekkers so an assailant was sent,” a Sierra Leonean police source claims.
The president himself urged police action but no killer was caught. “There was no proper investigation. They let it go,” added the source. Justice campaigners claim they were “obstructed” by the authorities. Police would not comment.
Such unsolved killings have chilled the country. Residents describe a climate of fear. “Targeted assassinations, cover-ups and impunity. We are terrified,” says one local politician.
Most feared are the “commandos”, Leijdekkers’ Turkish, Dutch and Serbian bodyguards, armed with pistols and assault rifles.
Journalists attempting to document Leijdekkers risk arrest, as happened to the Dutch reporter Sophie van Leeuwen, who travelled to Freetown last year.
A 24/7 police surveillance operation was instigated. At one point, officers watched her drive past Leijdekkers as he drank in the Sky Bar.
On her sixth day in Freetown, she was detained for several days on spying charges before being released. Her media files were deleted.
Politicians are similarly silenced. Abdul Kargbo, leader of the opposition, alleges that he was threatened after raising trafficking concerns. “They sent people to advise me to stay off [the issue],” he says.
Leidjekkers shows little sign of lying low, openly enjoying his favourite nightspots, Scarlet, Lor and the Sky Bar.
But observers report an increase in security; more armed guards, more lookouts and increasingly rigorous counter-surveillance. Drivers are frequently rotated. His fleet of vehicles are routinely changed. When Leijdekkers makes a journey, reconnaissance teams are dispatched 24 hours in advance. “He seems more paranoid,” says a source.
His caution might be valid. Twice, Dutch special forces have been positioned off the west African coast preparing to seize him. Aborted at the last minute, the operations will have jangled nerves. “His biggest fear is a mole,” says a Sierra Leonean source.
Several trusted lieutenants aside, Leijdekkers’ business is largely a one-man show. “It makes his network difficult to infiltrate; it can absorb the arrest of senior figures while easily getting rid of juniors.”
His willingness to eradicate any perceived weak links can be seen, sources allege, in the deaths of a specialist police unit. Leijdekkers, they claim, feared the team knew too much, including where Jalloh was buried. Two months after the shopowner disappeared, a police vehicle crashed, killing three officers. The official account was that it was an accident.
Days later, a fourth officer of the unit was found hanged. “His family knows their son would not hang himself. No investigation was mounted,” says a police source.
Leijdekkers’ arrival has also brought a surge in cocaine’s popularity among Freetown’s middle classes, particularly the Lumley beach nightclubs. The drug’s street price is the lowest in west Africa.
Abubakar Sesay, 32, a cocaine addict in Freetown, says dealers operate with political protection: “The bulk is mainly for export to Europe, but a small quantity is sold locally through criminal networks facilitating the trafficking trade.”
Experts already warn that cocaine poses a serious public health concern, particularly if processed into cheaper crack cocaine. “We’re already seeing overdoses,” says a drugs campaigner.
Despite its relatively low street price, the drug’s wider popularity in Sierra Leone is still limited by its cost, as nearly half of the population live in extreme poverty.
Very few people benefit from Leijdekkers’ largesse, with sources estimating only a “few hundred” of the country’s nine million people share in the profits. Yet cocaine has warped the country’s economy. One dish at Lor restaurant can cost £270 – five months’ pay for the average Sierra Leonean.
A slew of luxury car showrooms line Wilkinson Road; new apartments abound. “My driver showed me a huge multi-storey building built by a police officer. Not a regional commander – a traffic cop!” says the politician.
Fresh construction linked to Leijdekkers is emerging across west Africa. Operating bases have been established within Liberia, Guinea Bissau and now Ghana. Using diplomatic passports, Leijdekkers and his men roam the region with ease. Witnesses describe Liberian police applauding his convoy as it crossed the border.
On 21 July, the biggest drugs bust in Liberia’s history was announced when almost 4 tonnes of Leijdekkers’ cocaine, worth £235m, was found near its capital, Monrovia.
The previous day, sources say Leijdekkers returned to Freetown from Liberia. They also recognised the man arrested with the Monrovia cocaine, who was seen with Leijdekkers in Freetown.
Leijdekkers “frequently” visits Guinea Bissau, courting the junta that seized power last November.
There is scrutiny, too, in Ghana where last month several of Leijdekker’s network were arrested.
As gifts go, they caught the eye. On 23 June 2026, EU officials gave two sleek speedboats to Bio’s government at a ceremony in Freetown. The vessels were for the same military co-opted by Leidekkers to help tackle drug trafficking – one of many EU offerings made despite detailed warnings over Leijdekkers’ influence in Sierra Leone.
In a deal signed before Leijdekkers arrived in Freetown, Brussels sanctioned a €352m aid package running until 2027. So far, €245m has been paid.
In August 2024 – weeks after Dutch intelligence confirmed Bio’s government was harbouring Europe’s chief cocaine importer – the EU agreed to give an extra €90m to Sierra Leone.
In January 2025, another €35m was unlocked at a Freetown meeting with EU officials. Other deals involved tens of millions of EU taxpayers’ money paid directly into Sierra Leone’s treasury.
After the Arconian seizure, on 9 June 2026, Brussels opened the European chamber of commerce in Freetown to boost investment. Its inaugural president was the Sierra Leonean head of the shipping company whose employee John Conteh died at Freetown’s port.
Strengthening democracy was a core ambition of European investment in Sierra Leone. Since Leijdekkers arrival, the EU has spent €5.6m on the issue: not enough to prevent recent allegations that he financed $100,000 bribes in an attempt to corrupt its electoral system.
The Dutch justice minister, David van Weel, exasperated with Bio’s refusal to extradite Leijdekkers, wants Brussels to freeze development aid to Freetown. To date, just €18m of funding has been suspended.
In summer 2024, as evidence indicated that Bio’s government was protecting Lijdekkers, Sierra Leone assumed the rotating presidency of the UN security council.
In June 2025, after becoming chair of Ecowas, Bio led a committee demanding a permanent African seat on the security council. The UN body, which is mandated to impose sanctions on a country controlled by a drug lord, seems unwilling to target one of its lamentably few African voices.
“There was no appetite. Leidjekkers never came up,” says a European diplomat.
Bio doubled down on his statesman persona. Ten days after the Arconian was seized, he met the French president, Emmanuel Macron, before flying to London for his speech at Oxford.
In September, Bio addressed world leaders at the UN general assembly with a speech on “restoring trust”. A New York meeting with Kristalina Georgieva, managing director of the International Monetary Fund, saw Bio’s economic policies feted. Anti-narcotics investigators were gobsmacked.
Even Leijdekker’s 32-year-old wife, Agnes, is accredited to Sierra Leone’s UN mission in New York.
In London, where Bio’s wife, Fatima, until recently had a council flat, a dedicated team is investigating Leijdekkers’ sprawling UK connections.
Sharing daily briefings with their Dutch counterparts, Britain’s National Crime Agency has identified interlinked trafficking networks. “Intelligence is telling us that he’s linked to an awful lot of things. We have a number [of UK cocaine importations] we think he was involved in,” said a UK source.
The British government has not aired any concerns over Bio’s government.
It resembled a scene from Sinaloa, the Mexican region where drug cartels use brazen violence to subjugate the state and send a show of force. It was the quiet Dutch village of Overasselt where, on 1 September this year, dozens of heavily armed men descended. Leijdekkers’ hastily assembled “narco-army” opened fire on a rural warehouse, killing a security guard and, when police arrived, seriously wounding two officers.
In the pre-dawn chaos, 34 of the narco trafficker’s foot soldiers were arrested. A cache of high-velocity weapons was found nearby.
For Europe’s police, it was the realisation of a long-dreaded nightmare: Latin America’s cartel-style violence had arrived.
Leijdekkers attack on Overasselt was completely out of character. Intelligence updates had long chronicled a trafficking network characterised by meticulous paperwork and finely tuned logistics to remain under the radar. Overasselt was the precise opposite. “He’s getting desperate,” a Dutch police source believes.
Having lost €812m on the Arconian, the Overassalet raid was prompted by the loss on 29 August of 1.2 tonnes of cocaine near the French-Spanish border.
Leijdekkers believed a rival had nabbed it. Within two days, he and associates had recruited for this outlandish raid. But Leijdekkers was wrong. It was police, in fact, who had intercepted the €50m cargo.
Days later, the fugitive faced another egregious blow when police officers confirmed they had caught Leijdekkers’ chief financier, a senior operator in a clandestine money transfer system dubbed “Dubai bank”.
Since the Arconian was intercepted, Leijdekker has lost up to 12 shipments – and the wholesale price of cocaine in Europe has risen from €12,000 to €22,000 a kilo.
His cumulative losses, police believe, have left him in debt to the Colombian Cali cartel.
He also faces a gigantic monthly payroll inside Sierra Leone. A cornered Leijdekkers is a dangerous proposition. Having outlasted former accomplices, such as the alleged crime boss Daniel Kinahan, recently extradited from Dubai to Ireland, and the convicted Moroccan-Dutch trafficker Ridouan Taghi, sentenced to life in prison in 2024, Leijdekkers retains extensive influence within the sprawling criminal ecosystem in north Africa and Europe, the so-called Mocro mafia.
Police sources, who once insisted Freetown would “never, ever” extradite their wealthy guest, are now wondering if that might change. And for the Bio family, international pressure is escalating. Van Weel, the Netherlands’ justice and security minister, said work was under way to “sanction” individuals linked to Leijdekkers. The president’s office declined to comment, though there is no suggestion he is implicated in any suspected illegal activity linked to Leijdekkers.
Leijdekkers’ lawyer dismissed the allegations as “politically driven”. A subsequent statement read: “My client wants you to know that the information you got from anonymous sources is complete nonsense, probably nourished by the Dutch authorities and therefore not fit for publication.”
Sierra Leone stands on the brink, along with the rest of west Africa. A regional narco-economy, where fragile states are overwhelmed by entrenched corruption and ruthless criminal networks, remains a distinct possibility.
Like Jalloh, Leijdekkers may disappear from Freetown. He will probably surface elsewhere to assemble a fresh empire.
“There’s no sign of him retiring,” says a police source. “Every day, the guy’s growing his wings, expanding his network.”

Gothic getaways, un-adulting and trip snacking: Expedia ‘unpacks’ its top travel trends for 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
06:00:34 UTC
15:00:34 KST

Travellers will be going full Kate Bush, indulging their inner child and taking shorter breaks in between their bigger holidays next year and beyond.
‘Tis the season. No, not that season – there are still 11 weeks until Christmas. Not Halloween, either, or even Gilmore Girls-rewatch time.
We’re of course referring to the glorious season when all the industry trends reports are released, and the latest travel company to share its predictions is Expedia Group.
Pulling on insights from Expedia, Hotels.com and Vrbo, as well as a survey of 26,000 travellers across 16 countries, plus social media data, Unpack ’27 has identified five key travel trends.
“Travel is about creating memories, and Unpack ’27 uncovers the destinations and experiences shaping those moments,” said Ariane Gorin, CEO of Expedia Group.
“In 2027, travellers are being more intentional in choosing their next adventure, seeking experiences that are more personal and purposeful to them.”
The travel trends to know in 2027
According to Expedia Group, indulging your inner child will be the move in 2027, with travellers swapping the mundane facets of day-to-day life for playful getaways involving theme parks, water parks or other nostalgic activities.
Some 57% of travellers say they will book a so-called “un-adulting” trip in 2027, rising to 71% among Gen Z and Millennials.
Top options for embracing the trend? Disneyland Tokyo, Colour Factory Chicago and Park Xcaret in Mexico.
This year was all about “snackpacking”, aka trying crisps, chocolate and other supermarket treats, but in 2027, we’ll be embracing “trip snacking”.
Meant to satisfy a different type of appetite, trip snacking involves quick, spontaneous getaways that can ease the break between longer, less-frequent trips.
Some 79% of travellers are planning to book a one-night stay in the next year, with searches for one-night stays up 10% on Hotels.com.
Wuthering Heights hit screens in 2026, bringing with it a revival in appreciation for all things Gothic.
Some 56% of travellers have booked hotels specifically for the atmosphere or aesthetic, with 65% of these interested in booking a Gothic-style hotel, whether that be a historic castle or a destination steeped in folklore or the supernatural.
The numbers speak for themselves: The “Gothic Getaways” trend has seen a 20% increase year-on-year in demand for castles, according to Hotels.com.
“Skillcations” were a big trend in 2026, and that is set to continue in 2027 with “hobby hubs” – travellers specifically booking holiday homes for crafting weekends, photography retreats, mahjong game nights and antique-hunting breaks.
Last but not least, “heartland hideouts”, aka hidden gem destinations that are landlocked, are on the rise, too.

Walters explains choice of Walsh over Tedesco for World Cup opener

Reece Walsh was a surprise inclusion over James Tedesco for Australia's World Cup opener against New Zealand on Thursday night.
Kangaroos coach Kevin Walters said he chose Walsh because of Tedesco's heavy finish to the season.
What's next?
Tedesco is expected to start in Australia's second pool match against Fiji on October 25.
Kevin Walters has declared the battle for Australia's fullback berth remains wide open despite Reece Walsh winning the nod over James Tedesco to start in the Kangaroos' World Cup opener.
Walters claimed ahead of Thursday night's clash with New Zealand that Tedesco, the captain as Australia lifted the trophy four years ago, would have a chance to prove his worth in the group-stage game against Fiji in Brisbane on October 25.
Walsh, the hero of last year's Ashes whitewash, will don the No.1 jersey at Sydney's Allianz Stadium, but as for whether the Brisbane Broncos star will be first choice later in the tournament, Walters is keeping an open mind.
The Kangaroos coach indicated he had chosen to rest Tedesco and playmaker halfback Sam Walker following their exploits in the Sydney Roosters' NRL grand final win.
"I feel it's in the best interest of the team they get a spell this week and they'll play next week," Walters said on Wednesday.
"To be honest, I haven't decided that (fullback) position yet, that's why we're here, and they'll both get an opportunity.
"They're both Clive Churchill medallists, the last two, so I look at it that way. I'm very fortunate to have both of them in the team.
"They're different players, but I love what they both bring to the team. Teddy's the more experienced custodian and Reece is on the way up as such."
The one drawback to Walsh is his fitness, with Thursday's opener his first competitive match in close to two months after sustaining an ankle injury in clubland.
"He (Walsh) has had a good preparation and there's a few players in that position themselves, so it's good to get them around the group," Walters said.
Walsh will be part of a relatively settled Kangaroos spine, with Cameron Munster at five-eighth and Harry Grant at hooker.
Halfback Mitchell Moses is the only new addition to the key playmaking roles.
Moses was on last year's Ashes tour but didn't take the field, with the Parramatta skipper an understudy to Nathan Cleary, who has missed this World Cup following his compound ankle fracture.
"He's a very influential player, an experienced player, particularly his kicking game around the halves will be invaluable," Walters said.
"He gets his opportunity and I'm sure he's looking forward to taking it as well.
"They (Munster and Moses) are very calm and know what we need to do in different situations."
The Kangaroos have not lost to New Zealand on Australian soil since 2015, and while the Kiwis have a monster forward pack, Walters insists his side have the firepower to match them.
"It's a strong New Zealand side, certainly, but I feel like the guys that we have picked in the Australian squad, they're not mugs," the Kangaroos coach added.
"We've got Origin players, Test players, premiership winners, that's what the World Cup is all about: seeing the best players on the world stage."
