Bread on Uncle Milad’s Table: Masculinity, memory and Libya
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
06:00:25 UTC
15:00:25 KST

Breadcrumb
'Some people don't put love in their bread': How Mohammed Alnaas's award-winning novel unpacks masculinity in Libya
"My life is full of anticipation and anxiety," says Milad, the central character in Mohammed Alnaas’s Bread on Uncle Milad’s Table, comparing his life to the anxious wait for dough to rise, a feeling that runs through the novel as he struggles with the uncertain space between who he is and who he is allowed to be.
First published in 2021, Bread on Uncle Milad’s Table won the International Prize for Arabic Fiction in 2022, making Mohammed the first Libyan, and the youngest author, to receive the prestigious award.
Now, in Sawad Hussain’s English translation (HarperVia, October 2026), Mohammed’s distinctive voice comes through in all its intimacy: digressive, sensory and gentle.
That intimacy comes through in the way Milad tells his story, addressing an unnamed listener while repeatedly cautioning that his wife, Zeinab, is asleep and must not be woken, the care with which he guards her sleep becoming part of the atmosphere of his telling.
Those memories take him back to his childhood, where Milad grows up as the only boy among four sisters. His father, a baker, learnt the craft from an Italian mentor and teaches Milad the art of breadmaking in moments of rare tenderness and sudden rage.
"The heart, Milad," he would advise, "some people don’t put love in their bread."
But that tenderness comes with another lesson: love and affection are not to be shown to his sisters, because "you’re only meant to keep them safe and order them around."
The man Milad must become
For Milad, the love of bread and the demand to harden become intertwined, shaping one of the central pressures of his life.
While the novel is littered with self-deprecating humour, Mohammed is funniest in his treatment of the former Libyan regime. Gaddafi is a background force in the story and is always referred to by his chosen title, 'Brother Leader'.
The months also run on the calendar 'Brother Leader' invented, without missing a beat. This deadpan consistency turns the era’s forced theatrics into dark comedy.
In one scene, Milad waits in a room where a framed portrait of the 'Brother Leader' hangs on a wall while a propaganda song lists his virtues.
He is the ideal man: confident, virile, macho, powerful, all-controlling patriarch who "rode his horse to free the country."
He was everything that Milad was not. The image is what schoolboys were meant to grow into. The feeling of not being enough is a constant from childhood to adulthood.
It is this feeling that leads Milad to the "factory that would make a man out of him." His father’s final wish was for Milad to join the military, believing it would harden his son.
There, he meets Madona, a brutal trainer who takes a particular aim at him. Madona christens him "doughboy," and so begins the cycle of beatings and humiliations. The abuse intensifies until Milad attempts, without success, to take his life.
The attempts do not end with his time in the military. They continue afterwards, messy and undignified. Some are weirdly hilarious, interrupted, unsurprisingly, by domestic attentiveness. The effect on the reader is not so much horror as a protective tenderness.
But suicide here does not act as an abstract plot device. In Libya, men die by suicide at a higher rate than women. Milad is shaped by everything that pattern is made from: the lasting scars of military service and society’s narrow codes of honour. That he fails in these attempts is Mohammed’s deft hand. Even in the act of trying to die, Milad remains insufficiently a man.
The idea of what makes a man runs through everything Milad tells us: his childhood, his relationship with his father, the bond he shares with his sisters, the military, his marriage and his humiliations.
All are set against Libyan proverbs on manhood. Some counsel ferocity, insisting it is better to be a rooster for one day than a chicken for ten, or that the rider makes the mare. Another promises immunity, claiming that a man can do no wrong. One warns that a devil has many daughters.
Another advocates cruelty as a lesson, suggesting that "skinning the cat" will scare the bride. Yet it is the saying that opens the novel, and hangs over the story, that becomes its most pointed refrain: the whispered verdict on any household where the man cannot control the women inside, "it must be one of Uncle Milad’s."
Bread, music and memory
In his essay Kneading Words, translated by Nashwa Nasreldin (Arablit, 2022), Mohammed talks about learning to bake before writing the novel, and the care it shows.
Details like nurturing a yeast starter for years, the feel of dough under the hands, and the score of a baker’s blade “like a finger drawing in fine sand” are written with sensory details that can only come from a baker's observations.
Bread, he writes, "requires patience, precision and a touch of creativity." The story, too, takes time, adding texture through careful "kneading, shaping and reshaping."
That texture comes not only from bread, but from music. Songs by Abdel Halim Hafez, Fairouz, Cheb Khaled, Bob Marley and even the more obscure Libyan voice of Sadeq Bo Abaab, among many others, run through the story. They carry Milad’s longings and the small private freedoms he allows himself, like dancing to Layl as-Sahraneen as he bakes.
Of all the musicians Milad listens to, Ahmed Fakroun holds a particular place.
"No other musician could console me, assure me the way Ahmed Fakroun did," Milad says, as the lyrics of Hareb fil layali — "oh, you flee in the nights, from nights in the fog… the sorrow of your heart is in your heart" — give words to what he carries silently, making the novel feel as though it should be read with its soundtrack playing.
The same attention to small details shapes the way Milad tells his story. He is fastidious about his housework, but his narration obeys no such order. He wanders, doubles back, picks up a thread pages later, then digresses again into recipes and songs.
Sometimes, he moves on to a seemingly unrelated story. He reassures the listener: "You might be tempted to ask why I’m even telling you all this, and if it has anything to do with my story. It does."
For some readers, these digressions may feel indulgent, but this one found them charming.
The book asks its readers for the same patience dough demands. By the final page, the digressions and little details have built a full picture of Milad’s interiority.
We understand why, for instance, in the novel’s climax, Milad reaches for the old apron his father gifted him, and why Zeinab immediately realises what it means. The result is both intimate and capacious.
All of this makes Milad an easy character to care about, but for all his sensitivity, he is not a progressive hero. He is passive and easily swayed by louder, more insistent voices, a kind man socialised into a world that equates masculinity with dominance.
The same men, his father included, will weep over Umm Kulthum songs and later strike their wives. Milad notices this hypocrisy without articulating an alternative. He knows it, too: "I am not a big thinker or some intellectual."
That passivity has consequences. When Milad finally performs the role expected of him, the repercussions are devastating for him and for the women around him. For the reader, too, who has been invited to sit at his table and eat his bread.
Learning to be tender
The question of the man a society expects also connects Mohammed’s novel to the work of Tayeb Salih, whom he has named as a formative influence. His debut carries echoes, perhaps unconsciously, of Season of Migration to the North.
Both are confessional novels. Tayeb’s unnamed narrator listens to Mustafa Sa’eed, while Mohammed’s unnamed listener receives Milad’s monologue.
Mustafa and Milad are polar opposites. Mustafa performs the hyper-masculine role in Salih’s colonial encounter, while Milad is forced into it by his family, the military and his village’s mockery of his unmanliness.
The forces that made a Mustafa are scaled down to a village, a bakery, a marriage and a kitchen, producing instead a Milad: where Mustafa mastered the role demanded of him and was destroyed by it, Milad tried to resist and was destroyed anyway.
Yet for all that happens to him, what stays with us is Milad himself. We grow fond of him. How could one not? The man who flinches at loud voices, the "sunflower lover," the careful hands that waxed his sisters’ legs with syrup he made himself, the small mercies he extends even to those who once hurt him.
That tenderness returns us to the lesson his father teaches him at the beginning of the novel. Early on, Milad’s father teaches him that dough needs the right amount of air, and that too much or too little will ruin it. "Love," his father said, "is about giving it the right environment."
What happens, the novel asks, when the air stifles instead of lifting? When the heat is set by other hands to a scorching level? His name means 'birth', and the novel finally gives him that. He is at last "a man" by the warped standards he was forced into his whole life.
Sweet Milad. Kind Milad. Gentle Milad. Foolish Milad. What have you done, Milad?
Fifi Bat-hef is a Kenyan book reviewer with a bias for literary fiction
Follow her on Instagram: @fifi.bathef

Chinese researchers have built a self-propelled crawler robot that harvests iron from sand and have tested the device in the dunes of the vast Taklamakan Desert – an area the size of Germany – in northwestern China’s Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region.
In Frank Herbert’s classic science fiction novel Dune, mobile factories traverse the sands of the fictional planet Arrakis to extract the drug melange, also known as “spice”. The real-world device similarly travels across the desert, extracting valuable resources.
The rare earth-magnet-based separator, developed by researchers from Tarim University in Xinjiang, filters ferromagnetic materials from sand using dry magnetic separation.
According to the team’s study published in the Chinese-language journal Metal Mine, the Taklamakan contains “vast quantities of ferromagnetic materials”, with previous research estimating iron content in its sands of about 6 per cent.

Striking where it hurts: Ukrainian drones are having a tangible effect on the Russian economy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
05:59:57 UTC
14:59:57 KST

Russia’s losses from Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries have already reached 1% of GDP — and that's if Vladimir Putin is to be believed. Putin, of course, is hard to believe, but even 1% of GDP is an enormous sum — roughly half of the federal government's current budget deficit. And on top of that, mounting strikes mean the figure is likely only to rise — especially if the three recent attacks on Yandex data centers signal a new trend. According to The Insider’s estimates, each successful strike on an oil refinery costs Russia an average of around 23 billion rubles ($274 million), while a strike on an online marketplace warehouse costs 450,000 rubles ($5,350) per square meter. In the long run, these losses will weigh on the budget and drive down consumer demand — two key drivers of the Russian economy.
Average cost per unit
Unlike the production of crude oil, refining generates relatively little revenue for the Russian budget. When a refinery shuts down, the costs are borne by businesses: the refinery’s owner, fuel consumers, and intermediaries. Repair costs can be roughly estimated from equipment prices or the total cost of modernizing a refinery (since exact prices for individual units are rarely disclosed). For Russia’s large refineries, of which there are 37, several examples are available.
The Ministry of Energy estimated that 95 secondary-processing units were rebuilt and commissioned in Russia between 2011 and 2018, at a total investment of 1.6 trillion rubles. That works out to just under 17 billion rubles per unit, by a very rough estimate. Between 2019 and 2026, another 27 units were commissioned, against a target of 40, with investments totaling 512 billion rubles. That amounts to nearly 19 billion rubles per unit on average. The figures broadly corroborate each other and reflect rising costs, partly due to sanctions.
Bringing a single secondary-processing unit online costs 19 billion rubles – the average over the past seven years
Replacing imported oil-refining equipment with domestic alternatives has been a particular challenge. Foreign technologies dominated the original modernization projects, and after sanctions were imposed, the Ministry of Industry and Trade sought to promote import substitution. However, the industry continues to rely heavily on Asian suppliers.
There are also figures for individual companies. In 2023, Gazprom Neft ceremonially launched a new primary oil-processing complex in Omsk, costing more than 66 billion rubles. It replaced six older units built to previous environmental standards. In other words, replacing each old unit cost about 11 billion rubles.
Matthew Sagers, an expert at S&P Global Commodity Insights, estimated that damage from a single Ukrainian drone attack in 2024 could have cost anywhere from several million to tens of millions of dollars. Around the same time, Sergey Vakulenko wrote that refinery repairs could run into tens of millions of dollars.
If the energy truce proposed by Trump is agreed to, it would give Russian refineries time to carry out repairs. But if the deal Ukraine is willing to accept — but which Russia is not — falls through again and the Ukrainian Armed Forces step up their attacks on refineries, major overhauls may soon be necessary, according to one industry source. Such an overhaul takes at least six months, as the unit must be designed by an engineering institute, approved, manufactured, and installed.
Repairs involving imported equipment could take even longer, as the necessary components may simply be unavailable. Recovery from a fire can take longer still, requiring an assessment of the site, the dismantling of damaged structures, and the removal of debris.
What would it cost to repair the Moscow refinery?
On the night of Sept. 20, a drone attack damaged the Euro+ complex at the Moscow refinery. The complex, which includes an ELOU-AVT-6 primary oil-processing unit, was commissioned in 2020 at a cost of 98 billion rubles.
ELOU-AVT is an integrated processing unit in which crude oil undergoes atmospheric and vacuum distillation after desalting. A typical configuration includes an electrical desalting unit, an atmospheric distillation unit, and a vacuum distillation unit, often along with gasoline stabilization and fractionation units. Most of these components are available from Chinese suppliers, albeit in smaller capacities than the original equipment. A search for “atmospheric distillation column,” for example, returns numerous offers. An atmospheric distillation unit can also be ordered separately from China, although available prices are only rough estimates.
“The Russia factor for Chinese equipment is four,” one industry source told The Insider, explaining why equipment repairs are becoming more expensive. In other words, Chinese equipment delivered to Russia costs four times the price quoted on a website or in a catalog. Meanwhile, European equipment routed through China is prohibitively expensive and economically viable only for specialized items that cannot be sourced elsewhere.
The cost of Chinese equipment comparable to that used at the Moscow refinery can be estimated from several international projects involving Chinese contractors. In 2016–2017, China Petroleum Engineering & Construction Corporation (CPECC) modernized an atmospheric distillation unit at an Algerian refinery under a contract worth $408 million (approximately 23 billion rubles). The engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) contract covered the refurbishment of the atmospheric distillation unit, installation of a naphtha hydrotreating unit, and construction of a new control room.
At the Moscow refinery in Kapotnya, similar processes are part of the Euro+ complex: atmospheric and vacuum distillation in an ELOU-AVT-6 unit with an annual capacity of 6.6 million tons, as well as diesel fuel and naphtha hydrotreating. The Kapotnya refinery also has a unit for recovering sulfur from hydrogen sulfide, which was not included in the Algerian project.
A larger example is Kuwait’s Al-Zour refinery, which far exceeds the Moscow refinery in capacity. Its main processing units, including the atmospheric and vacuum distillation facilities, were built by China’s Sinopec Engineering in a consortium with Spain’s Técnicas Reunidas and South Korea’s Hanwha. The lump-sum turnkey (LSTK) contract ran from 2015 to 2019 and was worth $4.1 billion (equivalent to 265 billion rubles at the Central Bank’s average annual exchange rate). In addition to atmospheric and vacuum distillation and hydrotreating, the Kuwaiti project includes vacuum gas oil hydrocracking and a large elemental sulfur recovery unit. Similar facilities are also part of the Moscow refinery.
Another benchmark is China’s Zhongke refinery, with an annual capacity of 10 million tons. Built between 2017 and 2020, its first phase cost approximately $5.6 billion (around 360 billion rubles). Alongside atmospheric and vacuum distillation, it includes fluid catalytic cracking, hydrocracking, and an aromatics complex, as does the Moscow refinery.
However, an ELOU-AVT-6 unit cannot simply be bought off the shelf. Such facilities are not sold as finished products on the open market; they must be designed and built or reconstructed for a specific refinery. Publicly available figures offer only rough estimates for comparable units. In 2012, construction of a new ELOU-AVT-6 unit was estimated at 8.3 billion rubles. In Azerbaijan, dismantling and installing an operating ELOU-AVT unit with one-third the capacity cost $75–80 million in 2018, (equivalent to approximately 6–7 billion rubles at the time). In Russia, contracts for building new ELOU-AVT units comparable in capacity to the Azerbaijani facility were estimated at 14 billion rubles in 2017.
An ELOU-AVT-6 unit cannot simply be bought off the shelf: each must be built for a specific refinery. The price includes design, manufacturing and installation, and now runs to hundreds of billions of rubles
In other words, Chinese equipment for facilities comparable to those at the Moscow refinery can cost anywhere from several hundred million dollars to several billion dollars for an entire integrated refinery, depending on its scale and the range of secondary processing units.
The total cost of delivering equipment from China to Russia is three to four times the Chinese price, once logistics, customs duties, adaptation to Russian standards, and intermediaries’ margins are included. Repairs will therefore cost at least 25 billion rubles, with the upper end potentially reaching half a trillion rubles after markups.
The cost of the fuel shortage
Unfortunately, the full impact on the fuel market is difficult to assess. Rosstat has not published gasoline and diesel production data since May 29, 2024, leaving experts to guess. The most impressionistic approach is to look at gas stations — the length of queues and the level of tension among those waiting. But this is no basis for a serious assessment.
In early July, Ukraine’s General Staff put the share of affected refining capacity at 42.74%. The Financial Times estimated that by the end of July, 45% of capacity was nominally offline, with more than 30% actually idle. Refining output had fallen to 25–30% below normal levels. Alexander Shokhin, head of the Russian Union of Industrialists and Entrepreneurs, estimated the losses at 25–30%.
Experts broadly agree that Russian oil refining has fallen to 3.8–4.2 million barrels per day, down from 5.3–5.5 million barrels per day in 2024–2025 — a drop of 20–25%. The International Energy Agency forecasts a similar level of 4 million barrels per day. In September, it lowered its baseline forecast for the next 18 months.
Even an accurate estimate of lost refining output, however, does not tell us how much consumption has changed. That is crucial to assessing the indirect damage caused by the attacks. Short-term shortages can be partly offset by drawing on reserves, importing fuel, rerouting supplies, or increasing output at other refineries. The economic impact must therefore also be assessed from another angle: transport activity.
Sergei Vakulenko, an expert at the Berlin-based Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center, proposed using traffic accident statistics to gauge the severity of the fuel crisis, reasoning that they reflect the intensity of road traffic. His model showed that the number of accidents in July 2026 was 7.9% below the expected level, while the preliminary figure for August was 12.4% lower. The decline was particularly pronounced in more rural areas. Allowing for subsequent revisions to the data, Vakulenko estimated that gasoline consumption fell by 7.5–10% in August.
Payments by heavy trucks offer another indirect indicator. The Platon system charges vehicles weighing more than 12 metric tons a per-kilometer fee on federal highways, excluding toll roads. Monthly payments can be reconstructed from the operator’s reports by comparing the cumulative toll collections over time. (However, one adjustment is necessary, as the rate was 3.34 rubles per kilometer in 2025 but rose to 5.19 rubles in 2026.)
Using this method, The Insider calculated that between Aug. 15 and Sept. 15, 2026, truckers paid for 1.93 billion notional kilometers of travel, down from 2.4 billion a year earlier — a decline of about 20%.
Platon toll collections from August 15 to September 15 indicate that truck mileage fell by 20% year on year
A drop recorded over a single month is not enough to draw sweeping conclusions. But even if only one in ten trucks was taken off the road (rather than one in five), or all trucks kept running but traveled 20% fewer kilometers, the figures still point to a negative economic impact. After all, road freight is critical to the Russian economy.
As Putin himself said on Oct. 1: “Ukrainian forces began striking refineries and openly declared their goal: to damage our economy. Did they achieve it? Partly. By our estimates, we lost about 1% of GDP.” Notably, Putin did not specify the period covered by his estimate, but if he meant annual GDP, then the figure would be 232 trillion rubles, according to Finance Ministry projections. If true, that would put the losses from all the attacks at 2.32 trillion rubles — slightly more than a third of the projected 2026 budget deficit of 7.3 trillion rubles, and more than half the remaining liquid assets of Russia’s National Wealth Fund, which stood at 4 trillion rubles on Sept. 1.
Putin acknowledged that strikes on oil refineries had cost the Russian economy roughly 1% of GDP, but did not specify that this amounted to more than 2 trillion rubles
The estimate presumably includes destroyed property, repair costs, and losses caused by refinery disruptions — such as downtime, higher supply costs, and losses at businesses affected by fuel shortages. If Putin was referring to the current year, about 50 successful attacks on refineries were recorded in the first half of 2026, according to The Insider, followed by roughly the same number in July–September. That would put the average cost of each of the 100 successful strikes at 23 billion rubles (though this remains a very rough estimate based on an interpretation of figures released by the Kremlin).
Marketplaces: Goods burn, obligations remain
Russia’s retail sales totaled 61 trillion rubles in 2025. Though not a core economic sector, retail is just as vital to everyday life as the availability of fuel at filling stations. Alexander Maslennikov, deputy secretary of Russia’s Security Council, described the economic impact of strikes on warehouses belonging to the Wildberries online marketplace as “very limited” and “symbolic.” He acknowledged, however, that the attacks cause localized economic losses and affect small businesses.
The direct damage to the retail sector from strikes on Wildberries warehouses consists of the value of destroyed goods and damage to the warehouse infrastructure itself. Wildberries operates warehouses of varying sizes, and the Pareto principle applies to e-commerce too: 20% of products generate 80% of profits. In other words, 20% of the goods destroyed could account for 80% of the losses. Even so, some rough estimates of the damage are already available.
Following attacks on warehouses in Elektrostal (250,000 square meters) and Kotovsk (108,000 square meters), Kommersant reported that the cost of rebuilding the logistics complexes would range from just over 20 billion to 35.8 billion rubles. The variation reflects differing estimates of construction costs from industry sources, ranging from 60,000 to 100,000 rubles per square meter. The midpoint is 80,000 rubles per square meter, a useful benchmark for estimating damage from future attacks.
Estimating the value of goods destroyed by fire is even more speculative. Although products vary widely in price, we can assume that warehouses contain a roughly equal mix of cheap and expensive goods. On that basis, we can estimate the average value of goods destroyed per square meter. Ideally, we would use cubic meters, but warehouse capacity is not reported in those terms. Reports on fires also measure the affected buildings by floor area, not volume.
The value of goods destroyed in the fires in Elektrostal and Kotovsk was estimated at 150–170 billion rubles across a combined area of 360,000 square meters. That works out to an average of 444,000 rubles per square meter. In the attacks on warehouses in Krasnodar (150,000 square meters) and Nevinnomyssk (100,000 square meters), the value of destroyed goods was estimated at 100–120 billion rubles. That likewise comes to around 440,000 rubles’ worth of goods per square meter.
The average value of goods destroyed in fires at Wildberries warehouses is around 440,000 rubles per square meter, based on media reports
Other losses must also be considered. Every day that a distribution center remains out of operation costs tens of thousands of sellers when it comes to lost revenue, and it can take weeks for goods to be unblocked after an attack. Meanwhile, entrepreneurs’ working capital remains tied up and loan interest continues to accrue. Many lack financial reserves and are forced either to operate in the informal economy or shut down. Losing inventory depletes sellers’ working capital, as they must buy new stock to resume trading.
Even when insurance covers part of the losses, the wait for compensation itself represents a direct cost. Disputes between sellers and marketplaces are consequently increasing. According to SPARK, between July 15 and Sept. 15, Wildberries was named as the defendant in 599 new lawsuits, up 53.6% from the same period in 2025. Competitor Ozon’s main legal entity faced 236 new cases, more than twice as many as a year earlier.
For the government, this is a direct blow to the tax base, as the Finance Ministry loses VAT and corporate income tax revenue from an entire sector. If sellers’ lost revenue amounts to 445–508 billion rubles, the resulting tax losses can be estimated at 10–30 billion rubles. For sellers under the general tax regime, corporate income tax is calculated on profit margins of 15–25%, implying losses of 13–25 billion rubles.
Under the simplified tax regime, sellers pay 6% of their total revenue, which would mean tax losses of 26.7–30.5 billion rubles. A realistic estimate of the government’s one-off revenue losses is therefore 13–30 billion rubles. The lower end represents corporate income tax on a 15% margin applied to 445 billion rubles, while the upper end is the 6% simplified tax on 508 billion rubles. The actual mix of tax regimes could shift the estimate, but it provides a useful benchmark.
An alternative estimate, based on data from The Moscow Times, suggests even greater losses. According to the publication, Wildberries’ turnover has already fallen by a quarter due to sellers leaving the platform. With annual turnover of 6.1 trillion rubles, that implies 1.5 trillion rubles in lost revenue. VAT alone on that amount, at 20%, would total 300 billion rubles, excluding corporate income tax and taxes paid by sellers.
Moreover, a report by the Center for Tax Policy and the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Institute of Economic Forecasting estimates that the government could lose 440–690 billion rubles in marketplace-related tax revenue in 2026 because of the way these platforms operate. The attacks are only exacerbating this trend.
These are one-off losses, however. The long-term impact is more serious: depleted working capital will force some sellers out of business. Our calculations suggest that the loss of just 10% of active sellers would reduce annual tax revenue by 35–50 billion rubles and social insurance contributions by another 7–10 billion rubles. We assume that 10% of sellers account for roughly 10% of turnover — about 610 billion rubles out of 6.1 trillion. At a 6% simplified tax rate, that would mean 36.6 billion rubles in lost tax revenue. Social insurance contributions, normally around 30% of payroll, would add another 7–10 billion rubles, (although the exact amount is difficult to estimate).
The actual range could be wider depending on the mix of tax regimes, but we use this as a working estimate. In reality, the loss of working capital might force out 5% or 20% of sellers rather than 10%, significantly changing the outcome.
In any event, attacks on warehouses, like those on oil refineries, have also begun to fuel inflation. Prices on marketplaces rose by 10–30% within days of the attacks, and gasoline prices increased by 16.5% between January and August 2026 compared with the same period in 2025, according to Rosstat data. The year-on-year increase in August was 25%. Insurance payouts to businesses rose by a third in the first half of 2026, according to RBC. Higher insurance premiums will also feed through into prices over time.
Insurers are lowering their liability limits, and some risks are no longer covered at all. The loss ratio in terrorism insurance has exceeded 100%. Market rates for terrorism and sabotage insurance have risen tenfold over the past four years, according to Energogarant. Businesses are also rethinking their investment plans: why build a new production facility if a single attack could put it out of operation?
“Yandex”: The Ukrainian Armed Forces will find everything
Three of Yandex’s key data centers came under attack between Oct. 8 and 11. All three of the company’s supercomputers were housed at these facilities, with a combined computing power of 50.36 petaflops. Two of them — Lyapunov and Chervonenkis (the most powerful) — were located at the data center in Sasovo, Ryazan Region. “We cannot yet confirm that the equipment at the Sasovo data center can be restored,” Yandex said, warning that some services might become unavailable to users. Damage to the supercomputers would also affect the development of YandexGPT, the company’s neural network, which uses them for training.
The third supercomputer, Galushkin, was housed at the Vladimir data center, which shut down completely following a drone attack on the night of Oct. 11. Yandex also described its remaining resources as unstable and warned customers that its cloud platform was operating in emergency mode.
All of Yandex’s supercomputers may have been damaged. There is no reliable confirmation, but neither is there evidence to the contrary
Restoration could take up to six months. Sanctions restricting supplies of high-tech equipment will make repairs more difficult and expensive. The supercomputers ran on chips made by the U.S. company Nvidia, and the scale of the damage has yet to be officially assessed. Yandex spent 6 billion rubles building the Sasovo data center in 2011 and invested another 700 million rubles in its renovation ten years later, according to TASS. Investment in the Vladimir data center was expected to total around 9 billion rubles, according to Vladimirskie Vedomosti.
Many businesses, in Russia and abroad, rely on Yandex services hosted primarily at these three data centers. Cascading internet outages following the latest attack on Oct. 11 affected at least six countries, The Insider found. In Russia, two federal information systems — VetIS and Saturn, responsible for veterinary oversight and pesticide traceability — were switched to emergency mode. Russia’s Federal Service for Veterinary and Phytosanitary Surveillance attributed the disruption to a power outage in Vladimir Region.
Sources in the logistics industry reported that electronic waybills had stopped working for many companies. Their use had only just become mandatory. “A couple more strikes like this, and we’ll be back to paper,” one source said. T-Bank, ticketing services, online stores and cinemas, Russian Railways, and educational platforms also experienced problems.
The Russian economy rests on two main pillars: raw-material exports, which have funded the state budget, and domestic consumption, which generates demand and jobs. Drone strikes have hit both at once. The Ukrainian Armed Forces are targeting government revenue and consumer demand simultaneously, straining an economic model accustomed to offsetting structural problems through high oil prices, fast-turnover retail, or IT businesses whose services keep the system running efficiently and flexibly.

Russia attacked the railway in five regions, more than 100 trains are delayed
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
08:59:06 EEST
14:59:06 KST

Russia attacked the railway in five regions, more than 100 trains are delayed
Kyiv • UNN
As a result of the overnight strikes, railway infrastructure was damaged in five regions. There were no casualties; more than 100 trains are delayed.
Russia launched strikes on the railway in five regions of Ukraine during the night of October 14. Material losses are substantial. This was reported by Oleksandr Pertsovskyi, Chairman of the Management Board of the joint-stock company "Ukrzaliznytsia," on Facebook on Wednesday, UNN writes.
Another night of intense strikes on railway facilities. The enemy is trying to destroy everything it can reach: locomotive and carriage depots, repair enterprises, railway stations and terminals, not to mention rolling stock. This night, a massive wave of strikes on the railway covered the Kharkiv, Kyiv, Vinnytsia, Khmelnytskyi and Ternopil regions
According to the head of UZ, "they knocked out the power supply, our specialists restored it immediately, blocked key routes because of oversized vehicles—we organized alternatives and ensured passage."

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Tainan will begin removing railway crossings and related structures on Sunday, a day after the city's underground railway service is scheduled to begin.
Authorities will work to reconnect roads and develop greenways along a former 8.23-kilometer railway corridor. The project involves 17 rail crossing facilities, including eight street-level crossings, three vehicular overpasses, four underpasses, and two railway bridges or culverts, Tainan City government said Wednesday, per CNA.
Tainan's Bureau of Transportation said street-level crossings would be prioritized because their removal mainly involves dismantling tracks and leveling road surfaces. Removal of the Kaiyuan Road crossing will begin on Sunday and will include road paving and new traffic markings.
Work on the Dongfeng Road level crossing is expected to begin after Nov. 17. Construction will take place in three phases, with partial road closures and adjustments to traffic space intended to maintain vehicle access, per a press release.
Other demolition work includes a steel bridge on Changrong Road, Dongmen overpass, and Fulian underpass. The city said work would proceed after traffic-control plans receive the necessary approvals and would be coordinated with a broader greenway project.
The first phase of the underground railway project is scheduled to begin service on Saturday, moving trains below ground through central Tainan. The project is intended to improve connections between neighborhoods on either side of the tracks.

"Ukraine needs air defense, interceptors and reliable early warnings. Every minute of warning can give someone a chance to survive," she added.
The attack came days after Trump announced a deal allowing Russian diesel exports, following a conversation with Russian President Vladimir Putin on October 9.
Trump has said that, under the deal, the United States would immediately import 300,000 metric tons of Russian diesel, with millions more expected to follow.
The move has sparked criticism from European allies and from Democrats and Republicans, who warned it could embolden Putin to continue his war against Ukraine.
In a letter to Trump, a bipartisan group of 12 senators urged him to withdraw from the diesel deal with Putin, calling it "a gift to our adversary" and "a betrayal of our Allies."
"Granting Moscow the ability to sell Russian diesel freely in global markets damages American security interests and is a betrayal of the people of Ukraine," the senators wrote in the letter.
Meanwhile, former Ukrainian President Viktor Yushchenko addressed an open letter to Trump criticizing his deal with Putin on diesel fuel.

Rare earths company could be nationalised as China-linked investors fail to divest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
05:54:38 UTC
14:54:38 KST

Rare earths company could be nationalised as China-linked investors fail to divest
In short:
China-linked investors are defying federal government orders to divest from a Perth-based rare earths company.
Northern Minerals is seen as a key player in efforts by both the US and Australia to break China's stranglehold on the critical minerals supply chain.
What's next?
Resources Minister Madeleine King said "one option" is to nationalise the company, given the strategic national interest.
The Resources Minister Madeleine King says nationalising a Perth-based heavy rare earths company is an "option" for the government as China-linked investors continue to defy orders to divest from the strategically sensitive miner.
In May, federal Treasurer Jim Chalmers ordered six investors which hold around 17 per cent of Northern Minerals to divest by July 2 from the company, which is developing the Browns Range project in Western Australia's east Kimberley region.
But Northern Minerals told the ASX later in July that the companies still held most of the shares they had been ordered to sell.
Northern Minerals is seen as a key player in efforts by both the US and Australia to break China's stranglehold on the critical minerals supply chain and is already on track for about $500 million in funding from the Export Import Bank of the United States.
Madeleine King told the National Press Club on Wednesday that the uncertainty was "holding up" the development of the project, which is vital to developing alternative sources of dysprosium and terbium, critical minerals which are used in both renewable energy infrastructure and advanced military technology.
"It is one of the most significant heavy rare earth deposits on the face of the Earth, so it means a lot to us and our national interest and national security,"
she said.
The minister also appeared to leave the door open to nationalisation when asked if the government would be willing to take that step — although she stressed that no decisions had yet been made.
"I guess it is one option, but I wouldn't want to advance on any decision we're making there," she said.
She also appeared to confirm that the companies had failed to pay the fines imposed by the federal government for non-compliance.
Ms King said the government was "very active knowing what is going on" when it came to the project, and took aim at the China-linked investors refusing to sell, saying "failure to follow through or pay respects, quite frankly, to Australian government decisions, is a very serious matter we are looking at".
"There have been a number of decisions made by FIRB [the Foreign Investment Review Board] but also divestment decisions as well, and that has not been done by those who hold those shares," she said.
"That's not good."
The comments from the minister come after a rolling series of government interventions designed at protecting the company from Chinese entities stalking it.
In 2023, Mr Chalmers blocked a Chinese-linked investor Yuxiao Fund from boosting its stake in the company, and in 2025 he ordered another five companies linked to China to divest from it.
One of those Chinese investors launched an unsuccessful bid earlier this year to topple the company's leadership.
And at least some of the Chinese companies blocked from Northern Minerals seem to have made multiple efforts to circumvent federal government orders to divest from the company.
Earlier this year the Foreign Investment Review Board wrote to Northern Minerals, saying three of the blocked investors last year had simply transferred their shares to Hong Kong Ying Tak Ltd, one of the six companies ordered to divest earlier this year.
The Resources Minister said the saga highlighted the need for the federal government to press on with its review of foreign investment laws, which is due to wrap up next year.
The ABC has approached Northern Minerals for comment.

A US federal judge has ordered the White House to maintain press credentials for journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico while their lawsuit challenging a ban proceeds.
US District Judge Timothy Kelly granted the news outlets’ request for a preliminary injunction on Tuesday.
The order said the administration “shall not execute, implement or enforce the September 18, 2026 decision to revoke the White House ‘hard pass’ press credentials held by employees of CNN, MS NOW and POLITICO”.
The ruling maintains “the status quo since the Court’s entry of a temporary restraining order on September 24, 2026”, the order said.
US President Donald Trump announced on September 18 that he was barring journalists from the three outlets from the White House, accusing them of spreading “fake news”.
Three days later, the outlets filed a lawsuit arguing that the ban violated the First and Fifth Amendments to the US Constitution, which protect press freedom and due process, among other rights.
Kelly subsequently issued a temporary restraining order requiring the administration to reinstate the journalists’ press credentials while the legal challenge continued.

Sudan cannot afford to dismiss a chance for dialogue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
05:51:09 UTC
14:51:09 KST

Sudan cannot afford to dismiss a chance for dialogue
A new initiative faces serious questions about military influence, but its critics should not write it off prematurely.
More than three years into the war between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), Sudan is desperately in need of a political settlement. The fighting has caused immense suffering, and a military solution alone cannot rebuild the state or reunify its fractured society. Under such circumstances, any effort aimed at encouraging Sudanese-Sudanese dialogue deserves serious consideration rather than outright rejection.
In August, a self-appointed committee of 19 Sudanese public figures, chaired by Ahfad University President Qasim Badri, launched an initiative to prepare the ground for national dialogue inside Sudan. Its members had earlier met SAF chief General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and called for legal restrictions on opposition politicians to be lifted. The authorities subsequently issued a decree to drop certain politically motivated charges against Sudanese abroad returning for dialogue and grant participants temporary legal protections. These are limited but important confidence-building measures.
The initiative has nevertheless faced strong opposition. The civilian coalition Sumoud, led by former Prime Minister Abdalla Hamdok, and Ta’sis, an alliance that includes the RSF, have opposed the proposed internal dialogue. They question its independence and warn that holding talks in army-controlled areas could legitimise al-Burhan’s authority and entrench the country’s divisions. These concerns are legitimate and deserve serious attention. But the committee says it is not seeking to negotiate Sudan’s future or determine the agenda of a national dialogue. Its role is to help create the conditions for Sudanese political actors to engage one another directly. The question is whether it can fulfil that role without allowing one side of the conflict to dominate the process. Dismissing the initiative before it has had an opportunity to demonstrate its value would be premature.
The country’s political actors and civil society organisations remain deeply divided, previous mediation efforts have faltered, and the war continues to make comprehensive political engagement increasingly difficult. The committee’s initiative is an attempt to break the deadlock. Efforts to prepare for political dialogue should not be postponed until the fighting stops. Securing a ceasefire and ensuring humanitarian access are urgent priorities, but preparations for political dialogue can proceed alongside efforts to achieve them.
The committee’s members were not elected, and they do not represent every political constituency. Yet the committee’s legitimacy cannot be judged solely by how it was created. It must also be judged by whether it can help bring a broader range of political actors into a national dialogue.
Good intentions alone cannot resolve concerns about credibility. Political dialogue can succeed only if participants believe the process is fair and independent. The legitimacy required to facilitate a political opening is not necessarily the same as that required to negotiate a national settlement. But even a preparatory initiative must earn the trust of those it seeks to bring together.
The committee’s meeting with al-Burhan was a practical necessity. As army chief and head of the Sovereignty Council, he was in a position to respond to the committee’s demands for legal protections. Engaging with al-Burhan does not in itself amount to an endorsement of his authority. But if the initiative becomes too closely associated with the army, other political actors may view it as an extension of al-Burhan’s political agenda rather than an independent facilitator. The committee must therefore demonstrate that its engagement extends beyond the military authorities and that it is prepared to work with political forces that oppose them.
The initiative was launched in Khartoum, which is under army control. This raises a genuine concern about whether a process beginning in territory controlled by one side of the war can attract the confidence of political forces across the country. A national dialogue cannot be confined to one geographical or political constituency. Entire regions have experienced different realities of war, governance, displacement and insecurity. The committee must find ways to reach those living outside army-controlled areas, including Sudanese displaced by the fighting, and ensure they can participate freely and without intimidation.
Sumoud and Ta’sis’s decision to reject the initiative does not automatically invalidate the process. Their concerns deserve consideration, but outright rejection at this early stage risks closing off an opportunity for political engagement. At the same time, their absence matters. Sudan’s crisis is too deep and complex to be addressed by any single political current. The committee cannot expect every stakeholder to endorse its initiative immediately, but it must create conditions that persuade reluctant actors to participate. If it fails to do so, the initiative itself will have failed.
The African Union Commission and the Arab League have also welcomed the initiative, providing an important measure of regional support. Their endorsement lends weight to the effort to revive Sudanese-led political dialogue, although external backing cannot substitute for the confidence of Sudan’s own political forces.
The committee’s initiative should therefore be judged without excessive optimism or automatic suspicion. The legal measures announced following its engagement with al-Burhan are an encouraging first step, but the real test lies ahead. Does it help remove legal and political obstacles facing opposition actors in practice, not just on paper? Can it win the confidence of those who have rejected it? Can it ensure that Sudanese across the country’s political and geographical divides have an opportunity to participate freely?
What is clear, however, is that Sudan’s crisis will ultimately require Sudanese actors with profoundly different visions of the country’s future to sit together and engage one another politically. No committee can do that on their behalf. No external actor can do it for them. At best, a preparatory initiative can help create the conditions under which such engagement becomes possible. The concerns raised by its critics should not be dismissed, but neither should they be grounds for rejecting the initiative before it has had an opportunity to address them. Those who have rejected it should remain open to reconsidering their position if the committee demonstrates that it can build an independent and inclusive process. If it succeeds, it will have rendered an important national service.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

Israel returns 22 artifacts to Greece in first antiquities repatriation between Jerusalem, Athens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
05:49:11 UTC
14:49:11 KST

Israel on Tuesday returned a collection of 22 artifacts illegally removed from Greece, in the first repatriation of its kind between the two countries, as Athens renews its push to recover illegally taken and stolen antiquities from around the world.
Among the artifacts returned are fifteen ancient Attic vessels, six vases from Corinthian workshops, and one bronze statue of a female figure, all dating to between the 8th and 4th century BCE.
Of the Attic vessels, eleven are black-and-white, three are red-and-white, and one is ambergris, dating to the ancient and classical periods. The six Corinthian vases date to the ancient period, while the authenticity of the bronze female statuette requires further investigation.
The antiquities had been seized in 2020 during a joint investigation into illegal antiquities trafficking conducted by the IAA's Theft Prevention Unit, Israel Police, and the Israel Tax Authority. As part of the operation, the forces raided a gallery, warehouses and apartments in the Gush Dan area, where thousands of illegally acquired archaeological items from Israel and around the world were found.
They were officially returned in a Tuesday handover ceremony at the National Archaeological Museum in Athens, attended by Greek Culture Minister Lina Mendoni, Israeli Ambassador to Greece Pninat Yanay, and Israel Antiquities Authority's (IAA) Theft Prevention Unit Amir Ganor.
Mendoni said Israel's return of the 22 antiquities is especially significant, "marking the first time Israel has returned antiquities to Greece, serving as the starting point for closer cooperation between the two countries in the protection of cultural heritage."
Combating illegal antiquities trade
"This return confirms that cooperation between states can make a substantial contribution to combating the illicit trade in antiquities," she stated, noting that "The return of any cultural asset to its place of origin carries a broader symbolic and ethical dimension. It serves as a reminder that the protection of cultural heritage is a collective responsibility."
"I am confident that the cooperation between Greece and Israel will continue to yield tangible results in the safeguarding of cultural heritage."
In her own speech at the ceremony, Yanay explained that "Antiquities are much more than historical objects."
"They are moments from the past, frozen in time through art. They tell us who the people who created them were, what they believed in, how they lived, and remind us how deeply the past remains part of who we are today."
"For more than 2,000 years, these ancient objects have witnessed the rise and fall of empires, wars, revolutions, and enormous changes in our world. And through it all, they have survived," she said.
Becoming links in the chains between generations
"This celebration is not only about returning antiquities to their rightful home. It is also a celebration of something much greater and deeper: the special, strong, and profound friendship between the State of Israel and Greece," she wrote.
"Two modern states, two ancient nations, and two great civilizations that deeply understand the meaning of history, the importance of heritage, and the responsibility to preserve it for future generations. These antiquities belong to Greece’s past. Today, through their return, they also become part of the shared future of Israel and Greece."
'"Let us try to imagine a child looking at one of these ancient vessels today and feeling a spark of wonder," added Yanay. "They see what another child might have seen and felt 2,000 years ago, and thus become another link in the chain of generations that had been broken."
"For me, there is also something deeply moving in the thought that I have the privilege, as Ambassador of Israel, of placing this ancient object into your capable hands, and that my country had the honor of contributing to this significant moment and mission."
"The illegal trade in antiquities knows no borders, neither the boundaries of the law nor the borders between countries,” said Ganor. “Antiquities that are looted in one country find their way to another, causing irreversible damage to the cultural heritage of the country of origin."
"The illegal trade in antiquities serves as a cover for the financing of terrorism and organized crime, and it serves as a means of money laundering. Cutting off smuggling chains and preventing continued illegal profiting on the back of antiquities helps to thwart and prevent various types of criminal activity, and certainly helps to protect cultural heritage assets.”
Heritage Minister Amichai Eliyahu added that "The State of Israel is well aware of the deep connection between a people and its heritage, and the importance of preserving the historical evidence that tells its story."
"The return of these antiquities to Greece expresses our commitment to protect cultural heritage assets, and to act resolutely against the illegal trade in antiquities, wherever it takes place."
He continued, congratulated the IAA and both Greek and Israeli law enforcement agencies for their actions that led to the return of the artifacts.
"The strengthening cooperation between the countries expresses a shared responsibility to preserve the treasures of the past, for the sake of future generations," he said.
Israel, Greece expected to sign heritage MoU
As result of the cooperation between the IAA's Theft Prevention Unit and the Greek Antiquities Police in this case, a joint international enforcement workshop was held for representatives of the two units last month.
During the workshop, the two units discussed the possibility of expanding information sharing, identify items suspected of being looted, and trace antiquities trade routes.
In her remarks at the handover ceremony, Mendoni noted that during her visit to Jerusalem in March 2025, she discussed the expansion of cultural cooperation between Israel and Greece with Culture and Sports Minister Miki Zohar.
According to Mendoni, the return of these antiquities is a practical expression of the commitment that the two ministers discussed at their meeting. As well, a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) is expected to be signed between the countries, which will anchor their cooperation in the field of protecting cultural heritage assets.

Gigantic prehistoric snake discovered in India may have been one of the largest ever
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
05:44:39 UTC
14:44:39 KST

Gigantic prehistoric snake discovered in India may have been one of the largest ever
- Date:
- October 14, 2026
- Source:
- Scientific Reports
- Summary:
- A massive prehistoric snake discovered in India may have rivaled the largest snake ever known. Called Vasuki indicus, the 47-million-year-old giant could have reached up to 50 feet long, making it comparable to the legendary Titanoboa. Scientists believe its enormous body made it a slow-moving ambush predator, similar to a modern anaconda.
- Share:
A colossal prehistoric snake that lived in India about 47 million years ago may have been one of the largest snakes ever to exist. Known as Vasuki indicus, the ancient reptile could have reached an extraordinary 15.2 meters (50 feet) in length, putting it in the same league as Titanoboa, the enormous extinct snake long regarded as the largest ever discovered.
The remarkable discovery, described in 2024 in the journal Scientific Reports, came from fossils unearthed in Gujarat, western India. Researchers estimate that Vasuki measured between 10.9 and 15.2 meters (36 and 50 feet) long, although its exact size remains uncertain. Its enormous body and unusual evolutionary history offer a glimpse into a time when giant snakes inhabited the warm, tropical landscapes of ancient India.
Giant Snake Fossils Unearthed in India
Paleontologists Debajit Datta and Sunil Bajpai of the Indian Institute of Technology Roorkee identified the species from fossils recovered at the Panandhro Lignite Mine in Kutch, Gujarat. The remains date to the Middle Eocene, a period roughly 47 million years ago when Earth's climate was considerably warmer than it is today.
The researchers examined 27 fossilized vertebrae, the individual bones that make up a snake's backbone. Many were remarkably well preserved, and some remained connected in their original arrangement. The bones appear to have belonged to a fully grown animal.
The species was named Vasuki indicus in honor of Vasuki, the mythical serpent associated with the Hindu deity Shiva, who is traditionally depicted with the snake wrapped around his neck. The second part of the name refers to India, where the fossils were discovered.
How Big Was This Prehistoric Snake?
Although the scientists did not recover a complete skeleton, the preserved backbone provides important clues about the snake's enormous proportions.
Individual vertebrae measured between 37.5 and 62.7 millimeters (1.48 and 2.47 inches) long and between 62.4 and 111.4 millimeters (2.46 and 4.39 inches) wide. Their unusually broad shape suggests that Vasuki possessed a thick, cylindrical body capable of supporting tremendous weight.
To estimate its total length, the researchers compared the fossilized bones with vertebrae from living snakes whose body lengths are known. Two different methods produced estimates ranging from 10.9 to 12.2 meters (36 to 40 feet) and 14.5 to 15.2 meters (48 to 50 feet).
Those measurements place Vasuki among the largest snakes ever identified. Its estimated length rivals that of Titanoboa, the giant snake that inhabited what is now Colombia approximately 60 million years ago and is thought to have reached around 13 meters (43 feet).
However, the researchers caution that their calculations involve considerable uncertainty. Different methods can produce substantially different estimates, particularly when scientists must reconstruct an extinct animal using an incomplete backbone. It remains unclear whether Vasuki actually exceeded Titanoboa in length.
A Massive Predator That Likely Hunted by Ambush
Despite its intimidating size, Vasuki probably was not a particularly fast or agile hunter.
The researchers suggest that its enormous body and distinctive vertebral structure would have favored relatively slow movement. Rather than actively chasing prey, the snake may have relied on ambush tactics, remaining concealed until another animal came within striking distance.
Its hunting behavior could have resembled that of modern anacondas and large pythons, which can overpower prey through constriction. These snakes use their muscular bodies to tighten around captured animals, interfering with circulation until the prey dies.
Scientists suspect Vasuki may have hunted in a similar way, although its precise diet and hunting behavior cannot be determined from the surviving fossils.
Its anatomy also suggests that the snake may have spent much of its time on land or in shallow, swampy environments, rather than living exclusively in water. The ancient landscape surrounding the fossil site contained wetlands and marshes that could have provided suitable habitat for an enormous ambush predator.
Ancient India's Warm Climate May Have Helped Snakes Grow Enormous
The discovery also raises questions about why some prehistoric snakes reached sizes far beyond those of most species alive today.
During the Middle Eocene, the region where Vasuki lived experienced tropical conditions, with average temperatures estimated at approximately 28 degrees Celsius (82 degrees Fahrenheit).
Snakes are ectothermic animals, meaning they depend heavily on external sources of heat to regulate their body temperature. Warm environments can support the activity, digestion, and growth of large reptiles, potentially helping explain why exceptionally large snakes appeared during some of Earth's warmer periods.
However, temperature alone does not determine how large a snake can become. Food availability, suitable habitat, evolutionary history, and other environmental factors also influence body size.
A Lost Lineage of Giant Snakes That Spread Across Continents
Beyond its extraordinary size, Vasuki provides evidence of an ancient branch of snake evolution.
The species belonged to Madtsoiidae, an extinct family of snakes that survived for roughly 100 million years, from the Late Cretaceous to the Late Pleistocene. Members of this group occupied regions including India, Africa, Europe, South America, and Australia.
Unlike modern anacondas and pythons, Vasuki represented a separate evolutionary lineage within this long-extinct family.
The researchers found that its closest relatives included Madtsoia pisdurensis, a fossil snake from ancient India, and Gigantophis garstini, another large prehistoric snake known from North Africa.
These relationships suggest that a lineage of giant madtsoiid snakes originated on the Indian subcontinent before spreading into other parts of the world.
As India moved northward and collided with Asia around 50 million years ago, changing geographic connections may have allowed these snakes to disperse through southern Eurasia, including southern Europe, and eventually into Africa during the Eocene, approximately 56 to 34 million years ago.
Later Fossil Discoveries Reveal an Ancient World Filled With Snakes
Research published in 2025 has added important context to the discovery of Vasuki.
In a study published in the Journal of Paleontology, Datta and Bajpai described additional fossil snakes from Eocene deposits in western India. Their findings revealed a surprisingly diverse community of ancient reptiles, including aquatic snakes, another large member of the madtsoiid family, and other extinct snake groups.
Among the discoveries was Pterosphenus rannensis, an ancient aquatic snake species that adds to scientists' understanding of how these reptiles evolved and spread.
The researchers also identified another madtsoiid snake that appears to have shared a marshy environment with Vasuki. This suggests that the giant predator was part of a broader community of snakes occupying different ecological roles, rather than an isolated evolutionary oddity.
Evidence from the fossil deposits indicates that some of these snakes inhabited tidal environments, while others occupied swamps and marshes. Together, the discoveries paint a more detailed picture of the complex ecosystems that existed in India tens of millions of years ago.
What Modern Anacondas Reveal About Giant Snakes
Additional evidence about snake gigantism emerged from a separate 2025 study published in the Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology.
Researchers examining fossilized anaconda vertebrae from Venezuela found that these enormous snakes had already evolved large bodies by approximately 12.4 million years ago. Ancient anacondas reached estimated lengths of around 5.2 meters (17 feet), comparable to the size of many living anacondas.
The findings suggest that anacondas maintained their impressive size for millions of years, even as climates and ecosystems changed. They also show that prehistoric snakes did not necessarily grow larger simply because the planet was warmer.
Although anacondas are evolutionarily distinct from Vasuki, the research offers a useful comparison for understanding how different snake lineages became giants and adapted to their environments.
For Vasuki indicus, the full story remains incomplete. Its precise size, appearance, and behavior are still uncertain, but the fossil evidence establishes it as an extraordinary example of prehistoric gigantism.
Together with later discoveries from the same region, the ancient snake is helping scientists reconstruct a largely forgotten world in which massive serpents occupied the tropical landscapes of India.

- Debajit Datta, Sunil Bajpai. Fossil snakes from the Eocene of India: new material with comments on phylogenetic relations and biogeographic and paleoecological implications. Journal of Paleontology, 2025; 99 (2): 403 DOI: 10.1017/jpa.2025.10101

Global smartphone shipments have plummeted to their lowest level in 14 years
Kyiv • UNN
In the third quarter of 2026, smartphone shipments fell by 20% to their lowest level in 14 years. Samsung led the market with a 23% share.
The shortage of memory chips, which the technology press has dubbed "RAMageddon," continues to have a broad impact on the entire technology industry, and a new report shows that the smartphone market has just reached its lowest point in more than a decade. UNN reports this, citing 9to5Google.
Details
Counterpoint Research reports that global smartphone shipments fell by 20% in the third quarter of 2026, reaching their lowest level in 14 years. The last time smartphone shipments were this low was when Samsung released the Galaxy S3.
The decline affected not only overall shipment figures but also the market share held by major smartphone brands.
Chinese brands, including Xiaomi, Vivo, and Oppo, accounted for a smaller share of the overall market in the third quarter of 2026 compared with the same period a year earlier, while Samsung continued to hold the leading position with 23% of the overall market, and Apple held 22%, compared with 19% and 18%, respectively.
Counterpoint says that Samsung's overall shipments fell by only 3%, with the success of the Galaxy Z Fold 8 playing a major role in the company's performance this quarter. Meanwhile, a recent report claims that Samsung is currently not making a profit from selling Galaxy phones.
Meanwhile, Apple experienced a 22% year-over-year decline due to the absence of a standard iPhone 18. Oppo and Vivo declined by approximately 20%, while Xiaomi cut shipments by 30%.

Turkish police raid office of opposition TV channel, the broadcaster says

Turkey appoints trustee to run pro-opposition Halk TV amid opposition crackdown
ANKARA, Oct 14 - Turkish authorities appointed a government trustee to run pro-opposition broadcaster Halk TV, prosecutors said on Wednesday as police raided its Istanbul office, extending a crackdown on the opposition and prompting fresh concerns over media freedom.
The Istanbul Chief Prosecutor's Office said its financial crimes unit had conducted an investigation into Halk TV Chairman Cafer Mahiroglu over "bribery, tender-rigging, and laundering of assets derived from crime."
Prosecutors ordered the detention of 17 people, including Mahiroglu, and 11 have been detained, the statement said, with firms linked to Mahiroglu seized and the Savings Deposit Insurance Fund (TMSF) appointed as trustee.
Mahiroglu is currently outside Turkey and being sought by the authorities.
The channel's live broadcast was cut at 6:30 a.m. (0330 GMT), after which pre-recorded material began airing. "Hundreds of police" were inside and entry into the premises was not being permitted, it said on its website. A Halk TV programmer said negotiations with the trustee delegation to continue broadcasts had yielded no results.
The move comes days after Kemal Kilicdaroglu, the court-appointed chairman of Turkey's former main opposition Republican People's Party (CHP), publicly criticised Halk TV and Mahiroglu over its coverage. He said the CHP had complained to Turkey's RTUK television watchdog but no action was taken.
Kilicdaroglu lost the CHP leadership to Ozgur Ozel in 2023, but was reinstated by a court ruling in May amid an unprecedented legal crackdown on the opposition. He has refused to call new party elections, while his rhetoric has become more aligned with the government.
The CHP later criticised Wednesday's raid on Halk TV as a "shameful" example of "systematic pressure" on opposition media.
The European Parliament's Turkey rapporteur Nacho Sanchez Amor criticised the move on X, saying that the government was "not happy with controlling 90% of media" and was "aiming for the 100%".
"Amidst detentions of journalists & broad online censorship, freedom of media & expression will soon be just a memory."
CRACKDOWN ON PRESS FREEDOM
Wednesday's move makes Halk TV the fifth major Turkish news outlet to have a trustee appointed, following similar legal decisions for Flash TV, Eko Turk, Haberturk and Tele1.
Authorities have appointed trustees in recent years to take over many municipalities, previously seizing those run by pro-Kurdish opposition mayors in southeastern Turkey and more recently major municipalities - including Istanbul and its districts - won by the opposition, prompting some mayors to join President Tayyip Erdogan's ruling AK Party.
Rights groups and Western countries have criticised the government over its use of the judiciary, its record on rights, and its crackdown on press freedom in recent years as it establishes tighter control over mainstream media. Several opposition or independent outlets have experienced access bans, fines, and other restrictions.
The government says Turkey's judiciary is independent. It has not commented publicly on the latest moves against Halk TV.
Ozel, who now leads the main opposition New Party, condemned Wednesday's move, as did the pro-Kurdish opposition DEM Party.
"Dawn raid on a television channel, appointing a trustee — only dictators would do such a thing," Ozel said on X. "Those who appoint trustees to municipalities and trample the people's will have now appointed a trustee to Halk TV, watched by millions. Because THEY ARE IMPOTENT AND COWARDS!"
The raid on Halk TV came as Erdogan's biggest political rival, jailed Istanbul Mayor Ekrem Imamoglu, was expected to start his defence on Wednesday in a sweeping corruption trial of more than 400 defendants linked to the Istanbul municipality.
"On such a day, a trustee was appointed to Halk TV, one of the most-watched news channels in Turkey," Turkish Journalists' Union Chairman Gokhan Durmus told Reuters, adding Turkey was facing another "dark chapter" in terms of freedom of press and expression.
"It remains unclear what the fate of our 200 colleagues working inside (Halk TV) and its editorial line will be from now on." REUTERS

From Cairo to Tokyo: Can you guess these twin cities?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
05:40:18 UTC
14:40:18 KST

From Cairo to Tokyo: Can you guess these twin cities?
As a London borough moves to cut ties with Haifa, test your knowledge of the world’s twin cities.
Hackney, a borough in east London, is consulting residents until October 14 on whether to end its twinning with Haifa, Israel’s third-largest city, a link that dates back to 1968.
The Green Party-led council voted on July 28 to end the partnership in principle, citing its values and human rights commitments amid Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza. Councillors will make a final decision after the consultation and a review of the borough’s twinning policy.
What are twin cities?
Twin cities, also called sister cities, are places in different countries linked by formal friendship agreements. These relationships can support school exchanges, cultural events and civic visits, though many become inactive over time.
Can you guess which cities are twinned? Take our quiz below.
How twin cities began
Modern town twinning grew after World War II as a way to rebuild trust and foster peace. Coventry and Stalingrad (now Volgograd), both heavily bombed during the war, established a friendship link in 1944, often cited as the first modern city-twinning relationship.
The US city of St Paul and Japan’s Nagasaki established a sister-city partnership in 1955 to promote reconciliation after the atomic bombing of the latter in 1945. Cities have since formed links because of shared histories, similar roles as capitals or ports, or communities with roots in both places.
Why do cities cut ties?
Because twinning is often symbolic, ending a link can allow a council to make a statement. Several UK councils suspended or ended links with Russian cities after the 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
Prague’s relationship with Beijing also ended in 2019 amid a dispute involving Taiwan, after which the Czech Republic established a partnership with Taipei. Hackney’s proposal is the latest example of cities reassessing their international ties.

Speaking before Trump took the stage, Sullivan accused Peltola of planning to undermine Alaska’s oil and gas industry, which plays a major role in supporting the state’s economy even though production has declined since its peak in the late 1980s.
“Joe Biden, [Chuck] Schumer, their Democratic allies came after Alaska with a barrage of executive orders to shut down our state, kill jobs, drive up the cost of energy, and my opponent, Mary Peltola, not only did nothing to stop it, she enabled it,” Sullivan said.
In a statement, a spokesperson for Peltola’s campaign said the candidate “looks forward to working with President Trump to unleash Alaska energy and lower costs … when she’s elected to the United States Senate.”
“While Dan Sullivan continues to feel the fallout of his failed policies and support for the war in Iran, Mary spent the day talking with Alaskans … about how she will fight to lower their costs (and) take on DC corruption,” the spokesperson said in reference to Peltola’s campaign visit on Tuesday to Kotzebue, in north-west Alaska.
Peltola won a special election to the US House of Representatives in 2022 after the death of longtime Republican congressman Don Young, then a full term later that year. She was defeated in 2024 by Republican Nick Begich, who is seeking re-election this year.
Recent polls have the candidates neck-and-neck in a state that has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 2008.
