Jantar Mantar: What to know about Delhi's delisted protest site?
Jantar Mantar, in central Delhi, is an 18th century open-air astronomical observatory.
For over three decades, a stretch of road leading up to it was where Indians came to be heard, press their demands and hold those in power accountable. That was until last week when the Delhi Police delisted the iconic venue as a protest site.
What sparked the latest protests?
The move came days after a confrontation between thousands of police personnel and anti-government protesters led by India's Cockroach Janta Party (CJP).
The group, along with student organizations and activists, mobilized thousands to protest against a revision in electoral rolls which reportedly deleted 130 million voters.
While those deleted include dead and duplicate voters, critics argue the staggering number likely includes a vast number of eligible voters. India's poll body and the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party party have denied this.
Jantar Mantar has been the central rallying location for protesters demanding election Chief Gyanesh Kumar's resignation for overseeing the revision.
This is the same location that acted as a home base for the CJP-led youth protests in July over an exam scandal, which resulted in the removal of India's former education minister.
Why is delisting Jantar Mantar controversial?
Now, instead of Jantar Mantar, authorities have designated three alternative venues in Delhi. Campaigners argue those venues will reduce visibility and proximity to lawmakers as Jantar Mantar was surrounded by the nation's biggest institutions.
"Jantar Mantar is in the centre of the town, it is connected, it is next to parliament... it was a very important space for all protests," human rights activist Shabnam Hashmi told AFP. "This is nothing but a move to curb dissent," he said.
CJP leaders Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das were among about a dozen people who jumped barricades on Tuesday to enter the grounds of Jantar Mantar, despite the delisting a day earlier.
An Indian court has now sent Das and Ranka to five days in judicial custody over trespassing and other violations.

Left-wing All India Students' Association (AISA) on Wednesday demanded the "immediate release" of Cockroach movement conveners Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka after the duo were sent to judicial custody over trespassing amid protests.

Cockroach party conveners Ranka, Das sent to 5 days in judicial custody
Three leaders of India's Cockroach movement — Co-Conveners Saurav Das, Ashutosh Ranka and organizer Ajinkya Shinde — have been formally charged with multiple violations by authorities in India's national capital.
It all comes amid their protest against India's election chief over mass deletion of voter names from electoral rolls.
The trio was detained early Tuesday after they allegedly "sneaked" past police barricades to enter the grounds of Jantar Mantar in central Delhi, which until recently was a designated protest site.

"If the government thinks that sending our two leaders, Ashutosh and Saurav, to jail for five days will frighten them, it is absolutely mistaken," Shinde said, as per PTI.
He further called on "everyone" to "come together to bring an end to this dictatorial government."

France’s emissions are falling as fuel prices soar. Why is it still missing climate targets?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
05:02:49 UTC
14:02:49 KST

Despite using less fossil fuels, France is still far short of the 5 per cent annual reduction in emissions it needs to meet its climate targets.
France is getting an unexpected boost in its efforts to cut greenhouse gas emissions, but it comes with a catch consumers are feeling at the fuel pump.
Soaring fuel prices caused by the war in Iran have prompted people to buy less diesel and cut down on their gas use at home. That has helped bring emissions down 4.1 per cent in the first half of 2026, according to Citepa, a French organisation that measures air pollution and greenhouse gases to track the country’s environmental impact.
France is now on track to cut emissions by 2.8 per cent this year, up from 2.1 per cent in 2025. That would amount to 10 million tonnes fewer emissions than last year.
Even so, it’s still falling short of the pace needed to meet its long-term climate targets. France is aiming to halve emissions by 2030 compared to 1990 levels, but meeting that goal will require annual reductions of around 5 per cent.
Fuel prices hit French consumers
Much of the emissions reduction boils down to the cost of filling up the car. Fuel prices have surged since the start of the year, with diesel climbing 45 per cent after the war in Iran choked off oil supplies through the Strait of Hormuz.
People have simply bought less fuel since then. Diesel sales fell 7.3 per cent in the first six months of 2026. In that same timeframe, transport emissions dropped 4.5 per cent.
Emissions from homes and commercial buildings fell even more, dropping 12 per cent in the first half of the year mostly due to less natural gas use for heating, water and cooking.
But the downward trajectory is unlikely to last. Citepa expects emissions to fall just 1.3 per cent in the second half of the year, partly because France is using more gas-fired power plants to produce electricity for neighbouring countries.
The energy industry’s emissions are expected to rise by 3.6 per cent over the full year, even as transport and other sectors continue to record reductions.
France’s Ecological Transition Minister Monique Barbut called the decline “encouraging” but acknowledged it was “not yet enough to meet our climate targets”, according to AFP.
Global emissions could fall for first time since 2020
Elsewhere in Europe, emissions are on a steady – if slow – decline.
Germany’s emissions fell about 2 per cent in the first half of 2026 as demand for oil dropped. However, the think tank Agora Energiewende has warned the country could still exceed its annual emissions limit by around 10 million tonnes – the first time it will have done so since passing its landmark climate law in 2019.
High energy costs have also encouraged European households to find more affordable alternatives to fossil fuels. Heat pump sales rose 25 per cent in France, Germany and Poland early in 2026, and EV sales have also spiked since the start of the war. Meanwhile, solar power has saved the EU an estimated €37.4 billion in gas imports since it broke out in February.
Outside of Europe, emissions are also going down. In China, oil use fell 9 per cent in the second quarter of 2026, while carbon emissions dropped 1 per cent – the first time a decline in China’s emissions had been linked to oil rather than coal.
A recent report by Carbon Brief based on forecasts from the IEA suggests global fossil fuel CO2 emissions could fall about 0.5 per cent this year, which would be the first annual decline since stay-at-home orders caused them to plummet in 2020.
While the IEA expects oil demand to climb when the war ends, the widespread embrace of solar and wind power, nuclear energy, electric cars and heat pumps could keep fossil fuel use down even after their prices stabilise. Those technologies helped to prevent an estimated 3 billion tonnes of CO2 emissions worldwide in 2025, the agency reports.

Birdwatch: the paradoxical puffin – a comical bird with a fighting spirit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
05:00:46 UTC
14:00:46 KST

Few birds are as paradoxical as the puffin. It rivals the robin as Britain’s best-loved bird, yet most people have never seen one in the flesh. In spring and summer, they gather in large, noisy colonies to breed, but spend the autumn and winter far out to sea in the North Atlantic. And despite their small size, and gentle, clown-like appearance, puffins will fight to save their precious catch of sand eels from being seized by an opportunistic – and much larger – skua or gull.
Puffins, like penguins, have a very human quality, too. When the late Bill Oddie and I filmed puffins at a colony on Shetland, he memorably described them as “looking like old men in dinner jackets, waiting to go into supper at the club”, while the bird’s scientific name, Fratercula arctica, translates as “little brother of the Arctic”.
Their huge, colourful bill once earned them the name “sea parrot”, while “puffin” – meaning “fat” or “swollen” – was originally given to the young of another burrow-nesting seabird, the Manx shearwater. Confusingly, that species still retains the misleading scientific name Puffinus puffinus.
Now, like so many seabirds, puffins are in trouble. The sand eels, on which they rely to feed themselves and their single chick, are shifting north because of the climate crisis. Puffins are also threatened by avian flu, pollution and disturbance – ironically often caused by visitors to their colonies, over-eager to get closeup photos of these charismatic little birds.
The Puffin: A Biography, by Stephen Moss, is published on 15 October.

Cheese tart, corn salad, squash with ’nduja, radicchio salad: Joe Otway’s recipes for early autumn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
05:00:46 UTC
14:00:46 KST

Early autumn is one of the most generous and comforting times of year to cook with British produce: sweetcorn is at its peak, squash begins to sweeten as the weather cools and bitter leaves such as radicchio provide balance to the season’s abundance. Today’s recipes are simple celebrations of British ingredients, using just a handful of carefully chosen components to let each vegetable shine. Whether it’s a buttery cheese tart for sharing; a fresh, herby corn salad; sweet roast squash with warm, spicy ’nduja; or bitter leaves lifted with a floral dressing, they all rely on cooking with ingredients at their seasonal peak and allowing nature to guide the menu.
Cheese tart
Prep 10 min
Chill 30 min+
Cook 1 hr
Makes 4 individual tarts
90g unsalted butter, plus extra for greasing
120g plain flour, plus extra for dusting
110g mature cheddar, finely grated
70g whole eggs
25ml whole milk
10g ready-made English mustard, or to taste
110ml double cream
Sea salt and black pepper
First, make the pastry. Rub the butter into the flour until the mix resembles coarse breadcrumbs, then add 60g of the grated cheddar and knead gently until the mix comes together into a dough. Divide into four, wrap and chill for at least 30 minutes.
Meanwhile, make the custard. Blend the eggs, milk, remaining 50g grated cheddar and mustard until smooth, then stir in the cream by hand and season to taste.
Heat the oven to 180C (160C fan)/350F/gas 4, and grease and line four individual 8-10cm tart tins. Lightly flour a work surface, roll out each piece of pastry, then use to line the tins. Line each pastry base with baking paper, fill with baking beans or similar, then blind bake for 15 minutes, until lightly golden. Lift out the paper and beans, then return the tarts to the oven for a further five minutes, until the bases are crisp and golden.
Carefully pour the custard into each tart case until they’re almost full, then bake for another 15-25 minutes, depending on your oven (the actual temperature of domestic ovens varies a fair bit, after all), until the custard is lightly browned and just set with a slight wobble in the centre.
Leave to cool to room temperature, then serve, either with a bitter leaf salad or with one of the following two sides.
Corn salad with soured cream and oregano
Prep 5 min
Cook 15 min
Serves 4
Sea salt and black pepper
4 fresh sweetcorn cobs, or 1 400g tin good-quality sweetcorn
150g soured cream
100ml extra-virgin olive oil
Juice of ½ lemon
Sea salt
20g fresh oregano leaves, plus extra to garnish
30g parmesan, shaved
Bring a large pan of salted water to a boil, drop in the corn cobs, cook for four or five minutes, until tender, then drain and refresh. Once the cobs are cool enough to handle, cut off the kernels and put in a bowl (if you’re using tinned corn, skip the blanching stage and simply drain the water from the can).
Mix the soured cream with 20ml of the olive oil, the lemon juice and a pinch of salt. Blend the oregano with the remaining olive oil until fragrant. Dress the sweetcorn with the oregano oil, then season generously with salt and a little more lemon juice, if needed.
Spread the soured cream mix over a platter, spoon the dressed corn on top, scatter over a few more oregano leaves and finish with generous shavings of parmesan and a final twist of black pepper.
Roast winter squash with ’nduja
Prep 10 min
Cook 45 min
Serves 4
1kg winter squash (uchiki kuri is ideal, although butternut works well too), halved, deseeded and cut into skin-on wedges
5 tbsp olive oil
Sea salt
20g pumpkin seeds
120g ’nduja
2 tbsp good-quality honey
150g Greek yoghurt
1 tbsp lemon juice
1 small handful flat-leaf parsley, leaves picked and roughly chopped
Heat the oven to 220C (200C fan)/425F/gas 7. Toss the squash wedges with two tablespoons of the olive oil and a generous pinch of salt, then arrange on an oven tray and roast for 30-40 minutes, turning every 10 minutes, until tender and caramelised. Add the pumpkin seeds to the tray for the final 10 minutes of cooking.
Meanwhile, in a small saucepan gently warm the ’nduja, honey and the remaining olive oil until the mix comes together into a loose dressing. In a small bowl, mix the yoghurt with the lemon juice and a pinch of salt.
Spread the yoghurt on a platter, arrange the squash wedges and toasted pumpkin seeds on top, then spoon over the warm ’nduja dressing. Finish with the parsley and serve.
Radicchio with elderflower vinaigrette
Yes, elderflower is an early-summer flavour, but that’s why they invented cordial, so we can enjoy that gentle fragrance all year round.
Prep 10 min
Serves 4
3 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
2 tbsp elderflower cordial
2 tbsp white-wine vinegar
1 tsp dijon mustard
Sea salt and black pepper
2 heads bitter leaves – radicchio, treviso, chicory or endive will all work well here
40g hard sheep’s cheese, or pecorino
In a small bowl, whisk the oil, cordial, vinegar, mustard, and salt and pepper to taste, until lightly emulsified.
Trim the bases off the radicchio heads, then separate the leaves and put them in a medium bowl. Dress the leaves generously with the vinaigrette, then season with a little more salt and pepper if needed. Leave to marinate for five to 10 minutes, so the leaves soften slightly and absorb the dressing, then arrange on a serving plate and finish with generous shavings of the cheese.
- Joe Otway is chef/co-owner of Higher Ground, Bar Shrimp and Flawd, all in Manchester.

UK will not put tariffs on Chinese vehicles, says Jonathan Reynolds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
05:00:45 UTC
14:00:45 KST

The business secretary has hit back at European demands for British tariffs on Chinese imports, saying the government will not change its trade rules because of pressure from Brussels.
Jonathan Reynolds warned that the government would not bow to calls from other countries for the UK to hit Chinese vehicles with import taxes, despite political pressure to align with the EU in exchange for deeper future economic ties.
The EU imposed tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles in 2024 and last Friday agreed a 350,000 a year quota on Chinese hybrid cars amid fears cheaper alternatives are causing deindustrialisation and job losses.
Reynolds conceded that levying sanctions on Chinese goods was an option in the future, but he dismissed concerns from Brussels that the UK could provide a back door to the European market.
His comments highlight the divisions that remain between the UK and EU on trade and industrial policy, which could derail the prime minister’s attempts to move closer to Brussels.
“I just want to be clear: when we make any trade decision in terms of trade defence tariffs in relation to the EU, that’s based on the UK interest – it’s not based on any other country asking for that,” said Reynolds during a trade trip to India.
“In 2024, [we] looked at this issue carefully, and we keep it under review depending on what the needs of industry are … But it comes down to what is the fundamental nature of the UK automotive sector. It’s an export-led sector, so that’s what I’ve got to take into account.”
With Europe having imposed tariffs of up to 45% on Chinese electric cars, some believe that the UK has opened an alternative route into the EU for Chinese companies setting up in the UK to sell into the bloc.
Nissan, for instance, has agreed to look at building cars in northern England for the Chinese manufacturer Chery.
Reynolds rebutted those accusations, however, saying: “The UK currently has no major Chinese manufacturer based in its automotive sector, so we’re not making vehicles here and sending them to the single market through some sort of back door.”
His comments raise the stakes ahead of intense final weeks of negotiations before the long-awaited UK-EU summit, which Andy Burnham confirmed this week would be held in Brussels on 20 November.
The prime minister told the Commons on Monday he wanted a “serious dialogue” over the UK’s place in Europe, as he framed the summit as a possible first step to EU membership.
The new Made in Europe trade rules aim to protect European companies from subsidised Chinese imports, but British manufacturers worry they will also be shut out of supply chains.
The issue will not formally be on the agenda at the November summit, but British officials are hoping to use those talks to shape the European legislation.
Diplomats on both sides of the Channel say the summit will now be an early test of whether Burnham’s desire for a “real reset” in UK-EU relations is likely to bear fruit.
One EU official said this week that the UK’s negotiating position would determine whether it was worth pursuing more fundamental changes such as British access to the single market, a new customs union or re-accession.
Some in Brussels have been pushing for Britain to levy tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles in return for getting access to the European market under the new trade rules.
Reynolds has previously dismissed such an option in part because of the risk that Beijing could hit the UK with reciprocal tariffs, damaging British companies such as Jaguar Land Rover.
He said it would be to Europe’s detriment if it did not admit the UK into the scheme. “If you look at the impact analysis of such a policy, the consequences for the EU [of] excluding the UK are much more difficult,” he said.
“This is not just in the UK’s interest; it’s not in the EU’s interest because obviously we have integrated supply chains.”
Reynolds said the summit was an important milestone in EU-UK relations but also insisted that new trading terms for electricity, emissions and food and drink products would be a major achievement in themselves.
Speaking from a two-day trade delegation to Delhi and Mumbai, he acknowledged that the landmark free trade agreement he helped strike last year with India would become defunct if Britain does rejoin the EU.
“Obviously, if you enter those arrangements, you are doing things collectively. So there would be trade relationships with the UK that were based on Europe, the EU as a whole – that is how the European Union works in terms of its relationship.
“That’s why obviously when we were part of it, we didn’t have these separate bespoke arrangements.”
But he insisted that it remained worth continuing to push to broaden the scope of the agreement, as he unveiled a series of UK-India investments which officials say are worth over £1bn to the UK over the next 15 years.
The deal has already begun to reduce the price of Scotch whisky in Indian shops, after tariffs were reduced from 150% to 75%. Now British officials are keen to free up trade in services as well as goods, for example, pushing for both countries to recognise each other’s legal qualifications.
“There are some specific things regarding who can practice law and in which area,” Reynolds said. “I am confident over the medium to long term that this will improve over time.”
He added: “We’ve got to be cognisant of this long-term position with the EU. But frankly, there’s a job to be done here and now, which we’re doing.”

Global financial system is failing developing countries, says Ed Miliband
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
05:00:45 UTC
14:00:45 KST

The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, will claim the global financial system is failing developing countries, as he calls for a “new deal” for governments struggling under the burden of debt.
Promising to throw the UK’s diplomatic weight behind urgent reform, he will evoke the example of the Gleneagles summit under the last Labour government in 2005 – the culmination of the Make Poverty History campaign.
“The global financial system and indeed the global order is failing to serve developing countries on debt, on resilience and on climate. This is not just against our values but against our national interest,” Miliband is expected to say.
“In the interconnected world we live in, more than ever, the opportunities and challenges we confront are collective.”
Speaking in Bangkok on Wednesday, he will call for the World Bank and other multilateral development banks (MDBs) to use the resources they have available to lighten the load for governments trapped by hefty borrowing costs.
“We need action on developing country debt through the MDBs,” he is expected to say. “Action that leverages the balance sheets of the international financial institutions to support these countries to repay over longer time horizons, and crucially, refinancing, with better rates, to give them precious fiscal space.”
The foreign secretary will be in Bangkok to attend the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank annual meetings.
He opted to take up the UK’s seat on the bank’s board himself instead of leaving it to the development minister, Kirsty McNeill.
Labour’s manifesto in 2024 promised to restore the UK’s international reputation on development issues – but Keir Starmer subsequently slashed the aid budget to pay for defence.
Campaigners have long claimed the high interest rates paid by many developing countries mean the repayments crowd out vital public spending – including on tackling the climate emergency. In sub-Saharan Africa, more than three times as much is spent on debt servicing as on education.
Miliband will argue that making the global financial system work better for emerging economies will also help to attract more private investment – a key aim of the World Bank under the current president, Ajay Banga.
The UK is due to take up the presidency of the G20 group of nations next year – a key global forum for discussing global financial issues, including sovereign debt, which includes emerging economies such as China, India, South Africa and Brazil.
The chancellor, John Healey, will set out his own G20 priorities in Bangkok later this week, including mobilising more resources from the balance sheets of the IMF and the World Bank.
When the UK held the chair of the narrower G8 group in 2005, at the leaders’ summit at the Gleneagles hotel the UK secured agreements that eventually resulted in more than 30 countries receiving large-scale debt write-downs.
Miliband will say resources are now more constrained – but as well as debt refinancing for a large number of countries, he will demand an overhaul of the “common framework” for restructuring the debts of countries unable to pay.
The framework is widely criticised as too slow and cumbersome. Among other reforms, the UK wants to see changes to ensure private creditors cannot hold up negotiations – as has happened in recent cases including that of Ethiopia.
The foreign secretary will also call for overhauls to allow help to be made available more rapidly to countries in trouble. “We need finance teed up in advance of crises, so that governments get support in days, not months,” he will say.
Miliband will be speaking at the launch of a report by the Rockefeller Foundation that calls for a “surge” in affordable financing from the IMF and the World Bank to debt-burdened countries.
Tim Jones, the policy director of the campaign group Debt Justice, welcomed Miliband’s focus on the issue but said a litmus test of any plan would be whether private sector creditors bear some of the costs. “Action on debt relief is urgently needed. That must include private lenders sharing in the cost. Otherwise public money will just bail out private lenders rather than be used for investment.”

Palantir is worming its way into the British state – it’s time to curb this controversial US company’s influence | George Monbiot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
05:00:44 UTC
14:00:44 KST

What a world we live in. Imagine: gangs dragging civil servants off commuter trains and beating them up because they handed government data jobs to the wrong contractor – and the government is changing its procurement decisions as a result. Well, OK, it might not have happened yet, but it’s only a matter of time. As the former Labour deputy leader Tom Watson asks: “Do you want to let the rule of law lead procurement practice, or do you want mob rule to lead procurement practices?” No, I absolutely don’t want the latter, and it’s always good to get ahead of trouble.
But then I remember there are two common meanings of mob rule. One is intimidation by crowds of thugs. The other is a pejorative term for democracy. And while I’ve yet to see government procurement practices in the UK determined by pitchforks and flaming torches, democratic transparency could be a genuine threat to certain contractors. One might have hoped that Watson, who once took on the Murdoch empire, would have recognised the distinction. But then again, one might have hoped that Watson would not have taken a job as a senior vice-president at Palantir.
Over the past few years, this US company has been worming its way into the British state. It has landed contracts worth hundreds of millions with the Ministry of Defence, several police forces, the Financial Conduct Authority, the atomic weapons establishment and the NHS. Its superpower, according to a deep investigation by Peter Geoghegan and Lucas Amin in the London Review of Books, is that it is “willing to spend more on securing political access than almost all of its British and continental competitors”. It made abundant use of Peter Mandelson’s company Global Counsel, which seems, in turn, to have made abundant use of the UK’s remarkably flimsy lobbying laws. Watson is one of more than 30 former UK ministers and officials Palantir now employs.
Palantir’s contracts might have been awarded lawfully, but some of us might question the ways in which doors were opened for it. These include an unrecorded meeting between Boris Johnson, Dominic Cummings and the co-founder of Palantir, Peter Thiel, in Downing Street in 2019. It was invited back to Downing Street when the Covid-19 pandemic began a few months later, and was working in the NHS within days, on a contract for which it charged only £1. The mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, has criticised such loss-leaders, which can quickly lead to reliance on a company, at which point it can name its price.
Another controversial meeting was brokered by Mandelson in 2025, when he was UK ambassador to the US. Keir Starmer visited Palantir’s showroom in Washington, where he met the company’s global and UK chief executives, Alex Karp and Louis Mosley. They talked about defence spending. No 10, Geoghegan and Amin tell us, “refused to say whether Starmer knew that Palantir was a client of Global Counsel, in which Mandelson still held a stake of around a fifth at the time. The meeting was never declared on transparency registers.” A few months later, Palantir secured a £241m contract with the Ministry of Defence, without an open tender.
Now we learn that Martha Dalton, a key player in Andy Burnham’s campaign to win the Makerfield byelection, enabling him to become prime minister, was on unpaid leave from the lobbying company she co-founded, Lodestone. Lodestone had done extensive work for Palantir. And the Financial Times reports that Samantha Jones, then the lead non-executive director on the board of the health department, was an adviser to one of Palantir’s partners when the company was bidding for its huge and controversial NHS contract. Now she is permanent secretary in the same department.
There have been repeated allegations that some of Palantir’s products are rubbish. But, as the House of Commons science, innovation and technology committee warns, government agencies can quickly succumb to “vendor lock-in”: once you start using them, it can be very hard to stop.
Thiel, has claimed that “the NHS makes people sick”, and that we should “just rip the whole thing from the ground and start over”. The company is deeply embedded in the Trump administration, where it supplies software that helps ICE find undocumented people. It also works for the Israeli government on identifying targets in Gaza. When Karp was confronted by a protester who told him that “Palantir kills Palestinians”, he replied: “Mostly terrorists, that’s true.”
This is the company handling our critical information. After official denials, it turns out that NHS England has granted Palantir “unlimited access” to patient data. This is a huge issue. Identifiable patient data is supposed to be visible only to people directly involved in a patient’s care, or who have received the patient’s informed consent. There are widespread concerns about how this and other datasets might be used.
So, as Palantir runs into ever-greater controversy, it’s not hard to see why it might have hired Watson, who, with Burnham, was a minister in Gordon Brown’s government. I wouldn’t presume to speculate about what attracted Watson to the multibillion-dollar company.
In July, the government’s ethics and integrity commission recommended a major shake-up, enabling us to see all the encounters between lobbyists and ministers, aides and senior officials. I’ve heard this call many times before. The pattern is always the same: a scandal, followed by a call to action, followed by … little or nothing.
Before he became prime minister, David Cameron noted that lobbying “has tainted our politics for too long”. He would shine “the light of transparency” on it. Instead, he oversaw an act that was “more loophole than law”. It did nothing to protect us from lobbying by people such as Cameron – pulling strings, once out of office, among his old colleagues, to try to drum up government business for the bank Greensill .
You could almost believe that the real purpose of government was to do the bidding of corporations, foreign states and the ultra-rich. You could almost believe that some government ministers may have an eye on future opportunities when they resist effective reform.
So this is another key test for Burnham. Will he allow the mob rule of private business to keep dominating our lives, or will he ensure that government is for the people?
- George Monbiot is a Guardian columnist

World's oldest shipwreck found off coast of Turkey
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
06:00:35 BST
14:00:35 KST

World's oldest shipwreck found off coast of Turkey
- Published
The world's oldest shipwreck has been discovered off the coast of Turkey, archaeologists say.
They have dated it to between 4,400 and 4,700 years old, which is the Early Bronze Age, and is around the same time that the Great Pyramid was being built.
The ship's wooden structure has not survived, but the ceramic storage pots it was carrying were lying on the sea floor and, remarkably, some still contain traces of what they held inside.
The archaeologists who found the ship say it was about 10m in length and was a trade vessel carrying cargo across the Mediterranean Sea.
"The shipwreck is a time capsule at the bottom of the sea," said Prof Hakan Öniz, from Akdeniz University in Turkey, who led the Mediterranean Archaeology Association expedition.
The wreck is close to the shore of Kekova Island in Antalya, Turkey. The artefacts lie scattered across an underwater slope, just 30m beneath the waves.
Three large stone anchors were found, as well as more than 30 ceramic storage pots, called amphorae.
The fact that none of the ship's wood remained meant techniques like radiocarbon dating - which measures a form of carbon in organic materials - could not be used to determine its age.
Instead, archaeologists analysed the shape of the amphorae. Because pottery styles have changed over time, different styles are linked to particular periods.
The Kekova ceramics are distinctive, with two handles, a ridge in the middle and a flat base.
Öniz said this design matched other amphorae unearthed in Egypt and the Middle East that were known to be 4,400-4,700 years old.
"Comparing the decoration techniques… we can definitely say our wreck is Early Bronze Age. This is 100%."
Divers from the expedition brought the pots up to the surface, where they are now being carefully conserved after so many thousands of years underwater.
Dr Karin Sowada, an archaeologist from Macquarie University, Australia, examined the amphorae after they were recovered. Some were intact and she was surprised to see they still contained a viscous, glossy residue.
"I looked inside and nearly fainted. I could not believe how much [residue] was visible. It wasn't just like spots…. a lot of this material was still remaining," she said.
The team is now working to find out exactly what was being carried in the amphorae.
"It could be olive oil, it could be wine, it could be tree resins," Sowada said.
"It's possible that [the residue] could actually be the result of reuse of the jars. I mean, these jars are huge - they're not things that you just ship away and then never see again. People would have emptied these jars on arrival and potentially used them for many, many, many years."
The wreck and its cargo are also shedding light on trade in the ancient world.
The archaeologists say the ship started its voyage from somewhere along the eastern coast of the Mediterranean.
They believe it was taking goods to either the ancient city of Troy, in what is now north-western Turkey, or to the Minoan people in Crete.
Travelling by sea was fraught with danger, particularly around Kekova Island, where the strong currents and winds have claimed many ships.
There are hundreds of wrecks in the area, and the Mediterranean Archaeology Association specialises in finding and studying them.
Öniz says that when he is diving on the wreck his first thoughts are about the lives of the people who were connected to this vessel.
"We are the first humans who [have] touched these objects after 5,000 years.
"We are always thinking of the sailors... the producers of the amphora and the person who carried the amphora on their shoulders to the ship, and the women who were waiting for their husbands, and they unfortunately couldn't go back."
The shipwreck is owned by the Turkish Ministry of Culture. Its minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy said the artefacts that have been recovered would be put on display in the new Mediterranean Underwater Archaeology Museum in Antalya when it opens in the coming months.
The Kekova discovery now tops the list of the world's oldest shipwrecks.
Previously, the record holder was a wreck off the coast of Dokos, an island in southern Greece, which dates to about 4,200 years ago.
The oldest known intact shipwreck, where the wood is still preserved, was found in the Black Sea off the coast of Bulgaria. It dates to about 2,400 years ago.

Missile alert interrupts Saudi minister mid-speech (VIDEO)

The incident occurred at the Riyadh International Convention and Exhibition Centre, when warning notifications sounded simultaneously on the minister’s phone and those of audience members.
Al Rajhi, the human resources and social development minister, briefly acknowledged the alerts before calmly continuing his speech.
“We are under the protection of the Lord of the Worlds. God willing, may God turn their plot back upon them,” he told the audience.

Residents reported hearing several powerful explosions in the Saudi capital on Monday night, according to Al Jazeera. Riyadh has stepped up its air support for the offensive, intensifying strikes on Houthi-held territory in recent days. According to the group, Saudi bombardments have killed nearly 400 people since early September, many of them civilians.

Beyond the Box: What Shipping Container Architecture Gets Right and Where It Falls Short
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

Using shipping containers as the basis for a structure—also known as "cargotecture"—seems like a simple approach to building. Perhaps deceptively so. While it's true that containers are a quick, cost-effective, and often low-effort building material, and that they're durable and customizable, container conversions also bring their challenges. Without careful planning, the build process can be painful and the results underwhelming.
To understand whether containers are the right choice for a construction project, it's important to look past their industrial allure to the realities and constraints of steel boxes as a building material.
"Cargotecture" Challenges and Limitations
The use of shipping containers for architectural projects is an exercise in creating a beautiful and functional structure while overcoming an array of rigid constraints.
The most obvious is the width: at 2.44m, intermodal containers are only slightly wider than a caravan or motorhome. Side-opening containers can mitigate this constraint, or you can remove entire walls and connect two or more containers, though this brings engineering challenges, as will any alteration to the container's structure.
Another key hurdle is thermal conductivity. Containers are made from weathering steel, which gets cold in winter and hot in summer. Insulation and ventilation are critical, particularly for living and working spaces, but installing thick batts eats into the already limited space within the container.
There are a wealth of other challenges to navigate, from foundations to utility connections to the long-term mitigation of rust. Each, however, can be addressed through careful design and planning.
Overcoming Confines: Scandinavian-Inspired Tiny Home With Terrace
Despite a footprint of less than 14m², this tiny home uses a smart design to feel far larger. A clever internal layout creates distinct bed, kitchen, and bathroom spaces, while French doors open onto an outdoor terrace, extending usable space and bringing more natural light into the interior.
From Cramped to Open Plan: District 10 Container Building
Need more space than a container offers? Joining two or more containers can create a larger footprint, as demonstrated by this Dundee development, which uses more than 30 containers. Carefully removing internal walls and reinforcing the structure allows the individual units to function as a larger, more open-plan space.
Easy Access: Private Garage for Vehicle Preservation
Traditional containers feature doors at their ends, which can make access awkward, not just for home and workspace conversions, but for storage too. A car enthusiast faced this issue and solved it by converting a side-opening container that protects the vehicle while providing direct access.
Comfort in Extreme Temperatures: Dual-Layer Insulation
The thermal conductivity of steel means insulation is a must for any living or working space conversion. But extreme temperatures demand thick insulation, which can quickly eat into the limited space within a container. One approach is to combine internal insulation with external cladding, adding another layer of protection without taking up too much internal room.
Where Conventional Construction Still Wins
While shipping containers offer a range of advantages as a building material, for certain projects the cost-benefit analysis will still lean toward a traditional build. It's important to recognize the point at which extensive container modifications negate the financial and time advantages of modular steel.
This typically occurs when a build features complex geometries, wide-span clear spaces, or local zoning constraints that govern aesthetics. Container conversions can also have multi-decade lifespans, but they typically won't last as long as a traditional build.
Ultimately, containers shine in architecture when their intrinsic benefits—prefabrication, modularity, rapid assembly, the industrial look—are preserved, rather than modified beyond recognition.

ICC judge calls US pressure ‘most blatant attack on the court’ – interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

Almost immediately after former International Criminal Court (ICC) judge Navi Pillay was announced as this year’s Nobel Peace Prize laureate, Donald Trump’s administration struck the Court with sweeping sanctions. For ICC judge Kimberly Prost, however, the pressure from Washington is nothing new: the Canadian judge has been under personal US sanctions for nearly two years. “This is a pretty extraordinary attack on the court,” she tells LRT.lt in an exclusive interview.
When sanctions were imposed on her in February last year, Canadian judge Prost felt their impact immediately: her payment cards issued in the Netherlands and Canada were blocked. Although she managed to retain access to a few bank accounts, banking services remain very limited, and even small transfers are often blocked. The judge also lost access to paid services provided by Apple, Google, and Amazon, as well as the ability to travel to the United States. Even a French company distanced itself from the sanctioned judges and decided to stop paying their health insurance claims.
The latest blow from the United States is the imposition of sanctions on the ICC itself, aimed at financially paralysing the court.
“We're working to be resilient, but it's a very serious matter, which is why it's so important that everyone understands what's going on,” she stresses.
In an ironic twist, Prost, who recently visited Vilnius, was participating in the #Disinfo2026 conference, for which Lithuania also reportedly withdrew its support following pressure from the United States, according to media reports.
Nevertheless, despite the US attack on the ICC, Prost insists that it will neither break the judges’ resolve nor bring their work to a halt.
“The court will continue its important mandate to render justice,” she emphasizes.
You were sanctioned by the US a little over a year ago. What was your first reaction when you learnt about this?
We all – all of the judges, the elected officials and staff – knew that the executive order was there and they had always indicated that individuals would be added to the list as they were going along. It wasn't totally unexpected in the sense that I broadly knew that.
But I think I was taken aback because I didn't particularly see the basis where I was concerned, given my work. I just sort of processed it for a few minutes and then realized, okay, I'm going to have to adjust to this new reality.
Ironically, I worked for five years as the ombudsperson for the Security Council Al-Qaeda Sanctions Committee, so I was very familiar. I interviewed a lot of people subject to UN sanctions, but as it went along, it became clear that until you really experience it yourself, you don't have the entire perspective on what it's like.
How it has affected you personally and in your daily life?
It really does permeate your daily life because it affects things that are so average and sort of assumed.
First of all, all your credit cards are immediately canceled no matter what country they are issued. So, my cards were in Canada and in the Netherlands were immediately canceled, because of the influence of the United States in the financial and the SWIFT system.
Then there's the panic about banking services because literally banks can decide they don't want to do business with you, that could be a business decision even if they're, not American banks. <…>
Then there's all these services that are so permeating in our lives: computers, so “Apple”, “Apple Wallet” was gone obviously. “Google”, any services that are paid for. And you don't know what's going to be canceled and what's not, there's been a variation between the judges. So, the randomness also makes it even worse in some ways because there's no predictability. I make bank transfers, my bank will assist me, but will other banks receive the money or can people send from their banks to me? <…>
Then there's just the whole psychological effect of this, which is I've been in criminal justice work for pretty well all of my life, my colleagues – in human rights, criminal justice, and you're suddenly on a list with those purported to be involved in human rights violations, terrorism, and organized crime. You're put in the same category, that's very hard.
That just gives some of the idea of what we're dealing with. Obviously, I can't go to the United States. For some of my colleagues who have, for example, children in the United States, their visas get canceled or it's very complicated if you have a spouse or a child who happens to be American. I don't have those factors, although my siblings in Canada are very nervous about crossing the border. So far, they've made it.
The US say that you were sanctioned for your role in authorizing the ICC's investigation into US personnel in Afghanistan. Could you explain your this decision, and why do you think the sanctions were imposed?
I'm not really sure to tell you the truth.
My involvement is very limited. Six years ago, before this administration even took power, I sat on the appeals chamber temporarily, I'm a trial judge, replacing a judge, and we were faced with an appeal by the prosecutor of a pretrial decision refusing the authorization for the investigation in Afghanistan.
Why I was sanctioned six years after that, I have no idea.
This was at the very beginning, all of the allegations of a horrific crime by Taliban, ISIS, various military forces, and including a component of US officials and their activities in Afghanistan.
We unanimously, on the basis of what I consider overwhelming evidence and clear law, authorized the prosecutor to conduct the investigation, including the US portion. Now, the footnote to that is that about two years after, the prosecutor, who's faced with many competing areas of varying situations, decided to deprioritize the American component and focus on the other crime in Afghanistan and other situations.
So there is no investigation into the American component of Afghanistan, and I have no other involvement in anything, any of the investigations into the Israel-Gaza situation or Afghanistan.
And so why I was sanctioned six years after that, I have no idea.
I want to talk a bit about the broader pressure. President Trump and members of his administration have been highly critical of the ICC. At the UN he even described the court as “out of control”, you – “evil group of people,” and urged countries to leave the court. Has the ICC ever faced this level of political pressure?
Well, this is a unique angle. The ICC has long had issues that can involve geopolitics, if you put it that way, and these kinds of pressures. The United States, for example, at the early days under the Bush administration, was carrying out a campaign to have states who were parties, sign these, what we called Article 98 agreements, that they would never turn over US personnel. So that was a part of the same objection. But I would say this is pretty extreme.
I do have colleagues though, who are also subject to arrest warrants from the Russian Federation and have been convicted in absentia for their work related to the file in Ukraine. <…>
But this is a pretty extraordinary attack on the court. And what I emphasize here it's not because, “woe is me with what's happened in my life”. I can tell you, I sat on the Srebrenica trial, and I've sat on trials at the ICC, and what I see in people's lives by comparison, this is annoyances. But it's the purpose (and this is what makes this distinct), it's the most blatant attack rendered against the independence of judges and the rule of law – you must decide the cases the way we want or you must not do your job, or we're going to impose these measures.
That's a pretty shocking position for the government of the United States to take, in my view.
It's the most blatant attack rendered against the independence of judges and the rule of law
Following from that, when judges become targets of sanctions, and when the US appears to be actively and very openly devaluating the court's work, how significant of a risk is this, as you say, attack on the court, and how it affects the court's judicial independence?
I can assure you that it doesn't affect the court's judicial independence, and I think I've been very clear in every interview to say we will continue. We will continue to look at the evidence, the facts, apply the law, and do so objectively. Objectively, either way, not in favor, not in fear.
We will continue to do our job that way, and the court will continue its important mandate to render justice in these situations. I have no concern that that's ever going to stop. I don't see this as the end of the ICC, the Rome statute system or international law.
But we have to understand the seriousness of this attack. The secretary of state Marco Rubio said, “We want to tear down the ICC brick by brick,” in addition to the comments of the president in the General Assembly.
So their aim here is now no longer even a matter of speculation, and that's what we need to address. And these measures that they're using can be very crippling. They're not going to affect our core work, but all of the energy resources that have to be sent away from other measures we could be taking, are directed towards trying to protect the court, and now that's the threat – that they're going to hit the institution, which obviously has all sorts of implications for contracts and salary payments and all of those matters.
We're working to be resilient, but it's a very serious matter, which is why it's so important that everyone understands what's going on.
One of the biggest criticisms of international justice is that it struggles to reach the most powerful. The ICC has issued arrest warrants for Russian President Vladimir Putin and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Yet it is quite difficult at the moment to imagine either of them appearing before the court. What do you think needs to happen for such political figures to eventually stand a fair trial?
I'll answer that question sort of in the abstract.
I will say about the process: we have issued those arrest warrants for those individuals. Arrest warrants carry a lot of meaning in and of themselves. There are legal determinations made not just by the prosecutor, but by a chamber, that there's sufficient evidence to warrant the issuance of these arrest warrants. And all of our states' parties are under an obligation to arrest. So that's the process.
More broadly, though, I think if you look at the overall history of international criminal justice, we are not the first court to issue arrest warrants implicating sitting heads of states. Obviously, there was the case of The International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia of Slobodan Milošević and in addition, Charles Taylor in the Sierra Leone court was the subject also of proceedings.
What will happen in the ICC cases, only time will tell. But in those cases, it became a question of a long process. And ultimately, both Mr. Taylor and Mr. Milošević were tried. Mr. Milošević died before verdict, and Charles Taylor was convicted.
But I think it evidences that it is possible. It's certainly possible that arrest warrants will be executed, that the law will apply equally to everyone. And that's what the Rome Statute says – disregard official title capacity. So, I still believe that is always possible, and I hope that is possible as well in the context of the ICC. I know it is.
What we will see factually, only time will tell.
Lithuania has been one of the strongest advocates for accountability for crimes committed during Russia's war in Ukraine. We play an important role in a Special tribunal for the crime of aggression against Ukraine. I don't know if you saw, in Vilnius there is a large sign addressed to Russian president, which reads, “Putin, The Hague Is Waiting For You.” So again, I want to come back to this question that it is hard to imagine that he will appear there. How you personally view justice in such cases?
It's a great question. Ask me that on March 10th, 2027, at 5:00 PM, when I'm no longer a sitting judge.
I'm happy to speak to my vision of international criminal justice and the execution of these warrants. And I would say that, for example, back when I was at The International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia and Milošević had already been arrested, but I know people who were there at the very beginning who expressed the view that Mr. Milošević would never appear in the Tribunal.
Again, we look at the whole process, what international justice can do and we'll have to wait and see.
But the specific case, I'll just not comment on that.
And we do have Rodrigo Duterte. He's no longer head of state, but he arrived, and those warrants were also issued when he was still a sitting head of state. So time will tell.
Lithuania is a very important and has been a very active supporter of the ICC throughout the life of the court. Very committed, and I hope that that will continue.
Lithuania is so invested in the ICC because of our strong support for Ukraine. Lithuania in general shows very strong support for the ICC, but at the same time, we are receiving some signals from Washington. It has been said to Lithuania that the question of the ICC is particularly relevant for the countries hosting the US troops. As you know, with geopolitical and war threats, it is a very disturbing question for us. Although, I have to say that the US have not said explicitly yet that they will withdraw the troops, if we remain the member of the court.
What would you say to such countries as ours, which strongly support the ICC and international justice, but also face geopolitical pressure?
I would be simply taking that to a very high level. Lithuania is a very important and has been a very active supporter of the ICC throughout the life of the court. Very committed, and I hope that that will continue.
Every country has to manage their relationships with states. My country has to manage a relationship with United States, for example. I simply hope that every country will prioritize what is for me so fundamental to, as I like to refer to it, our global village, which is the rule of law, justice for victims and an end to impunity for atrocity crime.
And I hope that they will find other ways, I hope all our states will find ways through diplomacy, through support, through statements send a very clear message that they're always willing to engage and to consult, but those are our values and principles that have to be maintained. I very much hope that, and I am pretty confident that Lithuania will continue with that path.
To echo what the Prime Minister of the Netherlands Rob Jetten said in the General Assembly, which we're all quoting now quite a bit, “Hands off the ICC”.
So that's my hope.

Iran expanding attacks on ships beyond Hormuz to keep oil prices high; official vows full closure coming - report
A US military official said Iran has started using unarmed spotters in small boats to find targets, including US naval vessels, after much of its radar was destroyed
Iran is deploying new tactics against ships sailing through the Strait of Hormuz in a bid to keep oil prices high and influence the outcome of the US midterm elections, two senior Iranian officials said.
Tehran has tried to control the strait since the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran on February 28, restricting passage through a waterway that carried about a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas trade before the war. The officials declined to detail the new strategy, but one said Iran began using different offensive tactics in recent weeks against vessels it considered in violation of its restrictions.
Attacks on those ships have increased since, the official said. The shift covers both the type and pace of attacks and, they said, was approved at the highest levels of Iran’s leadership.
“The aim is to frustrate efforts by the United States and its allies to bring down global oil prices,” one official said. The other said Tehran would not let President Donald Trump lower prices before the November vote. “Just when they think they are getting close to the point where prices will fall, we will push them away from it. This is a game of chess,” the official said.
The officials said operations would also expand beyond the strait into the Gulf of Oman and farther afield. “Such vessels would be safe nowhere, even outside the Strait of Hormuz,” the second official said. Both said Tehran is moving toward a point where no vessel violating its restrictions could pass. “It will be complete closure soon,” one said.
Shipping data points to an escalation. There were at least five incidents involving tankers and other commercial ships around Hormuz in the past 48 hours, including drone strikes, according to maritime security sources and reports to UK Maritime Trade Operations.

- Britain accuses Iran's IRGC of directing foiled RAF Fairford terror attack | Yuval Barnea
- After the deadly attacks on Saudi Arabia, Iran offers to open dialogue between Riyadh and the Houthis | i24NEWS
Attacks have surged to their highest level since the war began, according to independent data. “There is a tempo increase in strikes, which looks deliberate,” one maritime security source said. Ships have also been hit off the coasts of Qatar and the United Arab Emirates in recent days.
A US military official said that after the US destroyed much of Iran’s radar capabilities, the Revolutionary Guards began using spotters to identify targets. Unwilling to risk its remaining fast boats, Iran has been unable to stop a ramp-up in oil exports through the strait, the official added.
The war, which costs about $3 billion a month, has become a key issue on the campaign trail. Trump is weighing next steps against Iran but has said he will not attack before the vote, while the US presses its naval blockade of Iranian ports. The Pentagon and Iran’s Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

US federal agents arrested a Saudi national who was an OpenAI engineer and charged him with installing a hidden audio recording device in an executive conference room at the AI company, the Justice Department said on Tuesday.
The case highlights growing security concerns around sensitive AI research as companies and governments compete fiercely for the talent and technology that could confer economic and strategic advantages.
Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, had worked as an engineer at OpenAI since July 2025, the Justice Department said in a statement. An email sent to an address associated with that name got no response, and it was not immediately clear who his lawyer was.
OpenAI discovered the recording device plugged into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive conference room at one of its San Francisco buildings on September 30, according to the department.
The thumb-sized device, which had a microphone and could connect to a camera, was concealed in toilet paper, according to an FBI complaint. It was installed on or about September 28, while its stored data was encrypted and inaccessible. Investigators later found a similar customized device in Alfozan's personal bag.
OpenAI said in a post on X that it used its internal AI models to identify the person responsible for planting the device and trace its origins.
OpenAI says employee intended to place additional recording devices in sensitive areas of its offices
The company said it had evidence that the employee intended to place additional recording devices in sensitive areas of its offices to secretly record meetings.
"At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data. The employee was terminated," the company said.
OpenAI referred the matter to the FBI, which is continuing to investigate. The Saudi embassy in the United States did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment.
"Abdulrahman Alfozan allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer's executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company’s super intelligence technology," FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement.
Alfozan also used an AI productivity agent to seek information about meeting-room calendars and capabilities for about a month through September 16, according to the FBI complaint. He has been a legal permanent resident of the US since September 2020.
Alfozan may face up to five years in prison
If convicted, Alfozan faces up to five years in prison, a $250,000 fine and three years of supervised release.
A LinkedIn profile showed that Alfozan studied at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and the University of California, Berkeley. It said he previously worked at Meta and Microsoft.
Reuters could not independently verify the details mentioned in his LinkedIn profile.
Separately, the Information reported that OpenAI was in early talks to acquire Trail of Bits, a startup that identifies and fixes vulnerabilities in open-source software. The talks were ongoing and could fall apart, the report said, citing people familiar with the matter.
OpenAI and Trail of Bits did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment.
OpenAI said on Friday it fired three researchers after an investigation found they had violated company policies on handling sensitive information.
The researchers, Jasmine Wang, Tomek Korbak and Mikita Balesni, had published a letter detailing the circumstances of their dismissal and arguing that the abrupt firings could create uncertainty among employees and undermine a culture in which researchers could raise safety concerns.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu claimed in an interview with Channel 14's The Patriots on Tuesday that he had never met with a foreign intelligence chief in his capacity as prime minister, despite official records showing that he hosted Egyptian intelligence chief Abbas Kamel at his Jerusalem residence in May 2021 and discussed security and diplomatic matters with him.
"When does an intelligence chief come and speak to a head of state? It hasn't happened to me once, OK? There's no such thing," Netanyahu said during the interview.
The remarks came after the prime minister confirmed that an Egyptian aircraft had landed in Israel in September 2023, just days before the October 7 Hamas attack.
Netanyahu denied meeting with the Egyptian intelligence chief on that occasion, saying he had been attending a memorial ceremony for fallen IDF soldiers at the time.
He also demanded to know whom the senior Egyptian official had met during his visit to Israel.
"I want to know who he met. I don't know," Netanyahu said, claiming that whoever had met the official was trying to "pin it on me."
However, in attempting to explain why it would be unlikely for an intelligence chief to meet with a prime minister, Netanyahu made a sweeping assertion that contradicts the documented history of his own meetings.
The official statement and photograph from May 2021
On May 30, 2021, the Prime Minister's Office published a statement titled "Prime Minister Netanyahu meets with Egyptian General Intelligence Chief Abbas Kamel and a delegation of senior officials headed by him."
The statement explicitly said: "Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu met today with Egyptian General Intelligence Chief Abbas Kamel and a delegation of senior officials headed by him at the Prime Minister's Residence in Jerusalem."
According to the statement, the two discussed strengthening cooperation between Israel and Egypt and regional issues, and welcomed the ties between the countries and their joint efforts on security and diplomatic matters.
The statement also said Netanyahu raised Israel's demand for the return of the soldiers and civilians who were being held in the Gaza Strip at the time.
The meeting also addressed mechanisms to prevent Hamas from building up its capabilities and from using resources intended for the civilian population.
The meeting was also attended by then-intelligence minister Eli Cohen and then-national security adviser Meir Ben-Shabbat, who had previously held an extended meeting with Kamel.
The statement was accompanied by an official photograph of Netanyahu and Kamel shaking hands, taken by Government Press Office photographer Amos Ben-Gershom.
A video of the meeting was also published on the prime minister's official YouTube channel.
In other words, this was not a meeting revealed retrospectively through anonymous sources, but a diplomatic event that Netanyahu himself chose to make public through his office.
Netanyahu also met with the CIA director
The meeting with the Egyptian intelligence chief is not the only instance that calls into question Netanyahu's sweeping claim.
In February 2024, Walla reported that then-CIA director William Burns had arrived in Israel and met with Netanyahu and former Mossad chief David Barnea as part of efforts to advance a deal to release the hostages being held in Gaza.
Netanyahu and Burns met again in Jerusalem in May of that year, against the backdrop of negotiations over a ceasefire and hostage deal.
Such meetings are a routine part of diplomatic and security relations between national leaders and the heads of foreign intelligence agencies, particularly when those officials are involved in sensitive negotiations or serve as envoys for their governments.

JERUSALEM - Liran Naaman said he spent €800 (S$1,148) to fly from Amsterdam, where he has lived for the past 11 years, to his native Israel, all to vote in the Oct 27 election.

“That’s why I’m going to vote,” the Parisian pensioner told AFP, noting that the last time she cast a ballot in Israel was in 1973.
Since then, she had felt it inappropriate to vote while living abroad. “But this year, it’s really different,” she said. “It’s about values.”
‘Crucial time’ for Israel
The relationship between religion and state is also a decisive factor for Tami Giniger, a startup consultant who will fly home from Bangkok to vote.
“This is a crucial time... for defining what is Israeli, what is Judaism, how these things work together,” she said.
“I do love that (Israel) is a Jewish state. But I don’t think that it needs to be fanatic,” she added.
The Aid Coalition has launched a non-partisan initiative, called Fly & Vote, to assist Israelis abroad who want to return for the election.
The programme provides information on the location of polling stations and identification requirements.
It also helps arrange travel by purchasing seats on commercial flights and reselling them, and in some cases has chartered aircraft.
Likud, Netanyahu’s party, filed a petition with Israel’s Central Elections Committee in early September, accusing the initiative of electoral bribery.
Aid Coalition president Jonathan Barsade told AFP the accusation had “no foundation whatsoever” and that the NGO does not provide financial incentives.
A settlement reached last week requires the NGO to stop selling additional flights as part of the programme, while allowing previously purchased tickets to remain valid.
‘You need to suffer with us’
While some Israelis abroad argue they should be allowed to vote at embassies, Naaman says he appreciates the requirement to return home and experience the country’s reality before deciding how to vote.
“Being in Israel gives a very different perspective than being abroad,” he said.
“When my family and friends come to visit (in Amsterdam), they’re always afraid that Europe has fallen and that everything has become horrible in Europe,” he said.
“And when I’m talking to them, I feel like (they) have Iranian missiles every Tuesday and Wednesday!” he said.
Relatives have criticised him for remaining abroad during the war while returning to vote for the country’s future.
“You need to be here and suffer with us in order to gain that privilege,” he said, describing their message to him.
Yet interviewees said Israeli politics continues to affect them deeply, despite the distance.
Giniger said she felt a “responsibility” to influence through her vote how “Jews and Israelis are perceived in the world today” at a time of rising anti-Semitism.
National elections, she argued, will shape Israel’s relations with the rest of the world.
“Those alliances and the way that the world sees us are crucial to us.”
Ariella Hanker, 44, a cancer research scientist in Dallas, was born in Israel to American parents.
An observant Jew, she grew up in the United States but has always felt strong ties to her country of birth.
After Netanyahu returned to power in 2022 and his government sought to advance a widely criticised judicial overhaul, she resolved to return for the next election.
“I don’t know that my vote really will affect anything,” she said. “But it’s more a personal thing. I don’t want to be complacent.”
“I’m just really worried about the future of a strong, democratic Israel. And I don’t want to blame myself for its downfall. I want to tell myself I did what I could to prevent it.” AFP

Israel could leave Syria but needs buffer zones in Gaza and Lebanon, ex-national security chief says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
04:52:36 UTC
13:52:36 KST

Retired Maj. Gen. Giora Eiland, former head of Israel's National Security Council, spoke Tuesday at the People of the State conference, the flagship event hosted by ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth. Eiland discussed what he described as Israel's fundamental mistake in 2007 that ultimately led to the October 7 massacre, as well as the differences between Israel's buffer zones in Gaza and Lebanon and the territory it holds in Syria.
"The great mistake always begins with an incorrect description of reality," Eiland said, referring to the Gaza Strip. "From 2007, through October 7 and to this day, the State of Israel has continued to make the mistake of mischaracterizing the reality in Gaza. The description is that there are two million unfortunate people there, and one day a terrible terrorist organization called Hamas came along, forcibly took over the Strip, and therefore it is right for us to fight Hamas, but we have nothing against the two million unfortunate people who found themselves in this situation."
"This naive description has nothing to do with reality," he continued. "In 2007, Gaza became a state in every sense, with clearly defined borders, an effective central government capable of collecting taxes, managing all the health care, education and sanitation systems, and so on. It has a completely independent foreign policy and its own army. The correct way to define what happened on October 7 is that the State of Gaza launched a war against the State of Israel."
Eiland argued that this flawed understanding of reality also shaped the IDF's assessment of Hamas. "For years, it was known that on the other side of the border there was a Nukhba force of at least 3,000 men, well-equipped and well-trained, with extremely high religious motivation, and just 10 minutes away from reaching any Israeli community or IDF base. Their clear and defined mission was to raid the State of Israel."
"In all IDF situation assessments over the years, from the division and command levels to the General Staff, when they discussed what might happen, they defined the worst-case scenario as a simultaneous attack by 60 terrorists. Wait a minute, you know they have 3,000, and you're saying the worst case is 60? How did such a huge gap emerge?"
"The answer is very simple. It is entirely philosophical," Eiland explained, arguing that the military's assessment was shaped by its definition of Hamas as a terrorist organization conducting guerrilla warfare through individual terrorists.
The sin of belief
According to Eiland, the same mistake was evident along Israel's northern border on October 7. "In 2014, Hezbollah established the Radwan Force, numbering 6,000 terrorists. Gradually, they moved closer to the border, building bunkers and infrastructure. The formal mission of the 91st Division is to defend the Galilee, but it did not prepare for defense."
"To do that, you need to implement the principles of defense: depth and reserves. What did the Galilee Division actually have at 6:30 a.m. on October 7? A thin line of outposts, no depth, no second line, no reserves and, most importantly, no available firepower capable of effectively delivering a large volume of fire against points of infiltration."
Eiland argued that the series of failures was not the result of a mistaken strategic conception, but something more fundamental.
"You first adopt a belief about what will happen and what will not happen, and from that moment you arrange the facts to fit that belief," he said. "Your brain is flexible enough to adapt reality to the belief instead of the other way around."
"That is worse than a mistaken conception, because a conception at least supposedly reflects a flawed thought process, but still a thought process. I'm talking about belief. Belief that has no rational basis, whose entire foundation is emotional and is built on many false assumptions that I developed over the years and never even examine."
Despite his criticism, Eiland identified two areas in which he believes the IDF has improved over the past three years. The first is basic military discipline, which he described as "appalling on October 7."
"The army has learned, and I think the improvement is real," he said.
The second improvement, he argued, is the recognition that Israel needs buffer zones along its borders. "In both Lebanon and Gaza, Israel cannot defend itself when there are communities along the border and, on the other side, an enemy 200 meters away with offensive intentions," he said.
However, Eiland argued that the situation along the Syrian border is significantly different. "There are many operational and tactical differences, and the need to hold territory in Syria is lower than in Lebanon," he explained.
He stressed that he was not proposing a unilateral Israeli withdrawal from the territory. "Israel can return to the border line provided there is an American plan guaranteeing that advanced weapons manufactured in Turkey or Russia will not enter Syria," he said.
"We can give up that particular enclave inside Syria. It is a risk worth taking, provided the strategic benefit we receive in return is far more important."

Over half of Amaha clients live with mental health concerns for a year before seeking help; 56% report self-harm thoughts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
04:51:15 UTC
13:51:15 KST

Many people struggle with mental health issues for over a year before seeking professional help
NEW DELHI: Mental health concerns can persist for months, sometimes years, before people seek professional help. By then, the distress may be affecting their relationships, work and ability to manage everyday tasks. More than half of people who eventually sought care had lived with their concerns for over a year, while 56.2% reported thoughts of self-harm before reaching professional support, according to the Amaha Mental Health Report 2026.The report is based on responses from 13,825 people who answered questions before beginning care with the mental healthcare provider between October 2025 and September 2026. Only 11.3% sought help within a month of experiencing mental health concerns.Dr Amit Malik, psychiatrist, founder and CEO of Amaha, said, “India’s progress in mental health must be judged by whether people can get timely, effective care, not simply by how openly we talk about it. These are the accounts of people who reached us; they should make us ask who is still unable to access care.”He added that friends, families and communities were vital to helping people recognise their needs and find care, and said finding treatment should not become “another test of a person’s resilience”.
Nearly 95% of respondents reported at least two concerns, averaging five each. Anxiety was most common (72.1%), followed by stress (67.5%), low mood (58.3%), relationship difficulties (55.6%) and sleep disturbances in over a third. The report also found a gap between self-reported distress and clinical diagnosis: 33% of those initially reporting stress were later diagnosed with depression, while among those reporting repetitive thoughts and behaviours, 32% were diagnosed with depression and 11% with obsessive-compulsive disorder.Before approaching a professional, many respondents relied on informal support or tried to manage their concerns on their own. More than half (54.5%) had spoken to friends or family, while 44.6% had turned to self-help resources such as books, apps, videos and online communities. Nearly a third had tried therapy previously, and 19.4% had used prescribed medication.Avoidant coping strategies, including excessive screen time, oversleeping and overworking, were reported by 82.7%. Another 15.4% said they had turned to alcohol or other harmful substances instead of professional support.The impact extended to everyday functioning. Only 12.3% said they could manage all their daily tasks, while 27.3% said they could not manage most tasks or any at all.
Young adults and working professionals formed the bulk of the cohort. Those aged 25–34 accounted for 51.3% of respondents, followed by 26.9% aged 18–24. Working professionals made up 64.3%, while students accounted for 15.3% and unemployed people 7.9%.Friends were the most frequently named contact in a mental health crisis (33.9%), followed by spouses (20.5%) and siblings (18.1%), underscoring the role of family and social networks in recognising distress and helping people access care.
Anuja Jaiswal is a Senior Assistant Editor at The Times of India, with an impressive 18-year career in narrative journalism. She specializes in health and heritage reporting, expertly simplifying complex health information to make it engaging and understandable for readers. Her deep dives into heritage topics are well-researched, resulting in captivating narratives that resonate with her audience. Over the years, she has worked in Chandigarh, Chhattisgarh and West UP, gaining diverse on-ground experience that shapes her storytelling.

HAMBURG, October 14. /TASS/. The first trial on the Nord Stream and Nord Stream 2 pipelines’ explosions is beginning in Germany four years after the terrorist attack. Ukrainian national Sergey K. will appear before the Hanseatic Higher Regional Court of Hamburg.
