INDIA bloc challenges SIR process but not its validity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
22:46:39 UTC
07:46:39 KST

NEW DELHI: Why did opposition INDIA bloc, after making special intensive revision (SIR) of electoral rolls the central point of its attack on Election Commission and govt, give up the challenge to the constitutional and statutory validity of SIR in their joint writ petition before Supreme Court?Opposition members, led by LoP Rahul Gandhi, stated in the petition that they were not challenging SIR's validity in view of the SC judgement on Bihar SIR, which was conducted by EC based on its June 24, 2025, decision.
That could be because SC in its May 27 judgement had examined the following questions - whether EC had the power to conduct SIR, whether SIR had a legitimate purpose and the process was proportionate to the object to be achieved, and whether the SIR procedure was contrary to Representation of the People Act and Registration of Electors Act, 1960 - and found there was nothing amiss in SIR's conduct or the process adopted to achieve the objective of weeding out voters who have died, shifted base or duplicate voters.SC had categorically ruled that SIR exercise "neither stands in direct conflict with RP Act and the 1960 Rules, nor does it detract from the constitutional imperative of free and fair elections".It had said, "The impugned SIR exercise, as conducted, satisfies requirements of proportionality. The measures adopted bear a rational nexus to the objective sought to be achieved, are not manifestly excessive, and are accompanied by sufficient procedural safeguards to prevent arbitrary exclusion."
Since the judgement was of May 27, and attained finality as no one sought its review or correction, the INDIA bloc petitioners could not have challenged SIR's validity, thus limiting their challenge to alleged irregularities in the process of SIR and large-scale deletion of voters without giving them proper opportunity to rebut deletion.SC, in its five-month-old judgement, had said, "The statutory framework of RP Act itself provides for a situation where EC may direct a special revision under Section 21(3), in such manner as it may think fit and for reasons to be recorded."It also said "a reading of the impugned order, dated June 24, 2025, reveals EC has recorded the basis" on which it decided to conduct SIR. "We are equally satisfied that, in its object and design, the impugned SIR bears a direct nexus to the constitutional goal of a free and fair election. Free and fair elections do not rest merely upon the mechanics of polling. They equally depend upon the integrity, accuracy and purity of the electoral roll which forms the foundation of the democratic process," it had said.
"The impugned SIR, therefore, is not a process designed to subvert the established procedure, but one intended to secure the constitutional mandate of free and fair elections by ensuring the roll on which election rests is accurate and reliable," it had said, adding SIR had a direct nexus with the object of ensuring purity and accuracy of the electoral roll.

Does Feminism Need More Than Liberalism?
Vanessa Yeung considers feminist responses to Rawlsian liberalism.
In most modern liberal democracies, women have the same legal rights as men, such as the right to vote, own property, and to seek employment. Yet, beneath a veneer of equality, deep-seated domestic power dynamics and patriarchal norms persist. This raises a fundamental question for feminist philosophy: Is liberalism enough?
At its core, liberalism champions the individual’s autonomous choice and wants this freedom equally for all. If liberty means liberty for all, then it means equal liberty for women and for men. Why then is there any need to be a feminist, when one can simply be a liberal? However, if we anchor our definition of liberalism to that popular version developed by the late John Rawls, then some modern feminist political philosophers, most notably Catharine MacKinnon and Susan Moller Okin, will say that liberalism isn’t good enough.
Nussbaum (top), MacKinnon (on the right) and Okin (on the left) by Gail Campbell 2026
Rawls’s Liberal Utopia
John Rawls was an American political philosopher who famously advocated for an egalitarian form of liberalism. He argued in A Theory of Justice (1971) that the just society is one that people would choose even without knowing what position they would occupy within it. He describes a thought experiment in which rational people design their future society while behind ‘a veil of ignorance’, which hides from them anything about their gender, wealth, race, or other background. For Rawls, this choice in these circumstances would create a presumption in favour of an equal society. He argued that two fundamental principles would naturally arise. Firstly, every person would have an equal right to a basic scheme of liberties (the ‘equality of opportunity’ principle); and secondly, social or economic inequalities would only be allowed if they also benefitted the least advantaged members of society (this he called the ‘difference principle’).
Together these two principles allow that inequality can be acceptable – if everyone benefits by it, and an unequal distribution of resources does not reduce any citizen’s basic rights and liberties. Rawls argues that individuals behind the veil of ignorance would vote in favour of these two principles, so that no one would be radically disadvantaged once they enter the game of life, as even the person in the most difficult starting position will still be empowered to succeed better than in other systems (this is the difference principle). In this sense, Rawls’ support for fair opportunity suitably accommodates general feminist ideology. Indeed, this basic framework for equality of opportunity initially appears perfectly compatible with feminism, as both men and women would equally thrive in Rawls’ vision of an ideal society. Behind the veil of ignorance, it would be rational to choose political institutions that protect women’s rights, since citizens could as likely as not be women themselves when entering society. So it seems that the principles of fair opportunity, equality of basic liberties, and the idea of the ‘veil of ignorance’ do strongly align with feminist principles. However, some feminists view Rawls’ liberalism as overlooking justice within the family.
Rawls presents his stance on feminism through ideas on justice within the family. The problem comes down to the traditional distinction between the public and private spheres. Rawls seems to assume the family is non-political, and so categorised as part of the private sphere. Unfortunately, removing the family unit from the world of politics could imply that families are not required to follow the Rawlsian (or other liberal) regulations for the public sphere, but instead have the autonomy to make other decisions on how resources are distributed. As a result, women within their families may sometimes remain subordinate and unequal, despite the public sphere operating on strong liberal ideas of freedom of opportunity.
Feminists Read Rawls
New Zealand philosopher Susan Moller Okin raised this issue in Justice, Gender, and the Family (1989), writing that Rawlsian principles are “deeply and pervasively gender-structured,” specifically because gendered social and moral norms operating inside the family are ignored, resulting in problems that fail to be resolved, such as domestic violence. In distinction from Rawls’ position, Okin says the family should be treated as political, because it operates as a social institution involving power dynamics, resource allocation, and diverging interests. And families do play a significant role both socially and politically. Okin also argues against Rawls’ assumption that removing barriers between the public and private sphere is the best way to bring justice to a family unit.
On the other hand, in Sex and Social Justice (2000), Martha Nussbaum defends the idea that liberalism is sufficient for accommodating feminism in social and political relationships, because liberalism “must respect and promote liberty of choice, and it must respect and promote the equal worth of persons as choosers”. She further argues that liberal insights are crucial to women. But she also identifies current international feminist issues that have not been addressed by liberalism, including educational inequality, social norms, and domestic labour. In contrast to Rawls, who moves from abstract rights to the general potential for human flourishing, Nussbaum uses a ‘capabilities’ approach, focusing on equality and fairness based on each person’s inherent potential. Nevertheless, she demonstrates that the capabilities view strengthens rather than replaces liberalism, and can adapt Rawls’ theory by extending his ideas of a just society to include material, social, and educational conditions for women to develop their capabilities. Thus Nussbaum presents feminism through an extended and ‘reformed’ version of Rawlsian liberalism – a solution that apparently fixes the flaws of abstract individualism and the neglect of the private sphere in classical Rawlsian liberalism. Yet despite Nussbaum’s defence of liberalism as being able to accommodate feminism, others argue that her version of Rawlsian liberalism as reestablishing the relationship between the public and private sphere might deviate so much from Rawls’ core principles that it can no longer be classified as a Rawlsian theory.
In complete distinction, Catharine MacKinnon argues in Toward a Feminist Theory of the State (1989) that liberalism is fundamentally incapable of accommodating feminist insights, particularly concerning social relationships, She argues that women live in a society so deeply imbued with patriarchal values that their decisions are not truly autonomous, as liberalism presupposes, since social conditioning has influenced women to generally simply accept male dominance.
MacKinnon’s views mirror Okin’s, to the extent that both say the private sphere is the main source of women’s inequality. MacKinnon cites the cases of human trafficking and sexual harassment to argue that society should sometimes intervene in the private sphere in order to achieve equality between genders. This directly contradicts Rawls’ version of liberalism. However, MacKinnon explores this issue through a more radical lens than Okin, since she also critiques the capitalist structure of society, and emphasises that the only way to finally resolve gender inequality would be to eradicate current oppressive power structures completely, and undertake a complete transformation of society’s beliefs and values.
For MacKinnon, political liberalism is flawed because it promotes only formal freedom, that is, the freedom to make legal decisions. She suggests that by contrast, feminism strives for the kind of freedom that Isaiah Berlin called positive liberty – the active ability of individuals to fulfil their own potential. (This is in contrast to negative liberty, which concerns what a person can do without being obstructed by others). Nevertheless, typical feminists might perceive MacKinnon’s radical ideas as unachievable in our contemporary world.
Conclusions
So can liberalism accommodate feminist insights into social and political relationships? The reformed Rawlsian liberalism put forward by Nussbaum seems the most realistic way forward. Feminism, at its heart, is a profoundly liberal idea, in that it aligns with the idea of the citizen as a free and dignified maker of choices. However, if to be compatible with feminism Rawlsian liberalism requires changes on the lines of Nussbaum’s re-interpretation of it, then one may ask whether it remains Rawlsian (or even liberal) at all. The more radical interpretations of feminism seen in MacKinnon’s argument suggest that reforms in liberalism itself will be necessary to accommodate feminist insights, since its current ideas on autonomy and neutrality are shaped for an underlying patriarchal framework. Ultimately, this debate illustrates that the ability of liberalism to accommodate feminist insights socially and politically may rely on how far it can be adapted to suit feminism’s progressive values.
© Vanessa Yeung 2026
Vanessa Yeung is an A-Level student from Tormead School in Guildford, Surrey.

To Philosophize is to Learn How to Say Goodbye
Scott F. Parker reflects on philosophy as a preparation for death.
The first day I visited my dad in the care facility where he was recovering from a serious infection in his prosthetic aortic valve, I got the clear impression that he was trying to feel out whether I would support his decision to stop treatment. “You people don’t know what it’s like in here,” he said more than once, allowing for a certain ambiguity as to whether ‘in here’ referred to the facility or to something more metaphysical. ‘You people’ included my mom and sister, both of whom lived in Portland, saw him frequently, and were understood in advance to be unreceptive to his appeals for mercy, no matter how subtle. In me, I gathered, he saw his hope for someone who wasn’t so sentimental as to prolong suffering by denying death, or, to put it another way, someone who would be willing to relieve suffering by hastening death. He was not wrong. Based on what I’d been able to discern from daily phone calls with my mom, herself a retired physician, it wasn’t unlikely that his decline would be permanent. Knowing what I knew of my father, it seemed cruel to ask him to go on in a state of dependence, unable to walk, unable to feed or wash himself, unable to carry on a coherent conversation or distinguish between people, days, or ideas. A man who strived for independence and clarity his whole life, the one time he’d had the energy to talk to me on the phone, he had sounded like a stranger – disoriented, confused, helpless.
Yet if I was ready to play my part in facilitating my father’s death, it wasn’t only from a sense of wanting to preserve his dignity, but also in the confidence that a lifetime of dedicated preparation had readied him for this moment. He was a philosopher both by nature and by application. For far longer than I’d had the chance to know him, he had been engaging with questions of meaning, truth, and reality as if his life depended on it. His commitment to philosophy was mysterious to me when I was young, but as a teenager I began to appreciate that it was born of necessity. Knowing what it meant to be human was life or death for him. As a child, my father suffered from severe OCD before such a diagnosis was available. His suffering was compounded by the notion of sin he internalized from his Catholic upbringing. The only treatment he was offered beyond prayer came in the form of heavy tranquilizers that consigned him to bed for long stretches of his adolescence. Things didn’t really improve for him until he began reading philosophy in his teenage years. He found, in its sober naturalistic attempts to discern the nature of reality, a sense of equanimity. In a calm moment, his obsessive thoughts and compulsive behaviors could be relaxed, even released. The world wasn’t the problem, he could see: thinking about it the wrong way was the problem. String enough calm moments together, and it’s possible to achieve something like a life.
After his most acute suffering had been relieved, he could see clearly that the reality of the human condition still remained: he, like everyone, and like everything living, was going to die. How was it possible to live in the face of that fact without terror, without comforting oneself with the promise of an afterlife? His answer to this question isn’t one I can succinctly summarize here, but it involves a constant engagement with the question itself. Philosophy, for my dad, is conducted with the human condition in mind as a preparation for death. In taking such an approach, he joins a venerable tradition that runs through Socrates, Cicero, Montaigne, and the existentialists. In Plato’s Apology, for instance, Socrates concludes his speech just prior to his unjust execution by the Athenian state with these words: “Now it is time that we are going, I to die and you to live, but which of us has the happier prospect is unknown to anyone but God.” Soon after, he will willingly drink the hemlock, leaving it to antiquity to make sense of his story.
Image © Susan Auletta 2026 Please visit instagram.com/sm_auletta
Since my dad introduced me to philosophy when I was a teenager, I have apprenticed myself in the same tradition. So, was I ready for his death? That was the question my dad’s health put to him directly, and indirectly to me. A lifetime of philosophy was being put to the test, I thought. And, I thought, I knew what the test demanded. Accept finitude. Don’t pursue every measure to extend life simply out of a terror of death. Welcome death, when it arrives, like an old friend, whose visit to paraphrase Montaigne, we have been expecting: “Ah, so today is the day you have decided to drop by. Come in!”
Easy enough to say, harder to achieve. But while there is a temptation to cling to life, there can be an opposing temptation to escape from it, and the line between accepting death and pursuing it can be quite thin. Like the suicide that might have earlier provided the most immediate (and permanent) relief from his OCD, the death now looming before my father promised him something he’d always desired: freedom from worldly entanglements. The needful body had asserted its absolute demands, but in so doing had exposed its limits. On the other side of the failing body was its complete absence – whether into pure mind or pure oblivion made little difference; any escape from the physical and its psychological overflow was preferable to the chronic pain and suffering that living entailed.
But was it a noble philosopher before me in the hospital bed, or a feeble old man?
My dad’s complaints were less metaphysical, I noticed, than personal. Like a Woody Allen joke, the food was both terrible and served in small portions. There were also too many pills, too many blood draws, too many visits from nurses, whose speech patterns were too bright and bubbly. Physical therapy was a waste of time. Come to think of it, the failures of the entire American medical system were on full display in this suburban care facility, “I’m not going to make it six weeks here,” he said – whether as a threat to leave or a promise to die was, once again, open to interpretation.
Am I giving an impression of a kind of immaturity? I mean to. He wasn’t here contemplating death with careful and wise detachment, but out of an immediate and reactionary frustration. Not that I wasn’t sympathetic. He had been sick for weeks and was not thinking clearly. He was confused about basic things, like what time of year it was or how long he’d been sick; how he’d arrived at the hospital and what exactly was wrong with him; how to check his email or treat people with kindness. Lost like this in time, neither could he understand the recovery he stood to make, nor indeed the recovery he was already making. In the four days I spent with him, he showed marked improvement physically, mentally, and emotionally. He still refused physical therapy, and sometimes, maddeningly, his antibiotics (it was important to him to affirm his autonomy however he could). But he could sit up longer, talk with more focus, smile briefly at his situation. If the recovery continued, where might he be in six weeks? Where might he be like after six months of home recovery? Was it wishful thinking on my part when I saw glimpses of recognition in him? Perhaps. But in those moments I read on his face an acceptance that life is as unpredictable as death, and that no one, not even he, controls the future. Call it God or call it life, the teacher was laughing, and the student could either be resentful, or join in the laughter.
The cruel irony of my father’s particular decline was that when he was closest to death he was least able to draw on the preparations he’d made for it. So philosophy went only so far: in his extremis, he was revealed to be not a disembodied thinker, but an embodied one – in a body that would fail and rot, and become, as Cornel West says, the stuff of terrestrial worms. Compromised as he was cognitively, he could not reason as to whether or not it was his time to go, and couldn’t see that it was not yet.
Maybe philosophy’s true consolations belong to the survivors. Had my father died suddenly from his infection, his death in a way would not have happened to him, as there would have been no more him to whom things happened. It would have happened to me and my mom and my sister, and whoever else was touched by his life. So maybe to philosophize is to learn how to witness death and proceed in life?
Had my dad died when he almost did, I would have been left to wonder about the meaning of his death. While I can’t know with anything like certainty what I would have thought and felt, I suspect gratitude would have played a part: gratitude for the inherited practice of holding death close in my consciousness and steeling myself against its various eventualities, which I found to be invigorating and life-affirming, the very opposite of morbid. Memento mori (the old admonition to ‘Remember that you must die’) is to me the sound of beauty and wisdom and, yes, love.
Everyone I or you meet is a corpse in the making. It is utterly clarifying and strangely consoling to remember that we – me, yes, but also you – are the stuff of terrestrial worms or the fuel for fire. The fact that we’re here is a source of wonder, especially given the fact that so soon we won’t be.
© Scott F. Parker 2026
Scott F. Parker is the author of Time Again: An Essay on Zhuangzi, Fatherhood, and Other Matters of Life and Death (Shanti Arts), amongst other books.

Brief Lives
Günther Anders (1902-1992)
Clive Webb on how Anders warned humanity about the moral costs of technological progress.
Günther Anders was a German Jewish philosopher who spent much of his life in exile. He devoted his work to understanding the moral consequences of modern technology. Born at the start of the twentieth century and shaped by fascism, world war, and the atomic age, he became one of the earliest and most uncompromising critics of the assumption that technological advance automatically amounts to an improvement. Anders argued that, on the contrary, humanity has entered an era in which its moral and imaginative capacities can no longer keep pace with the technological progress it’s bringing into being. Long before artificial intelligence, automation, or planetary ecological crisis became part of everyday discussion, he warned that modern societies were acquiring powers they were no longer able fully to understand, let alone control. Anders saw a widening mismatch between what human beings are capable of and what we can meaningfully imagine the consequences of.
A Life in Exile
Günther Anders was born Günther Stern on 12 July 1902 in Breslau, then part of Germany. His parents, Clara and William Stern, were leading psychologists who kept detailed developmental records of him and his sisters. Growing up as the subject of constant observation, Anders later suggested, gave him an early awareness of what it meant to be treated as an object rather than a person, a theme that would recur in his critique of modern technological societies.
During the First World War he was sent to a labour detachment in France and encountered wounded and traumatised soldiers. After the war, Anders studied philosophy in Hamburg and Freiburg. He completed his doctorate under Edmund Husserl, and later studied with Martin Heidegger. During this time, he met Hannah Arendt, whom he married in 1929. Academic success, however, eluded him. Unable to secure a university post, Anders moved to Berlin, working as a journalist and cultural critic. Following the Nazi rise to power in 1933, the political atmosphere rapidly darkened. He adopted the name ‘Anders’ – German for ‘different’ – partly because a less recognisably Jewish name made it easier to work in an increasingly hostile cultural climate.
When Anders later learned that his name appeared in a diary confiscated by the Gestapo from his friend the playwright Bertolt Brecht, he understood that time had run out. He fled Berlin on a night train, escaping first to Paris, and, after his divorce from Arendt in 1937, eventually moved to the United States.
Exile did not bring security. Anders worked briefly for the Office of War Information, but resigned after refusing to translate propaganda that racially stereotyped the Japanese. “I had not run away from the fascists to America in order to produce fascist American pamphlets,” he later remarked. He tried, and failed, to establish himself as a screenwriter in Hollywood, and for a time made ends meet working for a costume and theatrical property company. In 1950 he returned to Europe, settling in Vienna, where he lived for the rest of his life, which included two further marriages.
The Atomic Age
The event that most decisively shaped Anders’ philosophy came in August 1945. A radio report about the atomic bomb dropped on Hiroshima left him speechless. The bomb revealed what Anders would come to regard as the central fact of modernity: humanity has acquired the technical capacity to annihilate itself, yet lacks the imaginative resources to grasp what it’s done. So for Anders, the atomic bomb was not simply a weapon but a transformation in the human condition: it revealed a chasm between the power of what could be produced and the capacity to comprehend its consequences. In his words, “We are smaller than ourselves.”
Anders thought about Hiroshima obsessively, later publishing Burning Conscience (1961), a book based on his correspondence with Claude Eatherly, one of the airmen involved in the mission. He believed that Eatherly’s post war breakdown exposed a moral truth that society preferred to ignore.
From this point onwards, Anders became an uncompromising critic of nuclear weapons. With the onset of the Cold War, he argued that the ideological opposition between East and West was far less dangerous than the arsenals both sides were busily constructing. Philosophy, he concluded, could no longer afford the luxury of political neutrality.
That refusal of neutrality became concrete in the 1960s, when Anders was a member of the International War Crimes Tribunal led by Bertrand Russell and Jean-Paul Sartre, which investigated military atrocities in Vietnam. The tribunal had no legal authority, and its findings were dismissed by many at the time, yet for Anders its significance lay elsewhere: it was an attempt to bring acts of violence back within the compass of human judgement, and to insist that the vastness of modern violence does not absolve those who carry it out.
The Obsolescence of the Human
Anders’ most important work, The Obsolescence of the Human, appearing in two volumes (in 1956 and 1980), was an attempt to describe what he saw as the dawn of a new epoch, of a world in which human beings were increasingly overshadowed by the machines they’d made. At the heart of the idea lies Anders’ concept of the ‘Promethean Gap’ – the growing distance between what human beings can produce and what we can morally and imaginatively comprehend. Borrowing from the myth of Prometheus, who stole fire from the gods to give it to humanity, Anders argued that modern technology had placed in peoples’ hands powers they could not control, since what we could make, we could no longer responsibly imagine. Nowhere were these dynamics more dangerous than in the case of nuclear weapons. Nuclear annihilation exceeds our predictive and emotional capacities. Anders observed that it could be psychologically harder to kill one person than to kill millions, precisely because we can imagine the pain and suffering of an individual, but not the destruction of an entire population. “The apocalyptic danger,” Anders warned, “is all the more menacing because we are unable to picture the immensity of such a catastrophe.” When consequences cannot be imagined, the moral inhibitions that would normally restrain action begin to lose force. Thus the defining ethical question of the atomic age was no longer how humanity should live, but whether it would continue to live at all.
Closely linked to the Promethean Gap idea was what Anders called ‘Promethean Shame’ – a feeling of inferiority that arises when humans compare themselves to the technologies they have created. Surrounded by flawless machines that operate faster, more precisely, or on a far greater scale than human beings ever could, people come to see themselves as defective. For Anders, this shame isn’t a psychological weakness but an understandable response to technological conditions that systematically devalue humanity.
Technology & Responsibility
For Anders, nuclear weapons offered the clearest warning that humanity’s capacity to produce technologies had outrun its ability to responsively comprehend their consequences. With the creation of the bomb, he argued, humanity became simultaneously more powerful and more vulnerable than ever before. “Because we are the first Titans,” he wrote, “we are also the first dwarfs or pygmies.”
Gunther Anders with Hannah Arendt c. 1929
This failure of imagination was compounded, Anders believed, by the way modern technologies reorganise responsibility. As systems grow more complex, individuals increasingly act as operators following prescribed procedures rather than as agents exercising judgement, and decision making is delegated to machines using models and calculations. In such conditions, responsibility does not so much disappear as dissolve into the system. Moreover, to mistrust the output of the machine comes to feel irrational, even subversive. As Anders put it, to question the conclusions delivered by technical systems is to question “the very principle of our mechanised existence.” This surrender of judgement means that decisions of unimaginable consequences could be carried out as if they require no deliberation at all, because they’re automated.
Anders traced this pattern beyond weapons systems to the wider technological environment, particularly the rise of mass media. In his essay ‘The Phantom World of Television’ (1956), he argued that television does not merely transmit information but fundamentally restructures how human beings relate to reality. The paradox, Anders suggested, is that to encounter the world we now have to retreat indoors. Here, events come to us mediated through images, while the immediate world around us grows strangely unreal. “When that which is remote becomes familiar,” he wrote, “that which is familiar becomes remote. When the phantom becomes real, reality itself becomes a phantom.” In this sense, life is no longer lived, but consumed. Television (and by extension, phone screens) encourages passive spectatorship in place of direct engagement, reorganising perception and thinking around itself rather than around human needs. Once again, technology dictates the terms on which the world is encountered, widening further the Promethean Gap between human capacity and human understanding.
These concerns came vividly into focus with the Moon landing in July 1969. Like some 650 million others, Anders watched Neil Armstrong step onto the lunar surface via a TV screen. What should have been an occasion for existential reflection – a moment to glimpse the Earth from a cosmic perspective and sense its fragility – struck him instead as curiously diminished. The Moon had been domesticated, reduced to a familiar object within the décor of everyday life. Anders captured the moment with characteristic irony, imagining living rooms around the world arranged with “the record collection on the right, the bar on the left, and in between, the universe.”And for all the technological brilliance on display, nothing fundamental had changed in how human beings understood themselves or their responsibilities. Once again, the reach of human power had expanded, while the capacity to reflect meaningfully on its consequences lagged behind.
Why Anders Matters Now
For much of his life, Anders was treated as a marginal figure – too political for academic philosophy, too philosophical for political activism. Yet the problems he identified have only intensified in the years since his death. With several of his major works now appearing in English translation, Anders is finally being recognised as one of the twentieth century’s most prescient thinkers of technology, and his warnings speak directly to the pressures of the present. Although The Obsolescence of the Human became widely read in Europe, much of Anders’s work remained untranslated for decades. Only now is an English language readership catching up with a thinker who refused the comforting illusion that technological development necessarily amounts to moral progress.
Anders believed that responsibility begins with imagination – with the effort to picture realities beyond our immediate experience. Without making that effort, the gap between what we understand and what we can do threatens to become catastrophic. His core question therefore remains urgent: Can we still master the world we’re making, or have we already become obsolete in relation to our own creations?
© Clive Webb 2026
Clive Webb is Professor of Modern American History at the University of Sussex.

Fraudulent Hope?

Fraudulent Hope?
Alice Figes agrees with Ernst Bloch that hope can build worlds or destroy them, and philosophy’s task is to tell the difference.
Writing in the 1930s, the German philosopher Ernst Bloch (1885-1977) became fascinated by a lesser-known version of the Helen of Troy story that differs fundamentally from the Homeric tale. This older variant, preserved in fragments by the lyric poet Stesichorus, dramatised by Euripides in his play Helen of 412 BC, and later adapted by Strauss in his 1928 opera, has Helen never go to Troy at all. Thousands of ships are launched, ten years of brutal bloodshed ensue, an entire city is razed to the ground, all so Menelaus can retrieve what was stolen from him – the woman who had been declared the most desirable person ever to have lived. Yet in this telling the captive Helen was only a phantom. The goddess Hera, humiliated when Paris chose Aphrodite over her in a divine beauty contest, played a trick on these mere humans, fashioning out of cloud an image of Helen with the appearance of substance but nothing behind it – an eidolon. The real Helen was spirited away to Egypt, where she sat out the entire war in peace and relative uneventfulness. Menelaus knew none of this. When he finally locates the real flesh-and-blood Helen, his bewilderment gives way to deflation, because no actual woman could live up to what he had spent ten years idealising.
So, was it the woman’s fault that Troy was burned, or was it due to the gap between desire and its actualisation – in other words, to Helen’s very unattainability? For Bloch this older myth held the key to the most dangerous yet most necessary force in human life – one he would spend a career trying to understand.
Bloch fled Nazism in 1933, settling on the East Coast of America, where he moved in the orbit of the Frankfurt School. He was fascinated by the pull of the future – by our perennial orientation towards what he called the ‘not yet’. Writing through the darkest years of the twentieth century, he observed in his magnum opus The Principle of Hope (1954) how this drive towards the future can both emancipate and imperil.
His diagnosis was that the concept of the future had been dangerously neglected within Western philosophy. In the writings of the nineteenth century philosopher GWF Hegel he saw a static vision of the absolute, which he understood as a fetishization of completeness; while in Sigmund Freud’s work he saw a closedness – an understanding of the unconscious aimed merely at reconstructing what had already been, not venturing towards the unsettling novelty of the future, the horizon forever shaping human desires. Drawing on psychoanalysis, German Romanticism, Marxism, and Judeo-Christian messianic thought, Bloch then made the audacious claim that hope is not merely a feature of human consciousness but a “basic determination within objective reality as a whole” (POH, Vol 1, p7). Hope shows that the world itself is unfinished, and that humanity is oriented towards what does not yet exist.
It’s in this register that the older Helen myth does its work for Bloch. Menelaus becomes not simply a deceived husband but a metaphor for the human condition itself – a creature pulled forward by the anticipatory strength of his own desire; a force so powerful that he cannot see through the illusion. The phantom Helen is a paradigmatic example of what hope aims for when its forward pull outruns reality. Yet Bloch’s point is not to dismiss Menelaus as a fool, nor to dismiss hope as delusion. The deeper question the alternative myth poses for Bloch is whether the gap between desire and its actualisation is an innate human defect to be lamented, or potentially the very engine that drives human beings to make the world a better place.
Image © Miles Walker 2026 Please visit mileswalker.com
Hope For Transformation
The Principle of Hope established Bloch as one of the most ambitious modern philosophers. In this astonishing and encyclopaedic three volume work, Bloch traces an emancipatory vision of hope across millennia. He sees it in Moses leading his people out of Egypt towards a promised land most of them would never reach; in the radical preacher Thomas Müntzer, who in 1525 mobilised German peasants behind a dream of heaven brought down to earth, and who was executed for his troubles; in the European revolutionary fervours of 1789 and 1848, when the image of a different world propelled ordinary people to fight on the streets of Paris, Vienna, and Berlin. But for Bloch the not-yet did not belong only to political rupture. He found it in the soaring vaults of Gothic cathedrals, straining upward towards something they could not quite touch; or in late Beethoven, whose private self broke free of ‘the merely inner life’ towards a shared cosmic horizon (the trumpet call in Fidelio, signalling a rescue still to come, was for Bloch the very sound of hope); and in the canvases of the Expressionists, such as Marc, Kandinsky, or Kokoschka, which registered a content not yet thinkable – what Bloch called ‘the not-yet-conscious pressing towards form’. Hope, Bloch insisted, was the ‘warm stream’ of consciousness running beneath culture itself, and the surplus of human desire that could never be fully satisfied by any present arrangement, and which therefore kept history moving. The intellectual historian Cat Moir, rejecting Jürgen Habermas’s dismissal of Bloch as a ‘Romantic Marxist’, has recast Bloch as a speculative materialist ahead of his time – a thinker for whom matter is perennially in movement, pregnant with possibility.
What’s remarkable about Bloch’s idea of hope was that he was devising it in the 1930s, as the home he had always known crumbled around him. For all he knew, the Third Reich would win the war and fascism could become the new global order, as it found support even in the United States. His extended family were either fleeing Germany or being sent to the death camps, and his closest intellectual companion, Walter Benjamin, took his own life on the Spanish border in September 1940, believing that escape from the Nazis was impossible. Bloch, who had escaped, kept writing – and what he wrote about, in the teeth of catastrophe and despair, was hope. He connected to a utopian tradition he saw as old as the writing of history itself, which he had traced in his previous works Spirit of Utopia (1918) and Heritage of Our Times (1935). In these works, Bloch had transformed that tradition, wresting ‘utopian’ from its long-standing pejorative use, and also shifting utopianism from the static blueprints associated with Plato, Thomas More, William Morris, or Edward Bellamy, towards a process-based utopianism. To Bloch, hope was a force that had always belonged to the dispossessed and those in pursuit of humanisation and democracy. Longing intensifies through deprivation, and the dream of a transformed world burns brightest where the present world is unbearable.
What’s most striking is where Bloch was willing to look for this utopian current: in religion. After the French Revolution, most materialists, Marx above all, had dismissed religion as ‘false consciousness’, the residue of a superstitious age that progress would sweep away. Yet despite his atheism, Bloch refused this dismissal. For him religion was one of the great archives of human longing, ‘’a speculative apprehension of the future” that had carried the utopian impulse across millennia. He read the Hebrew prophets, Jesus’s Sermon on the Mount, and the Christian utopianism of the late Middle Ages, not as the ideological wallpaper of bourgeois society but as registers of a desire for transformation. Moses was for him the prototypical prophetic founder, the figure who embodied his own teaching. Müntzer’s revolt early in the Reformation drew its force from a Christian idea of the ‘last days’ bent into political insurgency. Moreover, the Christian ideal of loving one’s neighbour, Bloch suggested, echoed the Marxist vision of a stateless community in which human beings might at last live as equals. To dismiss all this as mere delusion is to throw away one of the richest seams of utopian energy the human species has produced, which Bloch, employing theological language for atheist purposes, called ‘transcendence without transcendence’. Indeed, Bloch was the first to argue that Marx himself was an unwitting utopian: that for all Marx’s celebrated demolition of contemporary utopians Saint-Simon, Fourier, and Owen, the classless society at the heart of Das Kapital was unmistakably utopian in form. It was an image of a redeemed society.
Ernst Bloch by Darren McAndrew
Hope’s Darker Currents
Yet Bloch knew that the same force that propelled prophets and revolutionaries towards a more just world could easily be diverted, hollowed out, and turned against the very people it moved. This is what drew him to the older Helen myth rather than Homer’s version. In Homer, the Trojan War ends in possession. Menelaus reclaims his wife and he forgives her for her infidelity, because her supernatural beauty stuns him into forgiveness. In Stesichorus’ and Euripides’ version, by contrast, there’s no Helen to win – only a phantom that had mobilised armies for nothing. The gods who tricked Menelaus had grasped something essential: it was not Helen herself who launched the ships, but her withholding, leading to her transformation into an ideal – Hera understood that an image suspended just out of reach could mobilise armies and raze cities precisely because it could not be obtained. Drawing on existentialism and phenomenology, Bloch placed this gap between desire and attainment at the heart of what it is to be human: we are constituted by ‘lack’ – by the felt absence of what we are not yet, of what the world is not yet, and our forward motion is the perpetual labour of closing that distance. The world is on the move in search of its essence. The gap between desire and its attaintment is not a defect of human existence, then, but its structure: we are the kind of beings who yearn. And it is precisely this yearning, Bloch saw, that makes us so dangerously vulnerable to those who seek to play God.
Bloch discussed this danger under the name of abstract utopia, by which he meant the utopian impulse cut loose from any concrete mooring in the present world, instead floating free as pure imagination. In our age of economic stagnation, historic levels of inequality, and climate devastation, this delusion runs through new forms. Every day we’re bombarded with false utopian images, that is, visions of a perfect life. (I call them the eidolons of the algorithm.) False visions of perfection are also present in the contemporary cult of self-optimisation – the looksmaxxing, the wellness regimes, the biohacking and clean-eating protocols – where the body itself becomes the canvas onto which the phantom ideal is projected, and perfection is to be carved from one’s own flesh. In Vincenzo Latronico’s acclaimed recent novel Perfection (2022), a young couple curate their Berlin lives through such contemporary images of utopia – of the monstera plants, the honey-coloured floorboards, the Danish furniture – only to find that the reality behind the catalogue photographs dissolves on contact, with the dust, the food stains, and the phone chargers that have to be cleared away to make the image possible. The curated image promises a life, but the life does not arrive. What arrives instead is the deflation Bloch named – the realisation that the gap between the phantom and actual existence can never be crossed.
Image © Miles Walker 2026 Please visit mileswalker.com
At the more predatory ends of the algorithm the consequences are far graver. The impossibly beautiful AI-generated women who flicker through the manosphere’s videos are phantoms manufactured not to be reached by the ordinary, often vulnerable young men they appeal to, but to keep their longing permanently deferred, as the false image cannot be attained. Some such men, lured by the financial ‘advice’ the influencers push, have ended up broke, sleeping in their cars, having staked everything on an curated dream that remains forever just out of reach. And the men selling the fantasy are not even the real winners: rather, they’re digital tenants on tech platforms owned by a much smaller, much richer class, who profit from every click of the rage cycle without ever appearing on screen, while what begins as lifestyle optimisation reveals itself, in time, as a Trojan horse of false promises.
This same dynamic, at its most dangerous, is what authoritarian movements have always harnessed for power. Hera’s trick was to suspend an image gleaming with the appearance of substance just beyond Menelaus’s grasp. Bloch saw demagogues of his own day learning to do precisely this, on purpose. In Heritage of Our Times and his essay on fascism, Critique of Propaganda (1937), he developed what was for him the central diagnosis of his age: that it was the far-right, not the progressive left-wing forces, that best understood the emotional, even libidinal power of the ‘warm stream’ – the appeal of spectacle and mythology in the mobilisation of the ‘not yet’ for its own political purposes. The fascists, Bloch saw, were unrecognised heirs to the religious imagination, drawing on the same archive of longing, but stripping it of its emancipatory charge and bending it to the legitimisation of their power. They had learned to manufacture eschatology: to create a redemptive vision that drew strict lines around who counted as redeemable and who did not. Such politics find its richest soil in times of economic precariousness. When ordinary people can no longer afford dignified lives and the future feels foreclosed, the warm stream of longing becomes most politically exploitable. The demagogue who arrives at such a moment offers not so much a programme as a feeling – that you, specifically, matter; that your suffering has meaning; and that someone, at last, sees you, and offers you a path of salvation.
Pandora, John William Waterhouse 1896
Educated Hope
For Bloch, writing in the 1930s with a caution that remains relevant in our own day, any politics which reduces itself to technocracy – to government through statistics, marginal policy adjustments, or ‘economism’ more broadly speaking – perilously leaves the warm stream unguarded. This was Bloch’s charge against the social democrats and leftists of his own day. Whoever identifies the gap and fills it with a utopian image (whether the ‘thousand year Reich’ or ‘Make America Great Again’) can gain extraordinary power. Man does not live by bread alone, Bloch wrote, especially when he has none. We live as much by the intoxicating ‘violin’ as by the bread – by the warm as well as by the cold stream – for it is humanity’s cultural achievements, in the end, that make life feel meaningful and history purposeful.
Bloch’s answer was not to renounce the utopian impulse. That, he saw clearly, was neither possible nor desirable. The warm stream cannot be drained without draining us of our humanity. The task, rather, is to channel this inextinguishable force into forms that cannot be turned against the people it mobilises. This is what Bloch called concrete utopia. Merely abstract utopia is the eidolon – the gleaming image suspended just out of reach. It’s typically the blueprint of a single visionary, manufactured from above to mobilise armies for dictatorial ends. But the concrete utopia is the future built from below, by ordinary people, out of the materials of the world they actually inhabit. The eidolon keeps people passive, gazing upward at a phantom that forever elusively promises to redeem them; concrete utopia asks them to recognise that the redemption they’re waiting for is something they’ll have to build themselves. Bloch’s wager is that the utopian impulse does not have to be handed down from on high, by Hera, the authoritarian demagogue, or the tech algorithm. It can be cultivated by human beings working together to repair, improve, and extend the institutions that already half-belong to them.
The phrase ‘concrete utopia’ is a deliberate paradox. Utopia literally means ‘no-place’ in Greek: to call it ‘concrete’ is to insist, against the grain of the word itself, that the not-yet is something we can actually build in the world as we find it. This is why, for Bloch, democracy is not a dry bureaucratic arrangement but the political form of hope itself. It is a bottom-up process of yearning towards a horizon of justice, the same yearning that has stirred every great emancipatory movement in history. A parliament, a trade union, a university, a town council, a public school, a free press, a courtroom in which the powerful can be held to account – each, in its imperfect way, is a concrete utopia in the making. Each is a piece of the not-yet that human beings have wrested from the gods and placed in their own hands.
But the possibility of a concrete utopia is not self-evident. Whether hope is a force for good or for ill has divided philosophers since antiquity. The Greeks themselves were ambivalent: when Pandora opened her box and loosed every evil into the world, the one thing that remained at the bottom was hope – left there ambiguously alongside what hope might cure and what hope might delude. Recognising the difference is what Bloch called docta spes – ‘educated hope’.
Raw hope, as the Greek gods knew, is the most exploitable resource on earth. It will reach for whatever’s dangled in front of it. Educated hope, though, is hope that has learned to read the world – to distinguish the genuinely possible from the merely promised, the tendency gestating within the present from the phantom suspended above it. This hope is, in Bloch’s striking phrase, willful rather than wishful – a discipline rather than a mood, sharpened by historical knowledge, sceptical of charisma, and attentive to the grain of what people are actually doing together. To be educated like this is to become harder to recruit by the deceivers: less seducible by the strongman’s promise, less willing to bleed for someone else’s redemption story, more capable of recognising when a war is being fought on one’s behalf and when it’s merely the instrument of power. This is why, for Bloch, good hope is finally a matter of pedagogy as much as politics. It’s a faculty cultivated, like any other, through reading, argument, memory, and the daily practice of democracy itself – not merely voting in elections, but the slow work of arguing with neighbours, organising with strangers, and holding power to account. And this, finally, is Bloch’s deepest insight: that the desirable ‘not-yet’ does not live in the things we might conquer but in the relations we might build – between neighbours, between strangers, between the powerful and those they answer to. The Homeric Helen was a trophy to be seized; the older Helen, an illusion to be seen through. The phantom is always an impossible fantasy. The real horizon is always an imperfect becoming. The education of hope is what teaches us to tell them apart.
© Alice Figes 2026
Alice Figes is a PhD student in the faculty of POLIS at the University of Cambridge. She can be found on Twitter @AlicheFrancesca.

When Truth Loses its Witnesses

When Truth Loses its Witnesses
Mohsen Askari on why not all political narratives should be treated as equal.
I am Iranian living in Istanbul, Turkey. In recent months, I have found myself sitting in rooms with other Iranians, all of us shaped in different ways by the same regime, the same history, and the same accumulated exhaustion. Yet when we speak about what’s happening in Iran, it often feels as if we’re describing different countries. One person sees resistance, another sees foreign manipulation. One sees the collapse of a dictatorship, another sees the danger of national humiliation. One sees war as the terrible price of liberation, another sees it as proof that liberation cannot come through bombs. One sees the Islamic Republic as defeated, another repeats its language of victory. One person speaks of ‘the people’, another asks, “Which people – and who gave anyone the right to speak in their name?”
This is not just ordinary disagreement. It produces a deeper shock. If people who speak the same language, who have lived under the same political order, have inherited the same wounds, and watched the same events unfold, cannot agree on what’s happening, what hope is there for historical truth? If even the present is already broken into incompatible accounts, can we possibly say we know the past?
Protest Gothenburg © Crannofonix News 2026 Creative Commons 4
Relativism Conceals Corruption
The apparently easiest answer to this problem is ‘relativism’: everyone has their own truth. Everyone speaks from their own pain. Every story is partial. Every account is constructed.
There is something right in this. Human beings do not experience history as raw data. We do not live through events as neutral recording machines. We remember through fear, loyalty, shame, class, exile, ideology, trauma, hope, and loss. The same event can enter different lives with different meanings. A person inside Iran may experience foreign pressure differently from a person in exile. A parent may hear ‘war’ differently from a young protester. Someone whose child has been killed will not speak in the same register as someone watching from a television studio. There is no ‘view from nowhere’.
But a dangerous mistake hides inside this truth. From the fact that all narratives are partial, it does not follow that all narratives are equal. Some narratives expose harm, some conceal it. Some help us understand a situation more fully, some make understanding harder. Some return agency to the wounded, some steal agency from them. Thus, a victim’s testimony, a regime’s denial, a propagandist’s justification, and a strategic analyst’s cold description of violence, are not simply four ‘perspectives’: they’re reports of four different relations to suffering, evidence, agency, and power, and some are better than others, in various ways. So the plurality of narratives should make us more careful in narrative assessment, not more relativistic.
This distinction matters because political violence does not only attack bodies; through the misinformation that attends the physical violence it attacks the conditions under which truth can be known, shared, trusted, and judged. It kills witnesses. It corrupts language. It destroys evidence. It floods public space with suspicion. It makes testimony sound partisan before it can even be heard. It turns grief into propaganda, and propaganda into ‘common sense’.
Hannah Arendt understood this danger clearly. In her 1968 essay ‘Truth and Politics’ she warned that factual truth is fragile because it depends on witnesses, records, and a shared public world. Mathematical truth can survive without public agreement, but factual truth cannot. If enough people deny that something happened, if records are destroyed, if witnesses are discredited, if language itself is made slippery, factual truth becomes politically homeless, and very short-lived.
Authoritarian regimes know this. Their greatest achievement is not making people believe the official story; it’s making people give up on the possibility of truth altogether. The dictator does not need everyone to say, “The regime is right.” It may be enough if people say, “Who knows? Everyone lies. Every side has its own story.” That is not skepticism. It is surrender disguised as sophistication.
The problem is not that politics contains narratives. It must. No society can remember everything, and no person can tell the whole of an event. The problem is that narratives do things: they classify actors, they assign motives, they distribute innocence and guilt. They decide whose pain counts as evidence, and whose pain becomes noise. Consider that in many authoritarian settings, protest is not described as protest. It is reclassified as infiltration, manipulation, rioting, sabotage, or ‘soft war’. This is not just a minor linguistic shift. Once protesters are seen as instruments of an outside power, they’re no longer seen as citizens with grievances. Their anger no longer has to be interpreted. Their suffering no longer has to be answered. Their deaths can be narrated as the restoration of order. The dead are no longer dead citizens, they are evidence that a conspiracy was defeated. This is a theft of agency. A person who risks their life to speak is transformed into a political puppet. A political demand from the opposition party becomes a security incident. State violence becomes management.
A narrative, then, is not merely a representation of reality, it is an intervention in reality. It can open moral attention, or close it. It can widen the space of responsibility, or narrow it. It can make the victim more visible, or make the victim disappear behind a theory. This is why the question ‘Whose narrative is this?’ is never enough. We must also ask: What does this narrative make possible? What does it make impossible? What facts must it deny? Whose suffering does it erase? Who becomes more powerful if this story is believed?
Bad Language
Miranda Fricker’s work on epistemic injustice gives us useful language for this problem. Testimonial injustice happens when a speaker’s credibility is unfairly reduced because the listeners have been prejudiced. Someone speaks, but their word arrives already discounted. In a political context this discounting can become systematic: the protester is treated as manipulated, the exile as hysterical, the grieving mother as emotional, the prisoner as unreliable. Meanwhile, the official is treated as serious because he speaks the language of order. This is not simply a mistake in listening, it is the political rearrangement of credibility.
Fricker’s second concept, hermeneutical injustice, is also relevant. This is the injustice people suffer when they don’t have the shared concepts needed to make sense of their experience. Something happens to them, but the available public language cannot yet name it properly. This problem is sharpened under authoritarianism because language itself is managed – killing becomes ‘restoring order’, disconnection becomes ‘security’, and so on. People are harmed, and then the language available to describe that harm is stolen or poisoned.
To recover truth, then, is not only to collect facts. It is also to recover the conditions under which testimony can be heard and experience can be named.
A similar linguistic problem appears when some people claim to speak for ‘the people’. In moments of crisis, everyone seems to invoke ‘the people’. Regimes claim to defend them. Opposition leaders claim to represent them. Foreign governments claim to help them. Media channels claim to show what they want. But under authoritarianism, the people are everywhere in speech and nowhere in power. That’s why ‘The people want [whatever]’ is often a dangerous political sentence. Sometimes it’s true, sometimes it’s wishful thinking, and sometimes it’s propaganda – the speaker’s own desire dressed in democratic clothing.
Hearing the People
This leads to a distinction that I have come to think of as ‘democratic audibility’. A population is democratically audible when people can form political judgments freely, communicate them without coercive distortion, and have them registered through credible public channels. This requires more than speech. It requires safety, access, institutions, trust, and the possibility of disagreement without terror.
This idea is close to the late Jürgen Habermas’s theory of communicative action and his concern with the conditions under which public communication can be rational and legitimate. But democratic audibility emphasizes something more basic, and more easily damaged in authoritarian contexts: the possibility of a people becoming hearable politically at all. A culture may be full of voices, and yet still be politically inaudible. This is especially true in the digital age, where visibility is easily mistaken for political audibility. A video can go viral or a hashtag can trend; but circulation is not political authorization, and loudness is not representation. The most visible voices are not necessarily the most legitimate ones – especially when fear, censorship, exile, wealth, algorithmic amplification, and unequal access determine who is heard.
In an authoritarian crisis this problem becomes severe. The person in the country may be unable to speak freely, while the person outside it may speak freely but not represent those inside it. The person with access to foreign media may be treated as the national voice, while the person without internet access vanishes from the record. And silence itself becomes unreadable, as the person who says nothing may be silent from fear, exhaustion, strategy, disagreement, or grief, or many other reasons.
This does not mean that no one can make political judgments. It means we must be honest about the damaged conditions under which such judgments are made. When a people has been deprived of free institutions, open media, secure communication, and basic safety, no claim to speak for them should be accepted without scrutiny.
Lost in the Woods of Rhetoric by Venantius J Pinto
Truth & Uncertainty
Truth also needs infrastructure. This may sound strange because we often imagine truth as a matter of mind or character: A truthful person is honest. A rational person follows evidence. A good historian checks sources. All this is right, but incomplete. Truth also depends on phones, cables, archives, courts, hospitals, journalists, witnesses, internet access, translation, memory, and trust. It depends on whether a mother can call her son, whether a video can be uploaded without being deleted, whether a doctor can record a cause of death honestly, whether a journalist can investigate without fear of imprisonment, and whether citizens have the same access to the outside world as officials and propagandists. When a state controls who can connect, it also controls who can testify. When only some people can speak, only some can upload, only some can bypass censorship, and only some can reach foreign audiences, then the public record is unequal before interpretation even begins.
A media blackout, then, is not merely an interruption of communication. It is an attack on the social conditions of truth. It not only stops people from speaking, it also prevents families from knowing, journalists from verifying, citizens from coordinating, and the outside world from hearing. It turns life into uncertainty.
In Persian, the word bī-khabarī means ‘being without news’. But in moments of political instability, this means more than just ‘lacking information’. It means not knowing whether your mother is safe, your brother is alive, your friend has been arrested, or whether the silence in your phone is technical, political, or final. For the philosopher, uncertainty may be a problem of knowledge. For the exile, it may be the sound of a phone that does not ring. And this kind of not-knowing is not empty; it is full of images, fears, guesses, rituals, and distress. People refresh apps. They wake in the night. They scan fragments of news. They interpret short messages as proof of life. ‘We are fine’ becomes both reassurance and a question generator: Fine how? Written freely? Sent under fear? Copied from someone else? Already out of date? The point is that bī-khabarī is not simple ignorance, it’s relational ignorance. It’s the absence of news from someone whose ordinary presence has helped hold your world together. A daily message from a parent is not just information. A photo, a message, a joke, a complaint about the weather, or a reminder to eat properly, may look trivial from the outside, but these small exchanges are how distance becomes bearable, as they’re how a person abroad continues to belong. When that rhythm disappears, the primary question is ‘Where am I in relation to those I love?’ So a blackout does not merely remove data, it removes the ordinary confirmations through which people remain real to one another. This is why the sentence ‘I am fine’ becomes semantically strange under an information blackout. In ordinary life, it may be enough. Under political oppression it becomes unstable: Are they fine, or protecting me? Are they speaking freely, or carefully? Are they safe now, or were they only safe when the message was sent? Does the word ‘fine’ describe reality, or is it a small act of mercy sent across danger?
Here truth becomes inseparable from trust. A message is not only judged by its content, it’s judged by tone, timing, background noise, delay, and the history of the relationship. People learn to interpret silence as evidence. But silence is a terrible witness. It can mean fear, sleep, arrest, technical failure, battery loss, injury, or nothing at all. The mind fills the gap because love cannot leave it empty. This is why not-knowing can be a form of suffering.
In ordinary epistemology, uncertainty is often treated as a lack – a missing proposition. But in political crises, uncertainty can be manufactured, weaponized, and prolonged. To cut communication is to force people into interpretation without grounds. It makes them search for signs while denying them reliable evidence. It makes the imagination do the work of the torturer. In such conditions, truth is not only a proposition, it is also reassurance. It is the daily confirmation that someone exists, speaks, breathes, and remains reachable. When that confirmation is removed, the world itself becomes less stable.
This is why political violence cannot be understood only through the visible act: the shooting, the arrest, the bombing, the lying speech, the bad law. It must also be understood through the damage done to relations. We depend on testimony not as an optional supplement to knowledge, but as a foundation of human life. Almost everything we know, we know because someone told us it, recorded it, preserved it, or made it available. To destroy trust in testimony is to destroy the world.
The work of Nobel Prize-winning Belarusian writer Svetlana Alexievich is important here. Her books do not give us one clear history of Soviet life, war, or disaster – they give us voices, often contradictory, wounded, self-deceiving, generous, bitter, confused, brave. She does not resolve them into a single official account. Yet she also does not treat all speech as equally truthful. The power of her work lies in preserving plurality without abandoning moral seriousness.
This is the balance we need. We must resist the fantasy of one story that explains everything. But we must also resist the lazy pluralism that treats every story as just another equally-viable angle.
Judging the Narrative
In his work on history and silence, Michel-Rolph Trouillot argues that silences enter history at many stages: when facts are created, when archives are assembled, when narratives are made, and when history is finally written. He means that the past is not only lost because time passes, but because power filters what survives. The same is true of the present. What we will later call history is being filtered now. Some voices are being recorded, others are being buried. Some deaths will become statistics, others will become symbols. Some testimonies will be translated, others will remain in private messages, family grief, or silence. Some narratives will travel because they are useful to powerful actors, others will remain morally true but politically weak.
So how should we judge narratives without pretending to be neutral gods? We can begin with a few tests:
First, what facts must this narrative deny? A story that survives only by refusing evidence deserves suspicion.
Second, whose suffering does it make visible? A narrative that notices only the pain of its own side is not necessarily false, but it is morally incomplete.
Third, whose credibility does it deflate even before listening begins? This is Fricker’s warning. If a person’s testimony is dismissed because they are a protester, an exile, a woman, a grieving parent, a prisoner, a refugee, or simply inconvenient to the preferred theory, then injustice is already underway.
Fourth, whose agency does it erase? If citizens become puppets, victims become tools, or protesters become instruments of powers, then something has gone wrong.
Fifth, who benefits if this story is believed? This does not automatically disprove the story, but it does reveal its political function.
Sixth, does the narrative allow complexity, or does it instead demand loyalty? Propaganda usually cannot tolerate mixed feelings. Human truth often begins with them.
Seventh, does the story help us judge, or does it exhaust judgment? Some narratives do not persuade us of a falsehood directly. They simply tire us intellectually until we no longer want to know the truth.
This last point is crucial. The crisis of truth in our time is not just that people believe false things, it is that many people become too exhausted to defend true things. They see an unending stream of competing videos, experts, accusations, corrections, countercorrections, and emotional rhetoric, and eventually they say, “I don’t know anymore.” Sometimes that sentence is intellectually honest. Sometimes it is the beginning of moral withdrawal.
The challenge is to keep judgment alive without making judgment simplistic. This is difficult because politics is complicated. Foreign intervention can be opposed without defending a dictatorship; a regime can be criminal without making every enemy of that regime virtuous; a protest movement can entertain many errors without losing its basic legitimacy; a person can fear war, yet understand why others welcome the weakening of an evil state. A person can be morally authoritative, yet still politically mistaken.
Complexity is necessary. But complexity should not become a hiding place for moral cowardice. (To say that things are complicated is sometimes the beginning of thought; sometimes, it marks the end of responsibility.)
Conclusions
The question is not whether we can escape political and historical narratives. We cannot. The question is whether we can develop the moral discipline of narrative judgment. Such a discipline requires humility, because no one sees everything. It requires courage, because some facts must be defended even when they’re inconvenient. It requires listening, because lived experience cannot be replaced by theory. It requires suspicion, because power often speaks in the language of reason. And it requires care, because behind every political narrative there may be someone whose grief is being used, denied, or forgotten. So in the end, the answer to propaganda is not merely counter-propaganda. It is also not the polite but misplaced relativism that says ‘Every side has its truth’. The answer is harder: it is to listen widely, judge carefully, and refuse to grant moral acceptability to narratives that depend on erasure.
The present will soon become history. But it will not easily become history fairly. Rather, it will pass through memory, media, archives, fear, translation, ideology, and power. Some of what matters most will be lost. Some of what is false will survive. Some of what is true will remain, but without witnesses. That is why we must strongly promote truth as a fragile public practice. In times of political oppression or instability, truth survives not by becoming simple, but by refusing to become indifferent.
© Mohsen Askari 2026
Mohsen Askari is an English instructor and interdisciplinary researcher at Boğaziçi University in Istanbul, writing on language, truth, testimony, education, and political thought.

Philosopher Miranda Fricker developed an influential analysis of what she calls epistemic injustice:
Testimonial injustice is when a speaker’s credibility is unfairly reduced because the listeners have been prejudiced against them.
Hermeneutical injustice is the injustice people suffer when they don’t have the shared concepts needed to make sense of their experience.
