DOJ arrests two, seizes 187 devices in North Korean laptop farm crackdown in Texas
Oct 13 - The US Department of Justice on Tuesday announced the arrests of two Americans accused of helping North Korean IT workers to steal identities and obtain fraudulent employment at US companies to earn money for the North Korean government.
The agency announced the arrests of Michael James Bostelle, of Pennsylvania, and Juan Cecilio Pena Carrillo, of Texas, on charges of wire fraud, money laundering and identity theft as part of the alleged scheme, the DOJ said in a statement.
• As part of the crackdown, the DOJ announced that the FBI conducted searches and took other action between September 21 and September 25 at more than 40 residences in Texas thought to be operating as “laptop farms” for North Korean IT workers, the DOJ said. The FBI seized roughly 187 laptops and other devices used to carry out the scheme.
• The indictment also charged Sun Sheng Ming, Pei Li Guang, Weng Shou Cheng, Han Guo Bin, Wang Jian Jun, Sheng Zhang Kun, Zhang Wei Ping, Zhang Li Ping, Yu Yang and Jin Long, all based in China, for their roles in the operation, according to the statement.
• According to an indictment unsealed on Tuesday, the Chinese-based operators directed Pena and Tey Michael Nolte, along with at least four other Americans, in the scheme. Nolte was named in the indictment but not charged.
• Nolte and attorneys for Pena and Bostelle could not immediately be reached for comment. Emails sent to addresses that the DOJ alleged were used by the Chinese-based participants went unanswered.
• Nolte allegedly recruited, managed and trained Bostelle and other Americans, who allowed their names and personal information to be used to permit the North Korea-directed operation to function, in exchange for proceeds from the scheme, the DOJ said. The Americans’ actions included receiving and hosting laptops belonging to US victim companies at their homes, to make it appear as if the North Koreans were legitimate employees operating in the US.
• The “massive” fraud impacted more than 70 U. companies, compromised the identities of 25 Americans, caused false information to be sent to multiple US government agencies, and generated at least $3 million in revenue for the overseas IT workers, the DOJ said.
• The US government has for years warned of North Koreans surreptitiously gaining employment at US companies to raise money for the North Korean government, access company networks and steal data.

Pope Leo’s lung operation ‘successfully completed’: Vatican
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
19:05:30 UTC
04:05:30 KST

Pope Leo diagnosed with cancer as doctors remove part of lung, Vatican says
- Pope Leo, 71, was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma after doctors removed the lower lobe of his right lung during surgery at Rome’s Gemelli hospital.
- The Vatican said the 90-minute operation was successful with no complications, and Leo is waking normally and expected to stay in hospital for about a week.
- His public events are cancelled until Oct 20, and the illness comes as he prepares for a busy papal schedule, including an 11-day South America tour in November.
AI generated
ROME – Pope Leo was diagnosed with a common form of lung cancer after surgeons removed a part of his right lung on Oct 13, the Vatican said in a medical bulletin, marking a significant health setback for the 71-year-old pontiff.
The Pope has lung adenocarcinoma, a common form of cancer, with tissue tests conducted during the operation confirming what doctors had suspected from preparatory examinations, the bulletin said.
He was admitted to Rome’s Gemelli hospital on Oct 13 for surgery to remove the growth that doctors had discovered in a recent routine health check.
The Pope’s lead surgeon,Stefano Margaritora, and his personal physician, Luigi Carbone, said in a statement that the procedure lasted about 90 minutes and was successful, with no complications.
“In order to make the procedure curative, the lower lobe of the right lung was removed using a video-assisted technique,” they said, making clear that the aim was to eliminate all cancerous tissue.
Human lungs have five lobes – three in the right lung and two in the left.
A medical expert said that in order to assess the pope’s case they would need to know the size of the tumour and whether the cancer had spread to his lymph nodes, information the Vatican did not immediately provide.
“While we have the diagnosis, we do not yet have the stage. This is critical to prognosis and treatment,” said Stephen Liu, a lung cancer expert at Georgetown University in Washington and division chief of hematology-oncology at MedStar Georgetown University Hospital.
“If this is a small lung cancer with no lymph nodes involved, surgery itself is likely to be curative,” he told Reuters. “But if final analysis reveals a greater extent of cancer involvement, this indicates a poorer prognosis.”
Resting in his hospital room
The Pope regained consciousness normally after the operation and later returned to his hospital room, where he was resting, the medical bulletin said.
The Vatican said earlier this week that he was expected to remain in hospital for about a week and all his public events have been cancelled until Oct 20.
Leo left the Vatican ahead of the surgery shortly before 1pm in Rome and was seen waving from the back of a black SUV as his convoy drove about 9km north of the Vatican to the Gemelli.
Upon arrival at the hospital, Leo shook hands with several officials, walked in front of a waiting crowd of well-wishers, some of whom shouted “Auguri” (best wishes), and headed in via the main entrance.
Leo, elected by the world’s cardinals in May 2025, is relatively young for a Church leader. He enjoys sports, including tennis, and is not known to be a smoker or to have had recent health issues.
The late Pope Francis, Leo’s predecessor, was hospitalised several times as he grew frail in his later years. He died aged 88 in April 2025.
Leo, who spoke in a firm, clear voice at his only public event on Oct 12, keeps a very busy schedule. He is due to make an 11-day tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from Nov 6 to 17, but it was not clear if this trip would still go ahead.
Typhoid fever
The Pope is the ultimate earthly authority for the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics and does not have a deputy who steps in when he is sick. When a pope is incapacitated, the business of the Vatican’s vast bureaucracy carries on as usual, holding off on any decisions that require papal approval.
Leo, born in Chicago in 1955 as Robert Prevost, served for decades as a missionary and bishop in Peru before becoming pope. In 1985, when he was a young priest, he came down with typhoid fever in Chulucanas, Peru and was hospitalised.
He recounted the experience in his only major interview given as Pope, in a book for Penguin Peru.
Leo said the pain was so bad that he asked God to die rather than continue suffering. He took his survival as a sign from God that “We need you here (on Earth),” he said.
“I never looked back,” said Leo. REUTERS

Blasts rock Saudi cities as Yemen conflict escalates

Loud explosions were reported in Saudi Arabia's capital, Riyadh, and near state oil giant Saudi Aramco's headquarters in Dhahran on Tuesday, as escalating hostilities with Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis fueled fears of a wider regional confrontation.
Six sources told Reuters that explosions were heard near Aramco's headquarters in Dhahran, which had been evacuated. One source reported seeing smoke rising from the facility, although the company had not issued an official statement confirming an attack or damage.
In Riyadh, a powerful blast was heard shortly after Saudi civil defense authorities warned residents of an incoming aerial threat.
"The city of Riyadh is facing a hostile aerial threat," an emergency alert sent to residents said.
The incidents followed threats by the Houthis to retaliate against Saudi airstrikes targeting rebel-held areas of Yemen.
Earlier Tuesday, the Saudi-led coalition carried out fresh strikes on the Houthi-controlled capital, Sanaa, according to the rebel-run Al Masirah broadcaster and local residents.
Witnesses reported powerful explosions hours after coalition aircraft targeted the al-Suhaba fuel facility west of the city.
The coalition had previously urged civilians to evacuate the Yemeni Oil Company facility and nearby storage areas ahead of possible strikes.
The company, however, said its storage facilities were empty and insisted that any attack would not disrupt fuel supplies. Despite those assurances, residents reported long lines at gas stations amid fears of shortages.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree warned that further Saudi strikes on Sanaa would trigger a "firm and painful" response against Riyadh.
The renewed violence follows a series of deadly Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, including a strike on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Saturday that killed at least 13 people and wounded more than 300.
Saudi authorities are investigating how their air defenses failed to intercept the missiles and drones used in the attacks.

The latest escalation comes as Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces battle the Houthis for control of strategic territory near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a vital shipping corridor connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.
Fighting intensified last month after Houthi forces seized key positions overlooking the waterway, prompting a Saudi-backed offensive to regain control.
Saudi Arabia's Cabinet warned Tuesday that the Houthis would face consequences for continued attacks on the kingdom.
"The Kingdom will not allow any threat to its security or to freedom of maritime navigation in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab Strait," the Cabinet said in a statement carried by Saudi state television.
Meanwhile, Yemen's Interior Ministry said Houthi attacks on the southwestern city of Taiz had killed six people and wounded 18 over the previous 24 hours.
A commander with Saudi-backed government forces said Houthi fighters had reached the outskirts of Taiz, with some entering the city despite fierce resistance.
Speaking on condition of anonymity, the commander said the rebels had deployed substantial forces supported by short- and medium-range ballistic missiles.
He identified the Kahboub mountains, which overlook the Bab al-Mandab Strait and the southern port city of Aden, as a critical battleground, adding that government forces had requested reinforcements.
The widening confrontation has disrupted regional aviation and raised concerns over commercial shipping through one of the world's most important maritime routes.
The Houthis renewed warnings Tuesday against using Saudi airspace, while several airlines have suspended flights to the kingdom following attacks on airports.
Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty condemned the attacks during a phone call with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, urging the Houthis to immediately halt strikes against Saudi Arabia.
"There is no justification for these attacks, and they cannot be accepted," Abdelatty said, according to an Egyptian statement.
He also called for renewed diplomatic efforts to resolve the conflict between Iran and the United States and prevent further regional instability.
Washington has provided Saudi Arabia with intelligence, targeting assistance and military planning support but has so far refrained from directly striking Houthi positions.
Saudi Arabia has sought greater U.S. military involvement as the fighting intensifies, although analysts warn that direct American intervention could prompt the Houthis to further disrupt shipping through the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
The latest developments underscore growing concerns that the conflict in Yemen could expand into a broader regional confrontation, threatening energy infrastructure, civilian aviation and international trade.

TOI explains: Why can’t Bengaluru protest outside Freedom Park?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
19:02:25 UTC
04:02:25 KST

A Karnataka high court order and a police licensing regime have made Freedom Park Bengaluru’s default protest venue. But the governing police order also gives the police commissioner discretion to designate another suitable venue, meaning the legal position is more nuanced than an absolute ban on demonstrations elsewhere. Here’s everything you need to know about why Bengaluru cannot protest outside Freedom Park:Bengaluru has confined protests to Freedom Park. The practice emerged from a suo motu Karnataka High Court case initiated in 2021 over the effect of demonstrations on traffic and the rights of people not participating in them.
How did the restriction begin?On March 3, 2022, a division bench of the Karnataka High Court passed an interim order directing the state government to ensure that no protests, processions and similar activities were held anywhere in Bengaluru except at Freedom Park, Gandhinagar. The court also directed that such activities be organised without adversely affecting traffic, especially during rush hours, and that action be taken where traffic was disrupted.On August 1, 2022, the High Court disposed of the case. In paragraph 4, it recorded a submission that protests, marches and dharnas would be permitted only at Freedom Park, and that the state was obliged to ensure compliance with the 2021 licensing order.
In paragraph 5, the operative direction required authorities to ensure compliance with that order “in letter and spirit” and to continue action against those violating it.What does the police order say?The Licensing and Regulation of Protests, Demonstrations and Protest Marches (Bengaluru City) Order, 2021, published in the state gazette in January 2022, is the rule currently governing protests in Bengaluru. It says no protests, demonstrations, dharnas or protest marches may be held in the city without a licence under the order.Clause 4.1 identifies Freedom Park as the venue for protests in Bengaluru. However, it also says that, depending on the situation, the commissioner of police may designate any other suitable place in the city for that purpose. The licensing authority may approve the number of participants at Freedom Park based on the type of programme, duration and available capacity.So, are protests outside Freedom Park illegal?Not necessarily in every circumstance. The 2021 order does not expressly prohibit protest marches, nor does it state that Freedom Park is the only possible venue: it identifies Freedom Park while preserving the police commissioner’s discretion to designate another suitable location.A legal backgrounder prepared by activists argues that the High Court’s final order did not itself direct that protests be held only at Freedom Park; it directed compliance with the licensing order. On that reading, the court’s judgment does not prevent rallies and does not mandate Freedom Park as the sole venue.The distinction matters because the March 2022 interim order did expressly restrict protests and processions to Freedom Park, while the August 2022 final order required enforcement of the 2021 licensing rules. The two must be read alongside the licensing order before drawing a definitive legal conclusion.
Why does this matter?Activists argue that concentrating demonstrations at one venue reduces their visibility and makes it harder for groups to draw public attention to local grievances. The backgrounder says the restrictions have affected workers, farmers, Dalit activists, sanitation workers and residents seeking to protest on issues in their own localities.The debate is ultimately about balancing traffic management and public convenience with the constitutional right to assemble peacefully and express dissent. For now, Freedom Park remains Bengaluru’s designated and practically dominant protest venue. Whether the police commissioner’s discretion to permit demonstrations elsewhere is exercised, and on what terms, remains central to the controversy.
Chethan Kumar is a Senior Assistant Editor with the Times of India. Aside from specialising in Space & Science, he has reported extensively on varied topics, with special focus on defence, policy and data stories. He has covered multiple elections, too. As a young democracy grows out of adolescence, Chethan feels, there are reels of tales emerging which need to be captured. To do this, he alternates between the mundane goings-on of the Common Man and the wonder-filled worlds of scientists and scamsters, politicians and soldiers. In a career spanning nearly 18 years, he has reported from multiple datelines — Houston, Florida, Kochi, Hyderabad, Chennai, Sriharikota (AP), NH-1 (J&K Highway), New Delhi, Ahmedabad, Raichur, Bhatkal, Mysuru, Chamarajanagar, to name a few — but is based out of Bengaluru, India’s science capital that also hosts the ISRO HQ.

US Army unveils new warfighting guidance to align with evolving battlefield threats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
18:58:15 UTC
03:58:15 KST

Diyar Güldoğan
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
The US Army is introducing new operational warfighting guidance designed to align its doctrine, training, force structure, and technology investments with evolving battlefield threats, Gen. Christopher LaNeve, vice army chief of Staff, said Tuesday.
Speaking at the Association of the United States Army’s Eisenhower Luncheon, LaNeve, who is also serving as acting army chief of staff, outlined the army’s new guidance, How the Army Fights, which was published last week.
The document is intended to establish a common framework for how the army contributes to joint military operations, drawing lessons from conflicts including Russia’s war in Ukraine and fighting in the Middle East.
"Upfront, I’ll just say, How the Army Fights is not a departure from Multi-Domain Operations. The purpose of this document is to provide warfighting guidance that enables every single leader to understand their role in Multi-Domain Operations," he said.
LaNeve said the changing battlefield, characterized by widespread unmanned aerial systems, persistent surveillance, increasingly precise long-range fires, and the growing importance of cyber and space capabilities, requires the army to adapt how it fights.
He outlined four interconnected elements at the heart of the new guidance: convergence, strike, close battle, and endurance.
"Together, these four elements of land power provide the US Army, within the Joint Force, the ability to fight and win our nation’s wars," he said.
The army plans to expand the integration of autonomous and unmanned systems across its formations, including the introduction of military occupational specialties focused on unmanned aerial systems and robotics.
LaNeve also announced that the Futures and Concepts Command had been redesignated the US Army Futures and Autonomous Systems Command, or FASCOM, following the establishment of the Autonomous Warfare Command.
"The army is not turning its back on modernization. We are sprinting towards (it)," he said.
LaNeve called on defense industry partners to support army efforts to field effective technologies at scale, stressing that innovation must be linked directly to battlefield requirements.
The ultimate objective, he said, is to preserve the Army’s position as the world’s leading land power and ensure it remains prepared to respond whenever the nation calls.

If You Cannot Say Genocide: Essays on Conscience and Witness
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
18:56:56 UTC
03:56:56 KST

“What task is left to art when words are turned into weapons?” Yahia Lababidi’s If you Cannot Say Genocide: Essays of Conscience and Witness explores the depth of this question impressed upon the reader in the preface. For the author, who is a Muslim of Palestinian descent, the question is pondered from a position of distance as an “inheritor of family dispossession”.
Written between 2023 and 2026, this collection of essays leans upon memory, literature, experiences, observation and reflection, through which disillusion exposes reality. While there is no chronology in Lababidi’s reflections, the preoccupation with words and meaning is persistent. For example, Lababidi writes of his posting as a speechwriter for the UN office in Cairo, where he encounters the politics of language. “I came to see that neutrality, posing as diplomacy, was a form of cowardice that did violence to my nature,” he writes.
Language shapes the rest of Lababidi’s reflections, exposing a world where meaning is determined by the politics of violence. Alongside language, Lababidi shares his own experiences, his awareness of living in the US as the government wields its power elsewhere in the world. But there are other nuances that Lababidi weaves in his essays.
“Memory is still alive, and it asks for responsibility. Distance has a way of laundering conscience. The longer we wait, the easier it becomes to confuse explanation with absolution. We need historians willing to write while the record is still unsettled, while consequences are still unfolding, guided by moral orientation,” Lababidi notes.
Many voices have practiced what Lababidi is insisting upon. The book makes many references to Palestinian writers, from Mahmoud Darwish, Edward Said and Ghassan Kanafani, to contemporary writes such as Omar El Akkad, Munther Isaac and Mohammed El-Kurd. In a way, these voices, particularly Kanafani and El-Kurd, stand in sharp contrast to the rest and even the author’s own reflections at times, who muses about the possibility of sustaining dialogue through cultural endeavours.
As the book continues, however, it becomes clearer that despite an ideal, colonialism is a brutal reality for Palestinians. The author’s distance from Palestine, not having experienced Palestine as Palestinians have experienced it throughout the decades until now, may account for the belief that art transcends. It makes for an uncomfortable read when one keeps in mind the brutality of Israeli colonial violence. But as the book continues, drawing upon Palestinian authors and their struggle from within, or from experience, the author’s voice emerges stronger. Palestinian voices speak through the pages of Lababidi’s essays, bringing a kaleidoscope of memories from artists, poets, writer and revolutionaries. Some stories relating to the Nakba are brought to the helm, and the Palestinian people’s resistance and endurance is shaped through the voices of those who survived the colonial atrocities. In this way, Lababidi’s reflections are accompanying slivers of history, such as when he states, “In our tradition, patience is greater than resignation.”
BOOK REVIEW: Wired to Steal: Zionism and the Shaping of the Western Mind
Written during the genocide, Lababidi’s essays also convey what the media conceals. “Numbers cannot contain this loss; they hide faces and extinguish stories,” he writes. Remaining conscious of language, Lababidi notes the importance of portraying the brutal reality as it is. There is more determination than anger, which suits a book that is dissecting language and what it conveys or seeks to hide. For Lababidi, contrary to the imperialist exploitation, language can convey humanity. It can also view the oppressor, in this case Israel, in its most basic form. “The jailer is never free,” he writes, while noting that colonialism depends upon control. “To normalise such injustice requires ethical numbing, which is another form of imprisonment.” The difference is that Israel has military might on its side.
On the other side of Israel normalising its colonial violence, Lababidi notes that the tools of surveillance and oppression translate into “tools of a structure that systematically erode psychological resilience.” This is a reality which, while acknowledged, is not talked about as much as Palestinian resistance and resilience.
Meanwhile, Lababidi also reflects on how Israel’s genocide in Gaza is managed through language: “The substitution is rarely defended. It happens mid-sentence, as though the speaker felt, in the act of naming, a resistance he could not sustain.” The erasure does not stop there. Lababidi continues, “Reconciliation is invoked before there has been agreement about what has taken place. The conversation advances beyond the wound, as if the wound were already understood.” But genocide has yet to be mentioned, instead of conflict and the multitude of futile synonyms used to conceal what Israel is exposing in plain sight.
And yet, as Lababidi writes, “what we are witnessing in Gaza is the collapse of that illusion.” Language can no longer sustain the deception of the oppressor; the oppression has revealed too much. “To name this genocide is to be honest. To call for Palestinian liberation is to insist that no people should live behind walls, under drones or under occupation,” the author insists. Language fails gradually and eventually the divide is unsurmountable. That space, however, provides opportunity to make language meaningful rather than employ the neutrality of both sides, for example, which the author names as “the purest expression of this invisibility.”
The book proceeds to a graceful conclusion when it gradually moves to criticising imperialism through exposing its own exploitation of language, as well as shedding the author’s own ideals. “Those beliefs lie in ashes,” Lababidi says, when he reflects on an earlier belief that “Israeli leaders sought an end to Palestinian resistance out of existential fear, not imperial ambition.” And yet, there is a bigger realisation – imperialism expects our desensitisation. How does one remain spiritually intact, Lababidi asks. The answer, perhaps, lies in language, in reclaiming its truth when one speaks.

RIYADH – The headquarters of Saudi Arabia’s state-owned oil company Saudi Aramco in the eastern city of Dhahran was attacked on the night of Oct 13, causing what the kingdom’s energy ministry said in a statement was a limited fire, as fighting between Yemen’s Iran-allied Houthis and the kingdom intensified.
The authorities responded to the incident in an administrative building at the headquarters complex late on Oct 13 and took necessary measures, the ministry said, adding that there were no injuries or deaths.
A company source told Reuters earlier that a ballistic missile hit the Aramco headquarters complex in Dhahran.
The source said an office tower in the complex was struck and that its top three floors were damaged. The source and two other people with knowledge of the matter said the building was on fire.
The complex hosts a major operations centre for Aramco, which oversees a vast network of onshore and offshore oil rigs, pipelines, refineries and export terminals.
The Houthis have for a week been firing ballistic missiles and drones at key Saudi sites in retaliation for the kingdom’s backing of government forces in Yemen’s reignited civil war.
Riyadh’s international airport has received four strikes, including one on Oct 10 that killed 13 people.
The Oct 10 ballistic missile strike on Riyadh airport was the deadliest in Saudi Arabia in a decade, with further attacks grounding flights across the country.
Earlier, six sources told Reuters they heard loud booms near the Aramco complex.
The Saudi-led coalition said fragments of a missile that it had intercepted and destroyed in Dhahran had fallen on a residential area, without providing further details.
The authorities also reported that drones and missiles were intercepted and destroyed in the capital, Riyadh, and the country’s southern region.
Four people were injured in Riyadh after fragments from two Houthi missiles fell following their interception and destruction, Saudi Civil Defence said on Oct 14.
The debris caused limited damage to 15 homes in the capital, the Civil Defence spokesperson said, adding that the injured were two women, a man and a child.
The Houthis had threatened a “harsh and painful” response to Saudi-led strikes on the Yemeni capital Sanaa, with spokesperson Yahya Saree saying targets could include the Saudi Aramco headquarters in Dhahran and an oil refinery in Riyadh.
The group has warned oil workers in Saudi Arabia to stay away from sites that could be targets.
The Houthis earlier on Oct 13 said Saudi Arabia was attacking Sanaa, and the Saudi-led coalition warned civilians to stay away from an oil depot on the city’s outskirts.
Houthi-run Al-Masirah television reported that the Saudi-led coalition had targeted the Yemen Petroleum Company’s Sabah central station, a fuel depot on the outskirts of Sanaa.
The coalition said in a statement on the evening of Oct 13 that it attacked the station and other sites in an operation aimed at “neutralising the capabilities of Houthis” to threaten Saudi Arabia, Yemen and international waterways.
The Saudi Cabinet, chaired by de facto ruler Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, issued a statement on Oct 13 before the strike on Saudi Aramco saying the Houthis would face consequences for their repeated attacks on the kingdom.
Reignited Yemen war
Saudi Arabia resumed its military campaign in Yemen in support of the internationally recognised government in a bid to reverse the Houthis’ sudden gains in September, when they swept down the Red Sea coast to the critical Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
The strait, the southern gateway to the Red Sea, has become a more vital route for Saudi and other global energy supplies since the start of the Iran war in February, when Tehran closed the Strait of Hormuz leading from the Gulf to the Indian Ocean.
While a government offensive that began a week ago pushed the Houthis from the area closest to the strait, the group remains embedded nearby and has made gains around the city of Taiz in October.
Saudi Arabia has been seeking wider support from allies for its campaign against the Houthis and to help it ward off their missile and drone attacks.
Washington, Saudi Arabia’s strongest ally and longtime security guarantor, has so far rebuffed Saudi efforts to bring it directly into the war against the Houthis.
The Yemen conflict has resumed as a spillover from the wider US-Iran war that began with the US-Israeli attack on the Islamic Republic on Feb 28.
Iran, Saudi Arabia’s long-time regional archrival, has offered to mediate between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, its foreign minister Abbas Araghchi said on Oct 11 in statements reiterated by the ministry on Oct 12. REUTERS

The mathematical secret behind why rose petals curl
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
18:53:35 UTC
03:53:35 KST

This article is from Proof Positive, our friendly newsletter that explores the joys and peculiarities of math. Sign up today for a weekly math essay and puzzle in your email inbox.
While they are undeniably beautiful, roses aren’t among my favorite flowers—too clichéd and romantic. I much prefer an indestructible cactus, a carnivorous plant or a hipster monstera, which, of course, is a must-have in any Japandi-style apartment. But after hearing about the research findings of physicist Eran Sharon’s lab at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, I’m reconsidering roses. From a mathematical perspective, the flowers are pretty cool—or at least their petals are.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
You can find many videos online explaining that the arrangement of a plant’s petals is related to the golden ratio or the Fibonacci sequence, indicating a deep connection between botany and mathematics. The reason isn’t that nature has a particular affinity for mathematics. Rather the most sunlight reaches the petals when they form an angle with one another that is irrational, meaning its measurements cannot be expressed as the ratio of two integers. The irrationality ensures that no petal is directly above another.
Such insights have fascinated mathematicians and physicists for decades, which is why they have taken a closer look at plant growth. How, for example, can the curly leaf shape of Lollo Rossa lettuce be explained? Why does a carrot bend when it’s cut lengthwise? Questions like these can be answered quite easily with a little math and physics. But the arrangement of rose blossoms has been a long-standing scientific puzzle.
Irregular Growth Leads to Tension
The shape of a leaf is influenced by many different factors, such as the speed of growth, the material and the environment it grows in. For example, if the edge of a leaf grows faster than its center, this can lead to a curled or wavy shape—as with Lollo lettuce. With carrots, on the other hand, the opposite is the case: the inside of the vegetable grows faster than its outside, but because of its firm structure, it usually retains a straight shape. If you quarter the vegetable lengthwise, the structure is weakened, and the insides of the pieces will bend outwards, making visible the pressure that has existed inside the carrot.
Rose petals, however, differ from other flower shapes. They are not simply wavy or curved but have almost triangular tips. Such irregular segments are distinct among flowers. And this raises questions: What distinguishes rose petals from the leaves, petals and shoots of other plants?
To find out, Sharon and his team dissected rose petals, devised theoretical models, created computer simulations and conducted experiments with rubber surfaces. They discovered that the shape of rose petals has a completely different geometric cause than that of other plants.
An Incompatible Geometry
The curling of flower petals can be explained mathematically: because of their differing growth rates, petals “want” to curl, but this is prevented by external factors—such as the tissue not being elastic enough. It’s like trying to flatten the surface of a sphere onto a plane—it’s simply impossible. This “Gauss incompatibility” leads to mechanical stresses that produce virtually all flower shapes.
Gauss incompatibility can only explain smooth and periodic patterns, however, as Sharon and his team were aware. But the shape of rose petals is neither periodic nor smooth: there are isolated locations where a point is formed. To understand this, the researchers first cut the petals into fine strips—once along the horizontal axis and once along the vertical axis. The team’s aim was to visualize the mechanical pressure acting on the petals, similar to cutting carrots to reveal their internal pressure.
The longitudinal strips of the rose petals did indeed curl up, suggesting that the petal preferentially curves in this direction. When cut along the horizontal axis, however, the petal segments remained unchanged. This means a petal possesses a kind of conical structure, which is compatible with a flat geometry and therefore shouldn’t create any internal tension. After all, a flat sheet of paper can easily be rolled into a cone or a cylinder. A rose petal can, in principle, be laid flat on a surface; this confirms that Gauss incompatibility isn’t what causes the unusual shape of the petal. But what causes it then?
Similar questions are addressed in mechanics and industrial manufacturing processes because it’s crucial to know whether a manufactured component exhibits internal stresses and could break. Besides the Gauss equations, which must be considered, there are other equations at play: the Mainardi-Codazzi-Peterson equations. These state, among other things, that the normal vector (the vector perpendicular to the surface) must be uniquely defined. And as Sharon’s team discovered, this isn’t the case with rose petals. They therefore exhibit a geometric incompatibility, albeit a different one than that of other flowers.
Imagine cutting a slice of a pie chart, a shape that roughly corresponds to a flower petal. Now the left side of the slice wants to curl up, and so does the right side—but in different ways. This creates a point in the circular segment where tension accumulates, which in turn leads to the formation of a pointed edge. This can even happen in several places, resulting in multiple points.
Sharon’s research group was able to confirm this mechanism, which had never been observed in nature otherwise, using computer simulations and experiments. Although the team cannot rule out the possibility of other natural processes exhibiting Mainardi-Codazzi-Peterson incompatibility, rose blossoms are currently the only known example.
And that’s what makes roses so unique. I’m still not sure if that’s enough to convince me of their beauty. But I’d never previously considered why flowers look the way they do, so I acknowledge that roses add some new insights into mathematics—and therefore appreciate them a little more.
And as physicist Richard Feynman pointed out in an interview in the early 1980s, looking at a flower with a scientist’s eyes raises “all kinds of interesting questions,” which, in his view, “only adds to the excitement, the mystery and the awe of a flower.”

Brazil's Flavio Bolsonaro reverses course, backs end to six-day workweek
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13

Brazil's Flavio Bolsonaro reverses course, backs end to six-day workweek
SAO PAULO, Oct 13 - Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro on Tuesday said he would back a popular labor reform to reduce the country's workweek, reversing his position in a bid to avoid handing a political win to President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, his leftist opponent in Brazil's presidential elections.
The measure, approved by Brazil's lower house in May as a constitutional amendment, would lower working hours in Latin America's largest economy to 40 hours a week from 44, effectively ending a common practice in some sectors, like retail, of requiring employees to work six days a week.
Bolsonaro, the son of former right-wing President Jair Bolsonaro, defied pollsters at the start of the month to lead President Lula in the first round of Brazil's election by securing 47% of votes cast. The two men will face each other in a runoff on October 25.
Cutting the workweek would mark the biggest overhaul in Brazilian labor rights in decades and a nationwide poll conducted by Quaest in July found nearly 70% of Brazilians support the change.
While the senator and his Liberal Party, PL, had long opposed cutting the workweek, arguing the move was designed to boost Lula's reelection prospects, Bolsonaro changed course on Tuesday, just a day before the Senate was expected to vote on the matter.
"Most Brazilian workers want to see the end of the six-day workweek, so I'm going to vote in favor of ending it," Bolsonaro told journalists, adding that the government would need to offset impacts on business.
Lawmakers aligned with Lula have pushed for a Senate vote before the runoff, hoping to secure approval while the president remains in office.
"It seems to me that, following public pressure and street protests, PL decided to vote in favor of ending the six-day workweek," Lula said during an official event on Tuesday.
The PL has yet to formally announce a change to its position.
"Despite Flavio's lead, the race is still wide open. So it's a smart move by him in avoiding wearing down support on an issue that has broad popular appeal," Leandro Gabiati, director at political consultancy Dominium, said.
While business groups say the measure could increase costs and hurt competitiveness, they will not be left too disappointed by Flavio's decision, Gabiati said.
"The business community still has many ideological and practical reservations about this government," he said. "It will not feel betrayed by Flavio's change." REUTERS

Russia arrests Japanese reporter for alleged espionage
Suspect was arrested on Russia’s far-eastern Sakhalin Island before being transferred to Moscow, says Russia’s FSB.
Russian authorities say they have arrested a Japanese journalist on the far eastern Sakhalin Island, accusing him of espionage.
The Federal Security Service (FSB) announced the arrest on Tuesday, saying the man was believed to have gathered information on Russia’s defence capabilities for Japanese intelligence. The charges carry up to 20 years in prison.
Russia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs named the journalist as Imai Yuki, who it said worked for Japan’s Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper.
The Japanese government was trying to verify reports of the journalist’s detention, according to an official at Tokyo’s embassy in Moscow cited by Japan’s Kyodo news agency.
The journalist was arrested on Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk, the main city on Sakhalin Island, as he was preparing to leave Russia, said the FSB. He was then flown to Moscow, where a court ordered him to be held behind bars pending the probe, the agency added.
A video shared by Russia’s TASS news agency, attributed to the FSB, shows masked officers appearing to handcuff the suspect in a hotel room, before transporting him to an interrogation room.
The suspect was then shown boarding a plane accompanied by two FSB servicemen, before appearing in a cage on trial in a Moscow court, which authorised his custody for nearly two months.
The Japanese man’s arrest comes amid a spike in tensions between Russia and Japan following Russian President Vladimir Putin’s trip in August to the Kuril Islands, the Moscow-controlled Pacific archipelago that is claimed by both countries.
The Sakhalin region includes Sakhalin Island and the four southernmost islands of the Kuril chain, which Japan calls the Northern Territories.
Russia and Japan never signed a formal World War II peace treaty, with the main obstacle being the unresolved territorial dispute over the Kuril Islands.
Authorities in Russia have arrested numerous foreigners for alleged espionage since it invaded neighbouring Ukraine in 2022.
One of the most prominent cases was the detention of Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich in 2023. He was found guilty of espionage by a Russian court, sentenced to 16 years and then freed in a major prisoner swap involving Russia and Western countries in August 2024.

Walmart plans to cover more than 250 prescriptions, including some insulin, inhalers and GLP-1s for diabetes, at no cost to its employees in 2027, the company confirmed to CNBC on Tuesday.
The retailer is also expanding existing benefits and adding new ones to attract and retain workers at a time when many other employers are offsetting rising healthcare costs with higher prices and scaled-back plan benefits. The announcement comes weeks before open enrollment for Walmart employees closes on Nov. 6.
Walmart, the biggest private employer in the U.S., will offer Novo's diabetes injection Ozempic and Eli Lilly's rival shot Mounjaro without charge for people with Type 2 diabetes after a new prior authorization.
But the company still does not cover GLP-1s from Novo and Lilly for the purpose of weight loss. Other large employers similarly don't cover those treatments for obesity or have recently dropped coverage to tamp down on their healthcare costs.
The latest benefit changes build on Walmart's yearslong effort to boost employee compensation after previously receiving criticism for the healthcare benefits and wages it offers. Walmart employs roughly 2.1 million associates worldwide, with about 1.6 million of those workers based in the U.S., as of the end of fiscal year 2026.
In a statement, the company said it's minimizing premium increases for its employees, raising rates for its starting plan by $1.50 per pay period to $39.80. Walmart told CNBC that's a smaller increase than the company made last year.
The company is also expanding an existing benefit that pays for employees to see cancer specialists at the Mayo Clinic or the Cleveland Clinic, according to a Tuesday letter to workers from Donna Morris, Walmart's chief people officer. Starting next year, employees under most plans can use that benefit to get a second opinion from a specialist for rare conditions such as ALS, multiple sclerosis and Parkinson's.
Among the other added benefits is up to 12 weeks of neonatal intensive care unit leave for parents, which can be added on top of regular parental and maternity leave, the letter said.
"The steps we're taking are based on years of planning and trying new things, which is allowing us to make meaningful improvements for associates without slashing benefits or significantly raising premiums," Walmart said in its statement to CNBC.

Cornell suspends fraternity parties after alleged campus gang rape case
Chapters face immediate emergency suspensions for violations amid a sweeping ban tackling fraternity parties at the US university.
Cornell University has suspended fraternity parties for the academic year and will give the New York State Police a role in investigating sex crimes on campus.
The Ivy League university announced the major changes on Tuesday, as it sought to reassure the rattled campus community amid the ongoing outrage over its handling of allegations that a female student was sexually assaulted at a fraternity house in 2024.
The accusations came to light after the former student, known as Jane Doe, filed a civil lawsuit last month.
In addition to the blanket suspension of all parties and social events at fraternity houses through the 2026-27 school year, Cornell President Michael I Kotlikoff announced a new “zero-tolerance” policy for violations, noting that any fraternity chapter that breaks the ban will face an immediate freeze.
“These measures will provide time for a thorough review of fraternity life at Cornell to determine whether and how it can safely continue,” Kotlikoff wrote in a letter addressed to the campus community on Tuesday.
The university president pledged to strengthen Cornell’s sexual misconduct response by adding a dedicated case manager to the Office of Civil Rights to guide survivors through the reporting process.
Kotlikoff affirmed that he will be transferring investigative authority from the university police to independent, trauma-informed investigators with the New York State Police in an effort to reform the handling of sexual abuse cases on campus and restore community trust.
Kotlikoff acknowledged that sexual violence extends beyond fraternities, saying Cornell must also confront a campus culture of excessive drinking and drug use and expand education about students’ responsibility to intervene when others are at risk.
Cornell also plans to add victim advocates and expand sexual violence prevention programmes, including education aimed at encouraging bystanders to intervene, he said, calling the various actions announced Tuesday “first steps toward systemic change on our campus”.
“We will take all necessary steps to address the conditions that led to Jane Doe’s experiences, and those of other survivors,” he said.
Doe’s lawsuit was brought against the Chi Phi fraternity at Cornell University and seven of its members, accusing them of drugging and gang raping her during a party on the night of October 19, 2024.
Following her initial allegations in 2024, Cornell shut down the fraternity and temporarily suspended the accused male students, two of whom were later expelled. But critics have said the university’s response was too lenient, prompting it to launch an independent review into its handling of the case, led by a former top US prosecutor.
“We must meet this moment by acknowledging where we have fallen short and taking meaningful action,” Kotlikoff said. “Cornell must be a place where safety is not an open question.”

Israel’s Yellow Line in Gaza advances, leaving displaced with nowhere to go
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
18:42:52 UTC
03:42:52 KST

Israel’s Yellow Line in Gaza advances, leaving displaced with nowhere to go
As Israel moves Gaza’s ‘Yellow Line’ westwards, displaced families in Shujayea face renewed danger, and nowhere safe to go.
Shujayea, Gaza Strip – Mahmoud Harzeen is pitching a tent about 200 metres from the yellow concrete blocks marking Israel’s so-called “Yellow Line”, preparing for his sixth move.
Each time the line inches closer, the 35-year-old packs up and moves further back, trying to keep his family away from danger. But every move offers only temporary relief.
“Every time they move forward a little, we move back a little,” Harzeen told Al Jazeera.
The “Yellow Line” divided Gaza’s territory between Israeli and Palestinian control as part of the October 2025 “ceasefire” agreement.
Israeli forces withdrew behind the line, but have continued to move the demarcation deeper into Gaza. They now control about 65 percent of Gaza, according to the United Nations, up from the 53 percent agreed a year ago.
On October 11, Israeli forces moved the yellow concrete blocks several metres westwards in Shujayea, in eastern Gaza City. More of the neighbourhood was brought under Israeli military control and Palestinian families were forced to flee again, with Israel’s shifting boundaries further restricting where they can live and move.
For Harzeen, who supports a family of 10, the latest move is part of a yearlong search for somewhere his family can live.
He cannot remember the dates of each displacement. Instead, he recalled the places, one after another: Zeitoun, Sahat al-Shawa, al-Muntazah.
“About six times – every time the line advanced a little – I would feel that it was dangerous, so I would move back a little and try to live there for a while,” he explained.
His most recent move barely lasted one night. After spending time setting up the tent, he slept in it once before Israeli forces moved the “Yellow Line” forward again, getting too close for Harzeen’s liking.
“I pitched the tent and slept in it for one night,” he said. “The next morning, we took our bedding and our things and left.”
The threat extends beyond the movement of the blocks themselves. Harzeen described living amid drones, helicopters, artillery fire and stray bullets, with shrapnel posing a constant danger to people sheltering nearby.
The nights when the line advances are particularly frightening, he said, recalling tanks, troops and heavy shelling as the blocks were moved.
Israel has continued its attacks despite the “ceasefire”, killing nearly 1,500 Palestinians in the last year. Israel has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians since the war started in October 2023.
“The night they move the line, there are tanks, infantry coming down, and shells being fired,” he said. “All of that happens just so they can move the yellow block a little further forward.”
Most people in Gaza have been displaced multiple times as a result of Israel’s genocidal war and the accompanying large-scale destruction of buildings across the enclave. That leaves little space to pitch tents in safer areas and soaring rent that Harzeen cannot afford.
Now he is preparing for the possibility of moving again. “They will probably move it forward again,” he said. “Every time we have to flee, we have to move closer to it. We keep moving.”
Fleeing at night, returning in the morning
For Asma Ali, 32, the Yellow Line’s advance has turned displacement into a cycle of fleeing at night and returning in the morning, never knowing how long her family can stay in one place.
Ali, a mother of three from Shujayea, said her family has been displaced seven or eight times since the ceasefire began.
After staying in central Gaza City, they returned to Shujayea hoping to settle in the al-Mantar area. But then, a month later, renewed shelling and evacuation fears forced them to move again.
The family sought shelter at a school before moving to a house near a bus stop. After a night of heavy shelling, they left in the early hours of the morning and went to stay with family back in the centre of Gaza City. But the advance of the “Yellow Line” has left Ali uncertain about where her family could go next.
“Every night, we would flee, then come back in the morning,” Ali said. “You spend the night trying to find somewhere to stay, then return the next morning.”
“The night the Yellow Line advances is terrifying,” she said. “The shooting continues from the beginning of the night until dawn. You live in fear.”
Ali said her family lost their belongings – including gold, household items and her children’s clothes – when the dwelling they were staying in was destroyed.
Among the items lost was a brace for her son, who has a disability. She only had the brace for two days.
“It was gone in the blink of an eye,” she said.
The family has been trying to find somewhere safe to stay, but Ali said there is nowhere they can afford to go. Moving south is also difficult, with transport hard to find and little certainty that they will find a safe place there.
Asma’s request is simple: somewhere her children can sleep without the family having to flee again.
“The most important thing is somewhere safe for us,” she said. “Somewhere I can put my children and where we can rest and settle.”

====================================================================================================

'Unapologetic Zionism' and the end of Israel's democracy myth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
18:38:35 UTC
03:38:35 KST

Breadcrumb
'Unapologetic Zionism' and the end of Israel's democracy myth
A Muslim woman on a Tel Aviv beach, a hijab in a crowded street, “Arabs and Jews” sharing public spaces. It is precisely this imagery of everyday coexistence that Israelis often invoke to rebut accusations of apartheid. Yet the country's electoral politics tell a more complicated story.
On 23 September, Israel's Central Elections Committee voted to disqualify Ra'am and the Joint List, seeking to exclude the principal vehicles of Israel’s Palestinian parliamentary representation from the upcoming end-of-October election. The petitions invoked provisions intended to protect Israel's Jewish and democratic character, including prohibitions on supporting armed struggle.
Furthermore, the Balad Party leader, Sami Abu Shehadeh, was banned from the upcoming Knesset elections.
The same elections committee that had issued all these decisions also rejected attempts to disqualify far-right Jewish parties, including Itamar Ben-Gvir's Otzma Yehudit.
Although the Supreme Court overturned the decision, as it has repeatedly done over the past two decades, the irony remains hard to miss.
In 2021, against Arab consensus, Ra'am helped sustain an Israeli governing coalition, breaking a longstanding convention that kept independent Arab parties out of government. Yet five years later, the same party and its controversial leader, Mansour Abbas, found themselves fighting for the right to contest an election.
Exclusion
Today, as Israel swiftly shifts rightward, the boundaries of such participation are narrowing, bringing into sharper focus patterns of exclusion rooted in the state's earliest years, and potentially signalling a reversal in their political status.
Palestinians who remained after the 1948 Nakba, roughly 150,000, were incorporated into the electoral system while much of their population lived under military rule until 1966. They could vote for a parliament whose government restricted their movement, expropriated their land and treated them as a security and demographic threat.
The state wasn’t required to abandon the distinction between individual citizenship and nationality, which was reserved for Jews.
Therefore, Palestinian participation didn’t come with an equal claim to defining what Israel was, or the power to meaningfully improve their status. Nor did Palestinians have the right to return to the villages from which they had been expelled, while a Jew from Warsaw or Brooklyn could immigrate to Israel, acquire citizenship and enjoy preferential access to land and settlement opportunities.
Even in ethnic terms, they were reduced to merely “Arabs”, a generic label devoid of a distinct Palestinian identity, rendering them naturalised citizens in their own land. And simultaneously, or rather ironically, they were cast as an extension of the Arab World, while being severed from the wider cultural and linguistic environment to which they belonged.
Vote but not have a say
For decades, to maintain the state’s democratic image, the system managed this tension through legal restrictions, political bargaining, and institutional accommodation. It worked as long as institutions could absorb political challenges without fundamentally altering Jewish national primacy, while keeping the lid on the underlying conflict. This was, in effect, the achievement of what might be called suits-and-ties Zionism, largely associated with the Labour Party.
The occupation of the West Bank and Gaza in 1967 altered that environment profoundly. Territory that had occupied a central place in religious-nationalist imagination was now under Israeli control.
The impact on Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza was immediate, through military occupation and land seizures, whilst for Palestinian-Israelis the implications continued to be obscured by the longstanding arrangement that allowed them to “vote but not have a say”. A form of forced social bribe, so to speak.
Nevertheless, Israel has always had the power to withdraw the apparent “privilege” at its discretion. Over the past two decades, exclusionary politics have gradually gained freer rein. What has emerged, especially, is a more “unapologetic Zionism”. The religious-nationalist movements have moved from pressuring governments to exercising authority within them.
For Palestinian-Israelis, this convergence brought together ideological entitlement and the instruments of state power. What religious nationalism advanced as a matter of principle could brazenly be pursued through legislation, backed by the secular language of security and demography. This alignment found expression in electoral campaigns, such as “No loyalty, no citizenship” by the right-wing party Yisrael Beitenu in 2009, or a clip released on election day in 2015, in which Netanyahu warned that “the right-wing government is in danger. Arab voters are heading to the polling stations in droves.”
Protecting the Jewish state
Importantly, these campaigns coincided with, and were followed by, a growing body of discriminatory Israeli legislation, most notably the 2018 Nation-State Law, which reserved national self-determination exclusively for Jews and elevated Jewish settlement to a national value.
When the Arab party Balad submitted a proposed Basic Law entitled A Country of All Its Citizens, challenging the constitutional principle underlying the then-proposed Law, the Knesset Presidium refused to allow it to proceed to parliamentary debate. Supreme Court President Esther Hayut subsequently characterised Balad’s submission as crossing a red line, on the grounds that it negated Israel’s existence as a Jewish state.
Yet the significance of these proposals cannot be measured solely by their legislative success. From the perspective of “discursive institutionalism” and the political psychology of intergroup dynamics, political discourse both reflects and shapes collective attitudes.
Even unsuccessful bills, of which the Knesset has seen many, can signal a growing tolerance for exclusion, weakening social restraints on discriminatory behaviour and making previously contentious measures more politically conceivable. In this sense, the parliamentary arena becomes not merely a site of law-making, but a mechanism for renegotiating intergroup relations.
Such attitudes long predate the war in Gaza, although recent polling suggests they have intensified. A 2014–15 Pew Research Center survey found that 48% of Jewish Israelis supported expelling or “transferring Arabs from Israel”. Meanwhile, the 2025 Israeli Democracy Index found that support for government measures encouraging Arab citizens to emigrate had risen from 36% in 2019 to 53% in 2025. Only 16% of Jewish respondents believed Palestinian national identity was compatible with loyalty to Israel.
The irony is that Palestinian citizens have spent decades seeking to expand their influence within Israeli democracy, while movements determined to restrict that influence have gained power through the same institutions.
This contradiction has sharpened a longstanding Palestinian debate: whether electoral participation offers a way to change the system from within or merely legitimises its inequalities.
Mansour Abbas's entry into the governing coalition in 2021 tested the former proposition and yielded very few results. And today’s attempt to disqualify the principal Arab electoral lists, albeit overturned by the judiciary, marks a further step backwards.
Apartheid does not necessarily require the disappearance of democratic institutions; it can coexist with elections, courts and parliamentary representation when those institutions operate within an entrenched hierarchy of collective rights.
What Israel effectively operates on is a normalised two-tier conception of democracy. It is where political equality is recognised at the level of individual suffrage, however contested in practice, while remaining constrained by the institutional privileging of one national group over another, a principle treated as fixed and non-negotiable.
The legal significance, let alone the everyday implications for Palestinian-Israelis, lies not in individual instances of discrimination, but in whether they form part of an institutionalised system of domination, within which further exclusion can be pursued without fundamentally altering the existing political order. In other words, this version of ethno-democracy becomes the means of administering and perpetuating that hierarchy rather than a mechanism for overcoming it.
The late-October election may reveal just how far that transformation has gone, although the growing vulnerability of Palestinian-Israelis is already more apparent than ever.
Dr Emad Moussa is a Palestinian-British researcher and writer specialising in the political psychology of intergroup and conflict dynamics, focusing on MENA with a special interest in Israel/Palestine. He has a background in human rights and journalism, and is currently a frequent contributor to multiple academic and media outlets, in addition to being a consultant for a US-based think tank.
Follow him on Twitter: @emadmoussa

Pope Leo XIV undergoes successful lung surgery, Vatican says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
18:36:00 UTC
03:36:00 KST

Pope Leo XIV, 71, has been diagnosed with lung cancer after undergoing surgery in Rome on Tuesday, with doctors confirming that the lower lobe of his right lung was removed following the discovery of a malignant tumor.
The 71-year-old Leo returned to his room after the surgery at Rome’s Gemelli hospital, according to a statement from the Vatican spokesman, who promised further information at a later time. He had a scheduled operation to remove a nodule from his lung on Tuesday, which the Vatican said had gone smoothly.
Subsequent examination confirmed that the nodule was an adenocarcinoma, a form of lung cancer, the Gemelli medical team said.
The pope had announced his planned surgery on Sunday, saying the nodule had been detected during checks at a "very early stage" and was "well localized."
Leo had walked into Rome's Gemelli hospital through the main entrance earlier in the day and waved to dozens of well-wishers who had gathered to greet him. The Vatican said the surgery would be performed by a team led by Gemelli’s chief thoracic surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora.
The operation got under way as medical staff recited the Rosary prayer in the hospital chapel Tuesday evening. "Let us join together in prayer, asking the Lord to sustain our bishop, Pope Leo, and to comfort all those who are hospitalized here,” said the Vicar of Rome, Cardinal Baldassare Reina, at the start of the prayer.
The American pontiff has offered a rare level of transparency about the first publicly disclosed major health problem of his 17-month papacy. He revealed the discovery of the small, localized nodule during his Sunday noon prayer and announced that he would have it removed.
Oncologists say even if the nodule turns out to be cancerous, Leo’s prognosis is "excellent” since it will have been removed at an early stage.
The surgery, which is usually performed under general anesthesia, will require a weeklong hospital stay and the Vatican on Monday canceled all Leo’s audiences through Oct. 20.
"These are things that can be treated very well, if the words he used reflect the clinical situation,” said Dr. Lorenzo Spaggiari, director of thoracic surgery at the European Institute of Oncology, or EIO, in Milan, who is not involved in the pope’s care but knows the team at Gemelli.
But the decision clearly came as a surprise: While Gemelli has a specific papal apartment that past popes have used, complete with a private chapel on the 10th floor, Leo will actually be staying in a nearby room since the papal apartment is currently undergoing renovations, according to the Vatican press office.
Spaggiari said he expected the team at Gemelli would perform a biopsy to determine whether Leo has lung cancer followed by the removal of a section or lobe of the lung where the nodule is located.
Both could be done using robotic techniques, and could be performed consecutively, under the same anesthesia, with different specialist teams, Spaggiari said.
A sophisticated robotic bronchoscopy technology called ION allows a biopsy on nodules as small as 3 millimeters (1/10 inch), Spaggiari said. Both the Gemelli and the EIO have the technology, which has been available in Italy for just two years.
Gemelli also has robotic surgical technology, allowing the operation to remove the nodule to proceed "using a minimally invasive technique,” he said.
The technique involves the surgeon making four small incisions in the chest through which the instruments of the so-called da Vinci robot are inserted, he said. The surgeon then controls the robotic arms looking at a screen providing high-definition, 3D views of the surgical site.
"It’s a very well-established technology. This is something we have been doing for 20 years,” he said.
It wasn't known for certain what technique would be used on Leo. Gemelli has documented using both robotic procedures to diagnose and operate in under four hours.
The biopsy risk is "virtually zero,” while the surgical risk is very small, carrying a 0.6% to 0.8% mortality rate for patients in otherwise good health with good heart and lung function, Spaggiari said.
During the surgery, doctors would also remove lymph nodes that drain the segment or lobe. "If all those lymph nodes turn out to be negative, so stage one, then the outlook is very good,” he said, adding that no other treatment would be necessary.
The nodule was discovered during regular checks, the Vatican has said.
"I think he has had a bit of luck. They found something that was asymptomatic - a lung nodule, possibly a tumor. He might call it something else; we call it luck,” he said.
EIO advises patients not to fly for three weeks after surgery - which would give the pope just the interval needed to make his planned Nov. 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, depending on his recovery. The current itinerary for the trip is ambitious and the longest of his papacy to date, calling for Leo to clock just over 31,000 kilometers (19,000 miles) on a dozen flights and two helicopter rides, and a significant altitude change in Peru.
"He has decided to undergo surgery soon in order to not change his plans for future overseas trips, so there is no need to worry, as it is not an emergency,” said Tokyo Cardinal Kikuchi Tsutomu, who saw Leo on Monday.
A lung nodule is a small abnormal area measuring less than 3 centimeters (1.2 inches) that sometimes appears on a CT scan of the chest or abdomen. Often, the scans are done to investigate trauma or a lung infection, unrelated to a lung cancer screening. A nodule can be benign or malignant, and oftentimes surgical removal is recommended both to establish whether it is cancer and to treat a malignancy while it is still localized.
This is believed to be the second hospitalization for Leo, who is known to be sporty and in good shape, with weekly tennis games and swimming.
As a young missionary priest, he came down with typhoid fever in 1985, soon after arriving in Chulucanas, Peru. The illness and hospitalization were a cathartic moment for him to decide to stay in the poverty and discomfort of Peru after living in relative comfort in Rome - a decision that ultimately paved the way to his papacy, according to an interview Leo gave to Elise Ann Allen in 2025 for "Pope Leo XIV: The Biography.”
According to the book, Leo said he prayed to God to let him die rather than suffer the "horrible” pain of the fever. "I was hooked up to an IV, and I said, ‘If this is your sense of humor, Lord, I think you could do a little better.’
"Obviously, I survived; I recovered, but it turned out to be a very significant moment for me, because it was like, ’Well, you’ve already dealt with the illness; you already see what the needs are here - the order, the Augustinians, the church are telling you, ‘We need you here; go for it.’ I never looked back.”
___
Barry reported from Milan.
