The US Mission in Saudi Arabia on Tuesday urged Americans to reconsider travel to the kingdom, citing risks from Iranian and Houthi missile and drone attacks, armed conflict and terrorism, Anadolu reports.
In a post on US social media company X, the mission shared a travel advisory maintaining Saudi Arabia at Level 3, or reconsider travel, while designating the area along the Yemen border Level 4, or do not travel.
The US travel advisory system has two lower levels: Level 1, which calls for normal precautions and Level 2 for increased caution.
Under the advisory, US government employees working in Saudi Arabia require special authorization to use any airport in the country and are prohibited from traveling within 20 miles (32 kilometers) of the Yemeni border. They also require special authorization to travel to the provinces of Jizan, Asir and Najran, as well as the cities of Qatif, Taif and Yanbu.
The mission advised Americans in Saudi Arabia to take similar precautions.
The advisory said that since the outbreak of hostilities between the US and Iran on Feb. 28, there has been an ongoing threat of drone and missile attacks from Iran. It said commercial flights remain operational from Saudi Arabia but have at times faced significant disruptions.
It said Iran and the Iran-backed Houthis have launched missile and drone attacks into Saudi Arabia, targeting cities, infrastructure, airports, military bases, diplomatic sites and energy facilities.
The advisory said falling debris from intercepted missiles and drones also poses a risk and warned US citizens against photographing, filming or sharing information about interceptions or affected sites.

It cited terrorism, exit bans and the enforcement of Saudi laws governing social media activity among the risks facing travelers.
The advisory follows security alerts issued by the US Embassy in Saudi Arabia in recent days amid attacks and threats targeting the kingdom.
The embassy renewed its security alert on Monday for a third consecutive day following attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and an attack targeting King Fahd International Airport in Dammam.
The embassy warned of possible flight cancellations, airspace closures and other travel disruptions and urged US citizens to exercise caution at major airports.
Saudi authorities have reported missile and drone attacks targeting airports and other sites in the kingdom in recent days, while the Houthis have threatened further attacks on Saudi airports and oil facilities.
A Saudi-led coalition, meanwhile, has intensified military operations against Houthi positions in Yemen, including airstrikes in the capital, Sanaa.

Cholera cases surge in Yemen as conflict intensifies, WHO says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
17:18:45 UTC
02:18:45 KST

Cholera cases surge in Yemen as conflict intensifies, WHO says
Yemen has reported 8,034 suspected cases and 27 deaths this year, with a quarter of cases from the last four weeks.
Suspected cholera cases in Yemen have tripled in the past three weeks, the World Health Organization (WHO) warns, as civilians continue to escape renewed fighting and seek safety in unsanitary camps.
Ramped-up combat, which has pushed more than 200,000 people to flee their homes, drove suspected cases from 217 in the week of September 6-12 to 647 in the week of September 27 to October 3, the WHO said in a report on Tuesday.
“Families fleeing conflict are now facing another threat from diseases that can be prevented and treated,” said Annette Heinzelmann, the UN agency’s emergency director for the region.
“Without urgent funding and unimpeded access to safe water, vaccination and essential health services, outbreaks could spread rapidly among already vulnerable communities.”
Yemen had reported 8,034 suspected cases and 27 deaths this year, with a quarter of the suspected cases occurring in the last four weeks, the WHO said.
Five governorates hosting large numbers of displaced people in the southwest – Abyan, Lahij, al-Dhalea, Taiz and Aden – account for 92 percent of reported cases. The disease has also reached remote displacement camps in Hadramout in the country’s east that are particularly difficult for medical teams to access.
Emergency response underfunded
Cholera has ebbed and flowed for years as the conflict in Yemen has continued. In 2024, the WHO warned that the country was facing the “highest burden” of a global cholera outbreak. In 2017, a wave of the disease infected hundreds of thousands and killed at least 2,000.
Yemen was already suffering one of the “world’s worst humanitarian crises” and has seen an escalation of food insecurity and disease since fighting reignited between the Houthis and the government in July, shattering four years of fragile calm.
Cholera is an acute intestinal infection that spreads through food and water contaminated with the bacterium Vibrio cholerae, often from faeces. It causes severe diarrhoea, vomiting and muscle cramps.
Contracting the illness can be deadly when not treated with oral rehydration or antibiotics for more severe cases.
The Geneva-based WHO said it had only secured $3.78m of the $31m needed for its 90-day emergency response in Yemen.
The funding is intended to help expand disease surveillance in displacement sites, deploy rapid response teams, strengthen cholera treatment and improve infection prevention in health facilities and cholera treatment sites.

Greta Thunberg joins French student protests amid police clashes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
17:18:00 UTC
02:18:00 KST

Swedish activist Greta Thunberg joined French high school students protesting poor learning conditions Tuesday, as largely peaceful demonstrations were disrupted by clashes with police, who used tear gas to disperse crowds amid reports of thrown projectiles.
Four weeks into nationwide protests over teacher shortages, classroom overcrowding and dilapidated school buildings, more than 161,000 people took to the streets of major cities, according to interior ministry figures. That was down from 266,000 on a similar day of action a week ago.
The government has pledged to address the protesters' grievances, but with public finances already strained and borrowing costs at decades-high levels, it has limited options to invest in public services despite pressure from the streets.
The day started with pupils clustered outside schools with placards and megaphones. In Saint-Denis, a working-class suburb north of Paris, Thunberg joined one of the gatherings.
"We are inspired by the young people who are demanding their basic rights," she told reporters outside Lycee Paul Eluard, one of the schools where the protest movement first gained traction.
"Whether it's not funding schools enough, or the climate crisis, or social injustice crises ... it's about time that young people are stepping up and reclaiming that future."
In front of Paris City Hall, a youth orchestra played Antonin Dvorak's "New World Symphony." Some musicians had protest stickers on their cellos and violins.
The education ministry said 214 schools were closed, down from 800 on a similar protest day a week ago. It said 94.2% of high schools were open.
Six months out from a presidential election that polls suggest could usher in the first far-right government since World War Two, the youth protests, which have been supported by the left, have added to a sense of uncertainty and polarisation.
While most demonstrators marched peacefully on Tuesday, riot police charged and fired tear gas in locations in Paris, Lyon, Strasbourg and Nantes, while a fringe of protesters lit fires, vandalised property and hurled objects at police.
In central Paris, at least one car was set on fire during running confrontations between police and protesters down a central, tree-lined avenue.
In Lyon, the local authorities asked organisers to call off a march after a group of "hostile individuals" preceding the main procession vandalised shops and a petrol station and clashed with police.
While there was no immediate information on who was involved, it is not uncommon in France for street protests to attract so-called "casseurs", a fringe of rioters who seek to confront police and destroy property.
The protest movement and the police response have elicited polarised responses from leading contenders to replace Emmanuel Macron in next year's election.
Hard-left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon, who has a chance of reaching the runoff according to polls, joined one of the marches in Paris, where young protesters chanted his name.
"The police are losing their breath running after young people to beat them up and injure them," he said in a post on X.
"The only ones not losing their breath are the young people bravely protesting," he added, accusing the media of failing to show the extent of police brutality.
Far-right leader Marine Le Pen, the frontrunner in the presidential race according to polls, has denounced violence by protesters and called for those who have damaged schools - or their parents if they are minors - to pay for repairs.
The government has already introduced a bill that would allow precisely that. It is going through parliament.

Tens of thousands of demonstrators took to the streets across France on Tuesday in solidarity with high school students demanding better learning conditions, intensifying pressure on President Emmanuel Macron as he approaches the end of his term.
Some 161,500 people turned out, according to the interior ministry – more than double the 71,500 it gave for the last nationwide demonstrations on Thursday last week.
Unions helping organize Tuesday's rallies put the countrywide turnout at 480,000.
The numbers suggested snowballing street opposition to the government just six months before France votes for a successor to Macron, who is completing his maximum second mandate.
On Saturday, national demonstrations against the spiralling cost of living are to take place, and unions and student groups see the two protest currents fusing together.
The agitation comes as Macron's centrist government struggles to get a cost-cutting budget through parliament, in the teeth of worsening debt that has spooked the bond market.
Although most of Tuesday's demonstrations were peaceful, violence occurred on the sidelines of one of two marches in Paris, where the interior ministry said 41,500 people participated.
AFP journalists saw some cars set on fire and police fired tear gas as masked youths tried to erect barricades across roads and threw objects. Tear gas was also fired during a demonstration in Lyon.
Among those taking part in a demonstration in the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis was Swedish activist Greta Thunberg. She said she was there because "our future is being robbed".
University students were prominent in Tuesday's demonstrations, alongside teachers and union leaders.
They were also backed by far-left opposition France Unbowed (LFI) party, whose chief, presidential hopeful Jean-Luc Melenchon, was seen among crowds in Paris.
Thousands also marched in the cities of Nantes, Lyon, Lens, Strasbourg, Toulouse, Bordeaux and Marseille, according to police and AFP reporters.
"We stand in solidarity with the high schools that are worse off. We need real measures and proper dialogue, not repression," said 16-year-old Emeline, outside a Marseille school.
"We're here because we really feel we're not being heard by the government," said Nina, 17.
The student movement sprang up last month, with teenagers at France's lycees – high schools for those aged 15 to 18 – blocking the entrances to many schools to demand better classroom conditions.
Perceived heavy-handed reactions from police against the students drove many to join Tuesday's demonstrations.
One teen lost his hand when he picked up a police stun grenade during the protests, while another lost an eye, and another teeth when an officer fired a tear gas canister in his face.
Police have opened internal investigations into 34 allegations of violence against demonstrators.
Some 147 teaching staff have been injured in the protests, the education ministry said.
"We're not giving up the fight, whether it's for the high school students who were hit with a harsh crackdown, or for denouncing police violence," said Patricia, a 20-year-old university student in Paris who did not give her last name.
Some Indian tourists who wandered into the Paris demonstration said they were unnerved.
"Initially we were terrified," said Snehil Jain, a 45-year-old visiting Paris for a week with his wife.
"We had seen the media images of violence around these protests. But then we saw it was a peaceful protest, so we were OK then."
France's education ministry said 214 schools, mostly high schools, were closed Tuesday.
University student union l'Union Etudiante reported 90% of universities had closed nationwide to show support.
French students say they are determined to press their demands over absent teachers, dilapidated buildings, overcrowded schedules and other grievances.
They have dismissed a government pledge – made after last week's demonstrations – to send 3,000 substitute teachers to the 114 worst-affected schools.
"We are continuing the blockades. We are not budging," said Naouel, a high school student in Brest. She said she hoped the protests would continue after the half-term holidays, in late October.
Mariolino, a 16-year-old in Nantes, concurred. "Those who think the anger will disappear with the holidays just don't get it," he said.
On Monday, Macron had urged restraint from protesters, saying the issues "deserve time, consultations, discussion and respect".

An independent Premier League commission found Manchester City guilty of serious financial rule breaches between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons, including arranging "sham" contracts with commercial partners to artificially inflate revenue.
The club appealed the ruling, rejecting the allegations and maintaining innocence. Sanctions have yet to be determined.

Breadcrumb
Votes without power: What future for Palestinian citizens in Israel?
East Jerusalem - Israel's general election on 27 October, which will fill all 120 seats in the Knesset, is widely seen as a referendum on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
But it is also a contest over the political standing of Palestinian citizens of Israel, who make up about a fifth of the population, the descendants of those who stayed on their land during the 1948 Nakba.
Their votes may decide which coalition bloc eventually governs, yet nearly every major Israeli party is working to keep them out of any future government.
“In the dominant political discourse, Israelis often address Arab citizens as subjects, not as equal citizens,” Raafat al-Jawabra, a researcher on Israeli affairs, tells The New Arab.
Most Israeli parties, he argues, do not see Palestinian citizens as a natural political partner, instead using them in their campaigns as a subject for fear and mobilisation.
Ahmad al-Safadi, a Jerusalem-based analyst of Israeli politics, says the problem goes beyond the Israeli right and far-right parties and their electoral campaigns.
Israeli parties, including those on the left, treat the Palestinian vote as a way to strengthen their own electoral base rather than as the voice of a community whose crises of crime, poverty, unemployment, and discrimination need clear policy answers.
The numbers explain why their vote matters. A recent poll by local Channel 12 puts the bloc led by former army chief Gadi Eisenkot and Netanyahu's coalition level at 52 seats each, with Palestinian parties on 12.
Salim Brik, a political scientist who researches Israeli parliamentary and party politics, argues that if Palestinian turnout rises above 65 percent, it could reshape the distribution of seats, possibly to the point where a list allied with Netanyahu fails to cross the electoral threshold.
That arithmetic has shaped the campaign. Netanyahu's Likud and Bezalel Smotrich's Religious Zionism have largely dropped conventional persuasion on the economy, the cost of living, and post-war reconstruction.
They are instead campaigning on the fear of Palestinian citizens and a promise of territorial "Judaisation" in the Galilee and the Negev (Naqab).
If Palestinian participation could decide the outcome, then delegitimising Palestinian citizens and casting any government that relies on them as a security risk serve the same goal.
An election built on exclusion
The clearest expression of this logic was the attempt to remove Palestinian parties from the ballot. In September, the Central Elections Committee, made up of lawmakers, voted to disqualify the United Arab List (Ra'am) and the Joint List.
Likud and its far-right allies backed the move, accusing both parties of supporting armed struggle and rejecting Israel's status as a Jewish state.
Last week, the Supreme Court unanimously reversed the decision, as it has done with similar disqualifications before. But the campaign still produced a result.
Sami Abu Shehadeh, leader of Balad, withdrew his candidacy after justices signalled they were ready to disqualify him over an article he wrote on 8 October 2023. He denied supporting Hamas or the attack.
Itamar Ben-Gvir, who led the case against him, called the withdrawal a victory. Adalah, the legal centre for Palestinian citizens, called the whole effort an attempt to delegitimise Palestinian citizens and their representatives.
According to al-Safadi, the attempts by Netanyahu and his religious right allies to push Palestinian parties out of politics have failed. He also sees a risk for the right. Continuing this rhetoric may lead Palestinian citizens to see the election as a direct confrontation with policies aimed at their political presence.
“Anti-Arab rhetoric could end up increasing turnout among people who now believe their exclusion will affect their daily lives and their place in their own towns,” he argues.
This would reverse a recent trend. Al-Safadi says the racism that followed 7 October, the war on Gaza and military operations in the West Bank depressed Palestinian participation in earlier votes. The same pressures, now accumulated, may push voters the other way.
This is where the right's strategy becomes risky. Recent polling has shown Smotrich's party struggling to clear the threshold, and he has moved further to the fringe by announcing a joint slate with Zehut (Identity) chairman Moshe Feiglin. Netanyahu has warned that a divided right in 1992 led to "the Oslo disaster", Yasser Arafat, and Hamas.
Brik's analysis shows why these warnings matter. In a race this close, a far-right list falling just below the threshold would remove a block of seats from Netanyahu's camp. Higher Palestinian turnout is one of the few factors that could cause that.
“Influencing which lists survive,” Brik says, “is one of the main electoral tools available to Arab parties”.
Al-Safadi adds in this regard that “Arab parties have also strengthened their position through joint electoral frameworks and surplus-vote agreements, which can give them more weight when seats are allocated”.
The fear campaign is therefore aimed at two audiences. To Jewish-Israeli voters, it presents Palestinian citizens as a threat to be contained. Its effect on Palestinian voters is less certain: it could discourage them from voting, or it could mobilise them.
The demographic battle for land inside Israel
The second pillar of the campaign turns long-standing state policy into a campaign pledge. Judaisation programmes, land allocation to Jewish communities, and demolitions in unrecognised villages have a long institutional history, and since 7 October they have been recast as security measures.
With Smotrich in control of settlement-related portfolios, the line between ministerial policy and campaign promise has largely disappeared. The rhetoric of settling "inside the Green Line" brings the logic of West Bank settlement into Israel proper.
The Green Line refers to the 1949 armistice demarcation line drawn after the Arab-Israeli War.
Brik places these issues at the centre of Palestinian citizens' concerns, especially in the Negev, where unrecognised Bedouin villages face problems of planning, land, and demolitions.
He points to the positions of Smotrich and Ben-Gvir, tensions in Palestinian towns such as Majd al-Kurum, and rhetoric about strengthening the Jewish presence in the Galilee and taking control of land owned or used by Palestinian citizens.
These issues, he says, will be on the agenda of any government that includes Netanyahu, Smotrich, and Ben-Gvir.
Al-Safadi ranks land as “the issue gaining the most importance among Arab voters”. Many Palestinians, he says, see what is happening inside Israel, in Jerusalem and in the West Bank as part of the same struggle over land, presence and control.
He argues that the targeting of Palestinian homes and continued planning restrictions and demolitions may strengthen collective action within the community to hold on to the land.
In this framing, land stops being a matter of planning and becomes a question about the limits of citizenship.
How different is Israel's opposition?
The Israeli opposition offers no real alternative. Ra'am made history in 2021 as the first independent Palestinian party to join an Israeli governing coalition, in the government that briefly removed Netanyahu.
Al-Jawabra's reading of the current field suggests the alternative is narrow. Most Jewish-Israeli parties, he says, still reject a government that depends on Palestinian parties, and 7 October marked a turning point in rhetoric that delegitimises Palestinian political participation.
Netanyahu's camp is the most hostile, but al-Jawabra sees no fundamental difference between Avigdor Lieberman and Netanyahu, Smotrich or Ben-Gvir on alliances with Palestinian parties.
Eisenkot has said he does not want such an alliance, though his tone is softer. He has also not ruled out working with Ra'am, while denying reports that he promised it a place in government.
Al-Jawabra names only Yair Golan, leader of the Democrats, as a prominent Israeli politician openly willing to cooperate and ally with Palestinian parties.
The result is that one camp campaigns against Palestinian citizens, and the other campaigns around them.
Votes without power
Even a strong Palestinian result may not translate into power. Brik argues that Palestinian parties have so far failed to turn their parliamentary weight into real bargaining power on land, settlements, and civil rights.
With most Jewish parties refusing to rely on them as direct coalition partners, they may end up as "a partner from outside" rather than a central part of government.
Al-Safadi warns of a return to marginalisation if competing Jewish parties can build coalitions that do not need Arab support, however many seats Palestinian parties win.
That is the central contradiction of this election. Palestinian votes may be needed to block one camp from reaching 61, while the government that forms keeps Palestinian parties at a distance.
Higher Arab turnout increases the community's potential influence, but it does not ensure that Jewish parties will treat it as a coalition partner.
For Palestinian citizens, the vote is a test of their position inside Israel's political system: whether their electoral weight becomes political influence, or whether their votes remain a number in the calculations of Jewish parties.
For residents of the Galilee, the Negev, and Jerusalem, the answer will depend less on the results than on what the next government does about land, demolitions, and planning, and on whether issues of rights and equality reach its agenda or are again postponed behind security and demography.

His work focuses on Palestinian affairs, independent journalism, media freedom, and promoting the principles of editorial independence and professional journalism in Palestine

OpenAI’s blockbuster math proof isn’t what you think it is
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
17:11:03 UTC
02:11:03 KST

Mathematicians are finally making sense of the biggest event in decades for their field—and it’s stranger than anyone thought.
In early September OpenAI posted an inscrutable 166-page solution to the Navier-Stokes problem, one of math’s famed “million-dollar problems.” Initial accounts—including from the company itself—suggested that the proof, produced by an internal large language model (LLM), followed an approach devised by two Spanish mathematicians, Diego Córdoba and Luis Martínez-Zoroa.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The model’s purported reliance on this “Spanish program” sparked a very public conflict between the company and Tristan Buckmaster, a mathematician at New York University. Buckmaster had spent much of the past year using LLMs to carry out that program alongside Levent Alpöge, an employee of OpenAI’s archrival, Anthropic. The pair cried foul after OpenAI—whose public models Buckmaster and Alpöge had been using—announced a Navier-Stokes proof that seemed to build upon and then leapfrog over their hard-won progress. But the resemblance between the two groups’ methods now seems merely skin-deep.
“When you go to the details, it is a different approach,” says Gonzalo Cao-Labora, a mathematician at EPFL, the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology in Lausanne. Scientific American spoke with several groups of experts working through the OpenAI paper. All said that it’s increasingly clear that the company’s proof does not follow the Spanish program.
The Navier-Stokes equations are the math behind every fluid. OpenAI solved the million-dollar problem by uncovering a flaw in the equations. The company’s artificial intelligence concocted a situation in which the equations declared that the speed of a fluid’s flow should be infinite—a so-called blowup that can’t happen in real life.
OpenAI solved the problem with an “agent swarm,” some 10,000 copies of its new, math-adept LLM, which spent about 88 hours of computing time and 130 billion tokens collectively constructing a blowup. The company’s math team threw all its resources at the problem after learning of significant progress made by Buckmaster and Alpöge. Buckmaster has alleged that OpenAI then attempted to bribe and threaten him to prevent him going public with insinuations of malfeasance, which he ultimately did.
Even top experts have found OpenAI’s proof of blowup to be a difficult read. But the agents coded their arguments into Lean, a programming language used to automatically verify that the logical steps toward a conclusion in a given sequence are all valid. Several prominent research groups are now using both the Lean code and the paper, with the help of other LLMs, to get a simplified, bird’s-eye view of the math involved.
The proof does somewhat resemble the Spanish program in that both exploit the same “loophole” in the official framing of the Navier-Stokes problem that was given by the Clay Mathematics Institute. It permits a mathematician to coax the equations into blowing up by constructing a weird, unphysical force that “stirs” the fluid just right. But closer examination reveals that OpenAI’s proof builds its unnatural force in a totally distinct way. The proof’s similarities to Buckmaster and Alpöge’s progress are superficial.
Of course, the OpenAI result’s novelty doesn’t mean it wasn’t influenced by the Spanish program. In fact, OpenAI initially used a smaller team of agents to prove an intermediate result, and some experts say that this more modest squad did follow the program. But the 10,000-agent swarm apparently realized a different path was required to finish the job. Of course, regardless of OpenAI’s insistence that its model couldn’t have seen Buckmaster’s data (which the company reiterated in a statement to Scientific American), the “black box” nature of LLMs means we’ll likely never know the swarm’s exact chain of reasoning.
“I honestly don’t see a factual resolution of this,” says Camillo De Lellis, a mathematician at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, N.J. “It’s not anymore a matter of clearly verifiable mathematical facts.”
What’s important, and perhaps a harbinger of math’s future, is how long it took experts to realize all this. When OpenAI revealed its landmark achievement on September 8, company officials clearly and repeatedly stated that their proof followed the Spanish program. Their combative exchange with Buckmaster before the release seems to suggest that they believed as much. And they weren’t initially certain whether his work had been incorporated in their model’s training data.
That is, OpenAI didn’t understand its own model’s proof. And still, more than a month later, no one fully does.
Last week the company dumped some 400 more results on the community. In the pre-AI era, at least a dozen of those results could have merited any human mathematician a Fields Medal—math’s Nobel Prize. There already aren’t enough experts on Earth to keep pace with the onslaught, and there’s no sign that it’s slowing down.

Trump says US Senate as hard to defend as House in midterms

Trump says US Senate as hard to defend as House in midterms
WASHINGTON - US President Donald Trump said on Oct 13 Republicans face an equally difficult fight to retain control of the House of Representatives and the Senate in November’s midterm elections, despite forecasts showing a considerably tougher contest in the House.
“I would say equal,” Trump told reporters at the White House when asked which chamber would be harder for Republicans to defend in the Nov 3 vote.
Trump acknowledged the historical disadvantage facing the party of a sitting president, although he insisted that enthusiasm among Republican voters was surging.
“When you have a sitting president... no matter how good they seem to be, they’re at a big disadvantage, tremendous disadvantage,” he said.
“But I’m doing a tour right now, and I’m doing rallies. The level of enthusiasm for the Republican Party is way up.”
Trump’s assessment was striking because Republicans have been widely seen as particularly vulnerable in the House, while the Senate’s electoral map had initially offered them greater hopes of retaining control.
Election forecaster Decision Desk HQ gives Democrats a 77% chance of winning the 435-seat House, projecting that they will take 235 seats to the Republicans’ 200.
It also narrowly favours Democrats to capture the 100-seat Senate, giving them a 56% probability of victory and projecting a 51-49 majority.
Losing either chamber on Nov 3 would complicate Trump’s ability to push his agenda through Congress during the final two years of his presidency, while handing Democrats greater power to investigate his administration.
Trump has embarked on a campaign blitz in the closing weeks of the election, including rallies in traditionally Republican states where his party faces unexpectedly competitive Senate races.
History offers little comfort to the president.
The party holding the White House has almost invariably lost seats in midterm elections, with just three exceptions in the House since 1934, according to figures compiled by the American Presidency Project.
Franklin D. Roosevelt’s Democrats gained nine House seats in 1934, while Bill Clinton’s party picked up four in 1998 and George W. Bush’s Republicans gained eight in 2002.
The worst modern midterm drubbing came in 1938, when Roosevelt’s Democrats lost 72 House seats, followed by Barack Obama’s Democrats losing 63 in 2010.
Trump himself presided over a split verdict in his first midterms in 2018, when Republicans lost 41 House seats but gained two in the Senate. AFP

Baku arrests dozens as hijab ban empties schools
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
17:06:41 UTC
02:06:41 KST

Baku arrests dozens as hijab ban empties schools
TEHRAN — “I don’t have a single B on my report card. Is this the respect I get?” The girl standing at the school gate was crying, and the officials in front of her did not move. “Have I ever done anything wrong? And now you’re telling me I can’t enter the school. Why should I have to give up my religion?”
Video of the exchange spread across Azerbaijan within hours. Then Instagram and TikTok began failing for many users.
On September 21, the Cabinet of Ministers adopted Resolution No. 309, which bans school clothing that breaks uniformity or conflicts with the “principle of secularism.”
The text never mentions the hijab. On October 6, the same standard was extended to teachers, and by the second week of the month, principals in Baku and the provinces were stopping girls at the gate.
About 96 percent of Azerbaijanis identify as Muslim. For a girl who covers her hair, the decree offers two options: remove the scarf or stay home.
Classrooms empty, parents at the gates
Many families refused both. At School No. 69 in Baku’s Balakhani district, students walked out after classmates were barred and unfurled a banner saying the hijab is no obstacle to education. Students at School No. 322 in the capital did the same.
The pattern repeated in Masally, Jalilabad and the township of Hokmali. Boys joined the boycotts. In one Baku neighborhood, parents said they would keep their sons at home until the girls were readmitted. Footage showed students hugging teachers and sobbing outside locked doors.
Women on the staff have been given the same ultimatum. Zahra Hasanova, a teacher, was ordered to remove her scarf at work. “I am hurt,” she told Al Jazeera. “The hijab is a personal choice, and if one day I want to take it off, that should be my choice too.”
Arrests and a feed that would not refresh
Baku sent police. On October 12, the Interior Ministry reported 37 arrests in the capital, accusing the detainees of confronting school staff, damaging property and disturbing public order.
Criminal cases were opened under Article 233, which carries up to three years in prison. Local activists put the number of people taken into custody above 200.
The ministry has also cited violence: a school director’s car set on fire in the Garadagh district and an attempt to burn a school building, with no injuries. It has not shown who was responsible, and nothing connects the organizers of the school protests to either incident.
The online outage followed the same timeline. Instagram and TikTok stopped refreshing for most users, and X also degraded.
Many people could reach the platforms only through VPNs. Officials have not acknowledged a block, and independent monitors have stopped short of confirming one.
The sudden network throttling coincided with viral footage of barred students and empty classrooms, suppressing real-time organizing and obscuring state crackdown. By cutting off digital channels, Baku aims to curb outrage and enforce compliance.
The precedent and those who benefit
The so-called constitution guarantees freedom of religion in Azerbaijan. Practice has long run the other way.
Headscarf restrictions in schools in 2010 and 2012 produced street protests that police broke up with arrests.
In November 2015, the Baku government’s armed forces stormed the historically devout Shia town of Nardaran, launching a deadly assault that left several local believers martyred.
Following the crackdown, Taleh Bagirzade, head of the Muslim Unity Movement, was subjected to severe torture and handed a politically motivated 20-year prison sentence for organizing civil resistance against state anti-Islamic decrees.
Unsanctioned gatherings are violently dispersed, and independent media operate under constant pressure.
This time the dissent has reached the prisons. Polad Aslanov, a journalist already serving a long sentence on “treason” charges, began a hunger strike on October 8. A statement released through his family says he is using the only tool he has left to defend the constitutional rights of girls and teachers.
Demonstrators have also gathered outside the Azerbaijani consulate in Istanbul. President Ilham Aliyev, speaking at a party conference, told critics not to “interfere with our lifestyle.” Some observers read the remark as aimed at Turkey.
Observers note that the crackdown aligns with Baku’s foreign policy priorities as well as its domestic goals.
Aliyev has spent two decades building a controversial partnership with Israel, which buys a large share of its oil from Azerbaijan and sells Baku drones and other weapons, and he keeps a working relationship with Washington.
Baku has long treated its devout Shia population as a security risk. Enforcing the headscarf ban in the language of secularism lets the government act on that suspicion in terms its partners welcome, and neither capital has shown interest in objecting.
The bill is paid by Muslim families in a Muslim-majority country, who are being told that a girl’s education now depends on what she wears.

Sophocles’ “Antigone” on stage in Mahallat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Sophocles’ “Antigone” on stage in Mahallat
TEHRAN – The play “Antigone” by Sophocles is being performed at the Artists Forum in Mahallat, Markazi Province.
Directed by Rouhollah Soroush, the play will remain on stage through October 27. The cast includes Nasim Ostadhashem, Ali Baratali, Parham Parvaresh, Parastoo Rafati, Panisa Rezaei, Danial Sajadinejad, Amirsaleh Soleymani, Mehdi Azimi, and Mahdis Firouzi.
In Greek mythology, Antigone was a Theban princess and a character in several ancient Greek tragedies. She was the daughter of Oedipus, king of Thebes.
Antigone appears in three 5th-century BC tragic plays written by Sophocles, known collectively as the three Theban plays, with her being the protagonist of the eponymous tragedy “Antigone”.
In her eponymous play, Antigone attempts to secure a respectable burial for her brother Polynices. Oedipus's sons, Eteocles and Polynices, had shared rule jointly until they quarreled, and Eteocles expelled his brother. In Sophocles' account, the two brothers agreed to alternate rule each year, but Eteocles decided not to share power with his brother after his tenure expired. Polynices left the kingdom, gathered an army, and attacked the city of Thebes in the war of the Seven Against Thebes. Both brothers were killed in the battle.
King Creon, who has ascended to the throne of Thebes after the death of the brothers, decrees that Polynices is not to be buried or even mourned, on pain of death by stoning. Antigone, Polynices' sister, defies the king's order and is caught.
Antigone is brought before Creon, confessing her crime and foreknowledge of the king’s edict that Polynices neither be buried nor mourned, claiming the superiority of divine law to human law.
Antigone’s self-defense in defiance of Creon is passionate, courageous, and determined. Creon orders Antigone buried alive in a tomb. Although Creon finally has a change of heart—due to a visit from the soothsayer Tiresias—and tries to release Antigone, he finds she has hanged herself. Creon's son Haemon, who was engaged to Antigone, kills himself with a sword (after an unsuccessful attempt to kill Creon), and his mother, Queen Eurydice, also kills herself in despair over her sons’ deaths (Haemon and Megareus), which she attributes to Creon’s misrule and misjudgment. By her death, Antigone ends up destroying the household of her adversary, Creon.

Tehran Symphony Orchestra to perform “In the Italian Style” concert

Tehran Symphony Orchestra to perform “In the Italian Style” concert
TEHRAN- The Tehran Symphony Orchestra, conducted by Nasir Heidarian and featuring cellist Majid Esmaeili as soloist, will present a concert titled “In the Italian Style” at Tehran’s Vahdat Hall on October 20.
The performance is part of the orchestra’s autumn program and will feature works by Austrian composer Franz Schubert and Soviet-Armenian composer Aram Khachaturian.
The concert will open with Schubert’s Overture “In the Italian Style”, followed by Khachaturian’s “Rhapsody-Concerto”, featuring Esmaeili on cello. The program will conclude with Schubert’s “Symphony No. 2”, bringing together three orchestral works in a performance led by Heidarian.
Austrian composer Franz Schubert (1797–1828) was a central figure of the transition from the Classical to the Romantic era, celebrated for his melodies, expressive harmonies and contributions to symphonic and chamber music. His “Overture in the Italian Style” reflects the influence of Italian opera, particularly the lively, melodic style associated with Gioachino Rossini, whose popularity swept through Europe during Schubert’s lifetime. The work combines energetic rhythms, bright orchestral colors and a theatrical character.
Schubert’s “Symphony No. 2” in B-flat major, composed in 1814–1815. Written when the composer was still a teenager, the symphony reveals his engagement with the Classical traditions of Haydn and Mozart while offering glimpses of the melodic inventiveness that would distinguish his later music.
Aram Khachaturian (1903–1978), an Armenian composer born in Tbilisi, Georgia, became one of the leading figures in Soviet classical music, drawing on Armenian and other Caucasian folk traditions to create works known for their rhythmic energy, vivid orchestration and expressive melodies.
His “Concerto-Rhapsody for Cello and Orchestra”, composed in 1963 and dedicated to renowned cellist Mstislav Rostropovich, combines the structure of a concerto with the freer, episodic character of a rhapsody. The composition places considerable technical and expressive demands on the soloist, moving between lyrical passages and powerful orchestral exchanges.
The Tehran Symphony Orchestra regularly presents works by Iranian and international composers as part of its efforts to expand public engagement with classical music and enrich the country’s musical scene.

Restored “Bashu, the Little Stranger” to go on screen in Montreal

Unknown Publisher

Restored “Bashu, the Little Stranger” to go on screen in Montreal
TEHRAN- A restored 4K version of the late Iranian filmmaker Bahram Beyzaie’s acclaimed film “Bashu, the Little Stranger” will be screened at Cinéma Moderne in Montreal, Canada, on Wednesday evening.
The screening is scheduled for 8:30 p.m. local time, with English subtitles, offering audiences an opportunity to revisit one of Iranian cinema’s notable works exploring the human consequences of war, displacement and cultural differences.
According to the Public Relations and International Affairs Department of the Institute for the Intellectual Development of Children and Young Adults (Kanoon), the film’s restored version was prepared with the institute’s support at Roshana Studio to present the work to audiences in improved visual quality.
Released in 1989, “Bashu, the Little Stranger” follows a young boy from southern Iran who loses his home and family during the Iran-Iraq war. Fleeing the bombing, he takes refuge in a village in northern Iran, where he finds himself in an unfamiliar environment with a different language and cultural traditions.
There, he encounters Naii, a rural woman who gradually forms an emotional bond with the displaced child despite the barriers separating them. Their relationship becomes the heart of the film, illustrating how compassion and human connection can bridge differences in language, background and experience.
The touching acclaimed drama, however, carries subtle undertones about human emotions like love, acceptance, loneliness, and unfamiliarity.
Through Bashu’s journey, Beyzaie examines the effects of war on children and civilians, while addressing broader themes of displacement, identity, mutual understanding and the acceptance of others. The film portrays a child’s struggle to find security and belonging in the aftermath of violence, placing human relationships at the center of its narrative.
Widely regarded as a landmark in Iranian cinema, “Bashu, the Little Stranger” is also an important work in the country’s cinema for children and young adults. Its focus on the experiences of a war-affected child gives the film a perspective that extends beyond the battlefield, highlighting the lasting personal and social consequences of conflict.
In 1999, “Bashu, the Little Stranger” was voted the best Iranian movie of all time by a poll of 150 movie experts.
Born in Tehran in 1938, Bahram Beyzaie was a celebrated Iranian playwright, filmmaker and scholar whose work blended Persian mythology, epic literature, particularly Ferdowsi’s Shahnameh, and contemporary social issues.
Before turning to cinema in the 1970s, he had established himself as a leading playwright and historian. Often called the Shakespeare of Iran, he was admired for his mastery of Persian and his exploration of Iranian history and cultural identity through drama.
His notable works include “Ballad of Tara” (1979), “Death of Yazdgerd” (1982), and “Killing Mad Dogs” (2001).
After moving to the United States in 2010, Beyzaie continued his cultural and academic activities at Stanford University, teaching and researching Persian theater, cinema and mythology. His enduring creative commitment was also reflected in the manuscript “Dash Akol According to Marjan,” completed five years before his passing.
The Montreal screening forms part of efforts to introduce Iranian cinematic works to international audiences and bring restored versions of significant films to a new generation of viewers. The 4K presentation is expected to offer audiences an opportunity to experience Beyzaie’s work in enhanced image quality decades after its original production.
The screening also renews attention to a film whose themes of forced migration, cultural diversity and solidarity remain relevant to contemporary discussions about the human cost of war.

To turn invisible, we need to tweak the path light travels
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
17:00:00 UTC
02:00:00 KST

To turn invisible, we need to tweak the path light travels
Some animals have real-life ways to be see-through
It’s pretty hard to fight an opponent you can’t see. That’s what makes Invisible Woman an invaluable member of the Fantastic Four. She can disappear in the blink of an eye and take out entire factions of enemies, all while her adversaries kick and punch empty air.
Characters with invisibility powers — Marvel Comics’ Invisible Woman (aka Sue Storm), H.G. Wells’ Invisible Man and The Incredibles’ Violet Parr — can do all sorts of cool things. Escape embarrassing situations. Snoop on other people. Go places where they’re not allowed.
Short of a theoretical invisibility cloak, that kind of lurking is impossible for us. But some animals can hide in plain sight by turning nearly transparent.
Invisibility is useful for animals that spend a lot of time in places with no good hiding spots, such as the air or open ocean, says Kate Feller, a visual ecologist at Union College in Schenectady, N.Y.
The secret to invisibility is all about light. “The way we see things is when light is reflected back off of an object onto our eyes,” Feller says. The more light that can pass through something undisturbed, the harder it is to see that thing.
Light can’t easily pass through most animals, but those with nearly invisible body parts have tricks to get around this hurdle.
Animals get their colors from pigments, compounds that appear as different colors depending on which wavelengths of light they absorb and which they reflect. Green pigments, for instance, reflect green light and absorb all other colors. Invisibility requires getting rid of these colorful compounds.
Most baby fish lack pigments at first, helping them hide from predators. Some species stay see-through their whole lives. One is the ghost catfish (Kryptopterus vitreolus). With a body that’s fully transparent from gills to tail, it looks like a floating head from afar.
It’s hard to hide every body part, though. Eyes need light-absorbing pigments to see. And even clear stomachs will show up if animals eat colorful food. A ghost catfish eats only small bits of food and its long, thin, tubelike stomach stretches out a meal, helping the organ stay hidden, says Qibin Zhao, a physicist and materials scientist at Shanghai Jiao Tong University in China. Blood can’t be transparent either due to the iron-rich hemoglobin molecules that carry oxygen. So up close, the ghost catfish’s blood vessels are still visible.
But even pigment-free objects are not entirely invisible. Light travels at different speeds through different materials so will bend or bounce when it goes from one material to another. That can create a shine, like sun reflecting off a puddle.
That’s not a big problem for a glasswing butterfly (Greta oto): Its wings have fewer reflective scales than other butterflies’ wings. The wings are also covered in tiny wax bumps that make light’s transition from air to tissue more gradual, so light passes through the wings mostly undisturbed.
Invisible Woman uses a completely different vanishing trick than real-life transparent animals. Instead of letting light pass through her, she bends lights rays to completely avoid her body. The rays never even touch her, so they are not reflected or absorbed, making her invisible to any onlookers.
In 2006, scientists proposed that this same logic could be used to create an invisibility cloak. But in practice, a material that perfectly bends light rays is expensive, hard to make and can divert only a narrow band of light at a time. That’s just enough to make a single-colored object disappear but not an entire human.
And there’s another problem: With no light getting into the cloak, a person inside can’t see out. Luckily, Sue Storm has the ability to use cosmic rays to see while she’s invisible, allowing her to protect the world from supervillains like Doctor Doom.

Saudi Arabia strikes Yemen capital as Houthis vow to retaliate
RIYADH - Yemen’s Iran-allied Houthis said Saudi Arabia was attacking the Yemeni capital Sanaa on Oct 13 after a Saudi-led coalition warned civilians to stay away from an oil depot on the city outskirts, part of a rapidly escalating war between the sides.
The Houthis have for a week been targeting Saudi airports, including a strike on Riyadh on Oct 10 that killed 13 people, in retaliation for the kingdom’s backing of government forces against the Houthis in Yemen’s reignited civil war.
Houthi-run Al-Masirah television reported that the Saudi-led coalition had targeted the Yemen Petroleum Company’s (YPC) Sabah central station, a fuel depot on the outskirts of Sanaa.
The coalition said in a statement on Oct 13 evening that it attacked the station and other sites in an operation aimed at “neutralising the capabilities of Houthis” to threaten the kingdom, Yemen and international waterways.
It said the Iran-aligned group was using the sites in Sanaa, Hodeidah and Dhamar to “supply its arsenal of missiles and drones” to attack Saudi Arabia and commercial vessels in the Red Sea.
YPC said the facility did not currently hold any stocks of petroleum products and that targeting it did not affect oil reserves or supply chains.
However, the Houthis had earlier threatened a “harsh and painful” response to any strikes on Sanaa, with spokesperson Yahya Saree saying targets could include the Saudi Aramco headquarters in Dhahran and an oil refinery in Riyadh.
The group renewed earlier warnings it had issued to oil workers in Saudi Arabia, telling them to stay away from sites that could be potential targets.
The Saudi Cabinet, chaired by de facto ruler Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, issued a statement saying the Houthis would face consequences for their repeated attacks on the kingdom.
The Oct 10 ballistic missile strike on Riyadh airport was the deadliest in Saudi Arabia for a decade, with further attacks grounding flights across the country even as it hosts a major energy conference.
Reignited Yemen war
Saudi Arabia resumed its military campaign in Yemen in support of the internationally recognised government in a bid to reverse the Houthis’ sudden gains in September when they swept down the Red Sea coast to the critical Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
The strait, the southern gateway to the Red Sea, has become a more vital route for Saudi and other global energy supplies since the start of the Iran war in February when Tehran closed the Hormuz Strait leading from the Gulf to the Indian Ocean.
While a government offensive aimed at driving back the Houthis beginning a week ago pushed them off the area closest to the strait, the group remains embedded nearby and has made gains of its own around the city of Taiz in October.
Saudi Arabia has been seeking wider support from allies for its campaign against the Houthis and to help it ward off their missile and drone attacks.
Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan told Mohammed bin Salman on Oct 13 that Ankara would stand by the kingdom, the Turkish presidency said, but without giving details on any specific new line of support.
Turkey and Pakistan signed a mutual defence pact with Saudi Arabia this summer, though Turkey still needs to ratify the treaty in Parliament.
US President Donald Trump also spoke to Mohammed bin Salman on Oct 13, he told reporters, adding that the Houthis were “behaving very badly”.
He said he may ask Erdogan to intervene in support of Saudi interests.
Washington, Saudi Arabia’s strongest ally and longtime security guarantor, has so far rebuffed Saudi efforts to bring it directly into the war against the Houthis.
The Yemen conflict has resumed as a spillover from the wider US-Iran war that began with the US-Israeli attack on the Islamic Republic starting on Feb 28.
Iran, Riyadh’s longtime arch regional rival, has offered to mediate between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, its foreign minister Abbas Araghchi said on Oct 11 in statements reiterated by the ministry on Oct 12. REUTERS

Ethiopia had access to a coastline for decades until Eritrea gained independence from Addis Ababa in 1993. Ethiopia argues that restoring sea access is an existential issue but has said it would be restored through peace and dialogue.

Iran develops countermeasures against Starlink
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:52:05 UTC
01:52:05 KST

Iran develops countermeasures against Starlink
TEHRAN — Iran has developed technical capabilities to identify and disrupt unauthorized Starlink satellite internet terminals, while intensifying its efforts through international regulatory channels to compel the service to comply with telecommunications rules governing its operations inside Iranian territory.
Mohammad Amin Aghamiri, secretary of Iran’s Supreme Council of Cyberspace, said Iranian specialists had developed and tested several systems to identify and manage satellite communications, adding that one of these technologies had been deployed during unrest in December.
 
Aghamiri said approximately 80% of Starlink communication packets in Iran had been disrupted during that period, while much of the remaining traffic had become largely ineffective. 
He stressed that Iran’s countermeasures extended beyond interference with the Global Positioning System (GPS), saying domestic specialists had developed other technologies to identify satellite user terminals and interfere with communications between transmitters and receivers.
 
Identifying unauthorized Starlink terminals remains a priority for Iranian authorities, he added, arguing that the technology could be countered through a range of technical measures.
Beyond GPS interference: identifying and disabling terminals
Starlink, operated by SpaceX, delivers broadband internet through a constellation of satellites in low Earth orbit. Users connect through specialized ground-based equipment known as user terminals, which communicate with satellites passing overhead.
The system's architecture enables terminals to switch between satellites as their positions change, helping maintain connectivity. This network design also presents challenges for authorities seeking to identify individual terminals operating without authorization across a large territory.
Technical interference with satellite communications and the remote deactivation of user terminals are distinct approaches. The former seeks to degrade or interrupt the communications link, while the latter involves the satellite operator identifying a terminal's location and disabling its access to the network.
Iran's Supreme Council of Cyberspace secretary said the country's countermeasures were not limited to GPS disruption and that Iranian specialists had developed additional capabilities to address satellite communications. His remarks point to a broader focus on terminal identification and communications interference rather than reliance on a single technical method.
The International Telecommunication Union (ITU) has separately confirmed that Starlink has the technical capability to geolocate user terminals and disable them remotely. At its 100th Radio Regulations Board meeting, the ITU noted that Starlink had identified and disabled more than 2,500 terminals operating illegally in a particular area, demonstrating the system's capacity to restrict access geographically.
The ITU's findings are significant to Iran's argument that the operator can take more direct action against terminals operating in territories where its services have not been authorized.
Iran takes Starlink dispute to international regulators
Iran's objections to Starlink's operations are not confined to technical and security concerns. Tehran has pursued the issue through the ITU for several years, arguing that terminals transmitting from within Iranian territory must comply with the country's national telecommunications regulations and applicable international rules.
Aghamiri said Iran's Ministry of Communications had submitted multiple complaints and supporting documents to the ITU over the past two to three years. Tehran has also raised the matter with the relevant Norwegian regulatory authority and the US side, while Iran's Foreign Ministry has issued a formal warning to Norway.
The dispute centers on the authorization of satellite transmissions and the responsibilities of the administrations associated with Starlink's satellite-system filings. Under the ITU framework, satellite transmissions from within a country's territory must comply with applicable regulatory requirements, including provisions governing authorization to operate transmitting earth stations.
In October, Iran formally protested to Norway over the ‘continued failure’ to take effective action against unauthorized Starlink operations. The Foreign Ministry summoned Norwegian Ambassador to Tehran Paul Bjornstad and called for immediate measures to halt transmissions from terminals operating without authorization.
Iranian officials have also raised security concerns, believeing that the United States and Israel have used satellite communications infrastructure to support activities directed against the Islamic Republic. Tehran maintains that the operation of foreign communications equipment without its authorization raises questions of national sovereignty as well as national security.
What the ITU has decided
The ITU's Radio Regulations Board has examined the dispute since March 2023. Its decisions have repeatedly called on Norway and the United States to take appropriate measures to ensure that Starlink transmissions from unauthorized terminals inside Iran are stopped.
At its 101st meeting in March 2026, the Board concluded that Norway's actions were not compliant with obligations under relevant ITU resolutions and Article 18 of the Radio Regulations. It urged Norway and the United States to take all appropriate measures available to them to have Starlink immediately disable unauthorized transmissions within Iranian territory.
The Board also noted that Starlink had the technical capacity to locate terminals and deactivate them remotely. At the same time, it asked Iran to continue its own efforts, to the extent possible, to identify and deactivate unauthorized terminals.
At its 102nd meeting, held from June 29 to July 3, 2026, the Board reiterated its position. It noted that the dispute had remained unresolved since 2023 and that no response had been received from the Norwegian or US administrations on the latest submissions under consideration.
The Board again urged Norway and the United States to comply with the relevant provisions and called for immediate action by the operator to disable unauthorized transmissions inside Iran. However, it also reiterated that it lacked the authority to suspend satellite-system frequency assignments solely because the notifying administration had failed to comply with the relevant resolution.
The distinction is important: the ITU has pressed for enforcement of existing rules but has not ordered a blanket shutdown of Starlink's satellite network or suspended its frequency assignments.
A wider debate over satellite internet and national sovereignty
The dispute highlights a growing challenge in international telecommunications governance: how to regulate global satellite broadband systems whose signals can reach across national borders and whose user terminals can be transported into countries where the service is not authorized.
For Iran, the central issue is not simply access to satellite internet technology. Tehran argues that the operation of transmitting terminals within its territory must respect national authorization requirements and that the service provider and the relevant administrations have a responsibility to prevent unauthorized transmissions.
Aghamiri also pointed to Starlink's use in military conflicts, particularly Ukraine, arguing that satellite communications can support functions extending beyond ordinary civilian connectivity, including military command and control, drone operations, intelligence gathering and espionage networks.
His comments reflect Iran's position that satellite communications infrastructure must be assessed in light of its potential dual-use applications, particularly when deployed in a conflict environment. Such concerns have become increasingly prominent as commercial satellite networks play a growing role in military communications and battlefield connectivity.
The Iranian official also referred to statements by US officials and SpaceX chief executive Elon Musk concerning Starlink's wartime use, arguing that the technology should not be regarded exclusively as a civilian communications service.
For Tehran, the combination of technical countermeasures and international legal action represents a two-track response: developing domestic capabilities to address unauthorized satellite communications while seeking enforcement of international telecommunications regulations.
The unresolved ITU proceedings suggest that the dispute will continue to test the balance between the global reach of commercial satellite networks, the responsibilities of their operators and the regulatory authority of states over communications transmitted from within their territory.

Iran warns US against renewed military action, stresses readiness for diplomacy and defense

Iran warns US against renewed military action, stresses readiness for diplomacy and defense
TEHRAN — Iran has warned the United States against any renewed military action, saying the consequences would extend beyond the region, while reaffirming its readiness to pursue diplomacy on the basis of realistic proposals and mutual respect for commitments.
Kazem Gharibabadi, Iran’s deputy foreign minister for legal and international affairs, made the remarks in separate interviews with Russia’s RIA Novosti news agency and Al Araby television network, stressing that Washington must adapt to regional realities and abandon military threats in favor of a diplomatic solution.
“If the United States once again chooses the military option, the consequences will not be confined to the region,” Gharibabadi warned, according to his remarks to RIA Novosti. He said Washington must learn from past mistakes and decide whether to continue pursuing confrontation or engage in diplomacy.
The Iranian diplomat emphasized that Tehran had consistently maintained a constructive approach to negotiations and remained prepared for all possible scenarios. He stressed, however, that a diplomatic settlement required realistic proposals and a willingness by the US side to meet its commitments.
Iran finalizing response to US comments
In his interview with Al Araby, Gharibabadi said Iran was finalizing its response to US comments and concerns regarding the proposal Tehran had submitted in New York. Once consultations are complete, Iran will convey its final position through mediators, he added.
Gharibabadi said Iran continued to welcome diplomatic initiatives and had spared no effort to facilitate dialogue with relevant parties. Tehran’s continued engagement in the diplomatic process, he noted, reflected its political flexibility and commitment to finding a solution.
He nevertheless underscored that Iran’s preparedness to defend itself was no less firm than its readiness to negotiate, making clear that diplomatic engagement should not be mistaken for a lack of defensive resolve.
The deputy foreign minister also stressed that the United States must fulfill its own obligations if it expects progress in negotiations. Iran, he said, had not violated its commitments, while Washington had failed to honor its obligations under the Islamabad memorandum of understanding.
Tehran calls for US compliance with commitments
Gharibabadi argued that Iran could not reasonably be expected to demonstrate further flexibility while the United States continued to disregard its commitments. He said Washington needed to take corrective steps to restore the conditions necessary for diplomatic progress.
He added that the US side was already aware of Iran’s demands and conditions for normalizing the situation surrounding the conflict that began in late February. If Washington met those requirements, Tehran would be prepared to take the necessary reciprocal measures.
The Iranian diplomat’s remarks underline Tehran’s position that the path to de-escalation depends on practical steps, reciprocal commitments and an end to reliance on military pressure.
For Iran, diplomacy remains an available avenue for resolving the crisis, but it must be grounded in 'realistic proposals and the implementation of existing commitments.' Tehran has also made clear that its willingness to negotiate does not diminish its determination to defend the country against any renewed military aggression.

In Yemen's Taiz, shelling worsens and prices spiral

In Yemen's Taiz, shelling worsens and prices spiral
Oct 13 - With their city encircled by Houthi fighters, residents of Taiz say they face intensifying bombardment and dwindling supplies as the Iran-aligned group tightens its grip on surrounding areas.
Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city, has emerged as a major theatre of the conflict between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed government, after their war was reignited last month by the U.S.-Iran confrontation in the Gulf.
The Houthis cut off a main road from Taiz to Aden last week, leaving government forces encircled.
The International Organization for Migration (IOM) said the situation in Taiz had significantly deteriorated in recent days, and that people, basic supplies and humanitarian goods could not enter the city, driving up prices.
Yemen's internationally recognised government launched a campaign last week to recapture areas controlled by the Houthis, recovering ground near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a global shipping artery.
But the Houthis have kept up the pressure near Taiz, seizing the town of Mudiriyat al-Misrakh some 25 km (15 miles) south of the city on Monday, military sources said.
Residents reported heavy shelling of Taiz city on Monday night.
Government sources said the Houthis were to blame.
A spokesperson for the Houthis did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
"We lived a night of terror because of the continuous bombardment," said Ahmed Mahmoud, a resident reached by phone. "This morning there is calm and worry. The streets are empty."
Yassine Muqbil, another Taiz resident contacted by phone, said there had been widespread shelling and his child was too afraid to go outside.
Taiz city had an estimated population of almost 600,000, Katja Juric, IOM's Aden-based Head of Programmes, told Reuters. Government sources said 80,000 had fled in the latest fighting.
INCREASING PRESSURE
Military sources reported fighting in al-Dabab, 10 km (6 miles) from Taiz, and on Sabar Mountain, which overlooks the city to the south, saying government forces who had withdrawn from surrounding areas had regrouped in the city.
Yemeni government warplanes targeted Houthi fighters and equipment in Dabab and Misrakh, government forces said in a statement on Tuesday.
For the Houthis, seizing Taiz city would be a big boost 12 years since the war first erupted. It would leave oil-rich Marib as the last city under government control in northern Yemen.
Mohammed Al-Qadhi, a political and conflict analyst, said Monday evening's heavy shelling and the “tight siege” imposed by Houthi fighters indicated increasing pressure on the city.
"The Houthis know the value of Taiz governorate," he said, noting that its countryside overlooks the coastline and Bab el-Mandeb and that it had served as a bastion of "resistance against the Houthis and their ideology".
The Yemen war erupted in 2014 when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa, driving the government south.
Fearful of growing Iranian influence and chaos on its borders, Saudi Arabia led a military intervention against the Houthis in early 2015 to restore the government.
The resulting civil war triggered one of the world's biggest humanitarian crises and led to years of fighting and devastating airstrikes by the Saudi-led coalition.
The UN brokered a 2022 truce between the warring sides in Yemen that maintained peace until this year.
'CANNOT FIND FOOD'
In Taiz city, prices of basic goods have shot up.
"By God, we know families who cannot find their daily food," resident Nashwan Saad said on Sunday, adding that a sack of wheat had gone up by as much as some 40%.
IOM's Juric said access to Taiz city had been "significantly constrained", noting that a small bottle of water now cost up to $4. "The prices of basic commodities that are still available in the city have gone up significantly," she said.
"People are rushing to purchase and to stockpile basic commodities as they're anticipating a prolonged conflict and also further supply disruptions in the city."
Abdulrahman al-Qulaia, director general of the Ministry of Industry and Trade Office in Taiz, cautioned against panic.
"We appeal to the entire international community concerned with this matter, to humanitarian organisations and civil society organisations, to work seriously to provide these needs ... and lift the siege on the province." REUTERS

====================================================================================================

The journalists’ revolt against AI scraping
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:39:24 UTC
01:39:24 KST

In just a few short years, artificial intelligence (AI) tools such as ChatGPT and Claude have become mainstream technologies. The companies behind these innovative products tout their immense potential benefit for humanity, but this narrative, while not necessarily wrong, brushes aside that these models are built on the wholesale theft of copyrighted work and threaten to weaken further an already-fragile pillar of democracy: journalism.
That is why Editorial Perfil, a major Latin American publisher headquartered in Argentina (and the owner of Perfil, the newspaper where I am digital director), recently sued ChatGPT’s owner, OpenAI, and the company’s largest external shareholder, Microsoft, for the improper use of Editorial Perfil’s journalistic content in their AI products. In the damages suit brought before the Argentine Federal Civil and Commercial Court, we also accused these companies of “unfair competition” — in other words, abusing their oligopolistic position to our detriment.
While Editorial Perfil is the first Spanish-language publisher to file a copyright-infringement suit against an AI firm, it follows in the footsteps of the New York Times, which sued OpenAI and Microsoft over the same issue in late 2023. The Brazilian newspaper Folha de Sao Paulo brought a similar case last year, resulting in a content-licensing agreement earlier this year (an approach that OpenAI has taken with other publishers, including PRISA, the Spanish conglomerate behind El Pais).
We have been here before: Dominant search and social-media platforms also benefited from copyrighted news content without always sharing in the spoils. Search engines — such as Google’s “free” model — made news articles immensely more accessible by featuring them on their results pages. However, despite relying heavily on this copyrighted content to boost ad revenue, Google was not required to provide adequate compensation to the media companies that might employ hundreds of journalists to produce it. True, these distribution systems drove traffic to publishers’ Web sites, but the playing field was never level and increasingly tilted toward tech firms as they consolidated their power.
In the AI age, OpenAI and Anthropic (which owns Claude), as well as the entrenched tech giants such as Google and Meta (which owns Instagram and Facebook), have supercharged this dynamic. The chatbots and other AI enterprise products they have built on the back of increasingly sophisticated large language models answer Internet users’ questions directly, depriving news outlets of traffic and the chance to serve ads or sell subscriptions to potential readers.
These models required huge amounts of training data, much of which was copyrighted material illegally scraped from the Internet. Anthropic recently settled a class-action lawsuit in California by agreeing to pay US$1.5 billion to book authors who argued that the company had downloaded pirated copies of their works to train Claude. The models constantly thirst for more, particularly up-to-date information on current events.
At Editorial Perfil, we have identified multiple instances in which ChatGPT can replicate content from our historical archive in detail. It does the same with real-time news and would even prompt users to request a daily news recap so that they can avoid wasting time visiting multiple sites. It easily bypasses paywalls; for articles that it cannot find within Editorial Perfil’s own sites, it would use copycat Web sites that illegally reprinted them. Historical server data show that multiple bots are consistently crawling our content — not just from OpenAI, but from all the AI firms as well.
These flagrant abuses are self-evident to anyone with common sense. AI firms are not only stealing content, but also encouraging users to stay within their closed ecosystems, turning the Internet into an oligopolistic market. Yet they still try to argue that they are engaging in “fair use” of “publicly available” content. Unfortunately for OpenAI, it has already acknowledged the value of journalism through its many licensing deals. By contrast, Anthropic has avoided content-licensing agreements with news organizations.
The news industry has been in crisis ever since the digital revolution upended its business model more than two decades ago. A new, more sustainable model never emerged. While those of us in media failed to anticipate how the rise of the Internet would change everything, we tried to reinvent ourselves after the fact. However, the oligopolistic dominance of “big tech” has prevented us from making any real progress, and AI is exacerbating the crisis.
A decimated news industry is a bad outcome for everyone. It would not only result in a less informed public; it would also harm the parasitical AI firms themselves, cutting off an important source of training data. If they cannot be bothered to act in the public’s interest, they should at least look out for their own.
Agustino Fontevecchia is digital director at Perfil in Argentina.
Copyright: Project Syndicate

What began as a regional uprising quickly ignited a chain reaction across the empire, toppling a dynastic order that had endured for more than two millennia and ushering in one of Asia’s first republics — the Republic of China (ROC). From that moment, the 10th day of the 10th month became a date of epochal significance, not merely in Chinese history, but in the broader arc of Asia’s encounter with modernity. Yet today, as Taiwan marks Double Ten National Day, the holiday’s meaning has undergone a transformation

Qantas has been forced to ground a plane in Rome after bedbugs were discovered on the aircraft on its way from Perth, a source with knowledge of the incident said yesterday.
The parasitic insects were found in the front of the economy section of the Boeing 787 Dreamliner as it made its way from Perth to Rome for the QF5 flight on Friday last week, the source said.
Bedbugs are small insects that feed on the blood of some mammals, including humans, which can be hard to eradicate.
Photo: Reuters
As first reported by the Sydney Morning Herald, the aircraft had to be taken out of service for cleaning after its arrival in the Italian capital, resulting in the cancelation of the Qantas Rome to Perth service on Saturday.
A Qantas spokesperson said the flight was canceled to allow its engineers and maintenance teams to carry out a deep clean of the aircraft after “an issue identified on a small number of economy seats.”
The airline wanted to “sincerely apologize” to customers for the disruption, they said.
Affected passengers were given accommodation and rebooked on alternative flights within 48 hours of their original departure, Qantas said.
Its aircraft cabins were cleaned regularly and to an extremely high standard and treated with disinfectant every 50 days as a standard precautionary cleaning measure, the airline said.
Macquarie University parasitologist Michelle Power said the bedbugs had “more than likely” been brought on to the plane in someone’s luggage or on a passenger’s clothes and then escaped into the cabin.
“They’re associated with travel. People may go to a hotel that’s infested and because they like dark spaces and are attracted to the smell of human clothes, they make their way into someone’s luggage,” she said.
“They’re a flightless insect, without planes,” she said.
Bedbugs are not dangerous, even though their bites could be itchy and irritating, but they are difficult to get rid of and could hide in bedsheets and crevices for a long time without needing to feed, Power said.
