2026-10-13
16:38:52 UTC
01:38:52 KST

Tax revenue from securities transactions rose 71.2 percent year-on-year to NT$53.4 billion (US$1.66 billion) last month, a new September high, even as it marked the third consecutive monthly decline as market turnover continued to fall.
This year’s overall trading volume remains higher than last year, and securities transaction tax revenue last month still posted positive year-on-year growth for the 14th consecutive month, Ministry of Finance data released yesterday showed.
The stock market declined last month before rebounding later in the month and consolidating at high levels, the ministry said.
Photo: CNA
The TAIEX closed at 47,940.13 points at the end of the month, gaining 1,811 points or 3.93 percent, it said.
The average daily turnover of the local stock market was NT$1.032 trillion, down 5.8 percent month-on-month and marking the third consecutive month of decline. However, compared with the same month last year, it increased 71.8 percent, the ministry said.
The TAIEX yesterday closed down 960.65 points, or 1.95 percent, at 48,341.31, as investors took cues from overnight weakness on Wall Street amid escalating geopolitical unease and a sell-off of chip stocks across Asia.
In the first nine months of this year, cumulative tax revenue from securities transactions totaled NT$506 billion, rising 1.6-fold year-on-year and marking the highest level for the same period, the ministry said, adding that average daily stock turnover surged 160 percent year-on-year to NT$1.146 trillion over the period.
Overall, the nation last month collected NT$496.5 billion in tax revenue, up NT$81.3 billion, or 19.6 percent, from a year earlier and the highest September figure, the ministry said.
The growth was due to increases of NT$29.7 billion in business tax revenue, NT$25.4 billion in corporate income tax revenue and NT$22.2 billion in securities transaction tax revenue, it said.
Commodity tax revenue posted the largest decline of NT$1.1 billion in the month, it added.
In the first nine months of this year, cumulative tax revenue grew NT$700.4 billion, or 24.4 percent, to NT$3.571 trillion, as increases in corporate income, personal income, securities transactions and business taxes offset the decreases in revenue from commodity and land value increment taxes, the ministry said.
The January-to-September figure was 15 percent above the government’s budget for the first nine months and was 78.8 percent of its full-year target, it said.
It remains to be seen whether the tax revenue collected this year could exceed the government’s budgeted figure, as it must consider factors such as the stock trading volume in the coming months and the recovery of the local housing market, the ministry said.

Taiwan’s GDP to reach 10.7%, IMF says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:38:50 UTC
01:38:50 KST

The IMF has sharply raised its forecast for Taiwan’s GDP growth to 10.7 percent this year, the highest projected rate in the Asia-Pacific region, amid the ongoing artificial intelligence (AI) boom.
In its latest World Economic Outlook report released yesterday at its annual meetings in Bangkok, the IMF raised its forecast for Taiwan’s growth from the 5.2 percent it projected in April, making Taiwan the only economy in the world projected to post double-digit percentage growth this year.
Taiwan’s projected growth far outpaces that of neighbors in the Asia-Pacific region, including Japan at 0.7 percent, South Korea at 3.3 percent, Singapore at 5 percent and Hong Kong at 3.8 percent, the report says.
Photo: Ann Wang, Reuters
China’s economy is expected to grow 4.5 percent this year, while the US is forecast to grow 2.3 percent, the report said.
Despite the significant upgrade, the IMF’s latest forecast remains below the 11.05 percent growth projection released by the Directorate-General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics in August.
Global AI development has remained highly concentrated, both upstream, in the computing hardware required for AI training and inference, and downstream, in developing and operating frontier AI models, the IMF said.
Upstream, only a few economies produce advanced semiconductors on a large scale, it said, adding that Taiwan and South Korea account for 62 percent of net trade in AI-related computing hardware.
“Given the structure of supply chains for technology exports from these two economies, a handful of commodity exporters and other manufacturing hubs in East Asia are likely to see spillovers from this activity,” the IMF said.
Reflecting the nation’s robust export performance, the IMF projected Taiwan’s current account surplus would reach 22 percent of GDP this year, among the highest of any major economy.
The IMF also forecast Taiwan’s consumer price index would rise 2 percent this year, up from its April estimate of 1.5 percent, while the unemployment rate was projected to remain largely unchanged at 3.4 percent.
The IMF raised its global growth forecast by 0.1 percentage points to 3.1 percent for this year, compared with 3.5 percent growth last year.
“Two major transformative forces — geopolitics and technology — are reshaping the global economy, with their short-term impact gradually coming into view and their longer-term impact still largely unknown,” the IMF said in the report.
However, “technology is most recently playing out as a positive demand shock powered by investment in AI and related hardware and infrastructure,” the IMF said. “Trade flows show this most strikingly.”
While many advanced economies have been buoyed by rising investment in AI technology, poorer countries that are not benefiting from that boom face stark choices as they deal with high energy prices caused by the Iran war, it said.
“The global economy has been resilient, but that resilience is under strain, with risks tilted to the downside,” IMF chief economist Silvana Tenreyro told journalists in Bangkok.
The US’ war on Iran, launched in February, has plunged the Middle East into violence and seen global energy prices skyrocket as a result of Tehran’s retaliation.
The IMF report detailed that the twin economic forces of the war in Iran and the AI technology boom had created a “fragmented” world economy.
“Headwinds from a prolonged war and persistent geopolitical tensions could revive inflationary pressures, strain fiscal and external positions, and hit energy-importing and low-income countries hardest,” it said.
“At the same time, the current technology tailwind could stop abruptly if expectations about AI-related profits and productivity gains are reassessed, weakening investment and tightening financial conditions,” the IMF report said.

Lightmatter reveals plans for its new technologies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Lightmatter Inc, a US-based optical interconnect solution start-up, yesterday said it plans to ship its first near-packaged optics (NPO) engines and high-density laser network-interface cards (NICs) next year, adding that this would pave the way for full-scale copackaged optics (CPO) engine production in 2028 and 2029.
The company’s liquid-cooling and high-density laser NIC, called Guide NR, is light-source engineered to power next-generation CPO and NPO architectures in artificial intelligence (AI) data centers.
One of the CPO engines with detachable fiber array units is assembled in Taiwan by ASE Technology Holding Co (日月光投控), Lightmatter chief executive officer Nick Harris told a virtual media conference yesterday.
Photo courtesy of Lightmatter Inc
Lightmatter also counts Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC, 台積電), chip designer Global Unichip Corp (GUC, 創意電子) and passive fiber optic components maker Browave Corp (波若威) as its silicon photonics ecosystem partners in Taiwan.
Asked about the company’s commercial launches of new products, Harris said NPO and Guide DR could be launched next year and CPO in 2028.
“On the CPO side, we work with GUC, and there are others in Taiwan and elsewhere,” he said.
Initial, low-volume shipments of CPO are scheduled for next year, while high-volume deployment is expected start in 2028, Harris said.
The company’s photonic interposer technology, which is considered the most advanced and ultimate stage of CPO, will roll out on a very similar timeline, he said.
Silicon photonics is the next big breakthrough in artificial intelligence scalability, as it enables huge speedups for inference and training workloads, while traditional copper transmission reaches its physical scaling limits, he said.
The transition to photonics would coincide with the arrival of 224Gbps and 448Gbps copper-based SerDes technologies, he said.
Some Taiwanese companies have developed their first 400Gbps designs, but it remains highly unlikely that a standalone 896Gbps SerDes technology would ever materialize, Harris said.
Lightmatter already has technology capable of handling 1,600Gbps per optical fiber, which provides a scalable roadmap spanning from 400Gbps to 10Tbps per optical fiber, doubling the speed offered by traditional Ethernet technology, he said.
As the optical industry is facing acute laser and optical fiber shortages, Lightmatter uses bidirectional technology to halve optical fiber consumption, Harris said.
The company also uses a diversified supply chain and its proprietary Guide platform to mitigate laser shortages, he said.
The Guide platform relies on silicon-level integration known as Very Large Scale Photonics to drastically reduce laser usage, he added.
In the face of semiconductor capacity tightness, Lightmatter works with multiple foundries such as Intel Corp and Tower Semiconductor Ltd and packaging houses including Amkor Technology Inc to provide flexible options for customers ordering standard products such as Passage L20 and Guide, Harris said.
For custom product orders, clients secure their own semiconductor capacity, and Lightmatter builds on top of their allocated supply, he said.
Those clients are mostly industry giants, including hyperscalers and major semiconductor firms, he added.

Accountability in use of clinical AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:38:48 UTC
01:38:48 KST

Artificial intelligence (AI) is already reshaping Taiwan’s hospital wards. Squeezed by an aging population, nursing shortages and grueling paperwork, major medical centers are rapidly deploying algorithms. National Taiwan University Hospital uses large language models for medical records and International Classification of Diseases (ICD). Chang Gung Memorial Hospital integrates machine learning into disease prediction and triage.
Meanwhile, Taipei Veterans General Hospital has set up dedicated clinical review panels to audit algorithms throughout their lifecycle.
Most hospital AI tools in Taiwan still handle paperwork and triage, but that administrative line is already blurring. Systems are moving directly into diagnostic assistance and treatment pathways. Algorithms might not issue oncology diagnoses on their own, but they already prioritize which people gets urgent CT scans, flag suspicious lesions and suggest chemotherapy regimens.
When an algorithm errs, where does the liability fall? On the attending physician who trusted the screen? The hospital that procured the software? Or the vendor that wrote the black-box code? The danger in clinical AI is not only bad calculations; it is also the diffusion of responsibility.
Healthcare has paid dearly for overestimating software before. The Therac-25 radiation accidents in the 1980s killed and maimed people precisely because human oversight gave way to blind faith in automated code. The failure of IBM Watson for Oncology proved that sophisticated software collapses in real clinics when recommendations depart from clinical context and proven practice.
As legal academic Frank Pasquale wrote in New Laws of Robotics, AI must augment clinical judgement, not supplant it.
Pasquale’s core insight is straightforward: attribution must precede autonomy. In a hospital, an algorithm cannot be cross-examined and a providers cannot hide behind a proprietary model. Legal and moral responsibility must stay tethered to recognizable institutions and clinicians.
Aviation solved a similar dilemma years ago. When the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) introduced SMART — an automated tool for rerouting air traffic around severe weather — commercial airlines pushed back hard. Their concern was not whether the software worked, but who was on the hook if an automated route steered an airliner into a storm.
The FAA responded with a deliberate “start, crawl, walk, run” deployment: keeping human controllers firmly at the center of final routing choices until the operational logic was proven.
Clinical medicine needs the same posture.
The newly passed Artificial Intelligence Basic Act (人工智慧基本法) sets down broad principles: human oversight, transparency and accountability. However, broad statutory text does not tell an intensive care unit how to handle a conflicting drug alert.
Because fully autonomous clinical AI is not yet the standard of care in Taiwan, policymakers have a brief window to get the rules right.
Translating rules into clinical reality requires three concrete shifts:
First, tiered, risk-based oversight. Administrative tools for hospital bed tracking should not face the same regulatory friction as diagnostic algorithms that recommend surgery or radiation doses. Regulators must require rigorous clinical validation on local patient populations, transparent training datasets and an unobstructed right for clinicians to question and override recommendations.
Second, unbundled lifecycle liability. Responsibility must be divided by role, not blurred together. Developers must answer for model integrity and dataset bias. Hospitals must take ownership of local deployment and clinician training. Clinicians remain responsible for final treatment decisions within the software’s validated scope.
Third, post-market surveillance: Governance cannot stop at regulatory approval. Algorithms suffer from “data drift” as clinical protocols shift. Hospitals need multidisciplinary committees to track real-world errors, review patient outcomes and audit systems after vendor updates.
The transition toward healthcare AI is not an engineering race. It is a test of institutional credibility. The societies that thrive in the age of algorithmic medicine would not be those with the fastest processors, but those with the discipline to demand human accountability before automation outpaces oversight.
Hanson Wu is a healthcare policy professional with experience in pharmaceutical policy, health security and public affairs. He is a graduate healthcare policy researcher at National Taiwan University.

Yamamoto flounders in Milwaukee
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:38:48 UTC
01:38:48 KST

Yoshinobu Yamamoto finally flopped in a playoff game, and the Los Angeles Dodgers are heading back home with their bid for a third straight championship in serious jeopardy.
Yamamoto lasted just 2-2/3 innings for his shortest postseason start as the Dodgers lost 7-4 to Milwaukee on Monday to fall behind 2-0 in the National League Championship Series (NLCS). The Brewers continually fouled off pitches and drove up Yamamoto’s pitch count before knocking him out of the game.
“I don’t know the exact reason yet,” Yamamoto said through an interpreter. “I need to check the videos and then I can reflect on what happened today.”
Photo: AFP
It was quite a departure for a pitcher who was virtually unhittable last October.
Yamamoto, last year’s World Series MVP, entered 8-1 with a 2.14 ERA in 11 career postseason appearances. In Game 2 of the Dodgers’ NLCS sweep of Milwaukee last season, Yamamoto threw a three-hitter and pitched the first playoff complete game since Houston’s Justin Verlander threw one in 2017.
In three previous postseason starts following Dodgers losses, Yamamoto had gone 3-0 with a 1.23 ERA. The Dodgers were banking on him to deliver another gem to tie the NLCS as they continue their quest to become the first NL team to win three straight World Series.
“I think everybody’s so used to him being a robot that if he didn’t go eight innings, no hits, whatever, it wasn’t Yamamoto,” Dodgers shortstop Mookie Betts said. “It shows he’s a human being and it’s playoff baseball.”
Yamamoto was unable to protect two Los Angeles leads in the first three innings.
After the Dodgers scored in the top of the first, Milwaukee tied the game in the bottom half when Yamamoto allowed a one-out double to Brice Turang and William Contreras followed with an RBI single.
The turning point of Yamamoto’s night came in the third. The Brewers trailed 2-1 but had runners on first and second with two outs when Jake Bauers stepped to the plate.
Bauers worked the count full and then fouled off six straight pitches from Yamamoto before capping his 12-pitch plate appearance with a walk that loaded the bases.
“It was a blast, honestly,” Bauers said. “It was a blast. Any time you can get that locked in doing anything, it’s to me one of the most enjoyable experiences I think a human being can have.”
It was not very enjoyable for Yamamoto, particularly after Christian Yelich came up next and lined a two-run single to center. Yelich’s hit put Milwaukee ahead 3-2 and knocked Yamamoto out of the game.
Yamamoto ended up allowing two walks and four hits while striking out only one batter. He threw 75 pitches, including 36 in the third inning.
“He just didn’t have it tonight, which is very rare,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said.
The Dodgers pulled back ahead 4-3 in the fifth, but they could not maintain the lead and then Los Angeles’ lineup had no answers for Milwaukee’s bullpen. Milwaukee relievers Dustin May, JoJo Romero, Abner Uribe and Aaron Ashby combined to retire Los Angeles’ last 15 batters, continuing the Dodgers’ postseason slump.
Los Angeles got just three hits Monday and is 2 for 26 with runners in scoring position during the playoffs. Four-time MVP Shohei Ohtani hit his last homer way back on Aug. 18.
If the Dodgers do not start hitting, Yamamoto might not get another opportunity to pitch this postseason.
“Our job now is to win several games and give him another chance,” third baseman Max Muncy said, “because I know that next time out he’s going to dominate.”

The game helps students with ADHD pay attention in class and avoid triggering interpersonal conflicts, he said.
The first edition of the game took the silver award in a Japanese innovation competition, whose judges gave them valuable feedback to improve it to the refined version that won gold medals, he said.
Codesigner Cheng Hui-han (鄭暉翰) said Attention Master consists of six modes, including a “Whac-A-Mole” game and a memory game aimed at encouraging players to practice their ability to focus on a task, impulse control and patience.
The game uses algorithms to read body movements in modes centering on visual recognition, coordination and emotional regulation, he said.
An important element is that the exercises were gamified and capable of giving instant feedback to keep users entertained, Cheng said.
Liu said he used to serve on the panel of science fairs and the hard work of the students and teachers who guided them had never failed to impress.
Taiwanese students have won 106 gold medals in youth science and invention competitions in the past two years, thanks in no small part to the work of educators, he added.

Does muscle turn into fat if you stop working out?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:38:44 UTC
01:38:44 KST

“This is not true,” says Leigh Breen, a specialist in muscle physiology at the University of Leicester. But it’s a statement he hears a lot, particularly from people who have taken a long break from exercise. “They’ll often refer to the notion that their muscles have ‘softened’ or don’t feel as toned.”
The reality is that there’s no biochemistry linking the two types of tissue. Muscle and fat are distinct. “There’s no known process in the human body that would support muscle turning into fat, or vice versa,” says Breen.
He thinks the confusion comes from what happens when we stop exercising — particularly resistance training. We may begin to lose some of the muscle we built through training. And if we continue eating the same amount while exercising less, we may end up with an energy surplus, which can lead to an increase in body fat.
Photo: AFP
“This combination of a reduction in muscle mass and potentially an increase in fat mass can give the impression that one is turning into the other,” he says. “Which isn’t the case.”
If you take a couple of weeks off your usual training routine but remain relatively active, you’re likely to see fewer changes than if you are completely immobilized for an extended period because of an injury.
What we eat during an exercise break can also influence how much muscle and fat mass we gain or lose. Breen recommends keeping protein intake high while slightly reducing calorie intake.
Photo: EPA
Ultimately, our bodies are constantly changing, and small fluctuations in muscle and fat mass during breaks in our training are generally normal. “Slight fluctuations are generally nothing to worry about, as long as over the course of months and years consistent exercise and dietary habits have been maintained,” Breen says.

Saudis probe how defense systems failed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:38:38 UTC
01:38:38 KST

Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels yesterday again blamed Saudi Arabia for airstrikes overnight that targeted areas along Yemen’s northern border with the kingdom and its western coastline, while Saudi Arabia has launched an investigation to determine how its air defenses failed to intercept a barrage of missiles and drones fired by Houthis.
The rebel-run al-Masirah satellite television yesterday said that two airstrikes hit the Houthi-held Red Sea island of Kamaran, while a third hit al-Qanawis district, 55km northwest of Hodeidah.
The station also reported airstrikes in the province of Jawf, which borders Saudi Arabia.
Photo: AFP
Al-Masirah blamed Saudi Arabia for the strikes, but did not provide further details.
Saudi Arabia did not immediately respond to the claim, but the strikes came hours after air raid sirens blared in the Saudi capital and explosions were heard.
Meanwhile, officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to comment publicly, said an initial probe showed that Houthis fired multiple drones to pave the way for a mix of cruise and ballistic missiles to reach Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport, where at least 13 people were killed and more than 300 were wounded in attacks on Monday.
The Houthis possess ballistic missiles and advanced systems fitted with warheads that can change direction during flight and pose a challenge to Patriot interceptors and other defense systems used by the Saudis.
One of the officials said the investigation also aims to find out why air defense systems did not provide earlier warning of the attack in which the Houthi missiles and drones flew more than 1,000km to reach Riyadh.
The incident, one of a string of Houthi attacks since last week on Saudi airports, has exposed vulnerabilities in Saudi Arabia’s defense system and signaled a dangerous inflection point in an expanding Mideast conflict that began more than seven months ago when the US and Israel launched their war against Iran.
The Saudi-led coalition also said it had twice intercepted and destroyed ballistic missiles launched on Monday by the Houthis toward Riyadh. At least three explosions could be heard on Monday night in the city. Civil defense officials later said the danger had passed.
Saudi Arabia stopped issuing public warnings of imminent military attacks days before the series of deadly strikes on Riyadh airport, and the government has not said why there were no alerts in the past week.
The warnings had served to highlight the violence undermining the kingdom’s efforts to project an image of calm to its people and the world during its war with Houthis.
Their absence during the airport strikes raised questions about Saudi Arabia’s vulnerability to attack and about its ability to protect residents and visitors, four Western and Arab officials in the region and political analysts said.
It also reflected efforts to maintain a sense of normalcy, they said.
“They [the Saudi government] want to have it both ways: to launch a military operation and at the same time try to give confidence to the population and external stakeholders,” Middle East Policy Council senior resident fellow Sultan Alamer said.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:38:37 UTC
01:38:37 KST

Federal agents on Monday searched the home of Democratic US Representative Ilhan Omar, a startling escalation in a criminal investigation that brings renewed focus to the frequent target of White House derision in the final weeks of her re-election bid.
The search of the Minnesota congresswoman’s home so close to next month’s midterm contests that would determine control of the US House and the Senate was swiftly condemned by top Democrats in Congress, who raised questions about the timing given longstanding US Department of Justice (DOJ) protocol to avoid overt investigative steps involving political candidates in the direct run-up to an election.
Omar, an outspoken critic of US President Donald Trump, said she was being targeted as one of the Republican’s “political enemies.”
Photo: Reuters
The scope of the investigation was unclear, but Trump and officials in his administration have repeatedly referred to the existence of an inquiry into Omar, a Somalian-born Democrat whose status as an immigrant to the US and left-wing views have drawn scrutiny from the White House and other Republicans.
US Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin last month cited an “ongoing investigation” that he suggested was examining potential fraud in her family’s immigration paperwork.
“Something’s going to happen,” he said in a potential foreshadowing of the search.
In a post on X, Omar called the search an “attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.”
“For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation,” she said. “I will not be silenced.”
At a political rally in Ohio on Monday, Trump attacked Omar’s Somalian origins.
“She’s telling us about the Constitution, and she comes from one of the worst countries anywhere on the planet,” he said.
Although the Republican focus on Omar’s background dates back years, the search notably took place three weeks before the November midterms, in which Omar is seeking re-election. The DOJ has historically sought to avoid public investigative actions involving a candidate within 60 days of a primary or general election.
Top Democrats seized on the timing as the latest instance in what they said was the “continued corrupt weaponization” against Trump’s perceived adversaries.
“For years, Donald Trump and far-right extremists have relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Omar with vile personal attacks and baseless accusations,” a joint statement from US House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and other top congressional Democrats said. “Now, less than 30 days until the midterm election, his violent mass deportation machine has descended upon the home of a duly elected Member of Congress and her family.”
The DOJ said in a statement that agents had executed a judicially authorized search warrant in the Washington area related to an ongoing federal criminal investigation, but provided no other details.
The street around Omar’s home was blocked off on Monday morning as some Homeland Security Investigation agents removed boxes labeled “Seized Property Evidence.”
The operation came just days after Trump referred pejoratively to Omar at a rally in Tennessee as coming from a country of “crime and squalor” and suggested that US Vice President J.D. Vance “and our people” were investigating her.
Hours after the search, Trump told reporters he had “nothing to do” with it and it is “really up to the DOJ.”
Vance has in the past accused Omar of committing immigration fraud, an allegation she has denied, and has said the administration was looking for pathways to investigate her.

DNA and vehicle-tracking help recover stolen Renoirs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:38:37 UTC
01:38:37 KST

DNA left on a protective painting cover helped investigators recover two stolen Renoirs and uncover what they suspected were preparations for another art heist, a French prosecutor said on Monday.
Four men were given preliminary charges in the investigation into the Sept. 8 theft from the small Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer on the French Riviera.
The charges include organized theft and criminal association, Marseille Prosecutor Nicolas Bessone said.
Photo: AFP
One painting, Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano, sustained a tear, while the frame of Young Woman at the Well was slightly damaged, Bessone said.
He estimated their combined value at 4.2 million euros (US$4.7 million).
The thieves used an electric saw to cut through a fence, entered the museum through the ground floor and cut clips securing the frames of four paintings.
An alarm sounded and police officers arrived four minutes later, a swift response that “apparently caused the perpetrators to panic,” Bessone said.
“As they fled, they were unable to take all four paintings and abandoned two of them, which were later found in a protective sleeve,” he said.
The DNA found on the abandoned cover matched that of a 29-year-old already under investigation in a drug trafficking case in which police were tracking his vehicle, Bessone said.
Vehicle-tracking data showed that the suspect, accompanied by a 41-year-old man, went to the home of a third man shortly after the theft, Bessone said.
Police surveillance also showed that the 29-year-old on Oct. 3 visited the Maeght Foundation in Saint-Paul-de-Vence — home to a large modern art collection. The suspect then met with a fourth man known to police from art theft and forgery cases in 2001 and 2003.
The arrests were prompted by the “very strong suspicion that another heist was imminent,” Bessone said.
The two men suspected of carrying out the museum theft have been given preliminary charges of “theft committed by an organized gang” and “criminal association,” among other counts.
The two men, who have denied wrongdoing, were sent to prison pending further investigation, Bessone said.
The third suspect acknowledged receiving the paintings at his home and hiding them behind a wall built beneath a staircase after the theft.
Investigators recovered the Renoirs from the hiding place, Bessone said.
The fourth suspect acknowledged seeing photographs of the paintings, but said he did not immediately recognize them.
Both of those suspects were given preliminary charges of “concealment” of stolen paintings, and were released under judicial supervision and barred from leaving France.
Two additional people who had been arrested were released without charge.
The Renoir Museum occupies the final home of the leading French Impressionist painter Pierre-Auguste Renoir, who lived there until his death in 1919. It is the best-known attraction in Cagnes-sur-Mer, a Mediterranean coastal town between Cannes and Nice.
The theft revived painful memories of the spectacular theft of crown jewels from the Louvre Museum in Paris last year and renewed calls for better security and funding at the many cultural sites across France.
French Judicial Police National Director Christian Sainte on Monday said that the country “is repeatedly targeted by organized criminal groups that carry out theft operations targeting valuable objects that are part of our cultural heritage” in museums, castles, places of worship, private homes and art galleries.
French museums recorded 23 cases last year and about 10 this year, he said.

16:38:37 UTC

Shares in Taiwan tumbled nearly 961 points yesterday, tracking an overnight sell-off in US technology stocks after a Houthi attack on a Saudi Arabian airport sent crude oil prices soaring.
The New Taiwan dollar also fell sharply against the US dollar to close above the NT$32 mark for the first time in two months as investors shifted funds to the greenback as a safe haven amid escalating geopolitical unease.
South Korean and Japanese shares also led losses across Asian stock markets as technology firms plunged on fresh worries about the outlook for the artificial intelligence (AI) investment boom.
Photo: CNA
The TAIEX closed down 960.65 points, or 1.95 percent, at 48,341.31, with leading chipmaker Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (台積電) down 1.97 percent. The NT dollar lost NT$0.190 or 0.59 percent to close at NT$32.085 against the US dollar.
Turnover on the local main board totaled NT$1.125 trillion (US$35.22 billion), compared with NT$894.52 billion on Monday, Taiwan Stock Exchange data showed.
The three major institutional investors sold a combined net NT$198.446 billion of local shares, of which foreign investors sold a net NT$165.342 billion, the third-largest net sell-off on record, exchange data showed.
“The initial losses came after heavy losses among US semiconductor stocks overnight after attacks on a Saudi airport, sending oil prices higher,” Moore Securities Investment Consulting Co (摩爾投顧) analyst Adam Lin (林漢偉) said, referring to the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index’s 2.67 percent decline.
“Selling intensified as investors were stunned by falling technology stocks in Seoul this morning amid speculation about several developments, including a delay in shipments of Nvidia Corp’s Vera Rubin platform,” Lin said. “The expanded turnover showed that investors appeared to be panicking and scrambling to trim their positions.”
Memory supplier Nanya Technology Corp (南亞科技) slid 7.4 percent, tracking heavy losses by South Korean counterparts Samsung Electronics Co and SK Hynix Inc.
South Korea’s KOSPI tanked more than 6 percent at one point as Samsung and SK Hynix took a beating following reports that China’s CXMT Corp (長鑫存儲) had made progress on new technology to boost memory density, which other firms have been working on.
The firm was looking at releasing a new server-memory product based on the structure by the end of the year, the reports said.
Seoul closed down 5.5 percent, with SK Hynix off 10 percent and Samsung more than 7 percent down.
Japanese stocks were also sharply lower, with the Nikkei 225 losing 1.8 percent as chipmaker Kioxia Holdings Corp tumbled more than 13 percent, while Tokyo Electron Ltd was down more than 7 percent and Advantest Corp more than 8 percent.
Adding to the unease among traders were comments from Broadcom Inc CEO Hock Tan (陳福陽), who likened the recent investor AI buying frenzy to gambling.
“A lot of investors have no clue what they are investing in,” he said, adding that they “set very extreme expectations only to find out that it’s almost like they are in a casino.”
Tan also said that the industry had not yet found a sustainable model, pointing out that ChatGPT-maker OpenAI reported billions of dollars in losses.
“For now it’s still losing money, because they’re spending a lot on training,” Tan said. “So frankly, it doesn’t tell anything at this point except that there is a lot of potential revenue growth out of providing frontier generative AI models.”

Economists see AI boom sustaining Taiwan growth, urge diversification
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:38:34 UTC
01:38:34 KST

Economists attending the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok said strong demand for artificial intelligence (AI) chips is boosting Taiwan’s economic outlook, but urged the country to use the boom to diversify its economy and mitigate market risks.
The IMF yesterday raised its forecast for Taiwan’s economic growth this year to 10.7 percent from 5.2 percent it estimated in April, making Taiwan the only economy projected to post double-digit growth this year.
Iyabo Masha, director of the Intergovernmental Group of Twenty-Four (G24), told CNA that Taiwan’s growth is being driven mainly by its semiconductor industry, which is benefiting from strong demand in the AI sector.
Photo: Sirachai Arunrugstichai, Bloomberg
She said the industry could continue expanding over the next two to three years, although growth might slow as the sector stabilizes.
Masha urged Taiwan to take advantage of the current economic expansion by using additional government revenue and other resources to develop industries beyond technology.
Eric LeCompte, executive director of Jubilee USA Network, a nonprofit organization that advocates debt relief for developing countries, said AI could help Taiwan and other economies achieve strong growth even as many countries around the world struggle economically.
However, he warned that overly optimistic expectations for AI could inflate asset prices and trigger a market crash if the technology fails to deliver the anticipated returns.
"I think the most important thing for the Taiwan government if they’re really going to hedge their risk or not be as concerned about the risks is they need to diversify how their economy is growing and they need to diversify their job sector," he told CNA.
While Taiwan is in a favorable position in the short term, LeCompte said, its long-term resilience will depend on how effectively it uses the current boom to strengthen other parts of the economy.
Emma Rafaelof, an economist at the US-based Semiconductor Industry Association, recently told CNA that she was optimistic about AI’s continued growth, adding that cross-border cooperation would be needed to capitalize on the trend.
She urged the US, Taiwan and other economies to work together to support AI’s expansion.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:38:33 UTC
01:38:33 KST

Eleven people are missing after two merchant ships were yesterday struck by drones off Bulgaria in the latest spillover from the Ukraine war in the Black Sea.
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev summoned the Russian ambassador after drones struck a Ukrainian-owned cargo ship, while another vessel was also hit and sank further north off the coast of the NATO and EU member.
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said the alliance would adjust its defenses “as needed.”
Photo: Bulgarian Ministry of Interior via AP
The Ukrainian-owned cargo ship Chelsea 3 was “hit by three aerial drones,” and shortly afterward another ship was “struck” and sank, Radev said.
“We lack solid, clear evidence to level accusations against any specific party; however ... logic suggests the outcome works to the advantage of the Russian Federation,” he wrote, calling the attack “unacceptable.”
The presidency later identified the ship that sank as the HS Dignity, a Guinea-Bissau flagged cargo vessel that was en route to the Romanian port of Braila
It went down 17 nautical miles (31.5km) east of the Krapets, Bulgaria.
“According to information we got from the rescue center ... five people were rescued and 11 are missing. This is preliminary information,” a spokeswoman for the northeastern region of Dobrich said.
All 15 crew members aboard the stricken Chelsea 3 — seven Ukrainians and eight Azerbaijanis — had been rescued after it was hit 18 nautical miles east of Byala, Bulgaria, Radev said.
Rutte, speaking after a call with Radev, said NATO would continue to work closely “with our allies in the Black Sea.”
“We have already strengthened our posture along the eastern flank and will continue to monitor the security environment, adjusting our deterrence and defense posture as needed,” Rutte wrote.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen condemned the latest attacks, calling them “another front of escalation of the Russian war in Ukraine.”
Ukrainian Minister of Foreign Affairs Andriy Sybiga also blamed Russia, denouncing what he called Moscow’s “deliberate disregard for civilian lives and maritime security in the Black Sea.”
“The Black Sea is a lifeline for global food security. Russia is attacking it to weaponize hunger and hold the world hostage,” he wrote on X.
Amid mounting fallout from Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine, drone attacks have become increasingly frequent in neighboring countries.
The conflict has also spread across the eastern Black Sea, with at least 45 merchant vessels attacked over the past 12 months in areas previously not listed as high risk, the maritime risk management group Ambrey said last month.
No strikes were recorded in the areas in the preceding 12 months, Ambrey said, adding that the increase was driven by attacks further from the coasts of Russia and Ukraine.
Last week, two commercial vessels were hit in the Black Sea off Bulgaria in an attack widely blamed on Russia, although Bulgaria said the circumstances were unclear.
Nine Syrians and one Egyptian remain missing. That dual strike came a day after another ship caught fire and sank off the Romanian coast, killing one person and leaving another missing.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said the ship was hit by Russian drones.

Flu cases declining, but deaths still high
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:38:31 UTC
01:38:31 KST

There were 144 severe flu cases and 46 flu-related deaths last week, and extra flu vaccines have been purchased for a government-funded program to meet high demand this season, the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) said yesterday.
Flu and COVID-19 activity is slowing down, but both are still in an epidemic period, CDC Epidemic Intelligence Center Deputy Director Lee Chia-lin (李佳琳) said.
Influenza viruses were the most common respiratory pathogens spreading locally in the past four weeks, with influenza A (H1N1) accounting for 91.8 percent of tested cases, she said.
Photo: Taipei Times
Of the 128,847 medical visits for flu-like illness last week, 11.9 percent were emergency visits, above the epidemic threshold of 11 percent, but the percentage is declining weekly, she said.
More than 86 percent of the severe cases have or had underlying health conditions, Lee said, adding that the risk of developing severe illness should not be overlooked, especially among high-risk groups.
Flu activity is rising in Japan, Singapore, the US, Canada and Europe, she said.
While the recent wave of flu infections has passed its peak, deaths are a lagging indicator, so the 46 flu-related deaths reported last week was the highest weekly number this year, CDC Deputy Director-General Lin Min-cheng (林明誠) said.
Flu activity is expected to continue slowing and the epidemic period could end in the middle or late next month, he said.
Meanwhile, weekly medical visits for COVID-19 have been declining in the past few weeks, dropping a significant 35 percent last week to 5,261, Lee said.
There were 21 severe COVID-19 cases and 15 deaths reported last week, most of whom were older people with chronic conditions who had been vaccinated, she said.
As public willingness to get vaccinated is exceptionally high since this season’s government-funded program started on Oct. 1, the CDC would purchase another 200,000 to 300,000 doses of flu vaccines and 174,000 doses of Novavax’s COVID-19 vaccine, Lin said.
Beginning on Monday, the first batch of Novavax’s COVID-19 vaccine would be available for people aged 12 or older and eligible for the first phase of government-funded vaccination, while the additional purchases of vaccines are expected to be available from the second half of next month, the CDC said.
As most of the severe cases were unvaccinated high-risk groups — including older people, young children, people with multiple underlying health conditions or immunocompromised people — who are already eligible for vaccination, the CDC encourages them to get vaccinated as soon as possible, Lin said.
Meanwhile, 9,001 medical visits for enterovirus infection were reported last week, the CDC said.
The most common strain was Coxsackievirus A6, followed by enterovirus D68 and Coxsackievirus A16, it said.
Although enterovirus is not in its epidemic period, weekly numbers remain high, Lin said, adding that the centers continue to encourage people to wash their hands thoroughly with soap.

PSG and Man City tell two very different stories
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:38:29 UTC
01:38:29 KST

Manchester City and Paris Saint-Germain have reshaped soccer with the financial backing of Gulf state owners, but there is a stark contrast in the health of those projects ahead of their latest Champions League meeting on Wednesday.
City return to Champions League action for the first time since they were found guilty of breaking Premier League financial rules in a bombshell verdict which could threaten their place in the English top-flight.
PSG strived to follow City’s era of sustained success and are firmly established as Europe’s top dogs after successive Champions League titles to go along with their domination of French soccer.
Photo: Reuters
Abu Dhabi-backed City won the race against Qatar-owned PSG to become European champions first in 2023.
The triumph over Inter Milan in Istanbul that completed a treble of Champions League, Premier League and FA Cup was the pinnacle of City’s rise since a 2008 takeover fronted by Sheikh Mansour, the vice-president and deputy prime minister of the United Arab Emirates.
However, doubt hangs over City’s spoils from the past 15 years unless they can overturn the findings of the commission on appeal.
City were found to have used “sham” commercial deals with Emirati companies to inflate revenue and reduce costs to the tune of more than US$1.2 billion between 2009 and 2018.
No sanction has yet been meted out, but a severe points deduction or even expulsion from the Premier League are among the possible punishments.
The Premier League season has been thrust into turmoil while clubs await the appeal verdict, with City sitting top of the table after six successive wins, including a 3-0 rout of Liverpool on Sunday.
Winning the Champions League could be City’s only way back into the competition next season.
To do so they need to stop PSG’s quest to join a very select club of sides to win the Champions League or European Cup in three consecutive seasons.
Further UEFA action against City is unlikely as the club successfully fended off European soccer’s governing body when they attempted to act on the same leak of documents in 2018 that led to the Premier League’s case.
In 2020, City were found guilty of breaking UEFA’s Financial Fair Play rules, fined 30 million euros (US$33.6 million) and banned from playing in European competitions for two years.
City successfully overturned the ban at the Court of Arbitration for Sport, which ruled that most of the alleged breaches “were either not established or time barred”.
In the early days of Financial Fair Play rules, City and PSG entered into agreements with UEFA in 2014.
The French champions have managed to steer clear of such issues since, with president Nasser Al-Khelaifi becoming an influential figure, as a member of the UEFA Executive Committee and chairman of the European Football Clubs (EFC) organization.
At a meeting of the EFC in Copenhagen last month, Al-Khelaifi showed support for embattled City CEO Ferran Soriano.
“His career is fantastic and Manchester City did a lot of positive things also, but I am not in a position to judge,” said Al-Khelaifi. “I think that they have the right to appeal, so it is not the final decision.”

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:38:28 UTC

Fiji have appointed Rugby World Cup-winning coach Jake White to lead them through to next year’s tournament in Australia.
The South African, who led the Springboks to their 2007 World Cup triumph in France, makes his debut as Fiji coach in a Test against Japan in Tokyo next week.
He replaces Senirusi Seruvakula, who served as interim coach following Mick Byrne’s departure in April.
Photo: EPA
“Jake brings something that very few coaches in world rugby can claim -- the experience of leading a nation to Rugby World Cup glory,” Fiji Rugby Union Chairman John Sanday told a press conference with White yesterday. “We are not going to Australia simply to make up the numbers. We are going there with a determination to compete and challenge expectations, and demonstrate what Fiji can achieve when world class talent is supported by world class preparation.”
Fiji, ranked 10th in the world, have been drawn in Pool C with Argentina, Canada and Spain. They reached the quarter-finals of the last World Cup in France in 2023, losing 30-24 to England.
The Fijians have had a disappointing season this year so far, losing the Pacific Nations Cup final to Japan last month following successive defeats by Wales, England and Scotland in the inaugural Nations Championship.
White has coached mainly at club level since departing as Springboks coach after their World Cup win, having stints at French club Montpellier and the Canberra-based ACT Brumbies.
In his last coaching role, White took the Bulls to three United Rugby Championship finals in his five years at the team but lost them all.
The 62-year-old departed the Bulls after last year’s final defeat by Leinster, saying the Pretoria outfit needed a new voice.
He said on Tuesday he would relocate to Fiji and spend time with Super Rugby Pacific team Fijian Drua while watching local club competition to try to identify new talent.
“I’d like to say we want to have the best-prepared group of players ever to go to a World Cup,” he said. “That’ll be our challenge.”
His immediate task is to rebuild Fiji’s confidence before they meet Japan.
“To be fair about the Fijians, they have lacked a bit of confidence this year,” he said. “Technically, working on game management, that’s one area.”
“The theory for me is we want Fiji to play like Fiji but just give them a little bit more structure, a little bit more formation,” he added.

Social media data show DPP faces headwinds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:38:28 UTC
01:38:28 KST

Social media analytics show that Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) candidates in next month’s local elections, including Legislator Puma Shen (沈柏文), continue to face headwinds, despite strong online engagement, the party said yesterday.
DPP New Media Center director Juan Chun-ta (阮俊達) made the comments citing a study conducted by analytics consultancy QSearch from Monday last week to Sunday.
Shen, the party’s candidate for Taipei mayor — featured in 2,324,543 social media posts, with 42.8 percent of them negative and 28.2 percent positive, a “net negativity” rate of 14.6 percent, Juan said.
Photo: Liu Hsin-de, Taipei Times
His main opponent, Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) of the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT), featured in 1,643,538 social media posts, with 55.8 percent negative and 11.7 percent positive, or 44 percent net negativity, he said.
Lee Shu-chuan (李四川), the KMT’s candidate for New Taipei City mayor, was mentioned in 125,921 posts and had a 16.9 percent net negativity rating, he said.
Legislator Su Chiao-hui (蘇巧慧), the DPP’s mayoral candidate in New Taipei City, appeared in 100,004 posts and had a 0.8 percent net positivity rating — the only candidate in the greater Taipei area with a positive rating, Juan said.
The DPP does not need to belabor the positive aspects of the figures, but should instead call attention to hidden dangers behind the trendlines, he said.
The Chiang campaign’s attacks targeting Shen’s stance on drug policy and the death penalty, as well as personal attacks using a childhood parent-teacher notebook of the DPP candidate, have increased Shen’s negative coverage by 10 points in the past two weeks, Juan said.
Shen remains the underdog in the race across all polls, he said.
KMT supporters and the Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) base have been silent on social media due to low morale, but that does not mean they have lost the motivation to vote, he said.
In addition, negative messaging about DPP candidates is strong in closed chat groups on Line and Facebook, Juan said.
Although no foreign power has initiated a large-scale saturation cognitive warfare attack yet, bots have become increasingly sophisticated in manipulating public opinion and researchers have found an increasing number of bot campaigns, he said.
The public should remain vigilant about foreign-directed election meddling, he said.
Shen’s “ocean wave” has elicited a lot of enthusiasm in Taipei, but social media interest in other DPP candidates has declined in the past week, he said.
A voter’s perception of progress or lack of progress in a campaign could be affected by a social media “echo chamber” that does not correspond to reality, Juan said.
DPP supporters should openly endorse the party’s candidates to help boost real support, he added.

DPP takes New Taipei City lead
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:38:27 UTC
01:38:27 KST

Legislator Su Chiao-hui (蘇巧慧), the Democratic Progressive Party’s (DPP) candidate for New Taipei City mayor, has a 13.1 percentage point lead over her Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) rival Lee Shu-chuan (李四川), a poll released yesterday showed.
The poll, commissioned by the Taipei Trust in Democracy Association, showed that 43.1 percent of respondents said they would vote for Su, up 7.9 percentage points from a poll conducted in late August, while support for Lee was at 30 percent, down 4.7 percentage points.
It showed that 48.6 percent of respondents thought Su would make a suitable mayor, compared with 35.9 percent for Lee.
Photo courtesy of Lee’s campaign office via CNA
Independent candidate Su Hui-huang (蘇輝湟) received 1.5 percent support, 9.5 percent said they would not vote or would cast an invalid ballot and 15.8 percent were undecided, the poll showed.
Su Chiao-hui’s gains came from persuading undecided voters, as well as winning over some voters in traditionally KMT-leaning districts, said Tai Li-an (戴立安), who designed and analyzed the survey.
Her support among women rose by 11 percentage points, Tai said.
Photo: Lo Pei-de, Taipei Times
The share of Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) supporters who considered Su Chiao-hui suitable for mayor rose by 14.2 percentage points compared with August, while the share who considered her unsuitable increased by 4.6 percentage points, he said.
Many polling organizations do not release results showing wide discrepancies for fear of prompting rival camps to respond in ways that could affect the election, Tai said.
Political parties would continue to portray the race as close until voting day, he said, adding that KMT and TPP supporters might be less willing to disclose their preferences after seeing the poll results.
Asked about the poll on a talk show, Su Chiao-hui said she was surprised by the results, but would remain vigilant.
The rise in support might reflect positive public reactions to her interactions with Legislator Puma Shen (沈伯洋), the DPP’s Taipei mayoral candidate, she said.
Asked about Lee’s declining support and whether his age was a factor, she said that a candidate’s age should not be equated with an inability to implement policies.
Voters would support candidates whose attitudes and views keep pace with the times, she said.
Lee’s campaign office disputed the poll results, saying its findings did not reflect reality.
The DPP and KMT received similar shares of the party-list vote in the 2024 legislative elections, but DPP supporters outnumbered KMT supporters among the poll’s respondents by about 1.6 to one, the office said, adding that the survey’s sample was unrepresentative.
A TVBS poll commissioned by the New Taipei City Council’s KMT caucus showed Lee leading Su by 6.7 percentage points, it said, adding that Lee would continue to visit New Taipei City residents in all 29 districts to hear their concerns.
The poll interviewed 1,073 New Taipei City residents aged 20 or older from Tuesday to Thursday last week, with 750 interviewed by landline and 323 by cellphone. It had a margin of error of 3 percentage points at a 95 percent confidence level.
Additional reporting by Huang Tzu-yang and Weng Lu-huang

Syria says 18 suspects, including senior officers, detained over Assad-era chemical attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:35:28 UTC
01:35:28 KST

Şahin Demir
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
Syria said Tuesday that 18 suspects, including senior officers, are in custody and facing a specialized court over chemical attacks committed under the former Bashar al-Assad regime, according to the Syrian Arab News Agency (SANA).
Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani made the remarks at a joint news conference in Damascus with Sabrina Dallafior, director-general of the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW).
Al-Shaibani said Syria had provided the OPCW with more than 100,000 official documents and granted the organization access to records and witnesses as part of efforts to resolve the country’s chemical weapons file.
He said Damascus moved in June to correct the chemical weapons declaration inherited from the former regime, adding one production facility, two storage facilities and munitions that he said had previously been concealed.
According to al-Shaibani, the process culminated in August with the destruction of 42 declared chemical aerial bombs under OPCW supervision, which he described as the first verified destruction on Syrian territory since 2014.
He said Syria regained its full rights and privileges within the OPCW on July 9 and that discussions Tuesday focused on a roadmap toward the final closure of the country’s chemical weapons file.
Al-Shaibani said closing the file begins with ensuring justice for victims and preventing a recurrence of such attacks, adding that 18 suspects, including senior officers, are currently detained and appearing before a specialized court.
He said challenges remain, including mines, damaged sites and records that the former regime had either concealed or destroyed, complicating efforts to establish the full scope of its chemical weapons program.
For her part, Dallafior said visiting Syria had been a priority since she took office two months ago, including meeting victims and visiting sites in the country.
She said securing any remnants of the Assad-era chemical weapons program was a priority from a non-proliferation perspective and would help protect both the Syrian people and the wider region.
Dallafior said the OPCW, in cooperation with the Syrian government, destroyed a number of chemical weapons in July, describing the move as a milestone and a result of successful multilateral cooperation.
She added that the organization continues to investigate previous chemical attacks and identify those responsible, with the aim of preventing the use of chemical weapons again.
Syria joined the Chemical Weapons Convention in 2013 following a deadly chemical attack in Eastern Ghouta near Damascus.
In 2021, OPCW member states suspended Syria’s voting rights and other privileges over its failure to address issues related to the use and declaration of chemical weapons.
Following the fall of the Assad regime in December 2024, Syria’s new authorities pledged full cooperation with the OPCW to address the country’s chemical weapons file and locate and eliminate remaining chemical weapons and related materials.
In May 2026, Syrian authorities announced the discovery of previously undeclared remnants of the Assad regime’s chemical weapons program, including chemical munitions and materials related to the production of sarin.
The OPCW restored Syria’s rights and privileges on July 9 following increased cooperation between the country’s new authorities and the chemical weapons watchdog.

Iran pursues fate of pilots in Qatar, vows justice for Minab school victims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:34:28 UTC
01:34:28 KST

Iran pursues fate of pilots in Qatar, vows justice for Minab school victims
TEHRAN — Iran is pursuing diplomatic and legal efforts to protect its national interests, determine the status of Iranian pilots in Qatar and secure justice for the victims of the February 28 attack on a primary school in Minab, government spokesperson Fatemeh Mohajerani said on Tuesday.
Speaking at her weekly press conference, Mohajerani said the Ministries of Defense and Foreign Affairs were following up on the situation of the Iranian pilots in Qatar, adding that Doha had pledged cooperation and repeatedly expressed its readiness to help clarify their status.
 
She provided no further details about the pilots but said the relevant Iranian authorities were continuing their efforts to resolve the matter.
Iran preparing for all scenarios
Addressing the prospect of further restrictions on Iran’s transportation networks, Mohajerani said the government had prepared for difficult scenarios, including possible flight suspensions, sanctions targeting the country’s railway network and potential restrictions on land routes and border crossings.
She cautioned that some reports remained speculative but said the possibility of such measures reinforced Iran’s longstanding assessment that external pressure was directed not only at the country’s institutions but also at the daily lives of its people.
The spokesperson declined to disclose the government’s contingency plans, citing wartime conditions and the need to protect sensitive information.
Mohajerani also rejected the prospect of Iran’s civilization being destroyed, saying that any such objective pursued by the United States was bound to fail.
She described Iran as one of the world’s great civilizations and expressed confidence that attempts to erase its historical and cultural identity would meet the same fate as similar ambitions in the past.
Iran vows to pursue Minab school case until justice is served
Mohajerani separately reaffirmed the government’s determination to pursue international legal action over the attack on the Shajareh Tayyebeh elementary school in Minab, Hormozgan Province, on February 28, the first day of the US-Israeli military campaign against Iran.
She said the Vice Presidency for Legal Affairs and the Foreign Ministry were working together to pursue the case and secure the rights of the victims and their families.
The attack killed at least 175 people, including 168 schoolchildren, according to the figures cited in the report. The victims also included teachers, parents, sports players, and school staff.
Iran has pledged to continue seeking accountability through international legal channels, making the case a central part of its efforts to document the human cost of the war and pursue the rights of those affected.
Mohajerani said the government had decided to establish a special headquarters for Minab to coordinate relief, reconstruction and other initiatives following the attack.
The measure is intended to prevent overlapping or fragmented efforts by different organizations and ensure that activities in the affected area proceed in a coordinated manner, she explained.

Flooded streets, damage in Libya as heavy rains paralyse capital

Breadcrumb
Flooded streets, damage in Libya as heavy rains paralyse capital
Heavy rains flooded the streets of Libyan capital Tripoli on Tuesday, submerging vehicles and killing a bank employee, according to his employer.
The government ordered public services to launch urgent operations to drain the floodwater, while security forces announced the closure of the capital's ring road.
Jumhouria Bank announced on Tuesday the death by electrocution of one of its employees as he was entering the bank's headquarters in Tripoli, as floodwaters submerged utility boxes.
To reduce the danger, the General Electricity Company decided to cut power in some Tripoli districts.
Videos circulating on social media and in local media showed motorists managing at the last moment to scramble out of their cars as they fill with water.
Other buildings in the city centre were flooded, including the central hospital, where water entered the corridors, according to videos and images shared on social media.
On Monday evening, the National Meteorological Centre had forecast heavy rainfall across the entire north of the country, issuing a warning to people living near wadis and in valleys.
Every summer, local authorities try to prepare city streets before the rains by clearing drainage networks and manholes, which are often clogged by sand blown in from the desert.
Despite these efforts, the streets are regularly flooded.
On Tuesday morning, municipal trucks and Tripoli's road services were hard at work on the capital's main thoroughfares, pumping up the mud and debris carried into the city by the torrents of water.

US President Donald Trump has said that Washington continues to share intelligence with Ukraine and is working with both Kiev and Moscow to end Russia’s war, insisting that neither side has been cut off from US assistance.

Critics argue that the arrangement could conflict with US restrictions on Russian energy imports imposed following Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine.
Asked whether Russia could use proceeds from the deal to buy more bombs, Trump declined to address the potential military implications directly.
“That’s a diesel deal, not for us. That’s being released into the world. That’s not being released to us,” he said.
Trump’s remarks came as his administration continues to present negotiations as a route towards ending the war, while questions remain over the terms of any potential settlement and the role of continued US support for Ukraine.

London Bombs, London Blames
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:31:41 UTC
01:31:41 KST

London Bombs, London Blames
Iran rejects Fairford attribution as baseless, says London cannot evade accountability for role in aggression against Iran: Foreign Ministry
TEHRAN – Iran's Foreign Ministry has strongly condemned Britain's accusation linking Tehran to an alleged security incident at RAF Fairford air base, dismissing it as an ugly plot designed to fuel Iranophobia and evade accountability for London's direct participation in the ongoing American-Zionist military aggression against the Iranian nation.
In a formal statement issued late Monday, the Ministry said the British government's claim attributing the alleged incident to Iran is categorically rejected, holding London and the designers and perpetrators of what it called a clumsy false-flag operation responsible for all consequences arising from the fabrication.
"The government of Britain cannot, without presenting solid evidence and reasons, shirk its political and legal responsibility for its claims and their possible consequences by hiding behind ambiguous phrases," the statement said. " Resort to terms such as 'highly likely' and 'almost certainly' to insinuate the credibility of attributing the alleged incident to Iran is a blatant attempt to evade responsibility for baseless accusations."
The Ministry further recalled Britain's track record of fabricating security claims against other countries – which in some cases have led to devastating tensions and conflicts in West Asia – stressing that London must be held accountable for insisting on an approach that undermines international peace and security.
The strongly-worded rebuke came hours after British Prime Minister Andy Burnham told Parliament on Monday that a suspected plot last month against RAF Fairford, a U.S.-operated bomber base in southern England, was "highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran" and "almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps."
"We will not tolerate these threats on our soil," Burnham claimed, pledging to "crack down on Iran's use of criminal networks, using our full range of powers to target them and their funding streams" and to bring further sanctions to restrict the capacity of Iran and the IRGC.
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced that London had summoned the Iranian ambassador and imposed sanctions on two Iranian nationals – Ruhollah Bazghandi, described as head of IRGC counterespionage operations, and Shahram Ali Reza Tamarzadeh Jakki, described as a facilitator for the Zindashti criminal network – including asset freezes, travel bans and director disqualification, for their alleged role in facilitating hostile activity.
Iran's Ambassador to London, Seyed Ali Mousavi, who was summoned by UK Minister for the Middle East Stephen Doughty, categorically rejected any Iranian role and urged the British side to present evidence supporting its allegations if it possesses any, according to IRNA. He also expressed Tehran's readiness to cooperate with the investigation to clarify the facts.
The Iranian Embassy in London had already on September 28 "categorically" rejected "unfounded and malicious speculations" linking Tehran to the arrests near Fairford, warning they would only fuel Iranophobia propaganda in Britain.
The diplomatic escalation was accompanied by a joint political statement issued Monday by the foreign ministers of 29 countries – including the UK, the United States, most European states, Canada, Australia and New Zealand – condemning "in the strongest terms Iran's use of violent attacks, including acts of lethal plotting, arson, sabotage, cyber-attacks, and other hybrid activities against us and our partners."
The statement explicitly endorsed London's attribution, saying: "We recognise the United Kingdom's attribution of Iran's involvement in the incident at RAF Fairford on 27 September. The UK has also concluded this event demonstrates the IRGC's continued willingness to project hostile activity beyond its borders through covert networks and proxy actors."
Tehran says that cascade – from an unexplained local arrest to prime-ministerial attribution to instant multilateral endorsement and fresh sanctions, all without a single document made public – is precisely the hallmark of a coordinated smear campaign.
What actually happened at Fairford?
According to British police and media reports, in the early hours of September 27, five British men in their 20s were arrested in the vicinity of RAF Fairford on suspicion of terrorism and explosives offences. Two more arrests followed in subsequent days, bringing the total to seven. Counter Terrorism Policing launched an investigation into a suspected foreign state link.
Yet more than two weeks later, the source and nature of the threat remain shrouded in mystery. No one has been charged. All suspects have been released on bail under strict conditions.
Police later acknowledged they had found only a quantity of accelerant – gasoline – in three vans linked to the initial suspects, but no explosives, no detonators, no drones, no weapons-grade material. Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood told Parliament the coordinator was assessed to be "a known individual based in Iran," but she did not name that person nor disclose any supporting communications, financial records, travel data, or other intelligence.
U.S. officials, speaking anonymously to Reuters, spoke of a suspected Iranian plot to carry out a "complex drone attack" on the facility. Last week, U.S. President Donald Trump claimed an Iran-linked threat intended "to kill as many American troops and destroy as many U.S. planes as possible" had prompted a decision to withdraw American bombers. The Pentagon confirmed the B-1 and B-52 bombers stationed at Fairford have now been redeployed to their home bases.
London then upgraded its language in stages: first "strong indications," then on Monday "highly likely coordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed by the IRGC." The two Iranians sanctioned on Monday were not explicitly identified as the organizers of Fairford.
For Tehran and for independent legal observers, that timeline raises far more questions than it answers.
A terrorism plot without terrorists?
The first and most serious ambiguity, Iranian officials stress, is elementary criminal procedure: if this was a genuine terrorist operation against a strategic NATO air base, why are all alleged perpetrators free on bail?
Under British counter-terrorism law, police can detain suspects for extended periods with judicial approval when the threat is deemed grave and evidence is substantive. The unconditional release – without charge, without presentation to a court of any explosive device, without even an official charge sheet linking the men to any foreign handler – is difficult to reconcile with claims of an IRGC-directed mass-casualty plot.
Second: how can a government accuse a sovereign state of directing an attack while admitting it has no evidence to show? Burnham offered no photographs, no intercepted communications, no money trail, no travel records, not even a surname of the alleged coordinator in Iran. Miliband's sanctions designation speaks of "facilitating hostile activity" in general terms for Europe and the U.S., not of commanding the Fairford vans.
Iran's Foreign Ministry put it bluntly: London cannot hide behind "highly likely" and "almost certainly." Those phrases, Tehran notes, have a notorious pedigree in British politics – from the Iraq WMD dossier to the Skripal affair – where probabilistic language was later used to justify concrete sanctions, expulsions and even war, without ever meeting the standard of proof.
Third: what was actually found? Gasoline in vans is not a military capability. It is legally purchasable at any petrol station, and British police themselves confirmed no explosives were present. To extrapolate from jerry cans to an IRGC external operation to kill Americans en masse is, in Tehran's view, a leap that no court would accept, but one that fits a propaganda need.
Fourth: who are the suspects? All are British nationals in their 20s, with no announced Iranian nationality, no announced travel to Iran, no announced IRGC affiliation. If Tehran had recruited and directed them, London has shown no recruitment chain. The claim of direction by the IRGC's counterespionage chief, Bazghandi, was asserted without any published link to Fairford at all.
"How do they accuse Iran while they do not even have a small clue to present?" an Iranian diplomat asked. "If they have documents, present them. If they are willing to cooperate, as Ambassador Mousavi has offered, accept cooperation. Trial by press release is not investigation."
Tehran sees in this pattern what IRNA on Monday called "a coordinated wave to smear Iran" – a series of suspicious incidents recently attributed to Tehran by the U.S. president and senior Western officials without offering any evidence.
The bombers that fled: why Fairford matters
The irony, Iranian analysts note, is that while London portrays itself as a victim of extraterritorial threats, Fairford itself has been an active platform for extraterritorial aggression against Iran.
RAF Fairford, about 160 kilometers (100 miles) west of London in Gloucestershire, is not an ordinary Royal Air Force station. It is the U.S. Air Force's preferred forward operating location in Europe for heavy bombers. Its 3,000-meter runway, vast munitions areas and specialized maintenance facilities allow it to host B-52 Stratofortress and B-1 Lancer bombers that cannot be permanently based in crowded continental bases.
Since the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran began on February 28 – with surprise strikes that martyred several Iranian leaders and officials, including the Leader of the Islamic Revolution Ayatollah Seyed Ali Khamenei, according to regional reports – Fairford has served as a critical staging point for American air operations against Iran.
In other words, U.S. bombers took off from British soil, refueled by NATO tankers, guided by NATO intelligence, to bomb Iranian territory. Their sudden withdrawal last week under the pretext of an Iranian threat only confirms, in Tehran's assessment, the base's combat role: you do not evacuate strategic bombers from a base that has nothing to do with the war.
Iran has repeatedly and openly stated a clear legal doctrine: any base used to attack its territory is a legitimate military target under the right of self-defense enshrined in Article 51 of the UN Charter. That is a public, state-level deterrent posture – the opposite of covertly hiring young Britons with gasoline cans. Conflating the two, Tehran argues, is deliberate.
Britain's hidden hand in the war on Iran
Far more significant than one night in Gloucestershire, Tehran says, is Britain's sustained, if less visible, participation in the war that began in February.
London has provided three layers of support to the American-Israeli aggression, Iranian officials and Western reporting indicate:
First, basing and logistics. Beyond Fairford, Britain has opened its airspace, its Cyprus bases at Akrotiri and Dhekelia, its intelligence facilities and its naval logistics to the U.S. war effort. RAF tankers have supported air bridges toward West Asia. British officials have not denied that U.S. aircraft engaged in operations against Iran have transited UK-controlled infrastructure.
Second, political and intelligence cover. London, alongside Paris and Berlin, has consistently endorsed Washington's narrative of Iranian escalation while remaining silent on the initial U.S.-Israeli strikes and on repeated Israeli attacks on Iranian nuclear, military and civilian infrastructure – including the strike on a girls' school in Minab that martyred schoolchildren. British intelligence-sharing within the Five Eyes and NATO frameworks has fed directly into targeting and missile-defense operations in defense of Israel and Gulf-based U.S. assets.
Third, direct military engagement. The British government admitted its forces participated in what it termed defensive actions against Iranian missiles and drones aimed at Israel and at allied interests in the Gulf, positioning Royal Navy destroyers and RAF fighters as a shield for the aggressor while claiming non-belligerency.
It is this complicity, Tehran argues, that London now seeks to obscure by casting itself as the victim of Iranian terrorism. Accusing the IRGC of plotting on English soil shifts attention from English runways being used to bomb Iranian cities.
"The ugly plot to advance the Iranophobia campaign and escape accountability for participation in the American-Zionist military aggression against the Iranian nation," as the Foreign Ministry phrased it, is therefore not rhetorical excess but a legal argument: a co-belligerent cannot claim the immunity of a neutral and then criminalize the self-defense discourse of the state it helped attack.
International law scholars sympathetic to neither side have similarly warned that the 29-country statement – which speaks of Iranian "lethal plotting, arson, sabotage, cyber-attacks" without referencing the ongoing bombing of Iran, the U.S. withdrawal of bombers from a combat base, or Britain's own admitted hosting of strike aircraft – presents a one-sided picture that undermines its credibility.
Tehran's position is unequivocal: it had no involvement in Fairford, it is ready to assist a genuine technical investigation, and it demands evidence. Until London produces verifiable proof – names, transfers, communications subject to judicial scrutiny – the case will be remembered, in Iran's words, alongside previous fabricated security dossiers that paved the way for aggression in West Asia, not as counter-terrorism but as information warfare to sustain an unlawful war.
