Ethiopian troops enter town on border with Eritrea, stoking war fears
Oct 13 - Ethiopian government troops have advanced to a town on the border with Eritrea previously controlled by Tigrayan rebels, people in touch with residents said on Tuesday, as diplomats scrambled to avert war between the Horn of Africa neighbours.
Witnesses and a conflict monitor said Eritrean troops had crossed last week into Zalambessa, near Ethiopia's northernmost point, in support of the rebels, but it was unclear if the Eritrean troops or rebels were still present on Tuesday.
Asmara has denied any incursion into Ethiopia and asked the UN to take deterrent measures against Ethiopia. It argues that Addis Ababa's accusations of an invasion by Eritrean forces amounted to a "declaration of war".
Fighting broke out in Ethiopia last month as a rebel alliance led by the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) went on the offensive, reigniting a war that killed hundreds of thousands between 2020-22.
With Addis Ababa and Asmara now on opposing sides again, conflicts raging elsewhere in the region and tensions high across the Red Sea, there are fears of broader contagion of violence this time around.
The Ethiopian government's counter-offensive has driven rebels from a string of towns, forcing them to retreat north.
By Tuesday, the army had reached Zalambessa, a town with a population of around 15,000 on the Ethiopian side of the border with Eritrea, according to six sources. The sources included four people in touch with residents, a diplomat and an expert on the conflict in touch with the warring parties.
A spokesperson for a pro-government militia did not confirm the military taking control of the town.
Spokespeople for Ethiopia's military and Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
DUELLING UN LETTERS
Having been locked in conflict for years, Ethiopia and Eritrea made peace in 2018 and Eritrea fought in support of Ethiopia’s federal government during a 2020-2022 civil war in Tigray, but relations have since soured again.
Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of backing the rebels and wrote to Security Council members, stating that Eritrean troops had advanced up to 60 km (37 miles) inside Ethiopia.
Eritrea's Foreign Minister Osman Saleh has asked the Security Council to take action against Addis Ababa in a letter seen by Reuters, invoking Chapter VII of the UN Charter, which allows for measures ranging from sanctions to military action.
On Tuesday, Security Council members were due to hold a closed-door meeting on the situation in the Horn of Africa, the Greek presidency of the Security Council said.
The issue of sea access has also roiled relations.
Ethiopia had access to a coastline for decades until Eritrea gained independence from Addis Ababa in 1993. Ethiopia argues that restoring sea access is an existential issue but has said it would be restored through peace and dialogue. REUTERS

SARAJEVO, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- BiH Deputy Foreign Minister Josip Brkic said NATO has urged Bosnia and Herzegovina (BiH) to increase defense spending to meet the alliance's standards, as the country currently spends about 1 percent of its gross domestic product (GDP) on security, local media FENA reported on Tuesday.
Brkic, who chairs the BiH-NATO Cooperation Commission, said NATO member states and alliance officials had expressed particular interest in increased allocations for the country's armed forces during talks at NATO headquarters in Brussels.
BiH needs to gradually raise its defense spending and demonstrate the political will to strengthen its capabilities, primarily in its own interests, Brkic said.
The ratio of 2 percent of GDP has long been a NATO benchmark on defense spending. However, at the 2025 summit in The Hague, NATO leaders agreed to raise annual defense-related spending to 5 percent of GDP by 2035.
BiH joined NATO's Partnership for Peace programme in 2006 and was invited to participate in the Membership Action Plan in 2010. BiH is not a NATO member, and participation in the Membership Action Plan does not guarantee future membership. Currently, its cooperation with NATO focuses on defence reform, military capacity building and security cooperation. ■

RIYADH, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Saudi Aramco President and CEO Amin H. Nasser said Monday that global crude oil inventories were approaching dangerously low levels and could take up to two years to replenish.

Roundup: DR Congo's Ebola cases top 9,000 as vaccine trial nears launch
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
00:28:47 CST
01:28:47 KST

Health workers carry out disinfection work at an Ebola treatment center in Bunia, capital of Ituri Province in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), on Oct. 12, 2026. The Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has recorded more than 9,000 confirmed cases of Ebola since the outbreak was declared on May 15, with the death toll rising to 4,381, according to the latest situation report released Tuesday. No vaccine or treatment has yet been specifically approved for the Bundibugyo ebolavirus, although clinical trials are underway. (Xinhua)
KINSHASA, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- The Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has recorded more than 9,000 confirmed Ebola cases since May, as preparations for a vaccine trial near completion.
The country's task force on Ebola released a situation report on Tuesday, showing that 9,066 confirmed cases and 4,381 deaths had been recorded as of Oct. 11, bringing the overall case fatality rate to 48.3 percent. A total of 2,389 patients have recovered.
The outbreak has affected 65 health zones across seven provinces. The eastern province of Ituri remains the epicenter, accounting for 73.8 percent of all confirmed cases, followed by North Kivu Province, which has recorded the highest case fatality rate at 57.1 percent.
Earlier this month, DRC Health Minister Roger Kamba said that the outbreak was becoming increasingly localized, with several affected health zones reporting no new cases for weeks.
However, World Health Organization Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus warned on Oct. 7 that while the epidemic was slowing in some areas, it continued to grow in others. He also highlighted persistent challenges, including the high proportion of deaths occurring in communities and gaps in contact tracing.
The outbreak was caused by the Bundibugyo ebolavirus, for which no vaccine or treatment has yet been specifically approved, although clinical trials are underway.
Ervebo, a vaccine approved against the Zaire ebolavirus, is being administered to frontline health workers under research protocols and through compassionate-use arrangements.
According to the latest situation report, 399 frontline workers had been vaccinated in Haut-Uele province as of Oct. 11. Yet its effectiveness against the Bundibugyo ebolavirus remains unproven.
The Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations announced Tuesday that final preparations were underway for Tumaini, a pivotal Phase 2/3 clinical trial to evaluate vaccine candidates against the Bundibugyo virus.
The trial, expected to begin in the coming weeks pending ethical and regulatory approval, will likely evaluate Ervebo first, followed by vaccines specifically developed against the strain as they become available.
Declared on May 15, the outbreak has become the largest and deadliest Ebola outbreak ever recorded in the DRC and the second-largest worldwide, after the 2014-2016 epidemic in West Africa. ■

Iraq's political parties have reached a final agreement with Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi to complete his government, with parliament expected to vote on nine outstanding ministerial appointments and four deputy prime ministers on Thursday, political sources told The New Arab.
The agreement could end more than five months of political deadlock that has prevented Zaidi from completing his cabinet since taking office in May, amid disputes between political blocs over the distribution of ministries and the selection of candidates.
Kareem Aliwi, a lawmaker from the ruling Coordination Framework, told TNA that a final agreement had been reached following talks between Zaidi, the alliance and representatives of other political parties.
"In the past few hours, following a meeting between the Coordination Framework and Zaidi, and in agreement with our partners in the other political blocs and parties, a final agreement was reached to hold a parliamentary session this Thursday to complete the cabinet," Aliwi said.
He added that parliament would also vote on four deputy prime ministers whose appointments had been agreed between the prime minister and the relevant political blocs.
The four candidates are Laith al-Khazali, brother of Qais al-Khazali, leader of the Asaib Ahl al-Haq movement; Mohammed Tamim, a former planning minister; Mohsen al-Mandalawi, head of the Al-Asas Iraqi Coalition; and Fares al-Barifkani, a former chairman of parliament's Health and Environment Committee.
Aliwi also revealed the nine candidates selected to fill the remaining vacant ministries:
- Safaa al-Kinani: Youth and Sports
- Yasser al-Maliki: Interior
- Haider Bahaa: Higher Education
- Mohammed al-Moussawi: Labour
- Nayef al-Shammari: Defence
- Yassin al-Ithawi: Culture
- Mohammed Ali al-Nuaimi: Planning
- Ali al-Dakhili: Tourism
- Mohammed Sahib al-Darraji: Digital Technology
According to Aliwi, all nine candidates have received the approval of Zaidi and the political parties involved in the negotiations.
He said the prime minister had also held individual meetings with the nominees in recent days before their appointments were finalised.
"These names have been approved by Zaidi and all political forces and will be passed during Thursday's session without any disagreements or obstacles," Aliwi said.
Salah al-Kubaisi, a senior figure in the Sunni Sovereignty Alliance, separately confirmed to TNA that an agreement had been reached to convene parliament on Thursday to complete the cabinet and appoint the deputy prime ministers.
Kubaisi said the breakthrough followed a series of negotiations and understandings between political parties aimed at overcoming the disputes that had delayed the formation of the full government for more than five months.
He described the planned parliamentary vote as an important step towards ending political paralysis and enabling the government to carry out its responsibilities.
The agreement, he added, demonstrated the importance of political consensus and the need to translate negotiations into concrete parliamentary action.
Iraq's parliament granted confidence to Zaidi's government in mid-May, approving just 14 of the proposed 23 ministers.
The remaining nine portfolios were left vacant as political factions failed to agree on candidates and the distribution of ministerial posts.
In early September, the ruling Coordination Framework announced that an agreement on the remaining ministries was close and that parliament could vote on the nominees within a week.
However, that deadline passed without a breakthrough, forcing political leaders to resume negotiations.
Repeated attempts to reach a compromise subsequently stalled over disagreements concerning key ministries, with political influence and electoral calculations further complicating efforts to complete the cabinet.
Thursday's planned vote would mark the first major breakthrough in the months-long dispute, potentially allowing Zaidi to begin governing with a full ministerial team for the first time since his appointment.

Suspected cholera cases surging in Yemen: WHO

Breadcrumb
Suspected cholera cases surging in Yemen: WHO
Suspected cholera cases tripled in three weeks in Yemen, the World Health Organization said Tuesday, warning that the growing disease burden was straining hospitals already treating war casualties.
The country's escalating war, combined with mass displacement, is fuelling the risk of infectious disease outbreaks, the WHO said.
Overcrowding, inadequate access to safe water and disrupted health services are exposing growing numbers of people to cholera, measles and other preventable diseases, it said.
Suspected cholera cases have tripled from 217 in the week of September 6-12 to 647 in the week of 27 September to 3 October, the WHO said.
The UN health agency said Yemen has reported 8,034 suspected cases and 27 deaths this year - with a quarter of the suspected cases occurring in the last four weeks.
Yemen's war - where a Saudi-led military coalition supports the government against the Iran-backed Houthis - has reignited months into the US-Iran conflict that has plunged the Middle East into crisis.
"Families fleeing conflict are now facing another threat from diseases that can be prevented and treated," said Annette Heinzelmann, the WHO's emergency director for the region.
"Without urgent funding and unimpeded access to safe water, vaccination and essential health services, outbreaks could spread rapidly among already vulnerable communities."
The UN's International Organization for Migration said Monday that more than 217,000 people had fled their homes in Yemen since the fighting escalated.
Yemen, one of the world's poorest countries, was already suffering a vast humanitarian crisis.
"The growing disease burden is putting additional pressure on health facilities that are treating thousands of people injured in the fighting," the WHO said.
Cholera is an acute intestinal infection that spreads through food and water contaminated with the bacterium vibrio cholerae, often from faeces.
It causes severe diarrhoea, vomiting and muscle cramps.
Cholera can kill when not treated, though it can be treated with simple oral rehydration, and antibiotics for more severe cases.
The Geneva-based WHO said it had only secured $3.78 million of the $31 million needed for its 90-day emergency response in Yemen.
The funding is intended to help expand disease surveillance in displacement sites, deploy rapid response teams, strengthen cholera treatment and improve infection prevention in health facilities and cholera treatment sites.

Pakistan Is Treating Every Grievance as Terrorism, and It’s Failing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:26:00 UTC
01:26:00 KST

Pakistan faces mounting political, economic, and security crises. But instead of addressing the underlying causes, the country’s rulers are hell-bent on targeting the opposition and treating it as the problem.
I have seen this approach firsthand in Balochistan, Pakistan’s militancy-ridden southwestern province. For years, the state has responded to political dissent and social, economic, and political grievances primarily through a security lens, via arrests, enforced disappearances, and extrajudicial killings. The consequences have been severe: such policies have pushed thousands of youths toward a violent insurgency. But this approach is no longer confined to Balochistan.
Recent developments in the northwestern province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa suggest that the same logic is increasingly being applied elsewhere. On October 11, Pakistan’s President Asif Ali Zardari declared a state of emergency and suspended the provincial government led by Sohail Afridi, an ally of imprisoned former Prime Minister Imran Khan. Pakistani media reports said Afridi had been arrested and his whereabouts remain untraceable.
Enforced disappearances are a longstanding practice in Pakistan, particularly in its peripheries. But the disappearance of a politician who was the chief minister until Sunday morning raises disturbing questions about the rule of law and the fate of ordinary citizens with far less visibility or political influence.
The scenes from Peshawar, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s provincial capital, tell a similar story. Security forces have filled roads with brightly colored shipping containers to prevent Khan supporters from reaching Islamabad. On October 4, Khan’s party, Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), took to the streets to demand his release. The federal government has defended the barricades and its latest actions as necessary to prevent unrest.
Such restrictions on political dissent go beyond the PTI.
In Balochistan, the authorities have confronted the Baloch Yakjehti Committee, a large grassroots movement against enforced disappearances and extrajudicial killings. Its popular crowd-puller leader, Mahrang Baloch, was sentenced to life imprisonment on June 22 by an anti-terrorism court, alongside fellow activist Sibghatullah, over the alleged killing of a paramilitary soldier during a protest in Pakistan’s new emerging port city Gwadar in July 2024. The court found they had incited the crowd. Baloch’s lawyers boycotted the proceedings, held inside Hudda jail, and called it a faceless trial.
In Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, the Pashtun Tahafuz Movement, another civil rights movement demanding rights for ethnic Pashtuns, has faced an intensive crackdown. Its soft-spoken, 34-year-old charismatic leader, Manzoor Pashteen, has been among those targeted, as the government has attempted to ban the movement and its leadership.
Authorities have used similar tools in Pakistan-administered Kashmir, long described by Pakistani leaders as the country’s “jugular vein.” On June 5, the Azad Jammu and Kashmir government designated the Jammu Kashmir Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC), a grassroots coalition that has organized protests over economic and political demands, as a proscribed organization under the region’s anti-terrorism law.
These are different movements, with different demands. But the state responds in a common way: it treats every political grievance as a security threat.
Laws such as the Fourth Schedule, once intended for terrorism, are also being used against lawyers, journalists, and political opponents. In particular, the controversial cyber law, the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (PECA), is frequently used against activists and journalists.
In January, an Islamabad court handed prominent human rights lawyers Imaan Zainab Mazari-Hazir and her husband, Hadi Ali Chattha, prison terms totaling 17 years over social media posts the state called anti-state. The sentences were to run concurrently, so they were to serve 10 years. In September, the Supreme Court suspended the sentences and ordered their release on bail. Within hours, authorities rearrested them in an earlier protest case.
Since the controversial 2024 elections, Pakistan’s Parliament, the judiciary, and the media have come under intense pressure. Citizens on the periphery, especially ethnic minorities such as Baloch, Pashtuns, and Kashmiris, have little reason left to take a political complaint to those institutions.
Meanwhile, the security crisis has worsened.
The Global Terrorism Index ranked Pakistan the country most affected by terrorism in 2025. It recorded 1,139 deaths and 1,045 terrorist incidents, with Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa bearing the brunt.
An Islamabad-based think tank, the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies (PICS), documented 606 deaths and 232 injuries from militant attacks and counter-militancy operations in July 2026 alone, the deadliest month of the year to date. Most of the dead were militants: 401, against 112 security personnel and 74 civilians. The raw numbers still argue against the idea that more force is closing the war.
Some years ago, Pakistan spent millions of dollars on fencing its roughly 1,600-mile border with Afghanistan to contain cross-border attacks from militants allegedly based in Afghanistan. But militancy continues. Islamabad has since taken the war across the border.
On March 16, a Pakistani airstrike hit the Omid Addiction Treatment Hospital in Kabul, a drug-rehabilitation center on the site of a former NATO base. Pakistan said it had struck a militant storage site. The U.N. mission in Afghanistan confirmed at least 269 civilian deaths and 122 injured. Amnesty International later said the strike should be investigated as a possible war crime.
Cross-border strikes have continued. On October 1, Pakistan launched airstrikes in Kunar and Helmand provinces in Afghanistan. The Taliban government said at least nine civilians, mostly children, were killed and 11 injured. The U.N. mission said at least 10 civilians, most of them children, were killed and nine were injured. Pakistan said the strikes targeted militant hideouts and claimed 22 militants were killed.
There is a clear contradiction here. Pakistan’s leaders want to be seen internationally as peacemakers and mediators. At home, they have refused to engage politically with Imran Khan, Mahrang Baloch, the Kashmir committee, and Manzoor Pashteen, and they have preferred force with Afghanistan as well. The economic cost of that instability is why Islamabad is asking Washington for a $10 billion exchange-stabilization facility to strengthen its foreign-exchange reserves.
Western governments should be careful not to confuse that request, or Pakistan’s field Marshal General Asim Munir’s usefulness in mediating with Iran, with a diplomatic settlement. Pakistan matters to the West because of its size, its nuclear weapons, its position between South and Central Asia, and its role in regional security. Engagement with the army should not mean ignoring a provincial capital closed off with containers, civil rights movement leaders tried under anti-terror laws, or a strike on a Kabul hospital. Nor should Pakistan’s leaders assume that economic assistance or geopolitical usefulness can substitute for public trust.
Militancy cannot be excused, and the state has a legitimate responsibility to protect its citizens. But military action alone, whether inside or outside Pakistan, is not resolving the political alienation underneath the violence. Pakistan’s leaders need to face the hard questions. Why are educated Baloch in Balochistan being drawn toward a deadly insurgency? Why has resentment among Pashtun youth against the state increased? Why have large crowds in Kashmir repeatedly taken to the streets?
The West has tried to build a relationship solely through military generals before. It did not produce a stable partner. It is unlikely to do so while the same generals answer political protest with emergencies, repress dissent with terror and cybersecurity laws, target Afghanistan with airstrikes, and then ask the West to finance the country for economic stability.

LingDuels?
« previous post |
Mayur Naik has invented "MathDuels: A Self-Play Benchmark That Grows":
… in which models occupy dual roles: each authors math problems under adversarial prompting and solves problems authored by every other participant. A generation pipeline produces and filters the problems, and a psychometric model jointly estimates solver abilities and problem difficulties, from which author quality is derived. Experiments across 19 frontier models reveal that authoring and solving capabilities are partially decoupled, and that dual-role evaluation exposes capability separations invisible in single-role benchmarks. As newer models enter the arena, they produce problems that defeat previously dominant solvers, so the benchmark’s difficulty co-evolves with participant strength rather than saturating at a fixed ceiling. [Abstract taken from today's lecture.]
There's an evolving MathDuels leaderboard here.
It would be interesting to try the same thing with the sorts of problems featured in the International Linguistics Olympiad ("IOL"), or the North American Computational Linguistics Open Competition ("NACLO").
My prediction is that at the start, current "frontier models" will generally do a bad job at solving such problems, and a worse job at posing them. But over time, they should improve, probably reaching the point of becoming useful research assistants, and perhaps even (in some sense) independent researchers?

Citing an unnamed diplomatic source, the newspaper said the Saudi crown prince opposed direct Israeli participation because cooperation with Israel could provoke anger among the Saudi public.
Another source familiar with the discussions said Netanyahu hoped joint military action against the Houthis would strengthen relations between Israel and Saudi Arabia and potentially pave the way for a normalisation agreement.
Saudi authorities have not publicly commented on the reported proposal.
The revelation comes as Saudi Arabia faces escalating Houthi missile and drone attacks, including deadly strikes on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh.
An attack on Saturday killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, while another strike on Sunday killed a Pakistani resident and injured 11 others, according to Saudi authorities.
Netanyahu condemned Saturday's attack and offered condolences to the victims' families, despite Israel and Saudi Arabia having no formal diplomatic relations.
The Israeli leader has long regarded normalisation with Saudi Arabia as a major diplomatic objective, building on the Abraham Accords through which Israel established formal relations with several Arab states.
However, negotiations between Israel and Saudi Arabia, which had advanced before October 2023, were derailed by Israel's war and genocide in Gaza.
Riyadh has repeatedly insisted that normalisation must be linked to the establishment of an independent Palestinian state, a position at odds with Netanyahu's opposition to Palestinian statehood.
The reported Israeli overture suggests Netanyahu is attempting to use Saudi Arabia's confrontation with the Houthis to revive prospects for rapprochement, despite the continuing political obstacles presented by the Palestinian question.
Israel has previously conducted its own military strikes against Houthi targets in Yemen, meaning the latest proposal concerns participation in the Saudi-led campaign rather than Israel's first involvement in the conflict.
Saudi Arabia intervened militarily in Yemen in March 2015, leading a coalition that included the UAE in support of the internationally recognised government after the Houthis seized Sanaa.
A UN-brokered truce in April 2022 substantially reduced large-scale hostilities, but renewed fighting erupted in July this year.
The latest escalation has seen Houthi forces make territorial gains along Yemen's Red Sea coast, prompting a Saudi-backed government counteroffensive and renewed attacks across the Saudi-Yemeni border.
Saudi Arabia has sought greater US assistance against the Houthis, while Netanyahu's reported proposal would bring Israel directly into a military campaign that has already strained Riyadh's defences.
For the Saudi leadership, the prospect of openly cooperating with Israel remains politically sensitive, particularly amid continuing anger over the genocide in Gaza and the absence of any progress towards Palestinian statehood.

Morocco's biggest party strikes deal to form coalition government
Morocco's largest political party is joining forces with three rivals to form a coalition government, pledging a "shared reformist vision" as it bids to address rising youth anger over economic inequality and corruption.
Prime Minister Fatima Ezzahra El-Mansouri's Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM) will enter government with the nationalist Istiqlal Party and two small left-wing factions, the Socialist Union of Popular Forces (USFP) and the Party of Progress and Socialism (PPS), the parties said in a joint statement on Monday.
PAM emerged as the kingdom's largest party following the 23 September election, winning 97 of the 395 seats in the lower house. Istiqlal came third with 65 seats.
King Mohammed VI appointed Mansouri as the country's first-ever female prime minister a week after the vote, tasking her to form the next government.
The coalition will have a narrow nine-seat majority in the assembly and will be expected to deliver on electoral pledges to tackle the rising cost of living, boost youth employment, and improve public services.
Her administration will take power amid rising social discontent over deteriorating public services and narrowing job prospects.
It will also oversee preparations for the World Cup, which the North African country will co-host with Spain and Portugal in 2030.
The tournament emerged as a flashpoint in the wave of anti-government demonstrations that rocked Moroccan cities last year, with Gen-Z protesters criticising the billions of dollars being invested in football stadiums at the expense of the country's underfunded healthcare and education systems.
September's election received one of the lowest turnout rates in the country's electoral history, with only 38% of voters turning up to vote. The low turnout means that PAM is forming the next government with the support of fewer than 5% of eligible voters.
PAM is a socially liberal party created in 2008 by an adviser to the king. This is the second time it has been in government after it entered a coalition as a junior partner of the National Rally of Independents and Istiqlal following the 2021 parliamentary election.

Shipping industry sources have reported signs that cargo movements through the strategic waterway may be slowing after oil flows approached prewar levels earlier this month.
Available data, however, have yet to show a clear decline in oil-loading activity at several major regional export terminals, and some shipowners have reported no significant disruption to vessel movements, said the report.

That was roughly twice the agency’s average daily number of reported attacks during the previous week, according to Bloomberg.
The increase in attacks appears to be prompting greater caution among ship operators. Bloomberg-compiled tanker-tracking data showed that more than a dozen supertankers and several Suezmax-class vessels had turned around or reversed course while approaching Fujairah in the United Arab Emirates, near the entrance to the strait.
Shipbrokers and some vessel owners operating in the region have also reported signs of reduced activity, particularly longer waiting times for ship-to-ship oil transfers. One shipowner involved in the operations said traffic had not slowed.
Ship-to-ship transfers have been instrumental in sustaining regional exports. The practice allows shuttle tankers to transport oil through the high-risk Strait of Hormuz before transferring their cargo to other vessels for delivery to international buyers.

Majority in US say Trump prioritises personal wealth over all else: Poll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:07:26 UTC
01:07:26 KST

Majority in US say Trump prioritises personal wealth over all else: Poll
A majority of US adults say President Trump and his family have inappropriately profited from presidency.
Most US adults believe President Donald Trump has placed his personal financial interests and those of his inner circle ahead of the country’s since returning to the White House in 2025, according to a new nationwide poll.
The poll, conducted by the Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research and released on Tuesday, suggests that public perception of the Republican president leans heavily critical: Over half of surveyed adults view Trump’s second term as self-serving by investing in his own business and commercial pursuits “a lot”. Roughly one quarter believe he focuses on national interests, but only 11 percent feel Trump represents regular Americans. Fifty-five percent of Republicans surveyed said that Trump has prioritised his personal business interests “a lot” or “some”.
Half of the respondents report that Trump has placed zero priority on people “like them”.
As Trump’s family business pulls in record funds from new ventures helped by his policies, the poll results suggest that most US adults think growing his own finances has been the north star of Trump’s presidency, at least to some extent.
Trump’s June financial disclosure revealed massive post-election influxes of foreign and corporate capital into his business empire, stemming primarily from over $1bn in cryptocurrency ventures after he loosened regulation on the industry, as well as from international real estate.
During his first year as president, the Trump Organisation – Trump’s multinational family-owned enterprise dedicated to property development and global brand licensing – made eight real estate deals with authoritarian or one-party foreign states. Some speculate these countries were highly motivated to maintain favourable relations with the US to keep Trump happy on fronts like trade tariffs, military protection and private business dealings.
The administration, meanwhile, has repeatedly dismissed concerns over Trump’s business conflicts of interest, maintaining that he acts solely in the interest of Americans.
In late September, a separate Reuters/Ipsos poll found that Trump’s approval rating has fallen to 32 percent – the lowest of his political career – as his fellow Republicans soured on his handling of the cost of living crisis amid the deeply unpopular Iran war.
The dip in performance and approval ratings follows a high point in January 2025, when the newly inaugurated president boasted a 47 percent approval rating right after taking office.
According to the AP-NORC poll, which surveyed more than 2,000 US adults in late September, general sentiment around the administration’s ethical conduct is highly polarised, with far more citizens feeling that the president has neither prioritised the country as a whole nor everyday Americans.
Just over 40 percent of respondents believe Trump has “done something illegal” vis-a-vis allegations of personal enrichment while in office, with another 18 percent viewing his financial dealings as “unethical but not illegal”.
Opinions surrounding the lawfulness of the president’s financial practices split sharply along party lines, with Democrats overwhelmingly viewing the actions as illegal, compared with about three in 10 independents and about one in 10 Republicans, who largely see his behaviour as justified.

UK spy chief says Iran is stepping up targeting of military bases

UK PM says RAF base incidents 'likely coordinated' by Iran
The head of the United Kingdom’s domestic spy agency has said Iran is ramping up attempts to strike sensitive military targets after a series of incidents at airbases in Britain, even as Tehran has denied any involvement.
In his annual speech, M15 Director-General Ken McCallum on Tuesday said there had been a major shift in Tehran’s calculus this year and that “Iranian ambitions to come at harder targets, like military sites”.
McCallum’s warning came after UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) was “almost certainly” behind a suspected plot against Royal Air Force (RAF) Fairford, an airbase used by US bombers to carry out strikes on Iran. The incident prompted the United States to withdraw its military jets from the facility over security concerns earlier this month.
UK airbase incidents
British police declared a major incident after three “suspicious” vans drove close to the RAF Fairford airbase in Gloucestershire on September 27. Five British men in their 20s were arrested “on suspicion of committing offences under the Explosives Act”, but all were released on bail.
Police said they found a supply of petrol in three vans linked to the suspects, but no explosives. The men were later released without charge on police bail “under stringent conditions”.
Two others were arrested later, including a British-Iranian national, but were later released. None of the men have been charged.
Two Latvian men were arrested for trespassing at RAF Molesworth, which is used by the US military and NATO for intelligence operations, on Friday. The men were also released on bail.
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said on Monday that the government was sanctioning two Iranians for their “role in facilitating or engaging in hostile activity on behalf of the Iranian regime”.
One is Ruhollah Bazghandi, the head of IRGC counterespionage operations, and the other is Shahram Ali Reza Tamarzadeh Jakki, whom British officials described as a facilitator for Iran’s Zindashti criminal network.

McCallum said he could not speak about the recent incident at RAF Fairford because it was an ongoing investigation, but added, “The RAF Fairford incident … is not unique. There have been other examples, not just in the UK but around the world.”
The spy chief said UK authorities had carried out 50 arrests over the past year to disrupt Iran-linked operations.
However, he said he doubted Iran’s ability to launch complex attacks, perhaps using explosive drones, due to the limited sophistication of operatives Tehran used in the UK.
“Given what we’ve actually seen in practice in the UK in recent years, that has not been anywhere near [that] level of capability,” McCallum said.
“That said, clearly it is the case that in countries closer to its own homeland, the IRGC has quite deep experience of using more conventional and hybrid technology in a more aggressive and sophisticated way,” the MI5 boss added.
Tehran has rejected accusations of involvement in the Fairford incident or any other accusations of harmful activity in Britain.

Navi Pillay’s Nobel Peace Prize: Restoring moral authority of peace through justice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:05:57 UTC
01:05:57 KST

Navi Pillay’s Nobel Peace Prize: Restoring moral authority of peace through justice
GOA, India - For a world fractured by double standards, the recognition of a lifelong defender of human rights is a reminder that peace cannot be separated from accountability. True peace is not achieved simply when the powerful agree to stop fighting. It is achieved when the vulnerable no longer have to live at their mercy.
The award of the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize to Navanethem “Navi” Pillay, the South African jurist and former United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, arrives at a moment when the meaning of peace itself is being contested. Wars continue to devastate societies, international institutions struggle to command respect, and the application of international law remains deeply entangled with geopolitical interests. In such circumstances, recognising a woman whose life has been devoted to confronting discrimination, defending victims and strengthening international justice carries significance beyond the honour bestowed upon an individual.
It is also an opportunity for the Nobel Peace Prize to reaffirm its essential purpose. The prize must stand for something greater than diplomatic prestige, political expediency or the celebration of whichever causes happen to enjoy the support of influential governments. Its enduring authority depends on its willingness to recognise those who challenge entrenched power, defend human dignity and insist that no nation, government or individual should stand above the law.
Pillay’s recognition is therefore important not simply because of what she has accomplished, but because of what her career represents: the conviction that peace without justice is an incomplete peace, and that international law loses its meaning when its protection is distributed according to political convenience.
From apartheid to the defence of universal justice
Pillay’s journey began in apartheid South Africa, where racial discrimination was entrenched in law and institutional power. Born into a family of Indian Tamil origin in Durban, she experienced the indignities of a system that denied equal rights and opportunities to the majority of the population. Rather than accepting the structures of exclusion surrounding her, she chose the law as an instrument of resistance.
Her contribution to the anti-apartheid struggle was not incidental to her later international career. As a lawyer, she defended people subjected to political imprisonment, challenged abuses of authority and worked to protect the rights of those whom the apartheid system sought to marginalise. Her professional choices reflected a fundamental understanding: laws do not become just merely because a state enacts them, and governmental authority does not confer moral legitimacy on discrimination.
The struggle against apartheid established a principle with continuing relevance across the world. A system cannot claim legitimacy while denying a section of humanity equal dignity, freedom and protection. Nor can oppression be transformed into justice simply by giving it a legal form.
This is a lesson that extends well beyond South Africa. Across West Asia and elsewhere, communities confronting occupation, displacement, discrimination and prolonged conflict understand the difference between peace proclaimed by political leaders and justice experienced by ordinary people. A settlement that leaves fundamental grievances unresolved may end a phase of violence without creating the conditions for lasting peace.
Pillay’s life offers a powerful reminder that the defence of human rights must begin with the people whose rights are denied, rather than with the political interests of those who exercise power over them.
International justice must not have political favorites
Pillay carried these convictions into the international arena, serving as a judge of the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, presiding over that tribunal, and later serving as a judge at the International Criminal Court. Her judicial work contributed to the development of international jurisprudence on genocide and sexual violence. The landmark Akayesu judgment, delivered during her service at the Rwanda tribunal, helped establish that sexual violence can constitute an act of genocide when the necessary legal elements are met.
This was more than a legal advance. It challenged the longstanding tendency to treat the suffering of women during conflict as secondary to the supposedly larger political and military narrative. It affirmed that atrocities committed against vulnerable people deserve the full attention of the law, and that survivors must not be erased from the historical record.
From Rwanda to every other conflict in which allegations of grave international crimes arise, the principle remains the same: victims deserve investigation, recognition and justice, while those accused must be afforded due process and responsibility must be established through lawful procedures.
As United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights from 2008 to 2014, Pillay occupied one of the most demanding positions in the international human rights system. The office required her to defend universal standards in the face of pressure from governments with different political systems, strategic interests and ideological commitments. Human rights could not be defended consistently if criticism depended on whether the government concerned was a friend or an adversary.
That remains one of the central crises confronting the international order. Governments frequently invoke international law when accusing their opponents, yet become defensive when the same standards are applied to their own conduct or that of their allies. Some violations provoke immediate outrage; others encounter diplomatic hesitation, political obstruction or carefully worded expressions of concern.
Such selectivity does not merely damage the reputation of international institutions. It weakens the confidence of ordinary people in the very idea of international justice. When the law appears powerful against the weak but cautious before the powerful, it begins to resemble an instrument of political management rather than a universal safeguard.
For countries across West Asia, this contradiction is especially consequential. The credibility of international law cannot be sustained if its principles are proclaimed universally but applied unevenly in situations involving occupation, civilian casualties, displacement and allegations of serious international crimes. No community should have to wonder whether its suffering will matter less because acknowledging it would inconvenience a powerful state.
Pillay’s legacy does not require the international community to accept every allegation without examination or every institutional decision without criticism. It requires something more rigorous: evidence must be examined, legal standards must be applied consistently, and accountability must not be abandoned because its consequences are politically uncomfortable.
Palestine and the credibility of international system
The question of Palestine brings these contradictions into particularly sharp focus. Decades of occupation, repeated cycles of violence, the dispossession of Palestinians and the catastrophic destruction and human suffering in Gaza have intensified demands for an international order that does more than issue declarations.
Pillay has been associated with efforts to scrutinise alleged violations in the occupied Palestinian territory, including through her work with the United Nations Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem, and Israel. The commission she chaired concluded in 2025 that genocide had been committed in Gaza. That finding has been strongly contested by Israel and must be understood in its proper institutional and legal context. Its existence nevertheless illustrates the significance of independent investigation when allegations concern crimes of the gravest order.
The broader issue cannot be reduced to whether governments welcome or reject a particular finding. The question is whether international institutions can investigate serious allegations independently, whether their findings receive a reasoned response, and whether credible processes of accountability can proceed without political intimidation.
For Palestinians, justice cannot mean simply the temporary cessation of bombardment while the conditions that deny them freedom, security and self-determination remain unaddressed. Nor can the language of peace be used to demand that victims abandon their claims while the structures responsible for their suffering remain intact.
Equally, the defence of Palestinian rights must rest on universal principles that protect civilians and uphold human dignity without exception. International humanitarian law, the prohibition of genocide and the prohibition of torture cannot be selectively invoked. They must apply irrespective of nationality, religion, political affiliation or military power.
This is the significance of Pillay’s career for the wider region. Her work invites governments and peoples alike to insist that international law be judged by its consistent application, not by the identity of those it protects or holds accountable.
The Nobel Peace Prize must recover its moral purpose
The Nobel Peace Prize has historically recognised people and movements whose struggles connected peace with freedom, equality and resistance to oppression. Its recognition of Martin Luther King Jr., Nelson Mandela and other figures demonstrated that peace is not simply the absence of armed confrontation. It is also the pursuit of social conditions in which human beings can live with dignity and without fear of arbitrary power.
Yet the prize is not immune to the political controversies surrounding international life. Its selections can generate legitimate debate over the relationship between peace, democracy, diplomacy and geopolitical alignment. The 2025 award to Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado, which the Nobel Committee justified by reference to her promotion of democratic rights and a peaceful transition from dictatorship, became part of precisely such a debate. Critics questioned the political implications of the choice, while its supporters defended the committee’s stated rationale.
The issue is not that every controversial decision invalidates the prize, or that its recipients must satisfy every political constituency. The greater danger is that repeated perceptions of political selectivity can diminish the moral authority of an institution whose influence depends on public confidence in the principles it represents.
The Nobel Peace Prize cannot settle every international dispute, compel governments to obey the law or substitute for functioning judicial institutions. But it possesses a powerful capacity to direct the world's attention towards struggles that deserve recognition. Its choices help define what the international community celebrates as peace, and what it is prepared to overlook.
Pillay’s recognition offers an opportunity to bring that purpose into sharper focus. Her career has not been built around the promise of an easy diplomatic solution. It has been shaped by the demanding work of defending rights, strengthening legal institutions and confronting the impunity that allows grave abuses to recur.
This is a conception of peace that should resonate across political boundaries. It does not belong exclusively to the West, the Global South, any particular religion or any geopolitical bloc. Nor should international justice be portrayed as the exclusive property of one political tradition. Its legitimacy rests on the proposition that every human being possesses dignity and that every state bears obligations under international law.
For Iran and other countries of the region, the award provides an occasion to engage with that universal proposition while continuing to scrutinise the institutions through which it is implemented. Defending international law requires neither uncritical acceptance of every Western position nor the rejection of international institutions simply because their decisions are disputed. It requires a consistent commitment to legal equality, national sovereignty, human dignity and accountability for serious violations.
The test of principle is whether it survives when its application challenges our own political preferences.
Peace is a responsibility, not a slogan
Pillay’s life brings the meaning of the Nobel Peace Prize back to the human beings whose lives are shaped by war, discrimination and impunity. A displaced family needs more than declarations of concern. A survivor of sexual violence needs more than sympathy. A political prisoner needs more than a diplomatic expression of regret. People whose homes, communities and livelihoods have been destroyed need institutions capable of protecting their rights and securing meaningful remedies.
Justice cannot restore every life or erase every wound. Nor should the pursuit of accountability become an excuse to reject negotiations that can save lives. Ceasefires, diplomacy and political settlements remain essential. But peace becomes durable only when they create a credible path towards freedom, security, recognition and justice.
The Nobel Peace Prize awarded to Navi Pillay should therefore be understood as a recognition of a lifetime spent defending the principles without which peace becomes little more than a temporary arrangement between those who possess power. It honors a woman who confronted apartheid at its foundations and carried that commitment into the international institutions charged with defending humanity against grave abuses.
The true measure of this recognition will not be the ceremony, the medal or the declarations that accompany it. It will be whether the principles associated with Pillay’s work receive renewed support, whether independent institutions are strengthened, and whether the international community becomes more willing to confront violations even when doing so carries political costs.
The Nobel Prize does not become meaningful simply because it honors a distinguished individual. It becomes meaningful when that recognition reminds the world of obligations it would otherwise prefer to evade. In an age when the language of peace is frequently invoked while justice remains elusive, Navi Pillay’s recognition offers a clear and demanding message: no nation should possess a license to violate human dignity, no victim should be considered expendable, and no government should be beyond scrutiny.
Peace requires justice. Justice requires accountability. And accountability must never depend on who holds the power.
*Ranjan Solomon is an author, researcher, and freelance writer focused on global and national justice.

PoderData/Aya interviewed 3,000 voters by telephone between Oct. 10 and 12, with a margin of error of 1.8 percentage points.
BTG/Nexus interviewed 2,002 voters aged 16 and older during the same period, with a margin of error of 2 percentage points.
The BTG/Nexus survey was commissioned by financial institution BTG Pactual. Both polls were registered with Brazil's Superior Electoral Court.
In the first round on Oct. 4, Bolsonaro received 47.03% of valid votes, while Lula secured 45.16%, according to the results.
The candidates will face each other again on Oct. 25, when Brazilians will choose their next president.

Burnham links RAF Fairford incident to Iran amid delicate relations with US
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham attributed recent threats to an RAF base in Gloucestershire to Iran on Monday, but this may cause further problems for him in future.
Five men were arrested near RAF Fairford, which hosted long range bombers for the United States, including B1 and B52 bombers, on 27 September, after the police received a call concerning suspicious activity in the area.
The men were arrested on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act, and on suspicion of preparing an act of terrorism. Two other men were subsequently arrested in connection to the incident. The men have all been released on bail.
Rob Geist Pinfold, a lecturer in Defence Studies at King's College London, told The New Arab that linking the incident to Iran could end up putting Burnham in a "tough spot".
"There was this hyping up that this was an imminent terror threat. The residents were evacuated. They were hosted at a local leisure centre, and then we went from that to the suspects being released on bail," Geist Pinfold said.
The US responded to the attacks by removing their planes from the base. Shortly after the US and Israel's attacks on Iran in February, the UK granted permission for the US to use RAF Fairford for operations against Iran. The base is strategically important because it has a long runway from which long-range bombers, including B-1 and B-52 bombers, can take-off.
"The UK government has to walk a very, very strange tightrope here of not being part of the war effort but the same time, unlike other European countries, allowing the US to use the bases in its territory as part of that war effort, which is why Iran painted a target on Fairford," said Geist Pinfold.
Support for the war on Iran is low in the UK. In April, 65% of Brits disapproved of US military strikes against Iran, according to a poll by Ipsos.
The US President is also unpopular among Brits. In September, a YouGov poll found that just 10% of people in the UK have a favourable opinion of Donald Trump. By comparison, 85% have an unfavourable opinion of him.
"This is a tough spot for Andy Burnham," Geist Pinfold said, "[He] might find himself doing the same thing as [former Prime Minister] Kier Starmer, trying to pretend the special relationship is still alive and well when there are very clear cracks in the surface."
"[The UK] certainly doesn't think the war was a good idea now but at the same time it doesn't want to alienate the US and at the same time it does see Iran as a national security threat," Geist Pinfold told The New Arab.
When asked if the UK might become more involved in the Iran war, Geist Pinfold said, "I would suggest it depends on what happens with our Gulf partners because at the end of the day, the UK like other European countries sees the Iran conflict as a threat to national security, but also potential opportunity simply because Gulf states are looking to diversify the security partnerships."
"For a country like the UK with a strong defence industry that also is looking for a quick fix, or at least a boost to its economy ASAP, that's a very, very attractive potential."

A large trial of genotype-guided antidepressant prescribing finds no early benefit but higher remission later
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
16:00:38 UTC
01:00:38 KST

A randomized clinical trial found that using genetic test results to guide the prescription of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) for depression did not improve symptoms after 3 months compared with usual care. However, among patients whose genetic profiles called for a different medication or dose, 48% of those in the genotype-guided group reached remission at 6 months, compared with 39% of those receiving usual care. The paper was published in JAMA Network Open.
Depression is a common mental health disorder marked by persistent low mood, loss of interest or pleasure, and other symptoms that can substantially disrupt everyday life. Its prevalence has risen over the past decade among adults, adolescents, and school-aged children. Uncontrolled depression is closely linked to suicide, which is now the second leading cause of death among adolescents and young adults.
One of the most widely used treatments for depression is a class of antidepressants called selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, or SSRIs. These medications increase the availability of the neurotransmitter serotonin in the brain by reducing its reuptake into nerve cells. Although SSRIs are commonly prescribed, they do not work equally well for everyone. They can also take six weeks or longer to produce a response, and can cause adverse effects that lead some patients to stop treatment.
Part of this variability may be related to genetic differences in the liver enzymes that break down SSRIs, particularly CYP2D6 and CYP2C19. Variants in the genes for these enzymes can make a person a poor, intermediate, normal, rapid, or ultrarapid metabolizer, changing how much of an SSRI remains in the body. Some other medications can also slow CYP2D6 activity, producing a similar effect. Genotype-guided prescribing uses genetic test results to help clinicians choose a medication or dose suited to how a person processes it.
The Clinical Pharmacogenetics Implementation Consortium has published guidelines for adjusting SSRI prescriptions based on these genes, but most psychiatry experts and practice guidelines have not endorsed routine genetic testing, citing insufficient evidence. Earlier trials have been criticized for relying on proprietary commercial algorithms, using small samples, or failing to meet their main goals.
Study author Kathryn V. Blake of Nemours Children’s Health in Jacksonville, Florida, and her colleagues conducted a large randomized clinical trial to test whether genotype-guided SSRI prescribing improves depression in routine clinical care. The trial focused on CYP2D6 and CYP2C19 and used publicly available guidelines rather than a commercial algorithm to generate recommendations.
Study participants were 1,460 people with depression treated at primary care, psychiatry, and family medicine clinics in nine U.S. health systems between 2021 and 2024. Participants were aged 8 years or older, had experienced depression for 3 months or longer, and were about to start or adjust SSRI treatment. They included 1,239 adults, with an average age of 41, and 221 children and adolescents, with an average age of 15; 75% were female.
Participants were randomly assigned either to a genotype-guided group or to usual care. All provided DNA samples, which were analyzed for variants in the genes for CYP2D6 and CYP2C19, but only the genotype-guided group’s results were returned during the study; the usual care group’s samples were analyzed after it ended.
For the genotype-guided group, clinicians received recommendations about which SSRI to prescribe and at what dose through electronic health record alerts, consult notes, or pharmacist consultations, based on established guidelines and drug labels. The recommendations also accounted for other medications that can slow CYP2D6 activity. Clinicians were not required to follow the recommendations. The SSRIs covered were sertraline, escitalopram, citalopram, fluvoxamine, and paroxetine.
The main analyses focused on the 692 participants (about 47%) whose genetic results were “actionable,” meaning guidelines recommended a different medication or dose for them. Depression symptoms were measured with Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS) questionnaires for adults and children, and with the Patient Health Questionnaire-8 as a secondary measure.
At 3 months, depression symptoms had decreased modestly in both groups, but the decrease was nearly identical, and side effects were similar as well. At 6 months, however, 48% of patients in the genotype-guided group had reached remission on the PROMIS measure, compared with 39% in the usual care group. Using the second questionnaire, remission rates were 30% and 21%, respectively.
The genetic guidance did change prescribing: at 3 months, 85% of patients in the genotype-guided group were taking a medication and dose consistent with their genetic profile, compared with 74% in the usual care group. Among patients whose results did not call for any change, the two groups did not differ.
“In this randomized clinical trial, genotype-guided prescribing of SSRIs did not improve control of depression symptoms at 3 months compared with usual care but was associated with higher depression remission rates at 6 months. These findings suggest a possible longer-term clinical benefit and indicate that future studies should focus on the durability and long-term impact of genotype-guided prescribing in the management of depressive symptoms,” study authors concluded.
The study contributes to the development of new ways to treat depression. However, the trial did not meet its primary goal of improving symptoms at 3 months, and the 6-month remission rates were secondary outcomes. Clinicians and patients also knew which group they were in, and patients could see their genetic results in their health records, which may have influenced how they reported their symptoms.
The authors also note that the study design did not include a formal diagnosis of major depression, so the sample may have included patients with milder forms of depression. About 15% of patients in the genotype-guided group with actionable results were still not receiving a gene-matched prescription at 3 months, and delays in treatment changes, which were not tracked, may help explain why differences did not appear until later.
The paper, “Genotype-Guided Antidepressant Prescribing for Patients With Depression: A Randomized Clinical Trial,” was authored by Kathryn V. Blake, Lindsay J. Hines, Michelle Liu, Rachel A. Myers, Jordan F. Baye, Kerri L. Cavanaugh, Benjamin Q. Duong, Leslie A. Hulvershorn, Carol A. Mathews, James W. Murrough, Lori A. Orlando, Natasha J. Petry, Emma M. Tillman, Azita Sadeghpour, Deepak Voora, Sara L. Block, Emily J. Cicali, Sabrina Clermont, Erica N. Elwood, Elizabeth C. Harris, Khoa A. Nguyen, Michelle A. Ramos, Marc B. Rosenman, Nandini Shroff, Saskia Shuman, Christina Wyatt, Carol R. Horowitz, Simona Volpi, Rajbir Singh, Renee A. Rider, Hrishikesh Chakraborty, Paul R. Dexter, Julie A. Johnson, Todd C. Skaar, Larisa H. Cavallari, and Josh F. Peterson.

Washington DC — She was visibly nervous. She relied heavily on notes. She took deep breaths. And veteran White House reporters found themselves witnessing a "briefest briefing" ever.
However, when Katie Zacharia delivered her first White House press briefing on Tuesday, she conveyed the US administration's key points and broke significant news during a high-pressure debut.
Taking the custom podium in the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room — a small theater in the West Wing of the White House — for roughly 14–15 minutes, including an eight-minute prepared opening statement, Zacharia began her briefing by stating that she was "honoured to work for" US President Donald Trump "and the American people", thanking the US president "for the trust that he has placed in me."
She highlighted Trump's recent Ohio rally, his "America First" priorities of "lower taxes, higher wages, and one of my favourites, secure borders."

"He is an energetic president. Attendance is at record highs as enthusiastic, hard-working Americans are lining up and packing arenas to support President Trump and Republicans," she added.
Zacharia, tapped by Trump to replace Karoline Leavitt, who resigned in August to spend more time with her two young children, claimed that US real wages rose by up to 2 percent under Trump administeration, but fell nearly 4 per cent under former president Joe Biden.
President Trump is the first president in modern history to actually lower prescription drug prices, delivering the biggest drop in 63 years, she added.

Guilfoyle resignation
Zacharia, a conservative commentator, a lawyer and former communications adviser to Trump's media company, however, gave reporters a big news on Kimberly Guilfoyle, the US ambassador to Greece.
"We have asked Ambassador Guilfoyle to resign," Trump's new press secretary told reporters. "She has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her well."
The announcement came a day after Trump confirmed he was considering dismissing Guilfoyle, a former television host and the ex-fiancee of Donald Trump Jr.
Guilfoyle has come under scrutiny following media reports regarding her financial dealings and ties with wealthy business figures.
According to US media reports, she asked a prominent Trump supporter Eric Deters to settle $100,000 in credit card debt ahead of her July 2025 Senate hearing.
Reports citing messages and recordings reveal Guilfoyle boasted of luxury trips and hotel stays funded by wealthy Greek business figures.
The State Department is reportedly investigating whether Guilfoyle received improper gifts.
Zacharia's disclosure regarding Guilfoyle's status was one of only three questions she addressed from reporters – Nick Gilbertson of Breitbart, Peter Doocy of Fox News, and Alina Shirazi of the Daily Mail.
She said her job was to amplify and expand Trump's agenda, describing the US leader as "his own best spokesperson." She also did not answer whether US will stop intelligence sharing with Ukraine.
During remarks concerning her family, the California mother of four momentarily misspoke, stating, "my president — excuse me, my husband… That’s a good one", which drew laughter from the room before she regained her composure and continued.
Comparisons with Karoline Leavitt
Audible gasps were heard as she ended the briefing, citing Trump's departure on Marine One to Alaska to take no further questions.
"I've now been covering the White House for nearly four years — and that was without a doubt the shortest briefing I've ever attended. By a wide, wide margin," noted journalist Bernd Debusmann Jr.
A White House official interviewed by MS NOW's Jake Traylor immediately stated that Zacharia better improve — and quickly.
"Getting behind the podium is tough, but she got off on the wrong foot. She needs to get much better, fast, otherwise she’ll break Scaramucci’s record,” the unnamed official told Traylor.
Former White House communications director Anthony Scaramucci served for just 10 days during Trump's first term in 2017.
Zacharia's first press briefing lasted roughly 15 minutes, taking questions from just three reporters for five minutes, noted NBC News' White House correspondent Monica Alba.
"By comparison, Karoline Leavitt’s first briefing lasted around 47 minutes and she took questions from 20 different reporters."
Zacharia's supervisor, however, described her debut briefing as a "tremendous start".
"A tremendous start for the new White House press secretary," said Steven Cheung, White House director of communications.
"She commanded the room and effectively reminded the American people of all the great work President Trump and his Administration has done thus far."
Debut briefings are rarely easy, and the litmus test will come in subsequent briefings. Meanwhile, Zacharia must now build rapport with a White House press corps accustomed to combative exchanges, fast-paced political shifts, and a president who, she herself described, as "his own best spokesperson."

Centre asks states to go into ‘mission mode’ to curb stubble burning as farm fires rise in MP, Rajasthan

Centre steps up anti-stubble burning drive ahead of peak crop residue season (representative image)
NEW DELHI: The Centre on Tuesday asked Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Punjab, Haryana and Delhi-NCR authorities to work in “mission mode” to prevent stubble burning ahead of the peak crop residue burning season, flagging a sharp rise in farm fires in Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan.Union agriculture minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan and environment minister Bhupender Yadav chaired a high-level inter-ministerial meeting with state agriculture ministers and officials to review crop residue management and measures to control farm fires.“Very little time remains between the harvesting of the current crop and the sowing of the rabi crop. Therefore, the administrative machinery must step away from paperwork and work directly on the ground on a war footing,” the two ministers said, according to a statement from the agriculture ministry.States have been directed to hold immediate meetings with district magistrates to ensure strict monitoring and implement practical solutions, the ministry said.
Reviewing data from September 15 to October 12, Chouhan noted that stubble-burning incidents had declined by 53.3% in Haryana and around 32% in Uttar Pradesh compared with the corresponding period last year. Punjab had also recorded a fall.However, the rise in Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan prompted concern.
Madhya Pradesh's farm-fire count increased from 55 to 277, a jump of 452%, while Rajasthan's tally rose from 20 to 60, an increase of 200%.Chouhan directed the two states to identify affected districts and villages and immediately prepare special action plans. He also cautioned states reporting fewer incidents against becoming complacent, as a substantial portion of the harvest was still pending.The latest figures reflect the uneven spread of farm fires across northern and central India.Madhya Pradesh recorded 277 incidents by October 11, followed by Uttar Pradesh with 121 and Punjab with 118. Rajasthan reported 45 cases, Haryana seven, Uttarakhand three and Delhi one, taking the total across the seven states to 572.Stubble burning had been detected in 87 districts by October 11, with Amritsar recording 60 incidents, the highest among the seven states covered.
Farmers need affordable alternatives, says Centre
Chouhan said farmers had only 20-25 days between paddy harvesting and wheat sowing, making burning a quick and inexpensive way to clear fields despite its impact on soil nutrients, soil organisms and air quality in Delhi-NCR.“Simply telling farmers not to burn stubble is insufficient; we must provide them with easy, accessible and affordable alternatives,” he said.He said crop residue could be incorporated into the soil to serve as organic manure or removed for use in bio-CNG, bio-ethanol, electricity generation and fodder production.The government also aims to develop a system in which farmers can benefit from environmentally friendly practices, including through carbon credits.Chouhan urged states to promote short-duration crop varieties, including Pusa 2090 and PR126, instead of longer-duration varieties such as Pusa-44, to give farmers sufficient time to clear fields before the next sowing season.
Centre flags idle crop residue machines
The Centre has supplied more than 3.54 lakh crop residue management machines to states, including 26,109 during the current financial year. However, a central survey found that around 40% of older machines in Punjab and 48% in Haryana were idle or non-functional, news agency PTI reported.Chouhan directed states to repair existing machines alongside distributing new ones. He also called for the activation of Custom Hiring Centres to ensure that small and marginal farmers could access machinery at affordable rates.Between 2018-19 and 2025-26, the Centre released Rs 4,266.47 crore to states under the Crop Residue Management scheme. Punjab received Rs 2,056.50 crore, Haryana Rs 1,171.71 crore, Uttar Pradesh Rs 868.67 crore and Madhya Pradesh Rs 59 crore.For 2026-27, Rs 592.57 crore has been allocated, of which Rs 430.87 crore has been released.Chouhan expressed concern over slow utilisation of funds and urged Punjab to submit utilisation certificates for earlier releases so that the next instalment could be cleared without delay.
Monitoring to intensify after 3 pm
Yadav called for stronger enforcement and ground-level monitoring, identifying key districts in Punjab and Haryana for closer scrutiny.In Punjab, these include Sangrur, Tarn Taran, Amritsar, Patiala and Gurdaspur. In Haryana, the focus districts are Kaithal, Karnal, Kurukshetra, Ambala and Fatehabad.He stressed the need to integrate stubble-burning data with the Commission for Air Quality Management and the Central Pollution Control Board, while tracking harvesting schedules and weather conditions that affect air quality in the National Capital Region.
Yadav said monitoring should not rely on satellite data alone. District collectors should conduct ground assessments, while enforcement measures should include patrolling and flying squads, particularly after 3 pm, when satellites do not pass over the region.Chouhan also called for direct supply chains connecting farmers with thermal power plants that use stubble pellets for co-firing, compressed bio-gas plants and second-generation bio-ethanol facilities. He urged states to implement approved supply projects without delay and asked drought-hit regions to store crop residue safely for use as livestock fodder.The ministers said state governments would remain responsible for implementation, with the Centre providing technical, administrative and financial support.

Hezbollah announces aid for displaced in Lebanon, despite pressures
Hezbollah announced on Tuesday an aid programme for Lebanese who lost their homes in the war with Israel, with benefits capped at $14,000 per household, despite US and Lebanese sanctions on the militant group.
The announcement also comes despite US sanctions on Iran, which backs Hezbollah with weapons and resources, and tighter controls by the Lebanese authorities on Hezbollah's funding and supply routes, after the group emerged significantly weakened from two wars with Israel since October 2023.
At a press conference in Beirut's southern suburbs, the head of Hezbollah's Executive Council, Ali Daamouch, announced assistance of up to $14,000 per household for residents of Beirut and its southern suburbs, and $12,000 for other regions.
The assistance will go to displaced people whose homes have been destroyed or made uninhabitable, and to residents of areas in the south occupied by Israel, on the condition that beneficiaries do not have a second home, Daamouch said.
“The aim of the project is to support those directly affected who have been displaced from homes that have been destroyed or damaged and who do not have alternative accommodation,” he said.
Hezbollah will pay the assistance in four instalments over the course of a year, he added, without specifying the source of the funds or the number of beneficiaries the Shia movement can cover.
The aid announcement was the first from Hezbollah since it drew Lebanon deeper into war with Israel on 2 March in support of Iran, which the US and Israel began attacking on 28 February. Israel had already been striking southern Lebanon before that.
In December 2024, after an earlier war with Israel in support of Gaza, Hezbollah announced similar assistance worth $77 million to the displaced, describing it as a "a gift from the Iranian people and Hezbollah".
During the press conference, Daamoush said that "reconstruction and providing shelter for displaced people are the responsibility of the state," adding that the issue "must be kept out of political calculations". Hezbollah's critics say the state must not bear the burden for a war it did not choose.
Israeli attacks since 2023 have destroyed or damaged more than 290,000 homes, according to provisional figures from Lebanese authorities, particularly in the south of the country and in Beirut's southern suburbs, strongholds of Hezbollah.
The total cost of the two wars could exceed $27 billion, Prime Minister Nawaf Salam said in September, citing World Bank estimates.
He said the state, already reeling under a crushing financial crisis for the past seven years, does not have the means to rebuild southern regions destroyed by the war.
Despite a US-backed framework agreement signed between Lebanon and Israel in late June, Israeli strikes and demolitions have continued in southern Lebanon.

2026-10-13

Mücahithan Avcıoğlu
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
Turkish business leaders called for a renewed approach to Türkiye's EU accession process in an open letter to Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, saying closer integration would strengthen Europe's economic and strategic position.
The letter, published in Italian daily Corriere della Sera, said it is time to reconsider the approach holding back Türkiye's membership process and provide the country with a clear accession perspective.
Signatories included Foreign Economic Relations Board (DEIK) President Nail Olpak, Türkiye-Europe Business Councils Chair Mehmet Ali Yalcindag, and Türkiye-Italy Business Council Chairwoman Lale Cander.
"Europe will be stronger on the global stage if it fully harnesses the economic, technological, and strategic potential that Türkiye brings to a shared European future," the letter said.
The chairs of 26 business councils between Türkiye and EU member states said Europe had entered an era in which economic competitiveness, technological strength, and security are inseparable.
Geopolitical instability, rapid developments in artificial intelligence and advanced technologies, the energy transition, and the changing global economic order are reshaping Europe's interests, vulnerabilities, and ability to act, they said.
The letter reaffirmed the Turkish business community's commitment to European values and its determination to contribute to Europe's economic strength and global competitiveness.
Turkish companies and entrepreneurs have been integral parts of European value chains, industrial ecosystems, and innovation networks for decades, it noted.
The signatories said growing social concerns, demographic changes, and persistent geopolitical instability are shaping Europe's security environment, making deeper integration with Türkiye an important element of the EU's response.
While acknowledging challenges that both sides must address, they said global turbulence had made breaking the stagnation in Türkiye's accession process increasingly urgent.
"It is time to reassess the current approach that is hampering Türkiye's accession process," the letter said.
Providing Türkiye with a clear and unequivocal EU membership perspective would reaffirm the deeply interconnected futures of Türkiye and the bloc, helping restore strategic clarity and mutual trust, it added.
The business leaders called for a stronger roadmap, saying the dynamism of Turkish society and the EU's transformative power could help address existing challenges and move the accession process forward.
The letter also highlighted the potential for Türkiye's full integration into the EU's emerging economic security and defense architecture.
A modernized EU-Türkiye Customs Union would help strengthen Europe's competitiveness in a geopolitically fragmented world, it said.
