‘Block, blunt, break’: What’s in NATO’s new Russia war plan?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
14:52:22 UTC
23:52:22 KST

‘Block, blunt, break’: What’s in NATO’s new Russia war plan?
NATO’s top commander says he is revealing the plan to stop a Russian invasion of Europe, even though the threat is not ‘imminent’.
NATO’s top general has unveiled a new war plan for countering a Russian attack on members of the alliance, embedding lessons learned from the front lines in Ukraine.
Speaking about NATO’s so-called “theory of victory” at the Warsaw Security Forum on Monday, General Alexus Grynkewich, who has served as head of United States European Command and the Supreme Allied Commander Europe since 2025, said the plan rests on three strategies designed to stop an invasion in its tracks: “block, blunt and break”.
The announcement comes amid mounting warnings from European intelligence agencies of rising threats from Russia, including both the prospect of conventional military action and “hybrid warfare”, which can include tactics from cyberattacks to tampering with undersea cables.
In a bid to ease the alliance’s growing concerns, Grynkewich said: “What I want to do is assure the one billion citizens of our alliance that we’ve got this. We know what we need to do. We know how we would do it.”
But the new plan from NATO comes at a time when the alliance itself appears divided on how to deal with Russia, following a series of recent overtures from US President Donald Trump to Russian President Vladimir Putin, including his latest controversial plan for Russia to release stocks of diesel to global markets despite sanctions on Russian oil.
So, what’s in the new NATO plan, and what are European agencies warning about? How has Russia reacted? And is the alliance even on the same page on all of this?
What’s in the new NATO plan?
General Grynkewich told the Warsaw Security Forum that NATO does not view a military confrontation with Russia as “imminent or inevitable”, but that it will nevertheless be ready for one.
“Implementing the theory of victory I’ve described today would require me to issue orders that I hope to never give,” he said. “But let there be no doubt: should war come, we will block, blunt any attack, and then if it does not cease, we will break the forces conducting aggression against us.”
The “block, blunt and break” strategy, he explained, is aimed at stopping an attack rather than taking enemy territory.
Drawing directly on lessons learned on the front lines in Ukraine and from conflict in the Middle East, Grynkewich said the plan relies on the use of precision weapons with “affordable mass”, like drones, and other autonomous systems.
In the plan, he said, the alliance’s forces would “block” an attack at the border to halt enemy advances on the battlefield, then “blunt” the attack by hitting incoming troops from the air, sea, and land. Then, at last, they would aim to “break” the enemy by targeting the supply chain and command networks.
“If required, we will break the enemy’s forces and the operational warfighting system that is arrayed against us,” he said. “Enemy formations will be starved of replenishment. Enemy commanders will be unable to control their forces. Enemy forces and support capabilities will be reduced and destroyed.”
Are Russian threats in Europe on the rise?
Germany’s foreign intelligence chief, Martin Jaeger, warned last week that the country risked being drawn into a “violent conflict” with Russia, saying Moscow increasingly viewed Berlin as a principal adversary.
He cited an attempted drone attack on a Ukrainian cargo plane at Leipzig airport in August as an example of the escalating threat. Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt has also warned of a Russian-linked “shadow war” involving sabotage, cyberattacks and other covert operations.
In France, President Emmanuel Macron warned last month that the Russian hybrid threat facing France and other European countries had intensified in recent weeks, and ordered the preparation of plans to protect critical infrastructure.
The United Kingdom’s Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said that he had received confirmation upon entering office that Russia interfered in the 2016 Brexit referendum, although he did not publicly detail the evidence behind that assessment. Last week, he travelled to Berlin to meet with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, in part to discuss plans to combat Russian hybrid warfare.
Russia issued a nuclear warning to NATO late last month, saying it was prepared to use its arsenal, including nuclear weapons, if the alliance attempted to isolate Kaliningrad, a Russian exclave bordering Poland and Lithuania.
In July, Romania’s Defence Ministry said it had recorded 33 instances of Russian drones entering its airspace since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in February 2022. Eighteen of those incursions had occurred this year, and Romanian F-16 fighter jets had shot down three drones during the year.
Poland has also accused Russian intelligence services of orchestrating an arson attack on a Starlink satellite-internet station in Wola Krobowska last month. Warsaw described the incident as part of Russia’s hybrid warfare campaign against countries supporting Ukraine.
Norway, too, has issued similar warnings. Beate Gangas, head of the country’s Police Security Service, said this week that Europe is facing its most serious security situation since World War II, echoing concerns over suspected Russian sabotage and covert operations across the continent.
What has Russia said?
In August, Russia warned the UK that it could face “consequences” for supplying drones to Ukraine that have been used in long-range attacks inside Russian territory.
“London’s actions will inevitably carry consequences for which it will have to answer,” the Russian embassy in London said in a statement on August 17. “The deeper its involvement in the conflict and the greater its support for Kyiv’s terrorist machinery, the higher the price it will pay.”
Despite this, Russia is not preparing for “any kind” of conflict with Europe, President Vladimir Putin said last month. He added that Russia had “no real motive” to escalate tensions and criticised European countries that have suggested otherwise.
“Many in Europe talk about expecting an attack from Russia and therefore believe they must themselves prepare for hostilities, for a war with Russia,” Putin told reporters in St Petersburg.
“I want to emphasise once again: we are not preparing for any kind of hostilities with Europe,” he noted.
Putin added that Russia was considering its stance on whether to resume peace talks with Ukraine following recent Ukrainian attacks on Russia, particularly on energy infrastructure.
“On proposals to resume negotiations, yes, they are all on the table, and it is all possible. But after everything they’ve done, we will give careful thought to what steps we need to take in response,” Putin said.
Is NATO united?
Since taking presidential office in the US, Trump has repeatedly attacked other NATO members for not shouldering enough of the financial burden for defence. He has also been angered by NATO members’ general refusal to join in the US-Israel war on Iran.
As a result, there are fears that Trump cannot be relied on to provide support if it is needed within the NATO alliance, analysts say.
In August, after the Russian consulate in London warned of “consequences” for the UK for providing Ukraine with long-range drones, former Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Andrei Fedorov told the BBC that could include the possibility of attacks. He said many of the military experts currently advising the Kremlin are “convinced” that NATO would not respond forcefully if Russia were to hit the UK. “Trump will not allow NATO to answer,” he said.
The alliance is facing a deepening divide over Russia, as Trump pursues engagement with Moscow while European governments insist that Russia must remain under pressure if the war in Ukraine is to come to an end.
Last month, Washington invited Putin to December’s Group of 20 (G20) summit in Miami, in a move that was seen as potentially ending Moscow’s diplomatic isolation since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
The European Union responded that Russia remained a G20 member but said it would continue condemning the invasion regardless of whether Putin attended.
The divide deepened last week when Trump announced a deal allowing Russian diesel exports into US and global markets, temporarily easing sanctions on Russian fuel. His administration said the move could help lower energy prices and encourage Putin to return to peace negotiations.
Critics have warned that it would generate revenue for Russia while undermining Western efforts to constrain its war effort.
Meanwhile, Trump has also escalated his criticism of Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and suggested that Ukraine should elect a new leader willing to make a deal with Russia. Zelenskyy had called Trump’s diesel agreement with Putin “not fair and not honest”, arguing it would benefit Russia.
EU foreign ministers also insisted that European sanctions against Russia would remain in place despite Washington’s deal with Moscow.
On Sunday, Trump claimed in a Truth Social post to have instigated an “energy truce” between Russia and Ukraine, under which both sides would refrain from targeting each other’s energy facilities with long-range strikes. However, Zelenskyy said such a deal was “news to me” – although he also said Ukraine would respect such a truce if Moscow honoured it as well. Regardless, Russia, which also has not confirmed agreeing to an energy truce, continued striking Ukraine’s facilities on Monday, according to Ukrainian officials.

US threatens restrictions on military aid to Nigeria over child soldier concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
14:49:51 UTC
23:49:51 KST

Kabir Adeniyi
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
The US has placed Nigeria on its Child Soldiers Prevention Act blacklist, which could restrict military assistance, weapons sales, and defense cooperation unless President Donald Trump grants a waiver.
The designation was detailed in the US State Department’s 2026 Trafficking in Persons Report, which accused armed groups operating in Nigeria of recruiting and using children in their activities.
The report identified Boko Haram and the Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP) as groups that recruit, abduct and use children, including as combatants, spies, porters, messengers and guards. It said some children were as young as 12.
Countries on the list may face restrictions on international military education and training, foreign military financing, excess defense equipment and certain commercial licenses for military equipment. The restrictions are subject to presidential waivers and other legal exceptions.
The report said the restrictions would apply from Oct. 1 for the fiscal year unless a waiver or other applicable exceptions were granted.
The designation comes amid continued security cooperation between Washington and Abuja, including efforts to combat extremist groups in northeastern Nigeria.
The report also criticized Nigeria’s broader anti-trafficking record, saying Abuja had failed to meet minimum standards for eliminating human trafficking for the 15th consecutive year.
It said Nigerian authorities investigated 1,341 trafficking cases during the reporting period, but recorded 94 prosecutions and 97 convictions. Of 2,004 identified trafficking victims, 675 received government-supported assistance, according to the report.
The State Department also raised concerns about alleged corruption and official complicity in trafficking crimes, saying the government had not reported investigations, prosecutions or convictions of officials allegedly involved.
Despite the criticism, the report acknowledged some progress, including increased government funding for victim services and prevention programs, cooperation with foreign governments on trafficking investigations and the repatriation of Nigerians exploited abroad.
Nigeria has previously appeared on the Child Soldiers Prevention Act list, including in 2015 -2018 and 2020 - 2021. Previous US administrations waived restrictions, allowing military assistance and arms sales to continue.
The latest designation could complicate aspects of the security partnership, although the extent of any restrictions will depend on the application of the law and whether the US president grants a waiver.

14:49:44 UTC
23:49:44 KST

- Kim Jong Un opened a new underground-style defense museum displaying the Hwasong-20 ICBM, new missiles and drones.
- Among the exhibits is a new 4x4 armored vehicle closely resembling the Canadian Roshel Senator used by Ukraine in Kursk.
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un has opened a new national defense museum packed with the country’s missiles, rocket launchers and drones, and among the exhibits is a previously unseen 4×4 armored vehicle that closely resembles the Canadian-made Roshel Senator used by Ukraine.
State news agency KCNA reported on Oct. 13 that Kim attended the opening of the Defense Revolution Museum, run by the Second Economy Commission that oversees North Korea’s arms industry, on Oct. 11 and vowed to keep developing the country’s weapons. KCNA quoted him calling the museum a “precious monument” and did not give its size or location, though photos suggest at least part of it was built underground, with weapons lined up in long, tunnel-like halls.
The new armored vehicle shown in KCNA photos shares the overall layout and several hull details of the Senator, a Canadian armored car built on a Ford F-550 truck chassis that Roshel has supplied to Ukraine in large numbers. The North Korean version appears to have a lengthened body, suggesting it has been adapted to carry more troops in the back. KCNA did not name the vehicle or give any details about its protection, engine or how many are in service.
North Korean troops know the Senator from the battlefield. Ukrainian units used Senators during their incursion into Russia’s Kursk region in August 2024, where thousands of North Korean soldiers later fought alongside Russian forces to push Ukraine out. Russian troops have captured several Senators intact or lightly damaged, including one taken by naval infantry in the Kursk region that month, and a captured vehicle may have been handed to North Korea, which now appears to be building its own version. Roshel has delivered more than 2,000 Senators to Ukraine since Russia’s full-scale invasion, and open-source tracking project Oryx had documented 182 in Mrap version and 83 Senator IMV of them destroyed, damaged or captured by the end of 2025.
The museum’s largest exhibit is the Hwasong-20 intercontinental ballistic missile, which North Korea has displayed but not yet flight-tested, shown with a world map suggesting it could reach the United States and beyond. Visitors also see a new submarine-launched ballistic missile, the 600 mm super-large multiple rocket launcher and a range of drones developed under Kim’s rule.
Kim opened the museum a day after North Korea test-fired what KCNA described as a tactical ballistic missile, which state media said brought “an important change” in improving all of the country’s weapons systems. Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi condemned the launch. The museum opening also came as U.S. President Donald Trump said he might meet Kim during a planned trip to Asia in mid-November.

Aysu Bicer
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
The UK has urged Interpol to reject Argentina’s requests for the arrest of individuals involved in a major offshore oil project near the Falkland Islands, known in Argentina as the Islas Malvinas, warning that the moves could be politically motivated, according to a report by The Guardian.
British officials sent a letter to Interpol’s headquarters in Lyon, France, calling for caution in handling Argentine requests for detentions, including those targeting British nationals involved in the Sea Lion oil project.
The development comes amid rising tensions over the sovereignty of the British overseas territory, with UK officials describing Argentina’s actions as the most serious since the 1982 war.
The Sea Lion project, located in the North Falkland Basin in the South Atlantic, could triple the islands’ gross domestic product (GDP).
Argentine President Javier Milei has vowed to block the project, while his government has initiated criminal proceedings against Israeli company Navitas and its British partner, Rockhopper Exploration.
The UK government is concerned that Argentina is seeking to intimidate individuals and companies involved in the project and discourage future investment, according to the report.
Andrea Clausen, chief executive of the Falkland Islands government, confirmed that Argentina’s use of Interpol posed a threat.
“One would hope that Interpol wouldn’t necessarily take action,” she told The Guardian.
She added: “Certainly those of us who have an interest have had a look at certain sections of Interpol’s constitution to see what we think it could mean.”
Interpol reportedly responded to the UK’s letter by reaffirming its commitment to Article 3 of its constitution, which prohibits intervention or activities of a political character.
Red notices are requests to locate and provisionally arrest individuals pending extradition. Interpol screens such requests, but member countries independently decide whether to act on them.
UK officials remain concerned that Argentina could persuade member states that its requests are based on domestic law rather than political motives.
Argentina continues to claim sovereignty over the Falkland Islands, where 99.8% of residents voted to remain a British territory in a 2013 referendum.
The 1982 conflict lasted 74 days and killed 649 Argentine military personnel, 255 British military personnel and three islanders.

Why has search of Ilhan Omar’s home before US midterms caused controversy?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
14:41:11 UTC
23:41:11 KST

Why has search of Ilhan Omar’s home before US midterms caused controversy?
Federal agents searched Omar’s home in what she described as an attempt to ‘weaponise federal law enforcement’.
United States federal agents have searched the Washington, DC home of Democratic Congresswoman Ilhan Omar, a Muslim and a prominent critic of President Donald Trump, as part of an investigation that one source said was linked to alleged immigration fraud.
The predawn raid on Monday came three weeks before the US midterm elections on November 3, in which Omar is seeking a fifth term representing Minnesota’s 5th congressional district.
Omar called the raid an attempt to “weaponise federal law enforcement”, while top Democrats said the timing raised “serious questions”.
So why has the search caused such alarm? Here’s what we know:
What happened?
Agents from Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), part of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), executed what the US Department of Justice called a “judicially authorised search warrant”.
The department said only that it was part of “an ongoing federal investigation”.
The street around Omar’s home was blocked off on Monday morning, and agents were seen removing boxes labelled “Seized Property Evidence”.
Hours later, Trump told reporters he had “nothing to do” with the search, saying it was “really up to the DOJ [Justice Department]”.
What is Omar under investigation for?
Officially, it is unclear.
However, a person described as familiar with the investigation told the Reuters news agency that it relates to alleged immigration fraud, and that part of it concerns paperwork filled out by Omar’s late father when she was a child.
Omar fled Somalia’s civil war with her family when she was aged eight.
According to her House biography, the family spent four years in a refugee camp in Kenya before moving to the United States in the 1990s. She became a citizen in 2000.
Conservative websites have for years alleged that she “married her brother” to commit immigration fraud, claims Omar has dismissed as “disgusting lies”.
US Vice President JD Vance said in March, without offering evidence, that the administration believed Omar “definitely committed immigration fraud”. Her office called the claim fabricated and defamatory.
Last month, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told conservative podcaster Benny Johnson that “something’s going to happen” in the case.
“If we can prove that you shouldn’t have been here in the first place, we’ll deport you,” he said.
Why is the raid’s timing controversial?
Justice Department policy usually avoids taking any action whose timing would appear to affect an election or benefit a candidate or party. In practice, therefore, the department has historically avoided overt investigative steps against candidates within about 60 days of a vote.
Randall Eliason, a law professor at George Washington University and former federal public corruption prosecutor, said the raid appeared to break with that practice, though there is no way to enforce the policy.
“The idea is to avoid even the appearance of any kind of interference by the Department of Justice with the political process,” he said.
The norm’s most famous test came in 2016. On October 28, 11 days before the presidential election, then-FBI Director James Comey told Congress that the bureau was examining newly discovered emails linked to its investigation into Hillary Clinton’s private email server.
Clinton has blamed this, in part, for her defeat. A 2018 review by the Justice Department’s inspector general found Comey’s conduct “extraordinary and insubordinate”.
Electorally, little appears to hang on the outcome. Omar represents a very safe Democratic seat covering Minneapolis, which she won in 2024 by 50 percentage points.
On November 3, she faces Republican Dalia al-Aqidi, an Iraq-born former journalist who has called Omar “pro-Hamas”, in a rematch of the 2024 race.
The search fits a wider pattern, however. During Trump’s second term, the Justice Department has charged several of his perceived political enemies, including Comey himself, New York Attorney General Letitia James and former National Security Adviser John Bolton.
What has Omar said?
She claims she is being targeted as one of Trump’s “political enemies”.
“For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns,” she wrote on X. “This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced.”
Omar has previously described Trump’s focus on her as an “unhealthy and creepy obsession”, and says she and her family have received death threats that she blames on his rhetoric.
In early December last year, Trump took aim at the Somali community in Minnesota and called Somali immigrants “garbage“. “We’re going to go the wrong way if we keep taking in garbage into our country. Ilhan Omar is garbage. She’s garbage. Her friends are garbage.”
In January, a man sprayed her with vinegar at a town hall in Minneapolis. Anthony James Kazmierczak, who admitted attacking her because he disagreed with her progressive views, was sentenced last month to 14 months in prison.
Trump, meanwhile, returned to Omar’s origins at a rally in Youngstown, Ohio, on Monday this week.
“She comes from one of the worst countries anywhere on the planet,” he said, as the crowd chanted: “Deport.”
What are Democrats and other critics saying?
That the raid on Omar’s home is an abuse of power.
House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, joined by Representatives Katherine Clark and Pete Aguilar, called the raid “deeply disturbing”.
Trump’s “mass deportation machine has descended upon the home of a duly elected Member of Congress and her family”, they said, promising to “deliver full accountability”.
Minnesota Governor Tim Walz said Trump was “abusing his power to go after political opponents weeks before an election”.
Few Republicans have commented publicly. One who did, Representative Nancy Mace, wrote that if fraud was proven, Omar “should be denaturalised and removed from this country”.
Questions have also been raised about internal checks. A person familiar with the investigation told Reuters the department consulted its Public Integrity Section, which has historically approved investigations of members of Congress, before the search.
The Trump administration has cut the Public Integrity Section to about two lawyers as part of the sweeping government cuts he introduced after taking office in January 2025. Before that, the unit had 35 to 40 full-time lawyers.

Qatar faces 42% revenue drop as war on Iran hits gas exports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
14:39:50 UTC
23:39:50 KST

Qatar’s government revenues fell 42 percent in the first half of 2026 as the US-Israel war on Iran disrupted gas exports and damaged key energy infrastructure, Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani has said.
Addressing the annual session of the Shura Council in Doha on Tuesday, the emir said the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and damage to energy facilities in Ras Laffan Industrial City had disrupted a significant share of the country’s exports.
“It is only natural that the crisis would have a negative impact on public finances, as the total revenues declined by 42 percent during the first half of the year,” he said.
Qatar, the world’s second-largest liquefied natural gas (LNG) exporter after the United States, has been among the Gulf countries hardest hit by the conflict.
Iranian strikes badly damaged the Ras Laffan site, while restrictions on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz — the sole maritime route for Qatar’s LNG shipments — have further constrained exports.
North Field expansion continues despite disruption
Despite the setbacks, Qatar’s long-term plans to expand its gas production capacity remain on schedule, the emir said.
“Work on the expansion of the North Field Gas project is progressing according to the set plans,” Sheikh Tamim told the council.
The expansion of North Field, the world’s largest natural gas field, aims to raise Qatar’s total production capacity to 142 million tonnes of LNG annually by 2030. The field extends beneath the Gulf into Iranian territory.
The emir also reported significant progress on the Golden Pass LNG project in the United States, which Qatar is developing in partnership with ExxonMobil.
The projects are central to Qatar’s strategy to strengthen its position in global gas markets despite the immediate impact of the conflict on exports and public finances.
IMF forecasts sharp contraction in Qatar’s economy
The economic outlook remains challenging. On Tuesday, the International Monetary Fund forecast that Qatar’s gross domestic product would contract by 15.6 percent this year in its latest global economic report.
The revenue decline highlights the vulnerability of Qatar’s public finances to disruptions in energy production and exports, which underpin the country’s economy.
While the continuation of major expansion projects offers a longer-term prospect for growth, the pace of recovery will depend in part on the security of energy infrastructure and the reopening of shipping routes through the Strait of Hormuz.

Namibia's capital targets disaster resilience by 2030: mayor
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
22:39:48 CST
23:39:48 KST

WINDHOEK, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Windhoek aims to strengthen disaster resilience by 2030 as rapid urbanization heightens risks from floods, severe weather and house fires, Mayor Sakarias Uunona said Tuesday.
Speaking at the International Day for Disaster Risk Reduction in Namibia's capital city, Uunona said about one-third of Windhoek's population lives in informal housing, often in environmentally vulnerable areas exposed to natural hazards.
According to the 2023 Population and Housing Census, Windhoek had 486,186 residents, with an annual population growth rate of 3.3 percent. The mayor said the city's population is now expected to exceed 500,000.
Uunona said the city launched its Disaster Risk Reduction Strategy and Action Plan for 2026-2030 in June, setting a goal of becoming a sustainable and disaster-resilient urban center by the end of the decade.
The strategy focuses on improving disaster risk assessment and urban planning, strengthening coordination among municipal departments, investing in community resilience, improving disaster information systems and enhancing preparedness and early warning mechanisms.
The city also plans to establish a dedicated disaster risk reduction fund and explore partnerships with the private sector on risk-transfer and insurance products to strengthen its capacity to manage disasters.
Speaking at the same event, United Nations Resident Coordinator in Namibia Hopolang Phororo warned that the country could experience below-normal rainfall and above-average temperatures during the 2026/2027 rainy season as El Nino conditions intensify.
Phororo said the conditions could affect agriculture, water availability, food security and livelihoods, calling for early warnings to be translated into timely preparedness measures.
She added that the United Nations system in Namibia had helped mobilize more than 28 million U.S. dollars for climate and environmental priorities over the past year and provided drought-response assistance to more than 167,000 people.
The event was held under the theme "Resilience Starts at Home," emphasizing the role of households and communities in reducing disaster risks. ■

Formula 1 to return to Africa with 10-year deal in Rwanda
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
22:39:46 CST
23:39:46 KST

KIGALI, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Formula 1 will return to Africa for the first time in the coming years since 1993, after it was confirmed Tuesday that Rwanda will host races from the early 2030s under a 10-year agreement.
Rwandan President Paul Kagame announced the deal for the Formula 1 African Grand Prix at an event in Kigali, Rwanda's capital, attended by senior F1 officials.
"Today belongs to Africa. For more than three decades, the world's premier motorsport championship has raced without this continent, and that changes with this agreement," Kagame said.
He added that Rwanda is proud to host the African Grand Prix, and to share the "moment with more than 100 million fans across Africa, many of them young people who deserve to see the sport at home and to see themselves in it: as engineers, technicians, entrepreneurs and, one day, drivers."
The long-term agreement will see the first race in the country take place once a new purpose-built circuit in eastern Rwanda's Bugesera District has been completed.
The circuit is expected to be completed early in the next decade.
Kagame said the partnership is also an investment in Rwanda's future as the circuit in Bugesera will bring jobs, skills, tourism and new business to the country and region for decades.
In a statement, Formula 1 said the agreement marks a defining moment in F1's history.
"Today is a landmark moment for Formula 1," Stefano Domenicali, Chief Executive Officer of F1, said.
"With Rwanda joining the calendar from the next decade, our sport will race in every inhabited continent, bringing the World Championship closer than ever to fans around the globe," he added.
Africa first hosted an F1 World Championship race in 1958, when Morocco staged the season finale at the Ain-Diab circuit in Casablanca.
South Africa subsequently became the continent's main F1 venue, hosting its first World Championship race in 1962 at East London. The event remained there until 1965 before moving to Kyalami, near Johannesburg, in 1967.
The South African Grand Prix continued at Kyalami during the apartheid era, although the race was dropped from the calendar after 1985 amid growing international opposition to the country's system of racial segregation.
F1 returned to Kyalami for two races in 1992 and 1993 as South Africa transitioned away from apartheid, but the championship has not raced anywhere on the continent since.
In recent years, South Africa has sought to bring F1 back, with proposals involving both Kyalami and a potential street circuit in Cape Town, though a deal is yet to materialize. ■

German inflation confirmed at 3.3 pct in September, highest since 2023
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
22:39:33 CST
23:39:33 KST

BERLIN, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Germany's inflation rate was confirmed at 3.3 percent in September, its highest level in nearly three years, as surging energy prices continued to push up consumer costs, final data from the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis) showed Tuesday.
The reading, unchanged from a preliminary estimate released late last month, marked a further increase from 2.9 percent in August and 2.8 percent in July.
Energy prices jumped 14.9 percent year-on-year in September, accelerating from a 10.5-percent rise in August and marking their sharpest increase since February 2023, according to Destatis. Fuel prices surged 37.1 percent, while heating oil prices soared 74.9 percent.
"Once again, the development of energy prices was responsible for the increase in the inflation rate," said Ruth Brand, president of Destatis, noting that the sharpest increases were seen in fuel and heating oil prices.
To ease the pressure from soaring fuel prices, the German government introduced a fresh round of temporary fuel tax cuts on Oct. 1, aimed at reducing petrol and diesel prices by around 17 euro cents (0.19 U.S. dollars) per liter through the end of the year. The measure is expected to provide around 2.5 billion euros (2.8 billion U.S. dollars) in tax relief.
The latest move followed a similar tax cut in May and June, introduced after the outbreak of the conflict in the Middle East sent fuel prices soaring and intensified inflationary pressures in Europe's largest economy.
However, a recent analysis by the Munich-based ifo Institute found that the new tax relief had only been partially passed on to consumers. During the first five days of October, filling stations passed on an average of 15 cents per liter for diesel, compared with the 17-cent tax cut, according to the institute.
The institute also cautioned that the benefits of the tax cut were unevenly distributed, offering limited relief to low-income households and those who drive less, even as these groups continued to face high energy costs. ■

Interview: FAO chief economist calls for global cooperation on food security
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
22:39:33 CST
23:39:33 KST

ROME, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Rising prices, rather than food shortages, pose the biggest risk to global food security at present, a United Nations (UN) expert told Xinhua in a recent interview.
Speaking ahead of the World Food Forum, chief economist at the UN's Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), Maximo Torero, called for better coordination and innovation in order to make agrifood systems more resilient to shocks.
Food prices now carry a "risk premium," Torero said, rising not because food is scarce but because markets fear shortages in the future.
Disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, a route used for up to 30 percent of internationally traded fertilizers; renewed restrictions on Black Sea grain shipments; and a 90 percent chance of a strong El Nino are all adding to the risks, he said.
The pressure is already showing. The FAO Food Price Index, a benchmark of international food commodity prices, averaged 136.0 points in September, up 1.5 percent from August and 5.8 percent from a year earlier.
Torero said the situation is more complex than in 2022, when other exporters quickly made up for lost Ukrainian grain. Supplies of 25 to 30 percent of agricultural inputs are now restricted, and new fertilizer capacity takes five to 10 years to build.
Farmers are applying less urea, which could cut future yields, and switching from wheat and maize crops to soybeans. With freight costs rising and shipping through the Panama Canal and the Red Sea also restricted, "we're moving into a world of 'just in case'," he said.
Nevertheless, global cereal stocks remain ample, Torero said, with the FAO forecasting a stocks-to-use ratio of 31.7 percent for the 2026/27 season. The most pressing problem is affordability, with net food-importing countries in Africa, some in Asia, and small developing island states to be hit first.
Since it takes three to six months for commodity prices to reach retail shelves, consumers will feel the impact from the end of this year. The world is not yet in a food crisis, but the situation is slowly deteriorating, Torero warned.
He underlined that China, the world's largest food producer and consumer and a major importer, has been preparing for both natural and geopolitical risks by diversifying imports, keeping its market open and improving stock management.
China's urea exports are helping to bring down prices, he noted, expressing hope that this will continue and urging major producers and importers not to distort markets or restrict exports of farm inputs.
To strengthen resilience, Torero called for closer coordination among development banks, financial institutions and donors. He also urged greater investment in fertilizer alternatives such as green ammonia, more efficient fertilizer use, renewable energy for agriculture and better forecasting.
His view echoes the theme of the 2026 World Food Forum, "Innovate Today. Nourish Tomorrow." Its flagship event, currently being held at FAO headquarters in Rome from Oct. 8 to 16, brings together youth, scientists and investors, with 38 countries presenting investment opportunities.
The agrifood system has weathered repeated shocks in recent years, but "there is a limit to resilience," Torero underlined. While El Nino cannot be avoided, conflicts can, and "right now, we have to watch every risk," he said. ■

JUBA, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- South Sudan on Tuesday launched a three-day national workshop to establish a multi-agency platform to combat hate speech and disinformation, a key effort to strengthen conflict prevention and social cohesion.

Over the three-day workshop, participants will work to define institutional roles, strengthen links between early-warning mechanisms and preventive action, build a shared understanding of narrative threats, and foster national ownership of the new platform. ■

Japan's education minister apologizes for holding fundraising parties in violation of rules
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
22:39:28 CST
23:39:28 KST

TOKYO, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Japan's education minister Yoshihiro Seki admitted at a press conference on Tuesday that a ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) branch he heads had held political fundraising events within parliamentary office facilities in breach of the rules, and he apologized for the violations, local media reported.
The move came after Japanese newspaper Shimbun Akahata recently reported that the LDP's Hyogo 3rd electoral district branch, headed by Seki, had held political fundraising parties inside the members' office building of the House of Representatives in 2020 and 2024.
The lower house prohibits unapproved commercial activities and fundraising parties within the building complex under its internal regulations.
After reviewing the branch's political funds reports, Shimbun Akahata found that Seki's branch had held a fundraising event in the office building in December 2020, generating 2.44 million yen (around 15,400 U.S. dollars) in revenue, while expenses, including venue setup costs, totaled only about 46,000 yen.
In June 2024, the branch held a similar event in Seki's own office in the building, bringing in 810,000 yen while spending only about 82,000 yen on food, drinks and other items.
The newspaper noted that Diet members can use meeting rooms in the office buildings free of charge, which significantly reduces the cost of holding such events.
Hiroshi Kamiwaki, a professor at Japan's Kobe Gakuin University, said political fundraising parties are "effectively equivalent to political donations."
He noted that the disclosure threshold for buyers of political fundraising party tickets is higher than that for direct political donations, making it easier for ticket buyers to conceal their identities. "This is an egregious fundraising practice that exploits loopholes in the system," he said.
At the press conference on Tuesday, Seki said he had previously "not been sufficiently familiar with the relevant rules."
Seki joined the cabinet for the first time last month, when Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi reshuffled her cabinet, taking the post of minister of education, culture, sports, science and technology. He had previously been disciplined by the LDP over a high-profile political slush fund scandal, and his appointment made him one of the first disciplined lawmakers to enter the cabinet since the scandal came to light in late 2023. ■

ADDIS ABABA, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Ethiopia is taking concrete steps to cut greenhouse gas emissions by more than 70 percent by 2035, aiming to address the adverse effects of frequent extreme weather events that threaten livelihoods, the country's Minister of Water and Energy Habtamu Itefa has said.
The minister made the remarks on Monday while addressing the 65th plenary session of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), which is underway in the Ethiopian capital, Addis Ababa.
"Ethiopia has committed to a highly ambitious 70.3 percent reduction in greenhouse gas emissions by 2035," Itefa told the IPCC, a United Nations body responsible for assessing the science related to climate change.
Faced with mounting environmental challenges, the East African country is currently implementing coordinated initiatives to achieve its ambitious climate action target, primarily through renewable energy expansion, large-scale tree planting, and landscape restoration, he noted.
"Ethiopia is living on the frontlines of the global climate crisis. Irrespective of natural variations, anthropogenic climate change has severely disrupted our natural balance," Itefa said. "We are increasingly subjected to shifting and shortening rainy seasons, which bring both devastating floods and landslides, as well as frequent, extensive droughts."
He noted that Ethiopia is currently "aggressively expanding" its renewable energy matrix by harnessing hydro, wind, and solar power, while also extending the clean energy grid to neighboring countries to support Africa's transition to green energy.
Itefa also highlighted the country's flagship Green Legacy Initiative for significantly expanding forest cover and restoring degraded landscapes by enabling the planting of more than 66 billion tree seedlings nationwide since its inception in 2019, ultimately increasing the national forest cover from 17.2 percent to 23.6 percent. ■

Economic Watch: Global investors turn to "China Buffer" amid heightened uncertainty
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
22:39:07 CST
23:39:07 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- While surging government bond yields in several major economies raise risks to financial stability, China's market is becoming increasingly attractive to investors seeking to diversify amid heightened uncertainty.
Analysts said in a world where volatility has become the baseline, China offers what could be described as a "China Buffer," which is a combination of macroeconomic stability, industrial strength and huge potential that is increasingly hard to find elsewhere.
RISING APPEAL
Many active long-only funds globally have shifted their average China equity allocation from "underweight" to "benchmark neutral," ending four years of underweight positioning. Citigroup has moved further, upgrading Chinese equities to "overweight." Goldman Sachs, meanwhile, views Chinese assets as an attractive source of portfolio diversification.
The trend also extended to the bond market. Foreign institutions bought around 1.6 billion yuan of Chinese treasury bonds in August, marking the fourth consecutive month of increases, bringing their total holdings to nearly 2.03 trillion yuan (301.64 billion U.S. dollars), official data showed. Policy bank bonds also saw modest buying of roughly 600 million yuan.
The rise in foreign allocations to Chinese assets reflects a growing recognition among global investors of the resilience and dynamism underlying China's economy.
Official data showed the economy continued its steady, quality-oriented trajectory in the first eight months of 2026, with new growth drivers playing an increasingly supportive role. Value-added output of high-tech manufacturing rose 16.7 percent year on year in August, while investment in high-tech industries grew 5.2 percent in the January-August period.
Despite a turbulent and uncertain external environment, China's economy has maintained stable performance with strengthening new growth drivers, said Fu Linghui, a spokesperson of the National Bureau of Statistics, noting the country serves as an important growth pole and stabilizing anchor for global development.
Analysts believe that China's economy undergoing a sustained innovation-driven transition offers long-term structural opportunities in AI, advanced manufacturing and green energy.
Jason Hsu, founder and CIO of Hong Kong-based quantitative asset manager Rayliant Global Advisors, said overseas investors are shifting their focus from China's internet platforms and e-commerce to semiconductors, AI, robotics, advanced manufacturing, new-energy supply chains and automation.
China's growing importance in these sectors could drive a long-term re-rating of its capital markets, as investors seeking exposure to the next decade's technological advances would find it increasingly difficult to overlook China, he said.
Echoing Hsu's words, Eric Lin, head of APAC Research, UBS, said many overseas investors have recognized that China's AI supply chain is becoming an indispensable part of global technology investment portfolios, and some foreign capital is increasing its exposure with real money.
STABILITY AND OPENING UP
More importantly, analysts said Chinese assets are gaining appeal as stability becomes increasingly scarce in an uncertain world.
China is offering the world "security and certainty," underpinned by energy security, resilient supply chains, differences in macroeconomic policy cycles and ample foreign exchange reserves, as well as steady positive returns, attractive dividends and more predictable growth, noted Zhang Jundong, a macroeconomic analyst at China International Capital Corporation.
"Buying China means buying safety," said Liu Yuhui, a seasoned economist, noting that the integrity of China's supply chains and the stability of its vast market are becoming an anchor amid global turbulence.
China's continued opening up is reinforcing this trend.
The China Securities Regulatory Commission recently reiterated its commitment to further expanding high-standard financial opening up, improving cross-border investment and financing convenience, and optimizing the qualified foreign institutional investor regime and stock connect mechanisms.
Notably, issuance of panda bonds and dim sum bonds combined surpassed 1 trillion yuan in the first eight months of the year. "The expansion of cross-border bond varieties sends a clear signal of China's institutional opening up to international markets and is an important pillar supporting the rising global allocation value of renminbi assets," said Pang Ming, a researcher with the China Chief Economist Forum.
International investors' journey into China's capital markets is only just beginning, said Bonnie Chan, chief executive officer of Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Limited, adding that whether in equities or bonds, the room for holdings to grow will be enormous. ■

Interview: Cooperation with China helps Kenya advance vocational training: official
China

NAIROBI, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Cooperation with China is helping Kenya accelerate Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) reforms and build the skilled workforce its industrialization needs, Kenya's Cabinet Secretary for Education Julius Migos Ogamba has said.
Kenya aims to deepen its TVET cooperation with China further, Ogamba told Xinhua in a recent interview. The two countries have cooperated in the sector for years, with Chinese-supplied equipment now installed in most Kenyan TVET institutions, he said.
The cooperation goes beyond equipment supply to include technology transfer, he said, noting that after equipment is delivered, China provides targeted operation training for Kenyan technicians.
China has also partnered with some Kenyan institutions to build model centers for training, production and innovation, opening opportunities for students from other institutions to join exchange programs and work with Chinese technology, Ogamba said.
With that support, Kenya is now producing more graduates with professional skills, he said, adding that the government is committed to continuing the partnership "because it has borne fruit."
Drawing on the first three phases, Kenya has discussed a possible fourth phase of cooperation with China, hoping to widen coverage and standardize the equipment, Ogamba said.
TVET is now central to Kenya's industrialization, which cannot be achieved without workers who combine professional knowledge, technical skills and practical ability, Ogamba said. Kenya does not need to start from scratch, but can draw on China's experience and existing technologies to move faster, he added.
"In fact, I know that China has, for example, scrapped some programs that are not market-needed," he said.
Kenya must study what skills the market requires, adjust its curricula accordingly and build a more flexible system, he said.
With the rise of artificial intelligence and other advances, some equipment could become obsolete quickly and costly to replace, making it important to work with China and other countries to raise TVET standards at an affordable cost, according to Ogamba.
Ogamba said some Kenyans still regard TVET as "a second-rate program that people go to because they've not made it to the university."
"We want to remove that stigma, and let people undertake it by choice," he said.
Ogamba said he looked forward to the World Vocational and Technical Education Development Conference in Tianjin, China, as a chance to share experience with other countries and learn from those with mature systems, adding that the current period is vital for deepening and expanding TVET cooperation with China. ■

Hezbollah 'upgrading capabilities' for next war with Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
14:38:35 UTC
23:38:35 KST

Breadcrumb
Hezbollah 'upgrades weapons capabilities' ahead of potential renewed war with Israel
An alleged Hezbollah weapons shipment seized by Lebanese authorities last week has raised questions over the type of explosives the group is using to develop its arsenal, amid reports that it is preparing for another round of war with Israel.
Citing security and military sources, Lebanon’s French-language daily L’Orient-Le Jour reported that Hezbollah is working to rebuild its military capabilities, which have been significantly diminished by three years of conflict with Israel.
The sources said the group had used the relative calm of recent months to restore its military presence and capabilities in southern Lebanon, despite ongoing Israeli attacks and demolition of infrastructure.
Other sources close to Hezbollah have linked its reorganisation efforts to the recent interception of an explosives-laden vehicle. On 8 October, Lebanese police seized a truck carrying more than 500kg of military explosives, including TNT and C-4, along the central Dahr al-Baidar highway.
Two men who are in custody reportedly confessed to belonging to Hezbollah and said they were travelling from Baalbek in eastern Lebanon to Beirut’s southern suburbs, two traditional strongholds of the group that have been heavily targeted by Israeli strikes.
The Lebanese government has pledged to disarm all militias in the country, insisting that the state must have a monopoly on all arms and decisions on war. However, its efforts to rein in Hezbollah and disarm the group have so far failed.
According to sources cited by L’Orient-Le Jour, Hezbollah uses TNT and C-4 to develop fibre-optic-guided first-person-view (FPV) drones capable of carrying between four and six kilograms of explosives, up from around 2.5kg previously.
The sources also said the group had extended the fibre-optic cables connecting the drones to their operators from 20km to more than 30km, allowing them to target Israeli positions at greater distances.
The drones are reportedly being fitted with powerful explosives, as well as nails and steel ball bearings, to maximise casualties among Israeli forces. Hezbollah has already used such weapons against Israeli military drones in southern Lebanon, the report said.
Hezbollah has neither confirmed nor denied that the seized explosives belonged to the group. Hezbollah's political opponents have cited the presence of C-4 to accuse it of plotting political assassinations.
Moving further north of the Litani
Alongside efforts to replenish its reduced arsenal, Hezbollah has reportedly regrouped and maintained forces in areas near the so-called Yellow Line, Israel’s buffer zone in southern Lebanon, where dozens of towns and villages have been razed.
As Israel has expanded its occupation, particularly south of the Litani River, it has destroyed several forts that housed tunnels and underground complexes used by Hezbollah for decades.
Sources close to Hezbollah cited by L’Orient-Le Jour said the group had sought to strengthen its presence and capabilities north of the Litani around Nabatieh, Iqlim al-Tuffah and Rihan.
These areas are strategically important because of their elevated terrain and their proximity to routes connecting southern Lebanon with the Beqaa Valley, another Hezbollah stronghold. Israel is reportedly seeking to consolidate its control over the south and disrupt Hezbollah’s links with the Beqaa, parts of which are considered strongholds of the group.
The areas contain some of the south’s most strategically important hills, as well as sites housing central operations rooms that Hezbollah has reportedly been developing since before the 2006 war with Israel.
The report also said the underground facility known as Imad 4, which Hezbollah showcased in footage released in 2024, is believed to be located in the area.
Hezbollah is also reportedly preparing for further possible Israeli assassinations of its leaders and commanders. According to the sources, the group has drawn up plans to evacuate accommodation used by senior figures, particularly in Beirut’s southern suburbs.
Much of Hezbollah’s senior command structure has been eliminated, while thousands of its fighters are believed to have been killed over the past three years.
The conflict between Hezbollah and Israel began in October 2023 and was dramatically escalated by Israel into a full-scale war in September 2024. Fighting resumed on 2 March this year, alongside the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Reports have increasingly suggested that the wider confrontation with Iran could resume after the Israeli elections and US midterm elections, both expected within the next three weeks. Such an escalation could also reignite fighting on other regional fronts, including Lebanon.

'We've found missing head of 11th century Khajuraho Vishnu idol, will be restored soon': ASI chief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
14:38:13 UTC
23:38:13 KST

Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) has found the missing head of an 11th-century Vishnu idol at Khajuraho, whose restoration became the subject of a recent controversy involving the Supreme Court, and plans to reattach it after expert examination.ASI has also introduced a three-year deadline for archaeological excavations to curb delays in research and cut approval times for most conservation projects to 15-20 days, director general Yadubir Singh Rawat told TOI in an exclusive interview. He also revealed plans for a preliminary excavation at Ujjain's Vaishya Tekri, where a Buddhist stupa could be larger than Sanchi's, although its actual scale and significance remain to be established.Controversy over the beheaded Vishnu idol at Khajuraho's Javari temple reached the Supreme Court last year when advocate Rakesh Dalal sought restoration, replacement or reconstruction of the seven-foot statue.While dismissing the petition, then CJI BR Gavai had remarked, “Go and ask the deity itself to do something now.”Though Gavai later clarified his remark in court and said he respects all religions and that his statement was taken out of context, his words drew criticism, and a lawyer subsequently attempted to throw a shoe at him inside the courtroom.
Rawat said the missing head had been found in an ASI store. “During a visit to Bhopal for the BRICS summit, I learnt that the statue's head—which had been kept in our store—had been found. The person in charge informed me that someone likely tried to break off the head to steal it but failed to do so. We are having experts examine it and will soon reattach it to the statue.”On delays in archaeological research, Rawat said ASI had introduced a three-year timeframe for completing excavation projects, with permissions continuing automatically across financial years. He acknowledged that some researchers showed enthusiasm during fieldwork but delayed finalising reports, holding up publication of findings.ASI had also granted circle officers financial powers ranging from Rs 50 lakh to Rs 1 crore, reducing the need for approvals from HQ. Rawat said most annual conservation programmes now received clearance within 15-20 days, except those requiring expert consultation.At Vaishya Tekri in Ujjain, a recent survey identified a cluster of Buddhist stupas and a water reservoir. Rawat said the structures differed from Sanchi because they were built using unbaked bricks. The last excavation there took place in 1973.ASI plans to begin with a limited vertical excavation to establish the site's significance before committing to a larger project estimated to cost Rs 60 crore. “The true picture will only emerge after excavation. We will proceed only after confirming its significance, although the site already falls within a protected area,” Rawat said.He said acquiring and excavating the entire site would require substantial resources, making preliminary investigation necessary to determine whether a full-scale project was justified.On encroachments at protected monuments, Rawat questioned the continued reliance on a colonial-era list prepared under the Ancient Monuments Preservation Act of 1904.“The root of this problem lies in the list prepared by British rulers in 1904 under the ‘Ancient Monuments Preservation Act’—a list that the then-central govt adopted post-independence without any review. The British had included cemeteries and graves of their obscure soldiers, horses, mules, and pets—which they deemed highly significant—among the monuments protected by the ASI. Before adopting that list, a review should have been conducted to determine what was truly important in the national interest,” he said.Rawat said a review in 1953 incorporated state monuments into a definitive list, but the central list remained unchanged. The resulting difficulties eventually led to 17 monuments being removed from it.Explaining disparities in funding, he said allocations depended on visitor numbers, maintenance requirements, security expenses and public facilities. Taj Mahal and Red Fort, he said, served as showcases for ASI, while Taj Mahal's maintenance required substantial expenditure because of its delicate structure and heavy tourist footfall. ASI paid around Rs 3 crore monthly for more than 200 CISF personnel deployed there.Rawat acknowledged that lesser-known monuments, including the pyramid-like Bhim ki Gada structure in Bareilly, had received inadequate attention. He said ASI circles had been instructed to prepare conservation and tourism development proposals for such sites.On skeletal remains excavated at Rakhigarhi in Haryana, Rawat said ASI had signed an MoU with Anthropological Survey of India and Birbal Sahni Institute of Palaeosciences. ASI would lead the project, while the two institutes would examine the remains to determine physical characteristics, age, diet, diseases, sex and other details. A one-year deadline had been set for submitting the report.For Uttarakhand, Rawat outlined plans to trace the historic walking route from Rishikesh to Badrinath and Kedarnath along the left bank of Alaknanda river.
He said references in Gita Press archives pointed to several temples and traditional halting places used by local and tribal communities that had not been adequately documented. Ancient markers or surviving remains could provide information about travel and settlement patterns.“There is also a need to trace the ‘Swargarohana Path’ taken by the Pandavas to Kedarnath, as described in the Mahabharata. It is my personal wish that this project be pursued with full dedication and in ‘mission mode’ by the concerned circle,” he said.
