North Khorasan, the province I almost missed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
14:37:18 UTC
23:37:18 KST

North Khorasan, the province I almost missed
TEHRAN - A friend’s suggestion was all it took to set me on the road to North Khorasan, one of the few Iranian provinces I had never visited and, until then, had rarely considered as a travel destination.
We set out to explore the province over three days, keeping costs low and relying on local guides and the knowledge of people familiar with the region. What followed was a journey through mountain strongholds, traditional homestays, Turkmen hospitality, living musical traditions, local festivals and a secluded valley where a man had spent years building a world of his own. By the end, I had discovered how easily a place can remain off one’s travel map until the moment one finally gives it a chance.
A train to the edge of the desert
We boarded the train from Tehran around midday, heading towards Jajarm, one of the southernmost cities of North Khorasan province. We would not be getting off in the city itself, however, but at Jajarm railway station, roughly 30 kilometers away. From there, our tightly scheduled exploration of the province would begin.
By the time we arrived, it was around 8 p.m. The long train ride had carried us away from the bustle of the capital and towards a landscape where the desert and mountains seemed to set a different pace for life.
Our first night’s accommodation was a modest traditional homestay near the railway line, tucked behind a small pistachio orchard. Built largely of mud brick and earth, the property consisted of perhaps six or seven rooms. It was not the sort of place that would appear in a glossy hotel brochure. That, as I would discover, was part of its appeal.
Our hosts, a middle-aged couple known affectionately as Uncle Ghorban and Aunt Zeynab, welcomed us with a warmth that made the long journey feel worthwhile.
Dinner was a traditional meal accompanied by local music. There were no polished dining tables or carefully staged decorations. Instead, the setting had the unpretentious charm of a family home where visitors were treated less like customers than guests.
We ate, listened to music and gradually settled into the rhythm of a place that seemed far removed from the hurried world we had left behind.
The accommodation was basic. We slept on simple mattresses laid on the floor, and nothing about the rooms could be described as luxurious. The walls were made of earth, the surroundings were quiet, and above us stretched a night sky scattered with stars.
I began to understand that comfort does not always come from the things we buy or the services we expect. Sometimes it comes from the absence of things that have come to dominate our daily lives: traffic, noise, constant notifications, crowded schedules and the persistent feeling that we should always be doing something.
The following morning brought some of the most memorable moments of the entire trip. Aunt Zeynab had prepared two kinds of local bread. One was plain, while the other was enriched with aromatic herbs, sesame seeds and black seeds.
The smell of freshly baked bread filled the space, making it difficult to think about anything else.
There was also strained yoghurt that had been stored in a sheep’s skin, along with fresh eggs and vegetables from the family’s own garden.
Then came the butter.
Our hosts used a simple traditional arrangement involving a sheep’s skin and wooden poles to make butter from milk. The process was a reminder of how everyday necessities were once produced through household labor and local knowledge, long before industrial food production made such tasks almost invisible to urban consumers.
Nothing was presented as an attraction. These were simply the things our hosts did, and had perhaps done for much of their lives. Yet for us, they offered a glimpse into a way of living that is becoming increasingly unfamiliar to people in large cities. Under that simple roof, I felt an unusual sense of calm.
Before leaving, we thanked Uncle Ghorban and Aunt Zeynab for their hospitality. It was a brief encounter, but it left a lasting impression.
Through the mountains of Raz and Jargalan
After breakfast, we set off towards the northern part of the province. Our destination was Raz and Jargalan, a district close to the border with Turkmenistan, where mountains, valleys and remote settlements preserve traces of a past that is not always easy to read from the landscape.
The drive took around four hours. It was a long journey, but the scenery gave us plenty of reasons to look away from the road and towards the surrounding countryside.
Among the most striking sights were ancient juniper trees, some of which were said to be hundreds of years old, with some estimated to be as much as 2,000 years old. Their twisted trunks and weathered branches seemed to embody the endurance of life in a landscape shaped by harsh weather and the passage of time.
North Khorasan has many such reminders of time’s passage, although visitors who hurry towards more famous destinations may never encounter them.
The region’s historical attractions were no less compelling.
At one point, we came across a large defensive structure perched high on a mountain. Our guide explained that it had served as a refuge during periods of invasion. When danger approached, people could retreat to the elevated stronghold and pull up the ladders used to reach it, making access difficult for attackers.
The location was striking, but the first question that came to my mind was not how the structure had been built. It was how people had managed to reach it.
Imagine a community suddenly threatened by an invading force. Families would have to abandon their homes, gather whatever possessions they could carry and make their way up a steep mountain path. Children, elderly people and those carrying food or other necessities would all have to negotiate the same difficult ascent.
Then, once inside, they would have to wait, uncertain about what was happening below and whether they would ever return to their homes.
The defensive advantages of such a place become obvious when viewed from a distance. But imagining the people who depended on it makes the history far more immediate.
A little farther along our route, we encountered another remarkable sight: a series of man-made caves cut into a mountainside, arranged in three levels.
According to our local guide, the lowest level had been used to keep animals, while the upper levels served other purposes associated with refuge and shelter.
Iran’s history is often presented through the grandeur of its palaces, mosques, monumental tombs and celebrated ancient cities. Yet the country’s past also survives in less conspicuous places: a refuge on a mountain, a room cut into rock, a mud-brick house or a path worn smooth by generations of footsteps.
These are places where history is not always written in inscriptions. Sometimes it is recorded in the landscape itself.
The mountain refuges also brought to mind the long history of insecurity experienced by communities across this part of Asia. Trade routes connected distant regions, but those same routes could bring armies, raiders and political upheaval. For people living in exposed settlements, the ability to seek shelter was not an abstract architectural concern. It could determine whether a family survived.
We eventually left that mountains behind and continued towards a different kind of encounter, one that would reveal another dimension of North Khorasan’s character.
A Turkmen welcome, with an unexpected pizza
By midday, we had reached a traditional accommodation run by a Turkmen couple and their two sons.
The atmosphere was different from that of our previous night’s homestay, but the same spirit of hospitality was immediately apparent.
Our hosts wore traditional Turkmen clothing and distinctive hats. Their appearance, manner and surroundings offered a glimpse of a cultural identity that has been preserved across generations in this borderland region.
North Khorasan is home to a diverse population, including Kurdish Kurmanji speakers, Turkmens, Persians and Turkic-speaking communities. The province’s cultural richness is not simply a matter of different ethnic groups living within the same administrative boundaries. It is visible in its music, languages, food, handicrafts, clothing and everyday social customs.
Here, cultural identities have developed through centuries of coexistence, exchange and adaptation.
Turkmen communities, in particular, have maintained distinctive traditions in carpet weaving, textiles, music and horsemanship, while their cuisine reflects both local resources and wider cultural connections across Central Asia.
Lunch at the guesthouse brought some of those culinary traditions to the table. The food combined Iranian and Turkmen influences, giving us an opportunity to sample flavors that felt familiar in some respects and different in others.
Then came the surprise: a pizza that our hosts described as their own creation. It was delicious.
I had not expected to encounter a distinctive house pizza in a traditional guesthouse near the border with Turkmenistan. Yet that small detail seemed to capture something important about the character of the place. Cultural traditions do not necessarily survive by remaining frozen in time. They often continue through the ability to absorb new influences while retaining a recognizable identity.
Once again, the welcome was informal and sincere. We were travelling on a limited budget, and our hosts made us feel that this was no obstacle to receiving generous hospitality.
After lunch, we headed towards a reservoir behind a dam for a short boat ride. The water offered a welcome change after hours of mountain roads and dry landscapes. The surrounding hills formed a quiet backdrop, and for a while we could simply enjoy the view without having to think about the next destination.
Before long, we were back on the road, leaving Raz and Jargalan behind and heading towards Shirvan.
After approximately three hours on the road, we reached Shirvan, where one of the most memorable encounters of the journey was waiting for us.
Our first stop was a traditional dutar workshop run by master instrument-maker Khosrow Haddad and his sons.
The dutar is a long-necked, two-stringed lute found in Iran and across Central Asia. Its name comes from the Persian words do, meaning two, and tar, meaning string.
Although the instrument looks relatively simple, its cultural significance is considerable. In parts of northeastern Iran, particularly among Kurdish and Turkmen communities, the dutar is closely associated with the musical traditions of the Bakhshi, performers who have historically carried songs, stories, poetry and local memory from one generation to the next.
A dutar is not merely a musical instrument. In the hands of a skilled performer, it can become a means of preserving a community’s sense of itself.
The workshop was also a shop where instruments were displayed and sold. Yet it felt much more like a place devoted to a lifelong passion than a commercial enterprise.
Master Haddad had spent more than five decades making dutars and teaching others to play them. His students shared his enthusiasm, and the atmosphere suggested that the craft was being sustained not only through technical instruction but also through personal commitment.
Master Haddad and his students took turns performing several local pieces, first individually and then together. The music filled the workshop, turning an ordinary room into a space where the outside world seemed to recede.
The sound was distinctive: sometimes gentle and reflective, sometimes energetic and rhythmic. The musicians’ movements were unforced, and their concentration was evident. They did not seem to be performing merely to entertain a group of visitors. They were sharing something they knew intimately and cared deeply about.
As the music continued, conversation gave way to listening.
In this workshop, the dutar seemed to connect the present with a much longer cultural past. The instrument’s two strings carried melodies shaped by local experience, while the musicians’ knowledge ensured that the tradition remained alive.
The performers were known as Bakhshis, a title associated with traditional musicians and storytellers in parts of northeastern Iran and Central Asia. Their role has historically extended beyond entertainment. Depending on the local tradition, a Bakhshi may preserve epic narratives, recount historical events, perform poetry and transmit the songs through which a community remembers its past.
We had planned to make a relatively short visit. But the evening continued, one performance leading to another, and the prospect of leaving became increasingly unappealing.
It was close to midnight when we finally departed.
That night, I realized that some of the most valuable places in a destination may be workshops like this one, where cultural heritage is not simply preserved behind glass but practiced, discussed and passed on.
We went to another traditional guesthouse late that night, tired from the journey but reluctant to let the experience fade.
The next morning, we were back on the road.
Farhangestan-e Kanimal: A lifetime collected under one roof
The following day’s itinerary included a private collection known as Farhangestan-e Kanimal, a two-storey building filled with objects that offered a different perspective on the province’s history.
The collection had been assembled by its elderly owner, a man of about 90 who had devoted considerable effort to bringing together materials from different periods of Iran’s past.
The ground floor contained books, historical documents, newspapers and magazines. Their range suggested an interest extending well beyond a single subject or period. The collection offered a glimpse into the changing ways Iranians had recorded events, circulated ideas and understood the world around them.
Upstairs, the focus shifted from the written record to the material culture of rural and nomadic life. There were objects associated with traditional households, village work and pastoral communities. Together, they evoked a way of life in which many everyday tasks depended on practical knowledge, locally available materials and tools that were often made to serve more than one purpose.
What made the visit especially rewarding was hearing the collection’s owner talk about it.
The owner guided us through the collection, sharing his knowledge and memories. At his age, he had witnessed an extraordinary span of social change, even if not every object in the museum belonged to his own lifetime.
The contrast between the two floors was especially striking. Downstairs, newspapers and documents recorded public events, political developments and changing ideas. Upstairs, household objects revealed the quieter history of how people lived.
Both are necessary to understand the past.
In a province such as North Khorasan, where rural and nomadic traditions have helped shape local identity, preserving these objects is particularly valuable.
Farhangestan-e Kanimal left me with a warm impression precisely because it was so personal. It was not simply a display assembled to attract visitors. It reflected the sustained curiosity of an individual who had spent much of his life gathering pieces of the past.
Beside the private museum was an apple orchard. With the owner’s permission, I picked two apples directly from the trees and ate them.
They were exceptionally crisp and fragrant, with a freshness and flavor that seemed entirely different from the apples I usually bought in Tehran.
I later learned that North Khorasan is known for its apple production. The province’s agricultural diversity is one of the less celebrated aspects of its identity, alongside its cultural heritage and natural attractions.
Wrestling, apples and the festive spirit of Shirvan
After lunch at a cozy traditional restaurant, we headed to a local event featuring koshti ba chokheh, a form of traditional wrestling associated with the Khorasan region.
The atmosphere was lively. People had gathered to watch the matches, and the event offered a glimpse into a sporting tradition that has long occupied a special place in the region’s social life.
Koshti ba chokheh is generally associated with local celebrations and communal gatherings, including Nowruz festivities and, historically, weddings. It has also been an important setting for demonstrating strength, skill and the qualities expected of a pahlavan, or champion.
The sport is rooted in a wider culture of wrestling across Iran, where physical strength has traditionally been linked to ideas of courage, honor, generosity and community standing.
In Khorasan, the local form has developed its own identity, with characteristic clothing, techniques and customs.
The wrestling event was also a reminder that cultural heritage is not confined to architecture, museums and handicrafts. It can be embodied in movement, physical skill, competition and collective emotion.
A short distance away, another celebration was taking place: the Shirvan Apple Festival.
The event featured apples and a range of apple-based products, including apple vinegar. Modest stalls displayed local produce, offering visitors an opportunity to see the agricultural side of the province’s identity.
The festival was particularly interesting because it brought together two different dimensions of local life. On one side was a traditional sport rooted in community gatherings. On the other was an agricultural celebration centered on a crop associated with the region.
Both were expressions of local identity, but in different ways.
In a stall that was in fact a vast tribal tent, some women were preparing different kinds of bread, and the sight of them working around the ovens gave the festival a warm, informal atmosphere.
At the festival, the women were not just selling food. They were demonstrating a skill and sharing something of the cultural world from which it came.
I bought several pieces, thinking that they would be a pleasant reminder of the journey when I returned home.
By then, North Khorasan had already offered us much more than I had expected: mountain history, living musical traditions, an elderly collector’s personal museum, exceptionally fresh apples and a traditional sporting event.
Yet the most extraordinary experience of the trip was still ahead.
The hidden valley of Estarkhi
It was early in the evening that we left the apple festival and continued towards Esfarayen.
It was during this drive that we reached the historical Estarkhi village, where I encountered a bizarre house that would become one of the defining memories of the journey.
To reach it, we first had to walk for about ten minutes down a dirt track on a steep slope. The path was quite narrow and, as far as I can remember, there was a precipice alongside it. By the time we arrived in the area, however, it was already dark. Still, we felt it would be a shame to leave without seeing the house.
After about ten minutes of walking downhill, we reached a small river, whose flowing water stood out in the silence of the night. We then followed an uphill dirt path for another two or three minutes before finally reaching the house.
The owner, a man named Ali, warmly welcomed us. He was middle-aged, with long, graying hair and a long gray beard. After serving us tea, he showed us the different parts of the house, which he had built with his own hands over many years, with very little in the way of resources.
The owner had created the place brick by brick, drawing on the materials and possibilities of his surroundings. The complex offered views of the wooded valley and mountains, while the nearby river and waterfall gave it a setting that felt almost separate from the outside world.
There were also treehouse-style rooms built around the sturdy trunks and branches of two walnut trees said to be about a century old.
I spent some time talking to the owner.
He explained that, during a period when he had very little money, he had gradually carved into the rocks using a pickaxe and a sieve, working slowly over the years to shape the site.
His account suggested a long process of trial, labor and patience rather than a project completed according to a conventional timetable.
What struck me most, however, was not only the physical work he had undertaken. It was the way he spoke.
He talked quietly, without any apparent need to impress his visitors. There was a remarkable calmness in his face and manner, and it seemed to extend into every sentence.
I had met many people during my years of travelling and reporting, but his presence affected me in a way I found difficult to explain.
Perhaps it was the contrast between the stillness of the valley and the relentless pace of Tehran. Or perhaps it was the sight of someone who had devoted years to creating a place according to his own vision, without rushing towards a quick result.
In an age when projects are often measured by how quickly they can be completed and how soon they can generate a return, there was something unusual about encountering a place that appeared to have grown at the pace of its maker.
I imagined him working through different seasons, returning to the same rocks, gradually changing the contours of the site and finding ways to make the buildings fit the terrain.
Such a project requires more than technical ability. It demands persistence, a willingness to live with uncertainty and a clear enough idea of the desired result to keep working when progress is slow.
The luxury of having nowhere to hurry
The longer I remained there, the more I thought about the meaning of travel.
There was something deeply appealing about the idea of staying in the historical village of Estarkhi to see its other gems and spending a morning without checking the time.
We eventually had to leave. The journey was not over yet. We still had to reach Esfarayen before midnight to spend the night.
One last night in Esfarayen
After leaving Estarkhi, we continued to Esfarayen, where we spent the night in another traditional guesthouse.
By then, the pace of the trip had begun to catch up with us. We had covered long distances, visited a wide variety of places and met people whose stories had added unexpected depth to the journey.
Our accommodation was modest, in keeping with the spirit of the trip. We were not looking for luxury, and the simple guesthouses had allowed us to experience something closer to local life than we might have encountered in standard hotels.
The next morning, we rose early and headed back towards Jajarm to catch our train to Tehran.
There was one important place we had hoped to visit but could not fit into the schedule: the historic city of Belqeys.
I was disappointed not to see Belqeys, but the omission also gave me a reason to return.
For a traveler, an unfinished itinerary is not always a failure. Sometimes it is an invitation.
The train arrived at Jajarm station about half an hour late.
As we waited and then settled into our seats for the return journey, I began to think about everything that had happened over the previous three days.
The trip had started with a simple suggestion from a friend. I had accepted because North Khorasan was a province I had never visited, without expecting that the experience would leave such a strong impression.

Guilfoyle quits Greece post amid latest allegations of improper profiting by Trump associates

Guilfoyle quits Greece post amid latest allegations of improper profiting by Trump associates
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Reports have accused Guilfoyle of offering access to Trump administration figures in exchange for help paying a $100,000 credit card bill, which she denies.
- The allegations come amid a much larger swirl of claims that Trump, his family and others in his orbit are improperly profiting off their positions.
Kimberly Guilfoyle resigned her post as ambassador to Greece on Tuesday, after being asked to do so by President Trump amid a wave of misconduct allegations she has denied.
Guilfoyle, a former Trump campaign surrogate and onetime fiancee of Donald Trump Jr., faced allegations including an offer to use her influence in Trump’s orbit in exchange for payments, according to the Wall Street Journal — adding her to a growing number of Trump administration officials, family members and employees who have been accused of improperly monetizing their ties to the president or his government.
That list includes Trump and his sons, who have been criticized for making billions through investments in industries that are regulated by the administration — including in cryptocurrency and drone interceptors — and for trying to sell early access to Trump’s posts on his social media platform. Trump Jr. has also faced criticism for having his lavish Bahamas wedding paid for in part by a Russian oligarch close to President Vladimir Putin.
The business ventures of Jared Kushner, the president’s son-in-law and one of the administration’s top negotiators in the Middle East, have also raised questions, as Kushner has been tied to Russian oil negotiations amid talks on how to end the war with Ukraine and reportedly tried to raise money for his private firm from governments in the Middle East.
Meanwhile, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and his son Brandon Lutnick, now chair of the financial services firm Cantor Fitzgerald, have been questioned over the firm buying up rights to refunds from Trump’s dismantled tariff scheme. Howard Lutnick, who previously served as Cantor Fitzgerald’s chairman, championed Trump’s tariffs.
In a statement posted to social media, Guilfoyle said she will “forever be grateful” to Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio for trusting her to represent the U.S. abroad, remains “unwavering” in her support for them and “worked tirelessly to advance President Trump’s America First agenda, strengthen our strategic alliance with Greece, and deliver meaningful victories for the American people.”
Guilfoyle, 56, who was once engaged to Donald Trump Jr., presented her diplomatic credentials to Greek President Constantine Tassoulas after being sworn in Sept. 29 in Washington.
The allegations against her are false, she said, and she won’t allow them to define her “decades of public service” and intends to “vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity.”
The Wall Street Journal reported last week that Guilfoyle messaged a Trump donor asking for $100,000 to pay off a credit card bill in exchange for access to administration officials, and for it to be sent in a way that wouldn’t leave a paper trail. “It won’t show up anywhere if you wire money to American Express,” she allegedly wrote to the donor via the encrypted Signal messaging app.
The Journal has also reported that Guilfoyle promoted a Greek construction and energy company and gave its lobbyists access to a private diplomatic meeting; told guests at a reception that the U.S. could undermine the Greek government if it wanted to do so; and boasted about luxury travel with energy company executives. The British tabloid the Daily Mail reported that Guilfoyle had alienated staff with questionable behavior.
The State Department’s inspector general is looking into the allegations, according to an unnamed U.S. official who spoke with the Associated Press. And top Democrats — including Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Long Beach), the ranking member on the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform — have called for investigations.
Guilfoyle’s resignation comes a day after Trump said that officials were looking into the claims and were “not happy.”
Guilfoyle’s unusual rise
Guilfoyle’s resignation caps an unusual, decades-long run in the public spotlight that has captivated many, particularly in California, where she was formerly married to Gov. Gavin Newsom.
Born to a Puerto Rican mother and Irish father, Guilfoyle was brought up working-class in San Francisco. She attended UC Davis and the University of San Francisco Law School, and then served as a prosecutor in San Francisco and Los Angeles. She was introduced to Newsom — a likely Democratic contender for president in 2028 — by Newsom’s father, and moved back to the Bay Area, where she resumed working as a prosecutor.
Guilfoyle and Newsom wed in 2001. He became San Francisco mayor in 2004, and the couple began attracting attention in Democratic circles, with Harper’s Bazaar dubbing them “the new Kennedys.” Guilfoyle at the time espoused many mainstream Democratic political beliefs.
She later moved to New York for a broadcast job with Court TV. When she and Newsom divorced in 2006, they cited the strain of the bicoastal relationship. She went on to become a Fox News commentator, before being forced out amid accusations of sexual impropriety, according to the New Yorker and other outlets.
She started dating Trump Jr. in 2018. And by the time the 2020 presidential campaign rolled around, she was serving as Trump’s campaign finance chair and gave a Republican National Convention speech in which she bashed California as a liberal wasteland.
Guilfoyle was again a prominent surrogate for Trump during the 2024 campaign, and the president nominated her to serve as ambassador to Greece just a month after his election, amid rumors of a split between her and his son. At the time he called her “a close friend and ally” for many years with “extensive experience and leadership in law, media, and politics” and a “sharp intellect.”
Other profits questioned
Democrats, who are seeking to retake control of the House in the Nov. 3 election, have started laying the groundwork to make the Trump family’s business dealings a centerpiece of their investigations into alleged corruption next year. They say examples abound.
In May, Trump Jr. married Bettina Anderson in a Bahamas ceremony that ProPublica reported was heavily funded — to the tune of hundreds of thousands of dollars — by a Russian oligarch with close ties to Putin named Umar Kremlev, who also attended the wedding despite Trump Jr. describing the guest list as “really small.” After the scandal broke, Kremlev said that Trump Jr. had repaid him for the wedding expenses. Democrats launched an investigation.
Guilfoyle, a San Francisco native, was previously married to California Gov. Gavin Newsom.
Democrats have also demanded documents from Cantor Fitzgerald to assess its buying up tariff refunds and the Lutnicks’ role in that venture. “The American people deserve to know whether Administration insiders and their closest family members deliberately positioned themselves to profit from these blatantly illegal tariffs while everyone else paid the price,” Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), the ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee, wrote in a February letter to the Lutnicks.
They and the firm have denied any impropriety.
Democrats have also criticized Trump’s new deals to license his name overseas, campaign ads paid for by taxpayers, acceptance of a plane from Qatar to serve as Air Force One, and efforts to create a fund for payouts to Jan. 6 insurrectionists and other political supporters.
In a July speech calling out those and other deals, Sen. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) noted that Trump’s most recent financial disclosure forms showed he had made at least $2.2 billion in income the preceding year — which Schiff noted was 3½ what Trump reported earning the year prior. “So, either he’s just become a much better businessman since he became president, or he is corruptly using his office to enrich himself. The same can be said for much of the rest of his family,” Schiff said.
Trump’s income included about $1.4 billion from his family’s cryptocurrency businesses, records show, much of which was earned through World Liberty Financial, a crypto firm whose backers have clear interests in Washington. Trump has defended his business decisions while in office as perfectly legitimate.

Russia builds giant bomber shelters at Engels air base
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
14:32:25 UTC
23:32:25 KST

- Satellite imagery shows Russia nearly finishing frames for the first three of 16 large aircraft shelters at Engels-2 bomber base.
- Each shelter measures about 63 by 63 meters, large enough to cover Tu-160 and Tu-95MS strategic bombers.
Russia has nearly finished the steel frames for the first three of 16 large aircraft shelters it is building at Engels-2, the main base for its strategic bomber fleet, satellite imagery published by open-source analysis group AviVector shows.
An Airbus Defence and Space image dated Oct. 12 shows three side-by-side shelter frames standing on new concrete pads at the base in Russia’s Saratov region, each linked to the airfield by a freshly paved taxiway. AviVector first spotted ground being broken in early September, reporting in a Sept. 6 post, based on imagery taken on Sept. 5, that work had started on the first of 16 planned shelters.
Each shelter measures roughly 63 by 63 meters (207 by 207 feet), with 7-meter (23-foot) side walls and a peak height of about 17 meters (56 feet), according to AviVector’s estimates. That footprint is large enough to cover a Tu-160 supersonic bomber, which is about 54 meters long with a wingspan of nearly 56 meters when its wings are fully spread, as well as the smaller Tu-95MS turboprop bomber. Behind the frames, workers have built earth berms that deflect jet blast upward when aircraft run their engines, a sign the shelters are meant for aircraft to start up and taxi from directly.
Engels-2 sits about 600 km (370 miles) from the front line in Ukraine and is home to the bulk of Russia’s long-range bombers, which fire cruise missiles at Ukrainian cities from inside Russian airspace. Ukraine has repeatedly sent long-range drones against the base since December 2022, hitting fuel and ammunition storage and, in the past few months, parked aircraft. In July, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the SBU had destroyed a Tu-95 at Engels, and a satellite image taken days later appeared to show the wrecked bomber. A second Tu-95 was damaged in an SBU Alpha drone strike on the base on Aug. 28.
Until now, Russia’s bombers at Engels have been parked in the open, where commercial satellites can photograph them and drones can find them. Covered shelters would hide which aircraft are present and give them some protection against drone warheads and debris, and Russian crews have also painted outlines of Tu-95 bombers on the tarmac at Engels to confuse drone operators and imagery analysts. Russia can no longer build new Tu-95s, so every airframe lost to a strike permanently shrinks its long-range fleet.
The structures visible in the imagery are steel frames that have yet to be clad, and it is not yet clear what materials will be used for their walls and roofs. AviVector has not given a timeline for completing all 16 shelters, and the Russian Ministry of Defense has not commented on the construction.

Hurricane Simon weakened to Category 1 off Mexico's Pacific coast on Tuesday, as authorities warned of continued heavy rainfall, strong winds and dangerous waves in western states.
The National Civil Protection Coordination (CNPC) reported the weakening in a post on US social media company X, urging residents in affected areas to remain alert as hazardous weather conditions persist.
Simon had maximum sustained winds of 150 kilometers per hour (93 miles per hour), with gusts reaching 185 kph, according to authorities.
The hurricane's center was located off the Pacific coast of Mexico, west of Cabo Corrientes in Jalisco and south-southwest of Mazatlan in Sinaloa.
Authorities warned that the storm could continue to generate heavy rainfall, strong winds and high waves along parts of Mexico's western coastline, despite its downgrade in intensity.
The National Meteorological Service (SMN) forecast heavy to very heavy rainfall in western Mexico, including areas of Jalisco, Nayarit, Colima and Sinaloa, raising concerns about possible flooding and landslides.
Jalisco, located along Mexico's central Pacific coast, and neighboring Colima could experience hazardous coastal conditions, while Nayarit, north of Jalisco, could also be affected by the storm's rain bands.
Sinaloa, further north along the Pacific coast, remained under close monitoring as Simon continued a northwestward trajectory.
The weakening does not necessarily mean the threat has ended, as heavy rainfall and dangerous waves can persist even after a hurricane loses intensity.
Simon strengthened earlier in its development, prompting authorities to monitor its trajectory and warn communities along Mexico's Pacific coast.
Authorities continue to track the hurricane as it moves over the Pacific, with its future path and the extent of its effects depending on changes in its intensity and movement.
Residents were advised to follow guidance from civil protection officials and remain alert to warnings as weather conditions evolve.

What the US PERM Freeze Really Costs India’s IT Industry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
14:19:00 UTC
23:19:00 KST

On October 8, 2026, the U.S. Department of Labor decided to stop processing PERM labor-certification requests from eight technology firms, including Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL Technologies, and Capgemini. The Department of Labor said it would neither accept new applications nor process pending applications involving the named companies.
PERM, or Program Electronic Review Management, is the initial step in the employment-based green card process for most immigrants applying under the EB-2 and EB-3 categories. In order to proceed to the next stage, employers are required to prove that they have tried to hire Americans for the jobs in question.
The processing of the applications has been suspended in accordance with 20 CFR § 656.31(b), which allows for the temporary interruption of services if there are grounds to believe that fraud or willful misrepresentation is involved.
Vice President J.D. Vance accused companies that employ people on H-1B visas of creating a caste of foreign indentured servants. Notwithstanding the administration’s justification, allegations must not be confused with provided proof of fraudulent activity.
On the heels of the H-1B controversy came reports of investigations into the J-1 visa program, involving dozens of American universities. In the context of Vance’s comments on H-1B visas and intensified scrutiny of J-1, the latest development suggest that the debate over the United States’ immigration policy and the prospects of its labor market will continue to gain momentum. This would, in the meantime, systematically erode India’s IT service sector’s integrative loop with American companies and vice versa.
The H-1B-to-green-card process has three basic stages: entering the United States, living there as a worker, and eventually receiving permanent residency. Each of these possesses its own restrictions.
Indian nationals comprise a significant part of successful H-1B applicants. A U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services’ FY2024 H-1B characteristics report said that Indians comprised 71 percent of successful applicants in 2024.
The H-1B has become an IT program. Infotech workers made up 32 percent of H-1B holders in fiscal year 2003 and averaged over 65 percent across the last five fiscal years. H-1B status permits temporary employment, subject to immigration rules and the conditions of the petition. Workers may continue working lawfully while their green card applications are delayed, provided their existing authorization remains valid.
PERM falls under the third step, which concerns the transition from being a temporary resident to receiving permanent residency. The suspension interrupts a stage of the process for affected applications, potentially delaying workers’ transition to permanent residency. Its consequences depend on the status of each application.
Given a massive backlog, the PERM suspension impacts individual workers. But its immediate relevance for corporate profits is limited.
The Cato Institute estimated the U.S. employment-based waiting list to contain approximately 1.8 million people in 2023, around 1.1 million of whom are Indians. This puts the portion of Indians in the queue at around 68 percent. The report estimated the time necessary to clear the backlog for Indian applicants to be up to 134 years, with approximately 424,000 Indians expected to die before obtaining a visa.
This might have more of an impact than it seems. Permanent residency is a significant factor in the worker’s life, affecting their decision-making and planning. Another obstacle in their employment-based residency application might disrupt their lives severely.
Even before the PERM suspension, the U.S. immigration system was becoming more expensive and unpredictable. The Trump administration announced a $100,000 H-1B fine announced in September 2025. That was later clarified by USCIS to be applicable only to petitions made after September 21, 2025, as a one-time payment rather than an annual renewal.
Employers are adjusting their strategies accordingly. An RBI survey tracked an erosion in on-site revenues, from $19 billion to $18.4 billion. These are wages paid to staff members who work at client facilities overseas. The reduction implies that the traditional approach of sending numerous Indian professionals to work overseas is being de-emphasized relative to other approaches to technology services delivery.
Nasscom data revealed that Indian IT revenue totaled $315 billion in FY2025-26, up 6.1 percent, with exports of $246 billion, up 5.6 percent. The industry employed some 5.95 million workers and created about 135,000 net jobs in the past fiscal year. An American client can continue to buy software development, consulting, maintenance, and other tech services from an Indian team without requiring those professionals to be based inside the United States.
A restriction on permanent residency might well impose genuine costs on workers while having limited impact on the revenue-generating capabilities of their employers. The impact will vary from company to company, project to project, and staffing model to staffing model, but the market’s response to the policy change need not reflect the impact on individual workers’ circumstances.
For Indian IT companies, the PERM freeze may prove a small financial blow rather than a major threat to their business model. Most of their American revenue streams do not rely on having every employee on their payroll based in the U.S., and the fall in on-site earnings suggests an industry growing more capable of providing services beyond borders.
For Indian professionals, the implications are more personal. A green card process that already takes years to complete has just become even more unpredictable for those considering applying, and for whose employers are affected. Even if their American jobs are unaffected, their plans for permanent residency may be set back.
For India, the long-term impact is harder to assess. Restrictions on immigration may motivate multinational companies to invest more in local infrastructure, creating jobs and cementing India’s role as a center for tech production. But it would also shift work away from Indian outsourcing firms and toward the captive centers of their American clients.
The short-term financial pain may be minimal. The anxiety for those affected, however, is far greater. And the longer-term challenge will be whether the U.S. can prevent a rush to move work to where it will have value, by closing access to where it currently does.
This moment also marks a troubling low-threshold point in India-U.S. relations, almost causing an irreparable harm to the long diplomatic relationship between the two countries. First, tariffs on Indian imports, and now restrictions on skilled human capital mobility from India to U.S. companies could erode and dismantle core areas of economic integration between the two countries, which were cementing a strong political bond as well.
Where this leaves India and its economic integration strategy viz-a-viz the U.S. (amidst a more conflicted relationship with China) should trouble policymakers more than it seems to do in the current scenario.

Pentagon awards $8.3M for 10-minute blood clotting test
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
14:18:25 UTC
23:18:25 KST

- DARPA awarded Abram Scientific up to $8.3 million to develop CoagCare, a handheld clotting test that delivers results in under 10 minutes.
- The work supports DARPA’s RAPIID program, which aims to field an FDA-authorized shelf-stable blood substitute kit as early as fiscal 2029.
DARPA, the Pentagon’s research agency, has awarded Abram Scientific a contract worth up to $8.3 million to develop CoagCare, a handheld device that shows how well a wounded person’s blood is clotting in under 10 minutes from a single drop, so medics can decide on transfusions far from a hospital.
The Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency funds high-risk technology for the U.S. Department of War, and over the past few years it has put a growing share of its medical work into one problem: keeping badly wounded troops alive until they reach surgery. Abram Scientific, based in Menlo Park, California, announced the award on Oct. 13, a year after DARPA gave it $2 million in October 2025 to shrink the device to a size that can travel with medics.
Uncontrolled bleeding is one of the leading causes of preventable death after severe injury, on the battlefield and in civilian emergencies, and the best treatment is whole blood given as soon as possible. Donated blood has to be kept refrigerated and expires within weeks, which makes it hard to stock at small outposts, aboard ships or with units that may wait days for evacuation in a large war. Military medics often fall back on “walking blood banks,” drawing fresh blood from fellow soldiers on the spot, but that only works when donors are close by and screened.
DARPA is trying to solve that with a program called RAPIID, short for Resuscitation and Prevention of Ischemia-Induced Dysfunction, launched in May. The 36-month effort aims to turn lab-made blood components, such as oxygen-carrying substitutes and dried plasma, into a shelf-stable kit medics can carry, with the goal of FDA authorization as early as fiscal 2029. It builds on an earlier DARPA program, FSHARP, in which a team led by the University of Maryland, Baltimore showed that synthetic parts could perform key functions of whole blood. RAPIID also needs fast bedside tests, because a medic has to know what a casualty’s blood is doing before deciding which substitute to give and how much.
CoagCare is meant to be that test. It pairs a compact meter with a single-use card and measures how thick and dense a drop of blood becomes as it clots, tracking the process from the moment a clot forms until it breaks down. Hospital machines that do the same job, known as thromboelastography and thromboelastometry, can take 30 to 60 minutes per test and need laboratory conditions, while CoagCare is designed to work despite the vibration inside ambulances and MEDEVAC helicopters.
“Rapid access to actionable coagulation information can be critical for saving lives in trauma care, when every minute matters,” said Abhishek Ramkumar, founder and CEO of Abram Scientific.
Under the new contract, Abram Scientific will tune CoagCare to guide doses of the blood substitutes being developed under RAPIID and set up production lines for the meter and its test cards. The company will also design a military version for frontline use, and because the military and civilian models take the same disposable card, one factory line can serve both.
Swiss plasma products maker Octapharma led a Series A funding round in Abram Scientific in February to speed up development and help the company apply for FDA 510(k) clearance, which would allow CoagCare to be sold for managing transfusions in civilian trauma and surgery. Abram Scientific holds 17 granted patents on the technology and is working toward that FDA filing while it builds the military version for DARPA.

White House says US ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle has been asked to resign
WASHINGTON – The White House said on Oct 13 that it had asked US Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle to resign following allegations of unethical conduct.
“We have asked Ambassador Guilfoyle to resign,” White House press secretary Katie Zacharia told reporters. “She has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her well.”
Guilfoyle, whom President Donald Trump tapped as his envoy to Greece, came under scrutiny in a series of reports by The Wall Street Journal alleging she solicited or accepted money, travel and other benefits from private individuals while using, or offering to use, her access to US officials and her diplomatic position to advance their interests.
Before her confirmation as ambassador in 2025, Guilfoyle sought US$100,000 (S$128,000) from Trump donor Eric Deters while offering to use her administration contacts to help him with tax and legal matters, and urging him to avoid putting discussions about money in writing, according to the Journal.
Trump expressed his displeasure with Guilfoyle on Oct 12, responding to a reporter’s question about whether she would be fired by saying he was “not happy”.
“We’re looking at it,” the President had said.
The Journal also reported Guilfoyle accepted private travel and hospitality from Greek businessmen while promoting their commercial interests, including encouraging Balkan governments to work with a company whose chief executive had flown her to Davos.
Guilfoyle’s representatives have disputed key parts of the reporting, and her lawyer has questioned the authenticity of the messages involving Deters.
The US Embassy in Athens told the Journal she followed State Department ethics and gift reporting requirements.
Congressional Democrats have called for ethics and public corruption investigations into Guilfoyle.
NBC News reported last week that the ambassador and the embassy in Greece were under investigation by the State Department’s inspector-general, citing people familiar with the matter.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio publicly defended Guilfoyle during a trip to Greece, saying she had been “a strong ambassador”.
But after additional allegations were published before he left Athens on Oct 8, Rubio refused to address the reports and criticised journalists for treating allegations from unnamed sources as established fact as Guilfoyle stood nearby.
Trump nominated Guilfoyle in December 2024, and she was confirmed as ambassador by the Senate in September 2025. She previously was a Fox News host for more than a decade and was engaged to Donald Trump Jr.
Greece has been an important NATO ally to the US, offering key military facilities to safeguard security in the Eastern Mediterranean, and it leads a European Union maritime mission to protect commercial shipping in the Red Sea. BLOOMBERG, REUTERS

‘English nationalist’ content creators film themselves in asylum seekers’ house
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:08:24 UTC
23:08:24 KST

A Home Office accommodation provider has launched an investigation after “English nationalist” content creators posing as contractors filmed themselves entering a property housing asylum seekers.
The video, titled “HMO Hunting in Leicestershire”, was posted to the Truthhurts101UK YouTube account, which describes itself as being run by an “English nationalist citizen journalist” and claims to cover “immigration, demographic change, policing and stories others overlook”. The footage was also posted to the associated TH101UK’s X account, where is has been viewed more than 300,000 times.
The video shows three men accessing the back entrance of a house in Leicestershire accommodating asylum seekers. The men enter via an unlocked back door and move through several rooms of the house, including the kitchen, where they examine the contents of the fridge. They repeatedly claim to be looking for “paperwork”, searching through a pile of letters near the front door and boxes discarded in the back garden. The man filming, who narrates the video, claims he is the first to “document” this property.
When the men filming encounter three men, who are believed to be asylum seekers living at the property, in the kitchen they tell them they are contractors sent to assess the property for repairs. They ask one man living at the property whether the property is run by Serco, a Home Office contractor used for asylum seeker accommodation, which the man confirms, and whether he has “paperwork”, which he says he does not.
When the man living at the property asks the man filming for his ID he briefly shows him a lanyard. It is unclear what information it shows.
In the footage, the man filming specifically names the street and the village where the house is located, and shows the exterior of the property and its surroundings, making it clearly identifiable.
A Serco spokesperson said: “We are aware of this post. We take issues of this nature extremely seriously and are investigating.”
A Home Office spokesperson said: “The safety and security of those housed in asylum accommodation, staff who work there and local communities are of the upmost importance to the government. We engage extensively with contractors, local authorities and the police and expect any instances of criminality to be taken seriously.”
A TH101UK spokesperson defended the footage, accused the asylum seekers of being “ticking timebombs” and questioned why the Guardian, which they described as “irrelevant” and a “rag”, was “scrutinising independent journalism”.
They added: “Don’t worry, I’ll keep asking the questions you should be.”
In recent years, there has been an increase of self-styled “auditors”, and far-right activists have attempted to gain access to hotels and other forms of accommodation housing asylum seekers, sometimes under the guise of wanting to carry out “inspections”.
When challenged, often by private security outside hotels, some have attempted to confuse the issue by quoting supposed “common law” principles, which have been taken up by members of the far right as a legal recourse that supersedes statutory laws.
However, the increasing use of houses of multiple occupancy (HMOs) as part of the government’s plans to phase out the use of hotels to house asylum seekers has given some of these activists a new target, with some obtaining addresses from publicly available documents and sharing details with one another in online groups.
TH101UK entered another asylum seeker property in Norfolk several months ago and posted footage online.
After the Guardian brought the footage to the attention of YouTube, a spokesperson confirmed that it breached its standards, and said that it had been removed from the platform.
A YouTube spokesperson said: “Harassment and cyberbullying are not allowed on YouTube and as part of this, we do not allow content that reveals someone’s personally identifiable information. Upon review, we have removed the flagged video for violating our harassment and cyberbullying policies.”
Louise Calvey, the executive director of Asylum Matters, expressed concern about the video. She said: “This is a premeditated invasion into someone’s home for clicks and attention. The people that court this are the very worst of us, they’re the ones the pose a threat – barging into people’s homes, filming in people’s private spaces. The audacity and sense of entitlement is breathtaking.
“Government must urgently take steps to improve protections, remove the details of shared accommodation sites of all descriptions from the public domain, support people accommodated as victims of crimes, and escalate quicker police responses.”

Happiness, not awe, may be the better emotional lever for openness to diversity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:00:14 UTC
23:00:14 KST

Feeling happy might do more to open people’s minds to social diversity than experiencing a sense of awe. New research published in the International Journal of Psychology indicates that a brief burst of joy leads to more positive attitudes toward inclusion, while awe has little effect. The findings challenge the expectation that awe would outperform other positive emotions in fostering acceptance of others.
Awe is an emotional response typically triggered by perceiving something vast and extraordinary that challenges a person’s usual understanding of the world, like a starry night sky or a towering mountain range. This feeling tends to diminish attention to oneself and make people view their surroundings as interconnected and meaningful.
Because awe encourages people to feel part of something larger than themselves, researchers have wondered whether it could help foster more positive attitudes toward diversity. The research, led by Jens Agerström, a professor of psychology at Linnaeus University, set out to test whether experiencing awe could encourage greater openness toward different social groups.
“Previous research has shown that people who are exposed to awe-inducing stimuli (e.g., vast and beautiful landscapes, moon landings) are more likely to act more prosocially (e.g., help another person),” Agerström told PsyPost. “We wanted to extend the research literature by examining whether awe can also make people more diversity oriented by, for instance, expressing more positive attitudes toward ethnic minority groups.”
Prior work provided reason to think awe might bridge social divides. For instance, a 2015 study found that awe shifts attention away from the self and promotes generosity: in one experiment, adults who watched an awe-inducing nature clip gave away more raffle tickets than those who watched a happiness-inducing one. Building on this, an experiment covered by PsyPost in 2023 found that experiencing awe, rather than joy, made children more likely to donate to members of an outgroup.
Happiness served as the comparison. Like awe, it is a positive emotion that tends to broaden people’s outlook and encourage helping and cooperation, which made it a solid benchmark. But the researchers expected awe to come out ahead, because awe is more strongly tied to a sense of a smaller self and a connection to others. Happiness also has a more mixed record: a 1994 study found that happy moods can lead people to rely more heavily on social stereotypes.
To test this, the researchers recruited 3,196 adults through the online research platform Prolific. The participants, who averaged about 40 years old, were randomly assigned to one of three groups, and each group watched a 28-second video designed to evoke a specific emotional response.
The awe group viewed majestic images of the universe, vast landscapes, and the Apollo 11 moon landing accompanied by sweeping music. The happiness group watched cheerful scenes of children playing and birthday parties paired with joyful music. A third, neutral control group saw everyday images of people studying or taking a coffee break with ambient background noise.
Immediately after watching the clips, the participants completed three questionnaires assessing their orientation toward diversity. The first survey measured general attitudes toward diversity, asking respondents if they value getting to know people from different racial or cultural backgrounds. The second survey measured diversity fatigue, which captures feelings of weariness or annoyance toward societal inclusion efforts. The third survey assessed social dominance orientation, which captures how much a person believes some social groups are simply inferior to others and that inequality between groups is acceptable.
The researchers found that the awe video did not measurably change how participants answered the surveys. On all three measures, the awe group’s responses did not differ statistically from those of the neutral control group.
Happiness, on the other hand, consistently shifted responses in a more inclusive direction. The neutral group’s average diversity attitude score was about 4.6 on a 6-point scale, and the happiness group scored about 0.08 points higher. The happiness group also scored 0.10 points lower on diversity fatigue (neutral group average: about 2.1 on a 5-point scale) and 0.15 points lower on preference for group hierarchy (neutral group average: about 2.4 on a 6-point scale).
When the two emotions were compared directly, the happiness group reported more positive attitudes toward diversity than the awe group and showed a slightly lower preference for social hierarchy, a difference that fell just short of statistical significance. The two groups did not differ reliably in diversity fatigue. The results held when the researchers excluded participants who finished unusually quickly or slowly and when they accounted for age and gender.
These shifts are small, but the authors note they emerged after a 28-second video and on measures thought to be fairly stable. The researchers suggest that happiness may promote social bonding, cooperation, and concern for others, which could carry over into more welcoming attitudes, though the study did not test this explanation.
“Brief inductions of awe do not seem to make people more diversity oriented,” Agerström noted. “Somewhat unexpectedly we found that happiness, which we used as a contrasting emotion, resulted in more positive diversity-related attitudes. Perhaps most interestingly, happiness seems to reduce social dominance, an individual difference characteristic capturing preferences for inequality and discrimination.”
The team’s biggest surprise, Agerström said, was “that happiness seems to triumph over awe when it comes to diversity.”
The lack of an effect for awe is in tension with research covered by PsyPost in 2025, which found that evoking awe through science fiction increased people’s identification with all of humanity. However, that earlier study measured a broad sense of global connection rather than specific attitudes toward demographic diversity and social equality.
“The main takeaway is that even a brief experience of happiness can make people more positive toward diversity and reduce diversity fatigue and social dominance orientation. Interestingly, the researchers did not find similar effects for awe,” said Ewa Palikot of the Institute of Psychology at the Polish Academy of Sciences, who was not involved in the study. “Like the authors, I expected awe to have a positive effect on attitudes toward diversity, especially since previous research suggests that awe can make people feel more connected to others and encourage prosocial behavior.”
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The study relied on a very short video clip to spark emotion. A 28-second video can easily lift a person’s mood, but it might not be intense enough to trigger the profound, transformative sense of awe that comes from standing at the edge of the Grand Canyon. It is possible that a stronger, real-world experience of awe would yield different results.
The researchers note, however, that in a pretest with 125 people, the awe video produced about as much awe as the happiness video produced happiness, so a weaker emotional jolt does not obviously explain the difference. The main study itself did not check how participants felt after watching.
The researchers offer a few possible explanations for why awe fell short. Awe is a complex emotion, and although their awe video produced very little fear, it did produce some surprise, which the authors suggest could prompt a disorienting search for order rather than curiosity and openness. It is also possible the video did not create the “small self” feeling thought to drive awe’s social benefits, something the study did not measure.
“The size of the observed effects of happiness was small and it is important to examine whether happiness has the potential to shape diversity-oriented behavior in real-world settings,” Agerström said. “For example, can a more joyful workplace reduce prejudice?”
Palikot cautioned against generalizing the experimental findings to everyday life. “It is important to remember that these findings do not mean that happier people are necessarily more open to diversity in everyday life,” she told PsyPost. “The researchers looked at how a brief feeling of happiness affected people’s reported attitudes right after watching a video. We still don’t know how long these effects last or whether they influence people’s actual behavior.”
The participants in this study also started out with relatively low preferences for social hierarchy, which left less room for their scores to drop, although the happiness effect still emerged.
“As is always the case, findings need to be replicated before strong conclusions are drawn,” Agerström emphasized. “Also, other awe-inducing methods (than those we tested) may have the potential to increase diversity. Future research needs to look into this.”
Looking ahead, Agerström said the team’s long-term plan is “to unobtrusively study effects of awe and happiness on diversity behavior.” Unobtrusive studies observe what people actually do without making the measured behavior obvious, which can reduce the pull to give socially desirable answers.
“From a cross-cultural perspective, I would be curious to see whether happiness and awe have similar effects across cultures,” Palikot said. “Previous research shows that happiness and positive emotions are not viewed in the same way in different cultural contexts. For example, in some East Asian cultures, emotional balance is more valued, and strong positive emotions like happiness can also be associated with negative consequences. This does not necessarily mean that these emotions have different effects on social attitudes, but I think it would be interesting to explore.”
The study, “Happiness, Not Awe, Makes People More Diversity-Oriented,” was authored by Jens Agerström, Magnus Carlsson, and Towe Nilsson.

Iron Dome architect behind new counter swarm system
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:00:15 BST
23:00:15 KST

A defence technology company founded in Washington and Israel has unveiled what it describes as the world’s first native counter swarm defence system, designed from the outset to engage large numbers of drones at once instead of picking off one target at a time, according to the company.
Skapion said the system has been designed by its founding architect, General (retired) Pini Yungman, who was the architect of Iron Dome and formerly general manager of Rafael’s air and missile defence division. It is built around what the company calls a native many-to-many architecture, allowing multiple interceptors to engage multiple targets at the same time.
The company said the mobile, fully kinetic system is designed to engage more than one hundred targets simultaneously with an interception rate above 97 per cent, at a significantly lower cost per interception than conventional air defence. A vertical launch arrangement gives 360 degree coverage, and the company said it is designed for deployment from ground, airborne and maritime platforms.
Ido Bar-On, co-founder and chief executive, said: “The next generation of threats cannot be defeated by simply stacking yesterday’s air-defense solutions. A swarm is not just a larger number of discrete drones. It changes the dynamics of the engagement, the number of simultaneous decisions, the speed at which they must be made and the economies of every interception. Native Counter-Swarm means designing the entire system from day one for simultaneous mass engagement.”
Most air defence systems were developed to engage single targets or small numbers of them, which creates capacity and cost constraints against simultaneous mass attack. Skapion cited the wars in Ukraine and Iran, where it said legacy air defence is being saturated by swarms built to exhaust the defender’s magazines and budgets.
A Shahed type one-way attack drone costs tens of thousands of dollars. The interceptors fired at it can cost hundreds of thousands or more, and the magazine on any launcher is finite, so an attacker who can generate enough cheap airframes wins on arithmetic even when every shot is defeated. Bringing the cost per interception down, and the number of simultaneous engagements up, is what several companies on both sides of the Atlantic are now chasing.
At the centre of the Skapion system is an AI command and control architecture that fuses data from the company’s own sensors or from third party systems, evaluates and prioritises threats, allocates interceptors and manages engagements in real time. The company said it can run with full end-to-end autonomy or with a single human operator in the loop, depending on customer policy, and that the open, sensor-agnostic design allows integration with existing command and control and other counter-drone systems.

Documents
Details
If consultation is to be undertaken on an amendment to the regulations or the implementation of new regulation, the MAA will issue an NPA. The NPA will explain the rationale behind the amendment, the possible impact on the regulated community (developed into an impact assessment (IA)) and set the deadline for comment/feedback. Feedback is important to further develop the IA.
Comments or enquiries on any NPA are to be sent to DSA-MAA-MRPEnquiries@mod.gov.uk by the date stated in the NPA. Please use the NPA Response Form template provided below to return your consolidated comments.
After the comments closure date, the NPA will be removed from the website.
NPA comment response sheets contain the collated MAA responses to individual NPA publications.
In the final preparation for publication similar Regulated Community comments have been consolidated into one response.
Some of the MAA responses to the Regulated Community comments may have been superseded by further internal review prior to the official publication of the new issue.

US singer alleges foreign funding for India’s ‘Cockroach’ movement
US donors opposed to Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi are funding the country’s youth-led ‘Cockroach’ protest movement, American singer Mary Millben has alleged, calling for a peaceful counter-movement. Her remarks come as two leaders of the group were jailed for five days following a protest in New Delhi.
Unnamed American donors are financing Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke and his movement, Millben claimed in a X post on Wednesday. She said such donors follow a pattern of recruiting US-educated activists to challenge conservative leaders in their home countries.
Dipke earlier rejected foreign-funding allegations, saying CJP organizers and friends pool money to finance protests.
The American singer performed India’s national anthem at an Indian diaspora event attended by Modi in Washington, DC, in June 2023, during his state visit to the US.
Millben backed Modi, saying the Indian prime minister would not yield to disruptive forces from the US. She did not identify the alleged donors, or provide evidence of any financial transfers.
To all the beautiful young patriots in India: This is not the time to be silent. @abhijeet_dipke and the @Cockroachisback are being funded by donors in the U.S. who are against Prime Minister @NarendraModi and your future under his leadership. Do not fear, my young patriots. Your Prime Minister, who has served India for 25 years, 12 years as Prime Minister, elected three consecutive terms, is not going to bow to disruptive forces from my country. And these select donors have a pattern globally - target conservative global leaders, find an U.S. educated person from the country, radicalize them, send them back to the country, and fund them to start chaos and destruction. None of them have been successful but have impacted the development and governance of the country. It is time for a new voice in #India, born, raised, educated on the soil of India, to RISE UP, organize, and peacefully protest the disruptive spirit of the Cockroach Party. There should always be a counter movement to uphold democracy and freedom. Rise up, young patriots! Rise up!
— Mary Millben (@MaryMillben) October 14, 2026
The Indian capital saw massive protests last week, spearheaded by the opposition despite police locking down the city. They were demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over a nationwide electoral-roll revision that has removed more than 130 million names since last year, including those recorded as deceased, relocated, or untraceable.
The ruling Bharatiya Janata Party has also accused CJP leaders and opposition politicians of attempting to destabilize India at the direction of foreign powers.
“This is not the time to be silent,” Millben wrote, urging young Indians to organize peaceful demonstrations against the CJP. “There should always be a counter movement to uphold democracy and freedom.”
CJP spokesperson Saurav Das and co-convener Ashutosh Ranka were sentenced to five days of judicial custody on Wednesday after joining protesters who climbed barricades to enter Jantar Mantar, a historic site in central Delhi, which the police had denotified as an approved protest venue.
The two were detained for allegedly violating undertakings to maintain public order that they had given following their detention last weekend.
The CJP emerged from a viral satirical post responding to remarks by India’s chief justice comparing unemployed youth to “cockroaches.” The movement has since organized protests over education, employment, and the alleged irregularities in voter lists.

In Bulgaria, unidentified individuals set fire to 11 of the 17 Starlink antennas providing communications to Ukraine, an MP says
Kyiv • UNN
Near Sofia, unidentified individuals set fire to 11 of the 17 Starlink antennas. The Bulgarian authorities said that an intensive investigation was under way and that security had been tightened.
Near Bulgaria's capital, 11 of the 17 antennas providing connectivity to the Starlink system, which is "actively used" during the war in Ukraine, were apparently set on fire. This was reported on Facebook by Bulgarian MP Ivaylo Mirchev, according to UNN.
Eleven antennas providing connectivity to the Starlink system (the communications network of SpaceX) were deliberately set on fire at a secret facility near Sofia. These antennas serve as the main communications channel with Musk's satellites in orbit, which are also actively used during the war in Ukraine
According to him, two masked unknown individuals set fire to 11 of the 17 SpaceX antennas providing Starlink satellite connectivity.
At the same time, the Bulgarian MP noted that no reports of the incident had come "either from the Ministry of Internal Affairs (of Bulgaria - ed.), or in the media, or from any other sources — as if this event had never happened at all".
Just a few days ago, at a meeting of the Consultative Council for National Security (CCNS), the head of the State Agency for National Security (SANS) assured me that the counterintelligence service was actively working to counter sabotage related to Russia. Obviously, they are not performing their duties properly... My colleague Bozhanov and I sent parliamentary inquiries to SANS and the Ministry of Internal Affairs. We will release additional information tomorrow in parliament
In addition
According to BNR News, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev refused to disclose details regarding reports of the deliberate arson of antennas used for the Starlink satellite system, citing an ongoing investigation.
"The investigation is ongoing, and it is proceeding very intensively. I urged the head of the State Agency for National Security (SANS) not to disclose details at this stage, despite your great curiosity. However, this is a matter of the near future. We are cooperating with partner agencies to successfully complete this operation. If the head of SANS and the police disclosed the established facts, we would not achieve the desired result; however, I can assure you that the investigation is under control," Radev said.
Meanwhile, Minister of Internal Affairs Ivan Demerdzhiev clarified that security measures concerning such facilities had been strengthened: "I can add — without disrupting the course of the investigation — that although responsibility for the security of these facilities rests with their owners, the structures of the Ministry of Internal Affairs have taken additional measures to protect similar facilities throughout the country."
Recall
Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov, the Adviser to the President of Ukraine on the Development of Defense Technology Areas, confirmed that this night SpaceX introduced speed restrictions on Starlink terminals while they are in motion.
The assumption that Musk's company could restrict the combat capabilities of the Ukrainian military prompted a sharp reaction from Poland, which pays for Starlink services for Ukraine.
"Hey, @elonmusk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again? — Poland's Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski asked Musk on the social network X. — We, your European customers, are watching you."
Reuters notes that Musk is a close political ally of Trump, and the assumption that SpaceX might restrict Ukraine's capabilities has intensified Kyiv's fears that Washington could end its support on the battlefield in order to force its former ally to make concessions.
