Sally Rooney halts book sales in Britain and even cancelled a trip due to fears of arrest — what happened
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:47:37 EEST
22:47:37 KST

Sally Rooney halts book sales in Britain and even cancelled a trip due to fears of arrest — what happened
Kyiv • UNN
Faber will no longer supply Sally Rooney’s books to Britain because of her support for the banned Palestine Action. The author fears criminal prosecution.
Writer Sally Rooney said she was forced to stop selling her books in the United Kingdom because of her support for the proscribed organisation Palestine Action, reports UNN, citing The Guardian.
Details
The Irish writer, author of such works as "Normal People" and "Conversations with Friends," said that because of her public support for the direct-action group, she could no longer receive royalties from sales in the United Kingdom.
After Palestine Action was proscribed last year, Rooney said she would direct proceeds from the sale of her books to support it. Supporting organisations proscribed under the Terrorism Act is an offence; the writer later cancelled a trip to the United Kingdom to accept an award, fearing arrest.
In a statement provided to The Guardian, the bestselling author said: "In July 2025, the direct-action group Palestine Action was designated a terrorist organisation in the United Kingdom. The following month, I wrote an article expressing my intention to continue supporting Palestine Action — an organisation that is neither proscribed nor deemed unlawful here in the Republic of Ireland."
"As a result, fulfilling contracts for the publication of my work in the United Kingdom may now be considered a serious criminal offence. Therefore, following consultations and discussions, and with my full agreement, my publisher Faber has decided that it can no longer supply my work to the United Kingdom market. I have made every effort to be open with the public about my beliefs and intentions, and I am entirely prepared to accept the consequences."
In a statement to the High Court supporting a legal challenge against the organisation's proscription — and warning of its impact on freedom of expression — Rooney said that her books could disappear from the shelves of British bookshops and that publishing new works in the country could become impossible.
Her books have received critical acclaim (she has been called "the voice of a generation") and achieved huge commercial success in the United Kingdom. Sales of the novel "Normal People" exceeded one million copies, while "Conversations with Friends" and "Beautiful World, Where Are You" each sold more than 500,000 copies. The BBC created television series based on "Normal People" and "Conversations with Friends"; the former attracted 62.7 million views, making it the broadcaster's most popular series of 2020.
Last year, Rooney said that the independent producer of the television adaptations had warned her that any payments for the series (both of which had aired before the proscription was introduced) would breach counter-terrorism legislation if the producer knew or suspected that she was using the money received to fund Palestine Action.
Under Section 15 of the Terrorism Act, it is an offence for a person to "provide money or other property, knowing or having reasonable cause to suspect that it will or may be used for the purposes of terrorism." The maximum penalty is 14 years' imprisonment. Faber, which publishes the author's work in the United Kingdom and Ireland, said: "The current law in the United Kingdom has created circumstances in which Faber cannot transfer to Sally Rooney funds earned by her in the country. For a publisher, a situation in which a writer's works are being sold but the resulting income cannot be passed on to her is untenable. Therefore, with Sally's full agreement, we have decided to stop supplying her work to the United Kingdom in any format. We are proud to publish her significant body of work and will continue to sell it in other territories."
We would add
It is believed that more than 3,700 people have been arrested in the United Kingdom for allegedly supporting Palestine Action since it was proscribed last July; most of them were detained over placards reading: "I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action."
Approximately 2,500 people have been charged, but none of them has yet appeared in court, as a legal challenge to the ban is ongoing and will be heard by the Supreme Court next month. Most of the arrests and charges concerned Section 13 of the Terrorism Act, which carries a maximum penalty of six months’ imprisonment.

The Verkhovna Rada approved two decisions to unlock €4 billion from the EU — next in line is a tax on parcels worth up to €150
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:39:32 EEST
22:39:32 KST

The Verkhovna Rada approved two decisions to unlock €4 billion from the EU — next in line is a tax on parcels worth up to €150
Kyiv • UNN
Parliament updated the property valuation system and created a group to select members of the Accounting Chamber. These decisions are needed for an EU loan.
The Verkhovna Rada adopted in the second reading a draft law on updating the property valuation system in Ukraine and also unblocked the competition for the Accounting Chamber. The documents are among the four decisions required to unblock EU macro-financial assistance under the Ukraine Support Loan program. Two more draft laws are still pending—on the taxation of parcels, which are to be considered on Thursday, October 15, UNN writes.
Details
Draft Law No. 13435 "On Property Valuation" was adopted in the second reading and in full with the votes of 271 members of parliament.
The document regulates public relations arising in the course of property valuation, the review of property valuation reports, the professional training and advanced training of valuers, regulation and professional self-government in the field of property valuation, and also establishes rules for determining the amount of property damage, including damage caused by the damage, destruction, or loss of property or other violations concerning such property as a result of an armed conflict.
Property valuation will be carried out by a single professional organization of valuers, which will provide training for specialists, quality control, and protection of their interests, with the aim of forming a professional judgment on the value of property (determining its value) or calculating the value of property.
The types of property value determined through property valuation are:
-  market value; 
-  fair value; 
-  investment value; 
-  other types of value provided for by international valuation standards and other regulatory legal acts in the field of property valuation.  
"Property damage caused by the damage, destruction, or loss of property or other violations concerning property, including as a result of hostilities, terrorist acts, or sabotage caused by an armed conflict, as well as the amount of costs for restoring property, shall be determined through an independent property valuation, and in cases established by the legislation of Ukraine, through a standardized property valuation," the document says.
As Olena Shulyak, Chair of the Verkhovna Rada Committee on the Organization of State Power, Local Self-Government, Regional Development, and Urban Planning, explained, instead of strict state control and bureaucratic procedures, the draft law strengthens the role of professional self-government. Valuers themselves and their professional associations will receive more powers and responsibility.
Shulyak added that for ordinary citizens and businesses, the valuation of an apartment, house, or enterprise would become more objective and understandable. The results produced by Ukrainian valuers will begin to be recognized by international investors and foreign banks.
Link to EU requirements
The aforementioned draft law is included in the list of conditions for the EU MFA (European Union Macro-Financial Assistance) program—macro-financial assistance from the European Union—and is also one of the structural benchmarks of the International Monetary Fund program.
It should be noted that, under the loan agreement and memorandum with the European Union for attracting a €90 billion loan, Ukraine must fulfill several conditions, including:
-  the Verkhovna Rada's adoption of legislation establishing a property valuation system that defines institutional roles and responsibilities concerning property valuation; 
-  the Verkhovna Rada's approval of the appointment of the three missing experts to the commission for selecting members of the governing board of the Accounting Chamber of Ukraine; 
-  the Verkhovna Rada's adoption of a law abolishing the tax exemption for international parcels, except for goods intended for security and defense purposes; 
-  the Verkhovna Rada's adoption of legislative amendments introducing taxation of income received through digital platforms. 
Rada ratified the attraction of a 90 billion euro loan from the EU28.05.26, 11:15 • 20296 views
What else Parliament approved
At its meeting on Wednesday, October 14, the Verkhovna Rada adopted a resolution establishing an advisory group of experts to conduct the preliminary selection of candidates for positions as members of the Accounting Chamber.
It consists of three representatives from international and foreign organizations, whose candidacies had previously been approved by a Cabinet resolution, including:
-  Lee Summerfield – Director of a department at the National Audit Office of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland (NAO); 
-  Igors Ludboržs – former member and dean of the European Court of Auditors (ECA); 
-  Pascal MUNIER – honorary magistrate of the Cour des comptes (Court of Auditors, the supreme audit institution of the French Republic).  
Three representatives from Ukraine who received the highest number of votes also joined the advisory group:
-  Mykola Marchenko (first deputy head of the secretariat of the parliamentary faction of the political party "Servant of the People") – 265; 
-  Hlib Vyshlinsky (executive director of the NGO "Centre for Economic Strategy") – 204; 
-  Myroslava Masliak (senior lecturer at Kharkiv National University of Economics) – 202. 
As Roksolana Pidlasa, chair of the Verkhovna Rada Committee on Budget, said, the establishment of the advisory group of experts is a condition of the Ukraine Support Loan (the macro-financial component) from the EU, with a deadline of August 2026, while the appointment of the full membership of the Accounting Chamber from among the candidates pre-selected by the group of experts is a structural benchmark of the cooperation program with the IMF, which must be fulfilled by December 2026. The funds from these programs are used to finance the state budget deficit and are disbursed in tranches subject to the fulfillment of the commitments undertaken.
Following the establishment of the group, the submission of documents by candidates will begin within a week of the vote in the Rada and will last 30 days. The advisory group of experts will then conduct testing and interviews and recommend at least two candidates for each position to parliament. The final decision rests with the Verkhovna Rada: it will appoint new members of the Accounting Chamber from among those recommended.
A citizen of Ukraine aged 30 or older may become a member of the Accounting Chamber if they speak Ukrainian and English or French, hold at least a master's degree, have at least seven years of total work experience and at least five years of experience in public control (audit), economics, finance or law, as well as an impeccable business reputation.
Today, two bills on abolishing the exemption for parcels worth up to 150 euros were also on the parliament's agenda, but it was decided to postpone the final vote until Thursday.
"We are now going to hear the amendments to the bills on parcels. Today, the amendments will be considered, while the confirmation, except for one, will take place tomorrow, and the substantive vote will be tomorrow (October 15 – ed.)," First Deputy Speaker of Parliament Oleksandr Korniienko said during the meeting.
It is worth noting that on Tuesday, September 1, the Verkhovna Rada once again failed to vote on bills abolishing the tax exemption for parcels worth up to 150 euros. The bills in question are No. 15460 and No. 15112-d.
On September 7, the Cabinet of Ministers approved and submitted to the Verkhovna Rada two related draft laws on the taxation of small postal and express shipments worth up to 150 euros ordered through marketplaces. The documents provide for the abolition of the tax exemption for parcels worth up to 150 euros.
Bill No. 15460 introduces amendments to the Customs Code of Ukraine (which regulates customs procedures, border-clearance rules and the 150-euro threshold for import duty).
Under the bill, VAT would be imposed on imported goods purchased through marketplaces starting from 0 euros.
Currently, international shipments worth up to 150 euros are not subject to import VAT or import duty. Under the proposed rules, the threshold itself would remain, but its effect would change: goods worth up to 150 euros would be exempt from duty only. Thus, VAT at the basic rate of 20% would already be charged from the first euro of the item's value.
For shipments costing more than 150 euros, the basis for calculating the duty would change. It would be charged at a rate of 10% of the parcel's entire invoice value, rather than only on the amount exceeding 150 euros.
At the same time, private, duty-free gifts worth up to 45 euros were expected to remain exempt from taxation. The new rules would not apply to the distance selling of alcohol and tobacco.
Government Bill No. 16051, which introduces amendments to the Tax Code of Ukraine, establishes rules for the assessment and payment of VAT on e-commerce and parcels; however, the government included provisions bringing the rules concerning politically exposed persons (PEPs) into line with the version agreed with the EU.
Incidentally, on June 9, the Verkhovna Rada adopted in its entirety Bill No. 15111-d on the taxation of digital platforms. On June 11, it was signed by Verkhovna Rada Chairman Ruslan Stefanchuk, and on June 12 it was sent to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for signature, since when the document has been "stuck" with the head of state.
The fact is that, during the second reading, a provision was submitted to the bill envisaging changes to the financial monitoring system for politically exposed persons (PEPs). It was included in the draft by the relevant committee and subsequently supported by the plenary chamber.
PEPs include current and former top officials: from members of parliament, ministers, and the president to heads of law enforcement agencies, members of the NBU Board, and ambassadors.
Bill No. 16051 provides for the exclusion from the list of politically exposed persons of heads of structural units of the central office of the National Bank of Ukraine and employees responsible for conducting financial monitoring at a bank in which the state owns more than 50 percent of the shares.
Under the legislation, banks and other financial companies are required to conduct enhanced financial monitoring of PEPs, their close relatives, and business partners.
PEP status is lifelong. At the same time, enhanced financial monitoring applies throughout a person’s tenure in a top position and for 12 months after their dismissal. However, banks and other financial institutions may continue to subject a PEP to enhanced scrutiny if they consider that the person remains risky.
The amendments introduced to the bill impose penalties on banks that decide to continue enhanced monitoring of a PEP’s transactions after 12 months have passed since the person’s dismissal from a top position.
According to some members of parliament, it is precisely because of this amendment that Zelenskyy has still not signed the aforementioned bill.
However, during its September 16 meeting, the Rada adopted an alternative bill—No. 16051-1—which abolishes the provisions concerning PEPs and stipulates that taxes on parcels will be credited to the special fund of the State Budget of Ukraine and directed toward meeting the needs of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
However, by the second reading, amendments concerning PEPs had also been included in Bill No. 16051-1; they are intended to unblock the signing of Law No. 15111-d on the taxation of income from digital platforms.

Archaeologists have discovered a sunken ship off the coast of Turkey that is up to 4,700 years old
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:30:28 EEST
22:30:28 KST

Archaeologists have discovered a sunken ship off the coast of Turkey that is up to 4,700 years old
Kyiv • UNN
Near the island of Kekova, they discovered the remains of an Early Bronze Age vessel with amphorae and anchors. It may be the oldest sunken ship.
Off the coast of Turkey, archaeologists have discovered a sunken Early Bronze Age ship estimated to be 4,400–4,700 years old. The vessel may have transported trade cargo across the Mediterranean Sea. The Independent reports, as cited by UNN.
Details
Although the ship’s wooden structure has not survived, archaeologists dated the storage pottery vessels and stone anchors found near Kekova Island to 2600–2400 BC. This could make the find the oldest known shipwreck in the world.
Previously, this status belonged to a ship that sank near Dokos Island in the Aegean Sea. It is dated to approximately 2200 BC.
Some of the amphorae found—large ceramic vessels with two handles—are similar to Early Bronze Age pottery from the Levant, which includes the territories of modern-day Lebanon, Syria, Israel, and Palestine.
The ceramic vessels were found scattered across the seabed at a depth of about 30 meters. The seabed is partly covered with sand and partly consists of rock.
One of the vessels resembled containers used during the Bronze Age to transport agricultural products, particularly wine and olive oil.
Near the sunken vessel, researchers also found two stone anchors with three holes and one anchor with a single hole. Similar artifacts have been discovered at other Bronze Age archaeological sites.
According to the researchers, anchors with three holes have parallels in Minoan, Cypriot, Anatolian, and Levantine archaeological contexts from the Bronze Age. The single-hole anchor is similar to those found off the coasts of Anatolia and the Levant.
It is not yet known whether these anchors belonged specifically to the discovered ship. At the same time, they may help provide a better understanding of the anchoring technologies used in the region during the Bronze Age.

On October 14, the Kyivskyi District Court of Odesa once again failed to continue considering the case concerning the medical negligence of Odrex private clinic doctors Vitalii Rusakov and Maryna Bielotserkovska, who are accused of improperly performing their professional duties while treating businessman Adnan Kivan. This time, the hearing was postponed at the request of defendant Rusakov, who, according to UNN sources, is on sick leave. As a result, three hearings scheduled for October 14, 15, and 16 were postponed at once. The next hearing is scheduled for October 20, reports UNN.
Details
This is not the first postponement of court hearings in October. The October 7 hearing did not take place because of a motion by the lawyer for the accused oncologist Maryna Bielotserkovska, who was engaged in another court proceeding. One of Rusakov's defense lawyers also failed to appear in court that day.
Although the court managed to continue considering the case on October 8, the next two hearings, scheduled for October 9 and 13, were postponed because of another motion by Bielotserkovska's lawyer. Three more postponements have now been added to these.
In fact, the criminal case in which the court must establish the circumstances of possible improper treatment and the patient's death continues to move from one postponement to another. The reasons for adjourning the hearings change, but the result remains the same — consideration of the case on its merits is being delayed.
It should be noted that the situation with the systematic postponement of hearings became more acute back in September. At that time, the court scheduled 13 hearings, expecting to intensify the examination of evidence. However, only six took place. The other seven were postponed, or the court was unable to continue considering the case on its merits.
The non-appearances of defense lawyers have already prompted a response from the court. Presiding Judge Viktor Chaplytskyi deemed the reasons for the doctors' lawyers' absences unjustified and sent the relevant information to the Qualification and Disciplinary Commission of the Bar. It is to assess whether the lawyers' actions contain signs of a disciplinary offense.
Reminder
The Kyivskyi District Court of Odesa is considering a criminal case against Odrex private clinic doctors Vitalii Rusakov and Maryna Bielotserkovska. They are charged under Part 1 of Article 140 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine — improper performance of professional duties by a medical worker.
According to the investigation, the actions or inaction of the medical workers during Adnan Kivan's treatment at the Odrex clinic may have led to the development of postoperative complications and sepsis, which, against the background of the oncological disease, could have caused the businessman's death. The court must provide the final assessment of the evidence and the issue of the doctors' guilt.

The Best Way to Respond to Passive-Aggressive Comments
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:07:29 UTC
23:07:29 KST

Have you ever left work at 5 p.m., only for a colleague to not-so-sweetly ask, “Going home already?”
If so, you’ve probably been the target of a passive-aggressive comment. The two halves of the very phrase “passive-aggressive” spell out the familiar dynamic, says Laurie Weingart, a professor of organizational behavior at Carnegie Mellon University who has studied how people express conflict at work. Someone is expressing opposition or anger—the aggressive part—but doing so indirectly. The words leave room for an innocent interpretation. The tone? Not so much.
That ambiguity puts you in an awkward position: Do you respond to what was said or what you think the other person meant—or give in to the urge to snip right back? We asked experts what to say when someone seems to be taking a dig at you but won’t quite say what they mean.
Why people default to passive-aggressive communication
Sometimes it feels safer to hint at a feeling than to say it directly. Admitting you feel some sort of way calls for a kind of vulnerability that a sarcastic remark does not. “Some people just haven’t learned how to say or don’t feel comfortable saying, ‘I’m hurt. You hurt my feelings,’” says Melissa Gluck, a psychologist in New York City. If you grew up around people who rarely said what they meant, the indirect approach might even feel normal.
There can also be something more specific behind a partner’s pointed comment. In research on romantic relationships, Levi R. Baker, a psychology professor at the University of North Carolina at Greensboro, found that people sometimes express displeasure indirectly because they’re unsure how much their partner cares. “People are really doing this to kind of test their partner,” he says. They’re signaling, “I’m upset with you, I’ve got some hurt feelings,” then waiting to see whether their partner notices and tries to find out what’s wrong. Underneath it all, Baker says, they may be wondering: “Do they care about me? Do they value me?”
Still, understanding where a comment might come from doesn’t make it feel any better to hear. It can leave you wondering whether you’ve been insulted—and how to answer an accusation the other person never quite made.
How to respond to a passive-aggressive comment
Weingart’s advice is to make your response “more direct and less intense” than the comment you just heard. Start by giving your friend a chance to be direct. If someone says, “Must be nice to have that much free time,” Brook McKenzie, a licensed chemical dependency counselor in Dallas who often helps families work through indirect communication and resentment, suggests responding: “I’m not sure how you meant that. Can you say it another way?” Another option: “It sounds like there might be something you want to say to me directly. Is there?”
The question should be an invitation, not an accusation. “Why are you being so passive-aggressive?” may be tempting, McKenzie says, but you’ll likely end up arguing about their tone instead of whatever is actually bothering them. Returning the sarcasm tends to cause the same problem, with two people annoyed instead of one.
If you’re talking to someone you’re especially close to, Gluck suggests a gentle opening: “I feel like something’s off. Do you want to talk about it?” That lets them tell you what’s wrong without requiring you to guess. If they say everything’s fine, you can take them at their word for the time being. “It’s not our job to become the feelings detective,” Gluck says.
If you have a good idea of what's underneath the comment, you can acknowledge that, too. Say your partner responds to your plans with friends by remarking that you certainly have time for everyone else. Baker suggests reassuring them that you want to spend time together and proposing a plan: “I’m going out tonight, but I’d really like to have dinner with you tomorrow.” You don’t need to cancel your plans to show that you care.
At work, clarity may serve you better than a conversation about feelings. If your boss says, “Leaving already?” when your workday is over, Weingart suggests asking: “Is there something else you need me to do before I leave?” A coworker’s jab may warrant even less: “Yep, the workday’s over. Have a great weekend.” Either response avoids assuming you know what the other person meant.
And sometimes the best response is no response. If a friend makes one out-of-character comment on a rough day, Gluck says, you can let it pass. If it keeps happening, that’s a different conversation.
What to do when someone is repeatedly passive-aggressive
A pattern deserves a more direct approach. If a friend repeatedly jokes that you never make time for them, Gluck suggests naming both what you’ve noticed and how it lands: “This isn’t the first time you’ve made that comment. It’s starting to hurt my feelings, and I’d like to know if something’s bothering you.”
The same pattern can emerge in families. Say you tell your mother it upset you when she criticized you in front of relatives, and she replies, “I guess I’m just a bad mom.” Gluck suggests saying: “That’s not what I said. I was trying to tell you how I feel, and it hurts when you put those words in my mouth.” That brings the conversation back to what she said in front of your relatives, instead of turning it into a debate about whether she’s a good mother.
What if they insist they were just joking? Weingart recommends separating their intention from the effect: “You may not have meant it to be hurtful, but that’s how it sounded to me.” You don’t have to prove what was in their head to explain what happened on your end.
It’s also fair to be clear about what you’re willing to do next. Consider borrowing McKenzie’s go-to line for recurring comments: “I’m willing to have difficult conversations with you. I’m not willing to keep guessing what you mean.”

EU's new Lebanon security mission explained, and what's next
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:56:41 UTC
22:56:41 KST

Breadcrumb
EU's new security mission to Lebanon explained, and what's next
The European Union has agreed to establish a new security mission in Lebanon as the country faces mounting uncertainty over the future of UN peacekeepers amid continued Israeli attacks and its occupation of parts of the south.
Approved on Monday at the request of Lebanese authorities, the mission will operate under the EU's Common Security and Defence Policy, with an initial mandate of three years.
The move comes as the United States opposes extending the mandate of the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL), which expires on 31 December 2026, raising concerns about a potential security vacuum along Lebanon's southern border.
While the European mission is intended to strengthen Lebanon's army and security institutions, it will not replace UNIFIL or carry out peacekeeping operations.
So what exactly will the new mission do, when will it begin, and what does it mean for Lebanon's security?
What is the EU's new mission in Lebanon?
The mission is a European initiative designed to strengthen Lebanon's security institutions, improve border management and support the Lebanese state's ability to exercise authority across its territory.
It was established by the Council of the European Union following a formal request from Lebanese authorities and will operate under a unified political mandate.
Unlike a conventional peacekeeping force, the mission will not deploy troops to patrol Lebanese territory or monitor ceasefire violations.
Instead, it will provide technical assistance, specialised training and strategic advice to the Lebanese Armed Forces and Internal Security Forces.
Its work will extend beyond southern Lebanon, with a broader focus on strengthening state institutions and improving security capabilities nationwide.
EU sources told The New Arab that the initiative is separate from ongoing discussions about UNIFIL's future.
When will the mission begin and how long will it last?
The mission could begin operations in late 2026 or early 2027, according to EU sources who spoke to TNA.
However, no final start date has been agreed, and the number of personnel who will participate remains undecided.
The EU is expected to announce further details as decisions are finalised.
The mission has been granted an initial three-year mandate, although the precise arrangements for its deployment and activities have yet to be confirmed.
Unlike UNIFIL, which operates under UN Security Council resolutions, the European mission does not require Security Council approval because it was established through a bilateral agreement between Lebanon and the EU.
What will the European mission actually do?
The mission will have two main components, military and civilian, working under a single political mandate.
The military component will support the Lebanese army through training and advisory assistance in several areas, including border security, maritime operations, intelligence gathering, surveillance and reconnaissance.
It will also help strengthen the army's ability to monitor and control land borders, combat smuggling and improve coordination between security units.
The civilian component will focus on Lebanon's Internal Security Forces, providing specialised training to improve operational capabilities and establish sustainable training programmes.
These will cover areas such as cybercrime investigations, anti-smuggling operations and internal security.
The mission will also help improve security management at Lebanese ports, including the Port of Beirut.
The broader objective is to strengthen Lebanon's state institutions and contribute to long-term stability in line with UN Security Council Resolution 1701.
Will the EU mission replace UNIFIL?
No. European officials have explicitly ruled out the mission replacing UNIFIL or serving as the alternative international force currently under discussion.
The two missions have fundamentally different responsibilities.
UNIFIL was established in 1978 under UN Security Council Resolutions 425 and 426, with its mandate expanded following the 2006 war between Israel and Hezbollah under Resolution 1701.
Its responsibilities include monitoring the cessation of hostilities, supporting the Lebanese army and helping the government extend its authority across southern Lebanon.
UNIFIL peacekeepers maintain a physical presence throughout the south, including along the Blue Line separating Lebanon and Israel.
They conduct patrols, monitor military activity and work alongside Lebanese forces.
The EU mission, by contrast, will not carry out operational deployments, patrol borders or monitor ceasefire violations.
EU sources said the missions would also have different geographical areas of focus, with the European initiative extending beyond southern Lebanon.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas emphasised the distinction during her visit to Beirut last week, while stressing the importance of avoiding a security vacuum if UNIFIL withdraws.
Why is UNIFIL's future under threat?
UNIFIL's mandate is due to expire on 31 December 2026, amid US opposition to extending the peacekeeping operation.
Washington and Israel have criticised UNIFIL's performance, arguing that it failed to prevent Hezbollah from building its military infrastructure in southern Lebanon.
The United States has also pushed for new security arrangements, including direct military coordination between the Lebanese and Israeli armies.
Lebanon has resisted such proposals, instead calling for UNIFIL's mandate to be extended or for a replacement international force to operate under UN authority.
Lebanese MP Najat Aoun Saliba told The New Arab that 14 of the Security Council's 15 members were prepared to support extending UNIFIL's mandate, but Washington remained opposed.
Saliba is among 86 Lebanese MPs who submitted a legal memorandum calling on the Security Council to reconsider Resolution 2790, particularly the timing and mechanism of UNIFIL's withdrawal.
She warned that implementing the resolution under current conditions would be extremely difficult because Israeli forces continue occupying Lebanese territory.
One particular concern involves the transfer of UNIFIL positions and facilities to the Lebanese army.
Saliba argued that where these positions remain under Israeli occupation, transferring them to Israeli forces instead would effectively consolidate that occupation.
What happens to southern Lebanon if UNIFIL leaves?
The potential withdrawal has raised serious concerns about border monitoring, civilian protection and the ability of the Lebanese army to fill the gap.
Saliba warned that more than 10,000 residents of three southern Lebanese villages, Debel, Ain Ebel and Rmeish, could become completely isolated without an alternative to UNIFIL.
The peacekeeping force currently helps maintain a humanitarian corridor serving these communities, which have faced increasing pressure as Israeli occupation expands around their villages.
Residents are also dealing with the weakening presence of Lebanese state institutions and limited access to essential services.
Saliba warned that UNIFIL's departure would leave important border positions along the Blue Line without international observers.
"UNIFIL is responsible for the border points demarcated by the Blue Line," she said.
"If it leaves the south, these points that safeguard Lebanon's borders will be left open and unattended."
She stressed that the central concern was the absence of international monitors to help protect Lebanon's borders.
Could another international force replace UNIFIL?
Discussions are continuing over the possibility of establishing an alternative international force, although no agreement has been reached.
Lebanon wants any replacement to operate under the United Nations, maintaining international oversight of the southern border.
Washington has not ruled out an alternative force, according to Saliba, but the negotiations remain complicated by US and Israeli demands for new security arrangements.
Among the proposals is direct coordination between the Lebanese and Israeli militaries, an arrangement Beirut opposes.
The EU mission will operate independently of these negotiations and will not assume the responsibilities of any future international peacekeeping force.
For Lebanon, the European initiative could provide valuable long-term assistance to its military and security institutions.

====================================================================================================
